What he shows us is that God’s justice and his mercy meet in one place. So read the hard passages in the light of Christ, not against him. Where they puzzle you, trust the character of the God you have seen in Jesus while you keep studying.

In a sentence. The law came through Moses, but grace and truth through Jesus Christ; no one has ever seen God, but the unique Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, has made him known.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test. Every one of us is carrying a picture of God assembled out of odds and ends: what our father was like, what we were told as children, our own temperament, the last sermon that frightened us. Take one thing on that picture that you are fairly sure of: that he is disappointed in you, say, or reluctant, or watchful, or hard to get hold of. Now ask where you would find that in Jesus Christ. Not whether you can defend it from a text somewhere; whether you can find it in him. If it is not in him, it is not in God, because he is the exegesis and there is no other copy.

For worship. The prologue opens with a locked door, no one has ever seen God, and it does not leave the door locked. It says the one person in existence who has never been anywhere but the Father’s side has come out and told us, and the telling was a life. Nobody has seen God. And a man who had been leaning on his chest wrote that sentence down. Do you want to know what God is like? Look at Jesus, and adore.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son.” “At the Father’s side” is literally “in the bosom of the Father” — the place of closest intimacy.

parallels.desc: no one may see me and live
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is, he states plainly that he is not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet, but the voice in the wilderness Isaiah spoke of, calling people to make the Lord’s road straight. Asked why he baptises, he says he baptises with water, but among them stands one they do not know, whose sandal he is unfit to untie. Next day, seeing Jesus, John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin, the one who ranks above him because he was before him. John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign God had given him of the one who baptises with the Spirit; so he declares that this is the Son of God. The following day two of John’s disciples hear him call Jesus the Lamb of God and follow Jesus. He asks what they are looking for; they ask where he is staying, and he invites them to come and see. One of them, Andrew, brings his brother Simon, telling him they have found the Messiah, and Jesus names Simon Cephas, Peter. Next day Jesus calls Philip, who tells Nathanael they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs at Nazareth, but comes, and Jesus greets him as a true Israelite without deceit and says he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises he will see greater things: heaven opened and God’s angels going up and down on the Son of Man.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gathering of the first disciples in John 1 is a theology of testimony: John testifies to Jesus; Andrew testifies to Simon; Philip testifies to Nathanael. The gospel spreads through personal witness. Each person who encounters Jesus becomes a testimony to others. The titles accumulate — Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man — each one true, each one partial, each one pointing toward the one who exceeds all titles. Faith begins with testimony, but it must end with personal encounter: 'Come and see.'

Two guards belong to this section. The first concerns the phrase the Jews, which appears here for the first time and some seventy times in the Gospel: in John it functions as shorthand for the Jerusalem religious authorities, not for a people. The author is a Jew, every disciple is a Jew, and Jesus says in this same book that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). What is recorded is an argument inside a family about the family's own hope, and reading it as one people's verdict on another inverts it — a misreading Christians have made at terrible cost.

The second concerns the Lamb. Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (v. 29) should not be assigned lazily to one background. John's own frame is Passover: he alone dates the condemnation to the hour the lambs were killed (19:14) and applies the Passover regulation about unbroken bones to the body on the cross (19:36). But the words spoken here — takes away the sin — echo Isaiah, since of all the candidate lambs only the servant of Isaiah 53 bears sin. Genesis 22 supplies the unanswered question (where is the lamb?), and the daily sacrifice explains why there had to be a last one. The verb is a present participle and the noun is singular: not a list of offences but the whole condition, taken up in order to be carried away.

The gathering of the disciples also settles the relation between this Gospel and the others. The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not an alternative version of this meeting but a later and decisive summons; here men are introduced to Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave the nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern, not a defective one — which is also the burden of vv. 50-51, where a man who has believed for minutes is told he will see greater things, and the greater things turn out to include a cross.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Behold, the Lamb of God' is the most comprehensive atonement statement in the New Testament: the lamb of Passover (Exod. 12), the lamb of the daily sacrifice (Exod. 29:38-42), the suffering servant who is led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and the apocalyptic Lamb who alone is worthy (Rev. 5) — all in one person. And Andrew's first act after meeting Jesus is to find his brother: the natural overflow of genuine encounter with Christ is the desire for others to share it.

The pastoral centre of this section is that nobody in it recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his own brother — the hardest possible person, and the one least impressed by him — with a five-word sentence containing no case at all. Philip's testimony is theologically magnificent and incomplete twice over (Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph — nothing of Bethlehem, nothing of the virgin birth), and John lets both gaps stand on the page because Nathanael came anyway. Nobody is waiting for a witness to be finished before he is useful.

Two cautions worth carrying out of it. Andrew won his brother the same day, and that is the exception rather than the pattern; Jesus' own brothers did not believe during his lifetime (7:5). Anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades is not being rebuked by this chapter. And I saw you under the fig tree should be handled on both sides: it is the comfort of the believer whose faithfulness nobody is counting, and it is exposure for the reader who would rather his private life stayed private — with the point being that the one who has complete access to it is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he mentions the tree and says nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him: who are you? He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed: I am not the Christ.

The narrative begins. After the prologue, John’s Gospel opens with a week of testimony (1:19–2:11), ending at the wedding in Cana. The eternal Word has been announced; now the story starts, and it starts with an interrogation.

The Jews. This is the first appearance of a phrase that will turn up some seventy times before the book is finished, and because it has been put to appalling use it is worth stopping over here, at its first occurrence. In John’s Gospel the Jews often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus: the men with institutional standing, who send delegations and convene meetings and eventually take a case to Pilate. It is not a term for a people. The plain facts settle it. John who wrote this book was a Jew. Every disciple in it is a Jew. Its central figure is a Jew who keeps the feasts, is called Rabbi throughout, and says in this same Gospel that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The delegation in this verse is Jewish, and so is the man they are interrogating, and so is everyone else standing in the river.

What it does not mean. What is being described is an argument inside a family about the family’s own hope, which is the sharpest kind of argument there is, and the moment it is read as one people’s verdict on another it has been turned inside out. Christians have done that, at scale, with results that do not bear describing. The term must never be used to justify hatred of Jewish people. Read the phrase as the Gospel uses it: the authorities in Jerusalem, and not your neighbour.

Sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem. An official delegation, perhaps from the Sanhedrin, to investigate this new prophet. Priests and Levites are temple staff; Levites assisted the priests, and also served as temple police. They have come down from Jerusalem, roughly twenty miles and a considerable descent, to establish by what authority an unlicensed man is conducting a religious rite in the open country. This is not curiosity. It is an inquiry, and inquiries are opened when something has grown large enough to be a problem.

Who are you? It is the question the whole Gospel is about: who is Jesus? First they ask John. It is the right question, asked of the wrong man, by people who will shortly be standing within a few feet of the answer without recognising him.

He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed. Emphatic, and voluntary. Notice what John does with the opportunity, because it was a real opportunity. He had crowds. Luke says people were questioning in their hearts whether he might be the Christ (Luke 3:15). The country was ready, the delegation had come to him, and a career was available. He puts it down in the first sentence he speaks in this Gospel. The word is the one used elsewhere in the New Testament for confessing Christ. It is the vocabulary of standing up and saying a thing publicly when saying it costs you. Here the confession is a subtraction.

I am not the Christ. “I” is emphatic: I am not; someone else is. John’s first word is to deny that he is the Messiah. The negative precedes the positive in his testimony, and the herald’s glory is entirely derivative: John shines only by reflected light from the one who is the Light itself.

In a sentence. When the Jerusalem authorities sent priests and Levites to ask John who he was, he openly declared that he was not the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test worth running, because this temptation almost never arrives as an ambition. It arrives as an offer. Somebody credits you with more than is true: more wisdom than you have, more spirituality, more authority in their life than any human being should hold, and the correction would be awkward and would cost you something. Do you make it? Most of us let a small overestimate stand because pulling it down would be embarrassing. John pulled his down in front of a government delegation, at the height of his influence, when the misunderstanding running in his favour was the largest religious question in the country. True witnesses point away from themselves. Be clear about who you are not.

For worship. The first words out of the last prophet’s mouth are about who he is not, and it clears the ground for the only sentence he actually came to say. There is one who is the Christ, and it is not John, nor any preacher, nor any of us. The Anointed One of God needs no rival and will share his glory with no other. How good it is to belong to a Saviour so great that the greatest of the prophets could only say: not I.
verseByVerse.note: In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: whether he might be the Christ

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: what then? Are you Elijah? He said: I am not. Are you the Prophet? And he answered: no.

Are you Elijah? Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah. Malachi ends the Old Testament by promising that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5): the very last thing said before four centuries of silence, and therefore the thing everyone was still waiting for when the silence broke. John dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6). Jesus said John was Elijah, in the sense of fulfilling Elijah’s role (Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13). But John denies being Elijah literally returned.

I am not. Read the three answers in sequence and watch them shrink. I am not the Christ: a full sentence. I am not: three words. No: one. He is diminishing on the page as he speaks, and by the time they get a positive answer out of him in the next verse he will not claim to be a person at all, only a sound.

One says I am not, so another can say I am. There is something in the Greek that will pay dividends for twenty chapters. What John says here is egō ouk eimi, I am not. That is the exact formula, with a negative in it, that Jesus will use again and again without one: egō eimi, I am. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. I am the good shepherd. Before the door of Jesus’ great self-declarations is opened, the last and greatest of the prophets stands in it and empties the phrase of himself. One man says I am not, so that the other can say I am.

Are you the Prophet? The Prophet refers to Deuteronomy 18:15–18, the prophet like Moses whom God would raise up, to whom Israel must listen. Peter later identified him with Jesus (Acts 3:22). The delegation is working through the list of expected figures.

No. One word. John refuses every title.

So was John Elijah or not? Yes in role, no in person. The angel had told his father that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), which is exactly what Jesus later says he did (Matthew 11:14). Jesus is describing a role; John is refusing a reputation. What John will not accept is the popular version: the returned prophet as a figure in his own right, with his own following, around whom a movement could be built. His denial is not a contradiction but humility. He will not allow the crowds to construct an identity around him that would compete with the one coming after.

In a sentence. Asked whether he was Elijah or the Prophet, John said no to each.

On a Tuesday. A great deal of Christian exhaustion comes from quietly accepting jobs that were never ours: being the one who holds a family together, the one with the answers, the one whose faith everyone else is leaning on. Those roles are flattering while they last and they will break you, because they belong to somebody else. John is not being modest here. He is being accurate, and accuracy is lighter to carry. Try it as a question: what are people counting on you for that only Christ can actually supply? Not what you have failed to do; what you have been allowed to be, and should not be. Saying no to it will look like a loss of standing. It is the removal of a weight you were never built to take.

For worship. He gives them three answers and every one of them is a subtraction. It is the shortest self-description in the Gospels, and the man who gave it is the one Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11). The greatness was in the pointing. All the titles he refused belong to another, and that other wears them all: the true Prophet like Moses, the Lord whose day Elijah heralded, the Christ. Every crown John set down, Jesus picks up, and they fit.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah; “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah
a prophet like me
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him: who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself? He said: I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said.

Who are you? Again. Notice the pressure in their question, because it is very human.

We need to give an answer to those who sent us. They have to file a report. Somebody in Jerusalem is expecting a finding, and this man keeps saying what he is not. Give us something to write down.

I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness. What he gives them is barely anything at all (Isaiah 40:3). John describes himself not as a person with a title, but as a voice. Not a prophet, not a teacher, not even the voice of a man: a sound. And a voice is the one thing in the world that stops existing the moment it has done its work. It is not a monument or an office. You cannot preserve it. It exists only while it is being used, and then the words it carried go on without it. Jesus is the Word; John is only the voice.

Isaiah 40, the turn to comfort. Stage the verse he reaches for, because it is not a random proof text. Isaiah 40 is the great turn in that book: the end of the judgment chapters and the beginning of comfort, addressed to a people in exile who have concluded that God has lost interest. Comfort, comfort my people, it opens. And then a voice in the wilderness: prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. The picture behind it is a road gang. When a king was coming, riders went ahead of the royal party and the road was made ready: hollows filled, rocks cleared, the surface levelled, because a monarch does not pick his way over broken ground. That is the job John claims. He is not the king and he is not the escort. He is the man out in front with the news that someone is coming and the road is in no condition for it.

The LORD himself is coming. Two things follow from his choosing that passage. The first is that the one being announced is, in Isaiah, the LORD: God himself coming to his people. John applies it to a man who will walk up to him next morning. He has just made the prologue’s claim without using any of the prologue’s language. The second is that this comfort was spoken to exiles: people who had been waiting so long they had stopped expecting anything. That is who the announcement is for. Not the people who are ready, but the people who have given up on the road being used.

Make straight the way of the Lord. Prepare the road for the Lord himself, by repentance. And the road-making is the part we would rather not translate. Preparing the way is not decoration; it is demolition and haulage. What has to come down is whatever a king would have to step over, which, in the sermons John actually preached, turned out to be quite specific: what you do with your coat and your food, how you handle money that passes through your hands, whether you use your position to squeeze people (Luke 3:10–14). He did not tell them to feel differently. He gave them roadworks.

What does making straight the way look like for me? It means clearing out of the way whatever you know Christ would have to step over to reach you. Name it specifically: the grudge you are nursing, the money you are handling dishonestly, the habit you keep hidden, the relationship you know is wrong, the apology you owe. Confess it to God, and where it involves others, put it right. You do not do this to earn his coming; he is coming anyway, and he comes to sinners. You do it because a heart that is busy defending its rubble cannot welcome a king.

As the prophet Isaiah said. John knows his role from Scripture. He did not invent his identity; he found it written.

In a sentence. Pressed for an answer, John said he was the voice Isaiah spoke of, crying in the wilderness to make straight the way of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test for anyone in Christian work of any kind, paid or not. Ask what would remain of your ministry if your name were removed from it. If the honest answer is not much, if the thing only functions because people are attached to you, then you have built something other than a voice. A voice is content to be forgotten the moment it is understood, and it does not consider this a tragedy, because being forgotten was always the plan. Be a voice for Christ. It is the message, not the messenger, that matters.

For worship. They came for a name to put in a report. He gave them a job description and a piece of Isaiah, and no name at all. And the voice is gone now, and the Word it announced remains for ever (Isaiah 40:8). The LORD whose way John prepared has come down the road, to exiles who had stopped expecting him, speaking comfort. Blessed is the God who sends a voice ahead of himself, and then comes himself.

parallels.desc: the voice in the wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)

Sent from the Pharisees. John’s aside. Some manuscripts read some of them were Pharisees. A single verse in brackets, easy to read straight over, and it changes who is in the room. The first delegation was priests and Levites, temple staff, the professional clergy. This note tells us who was behind the sending, and it is a different constituency altogether. The Pharisees, strict interpreters of the law, would be concerned with John’s authority to baptise, and their concern will surface again throughout the Gospel.

Who the Pharisees actually were. It is worth knowing, because Christians have made the word into an insult and in doing so have lost the whole point of them. They were not the temple establishment; that was the priestly families, who were wealthy, political, and in many cases not especially devout. The Pharisees were a lay movement: a few thousand men, mostly ordinary tradesmen and teachers, who had made it their life’s work to take the law of God with complete seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. They tithed their herbs. They knew the Scriptures by heart. They believed in the resurrection, in angels, in the coming Messiah, and in a God who cared what you did on a Tuesday. Ordinary people admired them enormously.

The serious ones. Hold that steadily, because the tragedy of this Gospel depends on it. These were not obvious villains. They were the serious ones, the people you would have picked out of any crowd as most likely to recognise God at work. If sincerity had been enough, or knowledge of the Bible, or moral effort, or a genuine longing for the Messiah to come, they would have been first at the river and first at the cross. They had all four. It was not enough.

What it does not mean. The word has no business functioning as a name for other people. When a Christian says Pharisee he almost always means someone stricter than himself, and the usage is nearly the opposite of the truth. The Pharisee problem is not strictness. It is the state of a man who is so certain he is on God’s side that there is no longer anything God could do that would surprise him, and therefore nothing God could do that he would be able to recognise. That condition is available at every point on the scale of strictness, and it is most available to those who have been right about something for a long time.

Should I then distrust every careful, serious Christian? No. Taking God’s word seriously in the details of life is good, and the New Testament commands it. Nicodemus, a Pharisee, came to Jesus (3:1), and Paul was one before Christ found him (Philippians 3:5). The danger is not seriousness but self-trust: relying on our own record to stand before God, and refusing to be corrected by him. The cure is not to become careless but to become humble, to keep your Bible open in front of you rather than behind you, and to keep asking God to show you where you are wrong.

In a sentence. The delegation had been sent by the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in proportion to how much you know. What would it take to convince you that God was doing something you had not authorised: something outside your tradition, through people whose theology you would want to correct, in a form you find unimpressive or embarrassing? If no answer comes, that is worth sitting with. It does not mean you are wrong about the things you are right about. It means the mechanism by which you could ever be corrected has been quietly disconnected, and the men in this verse are what that looks like at scale. Religious authorities are often the first to question a genuine work of God. Don’t be discouraged by it, and don’t be one of them.

For worship. They travelled twenty miles to investigate. They asked reasonable, careful questions. They went home with a report. And the one they had been waiting for their entire lives was standing in the crowd the whole time. Yet he did not leave them to their system. He went on to eat with Pharisees, to answer them, to weep over their city, and to save one of the strictest of them on a road to Damascus. Praise the patient Lord who seeks even the self-assured.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: then why are you baptising, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet? John answered them: I baptise with water, but among you stands one you do not know.

Then why are you baptizing. The question only makes sense if you know why baptising was the provocative part. Baptism was associated with the coming of the messianic age, the cleansing God promised (Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1). Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism: there were stone pools for it all over Jerusalem, and a devout man might immerse himself many times in a month. But there was one washing that marked a person’s entry into the covenant people from outside. Later Jewish sources describe it for Gentile converts: a pagan who wanted to become a Jew was circumcised, brought an offering, and was immersed, washed clean of the paganism he was coming out of. Whether that practice was already established in John’s day is debated, but the offence was felt either way.

Jews washed like outsiders. Now put John in the Jordan. He is baptising Jews. Sons of Abraham, circumcised on the eighth day, keepers of the law, are wading into a river to be washed as though they needed to come in from outside. That is the outrage, and the delegation’s question is entirely reasonable given it: by what authority do you treat the covenant people as though they were outsiders? Only three figures could conceivably reorder Israel like that, the Christ, Elijah and the Prophet, and he has just told them he is none of the three. It was also the sharpest sermon anyone had preached in four hundred years, and he preached it without saying a word. Descent will not do it. Your ancestry will not do it. You need cleansing, and you need it in public, in cold water, where the neighbours can see.

I baptize with water. Only water: an outward sign. His answer does not defend his credentials at all. He changes the subject to the only subject.

But among you stands one you do not know. Already present, unrecognised. Every word of it is worth weighing. Among you: not coming, not somewhere else, not in Jerusalem where you have just come from. In this crowd. Stands: the verb is present and settled; he is not passing through, he is here, and he has been here while you were asking your questions. One you do not know: and these are the best-informed religious men in the country, standing within yards of him. They are investigating the wrong man.

What it does not mean. That last clause can be turned into a weapon against people who do not need it. It is not an instrument for making a settled Christian doubt whether he really knows the Lord. The people it is aimed at were confident of their standing and had come to audit somebody else’s. If you are worried by the sentence, it is a fair sign it is not describing you; the men it describes were not worried at all.

Was John’s baptism the same as Christian baptism? Not quite. John’s was a baptism of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming one; Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, a sign of union with the Christ who has now died and risen (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4). That is why the disciples Paul met at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:1–7). What the two share is the sign of cleansing and the call to turn. Like John, we hold that baptism belongs to those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 8:36–38), as the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches, while honouring brothers and sisters who baptise their children in good conscience.

In a sentence. Asked why he baptised if he was none of these, John said he baptised with water, but among them stood one they did not know.

On a Tuesday. There is a way of being near Christ for years, the services, the vocabulary, the diary, the opinions, which is nearness of the kind these men had to the Jordan: physically present at the event, and not in it. Long church attendance is no protection from it. The test is not how much you know about him. It is whether there is anything in your week that only makes sense if he is real. If everything you do would survive his non-existence unchanged, that is worth knowing now rather than later. Christ may be nearer than you think. Look for him, and speak to him.

For worship. They had come out to establish who John was. He tells them, in effect, that they have the wrong man under investigation, and that the right one is close enough to touch. That is still the wonder of the gospel. The Lord of glory stands among ordinary people, unannounced, unhurried, waiting to be known. He did not wait for the delegation to find him. He came and stood among them, and he still comes and stands among us.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie. These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptising.

Even he who comes after me. John borrows the language of a slave’s duty and declares himself unworthy even of that.

The strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job, the lowest task. There was a rabbinic saying about this, and it gives the sentence its edge. A disciple was expected to serve his teacher in almost every way a slave would: fetching, carrying, dressing him, waiting on him. But there was one duty considered too degrading to ask of a student, and it was the one to do with the feet: untying and carrying the sandals. So read what John is saying. He does not say he is unworthy to be the man’s disciple. He says he is unworthy to do the one job that even a slave’s list contained and a disciple’s list did not. He has reached for the lowest available rung and then said he cannot reach it. I am not worthy even to be his slave.

The King with a towel. Hold that, and then remember what happens twelve chapters from now. In an upper room, the one whose sandal strap John was not fit to loosen takes off his outer garment, ties a towel round his waist, kneels on the floor, and washes the feet of men who will every one of them fail him before morning (13:4–5). The task too low for the herald is the task the King performs. That is not a pleasant irony; it is the shape of the whole Gospel, and this verse is where the measurement is taken that makes chapter 13 unbearable.

In Bethany across the Jordan. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan, in Perea, not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Its exact location is uncertain, and it was obscure enough that early copyists were unsure of the name. John gives it in the flat manner of a man who was there and remembers where he was standing; his concern for precise places reflects an eyewitness.

Which bank. What matters is which bank. This is the crossing country: where the nation came out of forty years of wilderness and entered the land, where Elijah struck the water and went up in a whirlwind and left his cloak behind (2 Kings 2:8–13). John is standing at Israel’s front door, on the outside, telling the covenant people they need to come in again. And notice that the man himself is not the story of the location. This is the only spot in the chapter where the narrator pauses to say where all of this took place, and he says it after the sandal sentence, as if the address is a footnote to the self-abasement rather than the other way round.

Is it healthy to think of myself as unworthy? It depends what you mean. John’s unworthiness is not self-hatred or low self-esteem; he spoke with great boldness and never doubted his calling. It is simply an accurate measurement of himself against Christ. Next to him, the greatest of men is not fit to touch his feet. But the gospel does not leave us there. The same Christ who is infinitely above us kneels to wash us and calls us friends (15:15). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking truly of Christ, and then receiving gladly what he gives to the unworthy.

In a sentence. John said that the one coming after him was so great that he was not worthy to untie his sandal; this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan.

On a Tuesday. Think of the lowest job in your church: the one nobody puts on a rota because everyone assumes somebody else does it. Stacking the chairs. The bins after the meal. The lift home for the person who talks too long. Ask yourself, without answering out loud, whether you would be glad to be known as the person who does that and nothing else. John measured his own worth against exactly that scale and came up short, and Jesus called him the greatest man ever born. Then go and do it, for the one who washed your feet.

For worship. The greatest prophet felt unworthy to untie Jesus’ sandal. How great is our Lord! And how low he came: the feet John dared not touch were the feet that walked the road to Calvary, and the hands that John could not serve took a towel and served us. Majesty kneeling, glory with a basin: this is our God.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan — not the Bethany near Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: where John had been baptizing at first

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said: behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, after me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.

The next day. John marks the days of this first week (vv. 29, 35, 43; 2:1).

Behold, the Lamb of God. This is the interpretive lens for the whole Gospel, and everything depends on which lamb he means. The honest answer is that the question can be settled, not by choosing the most convenient option, but by letting this Gospel tell you which one its author had in mind. There were four lambs available to a Jewish imagination, and they are not interchangeable.

The lamb of Genesis 22. Isaac walks up a mountain carrying the wood for his own sacrifice and asks the question this verse could be an answer to: behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering? His father says: God will provide for himself the lamb (Genesis 22:7–8). And then God does not, not that day. A ram is caught in a thicket and a boy walks back down the hill, and the sentence about the lamb is left standing, unpaid, for two thousand years. When a man by a river points at another man and says, behold, the lamb, a very old question is being answered.

The daily lamb. A lamb every morning and a lamb every evening, in the temple, without a break, for centuries (Exodus 29:38–42). Constant, regular, and never finished, which was its own testimony, because a sacrifice you have to repeat tomorrow has not dealt with anything permanently (Hebrews 10:11–12).

The Passover lamb. A year-old male without blemish, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passing over that house (Exodus 12). The Passover lamb was not, strictly, a sin offering. It marked a house as belonging to God and turned aside the judgment falling everywhere else.

The lamb of Isaiah 53. Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, he opened not his mouth. And this is the only one of the four in which a lamb bears sin: the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all; he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:6–7, 12).

Let John decide it. Two things in his own account are decisive, and neither is in any other Gospel. First, he alone dates the crucifixion so that Jesus is condemned on the day of Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour (19:14), the hour the lambs were being killed in the temple. Second, when the soldiers come to break the legs of the crucified and find Jesus already dead, John alone tells you which Scripture was fulfilled: not one of his bones will be broken (19:36). That is the Passover regulation, from Exodus 12:46, about how the lamb is to be handled. So John’s frame is Passover. But the words spoken over him here, who takes away the sin of the world, echo Isaiah’s sin-bearing servant. The Baptist has done something no one before him had done: he has put the Passover lamb and the sin-bearing servant into one person and pointed at him.

The whole doctrine in one lamb. Take them together and you have the whole doctrine. Isaiah tells you how it works: the iniquity is laid on him and he carries it in our place. Passover tells you what it does for you: judgment is real, it is passing through, and it does not come into the house marked with blood. Genesis supplies the question, and the daily lamb explains why there had to be a last one. Jesus is the sacrifice God provides.

Who takes away the sin of the world! “Takes away” (airōn) means to lift up and to carry away, and both are needed, because he does not remove sin from a distance. He takes it up onto himself in order to take it away (Isaiah 53:4, 11–12; 1 Peter 2:24). And it is a present participle: not took away once, long ago, but taking away, described as what he is. Then the noun: the sin, singular. Not sins, not a ledger of separate offences to be worked through item by item, but the whole mass of human sin and guilt, treated as one object that can be picked up. And “of the world”: not of Israel only, but of people from every nation (11:51–52; 1 John 2:2).

Even my sin? People rarely doubt that Christ takes away sin in general. They doubt whether he takes away the particular thing they have never told anyone, the one that feels less like a sin than like a category. Look at the grammar again. If he had said sins, you might wonder whether yours was on the list. He said the sin, the whole weight of it, lifted as one load. Whatever yours is, if you come to him it is not too heavy and not too dark for the Lamb to carry; it was laid on him with all the rest (Isaiah 53:6). None who come will be turned away (6:37).

Where Christians differ: “the sin of the world”. Arminians take “the world” to mean that Christ died for every person equally, making salvation possible for all; they point to 3:16 and to 1 John 2:2, for the sins of the whole world. Verdict: in John, “the world” usually means humanity in rebellion against God, not every individual, and the point is the scope of Christ’s work: not Jews only, but Gentiles from every nation (10:16; 11:52). Christ’s death actually takes away sin; it does not merely make removal possible. It takes away the sin of all who are his, from all over the world. The gospel is offered freely to everyone (3:16), and none who come will be turned away (6:37).

Breaking the fence. What the phrase is denying is that this is a national arrangement. The men listening had come from Jerusalem; their categories were Israel and everyone else. John says the word that breaks the fence, and the rest of this Gospel will keep breaking it: a Samaritan woman, a royal official’s household, some Greeks who ask to see him. The same Gospel has the Good Shepherd laying down his life for the sheep the Father gave him (10:11, 15, 29), and those sheep are gathered from every fold.

After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me. As in verse 15: the eternal Word. Incarnation does not diminish deity; it expresses it.

The Lamb on the throne. One more lamb belongs on the list, and it is the one the writer of this Gospel saw for himself. In the vision on Patmos, John looks for the Lion of the tribe of Judah who has conquered, and turns to see a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, and the whole of heaven falls down before it (Revelation 5:5–6). The Baptist points at a lamb walking toward him on a riverbank. Decades later the same apostle is looking at the same Lamb on the throne of the universe, still bearing the marks. Whatever else the title means, it is not a stage he passed through. It is what he is called in glory.

In a sentence. The next day John saw Jesus and declared him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one he had said ranked above him because he existed before him.

On a Tuesday. The first word is an imperative: behold. Look. It is the thing the greatest prophet since Malachi most wanted anybody to do. He does not say understand it, or feel it, or resolve to do better about it. He says look at him, which is, as it happens, the one instruction a man carrying something too heavy is still capable of obeying. When guilt comes back today, over an old sin or a fresh one, do not argue with it from your own record. Look at the Lamb, and say: he took that away.

For worship. Stand back from the argument and watch what is coming down the riverbank. The one who put the ram in the thicket is walking toward the altar himself. The one who had accepted every offering Israel ever made, every bull, every goat, every pair of pigeons, every morning and every evening for fifteen hundred years, is coming to be the last one. All that blood was rehearsal. Every knife lifted in that country was pointing forward, and the thing it pointed at has just come round the bend of the Jordan on his own two feet, unbound, in no hurry, of his own accord. He did not have to be caught. He walked toward the man who would name him. Behold the Lamb of God, and worship.
verseByVerse.note: Lambs were offered daily in the temple and at Passover; Isaiah’s servant goes “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”

parallels.desc: the Passover lamb
God will provide the lamb

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptising with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.

I myself did not know him. That sentence needs a fact from another Gospel to land properly, and it is a startling one: they were relatives. Mary and Elizabeth were kinswomen; Gabriel told Mary so in the same breath as the announcement (Luke 1:36). These two men were born six months apart, and their mothers had spent three months of a pregnancy together. So I myself did not know him cannot mean he had never met him. John did not know him as the Messiah until God revealed it (v. 33). It means something far more useful to us: knowing Jesus as a relative, as a neighbour, as a face you have seen at family gatherings all your life, is not the same thing as knowing who he is. The Baptist had every natural advantage, and he says flatly that none of it told him. He had to be shown.

For the one raised in a Christian home. To the one who has heard it all since infancy and sometimes wonders whether familiarity has spoiled it: the greatest prophet in Israel’s history was in exactly that position and needed God to reveal it anyway, and God did. Proximity is not the qualification, and it is not the disqualification either.

For the one who distrusts his own certainty. To the reader whose faith feels as though it rests on a mood that comes and goes: notice where John’s certainty came from. Not from inside him. In the next verse we will find that God had told him in advance exactly what sign to watch for, and he watched for it, and he saw it. His confidence rested on something that happened outside himself, on a particular day, in front of witnesses. That is where yours rests too. The events this book reports did not happen inside anybody’s feelings, and they do not stop having happened on the mornings when you cannot feel anything at all.

But for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel. The purpose clause reframes the whole ministry. The baptising was never the point. The crowds were never the point. The entire operation, the wilderness, the camel hair, the preaching, the queues in the river, existed to create an occasion at which one person could be identified. Not to build his own following. It was scaffolding, and scaffolding is judged by the building, not by how impressive it looked while it was up. Every ministry is instrumental; the goal is always the unveiling of Christ, not the establishing of the minister.

But in Matthew, did John not recognise him? In Matthew, John protests: I need to be baptized by you (Matthew 3:14). The two fit together. John knew Jesus as a relative and a righteous man, and in Matthew he senses that Jesus is greater than he. What he did not know until the sign was given was that this was the one who baptises with the Spirit (v. 33). His protest in Matthew came at the baptism itself; his certainty came with the descending Spirit.

In a sentence. John said he had not known who Jesus was, but had come baptising so that he would be revealed to Israel.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your work is scaffolding for. Not what it achieves, not whether it is going well: what it is for, and whether that thing is a person. A ministry, a marriage, a job done Christianly, the raising of children: each of them can be measured by whether it ends in someone seeing Christ more clearly, or whether it has quietly become the building rather than the scaffolding. The purpose of your life and ministry is to reveal Christ to others.

For worship. He baptised thousands so that one man could be pointed at, and he seems to have thought that was a good return. He was right. God does not leave his Son to be discovered by our cleverness; he reveals him, on his own terms, by his own appointed means, and he made a whole prophet’s life into a lamp held up to show him. Blessed be the Father, who will not let his Son go unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And John bore witness: I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptise with water said to me: he on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove. At Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:10). John’s Gospel does not describe the baptism itself, but John the Baptist’s testimony to it. The dove evokes the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and the dove that returned to Noah with an olive leaf (Genesis 8:11): new creation and peace.

And it remained on him. “Remained” (emeinen): abode, stayed. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came on prophets and kings for particular tasks, and could depart (1 Samuel 16:14). On Jesus, the Spirit rests permanently (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). He has the Spirit without measure (3:34).

The first abiding. Stay with that word remained, because John has just used, for the first time in his Gospel, one of the two or three most important words in it. The verb is menō. It turns up around forty times before the book closes, and it is the word behind the whole of chapter 15: abide in me, and I in you; apart from me you can do nothing. Everything this Gospel will eventually say about the Christian life runs through that verb. And its first appearance is not about us at all. It is about the Spirit settling on the Son and not lifting off again. That order matters more than it looks. The abiding does not begin with your effort to hold on to Christ. It begins with the Spirit resting on Christ permanently, and everything downstream is a share in that. What is asked of us in chapter 15 was first true here, in a river, before anyone had been asked anything.

He who sent me. God. Notice how completely this scene depends on a spoken instruction. He who sent me to baptize with water said to me: John did not work it out, and he did not sense it. He was told in advance precisely what to watch for, and then he stood in the water and watched for it, perhaps for months, looking at every face that came down the bank. God gave him a sign specific enough to be checked, and then honoured it.

The Trinity at the river. What lands here is the whole Trinity in a sentence and a half, without a word of the later vocabulary: the Father who sends and speaks, the Spirit who descends and settles, the Son on whom he settles. Nobody in the scene is arguing for the doctrine. It is simply what happened at the Jordan, and the definitions came centuries later to protect the report.

This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. John baptises with water; Jesus with the Spirit. Set the two baptisms side by side and the difference is plain. Water is applied from outside; it goes on you, and it comes off. The Spirit is not applied. He is given, and he stays, because the one doing the giving is the one on whom he has already been seen to stay. The one on whom the Spirit rests will give the Spirit to others (7:38–39; 20:22). Fulfilled at Pentecost, and in every believer’s new birth (3:5).

Have I been baptised with the Spirit? If you belong to Christ, yes. This phrase has been used to make Christians anxious about whether they have had a second experience they may have missed. The New Testament’s own position is blunt about it: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), and in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is no category of Christian who is still waiting for the Spirit. If you belong to Christ, the thing John is announcing here has already happened to you, whatever it felt like at the time and whether or not there was anything to feel. You may and should ask to be filled afresh, to walk in step with him and to know his power more (Ephesians 5:18), but that is growth in what you have, not a gate you have not yet passed.

In a sentence. John testified that he saw the Spirit come down like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign God had given him that Jesus is the one who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Here is a better test than the anxious one. Do not ask whether you have had an experience. Ask whether anything in you objects when you sin: not guilt about being found out, but a genuine unease that was not there before. Ask whether the word Father ever comes out of you without being manufactured (Romans 8:15). Ask why you are still reading a page like this at all. Those are not feelings. They are the evidence of someone who has moved in. Thank him for it today, and ask him to fill you again.

For worship. The dove came down and did not leave. That is the whole announcement, and everything the Christian life is made of comes out of it. The Spirit who rested on Jesus without measure has been poured out from him on all his people, and he will not lift off from them either. The Father sends, the Spirit rests, the Son pours out: glory to the triune God, who has made his home with us.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.

I have seen and have borne witness. Perfect tenses: a completed action whose result is still standing. I have seen, and it is still true that I have seen; I have borne witness, and the testimony is still on the record. He is not describing a moment of enthusiasm. He is entering a statement that cannot now be withdrawn, and, in a Gospel shaped like a trial, that is exactly what a deposition is. The language is that of a witness in court, whose testimony carries weight because it rests on what he saw.

That this is the Son of God. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read the Chosen One of God (Isaiah 42:1). The alternative reading fits the scene with unusual precision. If that is what John wrote, he is echoing Isaiah: behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. That is exactly what has just happened in front of him: a servant, a choosing, and the Spirit put upon him and staying. And it would tie this sentence back to the Lamb of five verses ago, since the servant of Isaiah 42 is the same figure who by Isaiah 53 is led to the slaughter. Either way, this is the climax of John’s testimony. Jesus is the unique Son of God (v. 18), the purpose of the Gospel (20:31). Either reading is true and neither is at risk.

What would they have heard? It is worth knowing what the title would have meant to the men standing there, because it did not yet mean to them all that it means in the creed. In Israel’s Scriptures son of God could be said of the king: you are my Son; today I have begotten you (Psalm 2:7). So the crowd would have heard a claim about the Messiah, the anointed king. John, writing decades later for readers who have now read his first chapter, means all of that and the thing verse 18 said as well. The title grows as the Gospel goes on. It does not change its mind.

He came, he pointed, he went. And this is the last we hear from John the Baptist in this section. He appears again briefly in chapter 3, to say the sentence that sums him up, he must increase, but I must decrease, and then he is arrested and killed offstage, and this Gospel does not even narrate it. He gets no death scene.

What if my faithful service seems to have come to nothing? You are in good company. The greatest man ever born of women, on the Lord’s own assessment, has a public career of a few months, spends it telling people to look at somebody else, is imprisoned on a private grudge, and is executed to settle a dinner-party promise. From the inside it can have looked very like a wasted life. He had seen, and he had borne witness, and it turns out that is the whole job description. God does not measure faithfulness by visible results, and he forgets nothing done for his Son (Hebrews 6:10). Your testimony, too, stands in the perfect tense.

In a sentence. John declared that he had seen and testified that Jesus is the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Write down, in a sentence or two, what you have seen of Christ: not a theory, but what you know to be true about him and what he has done in your life. Then look for one person this week to whom you could say it plainly. A witness does not need to be eloquent. He needs to have seen, and to say so.

For worship. Join John’s testimony: this is the Son of God. The chosen Servant, on whom the Spirit rests, the Lamb led to the slaughter, the King of Psalm 2, the only Son at the Father’s side: all of these are one person, and the prophet who saw him staked everything on it. Two thousand years later the seeing and the witnessing are still standing, and the Son of God is still worthy of every voice that has ever said so.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God.”

parallels.desc: my Chosen One

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said: behold, the Lamb of God!

Two of his disciples. Andrew (v. 40), and probably John, the author, who never names himself. Something easy to miss is happening here, and it costs the Baptist everything he has left. He is not preaching to a crowd this time. He is standing with two of his disciples, his own men, the ones who had attached themselves to him, who fasted when he fasted and prayed the prayers he taught them (Luke 11:1).

He looked at Jesus as he walked by. “Looked” (emblepsas): gazed intently. He is not gesturing vaguely down the road, and that is what the two of them notice first: not the words, but where the man is looking.

Behold, the Lamb of God! Shorter, repeated. John points his own disciples to Jesus, knowing they will leave him. He says it in a handful of words. He does not preface it, or soften it, or ask them to stay in touch. He does not even repeat the whole of what he said the day before: the sin of the world, the ranking, the pre-existence. He simply says, behold, the Lamb of God, and lets it do what it is going to do. The next verse is the two of them walking off after somebody else.

The same sentence, again. This is now the second day running that he has said the same thing (vv. 29, 36). Not a new insight, not a fresh angle, not something worked up for a different audience. There is a whole doctrine of preaching in that. The pressure on anyone who has to speak regularly is the pressure to say something they have not said before, and the pressure is very often vanity. The preacher’s task is not novelty but faithfulness, not new revelation but the one gospel repeated. The man Jesus called the greatest prophet had one line and used it until it took his followers away.

The friend of the bridegroom. The cost is the part to sit with. He is not resigning at the end of a full career; he is at the height of his influence, and he is dismantling it deliberately, one pair of disciples at a time. When people came to him later complaining that everyone was going over to Jesus, he gave them the image of a best man at a wedding: the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice, and whose joy is now complete (3:29). Not resigned. Not managing a disappointment. The happiest man at the party is the one who is not the groom and never thought he was. He must decrease (3:30).

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated in ministry? Not in itself. Paul longed to see his converts and rejoiced in their love (Philippians 4:1). Wanting your work to bear fruit and your people to flourish is good. What John shows is where that desire must be held: under a greater joy in Christ himself. The test is not whether you ever enjoy being thanked, but whether you can rejoice when people outgrow you, leave for another church, or never mention you again, because they are following him. If that is hard, tell the Lord so honestly and ask him to make his glory sweeter to you than your own.

In a sentence. The next day John again pointed to Jesus as he passed, telling two of his disciples: look, the Lamb of God.

On a Tuesday. Here is the harder half of what most of us mean by humility. It is not difficult to say that Christ is greater than you. It is difficult to be glad when someone you have taught, prayed for and carried transfers their affection and their attention to him and stops needing you, and does it in front of you. John did not merely permit that. He caused it, on purpose, day after day. Point people to Jesus, even if it means they leave you to follow him.

For worship. Two of them heard it. One was Andrew. The other, unnamed, is almost certainly the man writing this down decades later, still remembering exactly where he was standing and what the old prophet said. And this is the glory of the Lamb: he is so worth following that the best of men counted it joy to lose his disciples to him. All our pointing ends at him, and he never disappoints those who are sent his way.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.

The two disciples heard him say this. One sentence, and it contains the first use in this Gospel of the verb that will describe the Christian life from here to the last page.

And they followed Jesus. “Followed” (ēkolouthēsan): literally walked after him, and the word for discipleship. At this moment it means nothing more spiritual than walking behind a man on a road. That is worth noticing, because the word never quite loses that meaning. It does not mean they admired him, or agreed with him, or had settled anything. It means they got up and went the same way he was going, and were now some distance behind him with no idea what to say. They heard the testimony, and followed. Witness leads to following. The first disciples come to Jesus through the testimony of John.

How following usually starts. Stage what this actually looked like, because the next verse tells you. Two men are trailing a stranger down a road in silence. They have not introduced themselves. They have no question prepared. They are close enough to be noticed and far enough back to pretend they are not following, and the situation is becoming awkward, and it is Jesus who has to turn round and rescue it by speaking first. That is how following him usually starts, and it is worth saying plainly to anyone whose beginnings were unimpressive. There is a kind of testimony that makes conversion sound like a decision taken in a clear moment with full understanding. This is what the first one in this Gospel looked like: a sentence overheard, two men walking off after somebody without a plan, and an embarrassed silence that had to be broken from the other end.

So little to go on. The thing they had to go on was very small: a few words from a man they trusted, pointing at a man they did not know. No miracle had happened. Nothing had been explained. Everything in the next twenty chapters, the water into wine, the raising of Lazarus, the upper room, the empty tomb, is downstream of two men taking one sentence seriously enough to move their feet. And John loses them here. This is what his ministry produces: not a following, but a transfer.

What does following Jesus actually mean today? It means more than believing things about him; it means going where he goes. We follow him by trusting him for forgiveness, by listening to his words in Scripture and doing them, by taking up the life he gives us among his people, and by going his way when it costs us (Luke 9:23). It is a whole life, but it is lived one step at a time: the next obedience you know about, the next sin to turn from, the next act of love. You do not need to see the whole road. These two did not. You need to keep him in front of you.

In a sentence. Hearing John, the two disciples followed Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time somebody said something true to you about Christ, in a sermon, in a conversation, on a page. Did anything move? Not did you agree with it; agreeing is free. These two men heard a sentence they had heard before, and the difference this time was that their feet were involved. Has the witness you have heard about Jesus led you to follow him? Then take one step today that you would not take if he were not real.

For worship. The whole history of the church begins with two men walking awkwardly behind a stranger. He let them follow, and he has been letting sinners follow him ever since. He is the Good Shepherd who goes ahead of his sheep (10:4), and every road he walks ends at his Father’s house. Blessed is the Lord who lets us walk behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them: what are you seeking? And they said to him: Rabbi (which means Teacher), where are you staying? He said to them: come and you will see. So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.

What are you seeking? These are Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel. Stop at that fact before touching the content: the first thing the Word says once he has begun to speak is not a statement. It is a question, and it is a question about what you want. He does not ask what they believe. He does not ask what they have done, or whether they are sorry, or what they understand. He asks what they are looking for. The whole of the encounter is opened by an enquiry into desire.

The question the whole book asks. John has built his book around that verb. It is the same word (zēteō) that Jesus uses in the garden when the soldiers arrive with torches and he steps out to meet them: whom do you seek? (18:4, 7). It is the same word he uses on resurrection morning, when a woman is crying at a tomb she thinks has been robbed and a man she takes for the gardener says, woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking? (20:15). The first question in the book and one of its last are the same question. Nobody in this Gospel gets to Jesus without being asked it.

What if I came for the wrong reasons? Most people do. The question is aimed past the disciples at whoever is reading, and it is worth answering honestly rather than piously, because the pious answer is often not the true one. Most people come to Christ seeking something other than Christ: relief from a fear, a way out of a mess, certainty, respectability, a marriage saved, the return of a peace they remember having. Look at what he does with that. He asks the question, and then he does not screen anybody out on the strength of the answer. He does not say, wrong reason, come back when your motives are pure. The question is not a filter. It is the beginning of an education, and this Gospel is largely the record of people arriving with a small want and being given something they had not known to ask for. Come as you are, and let him change what you want.

Rabbi (which means Teacher). John translates Hebrew and Aramaic words for Greek readers.

Where are you staying? “Staying” (meneis): the same word as remained (v. 32), abiding. They want to be with him, to know him, not just ask a question. And notice that they duck his question. Asked what they are seeking, they answer with a question about an address. That is exactly what people do when a question goes too deep too fast: they change it into something practical. He lets them. He does not force the deeper conversation; he answers the question they were able to ask.

Come and you will see. An invitation to discover him for themselves. Not an argument, not a summary, not a leaflet: an address and an afternoon. Philip will repeat it (v. 46). It is worth guarding this against a use it often gets: it is not a recommendation to stop thinking. This is the Gospel that says it was written so that you might believe, on the basis of evidence deliberately selected and recorded (20:30–31). Come and see is not the opposite of examining the case. It is an invitation to examine it from close up rather than from the road.

And they stayed with him that day. “Stayed” (emeinan): abode. They asked where he abides, and the answer turned out to be that they could abide there too. The doctrine of chapter 15 is already running under this conversation, and nobody in it knows. This is the beginning of abiding with Christ (15:4).

For it was about the tenth hour. The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m., late enough that they stayed the night. Why on earth is that in the Bible? Because the man writing it was very probably the unnamed one of the two, and he is an old man now, and he still knows what time of day it was. He does not tell us what was said in that room, and you can feel the reader wanting him to. He remembers the hour. That is exactly how memory works around the afternoon your life divided in half: the content goes and the frame stays, the light in the room, where you were sitting, what time it was when you looked up. A precise detail, remembered by an eyewitness who never forgot the hour he met Jesus.

Does John use a different clock? Some think John counts hours from midnight, Roman style, which would make the tenth hour ten in the morning. That question matters chiefly at 19:14. Here the natural reading, counting from sunrise as Jews ordinarily did, is about four in the afternoon, which is why they stayed the rest of the day.

How do I come and see today, when Jesus is not physically here? Through the means he has given. He is present by his Spirit, and he speaks in his word. Read one of the Gospels slowly, from start to finish, asking at each page what it shows you of him. Pray, speaking to him as someone who is listening. Go where his people gather and his word is preached, and keep going. Ask honest questions and bring them to Scripture and to mature Christians. The disciples spent an afternoon in his company; you can spend your mornings there. The invitation has not been withdrawn.

In a sentence. Jesus asked what they wanted, they asked where he was staying, and he invited them to come and see, and they spent the day with him from about four in the afternoon.

On a Tuesday. Answer his first question in writing, honestly: what are you seeking from Jesus right now? Not what you ought to want; what you actually want. Then bring that answer to him in prayer, and ask him to give you himself as well as, or instead of, what you asked for. And spend some unhurried time with him today, even twenty minutes with a Gospel open. Come and see.

For worship. They came with a question about accommodation. They stayed until dark, and decades later one of them was still writing about it. The eternal Word, who was with God in the beginning, opened his door to two strangers on an ordinary afternoon and let them stay. He is still the host, and still asking what we seek, and still giving more than we knew to want. Praise the Lord who says, come and see.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m. — late enough that they stayed the rest of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him: we have found the Messiah (which means Christ).

Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. Always known in relation to his more famous brother. And this Gospel gives him three scenes, and he is doing the same thing in every one of them. Here he brings his brother. In chapter 6, with five thousand people to feed and the disciples calculating what it would cost, it is Andrew who says there is a boy here with five barley loaves and two fish, and then adds, honestly, but what are they for so many? (6:8–9). In chapter 12, when some Greeks come asking to see Jesus and Philip does not know what to do with the request, he takes it to Andrew, and Andrew takes them in (12:20–22). Three appearances, and every single time he is bringing somebody to Jesus: his brother, a boy with a packed lunch, and a group of foreigners nobody was sure were allowed.

The connector. He never preaches a sermon in the New Testament. There is not one recorded saying of his that is not either an introduction or a question. And the man he brought in this verse becomes the one who preaches at Pentecost and has two letters in the Bible. That is worth sitting with if your own gift feels like nothing much. Andrew is a connector, and connectors do not leave a record. Nothing he did would have looked like anything from across the room. But the whole of Peter’s life, the confession at Caesarea Philippi, the walk on the water, the three denials, the restoration on the beach, the sermon that added three thousand in a morning, enters the story because his brother could not keep quiet for an afternoon.

He first found his own brother Simon. His first act as a disciple: tell his family. Personal witness begins at home. Notice which brother it is: his own brother. The nearest possible person, and therefore the hardest. Nobody is less impressed by your spiritual development than the person who watched you grow up. Andrew has known Simon all his life, has presumably been out-talked by him at every meal they have ever eaten, and goes and tells him anyway.

What if my family has not believed after years of prayer? This verse gets used to prod people who do not need prodding. Andrew found his brother the same day, and it worked. That is not the pattern; it is the exception, and the New Testament knows it. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (7:5). The man in whose house they grew up could not persuade them, and they came in later, after the resurrection, at God’s speed and not his. If you have been praying for a brother, a son, a husband for twenty years and nothing has moved, this verse is not a reproach. It is a reminder that Andrew’s job was to fetch him, not to convert him, and that the fetching is the only part any of us has ever been responsible for. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the hour with God.

We have found the Messiah. Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) both mean anointed one, the promised King. Only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (also 4:25). After one evening with Jesus, Andrew was convinced. And there is an irony in the pronoun he does not notice. They found nothing. They were standing on a riverbank because a prophet was sent to tell them where to look, and Jesus turned round and spoke first, and in the next scene it will be Jesus doing the finding (v. 43). Every person in this chapter who says they have found him was found.

In a sentence. Andrew, one of the two, first found his brother Simon and told him they had found the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Name the person you would least like to raise this with: not a stranger, someone close, precisely because they know you too well for it to be comfortable. Now notice that Andrew’s opening line was five words long, contained no argument, and made no case. It was a piece of news and an invitation to come and look. That is the whole of what was asked of him. Who in your family or circle can you tell about Jesus this week? Be an Andrew.

For worship. He is remembered as Simon Peter’s brother. Simon Peter is remembered at all because of him. And behind both of them stands the Messiah who had already found them, the anointed King whom Israel had waited for through all its centuries, now sitting in a room on a riverbank, being introduced to fishermen. Glory to the Christ who is found by those he has first found.
verseByVerse.note: “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one” — the promised king.

parallels.desc: Andrew and Simon called by the lake

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said: you are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas (which means Peter).

He brought him to Jesus. The greatest thing Andrew ever did. The man who would preach at Pentecost was brought by his brother.

Jesus looked at him. “Looked” (emblepsas): a penetrating gaze, seeing who he was and who he would become. The verb is the same one used six verses earlier of the Baptist looking at Jesus: a deliberate look. Simon is being examined. And what comes out of the examination is not a verdict but a name.

You are Simon the son of John. Jesus knows him already. Watch the tenses, because the whole entry is in them. You are Simon the son of John: present tense, and it is the accurate description. Here is who you are, and here is whose family you come from, and I know both without being told.

You shall be called Cephas. Future tense. Between the two tenses there is a gap, and the gap is the rest of Simon’s life. The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean rock. Kēpha means a rock or a crag, and John stops to translate it for readers who do not have the language, which is itself a small piece of evidence that this happened, since a nickname that has to be explained to your audience is not one anybody invented for literary effect. It stuck so hard that Paul, writing to Greek-speaking churches twenty-five years later, still calls him Cephas by reflex (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9). A new name, as God renamed Abram and Jacob, signifying a new identity and calling.

A name before the evidence. Now the thing that ought to stop a reader. At this moment Simon has done nothing whatever. He has not confessed anything, left anything, promised anything, or been tested in any way. He has been standing in front of Jesus for a matter of seconds, brought there by his brother, and he has not yet said a word that anyone thought worth recording. The name is handed to him before there is a single piece of evidence for it. And the evidence, when it comes in, runs the other way. This man will take Jesus aside and tell him he has got the plan wrong. He will swear he is ready to die and then, a few hours later, in this same Gospel, stand at a charcoal fire in a courtyard and say three times that he does not know him. If you were naming him from his record you would not call him Rock. John knows all of that as he writes this verse. He was there for the courtyard. Simon was impulsive and unstable; Jesus would make him a rock. Not what he was, but what grace would make him.
