The compliment is being paid to the wrong man, by a man who does not know what he is saying, which keeps happening in this Gospel and will happen most famously when a high priest explains that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:49–52).

But you have kept the good wine until now. The best comes last. That is a picture of God’s ways: the old covenant was good, but the new is better (Hebrews 8:6). And the best is still to come: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). It is the shape of everything God does, and it runs against the shape of everything else. The world front-loads. The advertisement is better than the product, the first year of the job is the best year, the holiday is at its finest in the brochure, and youth is spent early. Almost every pleasure available to a human being is arranged so that the best of it comes first and what follows is a slow negotiation with the decline. God works the other way round. Israel got the shadow first and the substance later. The disciples got three years of walking about Galilee and then Pentecost. And the whole of Scripture ends not with a garden restored but with a city, and a wedding, and a supper.

What it does not mean. The best wine last is not an assurance that your circumstances will improve, and it must not be handed to someone as though it were. Plenty of Christian lives get harder rather than easier; health goes, work narrows, the people you love are buried one at a time, and there is no verse anywhere that guarantees the second half will be more comfortable than the first. What is promised is not a better stretch of road. It is a better end, and an end that is not the end.

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians argue that biblical wine was unfermented grape juice, and that Christians should abstain completely. Verdict: the wine Jesus made was real wine, as the master’s comment shows. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) while forbidding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free to abstain; they must never get drunk, and must be willing to abstain out of love for weaker brothers (Romans 14:21). Abstinence is a wise choice for many, but not a command.

Not a killjoy. The steward’s remark settles the question of whether it was real wine: a host serves the good wine first and the poor wine after the guests have drunk freely, which is a comment about what alcohol does to a palate and makes no sense of grape juice. But it is worth not over-reading. Nothing here licenses excess, and nothing here shames the Christian who abstains, whether from conviction or from hard experience of what drink has done in a family. What the sign does say is that the God who came among us was not a killjoy. His first miracle was not a rebuke or a healing but a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

What if alcohol has been a problem for me or my family? Then abstaining is not legalism but wisdom, and often love. Freedom to drink is not an obligation to drink, and Paul says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21); the brother may be you. If drink has a hold on you, the gospel offers forgiveness and real help: confess it honestly to God and to a trusted Christian, get practical support, and remove it from your home. And if a parent’s or spouse’s drinking has wounded you, this passage does not ask you to celebrate wine. It shows you a Lord who brings joy without ruin, and who can heal what drink has broken.

In a sentence. The master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine and, not knowing where it came from, praised the bridegroom for keeping the best wine until last.

On a Tuesday. If you have begun to suspect that your best days are behind you, that whatever you were going to be, you have now been, that the years when you felt most alive, most useful, most in love with God are in the past, tell yourself the steward’s sentence. On any account but this one that instinct would be correct. For anyone in Christ the arrangement has been reversed. And look for one way this week to obey him from the servants’ side, where his works are seen.

For worship. The steward’s compliment is a statement about the management of the whole universe: he has kept the good wine until now, and now has not happened yet. With Jesus, the best is always kept until last. Every joy we taste here is a cup from the jars of Cana; the feast itself is still being prepared. Look forward to the wedding supper of the Lamb, and bless the Bridegroom who has saved the best for his bride.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.

The first of his signs. John calls Jesus’ miracles signs (sēmeia), pointers to who he is: not just displays of power, but signs that reveal his identity. That is a deliberate choice, and you can prove it by what he never says. Matthew, Mark and Luke commonly describe the miracles as dynameis, acts of power, mighty works. John does not use that word for them at all. He uses the word for a signpost.

A signpost, not a show. The difference is the whole of his method. A mighty work invites you to be impressed by the one who did it. A signpost is not for admiring. It has no interest in itself; its entire value lies in pointing away from where it stands to somewhere you have not got to yet, and a traveller who stops at a signpost and praises the carpentry has missed the point. That is precisely what will go wrong with the crowds in chapter 6, who eat the loaves and want to make him king and are told they came looking for him not because they saw signs but because they ate their fill of the loaves (6:26).

Seven signs. John records seven signs before the resurrection: water into wine (2:1–11), the official’s son (4:46–54), the paralysed man (5:1–15), the five thousand (6:1–15), walking on water (6:16–21), the man born blind (9), and Lazarus (11). Each reveals something of who Jesus is. The counting is debated at the edges, but the pattern is not, and he tells you at the close exactly what he was doing: Jesus did many other signs, but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:30–31). And note that he calls this the first, and the Greek word is the one he opened the Gospel with. In the beginning was the Word. This was the beginning of his signs. The book is quietly starting again.

And manifested his glory. His divine glory (1:14), hidden in his humanity, shone through. Fourteen verses into chapter 1 John had written, we have seen his glory, a claim with nothing behind it yet. Here is the first instalment. What does this sign show? That Jesus is the Creator, who turns water into wine every year through the vine, now doing it instantly. That he brings the abundance and joy of the messianic age. That the old order of purification is replaced by the new wine of the kingdom. And it is done quietly, for a poor family, to save them from shame.

The glory in clay cups. Let that stand a moment. The glory of God, the thing that filled the tent until Moses could not go in, that drove the priests out of Solomon’s temple so that they could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:11), that Isaiah saw for one moment and cried out that he was undone, was in a back room in Cana, quietly seeing to it that a young couple were not humiliated on their wedding day. Nothing shook. Nobody fell down. The steward went on doing his job and the bridegroom accepted a compliment he had not earned, and the glory of the eternal God went round that room in cups.

And his disciples believed in him. The purpose of the signs (20:30–31). Which ought to stop you, because they already had (1:41–49). Andrew had said, we have found the Messiah; Nathanael had said, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. What are they doing believing again? Their faith deepened. Faith is not a switch that is thrown once and then stays where it was put. It is nearer to a thing that grows, and gets tested, and grows again, and this Gospel will show it doing both. The same men will be terrified in a boat, will be scattered on the night he is arrested, and one of them will announce that he will not believe the resurrection without putting his hand into the wound. If your faith today is recognisably larger or smaller than it was five years ago, that is not evidence of instability. It is the ordinary condition of everyone in this chapter.

Should I look for signs and miracles today? Look for what the signs were for. They were written down so that you may believe (20:31); the record of them is God’s chosen means of bringing you to faith now, and Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29). God still answers prayer, and he can heal and provide in ways that astonish us; we should ask him freely. But the apostolic signs belonged to the founding of the church, and we do not need fresh wonders to confirm a gospel already confirmed. A faith that keeps demanding new signs has missed the one they all point to. You have the signs, in writing, and the Lord himself.

His mother and his brothers. He goes down to Capernaum with his mother and his brothers and his disciples. That is the first mention of his brothers in this Gospel, and John will tell us plainly what their position was: for not even his brothers believed in him (7:5). The most natural reading is that they were Mary’s younger children. So the group walking that road together includes men who lived in the same house as the Son of God for the best part of thirty years, watched him at close quarters, are travelling with him now, and did not believe.

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brothers; Matthew names them (Matthew 13:55–56), and Paul met James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, take them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never says so, and the plain reading is the more likely.

For the one praying for family. Sit with this if you have been praying a long time for someone in your own family. Familiarity did not convert them. Proximity did not convert them. A flawless life lived in front of them for three decades did not convert them, and neither did this wedding. And yet James is later found leading the church in Jerusalem, called a pillar by Paul, and writing a letter that is in your Bible (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Somewhere between chapter 7 of this Gospel and chapter 15 of Acts, the brothers came in. What changed them was not more exposure. It was the resurrection, and Paul happens to record that the risen Christ appeared to James personally (1 Corinthians 15:7). Whatever passed between those two did in an afternoon what thirty years under the same roof had not. Keep praying.

And they stayed there for a few days. The last clause is nothing at all. After the first sign, after the glory, after the disciples’ faith took a step forward: a few quiet days in a fishing town with nothing recorded.

In a sentence. This first sign at Cana revealed Jesus’ glory and his disciples believed in him, and then he went to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples.

On a Tuesday. That last clause is worth having in mind the next time an ordinary fortnight follows a Sunday when God seemed close. It is the pattern. Most of the Christian life is Capernaum for a few days. Do not take the quiet as absence. Keep doing the next ordinary faithful thing, and let your faith grow there.

For worship. Jesus’ glory is seen in his care for ordinary people. The first time these men saw it, it consisted of a wedding present given to people who never found out who had given it, in a village nobody had heard of. That is our God: glory that stoops, power that serves, majesty that saves a young couple from shame. Believe in him, and let your faith grow, for he has more glory to show you than you have yet seen.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Near Passover Jesus goes up to Jerusalem and finds the temple courts full of dealers in cattle, sheep and doves, and money-changers at their tables. He plaits a whip from cords and drives out the traders and their animals, flings the coins to the ground, upsets the tables and orders the dove-sellers to take their goods away: his Father’s house is not a place of business. The disciples recall the psalm about zeal for God’s house devouring the righteous one. The authorities demand a sign to back his action. Jesus tells them that if they tear this temple down, he will rebuild it in three days. They scoff that Herod’s temple has been forty-six years in the building. But Jesus is speaking of his own body, and after he rises the disciples remember and believe both Scripture and his word. At the festival many trust in him because of his signs, yet Jesus does not trust himself to them, for he knows human hearts without being told.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is an act of prophetic authority: Jesus acts as the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Mal. 3:1), purifying the house of prayer from the commercial transactions that have turned worship into a market. The zeal that consumes him is zeal for the Father's house — the passion of the Son for the honor of the Father. 'My Father's house' — his first recorded words in Luke (2:49) and his claim here: the temple belongs to his Father, and he has authority over it because he is the Son.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word dwelt among us and we have seen his glory; here the tabernacle has become the temple, and John states that the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city in which John saw no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). My Father's house (v. 16) is the claim that licenses the whip — the same phrase Luke records from him at twelve years old in the same building (Lk. 2:49).

Verse 22 supplies this Gospel's account of how understanding arrives. The disciples heard the saying at the time and grasped nothing of it for three years; the resurrection made the old sentence legible and the memory surfaced with its meaning attached — which is the promise of 14:26 in operation. They believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken, two objects of one verb, with no distinction drawn between them.

Verses 23-25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. What is described is faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested — the crowd of chapter 6 who turn back at the first hard saying (6:66). John uses of them the identical phrase he used of the saved in 1:12, believed in his name: the difference is not in the vocabulary but in what the faith does when the wine runs out. Anxiety about whether one's faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described here were entirely untroubled. And Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing — the next thing he does is give Nicodemus the fullest account of the new birth in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling were not wicked in themselves but had invaded the sacred space set apart for prayer, turning the house of God into a place of commerce. The sign of the temple's destruction and raising in three days is the central sign of the entire Gospel: the cross and resurrection are the ultimate manifestation of Jesus's glory, the event to which all other signs point.

The anger of this scene needs handling in both directions. It is not incompatible with meekness: anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged, and he stops to make the whip of cords himself (v. 15) — this is deliberate, not a loss of temper. But the passage is not a warrant for aggression on God's behalf. Two things separate it from that: all of it is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself, since under personal injury he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23); and it is the Son acting in his own house with the owner's authority.

The searching application is not the easy one about churches selling things. It is the Court of the Gentiles question: whether anything in the ordinary operation of a congregation — its assumptions, its vocabulary, the things everyone knows and nobody explains — makes it hard for an outsider to get near God. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

And the chapter's last word runs straight into the next scene: the printers' chapter break hides a joint. Verse 25 ends he himself knew what was in man (anthropos), and John's next sentence begins Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus — the general statement and its illustration set against each other like a caption and a photograph.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.

The Passover of the Jews was at hand. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is why we think Jesus’ ministry lasted about three years. And Jesus went up to Jerusalem: the Lord has come to his temple, exactly as Malachi said he would (Malachi 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons. The trading happened in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles. Animals for sacrifice, conveniently sold on the spot to pilgrims, at a price. And let the verb do its work: he found those who were selling. He is not told about it; he arrives and looks. This is the Lord coming suddenly to his temple, and the first thing recorded is an inspection.

A trade with a rationale. It is important to see that the trade had a reason and was not obviously a racket. An animal brought for sacrifice had to be without blemish and had to be certified as such, and a lamb carried a hundred miles has a poor chance of passing inspection. It was far more practical to buy one on site, already approved. Nothing in that system is corrupt on the face of it. It is convenience, and it grew up because people needed it.

And the money-changers sitting there. Every adult male Jew owed an annual half-shekel temple tax, and it had to be paid in a particular currency. Money-changers exchanged coins with images of pagan rulers for the Tyrian shekel used to pay the temple tax, accepted because of the reliability of its silver, taking a commission. This trade was under the control of the high priestly family.

Rot by convenience. That is the first thing to say about it. The problem was not that somebody had smuggled something wicked into the temple. It was that a set of reasonable arrangements, each defensible on its own terms, had between them turned worship into a transaction, and had done so gradually, with nobody deciding it. That is nearly always how it happens. Institutions do not usually rot by scandal. They rot by convenience.

The court of the nations. Now the location, and this is the part most readers have never been told. The temple had concentric courts, and access narrowed as you went in: the innermost for priests, then Israelite men, then women. The outermost and by far the largest was the Court of the Gentiles, and it was the only place in the entire building where a non-Jew was permitted to come and pray. Beyond it stood a barrier with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who passed would have himself to blame for his death. Two of those stones have been dug up. The market was in that court. The only place on earth where a Gentile could come near the God of Israel had been given over to livestock pens, currency tables, and the noise and smell of a cattle market on a festival week. The provision for the nations had been turned into retail space for the insiders.

A house of prayer for all the nations. That is why, in Mark’s account of the later cleansing, the sentence Jesus cries out is from Isaiah and includes the clause we usually leave off: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations (Isaiah 56:7; Mark 11:17). The offence is not merely commerce in a holy place. It is that the arrangements of the religious had made it impossible for the outsider to pray.

Is it wrong for churches to sell things or handle money? Not in itself. Churches need money to pay ministers, care for the poor and support missionaries, and Scripture commands generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7). A bookstall or a collection is not a temple market. The question is whether money and convenience have begun to shape worship and push people out: whether the gospel is ever made to look like something you buy, whether the poor feel unwelcome, whether leaders profit from the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Watch the purpose, not merely the transaction.

In a sentence. At Passover Jesus went to Jerusalem and found people selling animals and changing money in the temple courts.

On a Tuesday. The usual application of this passage is about churches selling things, and it is not wrong, but it is easy and it is about somebody else. The harder question is the Court of the Gentiles one: is there anything about the way your church actually operates, its assumptions, its vocabulary, its arrangements, the things everyone knows and nobody explains, that would make it hard for an outsider to get near God? Not hard to enjoy; hard to get near. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space. What has crept into the worship of God that should not be there? And who could you make room for this Sunday?

For worship. The Lord came suddenly to his temple, and he came looking for the nations. The court the insiders had filled with trade was the court he meant to fill with worshippers from every tribe and tongue. And he has done it: the dividing wall is broken down (Ephesians 2:14), and Gentiles who were far off have been brought near by his blood. Praise the Lord of the temple, who makes room for outsiders.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons: take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.

Making a whip of cords. This is the passage people either enjoy too much or are quietly embarrassed by, and both reactions are worth taking seriously, because a great deal has been done in the world with the sentence Jesus made a whip. Begin with what the text actually says, since the Greek is more restrained than the paintings. He made a whip of cords, improvised, perhaps from the rushes used for animal bedding or ropes lying about a place full of tethered livestock; not an implement he brought. It was to drive out the animals, not to beat people. A deliberate, considered act, not a loss of temper: making a whip takes time.

He drove them all out. With righteous anger. And the phrase is followed immediately by with the sheep and oxen, which many read as specifying who the all were. It is grammatically possible to read it as including the traders, and honest to say the point cannot be settled from the words alone. What is beyond dispute is that no one in the scene is struck. There is no injury reported, no blood, no arrest, and the authorities who arrive a moment later do not accuse him of assault; they ask him for his credentials. Whatever happened, it was not a brawl.

And he poured out the coins … and overturned their tables. Coins scattering across the stone floor.

Take these things away. To the pigeon sellers, he speaks: the birds were in cages and could not be driven. Look at how the action is graded, because the grading is the giveaway. The animals are driven out. The coins are poured out and the tables turned over. And the pigeon-sellers are told to take them away. He does not tip over their cages, and one likely reason is that pigeons were the offering of the poor, the sacrifice prescribed for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), and released birds do not come back. Even in the middle of it, he will not destroy what belongs to people who have nothing.

Is this consistent with the gentle Jesus? It is, and the way to see it is to ask what anger actually is. Anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged. A man who can watch his own child be harmed and feel nothing is not gentle; he is absent. The reason this scene sits so oddly with us is that we have quietly redefined gentleness as the absence of strong feeling, when in Scripture meekness is strength brought under command. Everything here is under command. He does not snatch up a weapon; he stops and makes a whip of cords. Whatever this was, it was not a loss of temper; it was a decision. The Lamb of God has a holy wrath (Revelation 6:16), and it is the same love that weeps over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. This passage has been used to justify a great deal that has nothing to do with it. It is not a warrant for Christians to be aggressive on God’s behalf, still less to use violence. It is not cover for the man whose temper is a standing problem in his household and who has learned to call it righteous anger. Two things separate this from that, and they are not subtle. First, every scrap of it is aimed at the abuse of God’s honour and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself; when the injuries were personal he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). Second, this is the Son acting in his own house with the authority of the owner, which is precisely the authority the next verse is challenged about. If your anger is regularly about your own treatment, this passage is not about you.

Then is anger always wrong for me? No. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real evil, at cruelty, injustice, abuse, the dishonouring of God, can be right, and indifference to such things is not a virtue. But our anger is rarely pure, so Scripture surrounds it with fences: be slow to anger (James 1:19–20), do not let the sun go down on it, never take revenge (Romans 12:19), and do not let it harden into bitterness. Ask whose honour your anger is defending. Then bring it to God, act through right channels, and leave vengeance to him.

Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade. My Father’s house: Jesus claims a unique relationship with God. Not the house of God, not our Father’s house, but my. It is the same phrase Luke records him using at twelve years old, in this same building, to the parents who had been searching for him for three days: did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? (Luke 2:49). His first recorded sentence and this one make the same claim, about twenty years apart and in the same courts. That is what licenses the whip. He is not a reformer with strong views about temple administration. He is the Son, standing in his own family’s house, dealing with what has been done to it. And he names what it has become: a house of trade. Perhaps an echo of Zechariah 14:21: there shall no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day. The day of the Lord has come.

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry; the other Gospels place one at the end (Mark 11:15–17). Some think John moved it to the beginning for theological reasons. But the details and wording differ, and it is quite possible that Jesus did it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry.

Weighing the two answers. That is not the strained solution it sounds. The abuse was structural and profitable and would have resumed within a month of any one-off protest, and the details differ in ways that fit two occasions rather than one: here Jesus makes a whip of cords and speaks of my Father’s house, while in the other Gospels he quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah about a house of prayer and a den of robbers. The authorities’ question differs too. The other answer is that John, who openly arranges his material by theme and tells us plainly that he is selecting (20:30–31), has set this true episode at the front as the doorway into everything that follows. That would not be a claim that he invented anything or shifted a date to deceive; ancient writers were free to order true events for meaning. Either way the point of the scene is untouched.

In a sentence. Jesus made a whip of cords, drove out the traders and animals, scattered the coins, overturned the tables, and told them not to make his Father’s house a marketplace.

On a Tuesday. Ask what has been allowed to clutter your own worship: the phone in the pew, the mind running through the week’s accounts during the prayers, the habit of treating church as a service you consume. Ask him to clear it out, even if the clearing is uncomfortable. And if you have been nursing an anger you have called righteous, test it against this scene: is it for God’s honour and the good of the weak, or for yours?

For worship. Jesus is zealous for the purity of God’s worship. The Son came into his Father’s house and would not let it be cheapened. That same zeal burns for his people, who are now his temple, and he does not leave us cluttered and compromised. He cleanses. Ask him to cleanse your worship today, and adore the Son who loves his Father’s house enough to turn over its tables.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples remembered that it was written: zeal for your house will consume me. So the Jews said to him: what sign do you show us for doing these things?

His disciples remembered. Perhaps at the time, or later, after the resurrection (v. 22). And notice the verb, because it is going to matter in this chapter: it happens twice, and the two are not the same. Here the Scripture surfaces while the coins are still rolling. In verse 22 they will remember something else, and it will take them three years and a resurrection to do it. Both are recorded, which is a mercy, because most of us have had both.

Zeal for your house will consume me. Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the righteous sufferer, often applied to Jesus in the New Testament (15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). “Consume” means devour, eat me up. And there is something in the quotation that is easy to walk past and is almost certainly the point of it: the tense. In Psalm 69 the zeal has consumed the psalmist, a thing already done. What the disciples remember, and what John writes down, is will consume me. Future. So the sentence they find themselves remembering as they watch him overturn the tables is not merely, look how zealous he is. It is a prediction. This will eat him. His zeal for God’s house would literally consume him: it would lead to his death. The temple authorities are the ones who will finally move against him, and the cleansing of the temple was one cause of his execution.

Psalm 69 at the cross. Psalm 69 will not leave this Gospel alone. It is the long complaint of a righteous man hated without cause, and John will reach for it again at the cross when they lift up the sour wine (19:28–29). The zeal and the vinegar come out of the same psalm.

What is zeal, and why do I not seem to have it? What is being described here is not a temperament. Some people are naturally intense and some are not, and the intense ones are not thereby more godly; a great deal of what passes for zeal in religious life is simply a strong personality with a subject. What the disciples saw was not energy. It was a man who could not be indifferent to his Father’s honour because he loved his Father, and the zeal was the shape the love took when the honour was being damaged. So the question to ask is not, am I zealous enough? No one has ever answered that helpfully. Ask instead what it takes to move you. Everybody has something. Find the last thing that genuinely stirred you, that you could not simply let pass, and you have located what you love. And if it is not God’s honour, ask him to grow your love for him, and the zeal will follow.

What sign do you show us for doing these things? By what authority? Prove it with a miracle. The prophets sometimes did symbolic acts; let him prove he is a prophet. And there is an irony in it that only grows as the book goes on: what sign do you show us? is asked in a Gospel built entirely out of signs, by men who will be shown every one and believe none.

Querying the credentials. But look carefully at what they are and are not disputing. Nobody says the market should stay. Nobody defends the money tables or argues that the Court of the Gentiles was the right place for livestock. The abuse is conceded without a word. What is challenged is his standing to do anything about it: not you are wrong, but who authorised you? That is the characteristic move of an institution under criticism, and it has not changed in two thousand years. The safest way to avoid a charge is to query the credentials of whoever brought it.

In a sentence. His disciples remembered the Scripture that zeal for God’s house would consume him, and the Jewish leaders demanded a sign to prove his authority.

On a Tuesday. Are you zealous for God’s honour? Jesus’ zeal cost him his life. Notice this week where your own heart is stirred, by a slight to yourself, by a football result, by a political headline, by the name of God being mocked, and let the comparison teach you. And when you are rightly challenged about something wrong in you, resist the urge to query the credentials of the one who said it. Ask first whether it is true.

For worship. The zeal that cleared the temple was the zeal that carried him to the cross. He loved his Father’s house so much that it consumed him, and in being consumed he built a better one, made of living stones. The psalm of the hated righteous man is his psalm, and he sang it all the way to Golgotha for us. Praise the Son whose zeal for God was our salvation.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The Jews then said: it has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?

Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The sign he offers: his resurrection. Note first what kind of sentence this is. Destroy is a command, meaning if you destroy: go on, then; do it. You will destroy it; I will raise it. It is a challenge thrown at men who have just asked for his credentials, and it has the form of a dare that both parties know is not really a dare. They will not lay a finger on Herod’s stonework. They will, in about three years, do precisely what he has invited them to do to the temple he actually meant. “Raise up” (egeirō) is the word for resurrection.

How testimony gets bent. The words were twisted at his trial into a threat to destroy the temple (Mark 14:58). Witnesses are produced who say: we heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands. And as he hangs on the cross, those who pass by jeer: you who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days (Mark 15:29). Compare the pronouns. He said you destroy. They reported I will destroy. One word was moved, and the sentence changed from a prophecy about what they would do to him into a threat about what he would do to them. Nothing was invented. Something was shifted, and that was enough to hang a capital charge on.

It has taken forty-six years to build this temple. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years later puts this at about AD 27. This one exasperated remark by a hostile official is one of the main pegs on which the chronology of Jesus’ ministry hangs. And there is a bitterness in it they could not have known. The work went on until AD 63, just seven years before it was destroyed. In AD 70 the Romans burned it and pulled it down. They were boasting to the Son of God about a construction project that would stand complete for about seven years.

And will you raise it up in three days? They take him literally, and mock. It is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through this whole Gospel. They hear a claim about masonry and answer with a building schedule. In the next chapter a teacher of Israel will hear born again and ask whether a grown man can enter his mother’s womb a second time (3:4). A woman at a well will hear living water and point out that he has nothing to draw with (4:11). A crowd will hear bread from heaven and ask for a permanent supply (6:34). Every time, the misunderstanding takes the same form: the words are taken at the flattest possible level, and the flat reading is the one that keeps the hearer from having to deal with him. The natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Why did Jesus speak in riddles? Not to hide the truth from honest seekers, but to draw them in and to expose hearts. A saying like this one sticks in the memory and opens up later, which is exactly what happened to the disciples (v. 22). It also sifts the hearers: those who want to understand him keep asking, while those who have already decided against him take the flattest reading and walk away. Jesus never plays games with people who truly want him. When Nicodemus asks, he explains at length. When the disciples ask, he tells them plainly. If something he says puzzles you, do what they did: stay near, keep reading, and ask.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that if they destroyed this temple, he would raise it up in three days, and they scoffed that it had taken forty-six years to build.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the flat reading in yourself. When a word of Christ makes a claim on you, it is very easy to answer it at the level that lets you off: to argue about details, or to treat it as impossible, or to take it so literally that it could never apply. Take one saying of Jesus that unsettles you, and ask honestly what it would mean if he meant it.

For worship. They were not wrong about their temple; forty-six years of it could not be redone in three days, and nothing could. They were wrong about which temple was standing in front of them. He let them destroy it, and on the third day he raised it, never to fall again. The sign of Jesus’ authority is his resurrection. Believe it, and worship the Lord who builds in three days what no human hand could build in a thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

But he was speaking about the temple of his body. John’s explanation, and it is the key. Jesus’ body is the true temple, the place where God dwells with his people. Follow the thread John is pulling, because it runs the length of the Bible and this verse is the knot in the middle of it. In chapter 1 he wrote that the Word dwelt among us (1:14), the language of the tabernacle, the tent in the wilderness where the glory came down. Here the tabernacle has become the temple: the fixed house, the place you travelled to, the address where God could be met. And John says the address is a body. Not a building that contains the presence, but a person in whom God is present. The temple building will be replaced by Jesus himself. Through his death and resurrection, he becomes the meeting place of God and humanity (4:21–24).

No temple in the city. It ends where you would expect once you have seen the direction. At the very close of the Bible, John is shown the city that is the end of everything, and he records the one thing about it that startled him: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22). There is no building at the end. There was never going to be.

We are his temple too. And his people, united to him, become God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). The living stones are built on the living cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–5). Where Christ’s people gather in his name, God dwells; and each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Then does it matter where or how we worship? Where, much less than before. Jesus will tell the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (4:21–24). No building is holy ground in itself, and you can meet God in a kitchen as truly as in a cathedral. How, very much. We come to God only through Christ, the true temple, and we must worship him as he has revealed himself, not as we invent. And because the church is his temple, gathering with his people is not optional decoration; it is where he has promised to dwell (Hebrews 10:25; Matthew 18:20).

When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered. Understanding came after the resurrection, with the help of the Spirit (14:26). Read that carefully and notice what it concedes. They did not understand it at the time. They were standing right there. They heard the words with their own ears, they had every advantage of proximity, they were the inner circle, and it meant nothing to them for the best part of three years. Then it landed. Not through study, not through someone explaining it, but because an event occurred that made the old sentence suddenly clear, and the memory came up with its meaning attached. That is what he had promised would happen: the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (14:26). This verse is that promise working, recorded by a man who was on the receiving end of it.

For anyone in the middle of something they cannot read. There is a great deal of pressure on Christians to understand what God is doing while he is doing it: to have an account of the illness, the redundancy, the years that went nowhere, the prayer that was not answered. That pressure does not come from this book. The men closest to Jesus, watching the most important events in human history at a distance of a few feet, understood almost none of it until afterwards, and were not disqualified for it. What was asked of them was not comprehension. It was staying near enough to remember.

And they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken. Scripture and Jesus’ own words are placed side by side. One verb, two things believed, and no distinction drawn between them. A sentence he said in a courtyard is placed alongside the Hebrew Scriptures as the same kind of word. Nobody in the verse argues for that. John simply writes it down, and it is one of the highest claims in the chapter. Jesus’ word has the authority of Scripture.

Which Scripture? John does not name one. Passages such as Psalm 16:10, you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, and Isaiah 53 were among those the apostles later preached, and Jesus himself opened all the Scriptures to them after he rose (Luke 24:27). Their faith was in the whole Old Testament witness to his death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

In a sentence. He was speaking of his body as the temple, and after his resurrection his disciples remembered and believed Scripture and his words.

On a Tuesday. Think of a stretch of your life you did not understand while you were in it, and ask whether you understand any of it now. Most people who have walked with God for twenty years can name at least one thing that made no sense at the time and is now the very thing they would not give back. That is not a technique for the present difficulty; it will not tell you what this one is for. But it is evidence about how the Lord works, gathered from your own life, and it is worth having in hand while you wait for the rest. Meanwhile, stay near: keep reading his word, so that there is something for the Spirit to bring to your remembrance.

For worship. For a thousand years God had consented to be met in a house of stone: the smoke, the blood, the courts, the curtain, the one room no one could enter but once a year and never without blood. All of it was pointing beyond itself. Then a man stood in the middle of it and said the meeting place was himself; and three years later they took him outside the city and killed him; and, as the other Gospels record, the curtain in that house tore from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). The house was never the point. The Son was the point, and the house had been saying so, in stone, for a thousand years. Jesus is the true temple. In him you meet God, and you are part of his temple.

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.

Many believed in his name when they saw the signs. Faith based on miracles: real, but shallow. John recognises different kinds of belief. These are people whose faith has been produced entirely by spectacle. They saw signs, and they were impressed, and impressed is what they are. Nothing has yet been asked of them; nothing has yet cost them anything; the whole thing has been going well and they have been carried along with it. John is not saying their belief is fake. He is saying it is untested, and that Jesus, who can see the whole of a person, knows exactly what it is worth. Some who believed would later turn away (6:66; 8:31, 59).

But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them. A play on words that English cannot carry. They believed (episteusan) in him, but he did not believe (episteuen), entrust himself, to them. It is the same verb both times. They believed into him; he did not believe into them. John has put the two clauses side by side deliberately, and the effect in Greek is like a door swinging shut on its own hinge. He did not commit himself to their enthusiasm.

What happens to it. He also shows us what happens to this kind of faith. In chapter 6 a crowd of the same kind is fed on a hillside and follows him across a lake, and then he says something they find intolerable, and John records the outcome in one of the saddest verses in the book: after this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66). That is this kind of faith, four chapters later, meeting the first thing it did not like.

Because he knew all people. He knew the shallowness of their faith. This is not cynicism but knowledge: Jesus knows the difference between excitement about evidence and the saving faith that perseveres through suffering and offence. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one. Many want Jesus’ blessings without Jesus himself.

How do I know my faith is not like theirs? This is a frightening sentence, and it should be handled slowly, because it unsettles people who are already unsettled. If you are troubled by these verses, if you have read them and gone cold and started auditing your own conversion, notice that the people being described here were not troubled at all. They were delighted. Nobody in that Passover crowd was lying awake wondering whether their faith would hold, because nothing had yet happened to make them wonder. Anxiety about the reality of your faith is not a symptom of the condition described here. It is nearly always a symptom of caring whether it is real, which is the one thing this crowd conspicuously did not do. Look away from your faith to its object: true faith rests on Christ himself, not on the excitement of signs, and he keeps those who are his (10:28–29).

Same words, different outcome. Notice that John uses exactly the same phrase of these people that he used in the prologue of the saved: believed in his name (1:12). He does not have a separate vocabulary for false faith. The words are identical, and the difference does not lie in the words. It lies in what the faith turns out to do when the wine runs out. So the question is not, and never was, whether your believing began with the right feeling. Nothing in Scripture asks you to establish that. What it asks is whether you are still holding on to Christ. And those whom God has truly given faith he will keep to the end (Philippians 1:6).

Withholding, not withdrawing. There is a further comfort hidden in the sentence. He did not entrust himself to them, but he did not send them away either. He goes on speaking, and the very next thing that happens in this Gospel is that one member of the Jerusalem religious establishment comes to him at night with a compliment about signs, and gets the longest and tenderest explanation of the new birth anywhere in the Bible. Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing. It is a refusal to be naive, and it is the opposite of a dismissal.

In a sentence. At Passover many believed in Jesus because of his signs, but he did not entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone.

On a Tuesday. Try the test, and it is not about your feelings. Think of the last thing following Christ actually cost you: not an inconvenience, a cost. Money you will not get back, a friendship that cooled, a truth told when a lie would have been easier, a resentment you had every right to and let go anyway. If nothing comes to mind at all, that is worth knowing, and it is knowable now rather than later. If something does, then whatever you feel about your faith, it has already been out in weather, and this crowd never was. Faith based only on miracles may not last. Is your faith rooted in who Jesus is?

For worship. He is not fooled by crowds, and he is not cold toward seekers. He sees through every surface and goes on speaking to the people he sees through. And for those whom the Father gives him, he does entrust himself: he calls them friends, opens his heart to them, and lays down his life for them (15:13–15). Blessed is the Lord who is never naive and never unkind.

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.

And needed no one to bear witness about man. Two things finish the chapter. First, the word that keeps appearing where you would least expect it. This is a Gospel obsessed with witness: John the Baptist is called to bear witness, the works bear witness, the Father bears witness, the Scriptures bear witness, and by chapter 5 Jesus will lay out a whole case with the witnesses named one after another. And here, in the middle of it, John records the one subject on which he needed no one to bear witness. Everything about himself he was content to have testified to by others. About human beings he required no evidence, because he already had it all.

He himself knew what was in man. He knows the human heart perfectly, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Psalm 139:1–4). He knew Nathanael (1:47–48), and will know the Samaritan woman’s past (4:18), and Judas’ betrayal (6:64).

The chapter break in the wrong place. Second, and this is the thing to carry into the next page: verse 25 ends with the word man, anthrōpos. And the next sentence John wrote, before anyone had invented chapter numbers, begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. Same word, back to back. He knew what was in man, and here comes one. Nicodemus is not a new subject. He is the illustration of the sentence that has just been made, and John has arranged it so that the general statement and the particular case sit against each other like a caption and a photograph. The next chapter shows him with a man, Nicodemus, whose heart he reads: a good, learned, genuinely searching member of the ruling council who has understood nothing, and who is going to be told that what he needs is not more instruction but to be born. And Nicodemus opens his mouth in a moment and says no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him: the crowd’s exact position, in the mouth of the best-qualified man in Jerusalem. He is the sign-faith of verse 23 with a doctorate.

A comfort and a warning. Jesus knows the worst about us, and still loves us. And we cannot deceive him with shallow profession. That Christ knows what is in a man is either the worst news or the best, and most of us hold both at once on different days. It is the worst because there is no version of your life in which you get to present the edited copy. Not the account you give your friends, not the one you give yourself at three in the morning: the actual contents. He has read it. The one thing every human being spends real energy on, in one way or another, is managing what other people are allowed to see, and with him the whole apparatus is simply irrelevant.

Full-knowledge love. And it is the best for exactly the same reason, on one condition: that you know what he did after reading it. This is not a verse about surveillance. The man who knew what was in man went to Jerusalem anyway, into the hands of people whose contents he had read in full, and died for them. If he had loved us on the strength of a favourable report, the love would be worth nothing, because the report would have been wrong. There was no report. He looked. The cross is not an act of ignorance; it is love offered in full knowledge of human sin.

If he knows my heart, why should I confess? Because confession is not giving him information; it is agreeing with him. When you confess, you stop hiding and start walking in the light with him (1 John 1:7–9). He already knows; what changes is you. Confession breaks the power of secrecy, humbles pride, and opens you to receive the forgiveness he has promised. It is the difference between a child whose father knows what he did and a child who comes and says so. The father’s knowledge is the same. The relationship is not.

In a sentence. He needed no one to tell him about people, for he knew what was in every heart.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a short one. Is there anything you are hoping God has not noticed? Name it, silently, now. Then notice that the naming told him nothing, and that the chapter that follows this sentence is the one containing the words for God so loved the world. Be honest with him today about what he already knows, and receive what he offers.

For worship. He knew what was in man. He knew what was in Judas on the night he dipped the bread and handed it to him. He knew what was in Peter when he looked at him and called him a rock. He knew what was in the men who would drive the nails, and in the crowd that would ask for Barabbas, and in every soul that has ever come to him carrying a rehearsed version of itself. He read the whole of it. He did not look away, and he did not revise the plan. He went to the cross having already seen the worst thing about every person he was dying for. Jesus knows everything in your heart, and still loves you.

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Two scenes open Jesus’ public ministry, one in a village home and one in the temple, and both announce that something new has come. At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Jesus turns some 150 gallons of water standing in stone jars for Jewish purification into wine better than any served before. It is the first of the seven “signs” John records, and through it Jesus reveals his glory and his disciples believe. The prophets pictured the messianic age as a feast overflowing with wine (Isaiah 25:6; Amos 9:13); the water of the old purification rites gives way to the wine of the kingdom.

At Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives the traders and money-changers from the temple court with a whip of cords, forbidding them to make his Father’s house a market. Asked for a sign to justify his authority, he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” His hearers think of Herod’s building, forty-six years in the making; John explains that he meant his body, and the disciples understood after the resurrection. The meeting place of God and people is now Jesus himself. Many in Jerusalem believe because of his signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every human heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, visits Jesus by night and acknowledges him as a teacher sent by God, because of his signs. Jesus tells him that without a birth from above no one can see God’s kingdom. Nicodemus takes it literally: can an old man be born a second time? Jesus explains that entry to the kingdom requires birth by water and the Spirit. Human nature can only reproduce itself; the Spirit gives new life, unseen and unpredictable as the wind. Israel’s teacher should have understood. Jesus speaks of what he has seen, yet his testimony is refused. The Son of Man, who alone has come down from heaven, must be raised up as Moses raised the bronze serpent, so that all who trust him may have eternal life. The reason is God’s love for the world: he gave his unique Son, so that no one who believes in him will be lost, but will live for ever. The Son came to rescue, not to condemn. Believers face no condemnation; unbelievers are condemned already. The light has come, but people chose darkness because their deeds were evil and they feared exposure, while those who practise the truth come to the light gladly.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills. No human being can produce it, control it, or predict it; the Spirit sovereignly regenerates those whom God has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness — is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God's motive is love for the world; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. The light has come, and the verdict of each person is revealed by whether they come to the light or flee from it.

The kingdom of God — the dominant phrase of the other three Gospels — occurs in John only here, at verses 3 and 5, and never again. And the verb shifts between them: without this birth a man cannot see the kingdom (v. 3) and cannot enter it (v. 5). The problem is not that he is outside a door he can see; he cannot perceive the country. This is why argument alone never works, and why Nicodemus is the proof of it.

Verse 6 states the impossibility as a principle of kind, not of quantity: like produces like, and nothing in creation generates something of a higher order than itself. Flesh here is not the body — this Gospel has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world — but human nature working with its own resources, including the best of them. So the failure of religious effort is not a failure of sincerity or degree. Effort was never the mechanism.

Verse 16 requires two corrections that make it larger rather than smaller. So loved renders houtos, an adverb of manner rather than degree: in this way God loved — he gave. The size of the love is not asserted but demonstrated. And the world in this Gospel is not a neutral term for the planet's population but humanity organised against God (1:10; 7:7; 15:18-19). The object of the love was the thing set against him. Verse 17's not to condemn is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgement exists — verse 18 says the opposite in the same breath. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anyone; that the drowning is real is why it was launched.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Born again' (or 'born from above') is among the most comprehensive descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it captures the totality of the transformation (rebirth, not reform), its source (from above, from God), and its necessity (without it, the kingdom cannot be seen). Nicodemus's night visit is the first of several encounters in John where the darkness represents the condition of the human soul before the light breaks in. John 3:16 is not a formula to be memorized but a universe to be explored: every word contains inexhaustible depth.

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation, and the arc is the answer to anyone who thinks the night visit was a failure. He appears twice more, each time further into the open: in chapter 7 he speaks up in the council for due process and is shouted down (7:50-51); and after the crucifixion, when the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution in daylight with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39) — a quantity fit for the burial of a king, carried through the streets by a member of the Sanhedrin. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon.

The bronze serpent repays being staged rather than cited. Israel complains; snakes come; people are dying through the camp. God's remedy is not to remove the snakes but to have Moses cast an image of the very thing killing them and raise it on a pole — an image, commanded by the God who forbade images, of the instrument of death — and the only requirement laid on a dying man is that he look. It is deliberately the one thing someone face down in the sand can still do. (Israel kept the bronze snake, and seven centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and smashed it, calling it Nehushtan — 2 Kgs. 18:4. Even the instrument of mercy becomes an idol if the look lands on it rather than through it.)

Verse 10 is the verse for the reader who knows his Bible and feels nothing. Nicodemus knows the texts and can almost certainly recite them; what he has never done is apply the promise of a new heart to himself, because he has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Note the tone of the rebuke, though: Jesus asks a question, does not end the conversation, and goes on to give this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than anyone else receives in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.

Meaning first. John 3 is the chapter of the new birth and of the best-known verse in the Bible. Nicodemus, a respected Pharisee and teacher, comes to Jesus by night, and Jesus tells him that no one can see or enter God’s kingdom unless he is born again, from above, of water and the Spirit: a new life that only God can give. Then Jesus points to the cross: as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. The chapter ends with John the Baptist’s final testimony: Jesus is the bridegroom, the one from above, into whose hands the Father has given all things, and he must increase.

The link. Do not let the chapter number fool you into thinking a new subject has started. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in man (2:25). The sentence immediately before this one ended with the word man, and this one begins: now there was a man of the Pharisees. Same word, back to back, with nothing between them in the original. John has just told us that Jesus can read the contents of a human being, and now he opens one up in front of us to show what the reading looks like: Nicodemus, and Jesus reading his heart.

A man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. A Pharisee: devout, learned, moral, strict in keeping the law. The best of Jewish religion. And John has chosen the best specimen in Jerusalem. Not a tax collector, not a prostitute, not a man with an obvious hole in his life, but one of the serious ones, the movement that took the law of God with total seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. If anyone could enter the kingdom by his own goodness, he could. If a man could be got into the kingdom of God by conviction, learning, discipline, moral seriousness or religious office, this man is already inside. That is why John put him here. The point of Nicodemus is not that he is a hypocrite. The point is that he is the best we have.

A ruler of the Jews. Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of seventy-one men who governed the religious life of the nation. And in a few verses Jesus will call him the teacher of Israel, with the definite article, as though he held a recognised position rather than merely a good reputation.

This man came to Jesus by night. Perhaps for fear of being seen (12:42; 19:38): a member of the council calling on an unlicensed Galilean preacher whose first recorded act in Jerusalem was to overturn the temple furniture would not want to be seen doing it in daylight. Perhaps for a quiet, uninterrupted talk, as rabbis often studied at night. But John never uses the word carelessly. This is the Gospel that has already said the light shines in the darkness, that will say in a few more verses that people loved the darkness, and that records at the blackest moment of the story the words: and it was night (13:30). In John, night is symbolic: he came out of the darkness toward the light. Where he goes from there is the whole of his story.

Three appearances. He is not finished. This is the first of three appearances, and each one is further out into the open. Here he comes at night with a compliment. In chapter 7, when the authorities are moving against Jesus and the room is against him, Nicodemus speaks up, not bravely, but he speaks: does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? (7:50–51). He is shouted down. And then, after everything, when the twelve have scattered and the movement looks finished and there is nothing left to gain and everything to lose, Nicodemus comes to a Roman execution site to help bury the body, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39). That is a quantity fit for the burial of a king, carried by a member of the Sanhedrin in front of anyone who cared to look. He seems to have become a believer. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon. Whatever happened in the conversation that follows did not finish that evening, and it did not fail.

Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God. Respectful, and true as far as it goes. And notice the pronoun. We: perhaps other Pharisees thought the same; there are colleagues who think this and have not come. He arrives representing a committee, and he will leave having been told something that no committee can act on. But a teacher is not enough. A teacher come from God is a large thing to say and an infinitely small thing to say. It leaves Nicodemus in the position of a student, which is a position he understands and can occupy with dignity. What he is about to be told is that he does not need a better teacher. He needs to be born.

For no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him. The signs had convinced him that God was with Jesus. Every clause of that is true. It is also, precisely, the position of the crowd John has just described in 2:23: people who believed because they saw signs, and to whom Jesus did not entrust himself. A faith like that of 2:23, based on signs. Nicodemus is that crowd with a doctorate.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus secretly or hesitantly? It is not where anyone should stay, but it is where many begin, and Jesus did not turn Nicodemus away. He received a frightened, half-convinced man at night and gave him his fullest teaching on the new birth. If you are exploring the faith quietly, or a believer still afraid of what others will think, come anyway; he welcomes honest seekers. But do not stay in the dark. Nicodemus’ story moves toward the open, and so should yours. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him and his words, of him he will be ashamed (Luke 9:26). Ask him for courage for the next step into the light.

In a sentence. Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, came to Jesus at night and acknowledged him as a teacher from God because of his signs.

On a Tuesday. Respect for Jesus as a great teacher is not enough. You need what he told Nicodemus. Ask yourself honestly what you think Jesus is to you: an admired moral guide whose sayings you value, or the one without whom you cannot even see God’s kingdom? And if you have been keeping your interest in him hidden, for fear of colleagues, family or friends, take one small step into the open this week.

For worship. The best man in Jerusalem came by night to the Light of the world, and the Light did not send him away. The Lord who knew what was in man opened his heart to a cautious teacher and patiently led him, over three years, from a compliment in the dark to a king’s burial in the daylight. Praise the patient Saviour, who finishes what he begins in timid hearts.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.

Jesus answered him. Answered what? Nicodemus had not asked a question. Jesus does not answer the compliment; he answers the need, the question of his heart, cutting through polite compliments to his deepest need.

Truly, truly, I say to you. A solemn statement.

Unless one is born again. The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above”. There is a deliberate ambiguity in the word Jesus chooses, and it is the hinge of the whole conversation. It can mean a second time, and it can mean from above. Both meanings are intended: a second birth, and a birth from God above. The word will let Nicodemus hear the first, and hear it he does. That is not stupidity on his part; it is the natural reach of a mind that has no category for what is being said. A second natural birth would change nothing; flesh would still produce flesh (v. 6). What Nicodemus needs is not a repeat of the first birth but a birth of a different order altogether, one whose source is not below but above, not the womb but the Spirit. Not improvement, but a completely new beginning, a new life given by God. Nicodemus needed not more religion, but new life.

What does born again actually mean? It means that God the Holy Spirit gives a spiritually dead person new life, so that he is made alive to God, given a new heart that loves him, and enabled to repent and believe (Ezekiel 36:26; Ephesians 2:4–5). Theologians call it regeneration. It is not turning over a new leaf, having an emotional experience, or joining a particular kind of church. It is something God does in a person, as invisible as conception and as real as birth, and its effects show in a changed life: faith in Christ, love for God and his people, hatred of sin (1 John 5:1; 3:14). Every true Christian is born again; there is no other kind.

He cannot see the kingdom of God. Cannot experience it, enter it, perceive it. Without the new birth, a person is blind to the kingdom. Not a few people, but every person. Even the most religious. And notice the verb, because it changes when Jesus repeats himself. Here it is see the kingdom; in verse 5 it is enter it. Without this birth a man does not merely fail to get in; he cannot make out what he is failing to get into. The kingdom is not a locked room he is standing outside of, rattling the handle. It is a country he cannot perceive. That is why the argument never works from the outside: you cannot persuade someone toward a thing they are unable to see.

The kingdom, twice. A small statistic carries weight. The kingdom of God (in Matthew usually the kingdom of heaven) is the heart of Jesus’ preaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke: the headline of his message, the subject of most of the parables. In the Gospel of John it appears only here and in verse 5. The great theme of the other three Gospels surfaces once, in a night-time conversation with one man, and is used to tell him that he cannot get in as he is.

The wrong category. Nicodemus has spent his life on a project of improvement, and by any measure available it has succeeded. He is not being told that the project was fraudulent, or that he did it badly, or that he needs to try harder at it. He is being told it was the wrong category of thing altogether. You cannot educate your way into a family. You cannot be promoted into a bloodline. A man may study a language for forty years and speak it beautifully and still not be French. Grace is not the improvement of nature but its renewal, not the assistance of a willing heart but the giving of a new one.

In a sentence. Jesus told Nicodemus that unless a person is born again, from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Ask what would have to change for God to be more pleased with you than he is today. If the honest answer is a list, pray more, lose the temper less, be more generous, sort out the thing nobody knows about, then the answer is being given in the wrong currency, and this verse is aimed at exactly that instinct.
