And on its summit lay the rubble of the temple they had built, torn down by a Jewish ruler about a hundred and fifty years before. So the disagreement she raises is not a seminar topic. It is a ruin she can see from where she is standing, and the people who made it are the people this man belongs to.

But you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship. The great dispute between Jews and Samaritans. Is she changing the subject to avoid her sin? Both readings are available, and the honest thing is to hold them together, because the same words can be spoken by two very different people.

It may be deflection. It has all the marks. A man has just named the most painful arrangement in her life, and within one sentence she is discussing comparative religion. Anyone who has tried to talk to a friend about something real knows the manoeuvre: the sudden availability of a large, interesting, impersonal question at exactly the moment the small personal one became unbearable. Religion is uncommonly good for this. There is always a doctrine to argue about, and arguing is a great deal easier than being known.

It may be entirely genuine. Here is a woman whose life has gone wrong in the place where people look hardest for happiness, standing in front of somebody who has just proved he can see. If she has ever wanted to know where God can be found, where a sinner should go to offer sacrifice and find forgiveness, this is the only chance she will ever get, and she takes it with the first question that comes.

Jesus does not force a verdict. He answers the question. He does not say, we were talking about your husband. He takes what she asks and gives her the fullest teaching on worship in the Gospels, which is what he would do if it were sincere, and is also the only thing that would ever have helped if it were not. And he is about to tell her that the argument is over, and that neither side won it.

What should I do when someone turns a personal conversation into a religious debate? Answer the question briefly and honestly, as Jesus does, and then bring it back to the person and to Christ. Do not get drawn into a long argument about church history, other religions or the hypocrisy of Christians while the real matter waits. You might say: that is a fair question, and here is a short answer; but can I ask what you make of Jesus himself? Most debates of this kind are not won by winning them.

In a sentence. The woman said she could see he was a prophet, and raised the question of whether God should be worshipped on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. When you are the one changing the subject, when God puts his finger on something and you find yourself suddenly fascinated by an interesting theological question, notice it. Stop, and go back to what he was saying to you.

For worship. Jesus takes even our evasions and turns them into doors. The question she may have raised to escape him becomes the question through which he shows her the Father. That is the patience of Christ. He is not thrown off by our manoeuvres, and he is never in a hurry to win a point. He is after the person, and he will follow her down any road she takes until she finds herself in front of him.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.

Woman, believe me. A solemn and respectful address, the same he used to his mother at Cana and will use to her from the cross (2:4; 19:26). In English it lands cold; in that setting it is formal and courteous, and he speaks to a Samaritan at a well in exactly the register in which he speaks to his own mother. And believe me is a direct request for trust, as one person to another, before he says the thing that will cost her her side of the argument.

The hour is coming. The new age Jesus is bringing through his death and resurrection. In John the hour is always tied to his glorification (12:23; 17:1) and to the gift of the Spirit.

When neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father. The scale of this is easy to miss because it is so calmly put. Neither mountain. Not your mountain is wrong and ours is right, which was the whole content of the dispute, and half of which he is about to say. Neither. The argument is not going to be settled. It is going to be made obsolete. Jesus himself is the new temple (2:19–21), and after his resurrection God can be worshipped anywhere, through him. Within about forty years the Jerusalem temple would be rubble too, in AD 70, as the one on Gerizim already was.

The Father. The first time in this conversation he uses the name. She asked where people ought to worship; he answers by telling her who it is that is worshipped, and the name he chooses is the family one. Worship in the new age is the worship of children.

The end of holy places. What is dismantled here is older than the Samaritan question: the assumption, held by every religion and sitting deep in human instinct, that God is more available in some places than others. That there is a spot, the spot has to be reached, and getting there is most of the work. It survives in people who would deny holding it: the sense that prayer counts more in a church building than in a car, that the same words weigh more before six in the morning than at eleven at night, the low-grade grief of coming home from a place where God seemed close. This verse says the mountain has been closed, and that everyone who cannot get to the holy place, the housebound, the shift worker, the mother of small children, the prisoner, has not been kept away from anything at all.

Does this mean church buildings and gathering on Sunday do not matter? Gathering matters; the place does not. Christ abolished holy geography, not the holy assembly. Believers are commanded not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), and the gathered church is where the word is preached and the Supper shared. But the building is a roof, not a temple. God is not more present in the sanctuary than in your kitchen; he is present with his people, wherever they meet in Christ’s name. Love your church’s gathering because God’s people are there, not because the bricks are holy.

In a sentence. Jesus told her that the time was coming when the Father would be worshipped neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. You can worship God anywhere, through Christ. Your kitchen, your bus, your hospital bed can be the place where the Father is honoured. Pick one ordinary place you will be in today and pray there, deliberately, knowing he is as near to you there as he was to the high priest in the holy of holies.

For worship. The way into the holiest is open now through the blood of Jesus, a new and living way (Hebrews 10:19–20). No mountain has to be climbed and no city reached. The Son himself is the meeting place of God and man, and wherever he is, there the Father is worshipped. Blessed is the God who did not stay on Gerizim or in Jerusalem but came down to a well, and who now dwells by his Spirit in every believer as in his temple.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.

You worship what you do not know. One clause in these verses stops the whole passage from becoming what it is most often made into, and it should not be softened. Everything else here is so generous, the barriers down, the mountain abolished, a Samaritan woman receiving the finest teaching on worship in the Bible, that it is tempting to conclude Jesus is indifferent to the disagreement. He is not. The Samaritans had cut themselves off from the prophets and writings and kept only the five books of Moses, and the result was real impoverishment: a God known in outline, a knowledge incomplete and distorted.

We worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. He puts himself unmistakably on one side. He does not call Samaritan religion a different route up the same mountain. He calls it worshipping what they do not know. Jesus does not pretend all religions are equal. God revealed himself to Israel, and the Messiah came from Israel according to the flesh (Romans 9:4–5). Salvation is from the Jews, and Jesus himself is a Jew. He does not flatter her; he tells her the truth.

From, not for. The same sentence takes away any possibility of boasting. Salvation is from the Jews. The privilege was never a possession; it was a channel. Israel was the well the water came through, and a well does not congratulate itself on the water. The Jew hearing this is told his heritage is genuine and, in the same breath, where it was always headed.

But the hour is coming, and is now here. The hinge of the chapter. He has already said the hour is coming (v. 21); only now does he add that it is here. Something has already begun. The new worship is not entirely future. It is beginning at this well, in this conversation, with this woman, in the presence of Jesus.

When the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. In spirit: not tied to a place, but from the heart, by the Holy Spirit, who gives new birth (3:5). In truth: according to God’s true revelation of himself, now fully given in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Not Samaritan worship, which lacked truth, nor merely Jewish worship tied to a temple, but worship through Christ, by the Spirit.

For the Father is seeking such people to worship him. A wonderful statement, and every word of it is the wrong way up by ordinary religious instinct. Worship is what we do to find God; here God is the one out looking. She came to this well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road his countrymen avoided. That is not an illustration of the verse; it is the verse, happening while it is spoken. Not that God needs our worship (Acts 17:25); he seeks us for our good and his glory.

Is it narrow to say other religions do not know God? It is honest, and it is what Jesus says. Many religions contain true things about right and wrong, and every person has some knowledge of God from creation and conscience (Romans 1:19–20). But saving knowledge of God comes only through his own revelation, given to Israel and fulfilled in Christ, and no one comes to the Father except through him (14:6). To say otherwise would not be kind; it would be leaving people at a dry well. And notice the spirit in which Jesus says it: sitting with a Samaritan, asking for her help, offering her the gift. Truth about other faiths should always come with that kind of love.

What if I do not feel like much of a worshipper? Take heart from the last clause. You may have spent years with a low sense that the singing does not move you, that your prayers are dutiful, that others plainly have something you do not. This verse does not tell you to try harder to find God. It says the Father is out looking for worshippers. The search that matters is the one conducted from his end, and it has a far better record than ours. True worship is not measured by the strength of your feelings, but by whether you come to the Father through the Son, trusting what he has revealed.

In a sentence. Jesus said the Samaritans worshipped what they did not know, while salvation is from the Jews, but the time has come, and is here now, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for he seeks such worshippers.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray today, remind yourself that you are not trying to attract the attention of a reluctant God. The Father sought you first. Come to him as one who has been found.

For worship. The Father is seeking worshippers. The infinite God, who needs nothing from anyone, sends his Son down a despised road to find a woman at noon, so that she might know him and worship him. He sought Adam in the garden, he sought Israel in Egypt, he sought this woman at the well, and he sought you. We love because he first loved us, and we worship because he first came looking. Blessed be the seeking Father, the Son who came to seek and to save the lost, and the Spirit by whom the found cry, Abba, Father.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

God is spirit. One of the great definitions of God in John’s writings, with God is light (1 John 1:5) and God is love (1 John 4:8). Three words, and they need unpacking rather than admiring, because everyone nods at them and few could explain them to a child.

What it does not say. It does not say God is a spirit, one item in a category of ghostly beings; the point is not to classify him. It does not mean God is vague, an atmosphere, a force, or an impersonal energy behind things. The God described here talks, seeks, loves, sends, and is called Father in the same breath.

What it does say. God has no body and is not located. He is invisible, everywhere present, not confined to a mountain or a temple (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25). He cannot be run out of or run to. He does not occupy a spot that another spot lacks. A statue can be stolen, a temple burned, a mountain captured, and Gerizim had been. None of that touches him, because he was never on it.

And those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. Must: it is necessary, because worship must match the nature of the one worshipped. If God were a local deity, worship would be a matter of arriving. Since he is not, worship is a matter of being a certain kind of person in his presence, and every person is already in his presence all the time, which is what makes this comforting and uncomfortable at once.

Not sincerity against ritual. The phrase is often misread as heartfelt against formal. That is not quite it. Spirit here is the Holy Spirit, the one Jesus described to Nicodemus as the agent of the new birth and has just pictured as a spring inside a person. Truth is not mere sincerity either; in this Gospel truth is a person before it is a quality: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (14:6). So worship in spirit and truth means worship enabled by God’s own Spirit and shaped by God’s own revelation in his Son. Both halves are gifts. Neither is a technique. And it cuts both ways. It rules out worship that is correct and dead, the right words in the right order with nobody home. And it rules out worship that is warm and invented, deeply felt and directed at a God assembled from preference. Truth without Spirit is a corpse. Spirit without truth is a mood.

Where Christians differ: how should we worship? Some traditions emphasise elaborate liturgy, ritual and visual symbols; others, free and spontaneous worship. Verdict: Reformed churches have drawn from this verse, among others, what is called the regulative principle: worship should be shaped by what God has revealed in his word, not by human invention, and offered from the heart by the Spirit. External forms matter less than the heart, but worship must be true to Scripture: the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments. Held charitably toward brothers who differ in practice.

What does this mean for how a church worships? It removes sacred places, not the gathered church (Hebrews 10:25). It does not rule out order or form, a planned service or a written prayer. It rules out empty ritual on one side and worship invented to please ourselves on the other, which is why the Reformed tradition asks that worship include only what God commands (Westminster 21.1).

If God is spirit, how could Jesus be God in a body? God in his own being is spirit and has no body. In the incarnation the eternal Son did not turn into matter or stop being spirit; he took a true human body and soul into union with himself (1:14). So the invisible God is seen in Jesus (1:18; 14:9). This is not a contradiction of God is spirit but the wonder of it: the God who cannot be confined to a mountain chose to dwell among us in the flesh, so that we might know him and worship him in truth.

In a sentence. God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship him in spirit and truth.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a plain one. Ask what happens to your worship when the music stops, when the service is dull, the preacher is poor, the room is cold, and nothing at all is being generated for you. Something is left, or nothing is. That residue is the part that was in spirit and truth. The rest was the building. And this Sunday, check your worship: is it from the heart, by the Spirit, according to God’s word?

For worship. God is spirit: infinite, eternal, unchangeable, filling heaven and earth, dwelling in light unapproachable, and nearer to each of us than our own breath. No mountain could hold him and no temple contain him. And this God, who needs no house, has made his home in the hearts of those who believe. He gives the Spirit by whom we worship and the truth in which we worship, and then receives the worship he himself has given. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things. Jesus said to her: I who speak to you am he.

I know that Messiah is coming. The Samaritans did not use the word Messiah as Jerusalem did. Having only the five books of Moses, they had no royal prophecies of David’s line. What they looked for came out of Deuteronomy 18:15–18: a prophet like Moses into whose mouth God would put his words. They called him the Taheb, the one who returns or the restorer.

When he comes, he will tell us all things. That is what they chiefly expected: not a king who would reign, but a teacher who would settle everything, including the argument about the mountain. Which makes her sentence quietly poignant. She has been told something enormous about worship, and her response is essentially: one day somebody will come who can sort this out. Perhaps she is postponing the matter. Perhaps she is wondering. Either way she defers it all to a figure in the future, standing three feet from him.

I who speak to you am he. Literally, I am, the one speaking to you (egō eimi). It is a perfectly normal way of saying that is me, and it is also the beginning of the most loaded formula in this Gospel. Jesus will use I am of himself again and again (6:20; 8:58), and it echoes the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), until in chapter 8 the crowd picks up stones.

To her, first. Hold the whole scene together, because it is the most improbable arrangement of facts in the chapter. He has been in Jerusalem for a feast. He has spoken with a member of the ruling council by night and told him a great deal without ever saying this. His disciples have been with him for months and are at this moment in town buying lunch. And the first open, unhedged declaration in John that he is the Messiah goes to a Samaritan woman with a broken past, alone, in the heat, with nobody there to write it down. Not to the Sanhedrin. Not to Nicodemus. She said that one day someone would come and tell them all things. He said: I am he, the one talking to you now. It is the shortest distance between a longing and its object anywhere in Scripture.

Why does Jesus say so openly here what he hides elsewhere? The Samaritans expected a Messiah who would be a teacher and restorer, not a king leading a revolt. In Galilee and Judea the title would have brought crowds wanting to make him king by force (6:15). In Samaria his open claim carried less political danger, and it could be said plainly.

In a sentence. The woman said that the Messiah would come and explain everything, and Jesus told her: I who am speaking to you am he.

On a Tuesday. Many people postpone Christ the way she did: one day I will look into it properly, one day when life is calmer. But the one they are waiting for is already speaking. If you have been deferring something he has told you, stop waiting for a better moment. He is here now.

For worship. A whole people had waited for a prophet like Moses who would one day tell them all things, and the waiting was answered in six words to one woman at noon. The voice that once spoke from a burning bush, where Moses hid his face, spoke now from the wall of a well, and she did not need to hide hers. The one she had been waiting for had been waiting for her. He is still the end of every honest longing, and he still comes to the waiting heart with the same words: I who speak to you am he.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just then his disciples came back. They marvelled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said: what do you seek? or: why are you talking with her? So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.

They marveled that he was talking with a woman. Not even that she was a Samaritan; simply a woman. A rabbi did not talk with women in public, and rabbinic sayings warned against it.

The questions nobody asked. Yet no one said, What do you seek? or, Why are you talking with her? John records something that did not happen, and the wording is exact. Two questions nobody asked. The first is the question Jesus himself asked at the beginning of this Gospel when two men followed him: what are you seeking? (1:38). The disciples have the question available to them and do not use it, not on him and not on themselves. They had learned not to question him. Whether that is reverence or awkwardness John does not say, and it is probably both. They have learned that he does things they would not have advised, and they have not yet learned to ask why.

A familiar silence. There is a way of following Christ for years while never bringing him the question that is actually there: the prayer that was not answered, the person he did not heal, the passage that troubles rather than comforts. It is possible to mistake that for reverence. This Gospel is full of people who asked him poor questions and got somewhere; it has far fewer examples of people who asked nothing. Bring your honest questions to him in prayer and to his word. He is not offended by them.

So the woman left her water jar. A small, vivid detail that survives only because somebody saw it. She had walked out to that well for one reason, in the heat, carrying an empty vessel, and she went back to town without it. She came for water and forgot it, because she had found living water. It is not a symbol she intended. She simply left it, the way people leave things when something has happened that makes the errand irrelevant. And there is a practical edge to it: she would have to come back for it. Whatever happened to her did not remove the daily walk, the hundred feet of rope, or the heat. It removed the reason she had been coming alone.

Does this show that women may teach men in the church? Her witness was an invitation, come, see a man, and her neighbours then came to Christ himself and believed because of his word (vv. 39–42). Every believer, man or woman, is to bear witness to Christ like this. The authoritative teaching of the gathered church is a different thing, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12).

In a sentence. The disciples returned, astonished that Jesus was talking to a woman, though no one questioned him, and the woman left her water jar and went into town.

On a Tuesday. What will you leave behind when you meet Christ? Not necessarily your duties; she still had to fetch water. But perhaps the fear that made you do them alone, or the errand that had become your whole life. And what question have you never dared to ask him? Write it down and bring it to him today.

For worship. The jar stayed on the wall, and the one who had asked her for a drink had given her more than any jar could carry. He is the treasure for which people leave things behind, not because they are told to but because every errand shrinks beside him. The disciples stood silent before a scene they did not understand, and the woman ran. Both belong before him: the hush of those who cannot yet ask, and the haste of those who have found him and cannot keep it in.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to the people: come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ? They went out of the town and were coming to him.

Come, see. The woman who came to the well alone now runs to the people, with the words of Jesus and Philip on her lips (1:39, 46). She becomes an evangelist, and she evangelises her own community.

A man who told me all that I ever did. Look at what her testimony consists of, because it is a remarkably poor piece of evangelism by any standard we would apply. She has one fact, and it is about herself. She overstates it, all that I ever did, when he had named one arrangement. She cannot explain the living water, she has no doctrine of the incarnation, she got the mountain question wrong twenty minutes earlier. And the town emptied. She does not hide her past. The very thing that made her ashamed becomes her testimony. Notice what is missing: there is no and he did not despise me. She does not need to say the second half, because it is the tone of the whole sentence. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted. That is the entire content of her testimony, and it is the thing most people are most afraid of.

Can this be the Christ? The Greek frames it as a tentative question, something nearer to this could not be the Christ, could it? She does not preach; she invites them to decide for themselves. The tentativeness may be the strength of it. A woman marching back into town with a finished doctrine would be easy to dismiss. A woman asking a question she plainly cannot answer herself, in evident agitation, having left her water jar, is harder to walk past. People argue with a conclusion. They find it harder to argue with somebody who has obviously been changed.

They went out of the town and were coming to him. Her testimony worked. She did not attempt to close the argument. She got people into the same field as the man, and stood out of the way.

What if I do not know enough to witness? Then you are in exactly her position, and look what God did with it. You do not need a theology degree. You need to know what Christ has done for you and where people can find him. Tell the truth about your own life, invite people to come and see, to read a Gospel, to come to church, to meet him in his word, and let him do the rest. Keep learning, of course, so that you can give a reason for your hope (1 Peter 3:15). But do not wait until you know everything. She knew one sentence, and a town came out.

In a sentence. She told the townspeople to come and see a man who had told her everything she had done, asking if he could be the Christ, and they came out to him.

On a Tuesday. Write down in one sentence what Jesus has done for you, the plainest, truest sentence you can. Then ask God for one person to say it to this week, and an invitation to add: come and see.

For worship. The Lord chose a woman with a broken history to be the first evangelist of Samaria. He delights to use weak things and despised things, so that no human being might boast in his presence. And the wonder at the heart of her testimony is the gospel itself: he knows all that we ever did, and he does not cast us out. Blessed be the Saviour who turns our shame into our testimony, and sends the forgiven to tell the town.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying: Rabbi, eat. But he said to them: I have food to eat that you do not know about.

Rabbi, eat. They had brought food. The comedy of the scene is not accidental. A town is walking out across the fields toward Jesus because of something that happened while the disciples were shopping, and the disciples’ whole contribution to the moment is to press him about lunch.

They are being kind. He had been too tired to walk; they had gone to fetch food; they are now trying to get him to eat it. This is thoughtfulness, and it is completely blind. The largest thing that had happened all day was standing in front of them, and they were looking at a man who had not eaten. That is a fair description of a great deal of church life, and of most of us on most days. The failure is rarely a failure to care. It is that the caring runs entirely along the practical grain, the rota, the building, the meal, and the thing God is doing in the room goes unremarked because nobody was looking for it there.

I have food to eat that you do not know about. As with the water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a spiritual reality and is misunderstood. It is the third time in this chapter he has done this. She said water, and he answered with water that was not water. Now they say eat, and he answers with food they know nothing about. He does not reject the material thing; he takes the ordinary object already in the conversation and uses it as a handle on something the hearer has no other way of reaching. It is not evasion and it is not mysticism. It is the only way to speak about a realm people have never seen in words made for the one they have, and it is why almost everyone in this Gospel misunderstands him at first. He pays that cost in nearly every conversation, and never once sounds impatient.

Is it wrong to care about practical things in church? Not at all. Someone has to buy the bread, and the disciples were right to look after their tired Master. Practical service is honoured throughout Scripture (Acts 6:1–6). The danger is only that the practical becomes the whole of what we see. Do the rota and the catering gladly, as service to Christ, but lift your eyes while you do it. Ask, in every meeting and every task: what is God doing here, and with whom?

In a sentence. The disciples urged Jesus to eat, but he said he had food they did not know about.

On a Tuesday. There is a nourishment deeper than food. What feeds your soul? In the middle of your practical tasks today, stop once and ask what God is doing in the people around you.

For worship. The Lord who fed five thousand was fed himself by doing his Father’s will, and he is patient with servants who only see the lunch. He speaks heaven’s truths in earth’s words and bears with our slowness to understand. He has never given up on dull disciples, and he goes on lifting our eyes from the shopping to the harvest.

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the disciples said to one another: has anyone brought him something to eat? Jesus said to them: my food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.

Has anyone brought him something to eat? Literal again. It is the most human sentence in the chapter. They are not mocking; they have concluded, reasonably, that somebody must have got there first with a basket, and they are working out the logistics.

My food is to do the will of him who sent me. His answer redefines what has been sustaining him for the last hour. Not that he did not need food; he did, he was too tired to walk. But there is something that works in him the way food works, and he names it. His deepest satisfaction and sustenance is doing the Father’s will (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). Talking to this woman had refreshed him more than food. And it is worth pressing this: the Father’s will is described as food, which is to say it feeds rather than costs. That is not how obedience usually feels. Most people, if honest, would describe doing God’s will as expenditure, drawn from a limited account that has to be topped up later by rest or pleasure. Jesus describes it as intake.

And to accomplish his work. Accomplish (teleiōsō) means to complete, to finish. It is the work the Father gave him to do (5:36; 17:4), and it is the same root as the word he will cry from the cross: it is finished (tetelestai, 19:30). What he is doing at this well and what he does at Calvary are, on his own account, one work with a beginning and an end, and he is nourished by both.

Does this mean I am doing ministry wrongly if it exhausts me? No. The verse has sometimes been used to flog tired people, and it should not be. The man who said this had sat down twenty minutes earlier because he could not go on; both facts are in the same chapter on the same afternoon. Weariness in God’s work is normal and honourable, and rest is God’s gift, not a failure (Mark 6:31). What the verse says is that there is a kind of work which, whatever it takes out of the body, puts something back into the soul, and that this is the mark of work done for the Father rather than merely about him.

In a sentence. When the disciples wondered if someone had brought him food, Jesus said his food was to do the will of the one who sent him and to finish his work.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test worth running honestly. Think of two things you do for God: one that leaves you flat, and one that tires you and yet you would not give up. Both may be duties, and both may be right. But the difference is worth examining, because it is often the difference between a task you took on to be useful and a task the Father actually gave you. The first is a job. The second, in the vocabulary of this verse, is dinner.

For worship. The Son delighted to do his Father’s will. It was his meat and drink all the way to the cross, where he finished the work the Father gave him and cried, It is finished. There was never a moment when his obedience was grudging, and it is that perfect, glad obedience that is counted to all who trust him. And because he finished the work, our obedience can be food too: not a wage we pay, but the joy of children doing the will of a Father who has already given us everything in his Son.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not say: there are yet four months, then comes the harvest? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.

There are yet four months, then comes the harvest. Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring, and four months was the usual wait; perhaps it was a proverb. Whether a saying or the actual state of the crops, the point is that harvest is the one thing in farming that cannot be hurried. Everything else can be worked at; harvest arrives when it arrives, and until then a farmer’s whole discipline is waiting. Jesus takes the one agricultural certainty about delay and cancels it.

Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Picture what he is looking at. A woman has run back to a town, and the town is coming out across open country toward the well, a straggle of people in the middle of the day, perhaps in the white robes many wore, moving through the fields (v. 30). Ripe grain turns pale, white-gold. He is not offering an image. He is pointing. The harvest of people is ready now, not in four months, walking toward you while you are asking about lunch.

Already the one who reaps is receiving wages. The reward of gospel work is not entirely deferred; it is being handed over during the work. And the fruit is gathered for eternal life: people saved for ever. This harvest does not rot, when everything else a person spends a life gathering has a shelf life measured in decades at best.

So that sower and reaper may rejoice together. The generous clause. In ordinary farming the reaper gets the visible result. Here it is arranged so that neither can celebrate without the other. Somebody prayed for years and saw nothing; somebody else said one sentence at the right moment and saw a town come out. In this economy those two are paid at the same table, and the joy is shared.

Does this mean everyone around me is about to believe? No. Jesus is speaking of what God was doing that day in Sychar, and elsewhere he says the labourers are few and that many will reject the word. But the verse warns us that our estimate of readiness is nearly always four months behind the actual state of the field. God has his elect in every place (Acts 18:10), and the Spirit is often at work where we see nothing. So sow widely, pray boldly, and do not write anyone off. The last people anyone expected were already on their way.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to wait four months for harvest, but to look and see that the fields were already ripe, and the reaper was already gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper could rejoice together.

On a Tuesday. Almost every Christian has a mental list of the people who will never be interested: the family member who has made his views plain, the colleague who finds it all absurd, the neighbour who was rude about it once. The list feels realistic. Lift up your eyes. Take one name from that list and begin praying for that person by name every day this month.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest sees fields where we see empty roads. He ripens hearts in secret, by his Spirit, long before we notice, and he gathers his elect from every town into his barn. The fruit is for eternal life, and none of it will be lost. Blessed is the God who makes sower and reaper glad together, and who will one day gather the whole harvest home with songs of joy.
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For here the saying holds true: one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour. Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labour.

For here the saying holds true, One sows and another reaps. A proverb, and it holds true in the direction nobody wants: I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour. The disciples will reap a harvest prepared by others.

Others have labored. Who were the others? Samaria has a history, and Jesus is standing in the middle of it. Some of it is very old: Jacob dug the well the disciples are standing beside, Joseph’s bones are buried in the field, Moses sent Israel to that mountain to hear the blessings, and the prophets laboured for centuries. Some of it is recent: John the Baptist had been preaching not far away. And some is a matter of hours: Jesus himself, and a woman who went back to her town twenty minutes ago and did all the sowing there was time for. The disciples arrive with the shopping and walk into a harvest that centuries of history and one conversation had prepared. And in Acts the disciples would reap in Samaria what Jesus sowed here (Acts 8:4–25).

Somebody always got tired first. The word for laboured is the same root as wearied in verse 6. Every harvest anyone reaps was preceded by exhaustion the reaper did not feel and often never hears about.

And you have entered into their labor. Every gospel worker builds on others’ work. There is no room for pride (1 Corinthians 3:6–9). Nothing you are reaping is yours. The building was paid for by people who are dead. The doctrine you preach was fought for by people who were burned for it. The person ready to believe in front of you was worked on for years by somebody whose name you will never learn, quite possibly a grandmother who prayed, saw nothing, and died thinking she had failed.

What about the sower who never sees fruit? This is the verse for the discouraged sower: the parent who has prayed for a child for thirty years, the Sunday school teacher who watched most of a generation drift, the missionary who left with almost nothing to report. There is no promise that the sower sees it. There is a promise, one verse earlier, that when it is finally seen, he rejoices with the reaper. God does not forget any seed sown in faith; your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Keep sowing.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the saying is true, one sows and another reaps, and he had sent them to reap where others had done the hard work.

On a Tuesday. Name, out loud if possible, three people who sowed the gospel in you. Most Christians can do it in seconds, and most have never told any of the three. If any are still alive, write to one of them this week. And sow faithfully today, even if others reap.

For worship. The harvest belongs to the Lord. He appoints one to plant and another to water, and he alone gives the growth, so that the glory belongs to no servant but to him. Through all the generations he has been working one field, and every faithful labourer, seen or unseen, is part of one great work that ends in one great joy. Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, who wastes no seed and forgets no labourer.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony: he told me all that I ever did. So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.

Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony. The power of a simple personal testimony. John repeats her sentence rather than summarising it, so we know exactly what carried: he told me all that I ever did. That is the whole content. Not a doctrine of the atonement, not the two natures of Christ, not one of the things people are often expected to explain before they are fit to speak. A woman said, in effect: he knew everything about me and he did not turn away. A town heard it and walked out into the midday sun to see whether it might be true of them too. What makes the gospel travel is not first the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Everyone in that town had known the earlier version of her.

They asked him to stay with them. Stay (meinai) is John’s great word abide. Samaritans asking a Jew to stay: barriers broken. And it is a larger step than believing. It is one thing to be persuaded about a man; it is another to want him in the house for two days.

And he stayed there two days. A Jewish rabbi accepted the hospitality of a Samaritan town, which means he ate their food, off their plates, under their roofs, for two days. Every one of those actions carried a ritual cost in the eyes of the men he had left in Jerusalem. He had spent the morning refusing to be governed by the boundary, and now he spends two days living on the wrong side of it. Nothing in the text treats this as remarkable, which is the most remarkable thing about it.

Is the later giving of the Spirit in Samaria a pattern for us? In Acts the Samaritans receive the Spirit only after the apostles come. That was a later group, and a special moment in the spread of the church, when God showed that Samaritans were fully included in the one church of the apostles (Acts 8:14–17). These Samaritans in John truly believed, knowing Jesus as the Saviour of the world. Neither passage sets up a two-stage pattern for all believers. Everyone who truly believes in Christ has the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

In a sentence. Many Samaritans believed because of the woman’s testimony, and asked Jesus to stay, and he stayed two days.

On a Tuesday. Your testimony, however humble, can lead others to Christ. And when you do believe in him, ask him to stay: in your home, your evenings, your plans. Faith that keeps Christ at the town gate is not yet the faith of Sychar.

For worship. The Son of God was not ashamed to lodge with Samaritans. He ate at their tables, slept under their roofs and taught in their streets, because they asked him and he loves to be asked. He still abides with those who welcome him: if anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him (14:23). The Lord who stayed two days in Sychar does not lodge with his people for a visit; he and his Father come to make their home.

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman: it is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world.

And many more believed because of his word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his word brings them to faith.

It is no longer because of what you said that we believe. Not an insult. They are describing the only journey that ever ends anywhere, from someone else’s account to first-hand knowledge, and telling her, in effect, that her errand worked. A witness who is still needed after two days has not finished the job. They have heard for themselves: a personal encounter with Christ through his word, second-hand faith become first-hand.

And we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world. The summit of the episode and one of the boldest lines in the New Testament. Not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of all peoples, including Samaritans. The title appears in the New Testament only here and in John’s first letter (1 John 4:14). And it was not unused in the first century. It was imperial: inscriptions across the empire called the emperor saviour and benefactor of the human race. This is not a devotional flourish. It is a title lifted off the man in Rome and placed on a Jewish teacher in a Samaritan village, by Samaritans, people with no stake in Jewish hopes at all. Outsiders understood what insiders missed.

The ironies stacked in the sentence. The people who confess him as Saviour of the world are the people a Jew would not share a cup with. They reach it in two days. The teacher of Israel in the previous chapter, with the Scriptures and the training and every advantage, could not follow a sentence about birth. And the confession comes in the one chapter where Jesus has said that salvation is from the Jews, so the outsiders are not correcting him. They are the first evidence that he was right.

Does Savior of the world mean that everyone will be saved? No. It means that Jesus is not the Saviour of Jews only but of Samaritans and Gentiles too, of all who believe, as these Samaritans did. Paul calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe (1 Timothy 4:10). The title speaks of the scope of the offer and the reach of his rule, not of universal salvation.

What if my faith is still borrowed? That is where this whole town started, and where most people start: a parent, a minister, a book. It is a good place to begin and a poor place to remain, because a second-hand faith is only as durable as the person it leans on, and people move away, disappoint and die. The remedy is the one the Samaritans found: hear him for yourself. Read the Gospels as his own words to you, pray to him directly, and sit under the preaching of his word asking him, not the preacher, to speak.

In a sentence. Many more believed through Jesus’ own word and told the woman that they now believed not because of her testimony but because they had heard him and knew he was the Saviour of the world.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly: if the person whose faith first brought you to Christ walked away tomorrow, would yours still stand? Open one of the Gospels today and read it slowly, as if Jesus were speaking to you, because he is.

For worship. Jesus is the Saviour of the world, of every tribe and tongue and people and nation. Caesar claimed the title and is dust; Christ bears it and reigns for ever. He saves Samaritans and Gentiles, outcasts and officials, and his word still makes believers out of those who hear it. One day a great multitude no one can number will stand before his throne and cry that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, and among them will be a town from Samaria and a woman whose name we never learned.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee, though he has said a prophet is not honoured in his own country. The Galileans receive him, having seen what he did at the festival in Jerusalem. He returns to Cana, where he turned water into wine. A royal official from Capernaum, whose son is dying, hears that Jesus is back and comes to beg him to come and heal the boy. Jesus says that unless people see miraculous signs they will not believe. The official pleads with him to come before his child dies. Jesus tells him to go home: his son will live. The man takes Jesus at his word and sets off. On the way his servants meet him with news that the boy is alive and well. Asking when he improved, he learns the fever left at one in the afternoon the day before, the very hour Jesus spoke. He and his whole household believe. This is the second sign Jesus performs after coming from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign illustrates the highest form of faith: believing the word of Jesus without the supporting evidence of a visible miracle. Jesus speaks ('your son will live'), the official believes, and he goes. The confirmation comes later — the servants meet him with the news, and when he checks the timing, it matches exactly. This is the progression of faith in John's Gospel: sign-faith (the disciples at Cana), word-faith (the official), and ultimately cross-and-resurrection-faith (Thomas). Each stage is genuine faith; each stage is a step deeper into trust in the person of Jesus.

The two Cana signs are numbered (2:11; 4:54) and the counting then stops for the rest of the book, which means the numbering exists only to tie these two together. They frame everything between: a member of the ruling council who could not follow the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman who understood enough to fetch a town.

Watch what changes between them. At the wedding Jesus was present, the water was in front of him, and he instructed servants who were standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and does nothing but speak. The first sign needed his hands on the situation; the second needed only his voice, and the voice worked across a day's journey as though the journey were not there. The escalation is the direction of the whole book — and it prepares the position every reader after the ascension occupies: no touch, no presence, no visible confirmation, only a word and a distance and the walking. John says at the close that he wrote it down so that people who were never in the room might believe (20:30-31).

Note also that the man believes twice. In verse 50 he believed the word — trust in a promise about his son. In verse 53 he himself believed, with no object named, which in this Gospel is the word for what a person does about Christ rather than about a request. The household followed him; that is not a formula and must never be used to reproach faithful people whose households have not, but it is worth noting what they had to go on — a man who came home, a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.
verseByVerse.examples:
The official's faith is remarkable because he believes before he sees — he accepts the word of Jesus as sufficient ground for confidence when everything he can see argues for despair. This is the pattern of all mature faith: not the absence of evidence but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, prior to the confirming experience.

The finest detail in the episode is one word in the servants' report: the fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour. Jesus spoke at about one in the afternoon, and Capernaum is some twenty miles away and downhill — a distance a determined man could nearly cover by nightfall. The father did not cover it. He stopped for the night and came down the next day. Nobody whose only son is dying stops for the night if any part of him is still calculating. The most convincing evidence that this man took Christ at his word is that he did not hurry home.

Verse 50 is where the miracle actually sits, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had walked all day for one thing — to bring Jesus back down to the house — and he is sent home without him. Everything he came for is refused. What he has instead is five words about a child who was at the point of death when he left. And he went. Every hour of that walk the alternative explanation was available: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come.

The pastoral note belongs to the father's prayer, which was a bad one by any measure — no theology, no composure, one sentence repeated under pressure — and was answered immediately and generously. Nothing in the account suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. And his original assumption, that God must be brought to the place, should be treated gently rather than corrected: it is what people ask when they love somebody and are frightened. The answer he received was not smaller than the one he asked for. It was the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles.

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honour in his own home town.)

For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown. There is a genuine puzzle in this bracket and it is better named than smoothed over. The proverb says a prophet has no honour in his own country, and John then reports that Jesus went to Galilee, where the Galileans welcomed him. The reason given seems to contradict what follows.

Two solutions. The first is that his own country here means Judea, the land of his birth, and Jerusalem, where he has just been rejected: the temple authorities demanding his credentials, the Pharisees counting his disciples. On this reading the sentence explains why he left Judea. The prophet has no honour where he properly belongs, so he goes north. It also fits John’s habit of using his own for the people who should have received him and did not (1:11). The second is that the welcome in Galilee was no honour at all, and John says as much in the next verse: they welcomed him having seen what he did in Jerusalem. That is enthusiasm for a performer. A prophet is not honoured by a crowd that has come for the signs; he is merely popular, which is a different and less durable thing. The first is the more likely, since John has just shown Jesus rejected in Jerusalem and Galilee does in fact welcome him. Either way the verse does the same work. It casts a shadow over the applause before the applause arrives, so that the reader does not mistake the noise in Galilee for something better than the silence in Judea.

Being liked and being believed. They are not the same, and the first can be a considerable obstacle to the second. A church well thought of in its town, a Christian whom colleagues find pleasant company: neither is a bad thing, and neither is evidence of anything at all. The Galileans were delighted with him. Within two chapters many of them will have walked away (6:66).

Should I expect rejection from those closest to me? Often, yes, and it should not surprise you. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him for a long time (7:5), and he warned that a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36). Familiarity can breed a kind of deafness: they knew you before, and find it hard to take seriously what has changed. Keep living faithfully and lovingly among them, speak when there is opportunity, and pray. Jesus’ brothers were in the upper room after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).

In a sentence. After two days Jesus left for Galilee, though he himself had said a prophet has no honour in his own home town.

On a Tuesday. Those closest to Jesus are not always those who honour him most. If you are well liked at work and at church, give thanks, but do not mistake it for fruit. Ask whether anyone around you is believing because of your witness, or only enjoying your company.

For worship. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. The Lord of glory accepted being dishonoured in his own country, and walked on to the places where the Father sent him, not where he was applauded. He bore the contempt of the familiar so that strangers might be welcomed. The prophet without honour in his own country is the risen King, and one day every knee will bow to him, in Jerusalem as in Sychar.

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.

The Galileans welcomed him. Because of his signs in Jerusalem at the feast (2:23), not because of who he was. This is the sign-faith John introduced at 2:23–25: real as a beginning, insufficient as a foundation.

Set the two receptions side by side. John has arranged them to be compared, and the comparison is uncomfortable. The Samaritans had no signs; not one miracle is recorded in that village. They had a woman with a doubtful reputation, one sentence about being known, and two days of listening to him, and they arrived at the Saviour of the world, believing because of his word (v. 41). The Galileans had everything else. They were his own people. They had been up to Jerusalem and seen the signs with their own eyes. They welcomed him warmly. And what they had was an appetite, which he names in a moment and which chapter 6 will test to destruction: after the bread and the fish, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66).

What separates them. The difference is not information and it is not privilege. Both groups met the same person; one had far more evidence. What separates them is what they were looking for when they came. Spiritual sight is not proportional to religious advantage.

Warm approval with nothing underneath. This is worth sitting with rather than aiming at somebody else, because the Galileans are much the easier group to belong to. They were not sceptics or opponents. They were fans. They were pleased he had come, spoke well of him, and turned out when he was in the area. The most dangerous position in this chapter is not hostility. It is warm approval with nothing underneath it.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus because of what he can do for me? It is not wrong to begin there; most of us did, and Jesus welcomed the sick, the hungry and the desperate. The problem is staying there. Faith that wants only his gifts will leave when the gifts seem to stop. Saving faith comes to rest on Christ himself, as Lord and Saviour, and trusts him even when he gives nothing visible. If you came for help, keep coming, and ask him to show you himself, until you would want him even with nothing else.

In a sentence. The Galileans welcomed him, because they had seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast.

On a Tuesday. Here is a quick test. Ask what would have to happen for you to lose interest in Christ: not to renounce him, simply to drift. If nothing comes to mind, press harder, because everyone has a version. For the Galileans it was a hard saying. For many of us it would be a long enough stretch of God doing nothing visible. Naming the thing is not faithlessness; it is the beginning of knowing what your faith is resting on. Is your welcome for Jesus based on what he can do for you, or on who he is?

For worship. Christ is worthy to be loved for himself. His gifts are many and good, but he is better than all of them, the pearl of great price for which a man sells everything. He did not entrust himself to crowds who wanted only signs (2:24), yet he never stopped offering himself to them. He is not content to be admired, and he will not rest until his people treasure him above every gift.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.

Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. The site of the first sign. This will be the second (v. 54), and John is building a frame.

An official whose son was ill at Capernaum. A royal official (basilikos), probably in the service of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee. That places him among the leading men of the region: a court appointment, a household, servants, standing. Capernaum lies on the lakeshore; Cana is up in the hills, about twenty miles away, some thirty kilometres. In that country twenty miles is a hard day’s walk, and it is a climb.

He went to him. Take the measure of what this man does, because the distance is the point. A courtier left a dying child, walked all day into the hills on the strength of a report that a travelling teacher had returned to the district, and begged him to come. Nothing about it is dignified, and men in his position spent a good deal of energy on dignity. What he had was a boy at the point of death, and every door his rank could open had already been opened. When a man of standing goes personally rather than sending a servant, the ordinary machinery of his life has stopped working. Wealth and position could not save his son.

And asked him to come down and heal his son. Notice the assumption: come down. He needs Jesus present. Everything he has seen work in the world, physicians, officials, favours, requires the person to be in the room. He believes Jesus can heal, but thinks Jesus must be there. He is not lacking faith; he is exercising the only kind he has.

Is this the same as the centurion’s servant in Matthew and Luke? Probably not (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10). Here it is a royal official’s son, at Cana, and the man asks Jesus to come down; there it is a Gentile centurion’s servant, at Capernaum, and the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. The likeness is in the healing from a distance, which Jesus did more than once.

Is it wrong to ask God to come and be present in my crisis? Not at all. Many people pray exactly like this: Lord, be in the room at the operation, come to my son. It is what a person asks when they love somebody and are frightened, and the psalms are full of such prayers. What this story does is not rebuke the request but enlarge it. The answer, when it comes, is not smaller than he asked. It is the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles. Christ is not limited by where he is, and by his Spirit he is present with his people everywhere.

In a sentence. When Jesus returned to Cana, a royal official from Capernaum, whose son was dying, came and begged him to come down and heal him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your desperate needs to Jesus, as this father did. Do not send a servant, so to speak, by offering a quick and distant prayer about something that is breaking your heart. Go yourself: take time, name the person, plead with him.

For worship. Desperation is a great leveller, and Christ is the refuge of the high and the low alike. The courtier and the Samaritan woman, at opposite ends of society, both found that their need had brought them to the same feet. He is Lord over sickness and death, and no one with a dying child has ever walked too far to reach him. He is mighty to save and gentle with the broken-hearted.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to him: unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.

Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe. The you is plural, and that single grammatical fact changes the temperature of the verse. Jesus is not turning on a frantic father. He is speaking over his head to the Galileans in general (v. 45), the ones who saw the signs at the feast and came out to see whether there would be more. Faith that depends on miracles is weak faith. They want signs; the Samaritans believed his word. The father is standing in the middle of a diagnosis that is not mainly about him.

What was it for? It is a hard thing to have said in one’s hearing when one’s child is dying, and it is worth asking why Jesus said it. The clue is what happens next. Jesus does not, in the end, give this man a sign he can see. He gives him a sentence. The point of verse 48 is that the man is about to be asked to do what the crowd will not: take a word and go, with nothing in his hands. The apparent rebuke sets up the test, and Jesus is testing the official’s faith: will he believe without seeing? The father passes inside a verse.

Then are miracles bad for faith? No. John records Jesus’ signs precisely so that we may believe (20:30–31), and Jesus appeals to his works as evidence (10:38; 14:11). Signs are good when they point us to Christ and lead us to trust his word. The weakness Jesus exposes is a faith that will believe only if it keeps seeing: faith in the spectacle rather than in the one who performs it. The signs were given once for all and are written down for us. We do not need fresh ones to believe; we need to believe what has been written.

In a sentence. Jesus said that unless they saw signs and wonders they would not believe.

On a Tuesday. There is relief here for anyone who has prayed badly under pressure. When something is genuinely at stake, the words go, the composure goes, and what is left is a single sentence repeated. This chapter records such a prayer word for word, and records that it was answered at once and generously. Nothing suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. Do you need to see miracles to believe? Trust Jesus’ word.

For worship. Christ is not moved by eloquence but by need laid before him in trust. The same Lord who exposes the shallow appetite of the crowd bends down to the cry of one desperate father. He tests faith in order to strengthen it, never to crush it. He is the High Priest who sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and he hears the stammered prayer of a frightened parent as clearly as the psalms of the saints.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural — Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The official said to him: sir, come down before my child dies. Jesus said to him: go; your son will live. The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.

Sir, come down before my child dies. One of the great replies in the Gospels, and it is not an argument at all. He does not defend his motives, or protest that his faith is better than that, or engage with the theology of signs. He has one thing to say and says it again. And note the word for his son. Not the formal word of verse 47. The Greek here is a diminutive, paidion: my little boy. The rank has fallen off the man entirely.

Go; your son will live. Five words, and what they do not contain is as striking as what they do. No journey, no touch, no prayer. No condition attached, no instruction to believe, no if you have faith. Not even a gesture in the direction of Capernaum. The man asked him to come down, and Jesus declines to come down and answers anyway: just a word, from twenty miles away.

The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him. Sit inside that for a moment. He had walked all day into the hills for one thing: to bring this man back down to the house. He is being sent home without him. Everything he came for has been refused, and what he has instead is a sentence from somebody he has only just met, about a child who was at the point of death when he left. This is the faith Jesus looks for: believing his word, without a sign.

And went on his way. He did not wait for proof. That is the miracle in this verse, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had no evidence of any kind. There was no way to send word ahead or to hear anything until he arrived, and the arriving would take the rest of that day and into the next. The whole journey home was made on the strength of five words, and every hour of it the alternative explanation was available to him: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come. This is what it looks like when a promise is the only thing in a person’s hands. Not the absence of fear, for there is no reason to think he was calm, but the willingness to act as though the word were true while everything visible is unchanged and the clock is running.

Does this mean that a parent with enough faith can secure healing for a sick child? No. This was a particular word from Jesus to this man: your son will live. We have no such word about every illness, and the faith he commends is trust in what Christ has said, not confidence that he will do what we ask. A parent whose child was not healed did not fail to believe enough. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he loved (11:35), and his promise to his people is not that no child will die, but that whoever believes in him, though he die, yet shall he live (11:25).

What has Christ actually promised me, then? Far more than one healing. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37), that he will never leave nor forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), that nothing can separate them from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39), that he will raise them on the last day (6:40), and that he is preparing a place for them (14:2–3). These are words as certain as the one spoken at Cana. Faith takes them and walks home on them, often long before the evidence arrives.

In a sentence. The official begged Jesus to come before his child died, and Jesus told him to go, for his son would live, and the man believed Jesus’ word and went on his way.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test. Think of a promise God has actually made to you in Scripture, and consider what you would do differently this week if you believed it was settled. Most of us go on arguing our case long after we have said amen, which is the equivalent of standing in Cana refusing to start walking. Faith, in this verse, is not a feeling about the promise. It is the point at which a man turns round and starts down the hill.

For worship. His word is enough. The Word who was in the beginning speaks, and it is done; he commands, and it stands fast. A father turned his back on the healer he had come to fetch and went home with nothing but a sentence, and the sentence was worth more than the visit. Every promise of Christ is made of the same stuff: the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word that sent a man down the hill from Cana stands for ever. Blessed be the Lord whose promise is as good as his presence.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.

As he was going down, his servants met him. He is on the road to Capernaum, the next day (v. 52), and they have not waited at the house. Somebody in that household was so relieved that they set off up the road to shorten the wait by a few hours.

And told him that his son was recovering. Literally, was living: the very word Jesus had used. His word had come true. And notice that what they bring is not, at this stage, a miracle. It is the ordinary best news a household can send: the boy is better, the fever has turned. Nothing in their message suggests anything supernatural. They think they are reporting a recovery.

How God’s answers usually arrive. Not with a label on them. The relief comes, the door opens, the feared thing does not happen, and from outside it looks exactly like an ordinary good outcome of the kind that sometimes occurs. The father is about to ask one question that will turn a recovery into a revelation, and it is not a spiritual question. It is a matter of fact: when?

How can I tell whether something was an answer to prayer or just coincidence? Often you cannot prove it, and you do not need to. Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including the ordinary course of events (Matthew 10:29–30), so the recovery that looks natural is still his gift. But it is worth doing what this father did: go back and check. Note what you prayed for and when, and notice what happened. Over time a pattern of God’s faithfulness becomes plain. Give thanks for every mercy without needing to label it a miracle; all good gifts come from above (James 1:17).

In a sentence. On his way home, his servants met him with news that his son was living.

On a Tuesday. A great deal of what God does in a life goes unrecognised simply because nobody goes back and checks the timing: when the money came, when the letter arrived, when the person walked into the room, against when it was prayed for. Keep a simple record of your prayers this month, and look back at the end of it. Jesus’ word does what it says, even at a distance.

For worship. The word went ahead of the father and arrived first. While he was still on the hill road, the life Jesus had spoken was already in the boy, and the servants were already climbing to meet him. The faithfulness of Christ runs like that: his word never waits on our arrival to become true. His providence moves through ordinary days and ordinary news, and his kindness comes quietly up the road to meet his trusting children, in the plain clothes of a household saying the boy is better.

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him: yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him: your son will live. And he himself believed, and all his household.

He asked them the hour. He wanted to confirm, and the servants’ answer settles it: yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m. And there is a detail buried in the servants’ answer that is easy to read past and is one of the best things in the passage: yesterday. Jesus spoke at about one in the afternoon. Capernaum is roughly twenty miles away, downhill most of the way, a walk a determined man could nearly finish by nightfall, and could certainly finish by the next morning if he pressed on at first light. Unless yesterday simply means after sunset, when a Jewish day began, he did not press on. He stopped somewhere for the night, came down the next day, and met the servants on the road. Think what that means. A father whose only son was dying has been told the boy will live. If he had only half believed it, if any part of him was still calculating and frightened and needing to see, he would have run. Nobody in that condition stops for the night. The most convincing evidence that this man took Jesus at his word is that he did not hurry home.

The father knew that was the hour. Then the arithmetic lands. The hour the fever broke is the hour the words were spoken, twenty miles away, in a village in the hills. Nothing had touched the boy and nothing had been sent. There had been a sentence, a father walking down a road with nothing in his hands, and a fever going out of a child at that moment. Not coincidence.
