And he himself believed. John notes that he believed a second time. The first time (v. 50) was trust in a promise about his son. This time no object is named; he simply believed, which in this Gospel is the word for what a person does about Christ himself rather than about a request. His faith had grown from faith in a healer, to faith in his word, to full faith in Jesus.

And all his household. His whole family and servants believed, the first household conversion in John (compare Acts 16:15, 34). That is not a formula and it is not a guarantee. But notice what they had to go on: a man who came home, a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.

What if my household has not believed? Then this verse must not be used to reproach you. Plenty of faithful people have households that have not followed, and Jesus himself warned that families would be divided over him (Luke 12:51–53). Salvation is God’s gift, and each person must believe for himself. What this verse does give is hope and a pattern: pray for your whole household by name, live the faith visibly before them, and tell them plainly what Christ has done. God delights to save families, and he is not finished with yours.

Does the household believing support baptising whole households, including infants? Here the household believed; John says so. That is the pattern this commentary takes throughout the New Testament: those who were baptised, or counted as believers, were those who heard and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Our paedobaptist brothers read the household passages differently and see in them the covenant inclusion of children, and they hold that view with deep conviction and care for their children’s souls. We honour them as brothers. But this verse, at least, describes a household of believers.

In a sentence. Asking when his son had improved, the official learned it was the very hour Jesus had spoken, and he and his whole household believed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your whole household to believe, by name, today. And let them see the reasons for your faith: tell them the hour, the answered prayers and the faithfulness of God you have known.

For worship. The Word who was in the beginning, through whom the fever and the boy and every mile between them had been made, simply spoke, and the distance turned out not to matter, because it never had. He does not have to be near a thing to reach it; he is the reason it is there. And the life he spoke into one boy at the seventh hour spread through a whole house, until family and servants believed in a Lord who had never crossed their threshold. He is Lord of the distance, and Lord of the home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.

This was now the second sign. John counts, and the counting is deliberate. He has told us that the water made wine was the first sign (2:11), and now the second, and then he stops counting; the numbering never resumes. Its only purpose was to tie these two together, and they are tied at both ends: both at Cana, both after a journey up from Judea, both ending in belief (2:11; 4:53).

A frame around the chapters. Everything between the two signs sits inside the frame. Between Cana and Cana there is a night visit from a member of the ruling council who cannot understand the plainest thing, and a midday conversation with a Samaritan woman who understands enough to fetch a town. The man with everything missed it, the woman with nothing did not, and the section closes with a courtier of Herod’s believing on a word alone.

What changes between the first sign and the second. The first revealed his glory at a wedding; the second, his power over sickness and death at a distance. At the wedding he was present, the water was in front of him, and he gave an instruction to servants standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and does nothing but speak. The first sign needed his hands on the situation. The second needed only his voice, and the voice worked across a day’s journey as if the journey were not there. Both show that his word has creative power.

Why does this matter for me? Because this is the position of everyone who follows Christ after the ascension. We are the man on the road home: no touch, no visible presence, no sign before our eyes, only his word and a distance and the walking. The signs escalate so that the last one in this frame can be a word alone. And John says at the end of his Gospel that he wrote these signs down so that people who were never in the room might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:30–31). That is, so that there could go on being men and women walking home on nothing but his sentence, and finding that the fever had gone at the hour it was spoken.

In a sentence. This was the second sign Jesus did after coming from Judea to Galilee.

On a Tuesday. You have something the official did not: the whole written word of Christ. Read one of his promises today and walk on it, as though he had spoken it to you from twenty miles away, because in his word he has.

For worship. Each of Jesus’ signs reveals who he is: the Lord of creation who turned water into wine, the Lord of life who drives out death with a word. The glory that shone at the wedding shone again in a sickroom he never entered. And the same voice that spoke at Cana will one day speak at every grave, and all who are in the tombs will hear it and come out. Blessed be the Word made flesh, whose word is life, and whose glory is full of grace and truth.

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Chapter 3 showed Jesus with a respected Jewish teacher at night; chapter 4 shows him with an unnamed Samaritan woman at noon. Travelling north through Samaria, tired and thirsty, he sits by Jacob’s well and asks her for a drink, crossing three barriers at once: race, sex and religion. He offers her “living water”, a spring of eternal life welling up inside, and she misunderstands, as Nicodemus did. Then he gently exposes her life: five husbands, and the present man not her husband. She turns to the old dispute between Samaritans and Jews about where to worship; Jesus answers that the hour has come when the place no longer matters, for the Father seeks worshippers in spirit and truth. When she speaks of the coming Messiah, he tells her plainly, “I who speak to you am he.”

She leaves her water jar and brings the town to “come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.” Meanwhile Jesus tells his puzzled disciples that his food is to do his Father’s will, and that the fields are already white for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, first through her testimony and then through his own word, and confess him as “the Savior of the world.” Back in Cana, a royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son; Jesus simply says, “Go; your son will live,” and the man believes and goes. His servants meet him with the news that the fever left at the very hour Jesus spoke. This is the second sign: the word of Jesus gives life at a distance. Together the stories show the gospel crossing every boundary, and faith growing from hearing to trusting his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At a festival in Jerusalem, Jesus visits the pool of Bethesda by the Sheep Gate, where crowds of the blind, lame and paralysed lie under its colonnades. One man has been disabled for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be healed. The man complains that no one helps him into the water when it stirs, and others always get there first. Jesus commands him to stand, lift his mat and walk, and at once he does. Because it is the Sabbath, the authorities rebuke him for carrying the mat; he blames the man who healed him, whose name he does not know, as Jesus has disappeared in the crowd. Later Jesus meets him in the temple and warns him to leave his sin behind, lest something worse befall him. The man reports to the authorities that it was Jesus, and they start to harass Jesus for Sabbath work. Jesus replies that his Father is still at work and so is he. Now they are more intent on killing him, for he not only breaks the Sabbath but claims God as his own Father, making himself God’s equal.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath healing reveals Jesus's divine authority by the very nature of the opposition it generates. When Jesus says 'My Father is working until now, and I am working,' the Jewish leaders understand immediately what he is claiming: equality with God, the same authority over the Sabbath that God the Father has. This is not a misunderstanding that Jesus corrects; it is a correct understanding that Jesus confirms. The discourse that follows is the most comprehensive statement of the Son's relationship to the Father in the Gospels: the Son does nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing; the Father has given all judgment to the Son; the Son gives life to whom he will.

The Sabbath argument lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. They knew God does not stop working on the seventh day — children are born and people die on it, and the giving of life and the judging of the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never ceases. The accepted solution was that God is exempt, since the whole universe is his house and he carries nothing out of it. Jesus takes that exemption for himself (My Father is working until now, and I am working) and then, over the next few verses, claims precisely the two works it was famous for: giving life (v. 21) and executing judgment (v. 22).

Verse 18 must not be softened. John does not write that they thought he was making himself equal with God, or that they misunderstood; he reports it as what was happening. The narrator agrees with their reading of the words and disagrees only with what they did about it. This closes off the idea that Jesus was a teacher of ethics whom his followers later inflated: nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. The possessive is the point — his own Father, private and particular, in a way that made his working and God's working one working.

Neither charge is right as they put it. He was not breaking the Sabbath; he was breaking their reading of it, and never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God either — for the opposite reason. He made himself nothing. He was stating what was already the case, which is a larger offence than the one they charged.
verseByVerse.examples:
The thirty-eight-year illness is not incidental but emblematic: the man has exhausted every human resource and lies waiting for something that never comes by human effort. Jesus's intervention is sovereign and uninvited — the man does not ask for healing, does not know who Jesus is, and does not believe in him before the miracle. The healing comes entirely from Christ's initiative, which is the pattern of all saving grace. 'Do you want to be healed?' is the most searching question Jesus could ask, because chronic suffering can become a settled identity that is comfortable in its own way.

Do you want to be healed? sounds close to an insult to a man who has lain by a healing pool for thirty-eight years, and Jesus does not ask it of everyone he heals, which means it is meant for this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for that long: it goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine, until a life is built around the waiting and the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; most people can manage it in months. The question is the most respectful thing in the passage — he does not heal the man over his head, but asks somebody who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

This is the verse for the reader who long ago stopped asking for something: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the prayer abandoned around its fifth anniversary. The test is whether one can still say plainly what would be different if God moved — or whether the answer comes out as an explanation of why it will not happen, which is exactly what the man says next.

Two further mercies are worth naming. The healing came unrequested to a man who had given up asking, without faith, without confession, without his even knowing the name of the one who did it — grace arriving on its own initiative. And the mat was not left at the pool: a healed man walking away is a private mercy nobody need ever know about, but a healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. It is possible to be genuinely healed and entirely discreet about it. He is told to pick it up.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.

Meaning first. John 5 is a turning point. At a pool in Jerusalem, on the Sabbath, Jesus heals a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years, unasked and with no mention of the man’s faith. The leaders see only a broken rule, and when Jesus answers that his Father is working and so is he, they understand him perfectly: he is making himself equal with God, and for the first time they seek to kill him. His reply is one of the great passages on who he is: the Son does what the Father does, gives life to whom he will, will judge the world, and must be honoured as the Father is. Then, like a defendant in court, he calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. A man who could do nothing was made whole; the best-taught men in the nation had every witness and would not come.

The setting. Some time after the second sign at Cana, Jesus is back in Jerusalem for a feast. The scene is a pool just north of the temple, and this third sign leads straight to open hostility and the first plot against his life (v. 18).

A feast of the Jews. Unnamed; perhaps Pentecost, Tabernacles or Purim. John normally names the feasts, Passover already (2:13, 23), Tabernacles and Dedication later, and here he simply says a feast. It matters only because the chronology of the ministry partly hangs on it, and it is honest to say we cannot date the chapter precisely. John was not writing a diary.

By the Sheep Gate. The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple, where sheep for sacrifice were brought in (Nehemiah 3:1). The healing happens beside the gate of the sacrificial lambs, in the presence of the Lamb of God.

A pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda. The ESV notes other spellings in the manuscripts (Bethzatha, Bethsaida). Bethesda may mean house of mercy. It was a colonnade full of blind, lame and paralysed people waiting for water that mostly did not come, and someone had called it the house of mercy. That was either the bitterest name in Jerusalem or a prophecy, and on this morning it turned out to be the second.

Which has five roofed colonnades. For a long time this description was treated as proof that whoever wrote this Gospel did not know Jerusalem. A pool with five colonnades is an odd shape, since four sides need four porticoes, and no such structure was known; it was cited as evidence of a late book written far away from imagination. Then it was dug up. Excavations near the Church of St Anne uncovered a double pool north of the temple, two large basins side by side, with colonnades on the four outer sides and a fifth across the partition between them. Five, as John describes, though details of the layout are still debated. The writer knew the city in a detail that had been lost for centuries and could not have been guessed. That does not prove the miracle, and it should not be overstated. But it removes a confident objection and tells us what kind of book this is: an eyewitness account of a real place, by someone who could still see the layout in his mind, and who mentions it only because it was where the man was lying. And has is present tense, which may suggest John wrote before the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, or may simply describe the scene vividly.

Does archaeology prove the Bible true? It cannot prove the miracles or the gospel; those rest on the testimony of God in his word, received by faith through the Spirit. But archaeology has again and again confirmed the Bible’s places, names and details, and has often embarrassed confident critics, as it did here. That matters. Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas detached from history; it stands or falls on real events in real places. When the details John mentions in passing turn out to be accurate, it is a reasonable confirmation that he is telling the truth about the larger things as well.

In a sentence. At a Jewish feast Jesus went to Jerusalem, where there was a pool called Bethesda near the Sheep Gate, surrounded by five covered colonnades.

On a Tuesday. John’s details have been confirmed by archaeology. The Gospel is history you can trust. When you read it today, read it as the record of things that really happened, to real people, in places you could have walked.

For worship. The God of the Bible acts in history. He came to a real city at a real feast and walked into a real colonnade that has been dug out of the ground. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, at an address. And the house of mercy, which had been a house of disappointment for so long, became on that day what its name had promised, because the Lord of mercy himself had come to it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these lay a multitude of invalids: blind, lame, and paralysed.

A multitude of invalids, blind, lame, and paralyzed. The pool was a gathering place for the sick and disabled, hoping for healing. Paralysed is literally withered. Three words covering every kind of body that will not do what it is told. They are the very conditions Isaiah promised would be reversed when God came: then shall the lame man leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6). And they are the ones Jesus listed when the imprisoned Baptist sent to ask whether he was the one: the blind see, the lame walk (Matthew 11:4–5). So the colonnade is not merely a sad place. It is the exact address at which the messianic promise was due to be paid, and it was full of people for whom it had not been.

He walks into it. That is worth registering before anything else happens. The Son of God, in a city full of holy places, chose to spend part of a feast day in the one building where the concentration of untreated suffering was highest. Where suffering gathers, he does not withdraw.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel who stirred the water, so that the first person to step in was healed. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added to explain verse 7, reflecting popular belief. That is why the verse numbers jump from 3 to 5. Some think the pool was fed by an intermittent spring that bubbled up, which people believed had healing power. Nothing is lost: the man trusted the water and its legend; Jesus ignored the water entirely and healed with a word.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible is unreliable? No. We have thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, far more and far earlier than for any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a later copyist added a note. Modern Bibles are open about these places, as the ESV is here. No doctrine of the faith depends on a disputed verse. The very fact that we can identify such additions shows how well God has preserved his word.

A mercy for the quickest. Whatever was or was not true about that water, the belief around it had a cruel shape: whoever gets in first is healed. It was a mercy available to the quickest, which is to say to the people who needed it least, and closed to the man who had been there longest. Thirty-eight years of a healing system that rewarded the ones who could already move. Jesus does not touch the water. He does not carry the man to it, clear the queue, or make him first. He heals him where he lies, and the whole apparatus of stirring and racing and being beaten to it becomes, in one sentence, irrelevant. That is the difference between a mercy you have to qualify for and a mercy that comes to where you are.

In a sentence. Under the colonnades lay crowds of blind, lame and paralysed people.

On a Tuesday. The world is full of people waiting for help that never comes. Jesus comes to them. Where is the colonnade in your town: the care home, the hospital ward, the street where people sleep? Go there this month, as his servant.

For worship. Isaiah saw the day when the lame would leap like a deer and the blind would see, and for generations this colonnade was full of people still waiting for it. Then the one in whom the promise would be kept walked in under its roofs on a feast day. He came not for the healthy but for the sick. He would take the lowest place himself, at the back of every human queue, so that those who cannot move or compete might find that mercy had come to where they lay.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed — a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him: do you want to be healed?

An invalid for thirty-eight years. Do the arithmetic before moving on, because a number in a sentence goes past too easily. It is longer than many people lived then, longer than most careers. If he was struck down at twenty, he is nearly sixty, and he has spent the whole of his adult life on a mat beside a pool, watching other people get well. Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering in the wilderness after their unbelief at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 2:14), the years of waiting outside the promise. John does not say so, and the link is better held loosely than pressed.

When Jesus saw him. Out of the multitude, Jesus chose this one. He took the initiative; the man did not ask. Why this man? John does not explain. Grace is sovereign, and the mystery of God’s choice is assumed, not apologised for. And Jesus knew that he had already been there a long time, without being told (2:25; 4:18).

Do you want to be healed? The strangest thing Jesus says in the chapter. To a man who has lain beside a healing pool for thirty-eight years it sounds almost like an insult. Of course he wants it. And yet Jesus does not ask this of everyone he heals, so it is meant for this man and this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for thirty-eight years. It does not stay a clean, sharp thing. It goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine: the same spot, the same hours, the same near misses, until the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; it is what happens to human beings, and it happens fast. Perhaps he had given up hope, or grown used to his condition and the life of a beggar. Healing would mean new responsibilities. So the question is not cruel. It is the most respectful thing in the passage. Jesus wakes him to desire. He asks a man who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

What if I have stopped hoping for something? This question is for you too: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the sin confessed so often the confessing has gone hollow, the prayer abandoned around the fifth year of praying it. The question is not a rebuke for having stopped hoping. It is an invitation to say aloud what would be different if God moved, which is harder than it looks. God may answer as you ask, or differently, or in his own time; but he invites you to bring the desire to him honestly rather than bury it. Hope in God is never foolish, even when hope in the circumstance has worn thin.

In a sentence. Jesus saw a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, knew how long he had been there, and asked if he wanted to be healed.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you long ago decided to live with. Now notice whether you can still say plainly what you would want instead, or whether the answer comes out as an explanation of why it will not happen. That is exactly what the man at the pool does: asked whether he wants to be healed, he explains why he cannot be. Do you really want Jesus to make you whole, with everything that would change?

For worship. In a colonnade full of the forgotten, the Son of God stopped at one mat. He knew the thirty-eight years without being told, and he began not with a cure but with a question, because he heals people, not cases. He chooses freely and comes unasked; he speaks to the heart before he touches the body. The Lord who saw the one in that multitude sees the one in every crowd, and there is no length of waiting he has not counted.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sick man answered him: sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.

Sir, I have no one. The loneliest words in the chapter. Not I cannot walk; he takes that as read. What he names as his problem is not his legs. It is that in thirty-eight years, in a colonnade full of people, in a city of pilgrims, at the season of a feast, nobody had ever stayed close enough to put him in the water. The Greek is bare: a man I do not have. No friend, no family. The paralytic in Mark had four friends (Mark 2:3); this man had none. He is surrounded by people and alone, which is a particular kind of alone and the one most people would recognise.

While I am going another steps down before me. He believed the popular belief about the stirred water, and it had failed him for years: a cruel competition, in which the weakest always lost. And the detail is almost too painful to be invented. He has tried. He has hauled himself toward that water more times than he could count, and every time someone quicker got in first, and he dragged himself back to his place to wait for the next stirring. Thirty-eight years of nearly.

He does not answer the question. He does not say yes. Asked whether he wants to be well, he describes the system and his place at the bottom of it. Not one word is untrue and not one word is an answer. That is what thirty-eight years does to hope: it converts it into an explanation. He does not know who is speaking to him (v. 13), and has no faith in Jesus. His hope is in the water. He is talking to the answer while explaining why there isn’t one. The man in front of him has no interest in the pool, will not use the water, and does not require him to be first in any queue, and none of that has occurred to him, because for thirty-eight years the water was the only door there was.

Why does Jesus heal someone who showed no faith? Because grace does not wait for us to be ready. This healing is a picture of how God saves: not because we reached the water first, or had the right friends, or even knew who he was, but because Christ came to us and spoke. Faith is the hand that receives Christ, and God gives that hand too (Ephesians 2:8). In this man’s case the healing came first and the knowing later. That should encourage you to pray for people who seem to have no faith at all. Christ can begin where there is nothing.

In a sentence. The man answered that he had no one to help him into the pool when the water stirred, and someone always got there first.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you have no one, Jesus has come to you. And look around: who in your church, or street, has no one? Be the friend with strong arms. And if you are praying about a situation with one visible solution, the promotion, the diagnosis, the phone call, remember that it is hard to ask God for anything but the door you can see. This man wanted a friend to carry him and got his legs back instead.

For worship. When there was no man to help, the Son of Man came. He is the friend of the friendless, the helper of the helpless, the one who stays when everyone else has stepped down before us. A bruised reed he will not break. He was himself forsaken by all his friends, so that no one who trusts him need ever say again, I have no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: get up, take up your bed, and walk. And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.

Get up, take up your bed, and walk. Three commands, all impossible, and the man is asked to do what he has not done for thirty-eight years before there is any evidence that he can. Get up, from a man who has not stood. Take up your bed: the word is krabattos, not a bed in our sense but a poor man’s mat, the cheap pallet a beggar sleeps on and rolls under his arm. And walk. His word gives the power to obey. No pool, no stirring, no help needed. Jesus is greater than every superstition and every human remedy.

And at once the man was healed. After thirty-eight years, instantly. There is no touch and no prayer. The man has not asked for healing, has not expressed faith, does not know who is talking to him, and will still not know an hour later. Unlike most healings, nothing is said of his faith. This is grace arriving unrequested at a man who had given up asking, and it is why Bethesda has always been read as a picture of the gospel.

And he took up his bed and walked. Obedience, at once. And the mat is the point. A healed man walking away is a private mercy; nobody need ever know. A healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. Jesus could have said get up and go home. He tells him to carry the mat, on the Sabbath, in Jerusalem, at a feast, past the authorities. That is not carelessness. It is deliberate, and the rest of the chapter follows from it.

Now that day was the Sabbath. The sentence that starts the conflict. John withholds it until after the healing, so that the reader feels the joy first and the objection second, which is the order in which the man experienced it, and exactly the wrong way round for the men about to arrive. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by the rabbis’ rules, built on texts such as Jeremiah 17:21–22 and Nehemiah 13:15–19. Jesus knew it was the Sabbath. He chose this day.

Must Christians, then, keep the Sabbath? Christians differ here, and both views are held by faithful believers. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds, the day of rest now kept on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, and kept with joy as a day for worship and works of mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). (The 1689 London Baptist Confession says the same, 22.7–8.) Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ, the true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so that no day binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6), while still gathering gladly on the first day, the day of resurrection. Verdict: the second fits the New Testament best; the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it. Both agree with what this passage plainly teaches: the day was never meant to forbid mercy, and Jesus is Lord of it.

In a sentence. Jesus told him to get up, pick up his mat and walk, and the man was healed at once and walked, and it was the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word gives power to do what it commands, so obey his word today, even where it looks impossible. And notice the mat. It is possible to be genuinely helped by Christ and entirely discreet about it, to leave the mat at the pool. He told this man to pick it up. Is there some evidence of his grace in your life that you have been keeping out of sight?

For worship. He speaks, and the dead legs stand; he commands, and the thing commanded is done. The word that called the world out of nothing called a withered man off his mat. And he chose the Sabbath, the day of God’s rest, to give a man the first true rest he had known in thirty-eight years. His commands carry their own power, and his grace comes to those who did not even know to ask.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews said to the man who had been healed: it is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.

So the Jews said. In John, the Jews often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his disciples and the healed man were all Jews.

It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed. No joy that a man paralysed for thirty-eight years can walk. Only concern that a rule has been broken. The Mishnah lists carrying an object from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work. The rule mattered more than the man.

Be fair to them first. They were not inventing a rule out of nothing. The prophets had been explicit: take care, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 17:21–22). Jeremiah names the city and the gates. These men are standing in that city, watching a man carry a load, and they have a text. So this is not a case of religious people making things up. It is something more uncomfortable and far more common: people applying a real command of God, in a situation it was never written for, and being catastrophically wrong while remaining technically correct.

The lens and the subject. The arithmetic of the sentence condemns them. A man who has been paralysed for thirty-eight years is walking through Jerusalem carrying his own bed, and the whole content of their response is a citation. Not one question about how, not one word to him about what has happened. They see the mat, the mat is against the rules, and the man holding it is invisible. It is what happens when a system of rules becomes the lens rather than the subject. A miracle walks past and is processed as an infringement.

Lord of the day they were guarding. The Sabbath these men were defending was God’s sign of the rest he would give his people, and the giver of that rest had just given it. For thirty-eight years the man had carried nothing but his own helplessness; the one load he lifts that day is the proof that his real burden has been taken away, by the one who told him to lift it. The men at the gate see the fourth commandment broken. They are looking at what it pointed to, walking past them on two healed legs. In a few verses Jesus will tell them why: his Father is working until now, and so is he (v. 17). The Lord of the Sabbath had come to his own day.

Does this mean rules do not matter? No. God’s commands are good, and Jesus never broke the law of God. What he exposed was a way of handling God’s law that loses sight of its purpose: love for God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). The problem was not that they cared about obedience, but that they cared about their reading of a rule more than about the man in front of them and the God who had just healed him. Keep God’s commands; but never let your system of applying them blind you to his mercy.

In a sentence. The Jewish leaders told the healed man that it was unlawful for him to carry his mat on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that is uncomfortable for anyone who has been in church a long time. Think of the last time something happened in a Christian setting outside your expectations: an unfamiliar style, a convert with a chaotic life, someone doing good work with theology you would want to correct. What was your first movement? For most of us with any training it is assessment. That is not wrong in itself; discernment is a duty. But notice that it is first, and that these men were the best-trained people in the country, and their first movement was a rule, and the second never came at all.

For worship. The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul, and the Lord of the law came to fulfil it, not to destroy it. Where men used God’s good law to keep a healed man from rejoicing, Christ kept it perfectly in love, and bore its curse for those who had broken it. His mercy is the meaning of the law, and he will not let his law be turned into a wall against his grace.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he answered them: the man who healed me, that man said to me, take up your bed, and walk. They asked him: who is the man who said to you, take up your bed and walk?

The man who healed me, that man said to me. He shifts the responsibility, and his logic is sound. Someone with the power to end thirty-eight years of paralysis with a word plainly has standing to say what may be carried and when. If the healer had authority to heal, surely he had authority to tell him to carry his mat. That is not an evasion; it is an argument, and a good one. What he lacks is not reasoning. It is a name.

Who is the man who said to you? Read the two sentences side by side and notice what each party seizes on. He says: the man who healed me. They say: the man who said to you. They repeat his sentence with the healing surgically removed. Not who healed you, but who told you to break the rule. They are not interested in the miracle, only the offence. That is an editorial decision made in real time, the exact operation by which an inconvenient fact stops being part of a discussion.

The right question for the wrong reason. Yet the question they ask, who is the man?, is the only question that matters in this Gospel, the one the whole book exists to answer. They ask it to identify a suspect. But they ask it. There is something almost merciful in how often, in John, hostile people stumble on the correct question.

Be gentle with the healed man. He has had his legs for perhaps an hour. He does not know who healed him. And the first use anyone makes of him is as a witness in a dispute he did not know existed, questioned by the most powerful men in the city about an infringement he committed on instructions. He is not a theologian and has had no time to become one. People are often hard on him for later naming Jesus to the authorities, and some of it may be fair. But not everyone is at his best in that position, and this Gospel does not pretend otherwise about anyone.

What do I say when I am challenged about my faith and do not know much yet? Say what you know, as this man did. You may not be able to answer every question, but you can say what has happened to you and who did it. The man born blind in chapter 9 said: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see (9:25). That is enough to begin with. Then go and learn more, so that next time you can say more. And do not be ashamed to say, I do not know the answer to that yet, but I will find out.

In a sentence. He answered that the man who healed him told him to carry his mat, and they asked who it was.

On a Tuesday. Notice what people focus on when they hear of God’s work: the grace, or the rule-breaking? And notice what you focus on. When you hear that God has done something unexpected in someone’s life, what is the first question you ask?

For worship. Who is the man? His enemies asked it to name a suspect, and every page of this Gospel answers it: the Word made flesh, the Lamb of God, the Son of the Father, the Lord who heals. The question meant as an accusation holds the whole of our salvation in its answer. He let his enemies ask it, and at the last they answered it themselves without knowing, with a title fixed above his head on a cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (19:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.

For Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place. The man did not know who it was: healed without knowing his healer, grace before knowledge. Jesus slipped away to avoid publicity. He healed the man and was gone before anything could gather around it. It will not be the last time in this Gospel that he does the extraordinary thing and immediately makes himself scarce (6:15), and it is the opposite of what anyone building a following would do.

Set him beside the man born blind. The contrast is deliberate. That man is interrogated by the same authorities and grows sharper with every round: he argues, he mocks them, he tells them that if this man were not from God he could do nothing, and he is thrown out of the synagogue; then Jesus finds him, and he worships (9:38). This man is asked one question and produces a name. John puts the two accounts four chapters apart and expects them to be compared. One received his sight, lost his standing and gained Christ. This one received his legs, and what we are told afterwards is that he told the authorities who had done it.

Answered prayer is not conversion. The passage is honest about something uncomfortable: the healing did not, as far as we are told, save him. Every physical mercy in the Gospels is real, and none of them is automatically anything more. This man’s body was mended by the Son of God, and there is no clear evidence in the text that anything else was. That needs saying in a world where much prayer is for exactly this kind of mercy, and rightly. A marriage restored, a diagnosis reversed, a job that came in time: each may be a genuine gift from God and leave the recipient where they were.

Can someone receive God’s blessings and still not be saved? Yes, sadly. God is kind to all; he sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and many received healing from Jesus without following him (Luke 17:17–18). Blessings are meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), but they do not save by themselves. Only faith in Christ unites us to him. So do not measure your standing with God by your circumstances, good or bad. Ask instead: do I know him, trust him and follow him?

In a sentence. The man did not know who had healed him, because Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

On a Tuesday. God often blesses us before we know him well. Make a list of the good things God has given you this year, and then ask whether they have drawn you closer to the giver. Seek to know the one who has blessed you.

For worship. He gives and slips away, not seeking applause. The Lord does good to those who do not even know his name, and is content to be unrecognised in his kindness. But he does not stay hidden for ever: the healer who vanished into the crowd went looking for the man he had healed. His mercies come before our knowledge of him, and he will not leave us with the gift alone, because what he means to give is himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterwards Jesus found him in the temple and said to him: see, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you. The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.

Afterward Jesus found him in the temple. Jesus sought him again. The man had gone to the temple, perhaps to give thanks, now able to enter where his condition had kept him out, and it was the first thing he did with his legs. That is not nothing; any reader may think well of him for it. And the finding is deliberate. Jesus had slipped away rather than be identified, and now he goes looking for a man who does not know his face. The healing was the beginning of the errand, not the end. He does not consider the matter closed because the legs work. That is his way throughout this Gospel: he comes back for people. He comes back for the blind man after he is thrown out (9:35), and for Peter on a beach after the denials (21:15).

See, you are well! He has been made whole. In telling him to sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to him, Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin (9:3), but warns this man that sin has worse consequences than paralysis: eternal judgement. Perhaps his illness was connected to some sin. Physical healing is not enough; he needs to turn from sin. A body healed but a soul unrepentant would face something worse.

Am I ill because of something I did? Many readers carry that question quietly for years. John himself settles the general question four chapters on. The disciples see a man born blind and ask who sinned, this man or his parents, and Jesus rejects the premise: neither (9:3). Illness is not a scoreboard. In a world under the curse, bodies fail, and the failure is not a message decoded from the sufferer’s record. Job’s friends built a theology on the opposite assumption, and God told them they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7). Sometimes a particular sin does bring particular harm, and then repentance is the path. But you must not assume your suffering is punishment. If you are in Christ, the punishment for your sin was borne at the cross, and whatever you suffer now comes from a Father’s hand.

So what is Jesus saying here? Not that this man’s thirty-eight years were a sentence served, but the thing any of us most needs to hear on the far side of a mercy: there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat. He has given the man his legs; now he warns him about his soul, in the temple, where the man has rightly come. Taken at that level the warning stops sounding cruel and becomes kind. Sin is worth abandoning not because it made you ill, but because judgement is real, and the body you have just got back will not last for ever either.

The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him. Why? Perhaps naively, perhaps to protect himself, perhaps as testimony. Compare the man born blind, who boldly defended Jesus (9:30–33). This man seems to have reported him, and from then on the authorities pursued Jesus.

In a sentence. Jesus found him later in the temple, told him that he had been made well and should stop sinning or something worse would happen, and the man went and told the leaders it was Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Physical blessing is not salvation. If God has recently answered a prayer for your health, your finances or your family, thank him, and then let the mercy lead you further: turn from sin, and trust Christ.

For worship. The good Shepherd goes after the one he has helped, and does not leave him with half a cure. He loves us too well to heal our bodies and leave our souls in danger, and his warnings are as much mercy as his miracles. The one who said sin no more would himself bear the worse thing he warned of, the judgement sin deserves, so that all who turn to him might have what is better than legs: a heart made new and a life that will never end.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them: my Father is working until now, and I am working.

The Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. The tense means they kept on persecuting, and the cause was a pattern, not one incident.

My Father is working until now, and I am working. A staggering claim, and sharper than it looks, because it lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. God rested on the seventh day from creation (Genesis 2:2–3). But Jewish teachers knew perfectly well that God does not down tools on the seventh day. Children are born on the Sabbath and people die on it, and both require God: giving life and judging the dead were the two standard examples, acknowledged as divine work that never stops, along with sending rain and sustaining the universe. The accepted solution was that God is exempt: the whole universe is his house, so he is entitled to work in his own home on his own day. Jesus takes that exact exemption and applies it to himself. As my Father works on the Sabbath, so do I. Not God is allowed, therefore mercy is allowed, which would be an argument about ethics. He puts himself on the same side of the line as the one who is exempt, because he does God’s work. And then he spends the next dozen verses on the two divine works the rabbis had in mind: giving life and executing judgement. And my Father: not our Father. A unique relationship.

The rest of God and the work of God. The rest God took on the seventh day of creation was rest from making, not from holding. Every heartbeat since has been his work. There has not been an hour in the history of the universe when God was not sustaining it, and the reason anything exists this morning is not inertia.

Who actually kept the Sabbath that day? Consider what happened. A man who had not stood for thirty-eight years stood. He had spent every seventh day of nearly four decades lying on a mat beside a pool, and on this one he walked home. If any human being in Jerusalem entered into rest that day, it was him. The one accused of breaking the Sabbath is the only person in the story who gave anyone a Sabbath, and the men defending the day spent it drawing up charges. The day was made as a mercy, a weekly memorial of a God who finished his work. To turn it into an instrument for keeping a healed man from carrying his bedding is not strictness. It is a misreading of what the day was for.

Is God really working all the time, even in the boring parts of my life? Yes. My Father is working until now. God does not take weekends off from caring for his creation or his children. He is at work in the dull Tuesday as much as in the dramatic answer to prayer, upholding all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), working all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28), and completing the good work he began in you (Philippians 1:6). You may not see it. But you are never in a moment that God has left unattended.

In a sentence. The leaders persecuted Jesus for doing these things on the Sabbath, and he answered that his Father was still working, and so was he.

On a Tuesday. When you feel that nothing is happening in your life or your prayers, say this sentence to yourself: my Father is working until now. Then look for one place today where you can join in his work of mercy.

For worship. God is always at work, even on the day of rest. He never slumbers, never sleeps, never lets go of the world he made. And Jesus does what the Father does: he holds the stars in their places and a healed man on his feet with the same hand. Blessed be the Father who works until now, and the Son who works with him, and the Spirit through whom their work goes on in every heart and every hour.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

Seeking all the more to kill him. The first time John mentions the plot to kill Jesus, and the thread runs on through the Gospel (7:1, 19, 25; 8:37, 40; 11:53). He healed a man who had been on the ground for thirty-eight years, and they began to plan his death. John sets the two a verse apart without comment.

But he was even calling God his own Father. His own (idion): uniquely, personally, in a way no one else could. The word means private, particular, belonging to him and not to others. Jews called God Father collectively, the Father of the nation. To speak of God as one’s own Father, in the singular, in a way that made his working and God’s working the same working, was a different kind of sentence altogether.

Making himself equal with God. They understood him perfectly. Notice what John does not write. He does not say they thought he was making himself equal with God, or that they misunderstood him. He reports it flatly as what was happening. The narrator agrees with their reading of the words. What he does not agree with is what they did about it. Either Jesus was a blasphemer, or he is God. He does not deny it; the discourse that follows explains it. Those who say Jesus never claimed to be God have not read John 5.

The people who understood him best. This closes off one of the most popular ways of handling Jesus: the idea that he was a teacher of ethics whose followers later inflated him into something divine. The people who wanted him dead were the ones who understood him best. They were not offended by his ethics; nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. They killed him for who he said he was, and this verse is where the machinery starts moving.

Two charges, neither right as they put it. He was, they said, breaking the Sabbath. He was not; he was breaking their reading of it, and he never once broke the law of God. And he was making himself equal with God. He was not doing that either, for the opposite reason. He did not make himself anything. He was stating what was already the case, which is a different and larger claim altogether.

If Jesus is equal with God, why does he pray to the Father and obey him? Because within the one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory, and distinct in their relations (Westminster 2.3). The Son is fully God, and he is also the Son: from all eternity he delights to do his Father’s will. And in becoming man he took the form of a servant, humbled himself, and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6–8). So his prayers and obedience do not make him less than God. They show us God the Son living out, in our nature, the love and unity he has always shared with the Father.

In a sentence. The leaders were even more determined to kill him, because he was not only breaking the Sabbath but calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

On a Tuesday. If someone tells you Jesus never claimed to be God, open this chapter with them and read verses 17 to 23 together. And ask yourself: is my Jesus the one his enemies understood, or a smaller one who could never have been crucified for blasphemy?

For worship. The charge sheet, when it was finally drawn up, said that he made himself the Son of God (19:7). It was the only accusation ever brought against him that was true, and true in a sense the prosecution never suspected, since he had not made himself anything. He had come from somewhere, and the somewhere was his Father’s side, and he was on his way back to it by the road they were about to build for him. He claimed equality with God and died for the claim, and the empty tomb was the Father’s verdict that every word of it was true.

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus explains that the Son acts in perfect union with the Father, doing whatever he sees the Father do, because the Father loves him and shows him all things. Like the Father, the Son gives life to whom he wills, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that the Son may be honoured as the Father is. Whoever hears Jesus and trusts the Father has eternal life already and has passed beyond condemnation. Even now the spiritually dead hear his voice and live, and one day everyone in the tombs will hear it and rise, to life or to judgment. Jesus does not testify alone: John the Baptist bore witness, Jesus’ works bear witness, the Father bears witness, and so do the Scriptures, which his hearers study while refusing to come to him for life. They seek honour from each other rather than from God. Moses, their hope, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus; if they do not believe Moses, they will not believe Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse on the Son's authority establishes that Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet but the one to whom the Father has delegated the twin divine prerogatives of life-giving and judgment. These are not shared with any creature; they belong to God alone. Yet the Father has given them to the Son precisely so that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. The four witnesses — John, works, Father, Scripture — are not offered as proofs that compel belief but as witnesses whose rejection reveals the condition of the rejecting heart: no love of God, no desire for the glory that comes from God.

Life in himself (v. 26) is the highest thing said about God in the chapter. Everything that lives has life on loan — a tree from soil and light, a man from food and breath — and every such supply can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself is to hold it as a property rather than a supply, with nothing behind it that could fail; theologians call it aseity, and it belongs to God alone. That the Father granted the Son to have it is not an event in time and does not make it derived in the ordinary sense: it states the eternal relation between Father and Son. What the Father is, the Son is.

Verse 23 fixes the measure of honour with two words — just as — and forecloses the most popular way of handling Jesus. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ; it is not offered. And the direction is the reverse of what is usually assumed: the Father has given life and judgment to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. Withholding that honour is not modesty on God's behalf but a failure to give the Father what he has said he wants.

Verse 29 sounds like salvation by works and cannot be, since verse 24 gives life to whoever hears my word and believes. The good and the evil are evidence rather than currency — the visible form of a life that had already crossed from death to life, or had not. And the apparent contradiction between 5:31 (if I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true) and 8:14 (even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true) resolves by what each answers: the first concerns legal standing, the second factual accuracy. He does not need corroboration in order to be right; he offers it because they need it in order to be persuaded.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's claim to give life to whom he will (v. 21) and to execute judgment (v. 22) is either the most arrogant statement in human history or the most important truth in human history — there is no middle ground. The discourse forces a decision: either this man is deluded and dangerous, or he is who he says he is. The sequence of judgments in the discourse — present hearing (v. 24), coming resurrection (vv. 28-29) — establishes that the final judgment is already operative in every person's response to Christ.

Verse 35 is the saddest in the chapter and the tense is what makes it unbearable. He was a burning and shining lamp — the ordinary household oil lamp, the thing carried into a room after dark, and this Gospel has been careful that the Baptist was not the light (1:8). And they were willing to rejoice in it for a while. The whole country went out to the Jordan; it was the religious event of the decade; and it lasted about as long as such things last. By the time Jesus speaks, John's ministry is over. The mechanism has not changed — there is a way of consuming preaching as an experience, genuinely moved and warmly discussing it afterwards, and ending the season exactly where one started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous: it feels like a response and it is a reaction.

Verse 39's search was no casual reading — these men counted the letters and knew which word stood at the centre of the Torah. They got a preposition wrong: they thought the life was located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that Scripture gives life; he denies the address. The distance between the scroll and the person was about four feet, and they would not cross it. It is entirely possible to conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system — the tracing of themes, the resolving of difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage coming clear — and for the whole exercise to terminate in itself. The test takes ten seconds: after the last passage studied, did it end in knowing something, or in wanting him?

Verse 44 is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus calls believing impossible for a stated reason, and the reason is an economy. Doxa means both glory and reputation, and these men held a currency they issued to one another — standing, deference, the seat at the front — which can only be earned inside the system and therefore only kept by not leaving. The way out is in the same verse and is not an instruction to care less about honour: the glory that comes from the only God. He does not tell them to want no approval. He tells them they are seeking it from a bankrupt issuer.

And the chapter's arrangement is its own argument. It opens with a man who could not reach the water, had nobody, and did not know the name of the one who healed him — and he was made whole. It closes with the best-taught men in the nation, holding every witness heaven could produce, who would not come. He got up. The men with all the evidence stayed sitting down.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to them: truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.

The discourse. Jesus answers the charge that he made himself equal with God (v. 18). Not by denying it, but by explaining the relationship of the Son to the Father: perfect unity, with distinct roles.

The Son can do nothing of his own accord. Not weakness, but unity. The Son never acts independently of the Father. He is not a rival god setting up on his own. He does nothing apart from the Father, as the Father does nothing apart from him. And notice the direction of the sentence, because it is the opposite of what a critic would expect. It sounds like a limitation, but it works as the strongest claim in the paragraph. Anyone can do things independently of God; every one of us does it hourly, and that is what sin is. Only one person in existence can say that he never has, and that everything he does is what he sees the Father doing. It is not a confession of inability. It is a claim to be doing the Father’s own work, continuously and without deviation, which no prophet ever said.

The workshop. There may well be a picture underneath this. In that world a trade passed from father to son by watching. A boy did not attend a school of carpentry; he stood in his father’s shop from the time he could stand, and learned by seeing it done, and in time did the same work in the same way because he had never seen it done any other way. Everyone listening would have recognised the shape of it. Which makes the claim both homely and enormous. Take it as a picture of an ordinary trade and it is charming. Then look at what is made in this workshop: raising the dead and judging the world. Those are the two items named in the next verses, and they are on no human trade’s list.

For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. He does only what he sees the Father doing, in perfect knowledge of the Father’s will and perfect conformity to it. Whatever: everything. Not approximately, not partially, but exactly. The Son does all the works of God. Only one who is God can do everything God does.

For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. Eternal love and complete openness between Father and Son. The verb here is philei; in 3:35 the same love is expressed with agapa, and John uses the two interchangeably. What matters is what that love does: it shows. It withholds nothing. There are no works of the Father that the Son is not shown, and the reason given is love rather than policy. And the Father will show him greater works than healing a paralysed man: giving life and judging (vv. 21–22).

Where Christians differ: the Son and the Father. Arians (and today Jehovah’s Witnesses) read “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” as proof that the Son is inferior to the Father. Verdict: the passage teaches that the Son is equal with the Father in nature and power (he does whatever the Father does, gives life, judges, receives equal honour), while distinct in person and relationship (the Father sends; the Son is sent and obeys). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, three persons, equal in power and glory, distinct in relations (Westminster Shorter Catechism 6).

How can I explain the Trinity simply? Start with what the Bible says, not with an illustration. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. The three are not the same person: the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent by both. So God is one in being and three in persons. Most illustrations, water and ice and steam, or one man as father, son and husband, end up teaching an old error, that God is one person wearing three masks. It is better to say plainly: this is beyond us, and it is what God has shown us about himself, and it is the most beautiful truth there is, because it means God has always been love.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Son does nothing on his own but only what he sees the Father doing, doing everything the Father does, because the Father loves him and shows him all he does, and will show him greater works still.

On a Tuesday. You cannot do what the Son does, but you can learn from his way of doing it. Before the main decisions of today, stop and ask: what is my Father doing here? Do your work as a child learning in his Father’s workshop.

For worship. Father and Son are perfectly one in love and work. Before the world was made, the Father loved the Son and showed him all things, and the Son delighted to do all that the Father does. Into that eternal love, by grace, God brings his people: the Father loves us as he loves the Son (17:23). Blessed is the triune God, whose life is love and whose works are one.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son.

For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life. In the Old Testament, only God gives life to the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7). These are the two works the rabbis had identified as God’s alone, the two exceptions that proved he does not keep the Sabbath as men do. God gives life, because children are born on the seventh day. God judges the dead, because people die on it.

So also the Son gives life to whom he will. Jesus has just claimed the Father’s Sabbath exemption for himself. He now names, in order, the two works that exemption was famous for, and claims both. This is not a man drifting into grandiose language. It is a precisely targeted argument, delivered to people who knew which two items were on that list. The Son does what only God does. To whom he will: by his sovereign choice. Spiritual life now (v. 24), and resurrection life at the last day (v. 29). Salvation is the sovereign gift of the Son.

To whom he will. Not to whoever qualifies, not to whoever arrives first at the stirring of the water, which is what the man on the mat had believed for thirty-eight years and what had kept him on the ground. The whole first half of this chapter demonstrates that clause. Jesus walked into a colonnade of sick people, healed one, and left. Nobody has produced a satisfying account of why that man, and John does not attempt one. A Christ who healed everyone at the pool would be easier to admire and would tell us nothing about how mercy actually comes to anyone. What we have instead is a man who was not first in the queue, could not reach the water, had nobody, and got up and walked, and the only reason given is that the Son gives life to whom he will.

For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. The final judgement, which belongs to God alone (Genesis 18:25), is given to the Son (Acts 17:31). Two divine works, giving life and judging, and both belong to Jesus. It sounds administrative and is not. Every human being who has ever lived will be judged, and the one who judges is the one who was crucified. The bench is not occupied by a stranger to the case.

But Jesus also says he did not come to judge the world. How do these fit? He says it in 3:17 and 12:47, and in 8:15 he says, I judge no one. These fit together. He came the first time to save, not to condemn; the condemnation already rests on those who reject him (3:18). At the end, all judgement is committed to him, and he will judge (v. 27). And in 8:15 he means that he does not judge as they do, by outward appearance, by the standards of the flesh.

If the Son gives life to whom he will, is it unfair to those he passes by? No one has a claim on God’s mercy; if we did, it would not be mercy. All of us are sinners deserving judgement, and God would be perfectly just to leave us all to it. That he chooses to save any is pure grace, and that he saves a great multitude is amazing grace (Romans 9:14–16). And the same Christ who gives life to whom he will freely invites all: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). No one who wants to come is turned away. If you want Christ, that wanting is itself the sign that he is giving you life.

In a sentence. As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he chooses, and the Father has given all judgement to the Son.
