On a Tuesday. If you are a Christian, you did not get yourself to the water. Stop today and thank the Son by name that he gave life to you. And if you are praying for someone who seems far from God, take heart: the Son gives life to whom he will, and no one is too far gone for his voice.

For worship. Life and judgement are the two works no creature has ever held, and the Father has placed both in the hands of his Son. He gives life as freely as he chooses, answering no claim of merit because there is none, and calling men off mats who could never reach the water. He is sovereign in mercy and righteous in judgement, and both belong to him because he is God. Those who have his life in them now will find on the last day that the Judge on the throne is the one who raised them.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father. Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

That all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. The purpose: equal honour. The little phrase just as is the one to weigh, because it fixes the measure and leaves no room to negotiate. Not honour the Son highly. Not honour him more than any other teacher. Honour him just as the Father is honoured: the same kind, the same degree, the same worship, with no discount for the fact that he could be seen and touched and was tired at a well. Worship belongs to God alone; God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). If the Son is to be honoured just as the Father, the Son is God.

The Father wants his Son honoured. Notice the direction the honour runs. It would be natural to assume the Son’s whole purpose is to direct attention to the Father, and that any honour paid to him is a detour. The verse says the reverse: the Father has given life and judgement to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. The Father’s own design is that his Son be worshipped. Withholding it is not modesty on God’s behalf. It is a failure to give the Father what he has said he wants.

Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. This closes every exit. You cannot honour God while rejecting Jesus. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ. Every religion that respects God but denies Christ’s deity fails to honour God (1 John 2:23). That is the sentence which makes Christianity permanently awkward in polite company, and it is better stated than hedged. Many people are willing to say they believe in God, admire Jesus as a moral teacher, and regard his divinity as an unfortunate later addition. This verse says that arrangement does not exist, not because Christians are narrow, but because the Son himself refuses to be admired at a discount.

Is it right to pray to Jesus and sing to him, or only to the Father? It is right to do both. Ordinarily Christians pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, since through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18). But Stephen prayed to the Lord Jesus as he died (Acts 7:59), the first Christians called on the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and all heaven sings to the Lamb (Revelation 5:12–13). Since the Son is to be honoured just as the Father is, worship offered to him is not misdirected. It is exactly what the Father wants.

In a sentence. So that everyone will honour the Son as they honour the Father, for whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. Here is a quiet test. Listen to how you speak about Jesus when you are not in church: with colleagues, with family, in an argument. Most of us slide, without deciding to, into a register where he is a figure of great importance rather than a person to be worshipped. It is a defensible register, and it makes conversation easier. It is also the exact point at which honour begins to be withheld from the Father. Speak of him today as your Lord.

For worship. The Father has decreed that every knee shall bow to the Son and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, and he has decreed it to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). Honour given to the Son is never stolen from the Father; it is the glory the Father most delights to receive. There is no praise of Christ that needs holding back in case it overshoots. The man who sat tired on the wall of a well, and stood bound before a council, is owed the worship of the universe, and one day he will have it.

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. Hearing and believing is the way life is received, and the tense is present: already.

He does not come into judgment. No condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). Believers will stand before Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), but not to be condemned. This is the strongest assurance in the chapter. Not will be acquitted at the judgement: will not come into it. The case does not go to trial, because the one who would preside is the one already trusted, and the verdict was settled somewhere else.

But has passed from death to life. Perfect tense: has crossed over, and remains on the other side. From spiritual death (Ephesians 2:1) to eternal life, a complete change of state. Not is crossing. Not will cross when the accounts are settled. The border was crossed at a point in the past and the person is now on the other side. What this Gospel has said since chapter 3 in the present tense, whoever believes has eternal life, is here said in the past tense about the crossing itself. The believer is not a candidate for life awaiting a verdict. He is a person who has already emigrated.

An hour is coming, and is now here. Already happening. Two hours appear in these verses, and they are not the same hour. Here: now here. So these dead are not in graves. They are people walking around Jerusalem, going about their business spiritually dead and unaware of it, and some of them are about to hear a voice and start living. In verse 28 he will say an hour is coming and will not add and is now here, and that hour will involve tombs. Two resurrections, then: one going on in the room, one still ahead. The same voice does both.

When the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. The spiritually dead, who hear his voice in the gospel and are made alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). As Lazarus would hear his voice and come out of the tomb (11:43), the spiritually dead hear and live. Not that they decide to live; his voice gives life, and this is regeneration.

But Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. How can believers not come into judgement? Both are true (2 Corinthians 5:10). The believer does not come into judgement in the sense of condemnation (Romans 8:1); that verdict has been given. But his life and work will be reviewed for reward, and some will suffer loss though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What if I am frightened of the last day? Then hear this verse as Jesus meant it. There is a way of holding the faith in which the whole thing is provisional: a hope that the balance will come out right in the end, with a private suspicion that it may not. This verse forecloses it. If you have heard Christ’s word and believe the Father who sent him, the passing has happened. You will stand before Christ, but as one already acquitted, with your sins carried away by him. What remains for you is not a hearing but a homecoming. Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your feelings, but on the word of the Judge himself.

In a sentence. Whoever hears Jesus’ word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life, and the time has come when the spiritually dead hear the Son of God and live.

On a Tuesday. Say this verse aloud today, slowly, with your own name in it. And when you share the gospel with someone, remember whose voice gives life. Your task is to speak his word faithfully; his task is to raise the dead.

For worship. The voice that will one day empty the graves has already spoken into spiritual death and made the dead live. No accusation can reopen the case of one who believes, because the Judge has given his verdict, and he gave it at the cost of his own life: he came under judgement himself, so that those who hear him would not come into it. Blessed be the Son of God, whose word is life, and whose life was given so that our condemnation lies behind us for ever.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgement, because he is the Son of Man.

As the Father has life in himself. God is self-existent. He depends on nothing; life is his by nature. It is the highest thing said about God in the chapter, and it sounds like philosophy, so put it plainly. Everything that lives has life on loan. A tree has it from the soil and the light, an animal from what it eats, a man from his food and breath and the fact that his heart has not yet stopped, and every one of those supplies can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself means to be the one exception: to hold life not as a supply but as his own being, underived, with nothing behind it that could fail. Theologians call this aseity, from the Latin a se, from himself, and it belongs to God alone.

So he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. The Son too has life in himself: not borrowed, but his own (1:4). At first hearing this sounds like a contradiction, since a life that is granted would seem by definition not to be underived. The church thought long about this and arrived at the right place. Granted does not mean the Son once lacked it. It is not an event in time. The eternal Son receives life eternally from the Father, as the Son eternally comes from the Father (eternal generation). He is not a creature who was topped up. He is the Son, and what the Father is, the Son is. And as incarnate, he has it in his human nature too, to give to others.

And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man. The reason given is the last thing anyone would predict. Not because he is the Son of God, which is what the argument has been building. Because he is the Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away. But the plain sense is not lost in the allusion. As a man, he can judge humanity fairly, having lived as one of us (Hebrews 4:15; Acts 17:31). The one who will judge the human race was tired at a well, wept at a grave, was hungry and tempted, and knows from the inside what it costs to be one of the accused.

What difference does it make that God has life in himself? All the difference in the world. Because God depends on nothing, he cannot be worn out, run out or used up. He does not need you, and so his love for you is pure gift, not a deal. And because the Son has life in himself, the life he gives is not a borrowed supply that might run dry. It is his own inexhaustible life. Whoever is joined to him by faith is joined to the one source of life that can never fail, which is why Jesus can promise, because I live, you also will live (14:19).

In a sentence. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son life in himself, and authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. Everything you rely on today, your health, your income, your friends, your energy, is life on loan. Hold it gratefully and lightly. Draw your deepest life from the one who has it in himself.

For worship. The one who holds life in himself, and never borrowed a moment of it, took a body that could be killed. He did not need to. Nothing in him required feeding or resting or sustaining, and he consented to all three, and then to the loss of the whole of it. He had life in himself, and gave it away, and took it up again, and now gives it to whoever hears his voice.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement.

Do not marvel at this. He has just said that the spiritually dead are hearing his voice and living, which is astonishing enough, and his response to the astonishment is to say that it is the smaller of the two things. Wait until the graves. This time he says only that an hour is coming, not that it is now here: it is the last day.

When all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. The bodily resurrection of all the dead, righteous and wicked, at the end (Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Jesus will call, and every grave will open. Not only the believing dead or the notable dead: everyone who has ever been buried, in every century, in every unmarked place, in the sea and under the ash and in ground built over twice since. And the summons is a voice. Not only an angel with a trumpet, though there will be one. A voice, the voice of the man who stood in a Jerusalem colonnade and told someone to pick up a mat.

Those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. Both are raised in the body: the one to eternal life, the other to condemnation.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by good works. In John, the “good” is above all believing in Jesus (6:29: this is the work of God, that you believe in him). Good deeds are the fruit and evidence of saving faith, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Those who have truly believed will have lived differently.

Evidence, not currency. Read against the previous verses, where life comes to whoever hears his word and believes, this sentence cannot mean that the resurrection sorts people by their record. The good and the evil are evidence: the visible form of a life that had already crossed from death to life, or had not. Nobody is raised to life because their file was satisfactory. But nobody’s file is irrelevant either, and this Gospel will not let faith be a word said once with nothing following.

One resurrection or two? This verse speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs come out, the righteous and the wicked together (compare Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Premillennial Christians read Revelation 20 as teaching two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart, the first for believers and the second for the rest. The more likely reading is the one this verse gives: a single general resurrection at Christ’s return, with Revelation’s first resurrection referring to the new life believers already share with Christ.

What will the resurrection body be like? It will be your own body, raised, not a different one, just as Jesus’ risen body bore the marks of the nails (20:27). For believers it will be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), like Christ’s glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The unbelieving dead will also be raised bodily, to face judgement and conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). This is why the body matters in the Christian life: what you do with it now is done with something God intends to raise.

In a sentence. The time is coming when all the dead will hear his voice and rise, those who did good to life and those who did evil to judgement.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is not about performance. Ask what your life would look like to someone who watched it for a year without ever hearing you say anything about God. That is the level at which verse 29 operates. It is not asking for a score. It is asking whether the crossing has left any tracks. One day you will hear his voice from the grave. Are you ready for the resurrection of life?

For worship. Every grave that has ever been dug will be emptied by a sentence: the ones nobody remembers, the ones with nothing over them, the ones whose occupants have been forgotten so long that no living person knows a name to forget. All of them will hear a voice. And the voice will belong to a man who has been in a tomb himself, and came out, and knows the way. Blessed be the risen Lord, who holds the keys of death and Hades, and who will raise his people in glory.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgement is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.

I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge. The Son never acts apart from the Father, and so his judgement is perfectly just, because it is the Father’s.

Because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. Perfect submission (4:34; 6:38). That is the qualification for a judge: not superior intelligence but the total absence of self-interest. Every human court is compromised somewhere by what the judge wants. Here is one with nothing to gain.

If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true. The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself alone was not accepted in court (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus accepts the rule, and now calls his witnesses. The legal turn here is where this Gospel’s deepest structure comes to the surface. John the Baptist was introduced as a man who came to bear witness (1:7–8), and the vocabulary has never gone away. Now the case is formally opened, and what follows is a defence conducted according to the rules of evidence. Not true here means not legally admissible, rather than factually false.

But in 8:14 Jesus says his testimony about himself is true. Is that a contradiction? No; each answers a different question. Here he meets them on their own ground: you require corroboration, and you shall have it, and here are the witnesses. In chapter 8 he is answering a challenge to his knowledge, and his point is that he alone knows where he came from and where he is going, so his testimony, whatever a court makes of it, is accurate. One statement is about legal standing; the other is about truthfulness. He does not need corroboration to be right. He offers it because they need it to be persuaded.

He builds a case. He is under no obligation to argue. He is the Son who has just claimed authority to raise the dead and judge the world, and he builds a case as if he were a defendant with something to prove, because the men in front of him will move only on evidence, and he is prepared to give them evidence rather than stand on his dignity.

In a sentence. Jesus said he does nothing on his own, judging justly as he hears from the Father, and if he testified about himself alone his testimony would not count.

On a Tuesday. Seek God’s will, not your own. That is the path of true judgement. Before you form an opinion of someone today, ask what you stand to gain from it. A judgement with self-interest in it is already bent.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth will do right. He seeks nothing for himself and cannot be bribed, flattered or deceived. And this perfectly just Judge stooped to argue his case with sinners, offering evidence to men who were plotting his death, because he wanted them to believe. His justice is spotless, and his patience is beyond measuring.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.

There is another who bears witness about me. Some take the other witness to be John the Baptist (v. 33), but it is most likely the Father, the supreme witness, since verse 37 says the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me, and the sentence here has a solemnity that fits. The argument matters less than it seems.

And I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true. The Father cannot lie. And notice the settledness of the clause. He is not producing witnesses because he is uncertain and needs reassurance. There is a calm in that sentence which sits oddly beside the whole apparatus of a legal defence, and it is meant to. He knows. The case is being built for the benefit of people who do not.

The witnesses. Jesus now calls four witnesses, as in a trial: John the Baptist (vv. 33–35), his works (v. 36), the Father (vv. 37–38), and the Scriptures, including Moses (vv. 39–47).

There is another. There is a weight in the bare phrase that is easy to miss because it is so plain. He is standing alone in a hostile room. The disciples are not mentioned in this chapter at all; the healed man has just identified him to the authorities; nobody visible is on his side. He says: there is another. Not another party in the room, but another altogether. The corroboration comes from outside the building, from the one who sent him, and it does not depend on a single person present being persuaded.

How should I argue for the faith with someone who wants proof? From knowledge, not anxiety. Evidence is offered in Scripture constantly and without embarrassment; this Gospel is a marshalling of evidence, and says so at the end (20:30–31). So give reasons gladly: the eyewitness testimony, the empty tomb, fulfilled prophecy, the changed lives. But there is a way of arguing for Christ that has fear underneath it, and it communicates the fear rather than the case. Jesus never once sounds worried about the verdict. The truth does not depend on your winning the argument. Speak calmly, honestly and kindly, and leave the persuading to God.

In a sentence. Another testifies about Jesus, and his testimony is true.

On a Tuesday. If you have to hold a position alone today, in a family, at work, in a church that has gone somewhere you cannot follow, remember this sentence. It is not an encouragement to be stubborn. It is a statement about where the verdict actually comes from, made by a man about to be found guilty by every human authority he had.

For worship. Heaven is not neutral about the Son. The Spirit came down and remained on him at the Jordan, a voice from heaven answered him in Jerusalem (12:28), and on the third day the Father raised him from the dead. Every human court went against him, and the Father’s testimony stood. That verdict, given at the empty tomb, can never be overturned, and everyone who trusts the Son now lives under it.
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.

You sent to John. The delegation of 1:19. The first witness, and the reason he is admissible: they cannot dispute his standing, because they investigated him themselves. Priests and Levites were sent down from Jerusalem to find out who he was, and John told them, on the record, in front of their own officials. So Jesus is not appealing to a witness they might reject. He is producing the transcript of their own enquiry.

And he has borne witness to the truth. He testified that Jesus is the Lamb of God and Son of God (1:29, 34). Notice the tense: he has borne witness, and it stands. John’s testimony is still on the record, doing its work in a hearing he is not present at. He had said he must increase, but I must decrease, and by now the decreasing has gone a long way. He is not in the room. His witness is.

Not that the testimony that I receive is from man. Jesus does not depend on human testimony. He sets it aside in the same breath, and it would be a poor foundation if he rested on it, since the greatest man born of women is still a man.

But I say these things so that you may be saved. Even in conflict, Jesus seeks their salvation. He mentions John for their sake, because they respected him. Stop at that. He is under investigation by men who are already trying to work out how to kill him (v. 18). He is assembling a defence. And he says, in the middle of it, that the reason he is bothering is not to secure an acquittal but to secure them. It is not a courtroom manoeuvre. It is the disclosure of what the whole argument has been for. Every witness he calls is aimed at the salvation of the people conducting the prosecution, and he tells them so while they are conducting it. There is nothing else quite like it: a man on trial for his life, telling the court his defence is being offered for their benefit.

Does my witness matter if I never see results? Yes. Faithful testimony goes on working after the person who gave it can no longer give it: in rooms they never entered, in arguments they did not know were happening, long after they have been forgotten by everyone but God. John was in prison or dead when Jesus cited him. Your words to a child, a friend or a colleague may be called as evidence by the Spirit years from now. Speak truly, and leave the timing to God.

In a sentence. They had sent to John, who testified to the truth, and Jesus mentions it not because he needs human testimony, but so that they might be saved.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ hard words are spoken so that people may be saved. When you have to say something hard to someone this week, check your motive first. Are you speaking so that they may be saved, or so that you may be right?

For worship. The Lord pleads with his enemies. While they plotted his death, he argued for their life. That is the heart of the Saviour who came not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17), and who would die for his enemies (Romans 5:10). He wants the salvation of sinners more than his own vindication, and he still says to a hostile world, I say these things so that you may be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.

He was a burning and shining lamp. A lamp, not the light itself (1:8). The word is lychnos, an oil lamp, the ordinary household kind you carry into a room after dark. Not the sun, not a torch. This Gospel has been careful: John came to bear witness about the light; he was not the light. Here Jesus grants him the highest compliment available inside that limit. Burning: with zeal; shining: giving light. A lamp actually alight, which is more than can be said for much religious furniture. But still the thing you use until morning. And the tense is past: John was now in prison or dead.

And you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light. For a while: literally, for an hour. For a while they enjoyed John’s ministry, the excitement of a prophet (Matthew 3:5). The whole country went out to the Jordan; it was the religious event of the decade. And it lasted about as long as such things last. They did not take his message seriously, or follow where he pointed. Enthusiasm without repentance. And the tense makes it unbearable. The lamp had been carried into the room, and they had admired it, and it had been put out, and here stands the daylight it was lit for, and they are trying to work out how to kill him.

Reaction is not response. The mechanism has not changed. There is a way of consuming preaching as an experience: going out to hear a man who is genuinely alight, enjoying it, feeling something, discussing it afterwards with real warmth, and being at the end of the season exactly where you started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous. It feels like a response, and it is a reaction.

Is it wrong to have a favourite preacher? Not in itself. God gives gifts to his church, and it is right to thank him for preachers who help you. But the Corinthians turned admiration into parties, I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, and Paul rebuked them (1 Corinthians 3:4–7). The test of a good preacher is that he points away from himself to Christ, as John did, and the test of a good hearer is that he follows where the finger points. If you would stop going to church when your favourite preacher leaves, it may be the lamp you love and not the light.

In a sentence. John was a burning and shining lamp, and they were happy to enjoy his light for a while.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test. Think of a sermon or a book that genuinely moved you in the last two years. Now name one thing you do differently because of it. If nothing comes, that is not a reason for despair, but it is the exact condition this verse describes, and the people in it were not cynics. They were delighted. Enjoying a good preacher is not the same as obeying the message. Follow where the light points.

For worship. Christ is the light; every faithful preacher is only a lamp lit by him, burning for a while and then put out. The lamps pass, but the light of the world shines on, and the city to come has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. He lights lamps to lead us to himself, and he is himself the morning they were waiting for.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me.

The testimony that I have is greater than that of John. Better witnesses: first, the works that the Father has given him to accomplish, his signs and his whole ministry, culminating in the cross (17:4; 19:30). The phrasing is worth pressing. Not works he chose to perform as demonstrations, but works handed to him as an assignment, a list given by the Father to be finished. The same verb turned up at the well, when he said his food was to accomplish the Father’s work (4:34), and it will be echoed from the cross. The healing at the pool was not an improvisation. It was an item on a schedule, and so was every other sign in this book, and so was the last one.

Bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. The works show who he is (10:25, 37–38; 14:11). And they outrank the Baptist as evidence for a simple reason. John could only say what he believed; his testimony was a man’s word, and men have been wrong. The works are not statements at all. A man who had been on the ground for thirty-eight years is walking through Jerusalem carrying his bed, and the fact does not depend on anyone’s credibility. It simply stands there in the street, and either it happened or it did not.

And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. Perfect tense: a lasting testimony. When did it happen? He does not say here, and the Gospel offers several answers: the Spirit descending and remaining at the Jordan, which the Baptist saw and reported (1:32–34); the Scriptures, which he is about to name; and most simply the works themselves, since it is the Father who gives them.

A case that is not refused for lack of evidence. The stack is now three high and rising, and the point is cumulative. Each witness on its own could be argued with. Together they make the kind of case that is not refused for lack of evidence, which is exactly why the next verse turns from the evidence to the men, and stays there for the rest of the chapter.

Where can I see Jesus’ works today? In the written record first, given for this very purpose (20:31). But also in what he goes on doing by his Spirit through his church: sinners converted, drunkards made sober, enemies reconciled, the dying unafraid, the gospel spreading through every nation as he said it would. These are not new revelations, and they do not replace Scripture; but they are the living fruit of the finished work, and they bear witness too. Look for them, and tell others what you have seen.

In a sentence. Jesus has a greater testimony than John’s: the works the Father gave him, which show the Father sent him, and the Father’s own testimony.

On a Tuesday. Look at Jesus’ works. They testify that the Father sent him. Read one of the signs in John this week, slowly, and ask what it tells you about who he is.

For worship. Every work of Christ is the Father’s signature. The water made wine, the son healed at a word, the man on the mat, the bread in the wilderness, the blind man seeing, Lazarus walking out, and above all the empty tomb: each one says, this is the one I sent. And the greatest work of all was the one on the list’s last line, the work he finished on the cross. The Father gave the Son his works, and the Son accomplished every one.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.

His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen. This is the hinge of the discourse, and it should be felt as an insult before it is understood as a diagnosis. He is telling the most religiously accomplished men in the nation that they have never heard God’s voice, never seen his form, and do not have his word living in them: men whose entire lives were organised around the word of God, who had memorised it, argued it, taught it, and travelled to a feast in obedience to it. At Sinai, Israel heard God’s voice and saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12). But these leaders, despite their claims, do not truly know God. They have not heard his voice in the Scriptures, or seen his likeness, which is now visible in Jesus (14:9).

But Israel heard God’s voice at Sinai, and Moses saw his glory. What does Jesus mean? Jesus is not denying that; he is saying that these hearers have not truly heard or seen, since his word does not abide in them (v. 38). And no one has seen the Father as he is (1:18; Exodus 33:20); the appearances of God in the Old Testament were real but partial, and many believe they were appearances of the Son himself.

And you do not have his word abiding in you. They study it, but it does not live in them. The phrase looks ahead to the vine (15:4, 7). What these men do not have is not information about God, which they had in quantity, but God’s word taking up residence. It is possible to have the whole text and none of the tenancy.

For you do not believe the one whom he has sent. The proof. If they knew God’s word, they would recognise his Son. The word had not lodged in them, and the evidence is that when the Word of God stood in front of them they did not recognise him. That is not circular reasoning; it is the claim this Gospel is built on. The Father’s self-disclosure runs through the Son, so a relationship with God that bypasses Jesus is not a different route to the same place. It is not a route.

The trial has changed sides. It opened with Jesus in the dock producing witnesses. Somewhere in the last few verses the parties have swapped places, and the men who convened the hearing are now the ones being examined. And the finding against them is not that they weighed the evidence and reached the wrong conclusion. It is that the evidence was never the problem.

Why do good arguments sometimes change nothing? Because the difficulty is not always in the evidence. Anyone who has argued about the faith with someone they love knows the experience of watching a good case land on nothing. It is tempting to conclude that a better argument would have done it. Sometimes that is true, and the argument is worth improving. But this verse says there is a condition in which no quantity of evidence will be enough, because the problem lies in the heart. Knowing that keeps a person praying for someone, and not merely preparing for the next conversation. Only God can open the heart (Acts 16:14).

In a sentence. They had never heard the Father’s voice or seen his form, and his word did not live in them, because they did not believe the one he sent.

On a Tuesday. Does God’s word abide in you? Then you will recognise and believe his Son. Choose one verse today and carry it with you, thinking about it through the day, so that the word does not merely pass through you but takes up residence.

For worship. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known. The invisible Father, whose voice no sinner could bear and whose form no eye has seen, has shown his face in Jesus Christ. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He has not left us to guess at him: he has spoken by his Son, and by his word he comes to dwell in us.

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.

You search the Scriptures. They studied the Old Testament with great diligence, memorising, debating, counting letters. They knew which word stood at the centre of the Torah. Nobody has ever handled a text more carefully. They were serious Bible students.

Command or statement? It can be read as a command, Search the Scriptures, as the King James Version has it, and searching is rightly commended elsewhere (Acts 17:11). But the context favours a statement: they were searching, and missing the one the Scriptures spoke of.

Because you think that in them you have eternal life. They thought that studying the law and keeping it would give them life. Rabbis said: the more study of the law, the more life. The sentence turns on a preposition they got wrong: in them. The life was understood to be located in the text, obtainable by handling it, so that a sufficiently thorough student would end up with it. Jesus does not deny that the Scriptures give life. He denies the address.

And it is they that bear witness about me. The purpose of Scripture is to point to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). The whole Old Testament testifies to him. The Scriptures are the fourth witness in his case, and a witness points away from himself.

Yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life. The tragedy: Bible study without coming to Christ. Life is not in the Bible itself, but in the one to whom it points. They searched for life in the book, and missed the life standing in front of them. The problem was not their mind but their will: “you refuse”. Not you cannot, not you have not understood: you refuse. Men bent over scrolls for a lifetime, tracing every promise of the one who was to come, and the one who was to come stands in the room, saying so, having just healed a man in front of them. The distance between the text and the person was about four feet, and they would not cross it.

How does you refuse to come fit with No one can come to me unless the Father draws him? The inability is not that people want to come and are prevented, but that their wills are bound by love of themselves and their own glory (v. 44). They cannot because they will not, and that is why they are responsible. Only the Father’s drawing changes the will (6:44).

Am I in danger of reading the Bible like this? This is aimed at people who read their Bibles, so it is better felt than pointed at someone else. It is entirely possible to conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system: to enjoy tracing themes, resolving difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage finally coming clear, and for the whole exercise to end in itself. The pleasure is real; it feels like devotion; and it can go on for years without once arriving at a person. The remedy is not to study less but to study prayerfully, asking at every passage: what does this show me of Christ, and how will I come to him because of it?

In a sentence. They studied the Scriptures thinking that in them they had eternal life, but the Scriptures testify about Jesus, and they refused to come to him for life.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it takes about ten seconds. After the last passage you studied, did you end up knowing something, or wanting him? Both can be good. Only one is what the text was for. Read your Bible to come to Christ. Bible study that does not lead you to him misses the point.

For worship. The Bible is not the destination; it is the road, and every road in it leads to Christ. From the first promise in Eden to the last prayer of Revelation, the Scriptures are one long testimony to the Son. God did not give us his word as a puzzle to master but as a witness, and the one it points to stands at the end of every page, as he once stood before the scholars who searched them, saying, come to me and have life.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.

I do not receive glory from people. Jesus does not seek human approval or praise. He seeks his Father’s glory (7:18; 8:50). This first sentence explains why he can afford to say the second. He is not fishing. He has no stake in their good opinion, so his assessment of them is not coloured by what he needs from them, and a man who wants nothing from you is the only one who can tell you the truth about yourself.

But I know that you do not have the love of God within you. Love for God, or God’s love. The Greek permits both, and they are probably not to be forced apart, since in this Gospel the two are never far from each other. Despite their religiousness, they did not love God. If they did, they would love the one he sent (8:42). The diagnosis is not about their intellect but their affections. They are not mainly failing a logical test; they are failing a love test.

The most frightening sentence in the chapter. It is frightening precisely because these men would have passed every other test. Attendance, orthodoxy, knowledge of the text, moral seriousness, willingness to travel for a feast: all in order. What was missing does not show up on any of those instruments. And it explains the whole chapter. They had watched a man paralysed for thirty-eight years get up and walk, and their first and only response was a rule about carrying. Nothing in them leapt. A person who loves God is not able to watch God do something and feel only procedural concern; the loving gets in the way. Their reaction was not a failure of information. It was the accurate reading of an instrument that registered nothing because there was nothing to register.

What if I fear this describes me? Then take an honest comfort from it. The men in this passage were entirely untroubled by the question. The very anxiety a verse like this produces in you is a form of caring, and caring is not what is being diagnosed here. And the remedy, if it is needed, is not to work up an affection. Love for God is not manufactured by an effort of will. It is what happens when a person actually sees him, which is precisely what Jesus spent this chapter offering. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Look at his love for you in Christ, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5).

In a sentence. Jesus did not seek human praise, and he knew they did not have the love of God in them.

On a Tuesday. Religious activity is not the same as love for God. Do you love him? Notice what makes your heart leap: news of God at work, or only news that affects you. Ask him today to make you glad in what gladdens him.

For worship. The Son of God needed no one’s applause. He lived wholly for his Father’s glory, and in him we see what it is to love God with all the heart. And the love these men lacked is the very love he came to pour into empty hearts. He searches the heart, and he does not merely expose its coldness; he warms it with his own love.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?

I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. He comes with his Father’s authority, representing him, and he is rejected: his own people did not receive him (1:11).

If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. A prediction that has been fulfilled so often it is almost dull. False messiahs, who came on their own authority, were often welcomed. Josephus records many. In AD 132, Simon bar Kokhba was hailed as Messiah by Rabbi Akiba and led a disastrous revolt. People prefer leaders who flatter them. The man who arrives sent, accountable, pointing away from himself, is resisted. The man whose warrant is himself gets a hearing. The first requires submission to someone the follower did not choose; the second flatters the follower’s judgement.

How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another. The root of their unbelief: love of human praise. To believe in Jesus would cost them their reputation (12:42–43). Glory here means reputation, the opinion others hold of you. So the sentence describes a closed economy. These men held a currency they issued to each other: standing, deference, the seat at the front, the title in the street, the respect of colleagues who were the only people qualified to grant it. And that currency had a fatal property. It could only be earned from the people inside the system, which means it could only be kept by not leaving. Belief in Jesus would have cost every one of them everything the system paid. A man cannot pursue two kinds of honour issued by different authorities that exclude each other. He will take the one he is nearer to.

And do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? God’s approval is the only honour that matters. Notice the way out, in the same verse. He does not tell them to want no approval at all. He tells them they are seeking it from a bankrupt issuer. The glory that comes from the only God is real, and Christ will one day say to his servants, well done.

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely. Scripture values a good name (Proverbs 22:1), and elders must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). What is wrong is when people’s opinion becomes the thing you live for, so that it decides what you will say and do about Christ. The fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not to become careless of others, but to care more about God’s approval, which in Christ you already have, freely. Once you are secure in his, you can bear the loss of theirs.

In a sentence. Jesus came in his Father’s name and they rejected him, though they would accept someone coming in his own name, for they could not believe while they sought praise from each other rather than from the only God.

On a Tuesday. Here is the sharpest test in the chapter. Think of a decision you would make differently if nobody you respected ever found out: what you would say in a meeting, which opinion you would voice, whether you would mention Christ in a particular room. The gap between what you would do observed and unobserved is the exact size of the account you hold in the currency of verse 44. Whose praise do you seek? Love of human approval can keep you from Christ.

For worship. The Son came in his Father’s name and made himself of no reputation, despising the shame of the cross. He refused the glory men offered and received the glory the Father gave, and now he shares it with those who trust him: the glory that you have given me I have given to them (17:22). The praise of the only God is the only praise that lasts, and in Christ he has already said to his people, beloved.

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.

Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. Jesus does not need to. The reversal here is complete. They convened this hearing. They opened with a charge about a mat, escalated to a charge of blasphemy, and have been the prosecution throughout. Now the defendant says he will not prosecute. For one second it sounds like mercy, and then the sentence finishes.

There is one who accuses you: Moses. Moses, their great hero, the giver of the law they trusted, will be their prosecutor. Their own counsel is their prosecutor. The authority they invoked against him, the name that gave them standing, the badge of the whole system: Moses is bringing the case. The law they thought would save them will condemn them (Romans 3:19–20). Moses is the one on whom they had set their hope of salvation.

For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me. Moses wrote of Christ: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the sacrifices (Leviticus), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18). To reject Jesus is to reject Moses. And the claim is larger than a few predictions that, correctly identified, refer to Jesus, though there are such. It is that the whole body of his writing was about him. The lamb whose blood on the doorposts turned the destroyer aside. The bronze serpent lifted on a pole. The tabernacle and the glory that filled it. The priest who went in with blood once a year. The rock in the wilderness that gave water. Each was written down by a man who saw only part of what he was describing.

A dispute about what Moses was for. So the disagreement in this room is not between a Jewish teacher and a Christian innovation. It is a disagreement about what Moses was for, and Jesus does not concede an inch of him. He does not say Moses was a preliminary stage now set aside. He claims Moses as his own witness, stands on him, and tells the men holding the scrolls that they have misread the author they built their lives on.

Did Moses really write the first five books? Jesus treats it as settled that Moses wrote (compare Mark 12:26; Luke 24:27, 44), and he means the books of the law. Where did Moses write of him? Beyond the pictures already named, in the ruler from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and above all in the prophet like Moses: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me (Deuteronomy 18:15).

In a sentence. Jesus said he would not need to accuse them, for Moses, in whom they hoped, accuses them, since if they believed Moses they would believe Jesus, for Moses wrote about him.

On a Tuesday. There is a warning here for anyone who reads Scripture at all. It is possible to take a book God gave to point somewhere and turn it into a fortress: to use it to confirm what you already hold, to settle disputes with people you already disagree with, to establish standing among those who read it the same way. These men did that with Moses, sincerely, and when the subject of the book walked in, the book was what they used against him. Read the books of Moses looking for Christ. He is there.

For worship. The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Every lamb on every altar, every drop of blood on every doorpost, every word of the prophet from the mountain, was pointing to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. And the curse that Moses pronounced on all who break the law, Christ bore himself, becoming a curse for us. He is the Saviour of whom Moses wrote, who fulfils the law and redeems those who could never keep it.

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?

If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? They claimed to honour Moses, but did not truly believe what he wrote. If they will not believe the written Scriptures they revere, they will not believe Jesus’ spoken words. Faith in Scripture and faith in Christ stand or fall together. Jesus places his own words alongside Scripture. The chapter ends on a question, and it is left unanswered, which is the point, since the answer would have to come from the men it was asked of. The logic is simple. Moses wrote of Christ. They do not believe Christ. Therefore they do not, in any sense that matters, believe Moses, whatever they think they are doing when they read him.

The problem is not the medium. People who will not be persuaded by Scripture are not waiting for a better delivery. The modern hope that if the message were only presented more attractively the resistance would give way is answered, fairly gently, here. They had the writings. They had the works. They had the Baptist. They had the Father’s testimony. And they had the man himself, available for questions, doing the works in front of them.

Stand back and see the whole chapter. It opened with a man who could not get himself to the water, who had nobody, and who did not even know the name of the one who healed him, and he was made whole. It closes with the best-taught, best-connected, most scripturally literate men in the nation, who had every witness heaven could produce, and who would not come. Between the two lies the sentence that explains both: the Son gives life to whom he will.

Should I trust the Old Testament as much as the words of Jesus? Yes. Jesus puts Moses’ writings and his own words side by side, and treats doubting one as the road to doubting the other. He believed the Old Testament to be the word of God, quoted it as settling arguments, and said Scripture cannot be broken (10:35). The whole Bible is one book with one Author and one subject. The Old Testament is not a lesser Bible to be outgrown; it is the testimony to Christ that Jesus himself used. Read both Testaments with the same trust, because the Lord you love trusted both.

In a sentence. If they did not believe Moses’ writings, how would they believe Jesus’ words?

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself trusting the parts of the Bible you like and quietly doubting the rest, take this verse as a warning. Choose a passage of the Old Testament you find hard, and read it this week asking how it points to Christ.

For worship. The Scriptures and the Son speak with one voice, because they have one Author, and what that voice says is: this is my Son. Moses wrote, and the one he wrote of stood in the temple and was not believed by the men who held the scrolls. Yet the Son they refused still gives life, and he gives it through the very writings they searched and could not read. Every page now opens onto him, and whoever comes to him through them finds the life those pages were written to bring.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.<sup>44</sup>How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?<sup>45</sup>Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.<sup>46</sup>For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.<sup>47</sup>But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
5.overview:
The third sign takes place in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda, whose five colonnades archaeologists have uncovered near the Sheep Gate. Among the crowds of sick people waiting for the water to stir lies a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well, then tells him to pick up his mat and walk, and he does. But it is the Sabbath, and the authorities challenge the man for carrying his mat. When they learn it was Jesus, they begin to persecute him, and Jesus answers, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” They understand him exactly: he is calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God, and they now seek to kill him.

Jesus’ reply (vv. 19–47) is one of the richest statements of his identity in the Gospels. The Son does nothing on his own, but whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Like the Father he gives life to whom he will, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father. Whoever hears his word and believes has eternal life now and has passed from death to life; and an hour is coming when all the dead will hear his voice and rise, to life or to judgment. Then, as in a courtroom, Jesus calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, and the Scriptures. His hearers search the Scriptures for life but refuse to come to the one they speak of; they seek glory from one another, not from God. Moses himself, whom they trust, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee, followed by a huge crowd drawn by his healings. He goes up a hillside with his disciples. Passover is near. Seeing the crowd approach, he asks Philip where they could buy bread for them all, to test him, since he already knows what he will do. Philip calculates that even two hundred days’ wages would not buy each a mouthful. Andrew mentions a boy with five small barley loaves and two fish, but what use are they? Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men. He takes the loaves, gives thanks and distributes them, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. When all are satisfied, he tells the disciples to collect the leftovers so that nothing is wasted, and they fill twelve baskets. Seeing the sign, the people declare him the Prophet who was to come, and Jesus, knowing they mean to seize him and make him king, withdraws alone to the hills. At evening the disciples set off by boat for Capernaum in the dark, without him. A strong wind whips up the lake. After rowing three or four miles they see Jesus walking on the water towards them and are terrified, but he tells them it is he and not to fear. They gladly take him aboard, and at once the boat reaches the shore.
verseByVerse.theology: The feeding miracle and the sea-walking are connected signs: together they reveal Jesus as the one who commands both provision and chaos, who is both the Lord of creation and the bread of life. 'It is I' on the water (v. 20) is followed at once by the great 'I am' discourses of John's Gospel, beginning with 'I am the bread of life' in the discourse that follows. The crowd that wants to make Jesus an earthly king misunderstands the sign: they want the bread without the Bread-giver, the miracle without the meaning, the provision without the person.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' plan to divide the available food among five thousand is not faithlessness but the appropriate response of stewards who account for what they have. Jesus's question to Philip — 'where are we to buy bread?' — is a test, not a request for information. The walking on water is the most theologically revealing of the nature miracles: Jesus walks on the sea, which in the Old Testament is the domain of chaos and the realm only God can command (Job 38:16; Ps. 77:19).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.

Meaning first. John 6 is the chapter of the bread. Near Passover, on a hillside by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus feeds five thousand men from a boy’s five barley loaves and two fish, and the crowd tries to make him king by force. That night he walks on the sea to his disciples and says, I am; do not be afraid. The next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, he explains the sign: he himself is the bread of life, the true bread from heaven of which the manna was only a shadow, and whoever comes to him will never hunger. All whom the Father gives him will come; he will cast out no one who comes, will lose none of them, and will raise them up on the last day. The bread he will give is his flesh, given in death for the life of the world, and to eat his flesh and drink his blood is to receive him crucified by faith. The chapter that opens with the largest crowd in the Gospel ends with many disciples walking away, and with Peter’s confession: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.

The setting. Chapter 6 contains two signs (the feeding of the five thousand and the walking on the water) and the great discourse on the bread of life. It ends with many disciples leaving Jesus. A turning point in his Galilean ministry.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Before anything else, a fact worth having in hand: the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus recorded in all four Gospels. Not the raising of Lazarus, not the walking on water, not any particular healing: this one. Whatever else the four writers chose differently, every one of them thought a hillside, a boy’s lunch and a crowd sitting in the grass had to be in the account.

The Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore around AD 20 and named after the emperor Tiberius. John explains for readers outside Palestine.

Because they saw the signs. They followed for the miracles, not for who he was (v. 26). They had watched him make ill people well and wanted to see more of it, which is an entirely reasonable thing to want and is not yet faith. John is setting something up for the reader. This chapter opens with the largest crowd in the Gospel and closes with many of them gone. Between the two lies no scandal, no failure and no change of policy, only a sermon. The crowd does not shrink because Jesus disappoints them. It shrinks because he explains himself.

He fed them anyway. One word of fairness to the crowd before the chapter turns on them. They were following for the wrong reason, and he fed them anyway. He did not begin by correcting their motives; he began by giving them lunch. The rebuke comes the next morning, after the meal.

Is it wrong if I first came to Christ for what I needed from him? No; almost nobody arrives for adequate reasons. People come because something hurts, a marriage is failing, a child is ill, or the fear of dying has become concrete, and every one of those is a version of wanting the loaves. It is where practically everyone starts, and this chapter does not despise it. Jesus received the crowd and fed them. What he will not do is leave anyone there. The question is not why you first came, but whether you are now coming to him for himself.

In a sentence. Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, followed by a large crowd who had seen his healing signs.

On a Tuesday. Why do you follow Jesus: for what he can do for you, or for who he is? Make a list of the reasons you go to church and pray. Then ask how many of them would still stand if he gave you nothing more than himself.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest fed a crowd that had come for the wrong reasons. He is kind to the ungrateful and generous to the half-hearted, and he meets us where we are in order to lead us where we could never go alone. Bless the patient Shepherd who feeds the flock before he teaches it, and who will not rest until we love him for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.

Jesus went up on the mountain. The hills east of the lake. Like Moses going up the mountain (Exodus 19; 24). The whole chapter will echo the exodus: the Passover, the mountain, the bread in the wilderness, the crossing of the sea, the grumbling.

And there he sat down with his disciples. The posture of a teacher. Going up a mountain and sitting to teach is what Moses did and what a rabbi does, and Matthew opens the Sermon on the Mount with exactly this pairing (Matthew 5:1). But what follows on this mountain is not a sermon. It is a meal. The teaching about it does not come until the next day, in a synagogue. That is the order the whole chapter runs on: the bread first and the explanation second, and the crowd that was delighted by the first is offended by the second. It is possible to enjoy what Christ does and find what he says intolerable, and this chapter is the demonstration.

Withdrawal at both ends. He goes up the mountain with his disciples before the crowd arrives, and at the end of the day he goes up the same mountain by himself after they have gone (v. 15). The most public act of his ministry has a retreat on either side of it, and Mark tells us the second one was for prayer (Mark 6:46). The Gospels do not make a point of it; they simply keep recording it, the way one records something habitual.

How can I find time to be alone with God when life is so full? Jesus’ days were fuller than yours, with crowds pressing on him and needs everywhere, and he still withdrew. It was not a luxury for him but a habit. Begin small and regular: a set time, a set place, a Bible and a few minutes of prayer, even if it is in the car before work or after the children are asleep. Protect it as you would a meeting with someone you love. The aim is not a perfect routine but real fellowship with the Father, which feeds everything else you do.

In a sentence. Jesus went up a mountain and sat down with his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Take time to sit with Jesus, away from the crowd. Before the busiest part of your day, find ten minutes on your own mountain.

For worship. The Son who sat on the mountain as teacher is greater than Moses, who climbed Sinai to receive the law. Moses spoke what he was given; Christ is the Word himself. And the Lord who was about to do the greatest public sign of his ministry first sat quietly with his friends. Bless the Saviour who is mighty in public and tender in private, and who still calls his disciples apart to be with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, "Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip: where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?

Now the Passover was at hand. This is the second Passover John mentions (2:13; 11:55); the Passover setting colours the whole chapter. Passover recalled the exodus, when God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness. And at Passover the next year, Jesus would give his body and blood (vv. 51–56). It is the feast of bread: unleavened bread eaten in haste, a lamb killed, and behind it the memory of a nation fed in a desert with bread that came down every morning for forty years. Everything in this chapter, the wilderness setting, the bread, the manna argument, the flesh given for the life of the world, stands inside that feast, and John tells us so before a loaf is broken.

Seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him. Jesus sees the need. And notice who moves first. Nobody in this story requests a meal. There is no petition, no crowd complaining of hunger; in Matthew and Mark the disciples even suggest sending everyone away. The initiative is entirely his, taken while the crowd is still walking toward him with no idea it is about to be fed.

Jesus said to Philip. Philip was from Bethsaida, nearby (1:44); he would know where food could be bought. Jesus asks the local man.

Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat? An echo of Moses: Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? (Numbers 11:13). And note the pronoun: we. He does not say they. He includes Philip in a responsibility Philip has not accepted and could not discharge. That is how the test is set: not by asking Philip to do the impossible, but by quietly making the crowd’s hunger his problem too.

Does Jesus expect me to meet needs I cannot possibly meet? He expects you to care about them and to bring them to him. He does not expect you to supply what only he can. The pronoun we means Philip is included in the work, not left to do it alone. When you see a need too big for you, the hungry, the lonely, the lost, do not look away and do not despair. Bring it to Christ in prayer, offer what you have, and do the part he gives you. He knows what he will do.

In a sentence. With Passover near, Jesus saw a large crowd coming and asked Philip where they could buy bread for them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sees the needs around you. He asks what you will do. Name one need near you that you have quietly decided is not your problem, and ask him what your part is.

For worship. Before we ask, he sees; before we know we are hungry, he has planned the meal. The Lord of the Passover lifted his eyes on a crowd of strangers and took their hunger as his own concern. Bless the God whose care runs ahead of our prayers, and who sets his people at his table before they have thought to look for bread.
verseByVerse.note: This is the second Passover John mentions; the Passover setting prepares for Jesus’ words about bread and his flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him: two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.

He said this to test him. To stretch Philip’s faith. Would he look to his own resources, or to Jesus?

For he himself knew what he would do. Jesus is never at a loss. John’s bracket is one of the kindest in the Gospel. The outcome was never in question. The bread was going to arrive whatever Philip said. The test was not an audition he could fail at the cost of the crowd’s dinner. It was a question asked by someone who had already decided, so that the man being asked might find out what was in him.

Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was about eight months’ wages. Philip calculated, and despaired. He looked at the problem, not at Jesus. His answer deserves to be heard fairly, because he is often treated as the failure of the passage. He has made a rapid estimate of the crowd, the price of bread and the common purse, and concluded that even that sum would not give each a little. The sum is correct. His problem is not his arithmetic. It is that he was asked where and answered how much. The question was about a source; he replied with a budget.
