A man who converts every question about God’s provision into a question about available resources will always arrive at the same answer, and it will always be right, and always beside the point.

Why does God test us if he already knows what is in us? Not to inform himself, but to show us, and to strengthen us. The tests God sets are not entrance examinations with the result pending. He knows what he will do. The examination exists so that the person taking it discovers where his own arithmetic runs out, which is knowledge he needs and cannot get any other way. Testing also proves and refines faith, as gold is refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). And God never tests in order to make his children fall (James 1:13); he tests in order to make them stand.

In a sentence. Jesus asked to test Philip, already knowing what he would do, and Philip answered that eight months’ wages would not buy enough for each to have a bite.

On a Tuesday. When God tests you, look to him, not to your calculations. Is there a situation you have been treating as a budget problem rather than a question about God? Do the sums, by all means; then ask where the bread will come from.

For worship. The Lord is never at a loss. He knows the end from the beginning, and his plans are formed before our panic begins. Even his tests are kindness, for he tests only those he means to feed. Bless the God who knows what he will do, and who teaches us, gently, to stop counting denarii and start looking at him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: where am I to get meat?

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?

Andrew. Again bringing someone to Jesus (1:41; 12:22).

A boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. Only John mentions the boy and the barley. Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor, coarser than wheat, what you ate when wheat was beyond you. This is a child’s packed lunch of the plainest kind, and it is the only food in the story. The fish were probably small dried or pickled fish.

The Elisha story underneath. An echo of Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). A man brought Elisha twenty barley loaves, and Elisha said, give to the men, that they may eat; his servant objected, how can I set this before a hundred men?; and they ate and had some left. Barley loaves, an objection about the ratio, a command to distribute, food left over. Andrew’s sentence is almost the servant’s sentence, and any Jew who knew his Scriptures would have felt it. What differs is the scale: Elisha fed a hundred from twenty loaves; here it is five thousand from five. Jesus is greater than Elisha.

But what are they for so many? Andrew brought what there was, even though it seemed useless. That is all Jesus asks. Notice what Andrew actually does, because he is easy to patronise for the second half of his sentence. He is the only person in the passage who has gone and looked. Philip did the sum; Andrew went through the crowd and found out what was actually there. And he brings it, knowing it is absurd, saying so out loud, and bringing it anyway. That is not weak faith. It is the posture the chapter requires: hands out, holding something insufficient, with no idea what will happen.

What if what I have to offer seems ridiculously small? Then you are in good company: a boy with five cheap loaves. Jesus does not ask for enough; he asks for what you have. Your few hours, your small gift, your weak prayers, your stumbling words to a friend: put them in his hands and let him decide what they are for. The miracle did not begin with abundance but with an offering. Nothing in the Gospels suggests Jesus wanted the disciples to feel confident. He wanted the loaves.

In a sentence. Andrew said there was a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, but asked what use they were for so many.

On a Tuesday. Bring what little you have to Jesus. He can multiply it. Think of one small thing you have held back because it seemed too little to matter, and offer it to him today.

For worship. The Lord who fed Israel in the desert and multiplied bread through Elisha took a child’s lunch into his hands, and five thousand ate. He delights to use the small, the cheap and the overlooked, so that the glory is plainly his. Bless the Christ who does not despise the day of small things, and who turns barley into a banquet.
verseByVerse.note: Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: have the people sit down. Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.

Have the people sit down. Recline, as at a banquet.

Now there was much grass in the place. Spring, at Passover. Green pastures (Psalm 23:2). The good shepherd feeds his flock. It is the sort of detail nobody invents, and it does two things at once. It dates the scene, since grass in Galilee means spring, and it turns a hillside into a dining room. Mark, telling the same story, says they sat down in groups on the green grass, and that Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34). Four chapters later Jesus will say, I am the good shepherd, and this hillside is where the picture was first acted out.

About five thousand in number. Men; with women and children, many more (Matthew 14:21).

And when he had given thanks. Eucharistēsas, the word the church would take for its central meal. John mentions only thanksgiving, not breaking, perhaps pointing to the Lord’s Supper, which he does not otherwise describe. Jesus does what any Jewish head of a household did before eating, and presumably says what they said: blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. It is the most ordinary sentence in Jewish life. He says it over five loaves in front of five thousand people, and it turns out to be true in a way it had never been before.

He distributed them. Jesus himself gives. The other Gospels say the disciples distributed.

As much as they wanted. Abundance. Not a token. Not enough to go round, not a small piece each, which is what Philip had calculated could not be managed. As much as they wanted: every person on that hillside eating until they stopped wanting more, which almost none of them would have done at home.

Should Christians still give thanks before meals? Yes, and this verse is one reason why. Jesus gave thanks before he gave the bread, and Paul says that everything created by God is good and is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A short prayer at the table is not a superstition or a formality. It is a confession that every meal comes from the Father’s hand, and it keeps us from eating like the crowd, who enjoyed the bread and never looked up at the giver.

In a sentence. Jesus had the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, gave thanks for the loaves and fish, and distributed as much as they wanted.

On a Tuesday. At every meal today, give thanks deliberately, and name one thing on the plate you would not have if God had not provided it.

For worship. Christ gives as much as you want of himself. Come and eat. He is the Shepherd who makes his sheep lie down in green pastures and spreads a table before them; he is the host who never rations his grace. Bless the Lord whose giving has no bottom, who satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry with good things.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples: gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost. So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.

When they had eaten their fill. Satisfied, fully.

Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost. Only John records this command. God’s abundance is not wasteful. And “that nothing may be lost” anticipates v. 39: I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. The fragments picture the people Christ will not lose.

Extravagance and care. This is the strangest instruction in the story, and it tells you most about him. He has just produced food out of nothing. There is no reason of scarcity to save the scraps; the man who made the meal could make another. And the first thing he says after five thousand have eaten their fill is: pick up the bits, so that nothing is lost. Extravagance and carefulness are not opposites in him. The same person who gave them as much as they wanted will not have a fragment trodden into the grass. We tend to assume that generosity implies indifference to detail, that a being who can make more will not much mind what happens to this. He minds.

The word lost. The verb is apollymi, to be destroyed or lost, and it runs through the rest of the chapter and out into the Gospel. In a few verses Jesus will say the Father’s will is that he should lose nothing of all the Father has given him (v. 39). In chapter 10 no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand. In chapter 18, when the soldiers come, John says this fulfilled the word: of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (18:9). So the barley crusts in the grass are the first instalment of a promise about people. The one who sends men round a hillside so that a scrap of a poor child’s lunch is not wasted is the one who will not lose a single person the Father has given him, and the second sentence is easier to believe once the first has been watched.

Twelve baskets. More left over than at the start. One for each apostle, and perhaps for the twelve tribes of Israel. They began with five loaves and finished with twelve full baskets: the arithmetic of the kingdom, where what is handed over comes back larger than it went in.

What if I feel like a scrap, not worth keeping? Then this verse was written for you. Jesus sent his disciples to gather fragments, crumbs that anyone else would have let lie in the grass, so that nothing would be lost. If he cares for crusts, he cares far more for the people the Father has given him. Your worth to him does not depend on how whole or impressive you feel, but on his love and his promise. He does not lose what is his.

In a sentence. When everyone had eaten enough, Jesus had the disciples gather the leftovers so nothing would be lost, and they filled twelve baskets.

On a Tuesday. God’s generosity overflows, but he wastes nothing. Use his gifts carefully. Look at your money, food and time this week and ask where you are being careless with what he has given.

For worship. Not one fragment lost. The Lord who gathers crumbs into baskets gathers his people into his arms, and none of them will fall through his fingers. His generosity is boundless and his care is exact. Bless the Shepherd who counts his sheep and the Father who gave them, and the promise that on the last day not one will be missing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said: this is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world! Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world! “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses gave manna; this prophet gives bread. They are right, but they misunderstand. Their theology was correct: they had identified the man. Being right about who Jesus is and wrong about what he is for is not a small error corrected by more information. It sent five thousand people up a hill with a crown and no idea what they were doing.

They were about to come and take him by force to make him king. A political Messiah, to lead a revolt against Rome. Passover, the feast of liberation, heightened nationalist fervour. They wanted a king who would feed them and free them, on their terms. The verb is violent: harpazein, to seize, to snatch, the word used of a wolf carrying off a sheep (10:12). This is not a crowd offering him a crown. It is a crowd intending to make him take one. He is in real danger here, not from the authorities but from an adoring mob who have decided what he is for.

Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself. He refused. His kingdom is not of this world (18:36). The same temptation Satan offered (Matthew 4:8–10): a crown without a cross. Matthew and Mark say he went to pray (Mark 6:46). And what he refuses is not the kingship. He is the King, and he will say so to Pilate. He refuses a kingship on their terms: a bread-king, installed by acclaim, who solves the food problem and then the Roman problem and never goes near a cross. Given what he had come to do, the most dangerous thing available to him that afternoon was popularity. The largest crowd of his ministry wanted to crown him, and he walked away from them up a hill in the dark to talk with his Father.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to solve my problems? It is not wrong to bring him your problems; he invites it. It is wrong to try to make him king on your terms, a Saviour who exists to deliver your agenda. The crowd wanted bread and political freedom and no cross. Jesus will give far more than they asked, but in his way: through his death, by his Spirit, for eternity. When he does not do what you want, it is not because he cannot, but because he is King, and his plans are better.

In a sentence. Seeing the sign, the people declared him the Prophet, and Jesus, knowing they meant to force him to be king, withdrew alone to the mountain.

On a Tuesday. Don’t try to make Jesus the king of your agenda. Let him be king on his terms. And here is an uncomfortable test for anyone doing anything for God: think of the response you would most like your work to receive, and ask whether it would help or hinder what the work is actually for. There are successes that are failures at the level that matters.

For worship. He would not be crowned by a crowd, because he had come to be crowned with thorns. He refused the throne of bread so that he could take the throne of the cross, and from there the throne of heaven. Bless the King whose kingdom is not of this world, who chose the Father’s will over the people’s applause, and who reigns now over all things for the good of those he died to save.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would lead a revolt against Rome.

parallels.desc: my kingdom is not of this world

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.

His disciples went down to the sea. Mark says Jesus made them go (Mark 6:45), perhaps to remove them from the crowd’s political excitement.

It was now dark. In John, darkness often has symbolic weight (1:5; 3:2; 13:30).

And Jesus had not yet come to them. Alone in the dark, without Jesus. Two facts sit side by side, and the Gospel does not soften either. They are exactly where they should be, doing exactly what they were told. And it is dark, and he is not there. John does not write that Jesus had not come and therefore it was dark, as though the absence caused the darkness. He lays down two separate facts flat, with no explanation offered for either. Most Christian accounts of a dark stretch reach at once for a reason: there must be sin in it, or a lesson, or a failure of faith. Sometimes there is. Here there is nothing of the kind, and John does not supply one.

Not yet. The last words make it bearable. John writes sixty years later and knows how the night ended. He puts the yet in deliberately, and it is the only comfort in the sentence: not that the darkness is short, or that it means something, but that his absence has a term on it.

From the best day to the worst night. They are coming down off the best day of their lives: five thousand fed from a boy’s lunch, twelve baskets of surplus, a crowd trying to crown their master. That evening they are alone on black water. The distance between those two experiences is about six hours, and anyone who has had a high Sunday followed by a Monday will recognise the geography.

Why does God sometimes seem absent when I am trying to obey him? Because seeming absent is not the same as being absent. The disciples were in the boat by his command, and he was praying for them on the mountain (Mark 6:46–48) and watching them in the dark. Scripture is honest that believers pass through seasons when God feels far away (Psalm 13:1; 88). In them, keep rowing in the direction he sent you, keep to his word and prayer, and remember the yet. He has not forgotten you, and he will come.

In a sentence. In the evening the disciples set out by boat across the lake for Capernaum, and it was dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.

On a Tuesday. There are times when it is dark and Jesus seems absent. He has not forgotten you. If you are in such a season now, write down where he sent you and what he told you, and keep doing it until he comes.

For worship. The Lord who prayed on the mountain had his eye on the boat the whole night. The darkness is not dark to him, and the night is as bright as the day. He sends his people out across black water, and he is never not coming. Bless the Saviour whose absences are always only not yet, and whose arrival is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.

The sea became rough. The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds funnel down onto it. It is one sentence and says everything by saying almost nothing: no dramatics, no cry for help. The lake sits about seven hundred feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air spilling down the ravines meets the warm air over the water and produces squalls with little warning. Fishermen who had worked that lake their whole lives knew it and were still caught by it. This is not a supernatural assault. It is the weather, and the men rowing into it were professionals.

Sometimes the wind is simply the wind. It is worth stating what the verse does not say. It does not say the storm came because they had done wrong; they had done what they were told. It does not say it came to teach them a lesson; John draws no moral. A great deal of harm is done by assuming that every hardship in a Christian life is a message. Living in a world under the curse means that things break, bodies fail, and boats get caught out on lakes, and being in the middle of obeying God when it happens is not evidence of anything at all. What the storm does supply is the occasion. The men in that boat are about to see something they could not have seen on land in daylight.

Is every hardship in my life a sign that God is displeased with me? No. God does discipline his children in love (Hebrews 12:6), and sometimes trouble is the fruit of our own sin. But many hardships are simply part of life in a fallen world, and God uses them for our good without their being punishments (Romans 8:28). The disciples were in the storm because they obeyed. So do not torment yourself trying to decode every trial. Confess any sin you know of, trust your Father’s love, and look for the Lord who comes across the water.

In a sentence. A strong wind blew and the sea grew rough.

On a Tuesday. Obeying Jesus does not mean calm seas. The disciples were where he sent them, in a storm. If you are facing trouble while doing what is right, do not conclude that you took a wrong turn.

For worship. He sits enthroned over the flood; the Lord sits enthroned as king for ever. The winds and the waves are his servants, and no storm rises without his leave. Bless the Lord who sends his disciples into the storm and then walks into it after them, so that they may see his glory.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds are common.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them: it is I; do not be afraid.

When they had rowed about three or four miles. The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. Roughly halfway across, at the widest part of the lake, as far from either shore as it is possible to be. They had been rowing for hours into a headwind.

They saw Jesus walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19). The sea pictures chaos. Jesus walks on it as its master. A psalm says of the Red Sea crossing, your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen. And Mark, describing this night, says he meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48), which sounds like indifference until you know that passing by is the language of God showing himself, as he passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:22) and Elijah at the cave (1 Kings 19:11). This is not a display of power to impress fishermen. It is a man doing, in front of witnesses, the specific thing the Old Testament says God does.

And they were frightened. Terror. Resist the instinct to hurry to the comfort, because their terror was the right response, and John records it without embarrassment. Mark says they took him for a ghost and cried out.

It is I. Literally “I am” (egō eimi), the divine name (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10–11; 51:12). The God who walks on the sea says “I am”. It is a perfectly ordinary way of saying it is me, and translators are right to render it so. It is also the two words behind the burning bush, and the two words this Gospel will build seven declarations on, starting later in this chapter. John knows both senses. He has just told us that the man saying it is standing on a lake in a gale.

Do not be afraid. God’s word to his people throughout Scripture (Isaiah 43:1–2: when you pass through the waters, I will be with you). And the comfort is not what we would have written. Do not be afraid comes attached to the most awe-inspiring statement available. They are not told there is nothing to fear. They are told who it is, and the reason to stop being afraid is that the one on the water is the one whose sea it is.

Did Jesus really walk on water, or is this a story with a spiritual meaning? He really did. John presents it as something that happened, seen by named witnesses, on a particular night, at a measured distance from shore. The spiritual meaning depends on the event: it shows who Jesus is precisely because he did what only God does. If the Word made flesh could make bread out of five loaves and raise the dead, walking on the water he created is no difficulty. To make it a mere symbol is to lose the very thing it reveals.

In a sentence. After rowing three or four miles, the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water toward them and were terrified, but he said: I am; do not be afraid.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you are most afraid of this week. Then say to yourself the words he said on the lake, and notice that he does not promise the thing will not happen. He tells you who is coming toward you across it.

For worship. In your storm, hear him say: I am; do not be afraid. A man walked across the top of a storm in the middle of the night to reach a boatload of tired men, none of whom had asked him to come. The waves that Job says God tramples were under a pair of ordinary feet with the dust of a Galilean hillside still on them. And the first thing the voice out of the dark said was not a command or a rebuke. It was, It is I, and then, do not be afraid.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.

They were glad to take him into the boat. Or “they wanted to take him”. Fear became gladness.

And immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going. Another miracle. Psalm 107:29–30: he made the storm be still … and he brought them to their desired haven. With Jesus, they arrive. Psalm 107 describes men who go down to the sea in ships, who see the works of the LORD in the deep, who are lifted up and thrown down until their courage melts. They cry to the LORD, he stills the storm, and he brings them to their desired haven. That is this verse: the rowing, the terror, the calm and the arrival. John does not quote the psalm; he narrates it.

The shape, not the mechanics. John does not explain whether the remaining distance was crossed miraculously. He reports that the moment Jesus was aboard, they were there. They had rowed for hours and covered half a lake. He steps in, and the journey is over. Everything they had achieved by straining was real and was not enough; what finished it was his presence in the boat.

Does this mean my troubles will disappear if I have enough faith? No, and the passage itself guards against that. This crossing had a storm, hours of useless rowing and real fear, and none of it was cancelled afterwards. The rowing still happened. What the verse says is that the arrival did not finally depend on it. Christ does not promise that faith will make difficulties evaporate. He promises to be with his people in them, and to bring them home at last.

In a sentence. They gladly took him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the shore they were heading for.

On a Tuesday. Take Jesus into your boat. In the thing you are straining at today, stop rowing for a moment and pray, not for the wind to drop, but for him to be with you in it.

For worship. Take Jesus into your boat. He will bring you to your desired haven. Every believer’s crossing ends at the shore, not because our rowing was strong, but because the Lord of the sea is in the boat. Bless the Saviour who stills the storm, gladdens the frightened, and brings his people home.

parallels.desc: he brought them to their desired haven

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crowd follows Jesus to Capernaum, wanting more bread. He urges them to seek food that lasts, given by the Son of Man, and tells them the work God asks is faith in the one he sent. When they demand a sign like the manna, he declares that he is the true bread from heaven, the bread of life, who satisfies hunger and thirst for ever. All the Father gives him will come, none will be turned away or lost, and he will raise them on the last day. As they grumble at his claim, he teaches that no one comes unless the Father draws and teaches them. The bread he will give for the world is his own flesh; only those who eat his flesh and drink his blood have life and remain in him. Many disciples are offended and leave. Jesus says his words are Spirit and life, but some do not believe. When he asks the Twelve whether they will go, Peter replies that only Jesus has the words of eternal life; they know he is the Holy One of God. Jesus warns that one of the Twelve, Judas, will betray him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bread of Life discourse is simultaneously eucharistic (the language of eating and drinking Jesus's flesh and blood points to the Lord's Supper) and spiritual (the key interpretive statement is 'it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all'). The flesh and blood Jesus speaks of is not a literal cannibalism but the reception of his atoning death: to eat his flesh and drink his blood is to appropriate by faith the benefits of his sacrifice. No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws them; all who are given to the Son by the Father will come; all who come will be raised up on the last day. The sovereignty of grace and the necessity of faith are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: The Bread of Life discourse sheds light on the Lord's Supper without being confined to it: feeding on Christ is spiritual, received by faith, not a physical re-sacrifice. The mass defection at the end of the discourse — 'many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him' — is the most important event in John 6: it reveals that the crowd's 'belief' was not genuine, and that the true disciples are known not by enthusiasm but by perseverance. Peter's confession — 'you have the words of eternal life' — is the greatest response to a hard teaching in the Gospels: when you cannot understand what Jesus is saying, you remain because of who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

The crowd saw that there had been only one boat. They were puzzled: Jesus had not left in the disciples’ boat, yet he was gone. What John records is a piece of reasoning, and it shows how close a person can get to the truth by pure logic and still miss it. They had counted the boats. Their deduction is faultless: he cannot have crossed the lake. So they cross the lake in the boats that have arrived, and find him on the other side. And nobody asks the obvious question. A man they last saw on the eastern shore, who could not have taken a boat, is standing in Capernaum the next morning. That is not a puzzle about logistics; it ought to have stopped them where they stood. They notice the anomaly, cross the lake to resolve it, and open with a question about his timetable. It is possible to be extremely observant about Jesus and entirely incurious.

Other boats from Tiberias. Perhaps blown across by the storm.

Where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks. John calls Jesus “the Lord”, and stresses the thanksgiving. It is John’s own aside, using a title he rarely uses of Jesus during the ministry. He is writing decades later to churches who broke bread every week and gave thanks over it, and for a moment his vocabulary slips into theirs. The hillside is being remembered by a man who has since watched the same action performed ten thousand times at the Lord’s Table.

Can I be interested in Jesus without really knowing him? Very easily, and this crowd shows how. They paid close attention to where he was, worked out the clues, and travelled to find him, and every bit of it was directed at the surface. Many people today read about Jesus, discuss him, even admire him, without ever asking the question his actions force: who is this, that he does what only God does? The cure is to stop treating him as a puzzle and come to him as a person, asking him to show you himself.

In a sentence. The next day the crowd realised Jesus had not left with his disciples in the only boat, and other boats arrived from Tiberias.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is not limited by circumstances. He goes where he will. And notice the questions you ask about him. Are they about the surface, or about who he is?

For worship. The Lord who crossed the sea without a boat is not bound by the limits that bind us. He goes where he will, and he is already waiting on the far shore when we arrive. And the thanks he gave on the hillside is still given at his table by his people in every land. Bless the Lord who gives thanks and gives bread, and who is himself the bread for which we give thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

Seeking Jesus. Diligently. But for the wrong reason (v. 26). Give them their due first: they got into boats. It is several miles across that lake. Nobody in this verse is casual. The seeking is strenuous, organised and costly, the sort of effort most of us would be pleased to see in ourselves. And Jesus is about to tell them it was aimed at the wrong thing.

Effort is not evidence. That is the uncomfortable possibility this verse opens. It is entirely possible to work hard at religion, to travel, give, attend, serve and arrange a life around it, and for the whole of it to be in pursuit of something other than God. The energy proves the wanting. It says nothing about what is wanted.

To his own address. They end up at Capernaum, his own base, the town of the synagogue (v. 59). They cross a lake to find him and arrive at his address. And the search is still a failure, because finding Jesus and receiving him are two different things, as this Gospel said on its first page: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11).

How do I know if I am seeking Jesus for the right reasons? Ask what you would do if the benefits were removed. Suppose the specific blessing you associate with your faith were gone: the community, the sense of purpose, the moral order it gives your life, the hope of things going well. Suppose only Christ were left. Would you still cross the lake? No one answers that perfectly, and it is not asked to produce despair. Mixed motives are normal; even the apostles had them. The question is which way you are moving: toward wanting him more than his gifts. Ask him to make it so.

In a sentence. Seeing that neither Jesus nor his disciples were there, the crowd took the boats to Capernaum looking for him.

On a Tuesday. Seeking Jesus is good; examine why you seek him. Look at what you prayed for this week, and ask how much of it was for him and how much for his gifts.

For worship. Christ is worth seeking for himself. He is not a means to an end but the end itself, the treasure in the field, the pearl of great price. And though we seek him for poor reasons, he seeks us for his own, and does not stop until he has given us himself. Bless the Lord who is found by those who seek him, and who first sought them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here? Jesus answered them: truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.

Rabbi, when did you come here? Curiosity. He does not answer the question they asked. They want to know when he arrived; he tells them why they came.

You are seeking me, not because you saw signs. Not because they understood the meaning of the feeding, as a sign pointing to who he is. Note the strangeness of the clause, since they had seen the sign; five thousand of them had eaten it. He means they had not seen it in the sense the word carries in this Gospel. A sign is a signpost. They had eaten the signpost.

But because you ate your fill of the loaves. They wanted more free food. They saw the bread, but not the sign. Jesus exposes their motive: they want what he gives, not who he is. And the verb is faintly rude. Echortasthēte comes from the word for fodder; it is what you say of animals fed until full. He is not being cruel; he had given them the meal himself, and lavishly. But the description is exact: they had been filled up, and being filled up was the whole of what had happened to them.

The danger of every good gift. It does not announce itself. Nobody decides to want the gift more than the giver. It happens by the ordinary working of appetite: the bread was real, the hunger was real, the satisfaction was real, and a person can live for years on that circuit without once turning to look at where the bread came from.

Does Jesus mind that I pray for practical things? No. He taught us to pray, give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and he fed this crowd gladly. The problem is not asking for bread, but wanting only bread. Pray for your needs, freely and specifically. Then let every answered prayer turn your eyes upward, to the Father who gave it and the Son who is himself the bread of life. A prayer life that is all requests and no worship has begun to eat the signpost.

In a sentence. When they found him and asked when he came, Jesus told them they were looking for him not because they understood the signs but because they had eaten their fill.

On a Tuesday. Do you want Jesus, or just what he can give? Seek the Giver, not just the gifts. Take one blessing you received this week and spend five minutes thanking God not only for it, but for who he has shown himself to be through it.

For worship. He tells the truth to the very people he has just fed, because he loves them too much to let them settle for loaves. His rebukes are as kind as his bread. Bless the Lord who will not let us live on the signpost, but turns us to look at himself, the true and living bread.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.

Do not work for the food that perishes. Physical food is necessary, but temporary. Don’t make it the goal of your life (Isaiah 55:2: why do you spend your money for that which is not bread?). And the word perishes is the same verb as the fragments, that nothing may be lost. Ordinary bread perishes; that is its nature, and the loaves they ate the day before were already going stale.

But for the food that endures to eternal life. Spiritual nourishment that never runs out.

Which the Son of Man will give to you. “Work for” it, yet it is a gift. Not earned, but sought and received. It sounds like a contradiction, and it is not. The working is not the purchasing. A man may labour hard to get to where something is being given out without in any sense having earned it. What is forbidden is not effort but effort aimed at the wrong provision.

For on him God the Father has set his seal. A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. The Father has authenticated Jesus as his own, at the baptism and through the signs. He is God’s certified Son. A seal was pressed into wax or clay by a signet ring. Merchants sealed sacks of grain. The picture is deliberately ordinary: the Father has stamped his Son the way a supplier stamps a consignment, and the stamp guarantees that the contents are what they claim to be. So the question in front of the crowd is not whether the bread is good. It is whether they will accept the certificate of the only authority competent to issue it.

Does this mean I should not work hard at my job? No. Scripture commands honest work and says that if anyone will not work, neither should he eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Jesus is not condemning daily labour but warning against making it the goal of your life. Work hard for your bread, as service to Christ (Colossians 3:23). But do not work for bread as if it were what you were made for. Give your deepest energy, your hope and your heart to the food that endures, and you will find even your daily work changed by it.

In a sentence. Jesus told them not to work for food that perishes, but for food that lasts to eternal life, which the Son of Man, sealed by the Father, will give them.

On a Tuesday. How much of your energy goes into food that perishes? Seek the food that lasts. Look at your diary for this week and see how much time is given to what will not outlast you, and what to what will.

For worship. The Father has set his seal on his Son: this one is mine, this one is true, this one I stand behind. Every promise of the gospel carries the Father’s stamp. And the food the Son gives does not go stale or run out; it endures to eternal life. Bless the God who has certified his Son for us, and who gives freely what no labour could ever buy.

parallels.desc: why do you labour for that which does not satisfy?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said to him: what must we do, to be doing the works of God? Jesus answered them: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

What must we do, to be doing the works of God? They take “work” literally: tell us what to do, what deeds, what rules, to earn this food. Watch the plural become singular, because the whole exchange is in it. They ask about the works, plural: a programme, a list. It is the most natural religious question there is, and every religion on earth has an answer to it. Give us the list. Tell us the observances and the standard, and we will apply ourselves. There is real sincerity in it, because a list can be worked at, progress can be measured, and a person can know where he stands.

This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. Not works (plural), but one work: believe. Faith is not a work that earns salvation; it is the receiving of a gift. And it is “the work of God” in a double sense: the work God requires, and the work God does in us (v. 44, 65; Philippians 1:29). Salvation is not by doing but by believing in Jesus.

The easiest and the hardest answer. Easiest, because a man on his deathbed with no strength for a list can do it. Hardest, because it cannot be part-done, cannot be worked up to gradually, and offers nothing to measure. A list lets a person keep control of the transaction. Faith hands the transaction over.

If faith is not a work, why does Jesus call it the work of God? Because he is answering their question in their own words, and then turning it inside out. They asked what work they must do; he says the only work is to believe, which is to stop working for acceptance and receive it. Faith is not something we contribute that earns a reward. It is the empty hand that takes Christ. And even that hand is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8–9). So we are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and the good works that follow are the fruit of salvation, never its price.

In a sentence. When they asked what works God requires, Jesus answered that the work of God is to believe in the one he has sent.

On a Tuesday. Notice what happens in you when a sermon ends without steps to take, nothing to implement. If you feel a mild frustration, that instinct is the one in this verse, and it is worth knowing it is there. It is not a bad instinct. It is simply the one Jesus declined to satisfy. Today, before you do anything for God, rest in what he has done for you.

For worship. The only “work” God requires for salvation is to believe in Jesus. Rest in him. The work that saves was done by another, on a cross, and finished. God asks us not to add to it but to trust it, and then he gives the very faith he asks for. Bless the God of grace, who turns our anxious question, what must we do?, into the glad answer, believe in him whom he has sent.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him: then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written: he gave them bread from heaven to eat.

Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? Astonishing: they had just seen the feeding of five thousand. They want more. Perhaps a sign as great as Moses’ manna, which lasted forty years. One meal was not enough. Yesterday afternoon they ate bread that came out of nothing, with twelve baskets over, and this morning they ask what sign he will do, as though the account were empty. Gratitude has a shorter life than anyone expects, and it is not cured by the size of the mercy: the generation that walked out of Egypt through a parted sea was complaining about the food within about a month (Exodus 16:1–3).

That we may see and believe you. It sounds reasonable and it reverses everything this chapter teaches. They are proposing terms: produce the evidence, and belief will follow. That puts the sign in the position of proof and themselves in the position of assessors. Jesus never accepts that arrangement from anyone. He will tell Thomas that those who have not seen and yet believe are the blessed ones (20:29).

Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. Exodus 16. There was a Jewish expectation that the Messiah would bring back the manna. And the manna tells you exactly what they want. Moses, they say, gave bread daily for forty years to a whole nation; one hillside meal, however impressive, was a single afternoon. The challenge is not so much prove yourself as can you keep it up? They are negotiating for a supply.

He gave them bread from heaven to eat. Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4. They challenge Jesus to match Moses. They quote Scripture correctly and use it as a weapon against the man standing in front of them. Jesus is about to take the sentence apart word by word and show they have misread its subject, the same thing he did with Moses at the end of chapter 5.

Why doesn’t God give more signs to convince unbelievers? Because more signs do not produce faith in an unwilling heart. This crowd had just eaten a miracle and wanted another. Jesus said of others that if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). God has given sufficient evidence: the signs written in the Gospels, the resurrection, and his word. What the unbeliever needs is not more light outside but new sight within, and that is the Spirit’s work. So pray for unbelievers, and keep showing them Christ.

In a sentence. They demanded a sign to make them believe, pointing out that their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness, bread from heaven.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief always wants more signs. Believe what God has already shown you. Write down three things God has done for you in the past year, and let them answer the voice that says, but what will he do for me now?

For worship. God has not been stingy with evidence. He fed Israel in the wilderness, he fed five thousand on a hillside, and he raised his Son from the dead. Every sign he gives is enough for faith and too much for any excuse. Bless the patient God who keeps giving to a people who keep asking for more, and who gave at last the sign of the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then said to them: truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven. God gave it, not Moses. He corrects their quotation in two places, and both corrections are in the grammar. First the subject. Exodus records God saying, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you (Exodus 16:4), and Moses told the people their grumbling was against the LORD, not him. The manna was never Moses’ to give. He woke up to it on the ground like everybody else.

But my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. Present tense: is giving, now. “True” (alēthinon): the real thing, of which the manna was a shadow. The manna fed bodies for a day; the true bread gives eternal life. That is the second correction, the tense. They said God gave: past, finished, a thing that happened to their ancestors. He says the Father gives: the action is not over. It is happening in the room.

For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven. Or “that which comes down”. The bread is a person: Jesus, who came down from heaven (3:13). Up to this point every hearer has assumed they are discussing a substance, and the substance has become a person without warning.

The manna was always too small a picture. Israel remembered it as the golden age of provision. It fell six mornings a week for forty years and kept a nation alive in a place where nothing grows. It also had to be gathered again the next day, went rotten if hoarded, stopped the moment they reached the land, and did not keep the generation that ate it from dying in the desert.

And gives life to the world. Not only to Israel, but to the world. It is the first time in this Gospel that the bread is given a scope, the same word John has used since the prologue for the world that did not know him, and it is spoken here, in an argument with hostile men, as the purpose of the bread.

How is the manna a picture of Christ? In several ways. It came down from heaven, as he did. It was given freely, by grace, to people who could not feed themselves in the wilderness. It had to be received and eaten, not merely looked at. It was enough for all who gathered it (Exodus 16:18). And Paul calls Israel’s food in the wilderness spiritual food (1 Corinthians 10:3). But Christ surpasses the type: the manna sustained a life that ended; he gives life that never ends.

In a sentence. Jesus said it was not Moses but his Father who gives the true bread from heaven, the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

On a Tuesday. Your soul needs daily bread as much as your body does. Before you check your phone tomorrow morning, gather your manna: a passage of Scripture, read slowly, with a prayer that Christ would feed you by it.

For worship. Jesus is the true bread from heaven. Feed on him. The Father did not send bread and then stop; he gives, now, today, his own Son to a hungry world. Every morning the table is spread again. Bless the Father who gives, and the Son who came down, and the Spirit who makes the bread of heaven our food.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: sir, give us this bread always. Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.

Sir, give us this bread always. Like the Samaritan woman (4:15), they still think of physical bread. They want a supply that never runs out. They are asking for the right thing and still mean the wrong one.

I am the bread of life. This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), the true vine (15:1). “I am” (egō eimi) echoes the divine name. Jesus does not just give bread; he is the bread. Not something he offers, but himself. Bread was the staple of life; without it, people died. Jesus is the essential nourishment of the soul.

Bread first. Each of the seven takes something ordinary, bread, a lamp, a doorway, a shepherd, a road, a vine, and says: that is not a picture of me; I am the thing itself, and every example you have met was the picture. And notice which comes first. Not light, which would be grander. Bread: the plainest, cheapest, most daily thing in the world, the item nobody notices until it is missing. Said in a synagogue, to people who had eaten the day before, in a district where a bad harvest meant a funeral.

Whoever comes to me shall not hunger. Coming to Jesus is like eating.

And whoever believes in me shall never thirst. Believing in Jesus is like drinking (4:14). Coming and believing are the same thing. The deepest hunger and thirst of the soul satisfied for ever. This is how this Gospel always speaks of faith: not an inward opinion but a movement toward a person.

The search is over. What is being claimed is easy to nod at and enormous. Every human being is running an experiment on what will finally satisfy, and every one of us has already found that the answers are temporary. He is not offering to improve the supply. He is saying the appetite ends in him, and that anyone who arrives will find the search is over.

What does it actually mean to feed on Christ day by day? It means to keep coming to him and keep believing in him, drawing your life from him as you draw strength from food. In practice: hear and read his word, because his words are spirit and life (v. 63); pray to him; trust his death for you afresh when you are guilty; come to his table; rest on his promises when you are afraid. Faith is not a single meal but a daily diet. You do not eat once and live for ever on the memory; you go back to the table.

In a sentence. When they asked for this bread always, Jesus said he is the bread of life, and whoever comes to him will never hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst.

On a Tuesday. Notice your hungers today: for approval, comfort, distraction, control. Each time you feel one, take it to Christ in a short prayer, and ask him to be what that hunger is really looking for.

For worship. Jesus is the bread of life. Come to him and believe, and you will never hunger again. The great I AM, who fed Israel in the desert, stands in a Galilean synagogue and says that he himself is the food of the soul. Not a teacher of bread, not a giver of bread only, but the bread. Bless the Lord who satisfies the longing soul with himself, and in whom every hungry search comes home.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.

You have seen me and yet do not believe. Seeing is not believing. They had seen the sign and the person, and still did not believe. Unbelief is not a lack of evidence. Why do some believe and others not? Jesus explains in the next verses. The sadness in the sentence is easily missed. Not you have seen my works, though they had. You have seen me. The thing that ought to have settled it is not an argument or a miracle but the person, and they have had him in front of them at close range, for a whole day, with a meal in between.

If only we had been there. This closes off an assumption almost everyone makes at some point: that if we had only been there, it would all have been obvious. It was not. Being present was not enough. The people who watched him make bread out of nothing and followed him across a lake are the people he describes as unbelieving. A man who could produce bread from nothing cannot, by any amount of saying it, make a person see what is in front of him. That takes something else, and the next verses name it.

Would I believe more easily if God gave me more evidence? Probably not, and this verse is why. The crowd had more evidence than you will ever have, and it did not produce faith. That is not because evidence is worthless, but because the problem lies deeper than the mind. Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ, opened to the heart by the Spirit (Romans 10:17). If you struggle to believe, do not wait for a sign. Go to the Gospels, read what he said and did, and ask the Father to give you eyes to see. That is a prayer he delights to answer.

In a sentence. Jesus said that they had seen him and still did not believe.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who have seen and heard and still don’t believe. Only God can open their eyes. Choose one person you have been trying to convince, and this week spend more time praying for them than arguing with them.

For worship. To see Jesus with the eyes is common; to see him with the heart is a gift. The Father who opens blind eyes has opened yours if you believe. Bless the God who does what no sign can do, and gives sight to those who had seen him and not seen him at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.

All that the Father gives me will come to me. The Father has given a people to the Son (17:2, 6, 9, 24). They are given before they come. “All” of them will come: not might, but will. None will be missing. This is unconditional election and effectual calling: the Father chooses a people, gives them to the Son, and draws them so that they certainly come (v. 44).

He is not counting the room. Notice the direction: this is a statement about the Father’s giving and the Son’s certainty, and there is not a word in it about the strength of anyone’s grip. It is also an answer to the situation Jesus is standing in. He is speaking to a crowd that came for bread and will shortly be abandoned by many of his disciples, and what he says about it is not that his ministry has failed but that everyone the Father has given him will arrive.

And whoever comes to me I will never cast out. And the other side: no one who comes will be rejected. “Never” (ou mē): the strongest negative in Greek. A wonderful assurance for anyone who comes to Christ, however unworthy. You do not need to wonder whether you are chosen before you come; if you come, he will receive you.

Never cast out. The verb is physical. To cast out is what you do to somebody at a door: it is used of the man born blind being put out of the synagogue (9:34), and of the traders driven from the temple (2:15). It is the language of being shown off the premises. So the promise is not, I will be tolerant of your failures, which is smaller. It is that there is no version of the story in which someone who came to him is put outside afterwards. And the promise does not depend on how a person came, well or badly, early or late, from conviction or desperation or sheer exhaustion; not on what they brought, nor on what they have done since. The only condition is whoever comes, stated so broadly that no one can be excluded by a technicality.

For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. Jesus’ mission is to do the Father’s will, which is to save all the Father has given him.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians teach that God chooses those he foresees will freely believe. Verdict: the text puts the Father’s giving first, and the coming second, as its result: all that the Father gives will come. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (also 6:44, 65; 10:26; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Yet human responsibility is real: everyone who comes is welcomed, and those who refuse are responsible (5:40). Both truths are taught together, and we hold them together.

How do I know if I am one of those the Father has given? By coming. You will never find your name by searching the secret counsel of God; it is not written where you can read it. But it is written where you can see its effect: whoever comes to Christ was given by the Father, and whoever comes will never be cast out. So do not ask first, am I chosen?, and wait for an answer before coming. Come to Christ now, as you are, trusting him. That coming is the evidence of the Father’s giving, and the promise of the Son’s welcome stands over you.

In a sentence. Everyone the Father gives Jesus will come to him, and he will never turn away anyone who comes, for he came down from heaven to do the will of the one who sent him.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what you are secretly afraid would get you thrown out: not sin in general, but the particular thing. Now read verse 37 again and notice that it has no exceptions clause, and that the man who said it knew everything about you before you came and made the promise anyway.

For worship. If you have come to Christ, he will never cast you out. And you came because the Father gave you to him. Rest in that. Before the world was made, the Father chose a people and gave them to his Son as a love gift; in time, the Son came down to receive them; by the Spirit, they come, every one. And at the door stands the Saviour who has never yet shown anyone off the premises. Blessed be the Father who gives, the Son who receives, and the Spirit who brings us home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.

This is the will of him who sent me. Jesus now spells out what the Father’s will is. It is a saving will, and the Son has come to carry it out to the end. He is quoting his job description, and it is stated as the Father’s will rather than the Son’s intention. So if a single person given to Christ were finally lost, it would not be a disappointment to the Son. It would be a failure of the Son to do what the Father sent him to do, and this Gospel has spent two chapters showing that he always does what he sees the Father doing.

That I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. “All that he has given me” is neuter in Greek (pan ho), the whole company of the given seen as one gift. “Lose” (apollymi) is the same word used of the fragments in v. 12: gather them up “that nothing may be lost.” The Shepherd who would not lose a crust of barley bread will not lose one of his people. This is the perseverance of the saints, grounded not in the strength of the believer but in the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son (10:28–29; 17:12; 18:9).

But raise it up on the last day. Salvation is not complete until the body is raised. Jesus’ keeping reaches all the way through death to the resurrection at his return. The phrase “raise up on the last day” comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54): it is the goal of everything Jesus does for his people. Keeping someone safe through this life is not the whole promise; anyone can be kept safe until they die, and everyone dies. What is promised is that the keeping extends through the grave and out the other side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that someone who makes a profession and then abandons Christ for ever was one of the given (see 1 John 2:19). Nor does it mean believers can live carelessly: those whom Christ keeps, he keeps believing and following (10:27).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Many Arminians teach that a genuine believer may finally fall away. Verdict: this verse rules it out. If one given to the Son were lost, the Father’s will would fail and the Son would have failed in his mission. The warnings of Scripture are real, and they are one of the means by which Christ keeps his own; but the outcome is certain.

What about the warning passages, like John 15:6 and Hebrews 6? Some Christians hold that Christ keeps only those who go on abiding in him, and that a believer may abandon faith and be lost (compare 15:6; Hebrews 6:4–6). But here the promise is not conditioned on our holding on: those the Father has given, Christ will not lose, but will raise up. The warnings are real, and they are among the means by which he keeps his own. He warns his sheep so that they will not wander, and his warning is one of the ways his hand holds them.

What if I fall into serious sin? Have I lost my salvation? If you belong to Christ, no. Peter denied him three times, and was restored (21:15–19). David fell into adultery and murder, and repented (Psalm 51). A true believer may fall grievously and for a time, bringing God’s fatherly displeasure and much grief on himself (Westminster 17.3); but he will not fall finally, because Christ will not lose him. The proof that you belong to him is that you cannot rest in the sin: you are grieved, you return, you confess. Run back to him now. The door he promised never to shut is still open.

In a sentence. The Father’s will is that Jesus should lose none of those the Father has given him, but raise them all up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Your perseverance rests in Christ’s hands, not in your grip. When you feel weak, remember: he does not lose what the Father has given him. On the day you feel least like a Christian, say this verse aloud, and let the Shepherd’s determination stand in for your feelings.

For worship. He does not say he will do his best. He says the Father has willed it and he will do it: lose nothing, raise it up. The Shepherd who gathered barley crusts so that nothing would be lost holds every one of his sheep, and none can snatch them from his hand. Bless the faithful Son, who finishes what the Father began, and who will stand on the last day with every one of his people, saying, here am I, and the children God has given me.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

For this is the will of my Father. The same will, now seen from the human side. Verse 39 spoke of what the Father gives; v. 40 speaks of what people do.

That everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him. “Looks” (theōreō) means to gaze, to look with attention. The crowd had seen him without believing (v. 36); this is seeing that leads to faith. The verse echoes the bronze serpent (3:14–15; Numbers 21:8–9): whoever looked, lived. “Everyone” is wide open: there is no one who looks and believes who is shut out.

Looking is the one thing required. It sends the reader back to the bronze serpent, where the dying were told to look and live, and forward to the cross, where John will quote Zechariah: they will look on him whom they have pierced (19:37). Looking is required because it is the one thing a person with nothing left can still do.

Should have eternal life. Present possession: has it now.

And I will raise him up on the last day. And future completion: resurrection at the end. Eternal life now, and resurrection then.

Election and the open invitation. Verses 39 and 40 stand side by side on purpose. One speaks of the Father giving, the other of everyone who believes. They describe the same people. God’s choosing never makes the invitation less sincere; it is what guarantees that the invitation will not be refused by all.

The pastoral order. Held next to verse 44, these verses produce the tension that has divided the church for centuries, and they are four verses apart in a single speech, so whatever the resolution is, Jesus did not experience them as in conflict. And the pastoral order matters more than the systematic one. Nobody has ever been kept out by the doctrine of election. The door has everyone written over it, and no one who looks to the Son will be turned away on the ground that they were not on a list. What the drawing explains is not who may come but why anyone does, and it is a question asked afterwards, looking back, by people already inside.

Can I freely offer the gospel to everyone if God has chosen only some? Yes, and you must. Jesus himself does both in the same breath. The offer is sincere: whoever looks and believes will live, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). You do not know who the elect are, and you are not asked to find out. You are asked to say to everyone: look to the Son and live. Election is not a reason to hold back the invitation; it is the guarantee that the invitation will not fall on deaf ears everywhere.

In a sentence. The Father’s will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and Jesus will raise him up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Today, when you feel guilty or afraid, do not look inward first. Look at the Son, lifted up on the cross for you, and believe. Then tell someone else to look.

For worship. Look to the Son and believe. That is all, and it is everything. The Father’s will is not hidden in a sealed book; it is proclaimed in the open street: everyone who looks shall live. Bless the God whose sovereign purpose and whose wide invitation meet in one Saviour lifted up, so that the dying may look and live.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?”

So the Jews grumbled about him. “Grumbled” (gongyzō) is a deliberate word. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling in the wilderness, the very place where the manna was given (Exodus 16:2, 7–8). They are acting out their fathers’ story while they talk about their fathers’ bread. “The Jews” in John often means the religious authorities and those who followed them in opposing Jesus, here people in the Galilean synagogue.

The picture is complete. John has built it carefully: bread from heaven, a crowd in a wilderness, a demand for a sign, an appeal to Moses, and now the murmuring, a low, sustained complaining that never quite becomes open revolt. The generation in front of Jesus is behaving exactly like the generation their argument depends on, and every one of them would have said the failure of that generation was the great cautionary tale of their history.

Because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven”. The claim to heavenly origin is what offends them.

Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? They know where he comes from, they think. They know his family. Ironically, they know only half the truth. John’s readers know he came from the Father (1:14), and many would know he was born of a virgin. Familiarity breeds contempt (compare Mark 6:3). And their objection is unanswerable on its own terms. They are not making anything up. They could probably have named the street. There is no way, from inside that information, to get to the conclusion that the man came down from heaven.

How does he now say, “I have come down from heaven”? Their objection is the incarnation itself: how can an ordinary man claim to come from heaven? This is still the stumbling block. God did not arrive in a form that made the conclusion easy. He came as somebody’s son, in a known family, from a town people could point to, and the very facts that make the story checkable are the facts that make it seem incredible.

How can Jesus have a human mother and come down from heaven? Because he is one person with two natures. As the eternal Son he came from the Father; as man he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). Joseph was his legal father, not his natural father. The crowd saw only the human side and thought it ruled out the divine. But the incarnation means that the one who came down from heaven really did grow up in Nazareth, and that the carpenter’s son really is the Word who was with God in the beginning.

In a sentence. The Jews grumbled because Jesus claimed to be bread from heaven, since they knew his father and mother and thought they knew where he came from.

On a Tuesday. Do not let familiarity with Jesus dull your wonder. The man of Nazareth came down from heaven. There is a warning here for anyone who has known Christian things a long time. The obstacle in this verse is not ignorance but familiarity, the settled sense that one already knows what there is to know about him, which never feels like resistance. It feels like being well informed. Read a Gospel this week as if for the first time.

For worship. The eternal Son came down from heaven and had a mother whose name the neighbours knew. He grew up in an ordinary house, in a town of no account, and worked with his hands. That is the glory of the incarnation: the Most High made himself so lowly that people could dismiss him. Bless the Lord of glory who hid his majesty in a carpenter’s son, so that he might be our bread.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.”

Do not grumble among yourselves. Jesus doesn’t argue with their objection about his family. He goes to the root: why they cannot believe.

No one can come to me. “Can” (dynatai) is about ability, not permission. It is not that no one may come, but that no one is able to come. Fallen human beings, left to themselves, are unable to come to Christ (3:3; 8:43; Romans 8:7–8). The whole of this Gospel has been demonstrating it: a teacher of Israel who could not follow a sentence about birth, a crowd who ate the sign and asked for another, men with every witness heaven could produce who would not come. The historic name for this inability is the bondage of the will. The will is not destroyed and it is not forced; it is bound, so that it chooses freely and always chooses against God until it is set free.

Unless the Father who sent me draws him. “Draws” (helkō) is a strong word. It is used of drawing a net full of fish to land (21:6, 11), of drawing a sword (18:10), of dragging Paul and Silas into the marketplace (Acts 16:19). It is not a gentle suggestion that might be resisted, but an effective pull. God’s drawing does not force anyone against their will; it changes the will, so that the sinner comes gladly. That is what v. 45 will explain: the Father teaches, and the taught come.

And I will raise him up on the last day. The one who is drawn is the one who is raised. The same person runs from the beginning to the end: drawn, comes, raised. None drop out on the way. The one who does the drawing also does the raising, and nothing in the sequence is left to the one being drawn.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people who want to come to Christ are turned away because they are not drawn. Anyone who wants to come has already been drawn. Nor does it excuse unbelief: people do not come because they will not (5:40), and they are responsible for it.

Where Christians differ: is the Father’s drawing resistible? Arminians teach that God draws everyone (citing 12:32) with a grace that can be resisted, so that some who are drawn do not come. Verdict: in this verse the one who is drawn is the one who is raised up on the last day. If drawing could be resisted, the verse would promise resurrection to people who never come. The drawing is effectual. In 12:32 Jesus says he will draw “all people,” meaning all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews (the Greeks of 12:20 have just asked to see him), not every single person. This is effectual calling: the Spirit’s work by which God persuades and enables us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered in the gospel.

What this doctrine is for. It is regularly used as a weapon, and it is not one. It is not a means of sorting other people into categories; nobody has been given the list, and this chapter shows Jesus preaching to a room he knows contains both. It is not a reason to stop pleading with anyone, since he is pleading with them as he says it. It is an explanation offered to people who already believe, and it answers one question: why me? Why did this land, when it did not land on the man beside me who had the same information and more sense? The only answer the chapter permits is that somebody came and got me. That removes the last possibility of taking credit for it, and it removes at the same time the fear that a faith I produced could be one I might fail to keep.

If no one can come unless drawn, why should I evangelise? Because the Father draws through means, and the chief means is the gospel spoken. The Father teaches (v. 45), and he teaches through the word preached and shared: faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:14–17). The doctrine of drawing does not make your witness pointless; it makes it hopeful. You are not trying to talk dead people into life by your own power. You are speaking the words that the Father uses to raise the dead. Speak boldly, pray earnestly, and expect him to draw.
