Roman Catholic teaching takes them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity; but the natural reading of the Gospels is that they were Mary’s later sons (Matthew 1:25 says Joseph did not know her until she had borne Jesus). Luke calls Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7), and the brothers appear again and again with Mary as her family (Mark 3:31; Acts 1:14). The other views arose to support a belief Scripture never teaches. What matters most for this chapter, though, is not the family tree but the fact that these were men who had grown up in the same small house as Jesus.

Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. Their advice sounds reasonable. Jerusalem was the centre; a Messiah should prove himself there, at the feast, with crowds from everywhere. “Your disciples” may mean the followers in Judea, or those who had turned away (6:66). And the phrase is spoken at arm’s length: your disciples, not ours. They are not part of it, and they say so in the way people do inside families, without quite saying it.

For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. They think like the world: if you want to be famous, go public. Jesus’ goal was not fame but the Father’s glory. Read it as advice rather than villainy, because it is entirely sensible. He has a following in Galilee and no standing in the capital; the feast will draw pilgrims from everywhere; if he wants a movement, he should be seen where the crowds are. Any modern adviser would say the same, and it is a perfectly sound observation about how reputations are made. That is exactly what is wrong with it. His kingdom does not advance by staged displays for the largest possible audience.

If you do these things, show yourself to the world. “If” reveals their doubt. They don’t deny the miracles, but they don’t trust him. It is the same temptation Satan put to him: prove yourself with a public display (Matthew 4:5–7). And there is a terrible irony in the words. He will show himself to the world. In this Gospel that is what the cross is: the lifting up, the public display, the moment when he is shown to everybody, written over in three languages for every passer-by to read (19:20). His brothers have named the right event and the wrong method, and they have no idea that the showing they are urging on him will happen at Passover and will kill him.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? It is not the centre of the gospel, and Christians who love Christ have disagreed about it. But it matters in two quieter ways. First, it is a question of reading Scripture honestly: the plainest sense of the Gospels is that Jesus grew up with brothers and sisters, and doctrines should be built on what Scripture says, not on what we would prefer it to say. Second, it makes the incarnation more ordinary and therefore more wonderful. Mary is blessed among women and is to be honoured as the mother of our Lord; she does not need a perpetual virginity to be honoured. The Son of God grew up in a crowded house, shared meals with siblings, and knew what it is to be misunderstood by his own family.

In a sentence. His brothers urged him to go to Judea and show his works to the world, since no one who wants to be known works in secret.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of advice that measures faithfulness by publicity. Jesus did not seek a platform; he sought the Father’s will. The pressure is everywhere now: grow the following, post the result, build the brand, be seen. Some visibility is simply the cost of telling people the truth, and nobody should hide a light under a basket. But ask of any plan, in your church or your own heart: is this aimed at making Christ known, or at making me known? The two can look identical from the outside for a long time.

For worship. The one whose glory fills heaven did not need to be seen at a festival. He had shared the Father’s glory before the world existed (17:5), and he laid it aside so completely that the brothers who ate at his table thought he needed their advice on how to be noticed. He bore it without a word of contempt. The Lord before whose throne all the nations will be gathered let himself be managed, misjudged and talked down to at home, and he was no smaller for it. His glory never needed our applause, and it has never been too proud to sit at our table.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not even his brothers believed in him.

For not even his brothers believed in him. John explains their advice. They had grown up with him and seen his miracles, and still did not believe (Mark 3:21). Eight words, dropped in as an aside, and they are among the most useful in the New Testament for a particular kind of grief. Consider what these men had actually seen. They had lived in the same small house with him for something like thirty years. They had watched him work, eat, sleep, keep the Sabbath and go to synagogue. Whatever there was to observe about the character of Jesus of Nazareth over three decades at close quarters, they observed it, and they did not believe. If moral excellence at close range were enough to produce faith, these four men would have been the first converts in history. Familiarity is the enemy of awe: they knew Jesus the man too well to recognise Jesus the Lord.

But that is not the end of the story. After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers were among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14). James later led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9) and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude. That is all we are told, and it is enough. Somewhere between this chapter and Acts 1, the risen Christ went to see his brother. The scandal of unbelief can be overcome, but only by resurrection: the same power that raised Jesus from the grave raised James from his unbelief.

The case was not closed. Take the person you have most nearly given up on. Now notice that if this chapter had been the last word about James, every reasonable observer would have concluded the case was closed: thirty years of evidence, no result. It was not closed. It was about six months from being reopened, and nothing that happened in the meantime looked like progress. The worst week of all, the week his brother was crucified, was the week that led to James’ conversion.

My family has watched my life for years and still does not believe. Have I failed them? Not necessarily. The most compelling life ever lived was on display in one household for thirty years and did not persuade the people in it. Unbelief is not proof that your witness was poor, and it is not proof that the case for Christ is weak. Faith is not produced by example alone; it is the gift of God, who opens blind eyes when he chooses (6:44). Your example still matters: live in a way that makes the gospel credible, apologise when you fail, keep loving them. But the burden of converting them was never yours to carry. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the timing with the one who went to see James.

In a sentence. Not even Jesus’ own brothers believed in him.

On a Tuesday. If your family doesn’t believe, keep praying. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe, until the risen Christ met them. Write down the name of the relative you have quietly stopped praying for, and pray for them by name today. And if you grew up around Christianity, take the warning in this verse: it is possible to have heard everything, to know the stories by heart, to have grown up in the very house, and still not to believe. Ask yourself whether you know him or only know about him.

For worship. For thirty years the eternal Son let his own brothers watch him at the table and the workbench and judge him ordinary, and he never forced their faith. When it came, it came as worship. James, who could have signed himself the brother of the Lord, wrote instead a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1); Jude called himself a servant of Jesus Christ, and only then a brother of James (Jude 1). The brothers who once told him to show himself to the world spent their lives showing him to it. He is patient with the people closest to him, and his patience wins.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.”

My time has not yet come. “Time” here is kairos, the right moment for a thing. John’s usual word is the hour (hōra), the fixed appointment of his death and glorification, which turns up at Cana (2:4) and in verse 30 and finally arrives in chapter 12 (12:23). Jesus lives by the Father’s timetable, not his brothers’. The right moment for going up to Jerusalem is not when his brothers think it would be effective, but when his Father says.

But your time is always here. For them, any time is fine. They have no mission to fulfil, and they are not under threat. There is no wrong moment for them, no appointment they are waiting on, nothing constraining when they may act. He does not mean it as a compliment.

The world cannot hate you. “The world” in John is humanity organised in rebellion against God. It cannot hate them, because they belong to it (15:19). This is one of the most quietly devastating sentences he ever addressed to his own family. Not does not: cannot. There is nothing in them for it to take offence at. They fit; they belong; they speak its language and want what it wants, and so the machinery of hostility never engages. He is telling his brothers that their safety is a symptom.

But it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil. Why does the world hate Jesus? Because he exposes it. Light shows up the darkness (3:19–20). People don’t object to Jesus as long as he is a teacher of kindness. They object when he says their works are evil. The world tolerates many kinds of religion and moral teaching; it cannot tolerate the claim that its basic direction is sinful and that only grace can save it. The cross is the world’s answer to that testimony.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that being disliked is proof of faithfulness. Many Christians are disliked for being rude, ignorant, harsh or politically obnoxious, and that hostility has nothing to do with Christ. The verse names the cause exactly: the world hates him because he testifies that its works are evil. The offence is the offence of having the truth told about oneself, by someone who loves you enough to tell it. So the test is narrow. Not, am I disliked? but, is there anything in my life that would make the world uncomfortable if it were paying attention? A faith with no friction at all may simply be a private faith. It may also be one that has quietly stopped saying the thing that causes friction.

But does God not love the world (3:16)? How can the world be the enemy? Both are true, and John holds them together. The world is humanity in rebellion against God, and God loves it anyway, not because it is lovable but because he is love. He loved it enough to send his Son into it, knowing it would hate him. So when Jesus says the world hates him, he is not describing a world God has given up on; he is describing the world he came to save. Christians are called to the same double stance: not loving the world’s rebellion (1 John 2:15), and loving the people caught in it enough to tell them the truth.

In a sentence. Jesus said his time had not yet come, though any time suited his brothers, because the world could not hate them, but hated him for testifying that its works were evil.

On a Tuesday. If the world never objects to you, ask whether you are telling it the truth. Think of the places where you are most at ease: the office, the club, the group chat. Would anyone there know, from the way you talk and live, that you think some of what is normal there is wrong? Not because you lecture them, but because your life quietly does not fit. If not, ask God for courage, and for love, which is the only thing that makes truth bearable to hear.

For worship. He could have been loved by the world. He had only to stop saying that its works were evil, to be a teacher of kindness and nothing more, and it would have praised him to the end. He would not. He loved the world too much to flatter it, and he let it hate him to death, so that the people who hated him could be forgiven. The light did not dim itself to be welcome in the dark.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come. After saying this, he remained in Galilee.

You go up to the feast. “Go up”: Jerusalem stands high in the hills, so one always went up to it. The pilgrim psalms are called the Songs of Ascents for this reason (Psalms 120–134), and the brothers would have been singing them on the road.

I am not going up to this feast. But then he does go (v. 10). Was this a lie? No. He refuses to go up in the way they meant, publicly, as a pilgrim seeking attention, and on their timing. When he does go, it is privately, and on the Father’s timing. Some see also a play on “go up”: the same verb is used of his ascending to the Father (20:17). He will not “go up” in that sense, to glory, at this feast.

A charge worth answering. The sentence has been used for centuries to accuse Jesus of lying. The third-century critic Porphyry pressed exactly this point, and it is still raised. It should be met head on rather than waved away, and it answers well, because the whole exchange is about a manner of going, not a matter of geography. His brothers were not offering him a lift to Jerusalem; they were urging a campaign: show yourself to the world (v. 4), go up publicly, with the crowds, and stake your claim. That is the going up he refuses. And John himself supplies the distinction in the very next sentence: when Jesus did go, he went not publicly but in private (v. 10). He did not do the thing he said he would not do. The man who would shortly refuse to come down from a cross was not a man who trimmed his words to make an afternoon easier.

For my time has not yet fully come. “Fully come” (peplērōtai, been fulfilled). The reason is the one he gave in verse 6. He is not managing his image with a convenient untruth; he is declining a schedule that was not his Father’s.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “I am not yet going up,” which smooths the difficulty. The harder reading, “I am not going up,” is better attested in early manuscripts and is more likely original, since a scribe would add “yet” to ease the problem, not remove it. So the honest course is to answer the harder text rather than shelter behind the easier, and as we have seen, the harder text needs no shelter.

If manuscripts differ, can I trust my Bible? Yes. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and comparing them lets scholars see clearly where a copyist slipped or smoothed. The great majority of differences are spelling, word order or small words like this “yet”, and none of them touches any teaching of the faith. Notice how this note works: the reading that looks harder is kept precisely because it is harder, which shows that the copyists were not freely inventing but were anxious about every word. Your Bible’s footnotes are not a sign that the text is shaky. They are a sign that it has been handled with great care.

After saying this, he remained in Galilee. He stays for now. The remaining is not passivity but restraint: the patience of one who knows that the hour has been set from eternity and cannot be rushed by family pressure or popular demand.

In a sentence. Jesus told his brothers to go up to the feast, but said he was not going to this feast because his time had not yet fully come, and he stayed in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. You will be pushed, by people who mean well, to do the right thing in the wrong way or at the wrong time: to confront too soon, to announce too early, to take the job before you have prayed about it. It is not stubbornness to say no to the method while keeping your heart open to the thing itself. Say plainly what you will not do, and then do what God has given you to do, in his way.

For worship. His brothers could not hurry him to Jerusalem, the crowds could not hurry him to a throne, and his enemies could not hurry him to a cross. And when the hour did come, nothing could stop him going up: up to Jerusalem, up onto the cross, up from the grave, and up to the Father’s right hand, where he reigns over every timetable in the world, including yours.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet” — “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”

Then he also went up, not publicly but in private. Not as part of the pilgrim crowds, not as a public show. He went quietly, on his own terms. Pause on the picture: the Son of God going up to the great feast of his own people, in a stream of pilgrims, unrecognised, deliberately not drawing attention. He walks the same road as everybody else, and nobody knows. And the secrecy is temporary, which is worth saying so that it is not mistaken for a policy. He goes up hidden in verse 10 and is teaching in the temple courts by verse 14. What he refused was his brothers’ method: the arrival, the entourage, the staged display. Days later he does the most public thing available to a man in Jerusalem, and does it alone.

The Jews were looking for him at the feast. The authorities expect him. They want to arrest him. Two searches are running in these verses and they will run through the rest of the chapter. The authorities are looking for him in order to end him. The crowd is looking for him because they cannot stop talking about him. And he is there the whole time, walking through the middle of both.

Where is he? “Where” is a key word in John 7 and 8: where he comes from, and where he is going (vv. 27, 34–35; 8:14, 21). And the question has a coldness to it. They will not use his name. It is the tone of people discussing somebody they have already decided about. Yet beneath the surface it is the deepest question there is: where is God? The answer John gives across twenty-one chapters is that he is here, in this man, at this feast.

The man they cannot find is the tent. There is a quiet wonder in the arrangement that John does not point out. The word for the feast comes from the same root as the verb he used in the prologue: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us (1:14). The whole city is sleeping under branches to remember the time God travelled with them in a tent, and the man they are looking for is the tent.

Is it ever right for a Christian to be secret? Sometimes discretion is wisdom, and Jesus himself shows it here. Believers in hostile countries meet quietly; a Christian may wisely choose not to announce every plan to people who mean him harm (Matthew 10:16–17). But there is a difference between discretion about our movements and silence about our Lord. Jesus hid his journey for a few days; he never hid who he was. If we are hiding our faith because we are ashamed of Christ, that is not wisdom but fear (Mark 8:38). Prudence protects the mission. Cowardice abandons it.

In a sentence. After his brothers had left, Jesus went up privately to the feast, while the authorities were looking for him there.

On a Tuesday. Wisdom is not cowardice. Jesus went where he was sent, and went wisely. And remember that he still walks unrecognised through crowds: in the stranger, the ordinary believer, the plain preaching of the word on a dull Sunday. The people who missed him at the feast were looking for someone grander. Look for him where he has promised to be.

For worship. The God for whom the feast was kept walked into Jerusalem unnoticed, a pilgrim among pilgrims. He who once filled the tabernacle with a glory so great that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35) came up the road dusty and anonymous, so that he could stand among his people and call them to himself. Our God is not a distant festival memory. He came close enough to be overlooked.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.” Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.

There was much muttering about him among the people. “Muttering” is the same word as “grumbled” in 6:41 (gongysmos), here meaning whispered debate. It is the wilderness word, the low sustained grumbling of Israel in the desert, and John uses it here of both parties, admirers and accusers alike. Nobody is speaking; everybody is murmuring.

Some said, “He is a good man.” A compliment that falls far short. Jesus never left that option open. A man who claims to be equal with God (5:18) and the bread from heaven (6:51) is either who he says, or not good at all. It is the kindly verdict, and the one most people still reach for.

Others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.” “Leading astray” (planaō) was a serious charge: the false prophet who leads Israel away from God was to be put to death (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Later Jewish writings describe Jesus as one who practised sorcery and led Israel astray. That is not name-calling. It is the formal accusation on which he will eventually be executed. And what is not on offer between the two verdicts is the third possibility, which is the point of recording the exchange. The one thing nobody in this verse says is that he might be telling the truth about himself.

Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him. “The Jews” here clearly means the authorities: the people themselves are Jews. Fear of the leaders silences everyone (9:22; 12:42). And notice who is silent. Not the opposition: they are talking freely. It is the people who think well of him who say nothing. The phrase becomes one of John’s refrains: it is why the blind man’s parents will not answer a straight question (9:22), why Joseph of Arimathea kept his discipleship quiet (19:38), why the disciples were behind locked doors on Easter evening (20:19). Jesus himself will name the root: they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (12:43).

Why can’t Jesus simply be a good man and a great teacher? Because of what he taught. A good man does not claim to be equal with God, to forgive sins against other people, to be the bread from heaven, or to be the one by whom everyone will be judged. If those claims are false, he is either deceived about himself on a scale no sane good man could be, or he is deceiving others, which is exactly the charge in this verse. The only verdicts that take him seriously are that he is a liar, or that he is the Lord. The good teacher who claims nothing is a figure people invented later to avoid having to decide.

Does John’s phrase “the Jews” make his Gospel anti-Jewish? No. John was a Jew, Jesus was a Jew, every disciple and nearly every believer in this Gospel is a Jew, and Jesus says salvation is from the Jews (4:22). In passages like this, “the Jews” plainly means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, as the sentence itself shows: the Jewish crowd is afraid of the Jews. The Gospel never gives any warrant for hatred of the Jewish people. Christians who have used it that way have sinned grievously, and contempt for Jews is a denial of the Christ who was born a son of David and wept over Jerusalem.

In a sentence. The people were whispering about Jesus, some calling him a good man and others a deceiver, but no one spoke openly for fear of the authorities.

On a Tuesday. Calling Jesus a good man is not enough. And whispering about him for fear of others is not faith. Speak openly of him. Think of the last conversation in which the subject came near enough that you could have said something, and you did not. Then ask honestly what you were afraid of. In most cases it is not persecution. It is the half-second of awkwardness, the sense of becoming the person who brings that up. The pressure in this verse was far heavier than ours, and the mechanism is the same. Next time, say one true sentence about him.

For worship. While the crowd whispered about whether he was good, he went on being good to them: teaching them, healing them, and walking towards a cross for them. He did not wait for them to speak openly of him before he died openly for them. And the Lord who was mumbled about in the courts of his own temple will one day be confessed aloud by every tongue, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”

About the middle of the feast. Around the fourth day of the seven. The timing is deliberate. He did not come with the pilgrims and he did not wait until it was over. He let the festival fill up, until the crowds were at their largest and the city had settled into the week, and then walked into the busiest place in Jerusalem and began to teach.

Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. Now he appears openly, in the temple courts, where rabbis taught, probably in Solomon’s Porch (10:23). Malachi had promised that the Lord whom you seek would suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). In the middle of a feast, without announcement, he does.

How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? “Learning” is literally “letters” (grammata), meaning knowledge of the Scriptures and their interpretation. It is not a claim that he was illiterate; Luke shows him handed a scroll in the synagogue and finding his place in it (Luke 4:16–17). “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi, the way Paul was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). A teacher was expected to cite his teachers: Rabbi So-and-so said, in the name of Rabbi So-and-so. That is how authority worked, and it is not a foolish system; it is how a community protects itself from anyone who turns up with a private revelation. Jesus quoted no rabbi, and yet he knew the Scriptures more deeply than any of them. They are not sneering, quite. They are trying to account for something that does not fit their categories. The same surprise is expressed about the apostles (Acts 4:13).

Does this mean training does not matter for preachers? No. The system was not wrong to ask where he had studied, and that question has saved the church from a great deal of nonsense. Paul was highly trained, and Scripture requires that elders be able to teach and hold firm to sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:15). Jesus is unique: his teacher was the Father, which no one else can claim. For everyone else, study is the ordinary way God makes faithful teachers. But the final test is not a certificate. It is whether a teacher’s words agree with Scripture and point to Christ. A trained man can be wrong, and an untrained believer can be right, and both must be weighed by the Word.

In a sentence. Halfway through the feast Jesus began teaching in the temple, and the authorities were astonished at his knowledge of the Scriptures, since he had never studied under a rabbi.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a degree to know the Scriptures well. Read them, slowly and often, and ask the Lord who wrote them to teach you. And when someone with no credentials says something true about God, listen before you correct their grammar.

For worship. Christ needed no teacher but the Father. His wisdom is not borrowed. The rabbis looked for a chain of teachers behind him and found none, because the chain ended in him: he is the Word who was with God in the beginning, and every true teacher who has ever opened the Scriptures has been borrowing from him. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he gives them freely to fishermen.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.”

My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. Jesus answers their question. He did have a teacher: the Father (5:19; 8:28; 12:49). His teaching is not his own invention; it comes from God. The Son’s school was eternal communion with the Father, a far greater authority than any rabbinic lineage.

If anyone’s will is to do God’s will. “Will” (thelē) means wants, wills, desires. The condition for knowing the truth is not first intellectual, but moral and spiritual: a will set on doing what God wants. This answers a question honest people actually ask: how could I know whether this is true? And the answer is not the one anyone expects. He does not offer an argument, a sign or a proof. Willingness first, knowledge second. This kind of truth is not available to detached inspection; a person determined to remain uncommitted while assessing the evidence has, by that very stance, put himself where the evidence cannot reach him.

He will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority. The person who truly wants to obey God will recognise Jesus’ teaching as God’s. The problem with unbelief is not lack of evidence but an unwilling heart (5:40; 8:43–47). Obedience and understanding go together. That can sound like a cheat, and it is worth saying plainly why it is not. There are many things a person can know while remaining entirely uninvolved: the boiling point of water, the date of a battle. There are other things that are only knowable from inside. Nobody has ever learned whether a person is trustworthy by studying them at a distance; you find out by trusting them. Nobody has ever discovered what music is by reading about it. To claim that God is known in the second way is not special pleading. It is a claim about what sort of being God is: not an object to be examined but a Lord to be obeyed. And the promise is remarkably wide. Not if anyone is clever, or educated, or has read the right books. If anyone’s will is to do God’s will. The condition is a disposition, not an achievement, and it is open to the least equipped person in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we can come to faith by our own good will, as if some people are naturally willing. John has just said no one can come unless the Father draws (6:44). The willing heart is itself God’s work. Whoever is of God hears the words of God (8:47). The verse describes how the Father’s drawing works: he gives a heart that wants to obey, and that heart recognises the Son’s teaching as God’s. But it does mean that the person who genuinely wants God’s will will never be left in the dark.

I want to believe, but I still have doubts. Does that mean my will is not set on God? No. Doubt is not the same as unwillingness. Many true believers carry questions for years, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 73; Mark 9:24). What this verse describes is the person who keeps God at arm’s length so as not to have to obey him. If you want God’s will, even weakly, and you are grieved by your doubts rather than comfortable with them, that wanting is itself his work in you. Bring your questions to him, keep reading his word, and keep obeying what you already know. Light comes along the road of obedience, often more slowly than we would like, but it comes.

In a sentence. Jesus said his teaching came from the one who sent him, and anyone who wants to do God’s will will know whether it is from God or from Jesus himself.

On a Tuesday. If you struggle with doubt, ask yourself: do I want to do God’s will? Obey what you know, and more light will come. Here is a test that can be run this week. Take the one thing you already suspect God wants of you: not a doctrine you are unsure of, but the plain duty you have been avoiding, the apology, the confession, the habit. Do that. Then see whether the intellectual difficulty is where it was. Very often the doubt was standing on top of the disobedience, and cannot survive its removal.

For worship. The Son did not speak on his own authority, though he had every right to. He who is God took the posture of one who listens, receives and passes on, so that what reaches us is nothing less than the Father’s own word. And the same God who speaks also gives the ears to hear. He does not leave us to find our own way to him; he makes us willing in the day of his power (Psalm 110:3), and then he shows us that the teaching was his all along.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?

The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory. A test for any teacher: whose glory does he seek? A teacher who speaks only from himself is out to make his own name. The test is portable and it still works. The criterion is not eloquence, or success, or even doctrinal accuracy on its own. It is the direction the man’s ambition points. Where does the credit end up? Who is bigger at the end of the sermon?

But the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Jesus seeks only the Father’s glory. That is the proof of his truthfulness. “No falsehood” (adikia, unrighteousness): there is nothing false or wrong in him. The word is not the ordinary word for a lie. He is not merely claiming to be accurate. He is claiming that there is nothing crooked in him at all, no bent motive under the straight sentence. It is the sort of thing that is either true or insufferable, and there is no third option. In him, it is simply true.

Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Jesus turns to the attack. They pride themselves on Moses, but they don’t keep his law. The change of register is abrupt. He has been reasoning; now he accuses.

Why do you seek to kill me? The proof: the law forbids murder, and they are planning one. They accuse Jesus of breaking the Sabbath, while they are planning to break the sixth commandment. It is the first time in the chapter that anybody says it out loud. John told the reader at verse 1, but no one in the courts has admitted it, and Jesus puts it in the middle of an argument about Moses, the most pointed place it could go. The charge is not exaggeration. Within months they will do precisely that, and it will be arranged by the men standing in front of him. He is reading their diary aloud.

How can I tell whether a preacher is seeking his own glory? Watch over time, not over a single sermon, because the test works over years rather than sentences. A man seeking Christ’s glory will make Christ large and himself small in his preaching; he will open the text rather than use it as a launch pad for himself. He will be accountable to others and will not build a ministry that cannot survive without him. He will be glad when someone else is preferred, slow to defend his own reputation, and quick to admit when he is wrong. Be wary of the teacher whose stories are mostly about himself, who cannot take correction, or whose church seems to exist to display him. And turn the test on yourself: when you serve, whose name do you most want remembered?

In a sentence. Jesus said that a teacher who seeks his own glory speaks for himself, but one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true; and though they had the law of Moses, none of them kept it, for they were seeking to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Test every preacher, and yourself, by this: whose glory is being sought? Before the meeting, the post, the lesson, or the conversation in which you are tempted to show what you know, ask quietly: Lord, let them see you, not me. Then notice how often that prayer changes what you were about to say.

For worship. There has only ever been one teacher in whom there was no falsehood at all. Every word he spoke aimed at his Father’s glory, and the Father answered by glorifying him (17:1). The men who held Moses in their hands and murder in their hearts stood before the only man who ever kept the law perfectly, and he kept it for them, all the way to the cross they were planning for him.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?” Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.”

The crowd answered, “You have a demon!” The crowd, many of them pilgrims, don’t know of the leaders’ plot. They think Jesus is paranoid, out of his mind. “Have a demon” was a way of saying mad (10:20). The same charge returns in 8:48, 52. And on the crowd’s part this is not so much hostility as alarm. A celebrated teacher has just announced from the temple courts that people are trying to murder him, and pilgrims from the provinces, who know nothing of the decision taken in chapter 5, conclude that he is unwell. That is the ordinary fate of anyone who names something the room has agreed not to see. The charge of madness is the cheapest available response, and it requires no engagement whatever. In this case the man was entirely correct, and was dead within six months.

Who is seeking to kill you? They don’t know. The leaders do (v. 25). It is worth keeping the two groups apart in this chapter, because John does. The crowd here is the festival pilgrims: ignorant, volatile and mostly well disposed. “The Jews”, in John’s shorthand, generally means the Jerusalem leadership, the men in verse 1 who had already decided. When the crowd asks who is seeking to kill him, they are telling the truth; they do not know. The reader has been told in the chapter’s first sentence, and so watches the exchange knowing what nobody in it knows.

I did one work, and you all marvel at it. The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath (5:1–9), which started the plot to kill him. “Marvel” here means they are disturbed and shocked by it, not admiring. His reply goes straight past the insult without a word of self-defence. And count how long ago that was. Chapter 5 was at an unnamed feast; chapter 6 was at Passover; this is Tabernacles, six months later. Many months have passed, and they are still on it. That is what he is pointing at with the word one. Not the scale of the offence but the arithmetic of the grievance. A single act of kindness to a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years has produced a settled determination to kill the one who did it, and the grievance has outlasted the memory of everything else he has done.

How should I respond when people think my faith is foolish or unhinged? Much as Jesus did: without panic and without retaliation. He did not argue about whether he was mad; he went straight back to the real issue. When people call your faith foolish, do not take the bait of defending your sanity or your intelligence. Gently bring the conversation back to Christ himself: what he did, what he said, why it matters. Paul was told he was out of his mind and answered with courtesy and the truth (Acts 26:24–25). And remember that if they said it of the Master, they will say it of his servants (15:20). It is not a sign you have failed. It may be a sign you have been clear.

In a sentence. The crowd said he had a demon and asked who was trying to kill him, and Jesus answered that he had done one work, and they were all shocked at it.

On a Tuesday. Notice your own grievances. Is there one act, by one person, that you are still holding against them months or years later, while forgetting everything else they have done? Jesus’ enemies nursed one healing into a murder plot. Ask God to show you any grudge that has grown larger than the thing it began with, and let it go.

For worship. Jesus bore being called mad and demon-possessed, for us. The Holy One, in whom the Spirit rested without measure, heard his own people say he had a demon, and he did not answer evil for evil. He went on teaching them. When we are misunderstood, we have a High Priest who has been there before us, and who was misunderstood all the way to the cross so that we could be understood, fully known and fully loved, by God.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.

Moses gave you circumcision. Jesus argues from their own law. The argument he is making is a standard rabbinic form, and his opponents would have recognised it instantly, which is what makes it so hard to answer.

Not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers. Circumcision was given to Abraham (Genesis 17:10–12), centuries before Moses, and the law confirmed it (Leviticus 12:3). It looks like a footnote, and it is a move in the argument. The obligation they allow to override the Sabbath is older than the Sabbath laws of Sinai. He is showing them that they already know how to rank two commandments when they seem to collide, and that they do it by asking which is older and deeper.

And you circumcise a man on the Sabbath. The law said a boy must be circumcised on the eighth day. If the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, circumcision went ahead, even though it was work. The rabbis agreed that this command overrode the Sabbath; the Mishnah puts it almost as flatly as Jesus does, that everything needed for circumcision may be done on the Sabbath. So their own practice admits that some works are right on the Sabbath. Jesus is not proposing a novelty. He is taking their own ruling and asking why it stops where it does.

What kind of thing wins. Notice why circumcision overrides the Sabbath in their own ruling. It is the sign of the covenant: it concerns a child being marked as belonging to God. The principle they have already granted is not administrative but merciful. When a rule and a person’s standing before God seem to collide, the person wins. Jesus is about to apply that to a man who had been on a mat for thirty-eight years, and it is their principle, not his.

Does this mean God’s commandments can be broken when they clash? No. God’s law does not contradict itself; the problem lies in how men had applied it. The Sabbath was never meant to forbid works of necessity and mercy, and even the confessions that keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath say so plainly, permitting works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8). Jesus is not setting one command against another. He is showing that the command, rightly understood, always had room for love. When we feel that obeying God and loving people are in conflict, the answer is not to drop one but to look again at what God actually commanded.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that Moses gave them circumcision, which came from the patriarchs, and that they circumcised on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Jesus reasons with his opponents from Scripture. Learn to do the same, patiently. When someone accuses you or the gospel, resist the urge simply to defend yourself or to win. Ask what common ground you share, what they already believe that points toward the truth, and start there, as Jesus does.

For worship. The Lord who reasoned so patiently about the eighth-day sign had received it himself: Luke tells us he was circumcised as a boy of eight days (Luke 2:21), marked with the covenant he had made with Abraham. He was born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). And what the sign promised, he gives: a circumcision made without hands, the putting off of the body of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), so that people from every nation are marked as God’s own, not by a knife but by his death and rising.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.

If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken. The argument goes from lesser to greater, a standard rabbinic method, which they called light and heavy. If it is right to perform circumcision, which affects one part of the body, on the Sabbath...

Are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well? ...how much more right is it to make a whole man well? Some rabbis themselves argued that if circumcision, involving one member, overrides the Sabbath, saving a life overrides it too. Jesus takes the argument further: healing is the very purpose of the Sabbath, a day of rest and restoration. The phrase he chooses is deliberate. One member against the whole man. If the part may be dealt with, how can healing the whole be a violation?

Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment. “Appearances” (opsis) means what is seen on the surface: they see only that he worked on the Sabbath. Right judgment looks at what was really done, and why. It looks beneath the surface to the purpose of the law. God himself looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). And notice what this verse does not say, because it is regularly quoted as if it said the opposite. It is a command to judge. Jesus is in the middle of telling a crowd that their verdict on him is wrong, and his complaint is not that they judged but that they judged badly.

So am I allowed to judge people or not? Yes and no, and Jesus’ two sayings fit together once you notice what each is about. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matthew 7:1) forbids the judgment that sets itself up as final, condemns the person, and applies to others a standard the speaker exempts himself from; it is followed at once by the log in one’s own eye. This verse requires the judgment that looks past the surface to the substance. The first forbids condemning. The second commands discerning. A Christian must tell right from wrong, truth from error, and a wolf from a sheep. What he must never do is sit in God’s seat over another person’s soul, or judge by rumour, appearance or prejudice.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Jesus never abolished the Sabbath in the Gospels, but showed its true purpose. Some Christians keep a strict Saturday or Sunday Sabbath; others see no special day at all. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day, the first day, when Christ rose, is a privilege for Christians, a day of worship and rest, to be kept not as a burden but as a gift, with works of mercy always in place.

What does keeping the Lord’s Day look like in practice? Begin with what it is for: meeting the risen Christ with his people. So put gathered worship at the centre and arrange the rest of the day around it, rather than fitting church into a busy Sunday. Rest from your ordinary work where you can, not as a rule to earn favour but as a gift that says your life does not depend on your labour. Make room for what refreshes the soul: the word, prayer, family, hospitality, visiting the lonely or the sick. Works of mercy and necessity are always in place: nurses, carers and parents of small children are not breaking anything. And do not make the day a burden for others; Jesus came to free the Sabbath from that.

In a sentence. If they circumcised on the Sabbath to keep the law, why were they angry that Jesus healed a whole man on the Sabbath? They should judge rightly, not by appearances.

On a Tuesday. Before you judge someone, look beneath the surface. Ask what was really done, and why. Take a judgment you currently hold about somebody. Ask which part of it rests on how the thing looked, and which on what you actually know. Then ask whether you would accept a verdict on yourself reached on that evidence. Judging by appearance is not only a failure of charity. It is a failure of accuracy.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath made a whole man well on the day of rest, and in doing so showed what the day had always been for. He is our rest. He finished his work on the cross, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of the week to make all things new. One day he will make his people whole, body and soul, and the rest God promised at creation will be ours for ever.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?”

Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said. Not the pilgrims, but locals who know what the leaders are planning. They live there; they hear things; and they are watching a man they know to be under sentence teaching in the temple courts unmolested. They know the plot that the crowd denied (v. 20).

And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! They are puzzled that the leaders do nothing. And there is a sting here that rewards attention. “Openly” is parrhēsia, freedom of speech, saying everything without holding back. Thirteen verses earlier John used the same word of the crowd: for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him (v. 13). The people who admire him whisper. The man with a price on his head speaks freely in the temple. John does not comment on the contrast. He lets it stand.

Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ? The Greek form expects the answer no. They are half joking, half wondering. “The Christ” (ho Christos), the Messiah, the anointed king. Their reasoning is not stupid. If the authorities wanted him, and he is standing in public, and nothing is happening, then something must have changed, and the only explanation they can think of is that the rulers have quietly come round.

The restraint nobody can see. They are wrong, and John will supply the reason four verses later: no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (v. 30). The inaction they are trying to explain is not a decision anyone in the building has taken. It is a restraint nobody in the story can see, exercised by someone who is not visibly present. That is the shape of a great deal of providence. Things do not happen, and everyone constructs a reason: he must have decided, they must have relented, the moment must have passed. Sometimes the real reason is simpler, and is not available to the people looking for it.

In a sentence. Some of the people of Jerusalem wondered why the authorities, who wanted to kill him, said nothing while he taught openly, and whether they had decided he was the Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of something that should have gone wrong this year and did not: the accident that did not happen, the plan against you that came to nothing, the word that was never said. You probably have an ordinary explanation for it. You may be right. But behind the ordinary explanation there is a hand, and it is worth thanking him for what you never saw.

For worship. The people of Jerusalem asked it half in jest: can it be that this is the Christ? It was the truest question of the week. He stood in the courts with a price on his head and spoke without holding back, because his life was never in the rulers’ keeping. No one takes it from me, he would say, but I lay it down of my own accord (10:18). The men who could not touch him that week did not take his life at Passover either. He gave it, and took it up again, and their half-joking question has an answer that fills heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from.

But we know where this man comes from. They know he is from Nazareth in Galilee. And the verb carries the deepest irony in the chapter. We know: the whole of this Gospel is the answer to that sentence. They know Nazareth. John’s readers have known since the first verse that he comes from the Father’s side, and that the true answer to where he is from is a place none of them has considered.

And when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from. Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding. Jewish writings speak of the Messiah being hidden until God revealed him. Others knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42). The popular idea may have grown from Malachi 3:1, where the Lord suddenly comes to his temple. So the crowd is working with two traditions that pull in opposite directions, and in this chapter they use both against him within fifteen verses. Here he is disqualified because his origin is known. There he is disqualified because it is the wrong one. Any candidate who satisfied the second would fail the first.

The irony. They think they know where he comes from. In fact, they know neither his birthplace, Bethlehem, nor his true origin, the Father in heaven. Their very objection is mistaken on both counts. And the pattern is worth noticing without becoming cynical about it, because it is a recognisable human habit and not a peculiarly Jewish one. When a conclusion has been reached in advance, the reasons arrive afterwards and do not need to be consistent with each other, since their job is not to establish the conclusion but to protect it.

So where did Jesus come from? Three answers, all true. As a man, he was born in Bethlehem, the town of David, as Micah foretold (Matthew 2:1–6), and grew up in Nazareth, which is why he was called a Nazarene. As the Son, he came from the Father, with whom he was before the world began (1:1; 17:5). And he came into the world by the Holy Spirit, conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). His enemies knew only the middle town of the three. Faith knows all of them: the eternal Son, born of a woman, raised in a despised village, so that no one could say God had come too high for them to reach.

In a sentence. They argued that they knew where Jesus came from, but no one would know where the Christ came from.

On a Tuesday. Beware of being sure you know all about Jesus. They knew his hometown, and missed that he came from heaven. Think of the reason you would give if you had to say why you do not take some claim of Christ seriously, perhaps a command you have quietly decided does not apply to you. Now ask whether you reached the reason before or after the conclusion.

For worship. The one whose goings forth are from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2), consented to have a hometown that people could sneer at. He came from the Father’s side to a carpenter’s house, and let men think they had him summed up. They knew where he came from as a man. They did not know that the man in front of them had made the hills that Nazareth stood on.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.”

So Jesus proclaimed. “Proclaimed” (ekraxen, cried out): a loud, public, solemn declaration (v. 37; 12:44). This is not the measured tone of the preceding exchange. He raises his voice in the temple courts.

You know me, and you know where I come from. This may be ironic: you think you know me. They know the earthly facts, but not the heavenly reality. It can be read as a concession, yes, you know the human facts and they are correct as far as they go, or with an edge, as near to sarcasm as he comes: so you know me, do you? The sentence that follows tips it toward the second. Whatever they know, it has left them ignorant of the one thing that would explain him: he has not come of his own accord, but was sent.

He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. “True” (alēthinos): genuine, real. The God who sent him is real, and they do not know him. A stunning charge against the religious leaders of Israel in their own temple. To reject the Son is to show you do not know the Father (8:19; 15:21). Weigh how large the claim is. He tells a courtyard full of devout people, at their own feast, in their own temple, that they do not know God. Not that they know him imperfectly; that they do not know him, and that he does. This is the charge that will not be forgiven. A man may say a great deal about God in that building and survive it. What he may not say is that the people whose whole life is organised around knowing God do not, and that he is the one who does.

I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me. Jesus knows the Father because he came from the Father’s presence. Here is his true origin, the answer to their question. And the ground he gives is not experience but origin. Not because he has prayed well or been taught well. Because of where he started: with God, as God (1:1, 18).

Can someone be sincerely religious and still not know God? Yes, and this verse is the proof. These men prayed, fasted, studied Scripture and kept the feasts, and Jesus says they did not know the one they worshipped. Knowing God is not the same as being religious. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3), and no one comes to the Father except through the Son (14:6). That is not a reason to sneer at sincere people of other faiths or none, but it is a reason not to leave them where they are. And it is a question to ask ourselves, gently and honestly: do I know God through Christ, or do I only know the religion?

In a sentence. Jesus cried out in the temple that though they thought they knew where he came from, he had been sent by the true God, whom they did not know, but he knew, because he came from him.

On a Tuesday. Knowing God comes through knowing the Son. If God feels distant or unreal to you, do not look for him in a feeling or a technique. Look at Jesus: read a Gospel, slowly, and ask at each page, so this is what God is like. Then talk to him about what you see.

For worship. No prophet, priest or rabbi had ever stood in the Father’s presence and come out to tell us what he saw. The Son had, for he is at the Father’s side and has made him known (1:18). He did not keep that knowledge to himself. He shouted it in the temple to men who had the scrolls and not the God of the scrolls, and then he opened the way into the Father’s presence with his own blood, so that people who did not know God could be brought home and know him as the Son knows him: as Father.

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, “When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?”

But no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. His claim to come from God enraged them, and they tried to arrest him. “His hour”: in John, the hour of his death, resurrection and return to the Father (2:4; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). No one could touch him before it came. Jesus was not a victim of circumstances. The timing of his death was in the Father’s hands. Now the word John has been holding back returns. Not kairos, the right moment, which is what he said to his brothers in verse 6. Hōra: the appointment. It has been running since Cana, and it will keep not coming until chapter 12, when Greeks ask to see him and he says that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. That hour is the cross. So what is protecting him here is not a bodyguard or a clever escape. It is an appointment with his own execution that has not yet fallen due. He is safe because he is going to die, and not yet.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me until my work is done? Not quite, and it is worth being honest about what the verse promises. It does not say God’s servants are always preserved until they have done everything we think they should do; Stephen was stoned early in his ministry, and John the Baptist was beheaded on a whim at a party. What it says is narrower, harder and more solid: nothing whatever happens outside the Father’s timing, including the things that look like defeat. The same providence that kept hands off Jesus in this verse will hand him over in chapter 18, and it is the same providence doing the same loving work. Your days are written in his book (Psalm 139:16). No accident, no enemy and no illness can shorten them by an hour.

Yet many of the people believed in him. Some believed. In John, belief can be shallow (2:23–25; 8:30–31), but here it is a start. In the middle of a chapter about hostility, arrest warrants and division, faith is quietly spreading. John reports it without comment, and he counts it.

When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done? They reason from the signs. This is not the deepest faith, but signs are meant to lead to faith (20:30–31). Their reasoning is modest and mostly right: could anyone do more than this? It is not a complete confession. It is not nothing.

Is faith that starts from miracles real faith? It can be the beginning of real faith, and Jesus does not despise it. He does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). John himself wrote down the signs so that we may believe (20:31). But faith that only wants more signs, and stops at what Jesus can do, has not yet reached who he is. The crowd in chapter 6 wanted more bread and walked away when he offered himself. True faith moves from the works to the person: from what he did, to trusting him, loving him and following him when there are no signs at all. Whatever first drew you to Christ, the question is whether you have come to rest in him.

In a sentence. They tried to arrest him, but no one could, because his hour had not yet come, and many of the people believed, asking whether the Christ would do more signs than he had.

On a Tuesday. Your life, like Christ’s, is in the Father’s hands. Nothing can touch you before his time. That truth is meant to make you brave, not careless. Name the fear that is most often in your mind this month, and set this sentence over it: my times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15).

For worship. The hour that kept not coming finally came, and he went into it willingly. He was protected from every arrest until the one that would save us, and then he gave himself up. The hands that could not touch him in the temple were permitted, at last, to nail him to a cross, because that was the hour the Father had appointed from before the foundation of the world for the salvation of his people.

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.

The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him. Talk of Jesus as the Christ alarms them. Notice what actually triggers the warrant. Not the teaching, not the Sabbath argument, not the claim in verse 29 to have come from God. It is verse 31: the muttering of the crowd, the fact that people are starting to believe. They move when the numbers move. And notice how they came to hear it. Muttering, in a festival crowd of tens of thousands, in whispers because people were afraid to speak openly (v. 13). That is not overheard by accident. There were ears in that crowd reporting back. What got reported was not a sermon but the mood of ordinary people, which tells you what the leadership was protecting.

The chief priests and Pharisees. Two groups who normally disagreed. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple; wealthy, at ease with Rome, and sceptical of the resurrection. The Pharisees were the lay party of strict law-keeping, and largely despised them. Together they made up much of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. They unite against Jesus. In this Gospel the two act together only to deal with him (7:32, 45; 11:47, 57; 18:3). Opposition to Christ has a talent for uniting people who cannot stand each other, and it will do it again at the trial, where a Roman governor and a Jewish council, and Herod and Pilate who had been enemies, find their way to the same verdict (Luke 23:12).

Sent officers to arrest him. The officers were the temple police, Levites who kept order in the temple under the chief priests. They were used to clearing the courts and removing troublemakers. They set out with a straightforward job and no reason to expect difficulty, and they will come back empty-handed, saying that no one ever spoke like this man (v. 46).

In a sentence. When the Pharisees heard the crowd talking about Jesus, the chief priests and Pharisees sent the temple police to arrest him.

On a Tuesday. Do not be surprised when people who agree on nothing else agree in opposing Christ, and do not be frightened by it. Every attempt to arrest the word by force, from Pharaoh to the present day, has met the same end. Pray for persecuted believers by name this week, and pray for the officers too.

For worship. The rulers of the temple sent its police against the Lord of the temple, and he did not lift a hand. He did not need to. The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:2–4). Every alliance of enemies who could agree on nothing else has broken against this same quiet man, and the only arrest that ever held him was the one he walked out to meet in a garden, saying to the soldiers, I am he (18:5).
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then said, “I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come.”

I will be with you a little longer. About six months remained before the cross. This is Tabernacles, in the autumn; he will die at Passover, in the spring. He answers a warrant for his arrest by announcing his travel plans, and the effect is to take the whole confrontation out of their hands. They think they are deciding whether he stays. He tells them he is leaving anyway, shortly, and for somewhere they cannot follow.

And then I am going to him who sent me. Jesus speaks of his death, resurrection and ascension as a going home to the Father (13:1, 3; 16:5, 28). He is not driven out; he goes.

You will seek me and you will not find me. A solemn warning. There will come a time when it is too late. The opportunity is now. Compare Proverbs 1:28 and Isaiah 55:6: seek the Lord while he may be found. It is addressed to men holding an arrest warrant: people who have him in front of them, who are seeking him at that moment in order to stop him, and who will one day want what he offered and find the offer withdrawn. That is not a threat aimed at the worried. It is a fact aimed at the comfortable.

Where I am you cannot come. Not “where I will be” but “where I am”: he speaks as the one who already belongs to the Father’s presence. Unbelievers cannot follow him there (8:21). He says something similar to the disciples later (13:33), but with a promise: you will follow afterwards (13:36; 14:3).

I am frightened that it may be too late for me. Is this verse about me? If you are troubled by it, that trouble is itself the evidence that it is not describing you. The seeking that fails in this verse is not the seeking of the frightened; it is the seeking of men who refused him to his face, and who would one day want rescue without wanting him. Scripture never shows a penitent sinner coming to God and finding the door shut. The whole burden of this Gospel is the opposite: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37), said to a crowd that mostly walked away. While you are alive and can call on him, the door is open. Call on him now.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would be with them only a little longer, before going to the one who sent him, and then they would seek him and not find him, for they could not come where he is.

On a Tuesday. Today is the day of salvation. Do not assume you can seek Christ later. If there is something you have been meaning to settle with God, a sin to confess, a step of obedience, a first prayer, do not leave it for a better week. And if you are praying for someone who keeps putting him off, tell them gently that the offer is real and that the time is not unlimited.

For worship. He went home to the Father by way of the cross, and he did not go alone. The place where his enemies could not come is the place he has gone to prepare for his friends (14:2–3). To unbelief he says, where I am you cannot come; to faith he says, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. The same words that warn the proud are the hope of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, ‘You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ‘Where I am you cannot come’?”

Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? They misunderstand again, thinking only of earthly places.

Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? The Dispersion (diaspora) means the Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, in the cities of the Greek-speaking world. More Jews lived outside Israel than in it. They mockingly suggest he will go and teach Gentiles, the lowest thing a Jewish teacher could do. They mean it as the reduction of his words to absurdity: the man is talking nonsense, unless he means something ridiculous, like going off to the scattered communities in foreign cities and teaching foreigners.

The irony. Their mocking guess was prophetic. Through his apostles, Jesus did go to the Dispersion and teach the Greeks. The gospel went from Jerusalem to the synagogues of the Dispersion and then to the Gentiles across the empire (Acts 11:20; 13:46). The letters of James and 1 Peter are addressed to the Dispersion. Within twenty-five years the message had gone to precisely those communities, by precisely that route, and the man carrying it was a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem. John is writing for readers who lived in those cities. When they reached this sentence, they were reading a mocking question that had turned into their own address.

Enemies who say more than they know. It is not the only time opponents of Jesus say more than they know. It will happen again at 11:50, when Caiaphas remarks that it is better for one man to die for the people, and John stops the story to point out that he was prophesying without the least idea of it. That is a quiet claim about how history is being run. The people most determined to stop this are not merely failing. They are being used, and their own sentences are being taken up and made true in a sense they would have found intolerable.

What does he mean by saying...? They cannot understand, because they are thinking on the wrong level. And notice what they do with his words. They quote them back, both halves, in full: you will seek me and you will not find me, and where I am you cannot come. Men who are dismissing something do not usually repeat it that carefully. It is the behaviour of people worrying at a sentence they cannot get out of their heads. They have no idea what it means, they are certain it is nonsense, and they cannot leave it alone.

In a sentence. They wondered where he could go where they would not find him, mocking that he might go to teach the Greeks among the scattered Jews, and puzzling over his words.

On a Tuesday. If you are not Jewish, you are reading this verse as one of the Greeks it mocked. Take a moment to see your own name in it, and thank God that the gospel came the long way round to reach you. Then ask who the Greeks are in your world: the people your church would find strange to teach. Go to them.

For worship. When Greeks did come asking to see him, at the next Passover, he said that the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified, because a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die before it bears much fruit (12:20–24). That is how he went to the Dispersion: not by leaving Jerusalem but by dying in it, rising, and sending his word after the scattered. Lifted up, he draws all people to himself (12:32), and the far cities his enemies sneered at are full of his worshippers.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”

On the last day of the feast, the great day. Probably the seventh day, the climax of the water ceremony, though some think the eighth day of solemn assembly. Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the Pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher each morning, in a joyful procession with trumpets, and poured out beside the altar, while the people sang the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) and prayed for the autumn rains. On the seventh day the priests circled the altar seven times. The ceremony looked back to the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and forward to the promised day when living waters would flow out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8, read at this feast) and from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12). The rabbis said that whoever had not seen the joy of the water-drawing had never seen joy in his life.

Jesus stood up and cried out. Teachers usually sat. He stands and calls out loudly, at the very moment the people are celebrating water. Picture it. For seven mornings the golden pitcher had come up from Siloam and the people had sung and waved their branches; on the great day the procession circled the altar seven times, and then it was over for another year. Into that moment a man stands up in the temple courts and shouts. The ceremony had been remembering water from a rock for a nation that would otherwise have died in the desert, and he offers, to anybody at all, what the ceremony had only ever pointed at.

If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. An open invitation to anyone. It echoes Isaiah 55:1: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters. What the ceremony pointed to, Jesus gives. He is the rock from which the water flows (1 Corinthians 10:4). To come and drink is to believe (6:35). And the terms are as wide as language permits. If anyone thirsts. Not if anyone is worthy, or prepared, or knows enough. The only qualification is an appetite, and it is the one qualification nobody can manufacture and nobody can fake, which is why it is the one he asks for. Nobody in that courtyard needed to be told they were thirsty.
