I judge no one. Not that Jesus never judges (5:22, 27), but that he did not come to judge as they do, nor was judging the purpose of his first coming (3:17; 12:47). The two halves of this saying look like a contradiction and are not. The resolution is in the timing. In his first coming he is not sitting as judge; that is not what the visit is for, and anyone who meets him now meets him as Saviour. The judging is real, it is his, and it is deferred. What he refuses is not the office but the timetable.

Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true. When he does judge, his judgment is right, for it is not he alone who judges, but he and the Father who sent him. They act together (5:30). His judgment is God’s judgment. The law’s demand for two witnesses was designed to protect against a false verdict; here the verdict comes from the Father and the Son together, in perfect knowledge and perfect agreement.

If Jesus will judge everyone, why does God seem to let things go now? Because the court has not yet sat, and the delay is grace. The reason a person is not being judged today is not that God has grown relaxed about sin. It is that he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). The interval is given to be used: for the unbeliever to turn, and for the believer to call others to turn. It is also a comfort to anyone who has been wronged and has seen no justice. Nothing has been forgotten. The judge is Christ, and his judgment is true.

In a sentence. Jesus said they judged by human standards, while he judged no one; but when he did judge, his judgment was true, because the Father judged with him.

On a Tuesday. Judging according to the flesh is not usually experienced as prejudice. It is experienced as noticing: the accent, the job, the clothes, the school. Its conclusions feel like observations, which is exactly what makes them so hard to revisit. Think of someone you summed up quickly and have not reconsidered. Give them a second look this week.

For worship. The judge of all the earth will do right, and the judge is Christ, who came first to save. He who will sit on the throne at the last came the first time to stand in the dock. The one who will judge the living and the dead was judged by men who judged according to the flesh, and he let them do it, so that his people could stand in the last judgment without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me.

In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). “Your Law” does not distance Jesus from the law; it emphasises that they are the ones who claim to live by it. Yet there is a quiet note of authority in the phrase. It is the tone of one who says, very well, let us proceed by your own procedure, and then names God as his co-witness. A prophet says, thus says the LORD. This is the Lord of the law himself, agreeing to be tried by its rules.

I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me. Two witnesses: the Son and the Father. Here is the deepest testimony there is, and it is not mere human evidence. On any ordinary reading it is an outrageous answer: the two-witness rule exists so that no man’s account of himself need be taken on trust, and he satisfies it by calling a witness nobody else can call and nobody present can cross-examine. But the second witness had already testified, publicly, three ways: in the works he gave Jesus to do (5:36), in the Scriptures (5:39), and at the Jordan (1:32–34). The men asking for him had been present for at least two of them.

But how can I believe a witness I cannot see? In the same way these men were meant to: through the testimony he has given. The Father’s witness is not hidden. It is in the works of Jesus, recorded so that you may believe (20:31); in the Scriptures, which from Moses onwards point to him (5:39, 46); and supremely in the resurrection, by which God declared him to be his Son (Romans 1:4). And the Spirit himself bears witness, opening our eyes to see what is there (15:26; 1 John 5:6–10). You are not asked to believe without evidence. You are asked to receive the evidence God has given, rather than demanding a different kind on your own terms.

In a sentence. Jesus said their law required two witnesses, and he had two: himself and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. The question in the courtyard was not a shortage of evidence. They wanted evidence that would let them remain the assessors: something produced on demand, on their terms. Notice whether you are doing the same, asking God for a sign while ignoring the testimony already in your hands. Open a Gospel and read the witness the Father has given.

For worship. Two witnesses, and both of them God. At the Jordan the Spirit came down and remained on him (1:32), and, as the other Gospels tell us, the Father’s voice owned him as his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17); at the empty tomb the Father spoke again, louder, by raising him from the dead. No court in heaven or on earth can overturn that testimony, and no cross-examination can shake it. The God who cannot lie has told us who Jesus is, and in telling us he has shown us what he is himself: a Father who delights in his Son, and gives him to the world.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him therefore, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.

Where is your Father? They want to see this second witness. Perhaps it is also a sneer at the rumours about his birth (v. 41). On its face the question is fair: he has named a second witness, and in any human court the next step is to ask to see him.

You know neither me nor my Father. They cannot see the Father because they don’t know the Son. The answer refuses the terms completely. He does not produce the Father, offer a sign, or argue. The witness they want to examine is not someone who can be summoned into the courtyard, and the only access to him is through the man they are cross-examining.

If you knew me, you would know my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (14:7–9). There is no knowing God apart from Christ. This is one of John’s plainest statements that Jesus is the revelation of God, and that every other road to the Father is closed (14:6). It is the point on which the Christian faith is least negotiable, and it should be stated without softening. Knowledge of God is not available around Jesus: not through sincerity, not through the law these men administered, not through the temple they were standing in.

These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering boxes stood (Mark 12:41). The great lamps of the feast also stood in this court. He spoke of light where the lamps burned. It was among the busiest, most public places in the whole temple. It is also where he would later sit and watch a widow put in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). He is standing beside the giving of Israel when he says that they do not know God.

But no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come. The Court of the Women was close to the council chamber. He spoke right under their noses, and still no one could touch him. The boldest claims in the chapter are made in the busiest place available, to the men who wanted him dead, and the sentence that follows is the flattest in the passage: no one arrested him. John explains it in a single clause.

What about people who love God but do not believe in Jesus? Jesus’ words are hard and clear: to know the Father you must know the Son, and to reject the Son is to show that you do not know the Father (5:23; 1 John 2:23). Many people are sincere, devout and morally serious without Christ, and we should respect their seriousness and treat them with love. But sincerity is not the same as knowing God, and Scripture says there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12). That is not a reason for pride; it is a reason for urgency and tenderness, because the God they are looking for has come in Jesus, and they need to hear of him.

In a sentence. They asked where his Father was, and Jesus answered that they knew neither him nor his Father, for to know him is to know the Father; he said this in the treasury, and no one arrested him, for his hour had not come.

On a Tuesday. When you catch yourself picturing God as harsh, distant or indifferent, set that picture beside the Jesus of the Gospels: crying out to the thirsty, touching the leper, weeping at a grave. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9), so let the Son correct the picture.

For worship. The God no one has ever seen has made himself known in his Son. We do not have to climb up to heaven to find out what the Father is like; the Son came down, and stood among the offering boxes, and said, know me and you will know him. All the fullness of God dwells in him bodily (Colossians 2:9), and every glimpse of the Father we will ever have, in this age and the next, will be in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he said to them again, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” So the Jews said, “Will he kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?”

I am going away, and you will seek me. As in 7:33–34, he is going to the Father, and where he is going they cannot come: heaven is closed to those who reject the one who opens it.

And you will die in your sin. The most frightening sentence in the chapter. “In your sin”: singular here, the root sin of unbelief (16:9); plural in v. 24, the sins that flow from it. To die in your sin is to die unforgiven, still carrying your guilt, and so to face God’s judgment with it. And the warning has hardened since chapter 7. There he said, you will seek me and you will not find me (7:34). Here the same warning comes back with a clause added. It is not being repeated. It is being completed.

One root, many fruits. The singular is deliberate and easy to walk past. The sin, singular, is named at verse 24: not believing that he is who he says. That is the root; the plural sins are the fruit. He is saying that there is one thing fundamentally wrong with these men, and everything else follows from it. Every sin will be brought into the light at the judgment, and none will be overlooked. But the decisive matter is a person’s relation to Christ, because he is the only one who can take sins away. To refuse him is to keep every sin one has ever committed.

>>>

Will he kill himself? A worse misunderstanding than in 7:35. Suicide was thought to send a person to the lowest depths of Hades, so they mean, perhaps, that he is going where they would never go. The irony is deep: Jesus will lay down his life, of his own will (10:17–18), but not as they imagine, and it will be they who put him to death. They have guessed, in mockery, that he intends to die by his own decision. They are wrong about the manner and the motive, and right about the fact. Once again his enemies prophesy without knowing it.

Can a believer die in his sin? No. A believer dies in the Lord (Revelation 14:13), with every sin forgiven, because Christ has borne them. Dying in your sin means dying without Christ, still carrying your guilt. If you trust him, even weakly, even with sins you are still fighting, you will not die in your sin; you will die forgiven, and wake in his presence. The warning is for those who refuse him. For those who come to him, the promise of 6:37 stands: he will never cast them out.

In a sentence. Jesus warned again that he was going away, and they would seek him and die in their sin, unable to follow; and they wondered if he would kill himself.

On a Tuesday. Do not carry your sin to the grave. If there is anything you have never brought to Christ, bring it today. And if someone you love is far from him, pray for them by name, and look for a way this week to tell them, gently, that there is forgiveness in him.

For worship. The truth was stranger and kinder than their sneer. He did go to death by his own decision, not in despair but in love, and he carried there the very sin they were about to die in. He went under the judgment sinners deserve, so that no one who trusts him need die in his sin, and then he went home to the Father, where they could not come, to open the way for all who would. He went where we could not go, so that one day we may be where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins.”

You are from below; I am from above. Two realms, two origins. They belong to the fallen world (3:31). He comes from heaven. He is not insulting them. He is explaining why the conversation keeps failing: two parties are using the same words, and one of them came from somewhere else. They are of this world, human life in rebellion against God; he is not.

Unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins. “That I am he” is literally “that I am” (egō eimi), with nothing added. This is the divine name. In Exodus 3:14 God revealed himself as “I am who I am,” and in Isaiah the Lord says again and again, “I am he” (Isaiah 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12), using in the Greek Old Testament the same words Jesus uses here. Isaiah 43:10 is especially close: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Jesus is claiming to be the God of Israel, come in the flesh. To be saved, one must believe that he is who he says he is. Salvation is not faith in faith, or vague faith in God, but faith in Jesus as Lord and God (20:28).

The bare name. Translators supply the pronoun because English will not tolerate the sentence otherwise, and they are right to; but the bare form is what the hearers got, and it is the form God used at the bush. The same absolute I am will come back at verse 28, and at verse 58 it will get him stoned. He is laying it down here quietly, three times over, before anyone reacts. And the condition attached to it is as narrow as anything he ever said. Not, unless you live well. Not, unless you keep the law, which these men were doing with more rigour than most people alive today could imagine. Unless you believe that I am. There is no version of this in which the identity of Jesus is an optional extra on top of a decent life. He has made it the hinge, in the temple, in public, and the men listening understood him perfectly.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus God? Jehovah’s Witnesses, Unitarians and others teach that Jesus is a created being, a lesser god or a great prophet. Verdict: Jesus here claims the divine name, and makes faith in it necessary for salvation. With 1:1, 5:18, 8:58, 10:30 and 20:28, John teaches plainly that Jesus is God the Son, one with the Father. This is not a secondary doctrine: unless you believe, you die in your sins.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse is spoken to men who had heard the claim plainly and were rejecting it, so its first force falls on everyone who has heard. But Scripture as a whole is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). That is why the church is sent to the nations. God is just, and no one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of, but for real sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). And the Reformed churches have held that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit. The right response is not to speculate but to go, and send, and pray.

In a sentence. Jesus said they were from below and he from above, they of this world and he not, and unless they believed that he is the I AM, they would die in their sins.

On a Tuesday. When you say the creed, or sing that Jesus is Lord, do not let the words slide past. Stop on one of them this week and say it slowly: Jesus is God. Then ask what difference it makes to the thing you are anxious about, or the sin you are tolerating, that the one who loves you is the I AM.

For worship. The fire that burned and was not consumed, the voice that sent Moses to Pharaoh, the God who said through Isaiah that before him no god was formed (Isaiah 43:10), stood in the temple in a human body and spoke the same name. The I AM came down from above to those who were from below, not to crush them but to be believed, so that people of this world could be made citizens of heaven. The name that made Moses hide his face now has a face of its own, and it is turned towards sinners.
verseByVerse.note: “That I am he” is literally “that I am” — the divine name.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe me, that I am he

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him.”

Who are you? The central question of the chapter, and of the Gospel. It may be a sneer: who do you think you are? After everything, the bread, the water, the light, the claim laid down twice already in this conversation, they still ask it. And they will go on asking it: Pilate will ask where he is from and get no answer at all (19:9). It is the question this Gospel exists to answer.

Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. The Greek here is notoriously difficult. The ESV reads it as an answer: I am what I have said all along. Others take it as an exclamation: why do I speak to you at all? The ESV’s reading suits the context: Jesus has been telling them who he is from the start. Either way the effect is the same, which is why the difficulty need not trouble a reader. He offers them nothing new. The obvious move, with a crowd this hostile and a claim this large, is to find better words. He does not. He has said it; the failure is not in the phrasing.

I have much to say about you and much to judge. He could say much more in judgment of them. He knows a great deal about the men in front of him, and says almost none of it. That is the more remarkable half of the sentence: the restraint of one who could expose every heart and chooses not to, yet.

But he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him. But his task now is to speak what the Father gives him (12:49–50). Nothing withheld, and nothing added on his own account.

Why do some people hear the gospel many times and never seem to understand? Because the problem is rarely the explanation. These men had heard Jesus himself, the clearest teacher who ever lived, and still asked who he was. Understanding the gospel is not only a matter of information but of a heart opened by God (6:44; 2 Corinthians 4:4–6). That should keep us from two mistakes: thinking that if only we found cleverer words, everyone would believe; and giving up on people who do not understand yet. Keep saying it plainly and lovingly, and pray that God will open their eyes.

In a sentence. When they asked who he was, Jesus said he was what he had told them from the beginning, and while he had much to judge in them, he spoke to the world what he heard from the true God who sent him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus has already told us who he is. The question is not whether he has spoken, but whether we have listened. If you are waiting for God to say something new before you obey what he has already said, start with what he has said.

For worship. He has told us who he is from the beginning, and he has never changed his story. In the beginning was the Word; and the Word still speaks, faithful and true, declaring to the world what he heard from the Father. He holds back judgment that he could pronounce, and speaks mercy instead. Blessed is the Lord who is patient with our slowness and keeps on telling us the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me.”

They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. He has named his Father again and again, and they are still blind to the obvious.

When you have lifted up the Son of Man. In John, “lifted up” (hypsoō) means both the cross and his exaltation (3:14; 12:32–33). It is the language of Isaiah 52:13 about the Servant who will be “lifted up.” They will lift him up on the cross, and that very act will be his exaltation. “You” will do it: they are responsible for his death. This is the second of three sayings about being lifted up, and they should be read as a set. The first was to Nicodemus: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up (3:14). The third comes in chapter 12, where John stops to explain that he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). The verb does double duty, and this Gospel never lets the two meanings come apart. The enthronement and the execution are one event.

Then you will know that I am he. Again “I am” (egō eimi). The cross will reveal who he is. Some will know it to their salvation (the centurion, Mark 15:39; the thousands at Pentecost, Acts 2:36–41); others to their judgment. There is a terrible courtesy in the sentence. He tells the men planning it that they will do it, and in the same breath that it will be the moment they finally understand. The knowledge comes too late to prevent the act and is caused by it. And the first person recorded as confessing him after his death was the Roman officer who had carried it out.

And that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me. The cross will also show his perfect obedience to the Father. Taught is a domestic word. The picture behind it is ordinary in that world: a son in a workshop, learning the trade by watching his father. He used the same image at 5:19–20: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, because the Father loves him and shows him everything. So the authority these men keep demanding an account of is not seized. It is the authority of the Son, received from the Father as a trade is handed from father to son.

Does this make the Son less than the Father? No. The Son is equal with the Father in being (10:30; 8:58), but he is sent and the Father sends; he obeys and the Father commands. That order is a matter of their relation, not of their nature. The Son does nothing on his own because he and the Father act as one. A son who does exactly what his father does is not less than his father; he is his father’s likeness. And the Son’s obedience is not a sign of inferiority but the glory of his love: he delights to do the Father’s will.

How is the cross a glory, when it looks like defeat? Because at the cross we see most clearly who God is. There his justice is satisfied, his love poured out, his wisdom displayed and his power at work, all at once, in one man dying for others (Romans 3:25–26; 5:8). What looked like the end of Jesus’ influence became the start of his worldwide reign. What his enemies meant as his shame, God made his throne. That is why Christians speak of the glory of the cross, and why Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).

In a sentence. They did not understand he was speaking of the Father, so Jesus said that when they had lifted up the Son of Man they would know that he is the I AM, who does nothing by himself but speaks as the Father taught him.

On a Tuesday. When you want to know whether God loves you, do not look first at your circumstances. Look at the cross. It is where the I AM was lifted up for you, and what it says does not change with the weather.

For worship. The name spoken at the bush was nailed to a Roman cross, and it was not dishonoured there. Lifted up between two criminals, the I AM did not cease to be God; he showed what God is: holy enough to judge sin, and loving enough to bear its judgment himself. The Son who learned every word from his Father never spoke his Father’s heart more plainly than there. And every sinner since who has looked to him has learned in the looking who he is, and lived.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him. As he was saying these things, many believed in him.

And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone. The Father is always with the Son, even when the world rejects him (16:32). It is a strange thing to say in the middle of a crowded courtyard, and it tells you what the loneliness of this chapter is. He is surrounded, and he is entirely unaccompanied: the crowd is hostile, the disciples are not mentioned once in the whole chapter, and his brothers do not believe him. The ground of his calm is not that the pressure is bearable. It is a person: the one who sent him has not gone away.

For I always do the things that are pleasing to him. “Always”: no one else could say this. It is a claim to sinlessness (v. 46; Hebrews 4:15). On the cross he would cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34): not because he had displeased the Father, but because he bore our sin, and in that very act was most pleasing to him. If anyone else said always, we would know exactly what to think of him. It is either the plain truth, or the remark of a man with no self-knowledge at all, and nothing in the record suggests the second.

Does this mean that when God feels absent, I must have displeased him? No, and it is important not to turn this verse into a formula that crushes people. Gethsemane and the cry from the cross forbid that reading. The one who always pleased the Father went into the dark anyway, and he did it so that those who have not always pleased him need not be abandoned. Believers may feel God’s absence for many reasons: grief, illness, exhaustion, or a trial God has sent to deepen their faith (Psalm 88; Isaiah 50:10). Sometimes sin is the cause, and then the remedy is confession. But your feelings are not the measure of his presence. His promise is: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

As he was saying these things, many believed in him. A note of hope. But the next verses will show that their belief was shallow. Not all who believe in some way are true disciples. In the middle of the most hostile exchange so far, faith is being born, and the next verse is going to test what it was worth.

In a sentence. Jesus said the one who sent him was with him and had not left him alone, because he always did what pleased him, and many believed in him as he spoke.

On a Tuesday. In Christ, your obedience is never alone. The Father is with you as he was with the Son. When you stand alone for what is right, at work, in the family, in a room where everyone else has gone along, remember that you are not as alone as you look.

For worship. The Son always did what pleased the Father, every hour of every day, and the Father was always with him. That perfect obedience, which we could never offer, he offered for us, and it is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). On the cross he was forsaken so that we never will be. Because he always pleased the Father, the Father is pleased with all who are in him.

parallels.desc: I am not alone, for the Father is with me

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells Jews who had believed him that if they hold to his teaching, they are truly his disciples; they will know the truth, and it will free them. They protest that as Abraham’s descendants they have never been anyone’s slaves. Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin; a slave has no permanent place in the household, but a son does, so if the Son frees them, they will be truly free. They are Abraham’s descendants, yet they want to kill him because his word finds no room in them. If they were Abraham’s children, they would act as Abraham did. They insist God is their only Father; Jesus says that if he were, they would love him, since he came from God. They cannot hear his word because they belong to their father the devil, a murderer from the start and the father of lies. They do not believe him precisely because he tells the truth; none of them can prove him guilty of sin. They accuse him of being a Samaritan with a demon. He denies it: he honours his Father, who will vindicate him. Whoever keeps his word will never see death. They scoff: Abraham and the prophets died; is he greater than they? Jesus answers that his Father glorifies him, and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They object that he is not yet fifty, and Jesus replies that before Abraham came into being, he is. They pick up stones, but he slips away from the temple.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage presents two competing genealogies: Abraham's children versus the devil's children. The distinguishing mark is not ethnic lineage but moral resemblance — you are of your father the devil if you do his works (lying and murder). This is not ethnic polemic but spiritual diagnosis: the unregenerate heart, whatever its ancestry, is in bondage to the father of lies. The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not philosophical insight but the person of Christ himself (v. 36). Freedom is not the absence of constraint but the liberation of the will from slavery to sin, accomplished by the Son who is himself free.
verseByVerse.examples: The stoning attempt at chapter's end is the authorities' answer to 'Before Abraham was, I am.' They understand perfectly: this is a claim to be the eternal God, the I AM of Exodus 3. They reach for stones because they reject the claim as blasphemy. For the Christian, reading this from the other side of the resurrection, this is the moment where the curtain is drawn back and the eternal Word stands visible in human flesh, claiming what was always true. The authorities stone the wrong person for the right reason — he is exactly who he says he is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

Meaning first. The rest of the chapter is a hard conversation with people who had, in some sense, believed. Jesus tests their faith, and it turns out to be shallow: by v. 59 they are picking up stones to kill him. The section teaches what true discipleship is, what real freedom is, and who a person’s true father is.

To the Jews who had believed him. Believed “him,” what he said, rather than believed “in him” (v. 30). John may intend no difference, but the conversation shows that their faith had not reached the root. This is the answer to the question every reader of this chapter eventually asks: how can people described as believers be told a few verses later that their father is the devil? They had accepted his claims; they had not given themselves to him. And the conversation that follows is the test that shows the difference.

If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples. “Abide” (menō): remain, continue, make your home in. The mark of a true disciple is not an initial response but continuing in Jesus’ word. Real faith lasts (15:4–10; Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14). Those who leave were never truly his (1 John 2:19). Which is why the first word Jesus says to them is a condition. If you abide in my word: not, if you agree with it.

And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. “The truth” is not just correct ideas, but the reality of God revealed in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Knowing him sets you free from sin (v. 34). Freedom is not doing what you want; it is being released from slavery to sin to become what God made you to be. The sentence is carved over the doors of government buildings and printed on university crests, and quoted constantly to mean that information liberates. It will not carry that. It has a condition in front of it and a definite article inside it. It is not truth in general; it is the truth, who is a person, promised to people who abide in his word.

Does abiding mean I can lose my salvation if I fail? No. Jesus is not describing a test you must pass to stay saved, but the mark that shows who is truly saved. Those whom the Father gives to the Son are kept by him, and no one can snatch them out of his hand (10:28–29). The same grace that brings a person to Christ keeps him continuing in Christ (Philippians 1:6). So abiding is both a command and a gift: we are told to remain, and God works in us so that we do. A true believer may stumble badly, like Peter, but he is brought back. What this verse warns against is a faith that never put down roots and so falls away when the word becomes hard.

So what does abiding in his word look like day to day? It means living in the Bible rather than visiting it. Read it regularly, not to tick a box but to hear his voice; let it shape what you think about God, yourself, money, sex, work and death. Sit under faithful preaching with his people. When the word says something you do not like, stay with it and ask for grace to obey, instead of drifting off. Memorise a verse and turn it over through the day. Abiding is less a technique than a home: the place you keep coming back to and living from.

In a sentence. Jesus told those who had believed him that if they continued in his word, they were truly his disciples, and would know the truth, and the truth would set them free.

On a Tuesday. Discipleship is not a moment, but a lifetime of staying in Christ’s word. Open it again today. And when you hear this verse quoted to mean that facts set people free, ask whether the freedom being offered would be recognisable to a slave. Most quotations offer relief from ignorance. Jesus offers release from ownership.

For worship. He who is the truth did not stand at a distance and shout instructions to prisoners. He came into our house of bondage himself, and now he invites us to make our home in his word, as he and the Father make their home with us (14:23). The chains we did not know we wore come off not by our cleverness but by our knowing him. And truth itself cannot prove false: what he loosens stays loosed, and the ones he frees he holds for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, ‘You will become free’?” Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.”

We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. A remarkable claim. Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; the Roman garrison stood beside the temple as they spoke. It was said by people fresh from a festival about living in tents after four hundred years in Egypt, members of a nation whose central annual meal, Passover, exists to make children ask why they were once slaves. They had not forgotten. Nobody forgets that. They meant something narrower and prouder: that as Abraham’s offspring they had never lost their standing before God, whatever the politics. And the scale of the denial is the point. This is what a person will say when the alternative is admitting bondage, and they said it in the one city where the evidence was standing in the street with a sword.

Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin. “Practices” (poiōn, present tense, keeps doing): habitual sin. “Slave” (doulos). Sin is not just something we do; it is a master that owns us (Romans 6:16–20). The worst slavery is not political but spiritual. And no one can free himself from it; a slave cannot buy his own freedom. Jesus does not argue about the history. He changes the subject to something they cannot check by looking out of the window, and he describes it with the one word that would have offended them most.

Is a Christian who still struggles with a habitual sin a slave of sin? Not in the sense Jesus means. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (v. 36): a believer’s standing has changed, and sin will have no dominion over him (Romans 6:14). He may still fight, and lose battles, and must keep fighting. But the slave in this verse is the one who serves sin as his master without wanting to be free; the believer hates the sin he struggles with and runs to Christ for help. The struggle itself is a sign that a new master has come.

In a sentence. They protested that as Abraham’s offspring they had never been slaves, and Jesus answered that everyone who keeps on sinning is a slave of sin.

On a Tuesday. The habit you can’t break is a chain. Only Christ can break it. Take the thing you would stop if you could: the temper, the drink, the screen, the way you talk about a particular person. You have decided to stop it before, probably more than once, and meant it. Now ask what the word is for a condition in which you genuinely will something and cannot do it. Paul spent a chapter on that question (Romans 7:14–25). A man who can stop whenever he likes has nothing to fear from this verse. Almost nobody is that man. So stop trying to free yourself, and ask the one who can.

For worship. We were slaves who called ourselves free, and Christ came to us not with a lecture but with a ransom. He took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7) and gave his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), so that slaves of sin could be bought back. The chains that no effort of ours could loosen fall off at his word, and the master he frees us to serve is the one whose service is perfect freedom: himself.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; they meant they had never inwardly accepted slavery.

parallels.desc: slaves of sin

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.

The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. A slave had no permanent place in a household; he could be sold or sent away at any time. A son belonged there for good. Perhaps there is an echo of Ishmael, son of the slave woman, who was sent away, while Isaac, the son of promise, remained (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:30). Being physically descended from Abraham does not secure a place in God’s house. The men in this courtyard are claiming Abraham as their father while Jesus describes a slave who does not remain in Abraham’s house, and they knew the story of the woman and the boy sent into the desert with a skin of water.

So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. The Son, Jesus, has the right to free the slaves of the house. “Free indeed” (ontōs, really, truly). The freedom he gives is real and permanent: freedom from sin’s guilt and power. The Son, the one who is permanently in the house, has the authority to change a slave’s status, and what he gives is not parole but adoption into God’s family for ever (1:12; Romans 8:15).

Freedom that cannot be lost. Measure this against every other freedom on offer. Political freedom can be lost by a change of government. Financial freedom can be lost in a market. Health goes. The freedom described here rests on the standing of someone who cannot be evicted from the house, and it is given, not earned, which means it cannot be forfeited by a failure, since it was never bought by success. And notice where the condition lies. If the Son sets you free: the question is not whether the slave improves, but whether the Son acts, and this Gospel exists to say that he did.

What does it feel like to be free indeed? It may not feel dramatic. Often it begins quietly: a conscience no longer crushed by guilt, because you know you are forgiven; the first real ability to say no to a sin that used to rule you; the strange new desire to please God rather than merely avoid punishment; the settled sense that you belong in the Father’s house and will not be thrown out. It grows over a lifetime. And its full flowering is still to come, when the children of God are finally set free from all decay and sin (Romans 8:21). Freedom is not doing whatever you want. It is wanting, more and more, what you were made for.

In a sentence. A slave has no permanent place in a house, but a son does, so if the Son sets you free, you will be truly free.

On a Tuesday. Live like a son, not a slave. A slave works in fear of being sent away; a son works because he is at home. If you find yourself serving God anxiously, as though one more failure would get you evicted, tell yourself the truth: in Christ you are a son, and the son remains for ever.

For worship. The eternal Son, who has always been at home with the Father, opened the door of that house to slaves and runaways and made them sons and daughters. He did not bring us in as servants to the kitchen but as children to the table. Abba, Father: that is the cry of the freed.
verseByVerse.note: A slave had no permanent place in a household; a son did.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman and her son

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father.

I know that you are offspring of Abraham. Physically, yes. The concession is generous, and it is easily overlooked in the heat of what follows. He does not dispute the genealogy anywhere in this exchange. The descent is real; it is simply not doing the work they think it does.

Yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. “Finds no place” (ou chōrei): makes no progress, has no room in you. They have shut the door to his word. Their plan to kill him shows it. It is not that they have not heard him; they have heard him for days and can quote him back. It is that there is nowhere in them for it to go. That is a more disturbing account of unbelief than the usual one. We picture rejection as a verdict reached after consideration. This is closer to a house with every room occupied: the word arrives, finds no space, and stands in the doorway. And the evidence he gives is not their arguments but their intention. Whatever a man says about God, what he plans to do to God’s messenger tells the truth about him.

I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father. Two fathers. Jesus speaks from his Father; they act from theirs. Who their father is, he will soon say (v. 44). And the verbs are carefully unmatched: seeing against hearing. He speaks from sight, from having been in the Father’s presence before the world was. They act on report, on something received at second hand from a source they have never examined. That is a fair description of how most evil actually spreads. Very few people have consciously met the father of lies. They have simply heard something, about a neighbour, a race, a rival, and acted on it without asking where it came from.

What fills the room where Christ’s word should be? Usually not one great rebellion, but many ordinary things: busyness, entertainment, worry, the opinions of the people we most want to please, a settled idea of who God is that we do not want disturbed. Jesus’ parable of the sower names them: the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desire for other things choke the word (Mark 4:19). Making room is practical. Turn off what crowds out silence. Bring your fixed ideas to Scripture and let it correct them. Ask God to clear space in you, and he will.

In a sentence. Jesus acknowledged they were Abraham’s offspring, yet they sought to kill him because his word had no room in them; he spoke what he had seen with his Father, and they did what they had heard from their father.

On a Tuesday. Is there room for Christ’s word in you? Make room today. And before you pass on the next thing you have heard about someone, ask where it came from, and whether it is true, kind and necessary.

For worship. The Son spoke what he had seen in the Father’s presence before the world began, and he brought it to people who had no room for it. He did not force the door, and he did not give up. He went on speaking; then he died for men who had no room for him, and rose to send his Spirit, who makes room in hearts that were full. Wherever his word is at last given a place, it does what it did in the beginning: it brings light and life where there was none, and fills the house with the Father’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “Abraham is our father.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did.”

Abraham is our father. They repeat it, sensing the insult. The exchange is worth watching as a dialogue: they shift ground each time, and he follows them exactly.

If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did. True children resemble their father. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6) and welcomed God’s messengers (Genesis 18). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7). The comparison is precise. Abraham welcomed strangers who came from God with a message, and set food before them under a tree (Genesis 18:1–8). These men are planning to kill one. And the grammar holds the verdict: it is a condition contrary to fact. He is not raising a possibility; he is stating, in the shape of the sentence, that the condition does not hold.

But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham received the truth gladly. They want to kill the one who brings it. And the phrase he uses of himself is deliberately small: a man who has told you the truth. Not the Son of God, not the light of the world, though he has said both this week. He reduces himself to the least contestable description available, and asks whether killing such a person is something Abraham would have done.

This is not what Abraham did. A family resemblance is missing. It is the whole argument in a sentence, and there is no answer to it that does not involve changing the subject, which is exactly what they do next. Yet there is mercy in it. What is required is not a different ancestry, which nobody can acquire, but a different faith and life, which God can give. He tells them what they are not, and at the same time what would make them what they claim.

Can I rely on my Christian family or background? No more than they could rely on Abraham. A Christian upbringing is a great gift, and God often works through families (Acts 16:31; 2 Timothy 1:5). But nobody is a child of God because his parents were. God has children, not grandchildren. Each person must come to Christ himself, by faith, and the evidence will be a family likeness: trusting God’s word, welcoming his Son, and doing the works of faith. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure the faith you were taught has become your own.

In a sentence. When they insisted Abraham was their father, Jesus answered that if they were his children they would act like him, but they wanted to kill one who told them God’s truth, which Abraham never did.

On a Tuesday. Ask what family likeness someone would see in you. Not your church membership or your background, but the marks of Abraham’s faith: trusting God when it costs, welcoming his word when it is uncomfortable, opening your home to strangers. Pick one and practise it this week.

For worship. Abraham set food before three strangers under the oaks of Mamre and found that the LORD had come to his tent (Genesis 18). His sons in the temple had God’s messenger in front of them and were planning his death. Yet Abraham’s greatest Son did not disown the family. He died for it, and widened it, so that the promise of descendants as many as the stars is kept not by bloodline but by grace, in people from every nation who believe God as Abraham did.

parallels.desc: Abraham welcomes the LORD’s messengers

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You are doing the works your father did.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God.” Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me.”

You are doing the works your father did. Their father, he implies, is someone other than Abraham.

We were not born of sexual immorality. “We” may be emphatic: we were not, implying, unlike you. They may be hinting at rumours about Jesus’ own birth; later Jewish writings spread a story that he was illegitimate. Or they may mean that they are not spiritually illegitimate, not idolaters, which the prophets called sexual unfaithfulness (Hosea 2:4). If it is the first, the argument has descended to this: cornered on Abraham, they reach for a rumour about his mother, and he does not stoop to answer it.

We have one Father, even God. They move from Abraham to God himself. It is the highest claim available to a Jew, and the last position there is.

If God were your Father, you would love me. The test of being God’s child is love for his Son. A child of God recognises his Father’s Son. You cannot love the Father and hate the Son (1 John 5:1). Not, you would agree with me. Not, you would be persuaded. You would love me, because children recognise the family, and a person who truly loves God will find himself drawn to the one God sent, often before he has worked out the theology. The test is about the heart, and it cannot be answered by argument, which is why the conversation is about to collapse into abuse.

For I came from God and I am here. “Came from” (exēlthon, came out from): from the Father’s side, from his very being. He did not come of his own accord; he was sent by the very one they claim as Father.

How do I know whether I love Jesus? Love for Christ is not first a feeling, though it often includes feeling. Jesus gave its marks himself: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (14:15). Love wants to be with him, in prayer and in his word. It treasures what he has done, and is grieved when he is dishonoured. It loves the people he loves, his church (1 John 4:20). It is sorry for sin because sin wounds him. If you find even a small and struggling version of these in yourself, that is the family likeness, and it is God’s work. If you find none, ask him to show you his Son, because no one who truly sees him remains unmoved.

In a sentence. When they protested that they were not illegitimate and that God was their Father, Jesus answered that if God were their Father they would love him, since he came from God and was sent by him.

On a Tuesday. Love for Jesus is the family likeness of God’s children. Do you have it? Tell him today, in your own words, why you love him, and if the words do not come easily, ask him to make you love him more. Then do one thing for him this week simply because you love him.

For worship. The Son came out from the Father, from his very heart, and stood among people who claimed God as their Father and did not know his face. He bore the slander about his birth in silence, the eternal Son of the Father allowing himself to be called illegitimate, so that we who were not God’s children could be adopted into his family. Those who love him are the Father’s children, and the Father loves them as he loves the Son (17:23).
verseByVerse.note: Their retort may hint at rumours about Jesus’ own birth.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies.

Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. “What I say” is his speech (lalia), the way he talks; “my word” (logos) is the message. The problem is not intellect but will. They are unable to hear, because they will not (6:44; 7:17).

You are of your father the devil. The hardest words Jesus says in John. Not all Jews, but these men, who want to kill him, show by their actions whose children they are. Spiritual parentage is shown by behaviour (1 John 3:8–10). Every unbeliever, Jew or Gentile, is by nature under the power of the evil one (Ephesians 2:1–3; 1 John 5:19). This is not an ethnic slur but a moral diagnosis, and it is not a permanent sentence. It describes the condition of every heart that the Son has not yet set free, and the next chapters show men of every kind being brought out of it.

He was a murderer from the beginning. They want what the devil wants, and what he has always wanted is death. The devil’s lie led to death in Eden (Genesis 3:1–5; Romans 5:12); the first murder followed soon after (Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12). The desire to kill Jesus is the devil’s family trait.

When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies. He does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him, and lying is his native language. The two marks of the family are murder and lying, and both were in the courtyard: they intend to kill the one who tells them the truth, and they refuse the truth itself. Every lie ever told traces its family tree back to the garden.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used horribly to justify hatred of Jewish people. That is a wicked distortion. Jesus himself was a Jew, as were all the apostles and the first church. He speaks here to particular opponents who were plotting murder, as the prophets of Israel rebuked Israel. The same diagnosis applies to every human being apart from Christ.

A family quarrel, from inside the family. No verse in this Gospel has been put to worse use, and a Christian reading John ought to know it. These words have been read from pulpits before massacres and quoted by men who planned genocide as though Christ had licensed what they intended. It is a straight inversion of the text. The speaker is a Jew, in the Jewish temple, at a Jewish feast, who has already said in this Gospel that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The Evangelist recording it is a Jew. The audience is not a race: John tells us at verse 31 that Jesus is speaking to particular people in a particular courtyard. A prophet of Israel rebuking the leaders of Israel is not an outsider attacking a people; it is the oldest and most Jewish thing in the Bible. Isaiah called them rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10). Nobody thinks Isaiah anti-Jewish. So the man who takes these words as a weapon against Jewish people has understood nothing. He sides against the Jewish Messiah, whose charge here is that his hearers intend murder, and then goes out to commit it himself, against his Lord’s own kinsmen. The verse condemns him. Paul, who felt the whole weight of this, said he could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers according to the flesh (Romans 9:3), and that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). That is the settled Christian mind.

Is everyone who is not a Christian a child of the devil? Scripture says that apart from Christ all of us were by nature children of wrath, following the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2–3). That is a description of the human condition, not a special insult for some. It includes the person reading this, before grace found him. So it gives no room for pride or contempt: the believer is a former member of that family, rescued by mercy. And it gives great hope: the Son came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) and to bring people out of that family into God’s. Treat unbelievers as people you once were, and whom God may yet adopt.

In a sentence. Jesus said they could not understand because they could not bear his word, for their father was the devil, a murderer from the beginning and a liar with no truth in him, the father of lies.

On a Tuesday. Every lie and every hatred has a father. Refuse his family likeness: speak the truth in love. Notice the small lies this week: the exaggeration, the excuse, the flattering untruth, the half-story that leaves you looking better. Each one is a word in the devil’s native tongue. Speak the truth, even when it costs you.

For worship. The father of lies was a murderer from the beginning, and he thought he had won when the Son of God was killed. But the Truth went to the cross and broke the liar’s power. The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he has done it, by dying and rising. The one who was called a demoniac is the one at whose name every demon trembles, and he brings children of the liar into the family of the God who cannot lie.
verseByVerse.note: The devil’s lie led to death in Eden; the first murder followed.

parallels.desc: “You will not surely die”

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?

But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. A stunning reversal. Not “although” but “because.” The children of the father of lies reject truth precisely because it is truth. To a heart shaped by lies, truth is not neutral. It is repellent.

Which one of you convicts me of sin? “Convicts” (elenchei): proves guilty. A challenge no other human being could make. Jesus invites his enemies to name a single sin. No one could. He is the sinless Son (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Stop and consider what it takes to ask that. He stands before men who have watched him for months, sent officers, looked for a charge: men with every motive to produce one. And he invites them to name a single thing. Nobody does. That silence is the loudest thing in the chapter.

The saints move the other way. Put the question in the mouth of the best person you have ever known, in front of those who know them best, and it becomes unbearable within a sentence. Every honest person’s self-knowledge runs the other way: the closer anyone gets to real goodness, the more sharply he sees his own failure. The saints are unanimous on this; the nearer they come to God, the worse they think of themselves. Here is one man who moves in the opposite direction: who is nearer to God than anyone has ever been and never once, in any record, confesses a sin. He teaches his disciples to pray, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12), and does not join in. He comes to a baptism of repentance, and John tries to stop him (Matthew 3:14). That is either a serious defect of self-knowledge, which nothing else about him supports, or it is simply true.

If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? If he is sinless, he is no liar. Their unbelief has no excuse.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus never sinned? Because our salvation depends on it. A sacrifice for sin had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5; 1 Peter 1:19). If Jesus had had a single sin of his own, he would have had his own account to settle, and nothing left over for anyone else. Because he owed nothing, he could pay what we owed. Because he was perfectly righteous, his righteousness can be counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). His sinlessness also makes him the perfect high priest: tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, and so able to help us when we are tempted (Hebrews 4:15–16).

In a sentence. Jesus said they did not believe him because he told the truth, and challenged them to prove him guilty of any sin, asking why, if he told the truth, they would not believe him.

On a Tuesday. Notice when the truth irritates you most: in a sermon, a friend’s honest word, a verse you would rather skip. The irritation may be the very sign that it is true. Thank God for the person who tells you the truth, and do not punish them for it.

For worship. For thirty-odd years in a fallen world he never thought an unclean thought, spoke a careless word, or failed to love God with all his heart. His enemies searched him for months and found nothing to name, and the Father, who searches every heart, found nothing either, and was well pleased. And then he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. The only man no one could convict was condemned, so that convicted sinners could go free.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God. The Jews answered him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”

Whoever is of God hears the words of God. Belonging to God comes first, and hearing follows (10:26–27; 18:37). Those born of God recognise his voice.

The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God. Their unbelief reveals their state. It is not that they are of God but fail to hear; it is that they do not hear because they are not of God. The logic runs backwards from the symptom to the condition. He does not say that they ought to listen harder. He says their failure to hear is the evidence of where they stand. It is chapter 6 seen from the other end. There, those who came had been given to him by the Father. Here, those who cannot hear were never his.

Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon? Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult. Samaritans were considered heretics and half-breeds (4:9). Perhaps they meant he was a traitor to Israel, or that, like the Samaritans, he rejected the true tradition. “Have a demon” means mad or possessed. Having lost the argument, they turn to name-calling. There is a nasty precision in choosing Samaritan: he has just questioned their true parentage, and they reply by questioning his. And it is richly ironic, because the Samaritans are the ones who called him the Saviour of the world after two days (4:42), which is more than Jerusalem has managed. The demon charge is the standard explanation for a man whose power is undeniable and whose claims are unacceptable: the works are real, so something is at work in him, so it must not be God. It requires no evidence, and it ends the conversation, which is its purpose.

If hearing depends on being of God, is it my fault if I do not believe? Yes, still. Scripture holds both truths together. No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (6:44), and yet those who refuse him are fully responsible, because they refuse what they could see is true and love the darkness (3:19). These men are not described as people longing to believe and prevented. They do not want to hear. And if you do want to hear, if you are reading this and something in you is drawn to Christ, that drawing is the Father at work. Do not wait to discover whether you are of God before you come. Come, and you will find that you are.

In a sentence. Jesus said that whoever belongs to God hears God’s words, and they did not hear because they did not belong to God; and they answered by calling him a Samaritan with a demon.

On a Tuesday. When people run out of arguments, they often reach for insults. Don’t be surprised when it happens to you, and don’t answer in kind. And watch for the same move in yourself: when you are losing an argument, do you reach for a label to stop having to listen?

For worship. The sheep hear his voice. Out of all the noise of the world, God’s children recognise the voice of their Shepherd, because the Father has given them to him and made them his own. He was called a Samaritan and a demoniac, and he went on speaking the words of God. And still today, in every nation, his sheep hear him and follow, and no insult has ever silenced him.
verseByVerse.note: Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge.”

I do not have a demon. He calmly denies the second insult. He doesn’t answer the first: he is not ashamed to be thought a Samaritan (4:40). It is the calmest sentence in the chapter. He denies it once, without heat, and moves straight back to the subject. There is no wounded dignity in it anywhere.

But I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. To dishonour the Son is to dishonour the Father (5:23). He does not say you dishonour God, which he could have. He puts himself in the sentence: his honour and the Father’s are the same currency, and slighting the Son is no lesser offence than slighting the Father.

Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge. He does not defend his reputation. The Father will vindicate him. Jesus entrusts his honour to God (1 Peter 2:23). He has just been called a Samaritan and a demoniac in public by men who have decided to kill him, and what he says is that his reputation is somebody else’s business. Somebody else is seeking his glory, and that somebody is the judge, and the case will keep. The man in this verse was executed on a false charge within six months, was publicly vindicated on the third day after it, and did nothing whatever to arrange either.

Should I never defend myself when I am slandered? Not never, but rarely in the way we want to. Paul defended himself when the gospel was at stake (2 Corinthians 11), and it can be right to correct a falsehood calmly, or to seek justice when real harm is being done; abuse and lies that endanger others should be brought into the light. But much of our self-defence is not about truth. It is about our reputation, and it is exhausting, never finished, and turns every insult into an emergency. Jesus shows another way: state the truth once, without heat, and then entrust your name to God, who judges justly.

In a sentence. Jesus denied having a demon, saying he honoured his Father while they dishonoured him, and that he did not seek his own glory, for the Father sought it and would judge.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you were described unfairly, and count how much of the following week went on it: the conversations, the mental rehearsals, the replies you drafted and did not send. Now ask what would change if your vindication were genuinely not yours to arrange. The injustice matters, enough that God has appointed himself to deal with it. It has simply been taken out of your hands and put into better ones.

For worship. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return. He left his name with the Father, and the Father did not forget it: he raised him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9). The one who would not seek his own glory now has all glory, and the hands that would not grasp at honour now hold the honour of every believer who has been slandered and kept silent.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.' The Jews said to him, 'Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death. The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’”

If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death. “Keeps” (tērēsē): holds fast, obeys, treasures. “Never” (ou mē … eis ton aiōna, not ever, to eternity). The believer will die physically, but will never experience death as the wages of sin, separation from God (5:24; 11:25–26).

Not a promise that the heart will not stop. The guard has to go on this one at once, because the verse has troubled people at gravesides. Every Christian who has ever lived has died, including every believer who heard him say it. The idioms see death and taste death mean to experience it as the thing it is, and what he denies is not the event but the encounter. The believer goes through the door; he does not meet what is on the other side of it for the unforgiven. Paul says the same: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55). The sting is drawn. The creature is still there, and Christians grieve at funerals like everyone else and are not asked to pretend otherwise. What has changed is what the bite does.

Now we know that you have a demon! Proof of madness, they think. Their reaction escalates. At verse 48 they said he had a demon. Now, they say, we know. The promise about death has settled it for them: no sane man says such a thing. They are within a hair of the truth and on the wrong side of it. This is indeed a claim that only a madman or God could make. They have named the alternatives correctly, and chosen.

Abraham died, as did the prophets. They think only of physical death. And it is the right objection, and a serious one. The greatest men in history are all in graves, and here is a Galilean promising what none of them could. If he cannot answer that, he is a fraud or a lunatic. His answer comes in chapter 11, at the tomb of Lazarus, four days dead, and it is not an argument.

He will never taste death. They change “see” to “taste,” a Jewish expression for experiencing death. It means the same.

What happens to a believer at the moment of death? The body dies and is buried, but the soul does not sleep or wait in some intermediate place of punishment. It goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory, because Christ’s death has paid in full; there is no soul sleep, because to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord. And that is not the end: at his return the body will be raised, glorious and imperishable, and body and soul will be together with the Lord for ever (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). So the believer can face death as a defeated enemy, still to be endured but no longer to be feared.

In a sentence. Jesus said anyone who keeps his word will never see death, and they took this as proof he was mad, since Abraham and the prophets had died.

On a Tuesday. Keep Christ’s word, and death loses its sting. You will never see death as the wages of sin. If you are afraid of dying, take that fear to him by name; he has been through it, and come out the other side. And if you have lost a believer, grieve, but not as those who have no hope.

For worship. Abraham died, and the prophets died, and Jesus died too. But he did not stay dead. He went down into death and broke it from the inside, and now he holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Because he lives, the believer will never see death as the enemy saw it. We will close our eyes in this world and open them in his presence. Death is swallowed up in victory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be? Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’”

Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The Greek expects the answer no. As the Samaritan woman asked about Jacob (4:12). The answer is, of course, yes. And notice how they cannot stop mentioning that Abraham is dead (vv. 52–53). The whole exchange has been about descent from a man in a grave. The one they are arguing with is about to say that he was there before Abraham was born.

Who do you make yourself out to be? The question of the chapter again. It is asked with contempt: the assumption is that he is inflating himself.

If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. He makes no claim of his own. He agrees entirely that self-declared greatness is worthless. A man who makes himself out to be something has, by that very act, made himself nothing.

It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, “He is our God.” The God they claim to worship is the one honouring Jesus. They are fighting their own God. Not, who is your God, but, of whom you say. He does not concede the claim; he reports it as theirs. And the sentence traps them from both ends: if the God they profess is real, he is the one glorifying Jesus, and their quarrel is with him.

How is Jesus greater than Abraham? In every way. Abraham was a creature; Jesus is the Creator (1:3). Abraham received the promise; Jesus is the promise kept (Galatians 3:16). Abraham believed God; Jesus is God. Abraham was justified by faith; Jesus is the one in whom we are justified. Abraham died and was buried; Jesus died and rose, and lives for ever. Abraham is the father of the faithful; Jesus is the Lord of the faithful, Abraham included, who rejoiced to see his day (v. 56). To honour Abraham rightly is to bow before the one Abraham longed for.

In a sentence. They asked if he was greater than Abraham and the prophets, who died, and who he thought he was, and Jesus answered that his Father, whom they called their God, glorified him.

On a Tuesday. Notice whose glory you are working for this week. When you are tempted to promote yourself, take a step back and let God do the honouring. What you glorify yourself with is nothing; what God gives is everything.

For worship. Abraham is in a grave, as they kept saying, and the one they were arguing with was not going to stay in his. The patriarchs and prophets are stars in the night; he is the sun, and every one of them shines with light borrowed from him. The Father who glorified him by raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand never needed his enemies to agree, and every honour God’s people have ever received came from his Son and returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.
