And would you teach us? Pride: a beggar can’t teach scholars. The whole thing is in a few words. Not, you are wrong; they never manage that. But, who do you think you are? Argument defeated, rank asserted.

And they cast him out. Out of the room, and probably out of the synagogue (v. 22). He has lost everything for confessing Jesus. His community, his standing, his family’s standing, and every relationship outside his own house. He is a man with new eyes and nothing else.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him. Jesus seeks him out. Rejected by the religious leaders, he is found by the Good Shepherd, who will speak in the next chapter of leading his sheep out (10:3–4). Jesus never casts out (6:37). Those cast out for his sake, he gathers in. Everything is in the two verbs. Heard: Jesus was not there, and it reached him. Having found him: the word implies looking. He went out into a crowded city and found one man who had just lost everything for defending him. Consider what the man had at that moment. He had no idea what Jesus looked like. He could not have gone looking if he had wanted to. Every road from where he stood was closed. And while he was standing in the street with nowhere to go, he was already being looked for. Sought before he knew there was anyone to seek him; sought again the moment he had nothing left.

Do you believe in the Son of Man? “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself. From Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure who receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus is asking a man who has just been stripped of his standing in Israel whether he will believe in the one to whom every kingdom is finally given.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “Son of God.” The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man,” and a scribe is more likely to have changed it to the more familiar confession than the other way round. The meaning is not changed: in John the Son of Man is the one who comes from heaven (3:13).

I have been rejected by a church or by Christians. Has Christ rejected me? No. Sometimes believers are put out unjustly, as this man was, and Christ sees it and comes looking for them. If you have been wronged by a church, bring it to him; he is the Good Shepherd, and he has not cast you out. At the same time, be honest: sometimes church discipline is a loving and right response to unrepented sin (Matthew 18:15–17), meant to bring a person home, not to destroy them. Whatever has happened, do not let the failures of Christians keep you from Christ, and do not give up on his people. Seek a faithful church where you can be known and cared for.

In a sentence. They mocked him as born in sin and threw him out, but Jesus heard and found him, and asked whether he believed in the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. Who has been pushed out of the circles you move in: the family, the friendship group, the church? Christ went looking for the cast-out man. Go and look for them.

For worship. When others cast you out for Christ, Christ comes to find you. The one who saw the man first, when he was blind and begging and unaware anyone was there, came back and found him again the moment the world had finished with him. That is the whole Gospel in one man’s afternoon. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and he has never stopped looking for those that everyone else has thrown away.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: brought forth in iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”

And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him? “Sir” (kyrie) can mean sir or Lord. He is ready to believe; he only needs to know who. It is the most attractive sentence in the chapter. Note the order: he commits before he knows the answer. He does not say, tell me who he is and I will consider it. He says he is ready to believe and needs only the name. And he is speaking to a stranger; he still does not know who is talking to him, because he has never seen the face.

You have seen him. A beautiful line. The first person this man has ever seen with his eyes may be Jesus. And now he sees him truly. He can say you have seen him only because of what happened at the pool. Any other person Jesus revealed himself to could have seen him at any time. This man could not have, until Siloam. The eyes he is using to look at Jesus were made by the man he is looking at, out of dirt.

And it is he who is speaking to you. As Jesus revealed himself to the Samaritan woman (4:26). Twice in this Gospel Jesus states his identity outright, without being pressed, and both times it is to someone with no standing at all: a Samaritan woman at noon, and an excommunicated beggar in a street. He has spent two chapters declining to give a plain answer to the men who run the temple.

How does Jesus reveal himself to people today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He no longer stands in the street to be seen with physical eyes; he speaks in Scripture, in the preaching of the gospel, and the Spirit opens hearts to see him there (Romans 10:17; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not second best. Jesus said that those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed (20:29). If you want to know him, go where he speaks: read a Gospel, sit under faithful preaching, and ask him to show himself to you. Like this man, you may find he has been speaking to you all along.

In a sentence. The man asked who the Son of Man was so that he could believe in him, and Jesus said he had seen him, and it was he who was speaking.

On a Tuesday. Christ reveals himself to those who want to believe. Ask him to show himself to you. Pray this man’s prayer in your own words: Lord, who are you, that I may believe in you more?

For worship. You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you. The Lord who made the man’s eyes let them rest first on his own face. He reveals himself not to the proud but to the humble, not to those who claim to see but to those who know they need sight. And one day every believer will see him face to face, and the first sight will be the Lord who sought us.

parallels.desc: I who speak to you am he

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him. Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

Lord, I believe. Now “Lord” (kyrie) in its full sense. The final step: from “the man called Jesus,” to “a prophet,” to “from God,” to “Lord.” The word he used for sir two verses ago now means what it means.

And he worshiped him. “Worshiped” (prosekynēsen): bowed down before him. In John this word is used only of worshipping God (4:20–24; 12:20). Jesus accepts it. Angels and apostles refused worship (Acts 10:25–26; Revelation 19:10). Jesus receives it, because he is God. That is the last step of the chapter, and it is not a title but an action. He began with the man called Jesus, moved to a prophet, then from God, and ends on his face.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “He said, ‘Lord, I believe,’ and he worshiped him. Jesus said.” Most scholars think the words are original: they are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including very early ones, and the omission may be accidental.

For judgment I came into this world. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), but his coming brings a separation, a verdict. His light shows who is who. Set against 3:17, it looks like a contradiction, and it is not. The resolution is in the chapter just told. Jesus came to give sight, and the giving of sight is itself a sorting: the man who knew he was blind can see, and the men who were certain they could see have spent forty verses proving they cannot. Nobody was condemned by a new verdict. They were exposed by a light, which is what light does.

That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Those who know they are blind receive sight. Those who think they see are confirmed in their blindness. The proud are blinded, the humble enlightened (Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 11:25; Luke 1:51–53).

Is it right to worship Jesus? Yes, and this verse is one of the plainest reasons. Scripture forbids worshipping anyone but God (Exodus 20:3–5; Matthew 4:10), and when Cornelius bowed before Peter, or John before an angel, they were told at once to stand up. Jesus never says that. He receives this man’s worship, and Thomas’ confession, my Lord and my God (20:28), because he is God the Son. The Father wills that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father (5:23). So Christians rightly pray to Jesus, sing to him and bow before him, together with the Father and the Spirit, one God.

In a sentence. The man said, “Lord, I believe,” and worshipped Jesus, and Jesus said he came for judgment, so that the blind would see and those who think they see would become blind.

On a Tuesday. Let your faith end where this man’s did: on your knees. Belief that never becomes worship has not yet seen Jesus clearly. Take a few minutes today simply to adore him: not to ask for anything, but to tell him who he is.

For worship. Bow before Christ as this man did. He is worthy of the worship due to God alone. Angels refuse it; apostles refuse it; Jesus receives it, because every knee in heaven and on earth will bow to him. A beggar in a Jerusalem street was the first in this Gospel to fall down before him, and he will not be the last. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your guilt remains.”

Are we also blind? The Greek form expects the answer no. Surely not us? They are not asking; they are inviting a denial, and they ask because they have understood him perfectly well.

If you were blind, you would have no guilt. If they knew themselves to be blind, and came to him for sight, their sin would be forgiven. Or: if they truly had no opportunity to see, they would be less guilty. That is the mercy in the sentence, and it is real. But no one in that crowd is in that position, and the answer sounds like a reprieve for a moment before it turns.

But now that you say, “We see,” your guilt remains. “Remains” (menei): stays, abides. The most dangerous condition is not blindness but the proud claim to see. The one who thinks he needs no light will never come to the light. Their claim to see is what keeps them in their sin. Compare Revelation 3:17. The whole weight falls on the claim rather than the condition. A man who knows he cannot see will ask for help. A man who is sure he can see will not, and there is nothing further to be done for him while he goes on saying it. And the last word of the chapter is remains, the same word this Gospel uses for abiding, turned the wrong way round. Some things stay because they have been given. This stays because it has been chosen.

Two kinds of blind men. That is the chapter in one line. One of them said, I do not know, twice (vv. 12, 25), and ended on his face worshipping. The others said, we know (vv. 24, 29), and we see (v. 41), and ended holding a verdict and nothing else. They were not defeated by an argument they could not answer. They were defeated by where it came from, and they would rather be blind than be taught by a beggar.

How do I know whether I am one of those who think they see? Ask whether you are still teachable. The Pharisees could not be taught by anyone below them. Ask when you last changed your mind about something because Scripture corrected you, or when you last let a doctrine you hold be questioned by someone with less standing than you. Ask whether you pray for light, or assume you already have it. This test is meant to catch the confident, not to crush the anxious. If you are worried that you might be blind, and want Christ to open your eyes, that very worry shows you are not where these men were. The humble cry, Lord, that I may see, is the cry he always answers.

In a sentence. When some Pharisees asked whether they were blind too, Jesus said that if they were blind they would have no guilt, but because they claimed to see, their guilt remained.

On a Tuesday. The first step to sight is admitting you are blind. Pray, “Lord, open my eyes.” Take the thing you are most sure you understand about God, and ask him this week to show you more of it than you have yet seen.

For worship. The Light of the world gives sight to the blind who know they are blind. He opened the eyes of a beggar and left the self-assured in their darkness, not because he was unwilling to give them light, but because they would not receive it. We were all born blind. If we now see, it is because he stooped to the dust and touched us. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18), and above all, the wonder of your Son.

parallels.desc: a guide to the blind

Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud<sup>7</sup>and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.<sup>8</sup>The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?”<sup>9</sup>Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” He kept saying, “I am the man.”<sup>10</sup>So they said to him, “Then how were your eyes opened?”<sup>11</sup>He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, ’Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed and received my sight.”<sup>12</sup>They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I do not know.”<sup>13</sup>They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.<sup>14</sup>Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.<sup>15</sup>So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”<sup>16</sup>Some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” And there was a division among them.<sup>17</sup>So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”<sup>18</sup>The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight<sup>19</sup>and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”<sup>20</sup>His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.<sup>21</sup>But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”<sup>22</sup>(His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue.<sup>23</sup>Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”)<sup>24</sup>So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”<sup>25</sup>He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”<sup>26</sup>They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”<sup>27</sup>He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”<sup>28</sup>And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.<sup>29</sup>We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”<sup>30</sup>The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes.<sup>31</sup>We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.<sup>32</sup>Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind.<sup>33</sup>If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”<sup>34</sup>They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out.<sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”<sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?”<sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”<sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”<sup>40</sup>Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”<sup>41</sup>Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ’We see,’ your guilt remains.
9.overview:
Jesus has just called himself the light of the world (8:12); now he gives sight to a man blind from birth, the sixth sign in John. The disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness; Jesus answers that it happened so that God’s works might be displayed in him. He makes mud with saliva, spreads it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, “Sent”, and the man comes back seeing. Then follows one of the most dramatic and humorous scenes in the Gospels, a series of interrogations. The neighbours cannot agree it is the same man. The Pharisees are split, because the healing happened on a Sabbath. The parents, afraid of being expelled from the synagogue, refuse to say more than that he is their son and was born blind. Questioned again, the man refuses to call Jesus a sinner: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.” When he asks, with an edge, whether they want to become disciples too, they insult him and throw him out.

Meanwhile his understanding of Jesus grows: “the man called Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then a man “from God”, and finally, when Jesus finds him after his expulsion, “Lord, I believe”, as he worships him. The Pharisees go the other way, from confident sight to blindness. Jesus says he came so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind; because they claim to see, their guilt remains. The chapter is a parable of conversion and of religious self-deception.

10.title: The Good Shepherd

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus contrasts the true shepherd with thieves who climb into the sheepfold another way. The shepherd comes through the gate; the sheep recognise his voice as he calls each by name and leads them out, but they run from strangers. When his hearers miss the meaning, Jesus says plainly that he is the door: whoever enters through him will be saved and find pasture. Thieves come to steal and destroy; he came to give life to the full. He is the good shepherd, who gives his life for the sheep, unlike the hired hand who abandons them to the wolf. He knows his sheep and they know him, as he and the Father know each other. He has other sheep outside this fold, whom he will gather into one flock under one shepherd. The Father loves him because he lays down his life freely, with authority to take it up again. Some in the crowd say he is mad and possessed; others reply that no demon could open blind eyes.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd imagery draws on the entire Old Testament tradition: God as shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34), the coming Davidic shepherd-king (Ezek. 34:23-24; Jer. 23:4), and the contrast between true and false shepherds throughout the prophets. Jesus claims all of these simultaneously: he is the door (the only legitimate access to God), the good shepherd (who gives rather than takes), and the one who lays down his life voluntarily (the self-giving that no hired hand would perform). The death is central: the shepherd metaphor cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice: the recognition of Christ by the elect is not achievement but gift. The sheep do not learn to recognize the shepherd's voice; they already know it because they are his sheep. This is Calvinist soteriology rendered in pastoral imagery: election precedes hearing, calling brings the elect home, and not one of the Father's sheep is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not sheep (v. 26); the church hears because she has been given ears by the Shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

Meaning first. John 10 follows straight on from chapter 9, with no break. The Pharisees have just thrown out a sheep of God’s flock, the man born blind, and Jesus has gone and found him. Now Jesus tells them who the true shepherd is. Behind the whole chapter lies Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David. Jesus says, in effect: I am that shepherd. The chapter moves from a picture (a fold, a door, a shepherd, a wolf) to the plainest claims in the Gospel: that he lays down his life for his sheep of his own accord, that no one can snatch them out of his hand, and that he and the Father are one. It begins with a beggar thrown out of a synagogue and ends with the Son of God holding his people in hands no power in the universe can open.

The setting. The healed man has been cast out (9:34), and Jesus has just said to the Pharisees that their claim to see is the very thing that keeps them blind (9:41). There is no change of audience. The men listening to the parable of the fold are the men who have just used the fold to throw a sheep out of it.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn double Amen that Jesus uses when he is about to say something that carries his full authority. No prophet ever spoke like this. The prophets said, thus says the LORD. Jesus says, I say to you, and puts his own word in the place where theirs pointed.

He who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way. Two facts about first-century sheepfolds unlock the whole discourse, and without them verse 7 sounds like a change of subject. The first kind of fold is the one described here: a walled enclosure in or near a village, often a courtyard beside a house, holding the flocks of several families overnight, with a solid door and a man paid to watch it. In the morning each shepherd came, was admitted, and called his own animals out of the mixed flock. Anyone who climbed the wall instead of using the door was obviously up to no good. The second kind was what a shepherd used out in the hills: a rough circle of piled stones with a gap in it and no door at all, because the shepherd lay down across the gap and slept there. Nothing came in and nothing went out except over him. He was the door. Hold on to that second picture. In six verses Jesus will say, I am the door of the sheep, and it will not be a new image but this one.

That man is a thief and a robber. The two words are not synonyms. A thief (kleptēs) works by stealth: he wants the animals and would rather not be seen. A robber (lēstēs) is a bandit, a man with violence in hand. It is the word John uses of Barabbas (18:40), and the word used of rebels and insurrectionists. So the flock is threatened from two directions at once, and always has been. There is the quiet exploitation that takes something and hopes nobody notices, and there is the open violence that does not care who sees. Jesus has in mind the false leaders of God’s people, and in the first place the Pharisees who have just cast out the man born blind. Every generation of the church has met both kinds, usually at the same time, and the marks are the same now as then: the man did not come in by the door, and his interest is in what the sheep can be made to yield.

But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The true shepherd comes openly, by the proper way, with the right to be there. Legitimate authority follows legitimate entry. He does not need to climb, because the door belongs to him; he does not need to hide, because he has nothing to take. Everything about how Jesus came fits this sentence. He came as the prophets said he would, born in David’s city, announced by the forerunner, doing in public the works the Scriptures said the Messiah would do. He did not slip into Israel’s life by a side window. He walked in by the door his Father had built for him over a thousand years of promise.

How do I tell whether a leader has come in by the door? Ask three questions. First, does he come through Christ and his word, or around them? A true shepherd points away from himself to Christ and is content to be measured by Scripture; a false one needs you to depend on him, his special insight or his new revelation. Second, is he accountable? Doors have keepers. A man who answers to no elders, no church and no one but himself has climbed the wall, however gifted he is (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Third, what is he taking? Watch where the money, the admiration and the control flow. A shepherd spends himself on the sheep; a thief spends the sheep on himself.

In a sentence. Jesus said that anyone who climbs into the sheepfold another way is a thief and a robber, but the one who comes in by the door is the shepherd.

On a Tuesday. Ask of any spiritual leader you follow, whether in your church, on a podcast or in a book: did he come by the door, through Christ and his word, or did he climb in another way? And then ask it of yourself, wherever you have any influence over others, as a parent, a teacher, a small group leader. Are you there to feed them, or to be fed by them?

For worship. The Shepherd of Israel did not break into his own fold. He came by the door he had promised, through the line of David, in the town of Bethlehem, at the hour the Father set. And he came openly, wanting nothing from the flock except the flock itself. Every thief who ever climbed the wall wanted what the sheep could give him. He alone came to give, and what he came to give was himself.
verseByVerse.note: A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, with a single doorway.

parallels.desc: the false shepherds of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.

To him the gatekeeper opens. The gatekeeper knows the true shepherd and lets him in. Some have said the gatekeeper is the Father, some the Spirit, and some John the Baptist, who opened Israel’s door for Jesus and then stood aside. But not every detail of a parable stands for something, and it is wise not to press this one. The gatekeeper is part of the scene: the man at the door who recognises the shepherd at once. The point is that Jesus is not an intruder. Heaven opens to him.

The sheep hear his voice. The sheep recognise him. They do not have to be persuaded; they know the voice the way a child knows his mother’s voice in a crowded station, before he has worked out where it is coming from.

And he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. This detail is drawn from life, and it is not a flourish. Shepherds in that world led their flocks rather than drove them, and often had names for their sheep, given for a marking, a habit, an injury; travellers in the Middle East have reported the same thing into modern times. A flock of a hundred is a hundred faces to the man who sits with them every day. So the picture is exact. Several flocks are mixed in the fold overnight. In the morning a shepherd stands at the door and calls, and out of the mass his own animals detach themselves and come, because they know the voice and the voice knows them. Nobody separates them by force. They sort themselves by recognition. “His own” (ta idia) is a possessive with warmth in it: Jesus knows his own people personally, by name, as God said to Israel, I have called you by name, you are mine (Isaiah 43:1).

Leads them out. The word (exagei) is the word used of God leading Israel out of Egypt. And John has just shown it happening. The synagogue authorities threw the man born blind out of their fold; Jesus went and found him (9:35). What looked like expulsion was an exodus. The man thought he had lost everything, and he had in fact been called by name out of a pen where he would have starved. And notice what the shepherd does with the sheep once he has them: he leads them out. The fold was safe, and the fold was not the point. Sheep kept permanently in an enclosure starve. The calling is always out of somewhere and toward pasture, which is the promise five verses later (v. 9).

When he has brought out all his own. All of them, not one left behind. He does not wait at the door hoping enough of them come. He brings them out, and the count is complete.

He goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. Eastern shepherds walked in front and the flock followed, which is not how sheep are handled in most of the world now. A dog behind a flock drives it; the animals move because something is pressing them from the rear. This is the opposite. The sheep move because somebody they trust is already moving, and every step of the road he asks them to walk he is walking a few paces ahead of them. There is a great deal of comfort in that, and it is worth taking slowly. There is no stretch of the road ahead of you that he has not already covered. Not the difficult part, not the frightening part, and not the last part, which he walked entirely alone so that nobody following him would have to.

Does Jesus really know me by name, among so many? Yes, and the number is no strain on him. Human attention is divided because we are finite; his is not. The Shepherd who calls the stars by name (Psalm 147:4) knows the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). You are not a case number in a vast administration of souls. He knows your history, your temperament, the sin you are fighting and the sorrow you have not told anyone, and he calls you as you are. On days when you feel invisible to everyone, including the church, you are not invisible to him.

In a sentence. The gatekeeper opens to the shepherd, his sheep hear his voice, he calls them by name and leads them out, walking ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice.

On a Tuesday. Whatever is waiting for you this week, a hard conversation, a hospital appointment, a decision you dread, he has gone ahead of you into it. You are not being driven from behind by circumstances. You are following someone who is already there. Listen for his voice in his word before you walk into the day.

For worship. The Shepherd knows your name. He called it when you were lost in the crowd of the fold, and you came out to him because his voice was the one you could not mistake. He goes before you into every day, and into the last day, through a valley he walked first and alone. A hired man counts sheep. This Shepherd names them, and the name he calls you by is one he will never forget.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and named their sheep; the sheep knew their shepherd’s call.

parallels.desc: who shall go out before them and bring them in

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers. This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.

A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers. True sheep will not follow false shepherds. The healed man would not follow the Pharisees; he had heard the voice that opened his eyes, and after that their voices simply did not sound like the same thing. There is a spiritual instinct in God’s people that recognises the voice of Christ and turns from other voices. The protection is not vigilance but familiarity. They do not identify the stranger by analysing him; they simply do not know his voice, and they move away.

The way to know a forgery. Here is a test that is more useful than it sounds. The way to recognise a false teacher is not first to study false teaching, which is endless and endlessly inventive. It is to know the real voice so well that the wrong one grates, and that is a matter of hours spent in the Gospels rather than hours spent on the internet. Bank staff are trained on genuine notes. This is the practical function of the doctrine of Scripture: the sheep who know the Shepherd’s voice in the written word can tell when a preacher contradicts it, even when they could not yet explain why.

They will flee from him. The flight sounds passive and is not. The sheep’s safety consists in moving away, quickly, without an argument. There is no suggestion that they engage the stranger, assess his credentials, or give him a hearing out of politeness. That is a permission worth granting plainly. Not every voice claiming to speak for God deserves a debate. Some of them deserve a closed door (2 John 10).

This figure of speech Jesus used with them. The word is paroimia: a proverb, a veiled saying, a picture with something hidden inside it. It is worth noticing because this Gospel never once uses the ordinary word for a parable. Matthew, Mark and Luke are full of parabolē; John has none. What he has instead are figures like this one.

But they did not understand what he was saying to them. This is not incidental reporting. It is the same failure as Nicodemus with birth, the woman with water, the crowd with bread, and the disciples with food. Again and again somebody has taken a picture literally and missed the thing it was carrying. The difference here is who is failing. These are the professional interpreters of Israel, and the figure they cannot follow is a figure about them. They miss it, and in missing it they prove the point: they are not his sheep, and his voice sounds to them like noise.

Christians do get deceived, so what does this promise mean? It means that the elect will not be finally and fatally led away from Christ, not that no believer is ever confused. Sheep can be frightened, scattered and misled for a time; Paul had to write to the Galatians because true believers had been bewitched (Galatians 3:1). But the Shepherd guards his own, and they come back to his voice. This is a comfort, not a licence for carelessness. The same apostle who says the sheep will flee from strangers tells us to test the spirits (1 John 4:1), and the means by which the Shepherd keeps his sheep from deception is precisely their knowing his word. So if you have been taken in by something, do not conclude you were never his. Go back to the voice, and let it correct you.

In a sentence. Jesus said his sheep will not follow a stranger but will run from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers, but the Pharisees did not understand this illustration.

On a Tuesday. Learn Christ’s voice in Scripture so well that you can tell at once when another voice is speaking. Read a Gospel straight through this month, slowly, and listen for how he speaks: the authority, the tenderness, the refusal to flatter. And when some teaching you meet makes Christ smaller, sin lighter, or yourself the centre, you do not owe it a long hearing. Walk away.

For worship. There is a voice in this world that the sheep cannot finally mistake, because it is the voice that called them into being and called them out of the dark. Ten thousand strangers have spoken since, clever and confident and sometimes in his name, and his flock has gone on recognising him. He has not left us to defend ourselves by cleverness. He has given us himself to know, and the knowing is our safety.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.”

So Jesus again said to them, Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. This is the third of Jesus’ great I am sayings in John, after the bread of life (6:35) and the light of the world (8:12). And here the second kind of sheepfold pays off. Out on the hills the fold had no gate; the shepherd lay down in the gap and his own body closed it. So the door is not a fresh metaphor laid on top of the shepherd. It is the same man in the same picture, describing what he does at night. The two images that look like a muddle (how can he be both the shepherd and the door?) are one image seen at two hours of the day. He leads them out in the morning; he lies across the entrance at dusk. Anything that wants them must go through him. There is only one way into God’s flock, and he is it (14:6).

All who came before me are thieves and robbers. Taken flatly, the sentence would sweep up Moses, Samuel, Isaiah and every prophet, and that cannot be meant by a man who has said that Moses wrote about him (5:46) and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day (8:56). The prophets pointed to him; they did not come instead of him. He means those who claimed to be saviours or leaders apart from him. The period was full of them. Judea produced a steady supply of men promising deliverance, gathering crowds and getting them killed; Gamaliel names two of them, Theudas and Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36–37), and there were more. They came claiming to bring the flock out, and what they actually did was scatter it. And beside them stood the corrupt religious authorities, who used the flock for their own position. They all came for themselves.

But the sheep did not listen to them. The qualifier that settles the meaning is in the sentence itself. The people of God had always listened to the prophets; whoever these men are, they are the ones Israel’s true sheep never followed. God’s true people were not taken in.

Is Jesus really the only way? Yes. He does not say he is a door, one entrance among many, but the door. That is not narrowness on his part but reality: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Salvation comes through conscious faith in him. That is exactly why the church sends missionaries, because the door must be shown to those who have not yet heard of it (Romans 10:14–15). But notice the other half of the picture, which is just as important: the door is open. The same verse that excludes every other way invites everyone to this one.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the door of the sheep, and all who came before claiming that role were thieves and robbers, but the true sheep did not listen to them.

On a Tuesday. Notice the little doors you are tempted to use instead of him: being good enough, being busy enough in church, having grown up in it, feeling the right things. None of them leads into the fold. Come to God today the only way anyone has ever come, through Christ, and come with nothing in your hands.

For worship. Christ is the door, and the door is a body laid across the gap. Every wolf that wanted the flock had to come through him, and on a Friday outside Jerusalem the wolf did, and the door was not broken. There is no other way in, and through him the way stands open to anyone, at any hour, from any distance. Blessed be the Shepherd who made himself the door.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.

If anyone enters by me, he will be saved. Open to anyone, but only by him. The offer is as wide as the human race, and the entrance is exactly one person wide.

And will go in and out and find pasture. A modern reader passes over this phrase; a Jewish hearer would not. “Go in and out” is a Hebrew way of speaking about living in safety, coming and going about your business without fear. Moses asks God for a leader who will go out before the people and come in before them, so that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd (Numbers 27:17), which is precisely a shepherd’s job description. The blessing of the covenant is, blessed shall you be when you come in, and blessed shall you be when you go out (Deuteronomy 28:6), and the psalm promises that the LORD will keep your going out and your coming in (Psalm 121:8). So the promise is not that the sheep will be shut in somewhere safe. It is freedom of movement under protection: a life with a door that opens both ways and somebody trustworthy standing in it. Salvation is not a cage. And at the end of the sentence: and find pasture. Not merely survive. Feed.

The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. That is the whole method, and it is a descending scale: take, end, ruin. Nothing is given at any stage. False shepherds take; they use the flock for themselves. And behind every false shepherd stands the one who was a murderer from the beginning (8:44). Whatever else is uncertain about the enemy of souls, his direction of travel is not.

I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. Here is the positive purpose of the whole gospel in one sentence. “Abundantly” (perisson) means over and above, more than the minimum, surplus, overflowing. Jesus gives not just survival but the fullness of eternal life, which is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). This is the bright side of the atonement: not merely rescue from death but the gift of life, not merely pardon but adoption, not merely forgiveness but an inheritance.

What it does not mean. There are few verses in the New Testament more systematically abused. This one has been made the charter of the prosperity gospel, read as a promise of health, money and success, on the reasoning that an abundant life must mean an abundance of things. The word says nothing whatever about possessions, and the context forbids importing them. The verse sits one sentence away from a shepherd being killed. The abundance on offer is defined by the man offering it, and what he is about to hand over is his life. Consider also who first received the promise and what it brought them. The eleven who heard it died, most of them violently, and by any material accounting they were worse off for having met him. Paul lists what his own abundant life came to, beaten, shipwrecked, cold, hungry, in prison (2 Corinthians 11:23–27), and then counts everything as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Abundant life is life with God, rich in him, whatever our circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13).

Then why does my Christian life feel so ordinary? Because abundance here is measured by what you have in Christ, not by how vivid each day feels. A child of a king is no less an heir on a wet Monday than on his coronation day. The life Jesus gives is real now: forgiveness that is complete, a Father who hears, the Spirit within, a people to belong to, and a future that cannot be taken. But much of it is still hidden with Christ (Colossians 3:3–4), and some of it you have hardly begun to draw on. If your life with God feels thin, the answer is not to look for a new experience but to go back to the pasture: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the company of his people. Sheep that are fed grow strong slowly.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the door, and anyone who enters by him will be saved and find pasture; the thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, but he came to give life in abundance.

On a Tuesday. Ask what would have to be added to your life for it to count as abundant. If the honest answer is a sum of money, a diagnosis reversed, a relationship restored, those are real and worth praying for, and the Shepherd is not indifferent to any of them. But everyone who has ever obtained such things has gone on to die, and none of it was what he was talking about. Abundant life is not a fuller diary or a fuller bank account. It is Christ. Drink deeply of him today.

For worship. The thief has only ever had three verbs, and none of them is give. Christ came with the opposite word in his mouth. He did not come to take a little less from us than the thief; he came to give more than we could hold, and the cost of the giving was his own life. Every good thing in the universe that is surplus, overflowing and undeserved flows out from him. He is not a tax on joy. He is the spring of it.
verseByVerse.note: “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety.

parallels.desc: this is the gate of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.

I am the good shepherd. The fourth I am saying. The adjective is not the ordinary word for good. Kalos means fine, noble, beautiful: the word for a thing well made or admirably done, as against agathos, which is moral goodness. The nearest English is probably the model shepherd, the one every other shepherd should be measured against. And the claim is enormous. In the Old Testament the shepherd of Israel is God himself: the LORD is my shepherd (Psalm 23:1); give ear, O Shepherd of Israel (Psalm 80:1); he will tend his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11). In Ezekiel 34 God promises two things that seem to pull apart. He will shepherd his people himself (34:11–16), and he will set over them one shepherd, his servant David (34:23). Jesus is both: God himself come to find his sheep, and David’s son set over them.

The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The whole weight of the claim falls here, and it is the strangest job description ever offered. Shepherds did risk their lives against wild animals and thieves: David fought a lion and a bear for his father’s flock (1 Samuel 17:34–36). But the point of David’s story is that he won and lived. A dead shepherd is a failure. He leaves the sheep worse off than before: scattered, unfed, and now with nobody to look for them. No employer in Galilee wanted a man who would die at his post; the animals were worth less than he was. So the sentence turns the whole trade upside down. Every other shepherd risks his life in order to save the flock, and the saving depends on his surviving. This one saves the flock by dying, and the death is not the risk but the method.

For the sheep. The little word is hyper: on behalf of, in the place of. This is substitution. He dies so that they live. The sheep were under a sentence they could not bear, and he stepped between them and it.

What does it mean that he died in my place? It means that the punishment your sins deserved fell on him instead of you. God’s justice is not set aside at the cross; it is carried out, on the Shepherd. He was pierced for our transgressions, the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:5–6), and he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). This is called penal substitution: penal because it is a penalty, substitution because it is borne by another. For you it means that God will never punish you for a sin Christ has already paid for. When guilt accuses you, do not answer it with your record. Answer it with his death.

He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep. The hired hand is the right contrast, rather than the thief. He is not wicked. He simply does the sensible thing: a wolf arrives, the animals are not his, and no wage is worth being killed for. Anybody would say he was right. He is the standard by which shepherds are judged everywhere, and against that standard the good shepherd is not a better employee but a different kind of person altogether. And the root is stated flatly: he does not own the sheep. Ownership is not a legal detail here but the thing that makes the death intelligible. The sheep are his, given to him by the Father (v. 29); losing one would be losing his own. The cross is not something imposed on Jesus from outside. It is the act of the owner, who would rather die than lose one of his own.

Sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. The wolf stands for anything that attacks God’s people: false teachers, whom Paul calls fierce wolves that will not spare the flock (Acts 20:29), persecutors, and the devil himself. Remember the verb “snatches” (harpazei). It comes back in verse 28, and there it is denied.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, unlike the hired hand who does not own them and runs from the wolf, leaving them to be snatched and scattered.

On a Tuesday. When you wonder whether you matter to God, do not look inward at your feelings first. Look at what the Shepherd did. A man does not die for a flock he is indifferent to. And when you are tempted to treat other believers as the hired hand does, as someone else’s problem, remember whose they are and what they cost.

For worship. The LORD is my shepherd, and he laid down his life for me. The God of Psalm 23 did not stay at a safe distance with a rod and a staff; he came down into the valley of the shadow himself, and went all the way into the shadow, so that the sheep could walk through it and fear no evil. No shepherd before him had ever saved a flock by dying. No shepherd after him will need to.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves.

parallels.desc: David rescues a lamb from a lion

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me.

He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. The root of his failure: he does not care. It is not that he lacks warm feelings, but that they are not his concern, not his business. He has no stake. And notice what his failure is not. He does not steal, betray or mislead. He runs, at the one moment when staying is the only thing that matters. Failure in this passage is not chiefly a matter of doing damage; it is a matter of absence when everything depends on presence. It is a warning for every pastor: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, not for shameful gain, but eagerly (1 Peter 5:2–4). And it is a warning for every parent, elder and friend whose care quietly evaporates when caring becomes costly.

I am the good shepherd. Said again, for emphasis. Against the hired hand who disappears when the wolf comes, here is the one who stays.

I know my own and my own know me. The word (ginōskō) means more than information. It is the knowledge of love and relationship, as when God says to Israel, you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Jesus knows his own personally, and has always known them: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). And they know him. Between a shepherd and an actual sheep the traffic is mostly one way; the animal has little to bring. Here it is mutual. There is no version of the Christian life in this picture that consists of a person believing correct things about a distant figure. The relation is two parties who know each other.

The order of the knowing. Here is comfort for the reader who feels his own knowledge of God is thin, which is most people who think about it honestly. Notice the order. He does not say my own know me, and I know them. The knowing that holds the relationship together is his, it was in place first, and it does not rise and fall with the quality of yours. Your grasp of him will always be partial in this life. His grasp of you is complete.

What should I do if my pastor behaves like a hired hand? First be fair: pastors are frail men, and tiredness, mistakes or a different style are not the same as not caring. Pray for him, and speak to him directly and kindly if something troubles you (Matthew 18:15). If the problem is real and continues, take it to the other elders, who are there to guard the flock. But if a leader is abusing anyone, spiritually, emotionally, physically or sexually, that is not a matter for patience. It must be reported, to the church’s leaders and, where the law is broken, to the authorities, and the vulnerable must be protected. The Good Shepherd’s care for the sheep never covers for the wolf.

In a sentence. The hired hand runs because he does not care for the sheep, but Jesus, the good shepherd, knows his own and they know him.

On a Tuesday. You are known by Christ, not as a number but as his own. Get to know him better in return: not more facts about him only, but time with him in his word and in prayer. And think of one person in your church whom you have quietly left for someone else to care about. Be there for them this week.

For worship. There has never been a moment when the Good Shepherd was absent from his flock because it had become too dangerous to stay. He stayed in Gethsemane while the disciples slept, stayed before the council while Peter warmed himself at the fire, and stayed on the cross when every other friend had gone. He knew his own then, by name, and he knows them now. To be known by him is the safest place in creation.
