the Lord knows those who are his

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.

Just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. This is the largest claim in the discourse, and it is easy to read straight past because it comes attached to the sentence before it. The mutual knowing of the shepherd and the sheep is measured against the mutual knowing of the Father and the Son. Not compared to it as a distant echo: the word is “just as,” and the same construction appears in chapter 17, when he prays that his people may be one just as the Father and he are one (17:21–23). Whatever is going on between a Christian and Christ is being described in the grammar of the life of God. Astonishing intimacy.

And I lay down my life for the sheep. Said for the third time (vv. 11, 15, 17), and each time with the same object. The death of Christ is for the sheep, those he knows as his own.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many Christians believe Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all and effective for those who believe. They have verses to stand on: he gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6), and he is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2:2). Godly and careful readers hold this view, and none of them is trying to make the cross smaller. Verdict: here Jesus says he lays down his life for the sheep, and in v. 26 he tells some of his hearers that they are not his sheep. His death has a particular purpose: to save those the Father has given him (6:37–39; 17:9). Paul speaks the same way: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). This is definite atonement. It does not limit the offer of the gospel, which goes to all, nor the sufficiency of his death, which is infinite. It means that the cross actually saves those it was meant to save; it does not merely make salvation possible. The texts about “all” and “the whole world” speak of the worldwide reach of the cross, to every kind and nation of people, not of a ransom paid for those who are finally not ransomed.

Then can I tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell everyone, with full sincerity, that Christ is offered to them, that his death is enough for any sinner, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (6:37). That is how the apostles preached: they did not first work out who the elect were; they called all people everywhere to repent and believe (Acts 17:30). The moment someone trusts Christ, he may say with Paul, he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Definite atonement does not make the invitation less real. It makes it certain that the invitation will not be refused by everyone, because the Shepherd has sheep and his death will bring them home.

And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. “This fold” is Israel; the other sheep are Gentiles who would believe. There is a distinction in the Greek that the older English translations blurred. Verse 16 uses two different words: a fold (aulē) is a pen, a structure, a set of walls, and the fold in view is Israel, with its law and its temple. A flock (poimnē) is the animals themselves. Jesus does not say the other sheep will be brought into this pen. He says the pens will stop being the thing that defines them, and there will be one flock under one shepherd. And notice the tense: before they have heard of him, they are already his sheep, because the Father has given them to him. God told Paul in Corinth, I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:10), before most of them had believed.

I must bring them also. “Must” (dei): it is certain, it is the Father’s plan. Not I hope to. This is announced in Jerusalem, years before Peter’s rooftop vision and the long struggle in Acts over whether Gentiles had to become Jews first. The Shepherd had already settled it.

And they will listen to my voice. Not might, but will. His voice will reach them through the gospel, preached by his servants, and they will respond: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). He is describing a future he intends to bring about, and most of the sheep in question had not yet been born.

What it does not mean. Mormon teaching claims that the other sheep were people in the Americas whom Christ visited after his resurrection. But the context is Israel’s fold and those outside it, the Gentiles, whom Jesus would gather through the preaching of the apostles (11:52; 17:20). There is no hint of another continent or another revelation, and the result is one flock with one shepherd, not two churches with two scriptures.

So there will be one flock, one shepherd. Jews and Gentiles together, one people of God, the dividing wall broken down (Ephesians 2:14–16). There will be no Jewish church and Gentile church, no first-class and second-class disciples. The unity of the church is grounded not in a structure but in one Shepherd.

If the sheep will certainly come, why should I evangelise? Because the way he brings them is through his voice, and his voice is heard in the gospel his people speak. They will listen to my voice is a promise about the means as well as the result: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14). Election is not a reason to keep quiet; it is the reason evangelism is not hopeless. Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth because God had many people there. So speak of Christ to your neighbour with confidence. You do not have to know whether he is one of the other sheep. You only have to let him hear the voice.

In a sentence. Jesus said he knows his sheep as the Father knows him, and he lays down his life for them, and he has other sheep outside Israel whom he must bring, who will listen to his voice, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd.

On a Tuesday. If you came into the faith from outside, the wrong background, the wrong family, arriving late and by a side door, you are exactly the category Jesus named in advance. You are not an afterthought or a second tier. And look around your church this Sunday at the people least like you. One flock. Treat them as the Shepherd’s.

For worship. Before there was a church in Rome or Corinth or anywhere beyond Judea, the Shepherd stood in the temple and spoke of sheep he already owned on the far side of the world. If you are a Gentile believer, you were one of the other sheep. He knew you before you knew there was a fold, he died for you by name, and he sent his voice across centuries and seas to bring you in. The knowing that binds you to him is patterned on the knowing between the Father and the Son. There is no deeper love in existence, and he has opened it to you.
verseByVerse.note: The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe.

parallels.desc: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father.

For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life. The Father has always loved the Son, before the foundation of the world (17:24). But he especially delights in the Son’s obedience to death, the love of the Father resting with joy on the Son who does his will. This is not love earned. It is love answered.

That I may take it up again. His death is not the end. He lays down his life with the purpose of taking it up again in the resurrection. The cross and the empty tomb are one intention.

No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. This is the plainest statement in the Bible that the death of Jesus was not something that happened to him. Set it against everything the story is about to do to him. Judas will decide to sell him, the council will decide to condemn him, Pilate will decide to hand him over, and soldiers will decide where to put the nails. Every one of those is a real human decision, and none of them is the cause. He says so in advance, in Jerusalem, months before any of them has made up his mind. At the arrest the soldiers fall back at his word (18:6). On the cross he bows his head and gives up his spirit (19:30). Jesus’ death was voluntary.

I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. The word is exousia: authority, the right and the power to act. He has it twice over, and the second is stranger than the first. A man might conceivably give his life away. Nobody has ever had the right to pick it back up. Who but God has authority over his own death and resurrection? And that recasts the resurrection completely. It is not a rescue, not the Father arriving to undo a disaster, but the second half of one continuous act by the same person. He put it down; he picked it up. John will make the point again with the face cloth lying folded in a place by itself (20:7), which is not what a rescue looks like.

But does not Scripture say the Father raised him? Yes: God raised him up (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4), and the Spirit gives life to mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). There is no contradiction. The Father, the Son and the Spirit act together in all God’s works. The Son took up his life again by the authority the Father gave him, as the next clause says, and by the Spirit’s power. One God raised Jesus from the dead, and each person of the Trinity was at work in it.

Voluntary is not the same as easy. This can be pushed into an error, so it needs a guard. To say the death was voluntary is not to say it was painless, or that his humanity was a costume, or that Gethsemane was theatre. The man who says no one takes it from me is the same man who will be in agony and ask for the cup to pass. Both are true, and holding only one produces either a stoic who never really suffered or a victim who was overwhelmed. He was neither.

This charge I have received from my Father. His death and resurrection are the Father’s command, freely obeyed. The last clause keeps it from being a solo performance. The most voluntary act in history was also an act of obedience, a combination found in only one place.

If no one took his life, are those who killed him not guilty? They are guilty. Peter holds both truths in one sentence: he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God’s sovereign purpose never makes human sin innocent, and human sin never defeats God’s purpose. That is a comfort for your own life too. The wrongs done to you are truly wrong, and God will judge them, yet none of them is outside his hand, and he can work even them for good (Genesis 50:20).

In a sentence. The Father loves the Son because he lays down his life to take it up again; no one takes it from him, but he lays it down freely, with authority to lay it down and take it up again, as the Father commanded.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think that Jesus’ love for you was reluctant, a grim duty he could not escape, remember this verse. He was not trapped. He chose you, with open eyes, knowing every cost. And when you are called to lay something down for others, do it as he did: freely, not under compulsion, out of love and obedience to the Father.

For worship. No one took his life. He gave it, for you. The soldiers thought they had arrested him, Pilate thought he had judged him, the priests thought they had finished him, and all the while the Son of God was laying down what he alone had the right to lay down. And on the third morning he took it up again, folded the grave clothes, and walked out. Death had never held anything it could not be made to give back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”

There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. The word is schisma, a tear, the word for cloth pulled apart, and this is the third time in four chapters (7:43; 9:16; here). John keeps using it because it keeps happening. Wherever Jesus speaks plainly, the room comes apart. And each time the split runs through the same crowd rather than between two settled camps. The people arguing here had all heard the same sentences.

Many of them said, He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him? The charge has two halves that do not usually travel together. He has a demon: that is the spiritual accusation, made again and again (7:20; 8:48, 52). And is insane: that is different, a claim that he is out of his mind. They reach for both at once, which is what people do when the real problem is that the claim is too large to sit with. A man who says he will lay down his life and take it up again does sound mad, unless he is God.

Why listen to him? The most self-revealing part of their sentence. It is a recommendation to stop listening. Notice that it is not an argument; it is an instruction about attention. And it is still the surest way to keep a conclusion safe: not to refute the thing but to establish that it does not need hearing.

There is no middle ground. The famous choice between madman, liar and Lord is set out most starkly here, because the people present understood the options exactly. A man saying what Jesus had just said about laying down his life and taking it up again is not a great moral teacher who has been misunderstood. He is possessed, or deranged, or telling the truth. His enemies could see there was no fourth position. It was later admirers who invented one.

What if my faith divides my own family? It is painful, and it is not a sign that you have failed. Jesus said it would happen (Matthew 10:34–36), and he never once softened his words to prevent division. Make sure the offence they feel is the offence of Christ and not of your manner: be patient, humble, honest, and kinder than you have to be (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not argue every meal; let them see the change. Keep loving them, keep praying for them, and remember that in this very crowd, the same words that drove some to say why listen drove others to ask the question in the next verse. Families divided over Christ are often families on the way to him.

In a sentence. His words divided the Jews again, and many said he had a demon and was mad, so why listen to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus leaves no middle ground. Either he is mad, or he is Lord. Notice when you are tempted to do what this crowd did, not to argue with something he says but simply to stop listening to it, and listen harder there.

For worship. He has been called mad by the sane and possessed by the religious, and he has never once lowered his claims to win back their approval. He did not need to. The words that sounded like madness in a winter courtyard are the words the church has sung for two thousand years: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He was not insane. He was the only fully sane man who ever lived, and he was telling the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

Others said, These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Their first sentence deserves as much weight as their question. They are testifying to the quality of what they have heard: not a miracle, not an argument, but the character of the speech itself. Whatever else is in dispute, these people have listened to Jesus talk about a shepherd laying down his life for his sheep, and they cannot make it fit the diagnosis being offered. It is a small thing, and it is the beginning of a great many conversions. Somebody hears him and cannot square the sound of it with the account they have been given.

Can a demon open the eyes of the blind? They point back to chapter 9, and their reasoning is sound. Opening blind eyes is God’s work: the LORD opens the eyes of the blind (Psalm 146:8). Whatever the enemy of souls does, he does not open eyes. The three verbs of verse 10 are his: steal, kill, destroy. Restoration is not in his repertoire and never has been. Every genuine healing in the Gospels is an argument that the power behind it is not the power that broke the world.

The man who is not in the room. The blind beggar has just been thrown out and is not mentioned again, and his eyes are still doing work. A division in the crowd is settled for some of them by the fact that a man who had never seen can see. That is worth having for anyone who has wondered whether a piece of God’s work in them mattered. He never appears again in the Gospel. He does not know this conversation is happening. And what was done to him is still, in a courtyard he is not standing in, stopping people from dismissing Christ. What God has done in you is also a testimony you may never hear about.

In a sentence. Others said these were not the words of a demon-possessed man, for no demon could open the eyes of the blind.

On a Tuesday. When you hear Christ dismissed, do what these people did: put the words and the works side by side. Read what he said, look at what he did, and ask whether anything evil or deranged could have produced them. Then tell someone what he has done for you; your changed life is one of his works.

For worship. His words and his works together testify: this is the Son of God. No madman spoke like this, and no demon ever made anything whole. Every eye he opened and every word he spoke came from the same source, the light of the world shining on those who sat in darkness. He opened a beggar’s eyes in Jerusalem, and he has opened ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the winter Feast of Dedication, the leaders corner Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He replies that his works already testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow; he gives them eternal life, and neither he nor the Father will let anyone snatch them away. He and the Father are one. They reach for stones, accusing him of making himself God. He answers from the psalm in which God’s word calls human judges “gods”: since Scripture cannot be overturned, how can they call it blasphemy when the one the Father consecrated and sent calls himself God’s Son? At least they should believe his works, and see that the Father is in him and he in the Father. Escaping arrest, he withdraws beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him, saying that everything John said about him has proved true.
verseByVerse.theology: The climactic declaration — I and the Father are one — is the theological summit of the Good Shepherd discourse and of John's presentation of Jesus' identity in the public ministry. The unity is not merely unity of purpose (though it includes that) but ontological unity — the unity of shared divine nature that the Jews correctly understand as a claim to deity (v. 33). Jesus defends the claim not by retreating from it but by appealing to the greater logic: if Scripture can call judges 'gods,' how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defense is not a reduction of the claim but an escalation of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe on the basis of John's testimony confirmed by Jesus' works. This is the pattern of fruitful ministry: the faithful witness of the forerunner, confirmed by the reality of the one the forerunner announced, produces lasting faith. The chapter ends not in Jerusalem with hostility but in the wilderness with harvest — a reminder that the gospel often bears its richest fruit outside the centers of established religion.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.

At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus, after the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes had defiled it by setting up an altar to Zeus and sacrificing pigs on the altar of God. It lasted eight days, in December, with lamps lit in homes. Later Jewish tradition (in the Talmud, Shabbat 21b) tells that when the temple was cleansed only one small jar of pure oil was found, enough for one day, and it burned for eight, which is why the feast became known as the Festival of Lights. Two months have passed since the Feast of Booths (7:2), where Jesus stood among the great lamps of the temple courts and said, I am the light of the world (8:12). Now the Light of the world walks through the temple during the festival of lamps. His light does not come from a jar of oil that might run dry, but from the eternal life of the Father, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5).

A feast about bad shepherds. There is a second connection running under this date, and it binds the two halves of the chapter together. Hanukkah was not only about lamps. It commemorated a rescue from bad shepherds: from Antiochus, certainly, but also from the high priests of Israel’s own establishment who had sold their office to Greek rulers and abandoned the covenant. Jason and Menelaus bought the high priesthood and delivered the flock to the wolf. That is exactly the charge Ezekiel had laid centuries earlier: Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep? And then came God’s answer: I myself will search for my sheep, and I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezekiel 34:2, 11, 23). So John places the Good Shepherd discourse immediately before the Feast of Dedication, and the feast is about the failure of Israel’s shepherds and God’s rescue of his flock. The men Jesus has just described as thieves, robbers and hired hands are keeping a festival that exists because their predecessors were exactly that.

It was winter. Not only weather. It is near the shortest days of the year, the dark end of the calendar, and John has already shown us what he does with the word night (3:2; 9:4; 13:30). Perhaps it also hints at the spiritual coldness of his hearers. The Light of the world walks a covered walkway in the cold, at the darkest point of the year, during the festival of lamps, and in a moment they will pick up stones.

And Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon. A covered portico along the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter wind. The early church later met there (Acts 3:11; 5:12), so that the place where Jesus was surrounded and nearly stoned became the place where his people gathered openly in his name.

Why it matters. At a feast celebrating a temple consecrated again, Jesus will speak of himself as the one the Father consecrated (v. 36), the true temple (2:21). At a feast remembering a political deliverer, the crowd wants to know if he is the Christ. Every thread of the festival is about to be pulled through him.

If the Maccabees are not in our Bible, how do we know this history? From 1 and 2 Maccabees, Jewish books written in the second and first centuries BC, and from the historian Josephus. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include the books of Maccabees, but Protestant churches, following the Hebrew canon that Jesus and the apostles used, do not treat them as Scripture (Westminster 1.3). They are valuable history, like any reliable ancient record, but they do not carry God’s authority. Notice that Jesus’ presence at the feast does not make it a command for Christians. He was a faithful Jew keeping a national festival of thanksgiving, and he used it to show who the true temple and the true light are.

In a sentence. It was winter and the Feast of Dedication, and Jesus was walking in Solomon’s colonnade in the temple.

On a Tuesday. Christ walked in the temple at Hanukkah as its true Lord. In whatever darkness or cold season you are in, he is the light that no darkness extinguishes. Thank him that your light does not depend on how much oil you have left.

For worship. The lamps of Hanukkah were lit for a temple that would be destroyed within forty years of this winter. The one walking through its colonnade was the temple they pointed to, the dwelling of God among men, and the light they could only remember. Every festival of Israel was a shadow cast by his coming. He walked among its shadows in the cold, and he did not burn out.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It fell in December. Solomon’s colonnade ran along the east side of the temple courts.

parallels.desc: Solomon’s Portico

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me.”

So the Jews gathered around him. “Gathered around” (ekyklōsan): surrounded, hemmed in, encircled. A menacing picture. It is the word of the psalm: dogs encompass me, a company of evildoers encircles me (Psalm 22:16).

How long will you keep us in suspense? Literally, how long will you lift up our soul? The idiom is genuinely ambiguous. It can mean keeping someone hanging; it can also carry the sense of vexing or provoking them, how long will you annoy us? Either way there is a complaint inside it: this is your fault. We would have settled the matter long ago if you had been clearer.

If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. They want a political statement they can either rally to or report to the Romans. At a feast that remembered Judas Maccabeus, the word Christ meant a liberator with a sword. That is exactly why Jesus avoided the title Messiah in public: when a crowd tried to make him king by force, he withdrew (6:15). He would not let them fill the word with the wrong meaning.

I told you, and you do not believe. That is the accusation to test, because people still make it. Has he in fact been unclear? He has said I am the bread of life, I am the light of the world, before Abraham was, I am, I am the door, I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life that I may take it up again. They have already reached for stones once (8:59), which is not the behaviour of people who found him vague. His answer is therefore not a dodge but a correction of the record. The information is not missing. The problem is not clarity but unbelief.

The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me. Then he does something generous. Having said that words have not worked, he points them to something that is not words. If the testimony is suspect because it is his own, here is testimony that is not a claim at all but a set of events: water made wine at Cana, a dying boy healed by a word, a man at a pool walking after thirty-eight years, five thousand fed on a hillside, a beggar with new eyes walking around Jerusalem. He is offering them the lowest rung on the ladder. Believe the evidence if you cannot yet believe the man.

Why did Jesus not simply say, Yes, I am the Messiah? Because the word in their mouths meant something he was not. To them the Messiah was a national liberator who would drive out Rome; to say yes plainly would have confirmed that error, and handed them a political charge. Instead he told them who he was in fuller terms than the title: the Son who does his Father’s works, the shepherd of Ezekiel 34, the one who is before Abraham. When he did say it plainly, it was to a Samaritan woman (4:26) and, at the end, under oath before the high priest (Mark 14:61–62), when there was no longer any danger of the word being mistaken for a rebellion. He is the Christ, but on his own definition.

In a sentence. The Jews surrounded Jesus and demanded he tell them plainly if he was the Christ, and he answered that he had told them, but they did not believe, and his works bore witness to him.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting for more evidence before you trust Christ, ask whether the problem is the evidence or your heart. Most of us already know enough to take the next step. And if you are praying for someone who keeps asking for proof, pray not mainly for better arguments but for opened eyes.

For worship. They surrounded him and demanded that he speak plainly, and he had been speaking plainly all along, in words and in works, and he did not turn away even from men who were looking for a reason to kill him. He offered them the lowest rung of the ladder. That is what our Lord is like: when the front door is shut, he looks for a window still ajar. The patience that stood in Solomon’s colonnade is the patience that waited for us.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.

But you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. This is the sentence in the chapter most likely to frighten a reader who is already frightened, and it needs handling with care. Notice the order. Jesus does not say, you are not my sheep because you do not believe, but you do not believe because you are not my sheep. Being his sheep comes first; believing follows. Who his sheep are is settled by the Father’s gift (v. 29; 6:37). This is election. It does not remove their guilt: they do not believe because they will not (5:40). But it explains why some believe and others do not.

Where Christians differ: does faith make us his sheep, or does being his sheep produce faith? Arminian Christians read the verse the other way round: people are not his sheep because they do not believe, and they could have believed if they would; God’s choice follows his foreknowledge of their faith. Verdict: Jesus says the opposite order. You do not believe because you are not among my sheep. Belief is the mark of the sheep, not the way of becoming one: all that the Father gives me will come to me (6:37), and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). God’s choice is unconditional, resting on his own grace and not on anything foreseen in us (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11–16). And yet these hearers were fully responsible for their unbelief, for they refused to come (5:40). Scripture holds both together, and so must we.

Who is being addressed. Read cold, at three in the morning, the verse becomes: what if I am not one? What if the reason faith is hard is that I was never given any? So notice first who Jesus is speaking to. These are men who have watched the signs for years, who have had the claims stated to their faces repeatedly and plainly, who have already reached for stones once, and who are at this moment trying to extract a sentence they can use at a trial. Jesus is not describing a person who is anxious about whether he belongs. He is describing men who are entirely untroubled and have made up their minds.

My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. Then notice what the mark of a sheep actually is, because he gives it in the next breath, and it is not a feeling. They hear; they are known; they follow. Not certainty, not warmth, not an absence of doubt. The sheep in this picture are not described as confident, and nothing in the passage suggests they can tell by looking inward. He knows them as his own (v. 14), and faith shows itself in following.

What if I am afraid I am not one of his sheep? Then do not ask whether you feel like a sheep. Ask what you have done with the voice. A person who has heard something in Christ that will not let him go, and who keeps turning back to him after every failure, is following, and that is the evidence this passage offers. Then do the plainest thing of all, which no doctrine of election has ever qualified: come to him. Nobody who came to him was ever turned away on the grounds of not being on a list; whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). The anxiety that says perhaps I am not one is answered the same way it has always been. Come, and find out.

If they could not believe, how can they be blamed? Because their inability was not a lack of opportunity or evidence but a refusal. They did not want him. No one is kept from Christ against his will while longing to come; the trouble with the fallen heart is precisely that it does not want to come (5:40; 3:19). God is not unjust in leaving people to the choice they themselves love. The wonder is not that some are left, but that any are drawn, and that he draws such people as us.

In a sentence. Jesus said they did not believe because they were not his sheep, for his sheep hear his voice, are known by him, and follow him.

On a Tuesday. Do not try to read the book of election from the outside. Read the voice. Listen to Christ in his word this week and follow what you hear, one obedience at a time. And when doubt says you are not his, answer it by coming to him again, not by examining your feelings again.

For worship. If you hear his voice and follow, you are his sheep, and you are his because the Father gave you to him before you had ever heard of either of them. Your faith did not make you his; his choosing you made you believe. There is nothing in that to make you proud, and everything to make you sing. He knew you first, and he knew you on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.

I give them eternal life. Take the promise apart, because it is built in layers and each one carries weight. Present tense: a gift already handed over, not a prize at the end. Eternal life is a gift, not a reward.

And they will never perish. The Greek (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna) is as emphatic as the language gets: a double negative with the subjunctive, strengthened by to eternity. They shall certainly not, ever, perish. It is the same construction as whoever comes to me I will never cast out in chapter 6 (6:37). Eternal life that could end would not be eternal.

And no one will snatch them out of my hand. The verb (harpazō) is the one from verse 12, where the wolf snatches. It is a word for violent seizure. What is being denied is not that anything will try. No wolf, no thief, no devil, no persecutor can take them.

My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. Then the second hand. The sheep are the Father’s gift to the Son, and the Father is greater than every enemy. The same promise is made twice, by two persons, about the same sheep, and the reason given is not the sheep’s grip but the Father’s greatness. Two hands hold the sheep: the Son’s and the Father’s. Double security, and neither hand is yours.

A textual note. The Greek of verse 29 is genuinely uncertain. The manuscripts divide between my Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and what my Father has given me is greater than all. Translations differ and both readings are defensible. Nothing in the assurance depends on which is right; on either reading the sheep are held by someone nothing can overpower.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Some argue that while no one else can snatch the sheep, a sheep may choose to leave. Verdict: “no one” includes the sheep themselves, and Jesus says plainly that his sheep will never perish. The sheep are kept not by their own grip on Christ but by his grip on them (Romans 8:38–39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). This is the perseverance of the saints. Those who fall away for good show that they were never his sheep (1 John 2:19). True sheep may stray and stumble, but the Shepherd brings them back.

The preservation of the saints. The doctrine is usually called the perseverance of the saints, and it could as well be called their preservation, since the verse puts the holding in his hand rather than in theirs (Westminster 17.1). They persevere because they are preserved, and they are preserved because the one who holds them is greater than all. No sheep the Father gave to the Son has ever been lost, and none ever will be: this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day (6:39).

Against presumption. This is said of sheep who hear and follow (v. 27). It is not a guarantee attached to a decision made once at fifteen and then abandoned, and the New Testament is not shy about people who went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The promise is made to a flock, and the flock is described by what it does. Anyone who says, I am safe, so I can live as I like, has not heard the Shepherd’s voice in this verse at all.

Against despair. This is the commoner need. The security here is stated as an impossibility from the outside: nothing can take them. But ask honestly what the fear usually is. Not that something will snatch. It is that the sheep will wander off, which sheep famously do. And the answer to that is in the Shepherd’s own words in another Gospel: he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, and when he has found it he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:4–5). The promise that they will never perish covers every way of perishing, including their own wandering.

What about Christians who fall into serious sin? A true believer can fall badly and for a time, as David did with Bathsheba and Peter did by the fire. Sin does real damage: it grieves the Spirit, darkens assurance, harms others and brings the Father’s discipline (Hebrews 12:5–11; Westminster 17.3). But a sheep of Christ will not be left there. The Shepherd pursues, convicts and restores, as he restored Peter on the shore (21:15–19). So if you have fallen, do not reason that you are lost; reason that he is coming after you, and turn back to him now. And if you feel no grief at all about a sin you are living in, take that as a serious warning, and come to him today.

What if someone I love has walked away from the faith? Grieve and pray, and do not give up. You cannot see the heart, and you do not know the end of the story. Some who wander are sheep who will be brought back, sometimes after many years; others, Scripture says, were never truly his (1 John 2:19), and only God knows which. Your part is not to pronounce, but to love, to keep the door open, to speak of Christ when there is an opening, and above all to bring him or her to the Shepherd in prayer. He goes after the lost one, and he is better at finding than we are at waiting.

In a sentence. Jesus gives his sheep eternal life, and they will never perish, for no one can snatch them out of his hand, or out of the hand of the Father, who gave them to him and is greater than all.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether you will make it, look at the hands that hold you. Rest in his grip, not yours. Your faith will waver this week; his hold will not. And let that security make you bold rather than careless: those who know they cannot be lost are free to spend themselves for him.

For worship. The one who said these words was a matter of months from having those hands opened with nails, and the holding did not stop. Nothing was let go of on the Friday. The grip that nothing in creation can break is the grip of hands that were themselves broken to make it secure. Around that hand is the Father’s hand, and the Father is greater than all. There is no wolf strong enough, no night long enough, no wandering far enough to take one sheep out of the hands of God.

parallels.desc: there is none that can deliver out of my hand

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I and the Father are one. The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.

I and the Father are one. Six words that hold the centre of John’s Gospel. “One” is neuter in Greek (hen): one thing, one in nature and purpose, not one person. If Jesus had said one person (heis), it would mean the Father and the Son are the same person, the old heresy of modalism. He does not say that. “I and the Father” are two; the verb “are” is plural. But they are one thing, one in being. Two subjects, one predicate: are keeps them distinct, one keeps them undivided. And in context he has just said that no one can snatch the sheep from his hand or from the Father’s. The hand of the Son and the hand of the Father do the same work with the same power, because the Son and the Father are one. This is the doctrine of the Trinity in a sentence: distinct persons, one God.

Two errors settled at once. The neuter word settles two errors that are both still met today. It will not carry the reading of those who say the Father and the Son are merely two names or modes of one individual, a view the early church met in Sabellius and which is taught today by Oneness Pentecostalism. John has already told us that the Word was with God (1:1), and you cannot be with yourself. And it will not carry the opposite reduction either, pressed by Jehovah’s Witnesses, that this is only two wills agreeing. Men do not pick up stones over a shared policy. They tell us themselves what they heard, two verses on: you, being a man, make yourself God.

Where Christians differ: is this only unity of will? Some say this means only unity of will and purpose, as believers are to be one (17:22). Verdict: it includes unity of purpose, but cannot stop there. The hearers took it as a claim to be God, and Jesus did not correct them; instead he went on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38). Believers share a unity of love; the Son shares the Father’s very being (1:1; 5:18).

The Jews picked up stones again to stone him. As in 8:59. They understood exactly what he meant (v. 33). This is the second time in about three months. The first attempt followed before Abraham was, I am; this one follows I and the Father are one. Their consistency is its own evidence: they reach for stones at exactly the two points where he identifies himself with God, and at no other point. What the church later put into the creeds was not an invention of the fourth century. It was already sitting in a sentence spoken in a temple colonnade in winter, by a man about to be stoned for saying it.

How can three persons be one God without contradiction? Because one and three are not said in the same sense. God is one in being: there is one divine nature, one will, one power, one glory. He is three in person: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly distinct, relating to one another in love (17:24). A contradiction would be one God who is three Gods, or one person who is three persons. The Trinity is neither. We cannot picture it fully, and every illustration fails somewhere, which is what we should expect if God is greater than his creation. But we do not believe it because we can picture it. We believe it because the Son himself stood in the temple and said both I and the Father, and are one.

In a sentence. Jesus said he and the Father are one, and the Jews picked up stones again to stone him.

On a Tuesday. When you pray to Jesus, you are not praying to a lesser being who will pass the message on. You are speaking to God. And when you feel unsure of the Father’s love, look at the Son: the Father is not different from him. They are one.

For worship. The Son is one with the Father. To see him is to see God, and to be held by him is to be held by God. The hand that holds the sheep is not the hand of a creature, however exalted, doing his best on God’s behalf. It is the almighty hand of the eternal Son, which is one with the Father’s. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: one God, undivided, and he has taken hold of us.
verseByVerse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek — one in nature and purpose, not one person.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?” The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”

I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me? A calm, ironic question with stones raised above him. But it is not mere sarcasm. The adjective is kala again, the word from the good shepherd: fine, noble, beautiful works. He is asking men holding rocks to name the beautiful thing they object to. And it is a real question in the sense that it forces them to state their actual charge, which they do, accurately, in the next sentence.

It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy. Stoning was the law’s penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16).

Because you, being a man, make yourself God. This is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone working out what Jesus claimed. These are hostile witnesses with every reason to play it down. If there had been any way to read his words as a lesser claim, a prophet, a teacher, a man specially favoured, they would have taken it, because stoning a popular figure at a feast was dangerous and they knew it. They did not take it, because it was not available. They understood his words as a claim to deity.

The direction is reversed. Their mistake was not in understanding him but in thinking he was making himself God. The truth is the opposite: he was God, making himself man (1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). They have the two terms right and the direction exactly backwards. Nobody in this story is climbing. And they are right about the man too. They say you, being a man, and the problem was never that they misread his humanity. It was standing in front of them, tired and dusty and not yet fifty (8:57). What they could not do was hold the two together: a man, and God. Everything since has turned on whether that sentence is a contradiction, and the church spent four centuries finding language careful enough to say it without collapsing one side into the other. The men with the stones had the whole problem in view and solved it the quick way.

Did Jesus ever actually claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies are the clearest witnesses. People sometimes say the idea that Jesus is God was invented by the church later. But here, during his lifetime, men who heard him tried to kill him for exactly that claim, and he did not withdraw it. He forgave sins as only God can (Mark 2:5–7), took the divine name I am (8:58), received worship (20:28), and said that to see him is to see the Father (14:9). A man who said these things and was not God would not be a good teacher. The only reason to worship him is that he is who he said.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of his good works they were stoning him for, and they answered that it was for blasphemy, because, being a man, he made himself God.

On a Tuesday. When someone tells you Jesus never claimed to be God, show them this verse. And take its question to yourself: is there any good work of his you are resisting? Any part of his goodness you hold at a distance because accepting it would mean bowing to him?

For worship. He did not make himself God; he is God, who made himself man for us. He came down so far that men could pick up stones against him, and they hated him not for any evil but for being exactly who he was. Every good work he had shown them came from the Father, and the best was still to come: the work of a cross, where the one they called a blasphemer bore the curse for blasphemers.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —

Is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? “Law” here means the whole Old Testament, as often in John. The quotation is from Psalm 82:6. The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s justice, exercising his authority among his people (compare Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9, where judges are called elohim). God then rebukes them for judging unjustly, and says they will die like men.

Read the whole psalm. It takes about a minute. God takes his place in the divine council and puts the “gods” on trial. They judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked (82:2); they will not defend the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted and the destitute (82:3–4); they walk about in darkness, and the foundations of the earth are shaken by their misrule (82:5). And then the sentence falls: nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince (82:7). That is the psalm. It calls them gods and then condemns them to death precisely because they are not. The word is a title of office, men entrusted with God’s own authority to judge, and the entire point of the psalm is to strip it off them.

If he called them gods to whom the word of God came. The argument goes from lesser to greater. If Scripture can call mere human judges gods, because God’s word came to them and they acted for him, how can it be blasphemy for the one whom the Father consecrated and sent to call himself the Son of God? And notice that his hearers did not take it as a retreat. They do not put the stones down; they try again to arrest him (v. 39). The claim of verse 30 stands.

Where Christians differ: who are the gods of Psalm 82? Some scholars read them as heavenly beings, the spiritual powers set over the nations, judged by God for their injustice. Others read them as Israel’s human judges. Verdict: the second is more likely. Jesus’ argument is that the word of God came to them (v. 35), and the psalm says they will die like men (Psalm 82:7), which fits human rulers far better. They were called gods because they held God’s authority, and judged because they abused it.

And Scripture cannot be broken. The word (lythēnai) means to be annulled, set aside, emptied of its authority. It is a remarkable statement of Jesus’ view of Scripture. He rests his argument on a single word in a short psalm, and says that word cannot be set aside. Even an obscure phrase in an obscure psalm carries God’s authority. This is the foundation of the doctrine of the inerrancy and authority of Scripture: Jesus himself held it, and his followers can hold no lower view than their Lord’s.

What it does not mean. Few verses in the Bible have been wrenched further from their meaning. “You are gods” is quoted by Mormonism to teach that faithful men and women may themselves become gods, and by Word of Faith teachers to tell congregations they are little gods with creative power in their mouths. To quote the psalm as a promise of divinity is to quote the indictment and mistake it for the reward. Nor is Jesus saying he is a god only in the sense the judges were. He is arguing from their own Scripture that his claim cannot be dismissed as blasphemy on principle, and then he goes further than the judges ever could: the Father is in me and I am in the Father (v. 38). The rest of Scripture allows no other reading: before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me (Isaiah 43:10); I am the LORD, and there is no other (Isaiah 45:5). The line between Creator and creature is never crossed by promotion.

What are we promised instead? Something better than the counterfeit and different in kind: not deity by nature, but adoption by grace. We become children of God (1:12), sharers in his life and holiness, and one day we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Sons, not gods. The offer of godhood was first made in a garden by someone else (Genesis 3:5), and it has never once been kept.

If Scripture cannot be broken, what about the parts that seem to contradict each other? Take them seriously and humbly, as Jesus took Scripture. Most apparent contradictions dissolve with careful reading: different writers choosing different details, rounding numbers, arranging events by theme rather than strict order, or using words in different senses, as Paul and James do with justify. Some remain hard, and it is honest to say so. But a difficulty we cannot yet solve is not an error we have proved. When you meet one, look at a good study Bible or commentary, ask your pastor, and hold on to the Lord’s own conviction while you wait for light.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that their Scripture called those to whom the word of God came gods, and Scripture cannot be set aside.

On a Tuesday. Treat every word of Scripture as Jesus did: it cannot be broken. Read it expecting God to speak, submit to it where it cuts across you, and when someone quotes a verse at you on the doorstep, read the whole passage it comes from.

For worship. The eternal Word stood under the written word and called it unbreakable. He who could have spoken any new sentence he liked rested his whole defence on one phrase of an old psalm. And he alone fulfils what the false gods of Psalm 82 failed to do: he defends the weak and the fatherless, he rescues the needy from the hand of the wicked, and he will judge the earth in righteousness. Arise, O God, the psalm ends, for you shall inherit all the nations (82:8). In him, God has arisen.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s authority. “Your Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole.

parallels.desc: “I said, ‘You are gods’”

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?

Do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world. There is a word in this verse that the English cannot show, and it is one of the finest details in the chapter. The verb is hagiazō: to set apart as holy, to sanctify, to dedicate. And the feast they are standing in is the Feast of Dedication, in Greek ta enkainia, the renewing, in Hebrew Hanukkah, which means exactly that: dedication. They are keeping the festival of a consecrated altar, an altar that had been defiled, torn down, rebuilt and set apart again for God, and whose rededication they had been celebrating for eight days with lamps. And Jesus says: the Father has consecrated me.

The true temple. The stone altar was dedicated by men and had to be rebuilt because it could be desecrated. This one was set apart by the Father before he was sent, and cannot be. He has already told them he is the true temple (2:19–21), the holy place where God dwells; now he tells them, during the feast of the temple’s reconsecration, that the consecration they are commemorating has been fulfilled in a person.

And sent into the world. The second verb should not be lost behind the first. Sending implies somewhere to be sent from. Consecrated before he was sent: he existed with the Father before coming. It is the quiet premise underneath the whole sentence, and it is the thing they have denied all along. At 7:27 they said they knew where he came from; at 9:29 they said they did not; and either way they had it wrong. Those two words contain the incarnation, dropped into the middle of a legal defence.

You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God? The argument’s force against the charge is simple. Blasphemy is a man claiming for himself a status he has not been given. If the Father himself did the setting apart and the sending, then whatever the Son says about his own status is a report rather than a claim, and the accusation collapses, not because the claim is smaller than they thought but because the authorisation is larger. If the judges could be called gods, how much more he, uniquely set apart and sent, can be called the Son of God.

Christians are called sanctified too, so is it the same thing? It is related, and the difference matters. Jesus was consecrated as the holy Son, set apart for his mission, with no sin to be cleansed from. We are sinners made holy because of him. In his prayer he says, for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth (17:19). He set himself apart for the cross so that we could be set apart for God. Your holiness is borrowed from his, and the Spirit is working it out in you day by day.

In a sentence. Jesus asked how they could accuse of blasphemy the one whom the Father had set apart and sent into the world, because he said he was the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. You belong to the one the Father consecrated. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). Ask what in your week needs to be cleansed and set apart again for God, as the Maccabees cleansed the altar, and ask Christ to do it.

For worship. Christ is the holy one, consecrated by the Father and sent for us. In him, God dwells among us. Every temple built of stone could be defiled and every altar torn down, but the Son of God was set apart before the world began, and he came into the world without losing one particle of his holiness. And he consecrated himself further still, to the cross, so that a people who had defiled everything they touched might be made holy and brought near.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.

If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me. This is the most accommodating thing he says to his enemies in the whole Gospel, and it is worth noticing how far down he is prepared to reach. He begins by handing them a test that could destroy him. He puts a condition on his own claim that could be checked. If the works are not there, he says, you are entitled to dismiss me. That is not the language of a man managing a following. Jesus invites testing; he does not ask for blind faith.

But if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works. Take that in. He has just been called a blasphemer by men with stones in their hands, and his response is to offer them a lower rung. Do not believe me, then. Believe the events. Start anywhere. He is not standing on his dignity or requiring that they come to him by the front door of full faith; he is trying to get them in by any opening still ajar. The works are evidence (14:11).

That you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father. The goal he names is not mere agreement but knowledge, and two verbs carry it: know, and understand. He wants them to arrive at the very thing they are about to stone him for. And the claim goes beyond anything Psalm 82’s judges could say. No human judge could say this. The Father and the Son dwell in each other; later theologians call it perichōrēsis, the mutual indwelling of the persons. It is the deepest statement of their oneness (14:10–11; 17:21).

Is it all right to believe because of evidence, rather than simply by faith? Yes. Biblical faith is not believing without reasons; it is trusting God on the basis of what he has shown. Jesus himself points to his works, John writes his Gospel so that by reading the signs we may believe (20:31), and the resurrection was proved by many proofs (Acts 1:3). Evidence alone cannot change a heart; only the Spirit can do that, as these hearers show. But the Spirit uses evidence. So do not be ashamed of asking questions, and do not despise friends who need reasons. Point them to the works, and pray that the Spirit will open their eyes to the one who did them.

Counting the works. Here is a test for the reader in a dry stretch rather than a hostile one. When the person of Christ has gone flat and the affections are not there, this verse permits a smaller move: look at what he has actually done. Not what you feel about him; the record. Faith that has lost its warmth can still count the works, and this passage says that is a legitimate place to stand while the rest comes back.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he was not doing his Father’s works they should not believe him, but if he was, they should believe the works, so that they would know the Father is in him and he in the Father.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not blind. Look at what Jesus did, and let it lead you to who he is. If your heart feels cold this week, do not wait for feelings; read one of his works in the Gospels slowly, and let the evidence warm you.

For worship. He stooped to men with stones in their hands and offered them the smallest door into the largest truth. And the truth on the other side of that door is beyond all our measuring: the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, an eternal life of love shared and indwelt, now opened to us, for he prays that we may be in them (17:21). The works were the window. The God behind them is the joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.

Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. Yet another failed attempt in this Gospel (7:30, 44; 8:20, 59; 10:31), and John never explains any of them beyond the hour. His hour has not yet come. No one can snatch the sheep out of his hand (v. 28); and no one can seize him out of the Father’s plan. The withdrawal is not retreat from danger so much as refusal to let the danger set the schedule.

He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first. John is doing something deliberate with this geography. “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John first baptised (1:28), and it is where this Gospel started: the Baptist standing in the water, pointing at him and saying, behold, the Lamb of God. So the public ministry, which opened there, now closes there. Everything between has happened, and he comes back to the spot where the first two disciples turned round and followed him. It is across the Jordan, outside Judea, beyond the reach of the temple authorities, on the far bank of the river Israel crossed to come into the land, and the stretch where Elijah was taken up. It is the threshold. He goes out over the boundary, stays a while, and will come back across it in the next chapter to walk toward a tomb (11:7), and from there toward his own.

And there he remained. A time of withdrawal, about three months before the final Passover. After a winter of stones and interrogations he goes back to the river and stays put. What happens next is the raising of Lazarus and then the last week. This is the quiet stretch immediately before all of it, and the fact that there was one, and that he took it, is worth having.

Is it cowardice for a Christian to step back from conflict or rest? No, not when it is done for the right reasons. Jesus withdrew more than once, not from fear but because his hour had not come, and he took his disciples apart to rest (Mark 6:31). Courage is not the same as walking into every fight, and faithfulness is not the same as never stopping. Withdrawing is wrong when it means abandoning a duty God has given you, as the hired hand did. It is right when it means waiting for God’s time, guarding your soul, or refusing to let other people’s hostility set your agenda. Rest is not desertion. It is often preparation.

In a sentence. They tried again to arrest him, but he escaped and went back across the Jordan to the place where John first baptised, and stayed there.

On a Tuesday. Is there a place where your faith began, a person, a church, a passage of Scripture, that you need to go back to in a hard season? And is there a quiet stretch God is giving you that you are filling with noise? Take it, and stay there a while.

For worship. Jesus withdraws and returns at the Father’s time. His life is ordered by love, not fear. No mob in Jerusalem could hurry him to the cross a day early, and no fear could keep him from it a day late. He went back to the river where the Lamb of God had first been named, and waited there for the hour when he would be that Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.” And many believed in him there.

And many came to him. A contrast with Jerusalem. Away from the leaders, people come.

And they said, John did no sign. Stop on that, because it is the only time in the New Testament such a thing is said of anybody, and it is said of the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11). No miracle. Not one healing, not one deliverance, nothing that would have drawn a crowd on its own account. What he had was a voice and a message, and he used them for a short time in a river valley and was then, as the other Gospels tell, imprisoned and beheaded. By any measure available at the time his ministry ended in failure: his own movement absorbed into somebody else’s, and himself dead in Herod’s prison without seeing what came of it. His greatness was in his witness.

But everything that John said about this man was true. And here, after his death, in the place where he had worked, ordinary people say it. They had heard him. They had remembered. And when the one he pointed to came back to that stretch of river, they knew him because of what a dead man had told them. He had called him the Lamb of God (1:29), the one who would baptise with the Spirit (1:33), the Son of God (1:34), and every word had proved true. The but in their sentence is doing the work. They concede what the Baptist lacked and assert what he had, and they rank the second above the first. No miracles, and every word accurate. It is a beautiful epitaph, and the greatest thing that can be said of any servant of Christ: what he said about Jesus was true.

And many believed in him there. The full construction, the real thing: faith in him. Faith flourishes where John’s witness had prepared the ground. Jerusalem, with the temple and the scholars and the festivals, produced stones. The riverbank produced believers. The chapter, full of rejection, ends with many believing, and it is the last thing this Gospel records before the greatest sign of all.

Should I expect miracles to confirm my witness? No, and this verse is a great relief. The greatest of the prophets did no sign at all, and his witness bore fruit years later. The miracles of Christ and the apostles had a special purpose: to confirm the new revelation as it was given (Hebrews 2:3–4). This app holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of that foundational age have ceased, while God still answers prayer and can heal as he wills. Many brothers and sisters see this differently, and we honour them. But on any view, the ordinary means God uses to bring people to faith is the faithful word of witness, spoken plainly and backed by a life. You do not need a sign. You need to tell the truth about Jesus.

In a sentence. Many came to Jesus across the Jordan, saying that though John did no sign, everything he said about Jesus was true, and many believed in him there.

On a Tuesday. You may never work a miracle. But you can tell the truth about Jesus, to a child, a neighbour, a colleague. Let that be your life’s witness. And if your work for God seems to have produced nothing spectacular, remember that the Baptist’s fruit came in late, at a place he had left, among people he could no longer count.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest remembers every true word ever spoken about his Son. He let his greatest prophet die in a prison cell without seeing the fruit, and then he walked back to the very riverbank where that prophet had preached and gathered the harvest himself. No faithful witness is wasted. Every sentence that points to the Lamb of God is kept, and at the right time, in the right place, it bears fruit to his glory.

The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.<sup>4</sup>When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.<sup>5</sup>A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers.”<sup>6</sup>This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.<sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.<sup>8</sup>All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.<sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture.<sup>10</sup>The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.<sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.<sup>12</sup>He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.<sup>13</sup>He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.<sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. This charge I have received from my Father.”<sup>19</sup>There was again a division among the Jews because of these words.<sup>20</sup>Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”<sup>21</sup>Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”<sup>22</sup>At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter,<sup>23</sup>and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.<sup>24</sup>So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me,<sup>26</sup>but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep.<sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.<sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.<sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.<sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.”<sup>31</sup>The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.<sup>32</sup>Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?”<sup>33</sup>The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ’I said, you are gods’?<sup>35</sup>If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—<sup>36</sup>do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ’You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ’I am the Son of God’?<sup>37</sup>If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me;<sup>38</sup>but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”<sup>39</sup>Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands.<sup>40</sup>He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.<sup>41</sup>And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.”<sup>42</sup>And many believed in him there.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 follows straight on from the healing of the blind man, whom the Pharisees had thrown out and Jesus had found. Against those false shepherds Jesus describes himself in two pictures from village life. He is the door of the sheepfold: those who enter through him are saved, and find pasture and abundant life. And he is the good shepherd, who knows his sheep by name, leads them out, and lays down his life for them, unlike hired hands who run from the wolf. The background is Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David. Jesus has other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must also bring, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. He lays down his life of his own accord and has authority to take it up again.

Two months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, which celebrated the cleansing of the temple by the Maccabees, the leaders surround Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he tell them plainly whether he is the Messiah. He answers that his works testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow him; he gives them eternal life, they will never perish, and no one can snatch them from his hand or from the Father’s. “I and the Father are one.” They take up stones for blasphemy. Jesus answers from Psalm 82, where human judges are called “gods”, arguing that Scripture cannot be broken and that the one the Father consecrated and sent is rightly called the Son of God. Escaping, he withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe in him.

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, his sisters Martha and Mary send word to Jesus, whom they know loves him. Jesus says this sickness will end in God’s glory, not death, and deliberately waits two more days before returning to Judea despite the danger. He tells the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he will wake him; when they misunderstand, he tells them plainly that Lazarus has died, and Thomas resolves that they will go and die with him. Lazarus has been entombed four days when they arrive. Martha meets Jesus, grieving that he came too late yet trusting him still. He promises that her brother will rise and declares that he himself is the resurrection and the life; she confesses him as the Christ, the Son of God. Mary comes and falls weeping at his feet, and Jesus, deeply stirred and troubled, weeps with them. At the tomb he orders the stone moved despite Martha’s fear of the stench, prays aloud to the Father so that the crowd may believe, and calls Lazarus out. The dead man emerges, still wrapped, and Jesus tells them to free him.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is a preview of Jesus' own resurrection and, through his, the resurrection of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is not merely a claim about what Jesus can do but about what he is: the source and substance of resurrection-life, the one in whom the age-to-come has already broken into the present. Those who believe in him will never die — not because they avoid physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24). Lazarus' resurrection is the bodily demonstration of what Jesus gives spiritually to every believer.
verseByVerse.examples: The weeping of Jesus (vv. 33-35) is one of the most theologically dense moments in the gospel: the one who knows he is about to raise Lazarus weeps with those who grieve. His tears are not ignorance of the outcome but solidarity with human grief, genuine compassion that does not remove itself from suffering even when it is about to overcome suffering. This is the incarnation at its most moving: God in the flesh does not observe human sorrow from a distance; he enters it, feels it, and weeps in it — before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.

Meaning first. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John’s Gospel. It shows that Jesus is the resurrection and the life, with power over death itself.
