It is also the turning point that leads to the cross: because of it the council decides Jesus must die (v. 53). The giver of life will lose his life for giving it. And the chapter shows us his heart as no other chapter does. He loves a family, delays on purpose, walks back into danger, weeps at a grave he is about to empty, and is angry at death. Then he calls a dead man by name, and the dead man comes out. Everything the Gospel has said about his authority over life (5:21–29) is here made visible on a Judean hillside, and the price of it is his own life.

The setting. Jesus is at this moment in Bethany across the Jordan, where the Baptist worked (10:40; 1:28). The message reaches him there about a man in Bethany near Jerusalem. There were two villages of that name, and the whole chapter is the journey from one to the other: from the place where his ministry began to a tomb two miles from the city that will kill him.

Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany. Six words set the whole problem of the chapter. “Lazarus” is a short form of Eleazar, meaning God helps, and the chapter will show what that name means. Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem (v. 18), on the road to Jericho; it is not the same as Bethany beyond the Jordan, where Jesus was staying. And this is not a stranger, nor a member of the opposition. This is the household Jesus stayed in when he came to Jerusalem, the nearest thing to a home he had in Judea, where he was fed and where he was known. So the illness in verse 1 is not a case. It is somebody’s brother, in a house Jesus loved, and the news is going to reach a man who could do something about it.

The village of Mary and her sister Martha. The sisters appear in Luke 10:38–42: Martha busy serving, Mary sitting at Jesus’ feet. There is a small tenderness in the way the household is described. Not the house of Lazarus, as a first-century listing would usually run, but the village of Mary and her sister Martha, with Lazarus attached to them. The women are the fixed point of the household.

It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair. John identifies Mary by an act she has not yet performed in his story; the anointing comes in the next chapter (12:1–8). He assumes his readers know it, which tells us how widely the story had been told; Jesus said it would be told wherever the gospel was preached (Mark 14:9). The wiping of the feet with her hair had become the thing she was known for. And so from the first verses the shadow of Jesus’ burial falls across the illness of his friend.

Is this Mary the sinful woman of Luke 7, or Mary Magdalene? No. Luke 7:36–50 describes an earlier and different anointing, in Galilee, by an unnamed woman known as a sinner, in the house of a Pharisee. Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus at Bethany days before his death (12:1–8). Mary Magdalene is a third woman, from Magdala in Galilee, from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons (Luke 8:2). Later tradition merged the three, but the Gospels keep them distinct, and it is worth keeping them distinct, because each of them is a separate testimony to his grace.

Did Jesus really need friends? He did not need them as God, who is complete in himself. But he was truly man, and a true man is made for friendship. He chose to have a home where he was welcome, people he loved by name, a table where he could rest. That is no weakness. It is a picture of what he is: the Son of God who has come near enough to be your friend (15:15). And it is a dignity he gives to ordinary Christian hospitality. A house where Christ is loved and his people are welcome is doing something he himself valued.

In a sentence. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Mary and Martha, was ill; this was the Mary who later anointed the Lord’s feet.

On a Tuesday. Jesus had friends, a home where he was welcome. Make your home a place where Christ is welcome: open your door to his people, keep his word at your table, and let tired believers rest there.

For worship. The eternal Son, who has the Father’s love from before the world began, chose a house in a village and three friends to love. He did not keep humanity at arm’s length. He let himself be fed and housed and grieved over, and when the illness came to that house it came to him. There is no home so ordinary that he will not enter it, and no sorrow in it that will not reach him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

So the sisters sent to him, saying, Lord, he whom you love is ill. The message is short, and it is a model of how to pray. There is no request in it. No come, no heal him, no please hurry, and these are women who plainly could have asked. They state the situation and the relationship and stop. Set that against the way most of us pray under pressure, where the instinct is to specify the outcome and then to keep specifying it. Their confidence is not in having framed the request correctly. It is in the fact that he loves their brother, and that he will know what to do with that information. “Love” here is phileō, the affectionate word, the love of friendship. Two verses later John will say Jesus loved them using agapaō. This Gospel moves between the two words without any clear difference of weight, which is worth remembering when much is built on the distinction in chapter 21.

This illness does not lead to death. This is the sentence that must be handled with care, because a bereaved reader will stop at it. Lazarus dies. By the time Jesus arrives he is four days dead and in a cave. So either Jesus was wrong, or he meant something the English does not immediately carry. The Greek is pros thanaton: toward death, in the direction of death. He is not predicting whether the man’s heart will stop. He is saying where the illness is aimed and what it ends in. Death will not be the end of the story. Its final outcome is not death but resurrection.

It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it. As with the man born blind (9:3), the purpose is God’s glory. And the glory of God is the glory of the Son: the Father is honoured when the Son is honoured (5:23). There is a double meaning here too. The Son will be glorified by the miracle, and also by the death it will bring him to (v. 53; 12:23). In John, Jesus is glorified on the cross. The sign that shows his glory is the sign that sends him to it.

If I pray for healing and the person dies, did God fail? No, and this verse should not be used to promise what it does not promise. Christians die of their illnesses, and this text has been quoted over sickbeds in a way that later looked like a broken promise. What it actually says is stranger and better: that for those who belong to him, an illness can pass straight through death and still not have death as its destination. God may heal, and we should ask him to. But his answer is never limited to the two choices of healing or failure. For a believer, death is not God’s defeat but the doorway to his presence and the road to resurrection. Pray boldly, and leave the shape of the answer to his love.

In a sentence. The sisters sent word that the one Jesus loved was ill, and Jesus said the illness would not end in death but was for God’s glory, so that the Son of God might be glorified.

On a Tuesday. Bring your needs to Jesus simply: Lord, the one you love is ill. You do not have to win his attention or prove your case. Tell him the need, remind yourself of his love, and trust him with the outcome.

For worship. The sisters had only one argument, and it was enough: he whom you love. They did not plead their own faithfulness or Lazarus’s goodness; they pleaded his love. That is still the ground on which every prayer stands. And the love they appealed to was greater than they knew. It was aiming, through this very illness, at the glory of God, and at a cross where he would be glorified by dying for those he loved.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.

Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. “Loved” here is agapaō, the deep, committed love. John is careful to say it before he tells us of the delay. He wants us to read what comes next with this sentence in our minds, so that we cannot misread the delay as indifference.

So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was. The little word “so” is the hinge of the chapter, and it should be felt as a shock. Not but; any of us would have written but. John writes therefore. The delay is the consequence of the love, not a suspension of it. Because he loved them, he stayed away. He meant to give them something far greater than a healing: a resurrection, and a deeper knowledge of who he is.

The arithmetic. Was Lazarus already dead? Probably, by the time the message arrived. When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (v. 17). Work backwards. The journey from Bethany beyond the Jordan to Bethany near Jerusalem took about a day. Before that, he waited two days. Before that, the messenger had to travel the same road, which took about a day. One plus two plus one. Lazarus may well have died soon after the messenger set out, before the message ever reached Jesus. So the delay did not kill Lazarus. Even if Jesus had left the moment the news arrived, he would have walked into a house where the man was already buried. The two days did not cause the death, but they ensured that no one could doubt he was truly dead.

The comfort for if only. That is a serious comfort for a particular kind of grief, and it should be given plainly to whoever needs it. There is a form of bereavement that spends years on the timing: if the appointment had been a week earlier, if we had gone straight to the hospital, if the prayer had started sooner. This passage puts a family in exactly that position, lets them say the sentence twice, and quietly shows that the arithmetic never worked. He was not late. He was doing something else. And the something else is uncomfortable to name honestly. He allowed a death he could have prevented, in a family he loved, in order to give them and everybody watching something a healing could not have given. That is what the text says. It does not make the four days pleasant, and John records no attempt to make them pleasant.

Why does God delay answering my prayers? Scripture does not give a single reason for every case, but this chapter gives us the deepest one: his delays are governed by love, not neglect. Sometimes he waits because he intends to give something greater than what we asked. Sometimes the waiting itself is shaping us, teaching us to trust him rather than our timetable. Often we will not know why until later, and some things not until we see his face. What you can know now is the sentence John put first: Jesus loved them. Read every delay in your life with that sentence in front of it, and keep praying.

In a sentence. Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, so when he heard Lazarus was ill, he stayed where he was two more days.

On a Tuesday. When God delays, it is not because he does not love you. It may be because he loves you too much to give you less than his best. And if you carry an if only about a death you could not prevent, lay it down before him. He holds the times, and he was not late.

For worship. Love that seems absent is often love preparing its greatest display. The Lord who stayed two days beyond the Jordan was not careless of Bethany; he was carrying the whole of it in his heart, and walking toward it on his own schedule. He is never hurried by our panic or slowed by our doubt. He comes at the hour that love has chosen, and when he comes he brings more than we dared to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.” The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”

Then after this he said to the disciples, Let us go to Judea again. Not let us go to Lazarus, which is what the errand is, but Judea, the place of danger. He names the province rather than the friend, and the province is where the stones are. He tells them what the journey costs before he tells them what it is for. And there is something in the pronoun. Let us go. He does not go alone and does not send them. Whatever is waiting in Judea, they are going into it together.

Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you. The disciples are not being cowardly, and their objection deserves respect. The authorities had tried, twice, in about three months (8:59; 10:31, 39), the last time at the Feast of Dedication only a few weeks before. They are afraid for him, and for themselves.

And are you going there again? The word “again” appears twice, once in Jesus’ mouth and once in theirs. For him it is a return to unfinished business. For them it is the second time into a place that nearly killed him. That is generally how a call sounds from the two sides. The one giving it has the whole picture; the ones receiving it can only see the last time.

The shape of costly obedience. It rarely announces itself as heroism. The disciples are not being asked to volunteer for martyrdom in a blaze of glory. They are being asked to walk down a road to visit a sick friend, in a district where the last visit ended badly. The danger is real, and the errand is ordinary. Much faithfulness looks exactly like that: a hospital visit that may be awkward, a conversation that may be costly, a return to a place where you were once hurt.

Should I take risks for Christ, or be prudent? Both, in their place. Prudence is not sin; Jesus himself withdrew when his hour had not come (10:40; 11:54), and he told his disciples to flee from one town to the next under persecution (Matthew 10:23). But prudence becomes sin when it is used to excuse disobedience. The question is not, is this safe? but, is this where he is going? If Christ calls you to a costly duty, to love someone difficult, to speak truth, to serve in a hard place, the danger is not a reason to refuse. And if he has not called you, there is no virtue in seeking danger for its own sake.

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciples they were going back to Judea, and they protested that the Jews had just tried to stone him there.

On a Tuesday. Is there a costly thing you are avoiding because the last time it went badly? Pray about it. If it is where Christ is leading, go, and remember he said, let us go. You will not walk into it alone.

For worship. Jesus walked toward danger to give life to his friend. He walked toward the cross to give life to us. The road to Bethany was the road to Calvary, and he took it with his eyes open, saying let us go, not because he did not count the cost, but because he had counted it and found us worth it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

Are there not twelve hours in the day? The picture depends on a fact of life before street lighting. The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset, whatever the season, so the hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter. When the light went, work stopped, and a man walking a stony Judean track after dark would fall. So the claim is about allotted time. The day has a fixed length, set by God. Jesus’ day is the appointed time of his ministry (9:4), and it cannot be cut short until it is finished. He is not saying the danger is imaginary. He is saying the clock is not kept by the men holding the stones.

If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. On the plain level: you can walk safely by daylight. On the deeper level: the one who walks in God’s will, in the light of Christ, walks safely. The disciples’ safety on this road is not a matter of the route but of whom they are following.

But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him. The last clause is the odd one. Not because there is no light outside, but because the light is not in him. The picture slips from the sun outside to something carried inside, which is where this Gospel has been going since chapter 1. The one without the light stumbles (12:35). Jesus is safe because he walks in his Father’s will, and his enemies cannot touch him until his hour.

The hard edge of the picture. Twelve hours is a fixed allowance. It cannot be shortened by enemies, and it cannot be extended by carefulness either. That cuts against the instinct behind the disciples’ question. They wanted him to stay on the far side of the Jordan because it was safer. He is telling them that safety cannot be manufactured by choosing a different road, and that the only truly dangerous position is to be walking somewhere he is not going.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me if I obey God? No. It is not a promise of long life or freedom from harm. This man’s own twelve hours had only weeks left in them, and most of the men listening would die violently for him. It is a promise that the ending is not in the hands of whoever is throwing the stones. Your days are written in God’s book (Psalm 139:16), and nothing can cut them short before he says. That frees you from two fears: the fear that your enemies control your life, and the fear that you must control it yourself by endless caution.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that the day has twelve hours, and whoever walks in daylight does not stumble, but whoever walks at night stumbles, for the light is not in him.

On a Tuesday. Walk in the light of God’s will, and you are safe, wherever it takes you. When anxiety tells you to protect yourself by staying away from what God has called you to, remember that your day has a fixed length, and it is in his hands.

For worship. The Light of the world walked toward Judea in broad day, unafraid, because his Father kept the clock. Every hour of his life was measured out and none was lost. He lived to the last minute of his twelve hours, and when the night came it was the night he had chosen, in which he went out to die for us. Our days are in the same hands.
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.” The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”

After saying these things, he said to them, Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep. Two things in this sentence are worth having, and the first is very small. Our friend. Not my friend, which is what he might have said about a man he loved and the disciples barely knew. He includes them in the friendship before he tells them the man is dead. It is a kindness so slight it is easy to miss, and it would not have been missed by them.

Fallen asleep. Sleep was a common picture of death for believers (Matthew 9:24; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). Paul uses it of those who have fallen asleep in Jesus; Luke uses it of Stephen, with the stones still flying. The noun built from it is koimētērion, a sleeping place, and that is where our word cemetery comes from. It is not a euphemism, and it is important not to let it become one. Sleep is not a nicer word for extinction; it is a claim about what death now is for those who belong to him. Sleep is temporary by definition, and it ends in the ordinary way: somebody says your name. That is precisely what is about to happen at the mouth of a cave.

But I go to awaken him. As easily as we wake someone from sleep, Jesus will wake Lazarus from death. The language is domestic, the ordinary language of rousing someone in the morning, and the domestic scale is the point. To everybody else it will be a resurrection. To him it is going in to wake somebody up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul sleeps unconscious between death and resurrection, as some teach. Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The believer’s spirit goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). The dead in Christ are conscious and at rest with him, waiting for the resurrection of the body (Westminster 32.1).

Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover. They take it literally: sleep is a good sign in illness. Their reply is not stupid, though it is usually treated as another comic misunderstanding. They are being sensible and slightly relieved: if he is sleeping, he is turning the corner, and there is no need to walk into Judea. Their literalism has a motive. It usually does.

What actually happens when a Christian dies? The body is buried and returns to dust, but the person, the soul, is immediately with Christ, made perfect in holiness, in conscious joy, awaiting the redemption of the body (Westminster 32.1). There is no purgatory and no unconscious waiting. Then, when Christ returns, the body will be raised, transformed and reunited with the soul, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 51–53). So when a believer dies, we may say truly that he has fallen asleep, and truly that he is with the Lord. Both are true, of the body and of the soul.

In a sentence. Jesus said their friend Lazarus had fallen asleep and he was going to wake him, and the disciples said that if he was asleep, he would get better.

On a Tuesday. If you have lost a believer you love, use the words Jesus used. They have fallen asleep in Jesus, and he will wake them. And if you are afraid of your own death, picture it as he described it: lying down to rest, and then hearing your name.

For worship. For those who belong to Christ, death is sleep, and he will wake us. He has made the grave a bedroom and the cemetery a dormitory. The last enemy has been turned, for his people, into a night’s rest, and the morning is certain, because the one who calls us friend has gone ahead to wake us.
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,

Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Another of John’s misunderstandings, and John records it in full, writing decades later, with no attempt to make the twelve look better. These men had been with him for years and had heard him speak in pictures constantly, and they still went for the literal reading. That is one of the small marks of an honest witness. Nobody inventing a founding story writes his leaders like that.

Then Jesus told them plainly, Lazarus has died. The word is parrēsia: plainly, openly, without veiling. And what he says plainly is three words. Jesus knows without being told. The plain statement is stark. There is a discipline in it worth naming. He had a better word available; he had just used it, it is true, and it is the word the church would keep. But sleep had been heard as getting better, and rather than let them travel to Bethany with a comfortable misunderstanding, he takes the comfort away and gives them the fact. He does not repeat the figure more slowly. He abandons it and says the flat thing, which is what he does throughout this Gospel the moment a picture has stopped carrying its load.

How should I speak about death, especially to children? Plainly first, then with hope. Do not let the tenderest words become an anaesthetic that leaves people confused. Children especially can be frightened by vague phrases: gone away, lost, gone to sleep, said without explanation. Say that the person has died, that their body has stopped working and will not work again in this life. Then give the hope, clearly: if they trusted Jesus, they are with him now, and he will raise their body one day. Jesus himself did it in that order. First the fact, then the promise. The sleep could be explained afterwards, and would mean something then.

In a sentence. Jesus had meant Lazarus’s death, though they thought he meant ordinary sleep, so he told them plainly that Lazarus had died.

On a Tuesday. Jesus does not avoid the hard word died. Neither should we. But we can say it with hope. When you sit with someone in grief this week, do not hurry past the reality. Name it, stay with it, and then speak of the one who is the resurrection.

For worship. The Lord who spoke so gently of sleep was not afraid of the word death. He looked at it plainly, called it by its name, and walked toward it, because he had come to deal with it. He needs no euphemisms. He is the one who will make death itself a word of the past, when there shall be no more death (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”

And for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. It is a startling thing to say about the death of a friend, and it should not be smoothed over. He does not say he is glad Lazarus died. He says he is glad he was absent, because his presence would have produced a healing, and a healing would have produced a smaller faith than what is now possible. The disciples already believed (2:11), but faith grows, and they will need more than they have for what is coming in Jerusalem.

But let us go to him. To him, though dead. Jesus speaks of a dead man as someone you can still go to, because to him the dead are not beyond reach.

So Thomas, called the Twin. Thomas’s name means twin in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent. We do not know who his twin was. But there is something twinned in the man himself all through this Gospel. He is the one who says the brave thing and the doubting thing, and both come from the same place: he will not pretend to a confidence he does not have.

Let us also go, that we may die with him. “Him” probably means Jesus. Thomas deserves better than history has given him. He is remembered for one sentence spoken in a locked room after the resurrection (20:24–25), and it has cost him his name in English. But this is the first time he speaks in the Gospel. He has concluded, reasonably on the evidence, that going to Judea means execution. He believes they are all walking to their deaths, and his proposal is that they go. That is not doubt. It is loyalty without hope, which is a rarer and harder thing than loyalty with it. Peter will promise to die with him too, within weeks, and will deny him before dawn. Thomas makes no promise. He simply proposes the journey, in a flat voice, expecting the worst. He would rather die with Jesus than live without him.

Is it all right to follow Christ while I am full of doubts and fears? Yes. Jesus did not wait for Thomas to become cheerful before he let him come, and he did not wait for perfect faith before accepting it. He works with what is offered and refines it along the way, as he did with Thomas a few weeks later (20:27–28). What matters is not how confident you feel but where you are walking. Bring your doubts with you, tell him about them honestly, and keep going in the direction he is going. Many of the best saints have followed in a flat voice for long stretches.

In a sentence. Jesus said that for their sake he was glad he had not been there, so that they would believe, and Thomas told the others that they should go too, to die with him.

On a Tuesday. Courage does not always feel cheerful. Thomas expected the worst and went anyway. Follow Christ even when you fear what it will cost. Here is the word for anyone who has served God for a long stretch without much sense of it going well: Thomas was not enjoying this. He went.

For worship. The Lord who was glad for his disciples’ sake was already planning to give them more than they could imagine. And the one Thomas expected to die with did die, not with them but for them, and then came back through a locked door to show his hands to the man who had followed him in despair. He honours the loyalty of the faint-hearted, and turns their flat obedience into a cry of my Lord and my God.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.

Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. The four days matter more than one fact about them. Burial in that world was usually on the day of death; the body was washed, wrapped with spices and laid in a rock tomb within hours, because the climate allowed nothing else. So four days in the tomb is four days from death, and in that heat decay was well advanced. There was also a popular Jewish belief, preserved in later rabbinic writings, that the soul lingered near the body for three days hoping to return, and departed on the fourth when the face became unrecognisable. Whether or not the family held it, everyone in the crowd would have known it. Three days left a theoretical margin. Four closed it. That is why John gives the number twice, here and again in Martha’s objection at the tomb (v. 39). He is establishing, as a witness establishes a fact, that Lazarus was beyond any hope of revival.

Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off. Literally about fifteen stadia, almost three kilometres, an hour’s walk. Close enough for mourners to come out from the city, and close enough that whatever happened would be in the temple courts by evening. He has arranged, or allowed, a situation in which the man is beyond all doubt dead and the witnesses are beyond all doubt numerous. This sign is not going to be deniable, and it is not going to be quiet. It is also, for exactly those reasons, the one that gets him killed.

Everything in public. Everything in this chapter happens in the open: in a road, in front of a crowd, at the mouth of a cave, rather than in a house where the family could have received their brother back in private. Jesus stops outside the village and stays there (v. 30). He never gets to sit down with the sisters before the sign. The whole thing is public, because the sign was never only for them.

Could Lazarus simply have been in a coma? Not after four days in a sealed tomb, wrapped in linen, with spices, in that climate, without water. Everyone present had seen death and buried their dead with their own hands; Martha expected the smell of decay (v. 39). The authorities, who had every reason to explain the event away, never suggested it; they took it as a fact and plotted to kill Lazarus too (12:10–11). John tells the details precisely so that we will know what kind of event this was. It was not a recovery. It was a dead man called back to life.

In a sentence. When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, in Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Is there something in your life you have written off as four days dead: a relationship, a habit you cannot break, a person you have stopped praying for? Bring it back to him. Nothing is beyond his reach.

For worship. No situation is too dead for Christ. Four days is not too late for him. He let every human margin close, every hope run out, every theory of recovery be shut in a cave, so that when life came there could be no doubt where it came from. He is the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17).
verseByVerse.note: After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. The ESV notes that the distance is literally fifteen stadia.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.

Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. The size of the crowd tells us something about this family. Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends and neighbours coming to sit with the family, weep, and bring food. Hired mourners and flute players often added to the lament (Matthew 9:23). These visitors came from Jerusalem, an hour’s walk, and they are still there on the fourth day, which suggests the family was well known. “The Jews” here is neutral: friends from the city. And it means the two sisters are not grieving in private. Every word either of them says to Jesus in this chapter is said in front of an audience, and so is everything he says back.

What the mourners were doing. Jewish consolation was a duty, not a social call. The mourners sat with the bereaved, said little, and stayed. The custom was not to speak until the grieving person spoke first, a discipline the friends of Job kept for seven days and then abandoned, at which point everything went wrong (Job 2:13). Nothing in this chapter suggests these people were doing it badly. They came, they stayed four days, and when Mary got up they followed her so that she would not cry alone.

So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him. Martha, the active one, goes out.

But Mary remained seated in the house. Mourners sat on the ground, and Mary, perhaps more crushed, stays. The sisters are true to their characters in Luke 10. And their two responses are not a lesson in which is better. John does not grade them, and neither should anyone else. One of them needed to move and one of them could not, and both receive everything. Martha meets him first and receives the greatest sentence in the chapter. Mary meets him second and receives his tears. Neither gets what the other got, and neither is short-changed. He does not have one way of dealing with grieving people.

What should I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little, at first. Your presence matters more than your words; the friends of Job did best when they were silent. Say that you are sorry, use the name of the person who has died, and do not hurry to explain the loss or rush to the hope. Avoid clichés that make the grief smaller. Offer practical help: meals, errands, company on the hard evenings. And keep coming after the funeral, when most people stop. When the time is right, and especially if the one who died was a believer, the hope of the resurrection is the greatest comfort there is. But let it be given as a gift, not as a reason to stop crying.

In a sentence. Many had come to comfort the sisters, and when Martha heard Jesus was coming she went to meet him, while Mary stayed in the house.

On a Tuesday. Go and sit with those who grieve. Presence matters more than words. Think of someone who lost a loved one months ago and whom everyone else has stopped visiting, and go this week.

For worship. The Lord of comfort does not deal with every grieving heart in the same way. He went to meet the sister who could move and waited for the sister who could not. He gave one a word and the other his tears. He knows each of his own, their temperament and their wound, and he comes to each in the way that each needs. The God of all comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3) is not a system. He is a Shepherd who knows his sheep.
verseByVerse.note: Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”

Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Grief, and perhaps a note of complaint. She believes he could have healed him. And Mary will say exactly the same sentence in verse 32, word for word. Two women, met separately, producing the same line. That tells you what had been going on in that house for four days. They had said it to each other. It was the thing that got said in the kitchen, and in the night, and every time somebody new arrived to sit with them, if he had been here, until it had worn a groove. Anybody who has sat in a house after a death will know the sentence. It has a hundred forms, and they are all the same form.

What Jesus does with it. It is not what a modern pastoral instinct would do. He does not correct it. He does not point out, though he could have and it was true, that he could not have arrived in time. He lets both of them say it, twice, and answers neither with the arithmetic. He answers them with himself.

But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you. Then Martha adds the thing that lifts her sentence out of pure lament. Faith in the middle of grief. She does not quite dare to ask for resurrection; verse 39 shows she did not expect it, when she objects to the stone being moved. What she has is something less specific and more lasting: a conviction that this man’s access to God is not affected by the fact that it is too late. That is a good place to pray from, and it is available to people who have run out of requests. Her faith is real, but not yet complete. She thinks of Jesus as one who asks God, not yet as the one who is himself the life.

Is it wrong to say to God, if you had been here? No. It is honest, and God would rather have your honest grief than polite silence. The psalms are full of it: why have you forsaken me? how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1; 22:1). Martha said it to Jesus’ face, and he did not rebuke her. What matters is where you say it. Martha brought her complaint to him, not away from him, and then she added but even now. Lament that is spoken to God is a form of faith. The danger is not in asking why, but in turning your back and refusing to wait for his answer.

In a sentence. Martha told Jesus that if he had been there her brother would not have died, but that even now God would give him whatever he asked.

On a Tuesday. If there is an if only you have been repeating to yourself, say it to him instead. Then add Martha’s two words: even now. Even now he hears, even now he is able, even now he loves.

For worship. You can bring your honest grief and your questions to Jesus, and still say: even now I know. He did not turn away from a woman who met him in the road with a reproach on her lips. He stood still and let her speak, and then he gave her the greatest words he ever spoke at a graveside. The Lord who is gentle with our complaints is the Lord who answers them with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”

Jesus said to her, Your brother will rise again. Jesus’ words are deliberately open. They could mean now, or at the end. It is what any well-meaning visitor would have said at a Jewish funeral, the standard consolation, entirely orthodox, and Martha takes it that way because that is what it usually means. He lets her. He does not correct her hearing of it or explain what he intends. He says the ordinary comforting thing and waits to see what she does with it.

I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day. Martha’s answer is entirely correct, and it is worth saying so before anything else, because she is often treated as having missed the point. She has not. Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age, based on texts like Daniel 12:2, many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, and Isaiah 26:19. The Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). Martha holds the orthodox hope, and Jesus never suggests she is wrong.

The gap the doctrine does not cross. What she is doing is what most Christians do at a graveside. The doctrine is intact. It is simply a long way off, and it is not touching anything. Notice the tense of the comfort. Everything true in her sentence is scheduled for the end of the world, and her brother is in a cave a short walk away, and there is a gap between those two facts that the doctrine does not reach across. That is exactly the gap Jesus is about to close, and the way he closes it is not by moving the last day nearer. It is by telling her that the thing she is waiting for is a person, and he is standing in front of her. She has the doctrine, and Jesus is about to show her it is a person.

What exactly is the resurrection on the last day? When Christ returns, all the dead will be raised bodily: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (5:28–29). Believers will be raised with bodies that are real, recognisable and their own, yet transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). It is not the soul escaping the body but the whole person, body and soul, made new. The body you bury is not discarded. It is sown like a seed, and what rises will be more fully you than you have ever been.

In a sentence. Jesus told Martha her brother would rise again, and she answered that she knew he would rise in the resurrection on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Doctrine is precious, but it is not the end. The resurrection is not only a future event; it is a living person, and he stands next to you. When you recite the creed this Sunday, I believe in the resurrection of the body, say it to him.

For worship. The Lord who waited to see what Martha would do with the ordinary words was about to fill them with more than she could hold. The resurrection on the last day is not a distant doctrine kept in heaven’s archive. It walked to Bethany on two feet. All our hope for the end of the world is gathered up in a person who stood in a road and spoke to a grieving woman, and who stands just as near to us.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”

I am the resurrection and the life. This is the fifth of Jesus’ I am sayings in John, and the one most often read aloud at funerals, which means most people have heard it in a building with a coffin in it. It is worth recovering what it cost to say. Martha has just placed resurrection at the end of history. Jesus takes the whole doctrine and places it in himself. Not I will raise the dead, which would be a claim to power. Not I bring resurrection, which would make him a channel. The thing she is waiting for on the last day is not an event he attends. It is who he is, standing in a road outside a village, having walked there. The power that will raise the dead at the end is present in him now.

Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live. The two halves that follow are not saying the same thing twice. This first half is for the dead. Physical death happens; though he die concedes it flatly. But it is not the end of the sentence. Believers who die physically will live, raised by him (5:28–29). This is the resurrection.

And everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. This second half is for the living, and it is the life. Believers who are alive now have a life that death cannot end. “Never die” means never die the true death, separation from God (8:51). Whatever happens at the graveside, what has begun in a believer does not stop. Physical death becomes a doorway. Both halves are needed, because a mourner is standing between them: one brother dead, one sister alive, and a promise that covers each of them.

What it does not mean. This verse is quoted badly in both directions. It does not promise that Christians will not die physically; Lazarus dies again, and so does everyone in the story. And it does not shrink to a metaphor about living on in memory or influence. The man saying it is about to show what he means by shouting into a cave.

Do you believe this? The question is put to Martha, and to every reader. Not, do you believe in a resurrection? but, do you believe this, about me? Four words, put to a woman whose brother has been dead four days, before anything has been fixed. He does not raise Lazarus and then ask. He asks first, with the stone still in place and the smell still expected, and requires her to answer on nothing but his word. The question is not whether the doctrine is believed in general. Martha believed it in general, and said so, correctly, one verse earlier. The question is whether it is believed of a particular person on a particular day when it has already seemed to fail. That is a different question, and it is the only one he asks.

What about those who die without believing in him? The promise is to whoever believes in me, and Scripture does not offer it to anyone else. Those who die outside Christ will also be raised, but to the resurrection of judgment (5:29), and they will face conscious, eternal punishment, separated from the life that is in him (Matthew 25:46). That is a solemn truth, and it should make us earnest, not cold. It is why Jesus asked Martha the question, and why we must ask it of others while there is time. And it is why we can leave the dead, whom we cannot judge, in the hands of the God who always does right (Genesis 18:25), while we plead with the living.

In a sentence. Jesus told Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, so that whoever believes in him will live though he dies, and whoever lives and believes in him will never die, and asked whether she believed it.

On a Tuesday. Answer his question today, not in general but about your own life and your own grave: do you believe this? Then let the answer shape the way you face illness, ageing and loss. A Christian can be sad at a funeral and still unafraid of his own.

For worship. Christ is the resurrection and the life. Death has no claim on anyone who is in him, because he is the life death cannot touch. Every grave of a believer is held in the grip of this sentence, and on the last day every one of them will open at his word. Answer his question at every graveside, and say it to him with Martha: Yes, Lord, I believe.
verseByVerse.note: This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”

She said to him, Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world. It is worth stating plainly how large this confession is, because it tends to be filed under Martha the busy one. John tells us at the end of his book exactly why he wrote it: these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:31). That is the purpose of the entire Gospel. And Martha says it, almost word for word. The confession the whole book exists to produce is placed in the mouth of a grieving woman standing in a road, before the miracle, with her brother still in the tomb. In Matthew it is Peter who says it and is called blessed (Matthew 16:16). In John it is Martha. It is one of the great confessions of the Gospel, as great as Peter’s (6:69).

The words of her confession. “I believe” is in the perfect tense: I have come to believe, and I still believe. And there are three titles. The Christ, the Messiah. The Son of God. The one who is coming into the world, the standing phrase for the long-awaited one, which she applies to a man in front of her while still holding the sentence if you had been here. She believes who he is before she sees what he will do. That is the order of grace: confession of Christ comes before the experience of his full power.

Who makes the great confessions in John. They are not made by the men who run the temple. They are made by a Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her, an excommunicated beggar who had been blind, and now a woman at the edge of a village who has just told him he arrived too late. John has been consistent about this from the beginning, and it does not look like an accident.

When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private. Privately, perhaps to avoid alerting the mourners, some of whom may have been hostile to Jesus. She does not announce it to the room full of visitors. Whatever is about to happen, Martha gives her sister the chance to go to him without an audience. It fails, since they follow anyway, but the intention was kind.

The Teacher is here and is calling for you. John has not recorded Jesus asking for Mary. Either it happened and is not written, or Martha understood that he wanted her. Either way, she knows her sister is sitting in a dark house and will not come for an invitation but will come for a summons. He calls each one personally, and Martha, who has just met him, does the first thing a believer does: she brings someone else to him.

Is it enough to believe the right things about Jesus? Martha’s confession is right in every word, and it is more than a list of facts. To believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, in the sense John means, is to trust yourself to him, as Martha did with her brother in a tomb. The devils believe facts and tremble (James 2:19). Faith says yes, Lord, and leans its whole weight on him. So hold the truth about Christ carefully, because it matters; and make sure it is not just in your head but is the ground you stand on when everything else has given way.

In a sentence. Martha confessed that she believed Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God, who was coming into the world, and then went and quietly told Mary that the Teacher was calling for her.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who is sitting in a dark house, too weighed down to come out on their own? Go and tell them, gently and in private if need be, that the Teacher is here and is calling for them.

For worship. The Teacher is here, and he is calling for you. Go to him. He drew from a grieving woman the confession that the whole Gospel was written to produce, and he drew it before he had done anything to earn it in her eyes, by his word alone. He is the Christ, the Son of God, the one who was always coming into the world, and he has come. Blessed is the one who believes it with her brother still in the tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Two words carry this passage: quickly, and still. Mary has been in that house for four days receiving visitors, and she has not gone out to meet him. Some read that as reproach and some as sheer inability, and John does not say. What he does say is that the moment she is told he is asking for her, she is on her feet. At his call, she goes at once.

Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. He had not moved. However long the errand took, he was waiting at the spot. He waits outside, perhaps to meet the sisters away from the crowd, or near the tomb, which would be outside the village. There is a picture in that worth keeping. He does not go into the house and gather everybody. He stands in a road outside a village where a family is grieving, sends for one of them, and stays put until she comes.

Inside the sound of it. And it is worth noticing what he is doing there. The next thing he will do is weep. Professional mourners would have been audible from some distance; Jewish custom expected flute players and wailing women even at a poor family’s funeral, and a family of this standing would have had a considerable number. So the road where he is standing is not quiet. He is waiting at the edge of the village inside the sound of grief.

In a sentence. When Mary heard, she got up quickly and went to Jesus, who was still outside the village where Martha had met him.

On a Tuesday. When Christ calls, go quickly. If his word has been calling you to something, to come back to prayer, to make something right, to trust him with a grief, do not wait until you feel ready. Rise and go.

For worship. The Lord of glory stood waiting in a road. He did not force his way into the house of mourning; he waited at its edge, listening to the wailing, until the one he had called came to him. He has waited for us like that, longer than we know, and when we came at last he was still in the place where he had promised to be.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Providence is doing something quiet here, and it should not be missed. The mourners follow Mary on a wrong assumption, made out of ordinary kindness, and it puts the entire crowd of Jerusalem witnesses at the graveside for what happens next. Nobody arranged it. They were being decent about a grieving woman and did not want her to cry alone. So the mourners become witnesses of the miracle. God’s providence gathers the crowd. They are wrong about her destination and right about the direction, and they arrive as witnesses to something none of them came for. And that is how the raising of Lazarus acquired the witness list that will, within days, get Jesus condemned.

Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet. The difference from her sister is in the body rather than the words. Martha met him standing and talked theology with him in the road. Mary fell at his feet. John says she saw him and fell: not that she reached him and knelt, but that the sight of him put her down. Four days of receiving visitors, and the composure held until the person she had sent for came into view. Anyone who has kept it together through the arrangements and then gone to pieces at the sight of one particular face will know exactly what this verse describes. And it is where she always is. Mary is at Jesus’ feet listening (Luke 10:39), grieving here, worshipping (12:3).

Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. The same words as Martha. But Mary says no more. She does not have a different opinion from her sister; the sentence is identical. She simply cannot say it upright. She has no confession yet, only tears. And that is the last thing she says in the chapter. Martha gets a dialogue, a question and the greatest answer in the Gospel. Mary gets one sentence, on the ground. What she receives in return is not an argument. It is his tears, which is what she needed and what an argument would not have been.

Is one way of grieving more spiritual than another? No. Martha talked and Mary wept, and Jesus received both with the same love, and neither is treated as having grieved wrongly. Some believers grieve with questions and activity; others grieve in silence and tears; most of us do both at different times. Do not measure your faith by how composed you are, and do not measure anyone else’s by how they cope. What matters is that both sisters brought their grief to his feet, or to his face. He meets each in the way each needs.

In a sentence. The mourners followed Mary, thinking she was going to the tomb, and when she reached Jesus she fell at his feet and said that if he had been there, her brother would not have died.

On a Tuesday. When you have no words, fall at his feet. You do not need to explain yourself or pray in tidy sentences. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.

For worship. When you have no words, fall at his feet. He understands tears. He did not ask Mary for a confession or a theology before he wept with her. The same feet she fell at would soon be anointed by her hands and then pierced by nails. The Lord who receives the speechless is the Lord who was led like a lamb that is silent before its shearers, and who knows the full weight of grief from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”

When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping. “Weeping” (klaiō): loud wailing, the public lament of mourning, the audible noise a Jewish funeral expected.

He was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. The verb here is the most important word in the chapter, and it is stronger than it first reads. The word behind “deeply moved” (embrimaomai) carries a sense of anger or indignation; the ESV’s margin gives it as he was indignant in his spirit (also v. 38). It is used of a horse snorting, and elsewhere of a stern rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5). So this is not a word for mild sympathy. Jesus is angry. “Greatly troubled” (etaraxen heauton) is literally he troubled himself: a deep inner agitation, which he does not merely suffer but takes up.

Angry at what? Not at Mary, who has done nothing but fall at his feet. Not at the mourners, who are behaving exactly as neighbours should. Some have suggested he is angry at their unbelief, but the text gives no sign of it, and the reading requires importing a rebuke that never comes. The answer that fits is death itself, the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and the devil who brought it, and the ruin sin has caused in God’s world. He is standing in front of a family destroyed by the thing he came to destroy, and he is about to walk to a cave and be shown what four days does to somebody who was loved. As he faces his friend’s grave, he faces the power he came to break.

God is not serene about death. That corrects a picture of God that many people carry: serene, above it all, receiving our griefs with infinite calm. He is not calm here. The one who made the world is standing in a village road, indignant at what has been done to it. Death is not natural, not friendly, not simply part of the circle of life. It is an intruder, and the Son of God is angry at it.

Where have you laid him? Then he asks the last thing anybody expects from one who knows all things. He is not asking for directions. He is doing what a man does when he arrives at a house of mourning: he asks to be taken to the grave. He goes to the grave.

Lord, come and see. The same words Jesus used to the first disciples (1:39), and Philip to Nathanael (1:46). There they were an invitation to see the Lamb of God. Here they are an invitation to see a tomb. He goes.

Is it right to be angry at death, or even at God, when someone dies? It is right to be angry at death, because Jesus was. Death is an enemy, and you do not have to pretend otherwise. Anger at God is different, and must be handled honestly. Bring it to him rather than nursing it, as the psalmists did. He can bear your raw words, and he will not despise them. But do not let it settle into a grudge that accuses him of evil, because the one who stood at Lazarus’s grave was not the author of death but its enemy, and he has already gone to war against it on your behalf.

In a sentence. When Jesus saw Mary and the mourners weeping, he was moved with indignation and deeply troubled, and asked where they had laid him, and they told him to come and see.

On a Tuesday. When death touches your life, do not call it natural or good. Christians may grieve with anger at the enemy, and still with hope, because the one who was angry at Lazarus’s tomb has overcome it.

For worship. Jesus is angry at death. He does not call it natural or good. He came to destroy it. The Prince of life stood in the road with indignation burning in him, and walked to the grave to do battle. And on another day he walked into death itself, through it and out the other side, so that death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55). Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The words behind “deeply moved” carry a sense of anger or indignation — at death itself and the grief it brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wept. So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”

Jesus wept. Three words in Greek (edakrysen ho Iēsous), the shortest verse in the English Bible, and one of the deepest. And there is a distinction in them that the English hides completely. The mourners in verse 33 are weeping with klaiō, the word for loud lamentation, the public noise of a funeral. What Jesus does is a different verb, used of him only here in the New Testament. Dakryō means to shed tears. Quietly. The tears themselves, without the sound. So the picture is not a man joining a wail. It is a man standing slightly apart in a road, surrounded by noise, with tears running down his face.

When it happens. Not at the news; he received that a day’s journey away and stayed where he was two more days. Not at the tomb. Here, at the sight of Mary on the ground and the crowd behind her. What breaks him is not the fact of the death, which he had known all week and had already announced. It is the sight of what it had done to people he loved.

He weeps anyway. Here is what makes this verse inexhaustible. He knows what is going to happen. He has said so twice. Very soon the man will walk out of that cave and the weeping will stop, and Jesus is the one who is going to do it. He weeps anyway. Why? Because he truly loves, and truly grieves with those who grieve (Romans 12:15). Because death is a real evil. Because he is truly man. That disposes of the idea, common and quietly cruel, that grief is a failure of faith, that a Christian who really believed in the resurrection would not be undone by a funeral. Here is the resurrection and the life, in person, minutes from proving it, in tears. If knowing the outcome were enough to stop the crying, his would have stopped.

So the Jews said, See how he loved him! Some of the mourners see his love truly. They read the tears correctly. It is the one thing in this chapter that the bystanders get entirely right.

Two natures in one chapter. Here is the full humanity of the Son of God: in the same chapter, he weeps like a man and raises the dead like God. He could have prevented the death, and there would have been no tears, no cave and no crowd. He could have raised the man from across the Jordan with a word, as he had healed the official’s son at a distance (4:50). Instead he walked a day’s journey to stand in the middle of it, let it reach him, and wept in front of a crowd. The shortest verse in the Bible is the answer to the oldest suspicion about God, that he is untouched, watching from somewhere the grief cannot reach. He came to where it was, and it reached him.

If Jesus is God, how could he weep? Because he is also truly man. The eternal Son took a full human nature, body and soul, and in that human nature he felt real sorrow, real tears, real grief. God in his own divine being is not overwhelmed by emotion or changed by what happens to him; he is unchanging and perfect. But that does not make him cold. The tears of Jesus show us the heart of God in a form we can see, a love that is moved toward us. When you are grieving, you do not pray to a God who has never felt grief. You pray to a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because he wept at a grave.

How long is it right to grieve? There is no fixed limit. Grief for someone you loved can return in waves for years, and that is not a failure. Christians grieve, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The difference is not that our grief is shorter but that it is held inside a larger hope. If grief has become despair, so that you cannot function, cannot pray, or no longer want to live, please tell someone: a pastor, a trusted friend, a doctor. That is not weakness of faith. It is the kind of burden God gives his people to bear together.

In a sentence. Jesus wept, and the mourners said, See how he loved him!

On a Tuesday. Christians grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Tears are not unbelief. Jesus wept. Let yourself grieve, and let others grieve without hurrying them.

For worship. God in the flesh stood in a road in a small village and cried about a death he was about to undo. The God who will wipe every tear from our eyes (Revelation 21:4) first shed tears himself. See how he loved him, they said, and they could have said it at the cross, where the tears were blood and the grave he faced was his own. There is no sorrow in your life that he holds at a distance. He has wept over it already, and he will wipe it away.
verseByVerse.note: This is the shortest verse in the English Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?” Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

But some of them said, Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying? Their question deserves to be taken at full strength, because it is the question, and softening it helps nobody. Notice what they concede in order to ask it. They accept the miracle of chapter 9, a few miles away, without argument. Their difficulty is not whether he can. It is why he did not. John does not tell us the tone. It could be a cynical taunt, and it could be bewilderment, and the words allow both. And that is exactly where a great many people are, and it is a more painful place than unbelief. Doubting God’s power is one kind of trouble. Believing in it completely and standing at a graveside is another.

Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. What he does with the question is worth watching: he does not answer it. Not a word of explanation, then or later. Nobody at the tomb is told why the two days happened; only the disciples had been told (vv. 4, 15). What he does instead is grow indignant again, the same word as verse 33, perhaps at their unbelief too, and walk to the tomb. That is the shape of the biblical answer to suffering more often than not. Job asked and received a whirlwind full of questions rather than reasons. Here the answer is a man walking toward a cave with tears still on his face and anger in his heart, about to do something about it.

It was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance to keep out animals and robbers. Some were cut horizontally into a hillside, others had steps leading down. The stone was usually a heavy disc or a block, and the body was laid on a shelf inside. John sets the scene in a few cold words, and the stone in them will turn up again within weeks, at a different tomb, rolled away.

Why does God not explain my suffering? Often he does not, and Scripture is honest about it. He did not explain to Job, or to the crowd at Bethany. But he did something better than explain: he came. The answer to the question why is often not a reason but a presence, God coming to where the grief is and acting in a way that transforms the question. You may not know in this life why it happened. You can know who is with you in it, and you can know the end of the story: resurrection, and every tear wiped away. Faith is not having every answer. It is trusting the one who walks to the tomb.

In a sentence. Some mocked that the man who healed the blind could have kept Lazarus from dying, and Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb, a cave with a stone across it.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to ask why he did not prevent something, ask it honestly, to him. Then look at what he does in this chapter: he walks toward the tomb. Wait for him there.

For worship. Jesus walked to the cave of death and stood at its door. One day he will stand at yours, and call. He did not answer the mockers with an argument. He answered with a resurrection. And at the end of all things he will answer every why of every grave in the same way, not with an explanation, but with a voice that empties tombs.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”

Jesus said, Take away the stone. Jesus could move it with a word. He tells them to do it. God often uses human obedience in his works. Notice what is asked of the human beings present. Not faith to raise the dead; to move a stone. The one thing in this scene that ordinary strength can do is the thing they are told to do, and the impossible part is not handed to anybody. That division of labour holds everywhere: obedience is generally something quite ordinary, done before there is any evidence it will matter.

Martha, the sister of the dead man. John slips in a phrase that is one of the quietest painful touches in the Gospel. The man has been Lazarus all chapter. Here, at the mouth of the cave, he becomes the dead man.

Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days. Martha’s objection is the most human sentence in the chapter, and it should not be treated as a lapse. Twelve verses ago she said, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God. Now she says this. Both are hers, a few minutes apart: the most complete confession in the Gospel and a practical objection about the smell, from the same woman in the same conversation. Anyone who has believed something on Sunday and not managed it on Tuesday has the whole of Christian experience in Martha. And she is right. Bodies were not embalmed; spices were used, but did not stop decay, and after four days in that climate it was well under way. Asking them to open the tomb is asking them to expose a family’s grief to something they will not be able to unsee. She is not being faithless. She is protecting her brother’s body, the last thing left to protect. Her faith of verse 27 is real, but she cannot imagine what Jesus will do.

Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God? His reply is a reminder rather than a rebuke. He does not argue with the chemistry. He recalls a promise: the glory of God of verse 4, which the messenger had presumably carried back, and the do you believe this? of verses 25–26. Believe, and you will see. In this Gospel, faith comes before sight.

Does God need my faith before he can act? Does my weak faith stop him? God is not limited by our faith; he raised Lazarus, who had no faith at all, being dead. Faith is not a power that makes God able. It is the empty hand that receives what he gives, and the eye that sees his glory when he shows it. Martha’s faith was weak at that moment, and Jesus did not cancel the miracle. He called her back to his word. So do not try to manufacture enough faith to earn an answer. Look at his promise, take the next step of obedience, roll the stone, and leave the power to him.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to take away the stone, and when Martha objected that after four days there would be a smell, he reminded her that if she believed she would see God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. What stone is Christ telling you to move? Perhaps a confession you have put off, a reconciliation you think is hopeless, a habit of prayer you abandoned because nothing seemed to happen. Obey, even when it seems pointless, and you will see the glory of God.

For worship. The Lord of life stood before a sealed tomb and a reluctant friend and said, did I not tell you? He is patient with the believer whose faith wavers between Sunday and Tuesday. He does not wait for our confidence to be perfect. He asks only for a stone to be rolled away, and then he does what no hand but his can do. The glory of God is seen by those who take him at his word.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”

So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes. Jews commonly prayed looking upward (17:1; Psalm 123:1). The stone is gone, the smell is expected, the crowd is waiting, and the first thing he does is look to his Father.

Father, I thank you that you have heard me. The tense is the thing here, and it is easy to miss. Past. Not hear me, which is what someone says before a miracle. He gives thanks before the miracle, as though it were already done. The thanks are for a prayer already answered, which means the asking happened earlier, unrecorded, perhaps when he first heard of Lazarus’s illness. The public prayer is not the request. It is the receipt. That explains why John shows us so little of Jesus praying and yet keeps showing us the results of it. The two days beyond the Jordan were not idle.

I knew that you always hear me. The Son is in perfect communion with the Father. This is a claim no one else in Scripture could make. Elijah on Carmel prayed, answer me, O LORD, answer me (1 Kings 18:37): a man hoping. This is a Son stating a fact about his home.

But I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me. Then the extraordinary aside. He tells the crowd, out loud, in the middle of a prayer, that the prayer is partly for their benefit. That is either an appalling breach of piety or a piece of complete transparency, and the difference is whether it is true. He is not performing a devotion he does not feel. He is saying openly that he does not need to speak in order to be heard, and is speaking so that they will know where the power is about to come from. Without the prayer, the raising would prove the wrong thing. A man who shouts into a tomb and gets a result looks like a wonder-worker, and the district had seen those. The prayer establishes what the sign is for: that the miracle comes from the Father, and that the Father sent him. It is not magic, nor a power of his own apart from the Father. Everything in this chapter is aimed at that sentence.
