Should I thank God before I see the answer? What if the answer is no? Yes, give thanks, but be clear what you are thanking him for. Jesus knew the Father’s will; we often do not. So we thank God not for an outcome we have decided on, but for the certainty that he hears us, that he is good, and that he will do what is best (Philippians 4:6–7; Romans 8:28). That kind of thanks is never misplaced, because even when the answer is no or not yet, he has heard, and his answer is love. Thanking God in advance is not a technique to secure results. It is trust speaking before it sees.

In a sentence. When the stone was removed, Jesus looked up and thanked the Father for hearing him, saying he knew the Father always hears him, but said it aloud so that the people would believe the Father had sent him.

On a Tuesday. Thank God before you see the answer. Faith gives thanks in advance. Before you pray about your hardest request this week, begin by thanking the Father that he hears you, for Christ’s sake.

For worship. The Son lifted his eyes, and heaven was open to him, as it had always been. Never once did he pray into silence. And because we are in him, the Father who always hears the Son hears us too, for his sake. We pray through the one whose prayers are never refused, and who ever lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25).
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed looking upward.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”

When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, Lazarus, come out. A loud voice, so that all could hear. The word is kraugazō, the word for a shout, used of a crowd bellowing (19:6). He has just prayed quietly to his Father. To the dead man he shouts. A command, not a prayer. An old saying, often credited to Augustine, has it that if Jesus had not named Lazarus, all the dead would have come out. And the name is the whole of it. This is the shepherd of the previous chapter who calls his own sheep by name (10:3), doing exactly that, into a cave. It anticipates the last day: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (5:28–29). One tomb, one name, on a Judean afternoon, as a demonstration of what he will do to every grave.

The man who had died came out. The simplest description of the greatest miracle. The man is still described as the one who had died. John does not dramatise it. He does not need to.

His hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth for the face, and spices between the strips. That raises a fair question: how does a man wrapped for burial walk? Jewish burial wound the limbs separately rather than swaddling the body into a single parcel, so a shuffle was physically possible; and there is no need to be too tidy about it, since the man had been dead four days and had just heard his name. But the wrappings do one more piece of work, and John will collect on it nine chapters later. Compare Jesus’ own grave clothes, left neatly behind (20:6–7). Lazarus comes out still wrapped; Jesus will rise leaving his behind. Lazarus will die again; Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). This is a resuscitation, a return to mortal life; Jesus’ resurrection will be the first of the new creation.

Unbind him, and let him go. Again, others help. John does not draw a lesson from this, but we may fairly apply it: Christ alone gives life, and his people help the newly living out of their grave clothes.

A picture of salvation. We were dead in sins (Ephesians 2:1–5). We could not respond, any more than Lazarus could. Christ called, and his voice gave life. This is regeneration, God’s effectual call: the dead hear and live (5:25).

Why do Matthew, Mark and Luke say nothing about it? It is a fair question, and it deserves a straight answer, because it is the objection most often raised against this chapter. If a man four days dead walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and it decided the authorities to kill Jesus (v. 53), why do the other Gospels not mention it? Part of the answer is how the four books are shaped. The first three concentrate on Galilee and bring Jesus to Jerusalem once, at the end; John is the one who fills in the Judean ministry, the feasts and the repeated visits to the city. And none of them is trying to be complete; John says so twice (20:30–31; 21:25). Nor were they shy of raisings: Mark and Luke both record the raising of Jairus’s daughter, and Luke tells of the widow’s son at Nain. There is a further suggestion worth weighing. The next chapter tells us that the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too, because on account of him many were believing (12:10–11). A man in that position, living a short walk from the temple, would not be helped by having his name published across the empire. The earlier Gospels leave several people anonymous whom John alone names: it is John who tells us that the disciple with the sword was Peter and the servant who lost an ear was Malchus (18:10). John writes last, a generation on, when those who might have suffered for being named were beyond harm. That may be the whole explanation or part of it; either way it is a better answer than the assumption that a story this size was invented late.

What did Lazarus experience in those four days? Scripture does not say, and that silence is deliberate. Lazarus is given no story to tell. What we know of death, we know from Christ’s word, not from those who claim to have returned: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And for the believer, what we are told is enough: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So be wary of books and testimonies that claim to describe heaven or hell from a near-death experience. They may be sincere, but they are not Scripture, and they often contradict it. We do not need them. We have the word of the one who has the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

What does unbinding look like in a church? Nobody in that crowd could have called Lazarus out. Every one of them could pick at a knot. The first thing the community is asked to do, in the presence of resurrection, is to get the grave clothes off somebody who is already alive. New believers often come out of the tomb still wrapped in old habits, fears, addictions, shame and confused ideas. The church’s work is patient: teaching them the word, welcoming them to the Lord’s Table after baptism, walking with them, praying, bearing burdens, and refusing to be shocked by the smell of the grave on them. We cannot give life. We can help someone who has been given it to walk freely.

In a sentence. Jesus cried out with a loud voice for Lazarus to come out, and the dead man came out, bound in grave clothes, and Jesus told them to unbind him and let him go.

On a Tuesday. Is there a new or struggling believer near you who is still wrapped in grave clothes? Ask how you can help: a meal, an hour of reading the Bible together, a phone call when they are tempted. And thank God for those who unbound you.

For worship. The voice that called Lazarus called you from spiritual death. One day it will call your body from the grave. The Word through whom all things were made spoke into a cave, and death let go of what it held, because death has no answer to that voice. He who calls the stars by name called one man by his, and the dead man came out. And on the last day the same voice will sound over every grave of every believer, and the whole sleeping church will rise.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth over the face.

parallels.desc: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many who saw the miracle believe in Jesus, but some report it to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees convene the council in alarm: if this man keeps doing signs, everyone will follow him and the Romans will destroy their temple and nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, tells them they understand nothing: better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish. John explains that he was unwittingly prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and also to gather God’s scattered children into one. From then on they plot his death, so Jesus withdraws from public view to Ephraim, near the desert, with his disciples. As Passover approaches and pilgrims arrive early to purify themselves, people look for Jesus in the temple, wondering if he will come, while the authorities order anyone who knows his whereabouts to report it so they can arrest him.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas' political calculation — sacrifice one man to save the nation — is simultaneously cynical expediency and unconscious prophecy. John explicitly identifies it as prophecy (v. 51): the high priest, by virtue of his office, spoke better than he knew. The death he plots as preservation of institutional power is the death that will actually accomplish the salvation of God's people — and not only of the Jewish nation, but of the scattered children of God throughout the world (v. 52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The decision of the Sanhedrin is the human side of the decree that was made in eternity: Christ was the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world (Rev. 13:8). Human hatred and divine love converge on the same event. The leaders plot what God has purposed; the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. The sovereign grace that works through human wickedness without being compromised by it is most visible at Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him. The sign leads to faith, as it was meant to (20:31). The mourners who came to console a family went home having seen the glory of God.

But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. The same event, the same crowd, the same afternoon, and two responses that could not be further apart. Others saw the same miracle and went to report it. That is the plainest possible refutation of the idea that a sufficiently impressive miracle would settle the question of faith for everybody. Here is the greatest sign in the Gospel, performed before witnesses, on a man they had buried themselves, in daylight. It converted some of them. Others went straight down the road to report it. And notice what the reporters did not do. They did not deny it. In what follows, the council’s discussion takes the fact entirely for granted. The evidence was accepted, and acted against.

Neither will they be convinced. Abraham said it in the parable: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). A different Lazarus, but the point stands. And then a man named Lazarus did rise from the dead, and they were not convinced, and within days they were planning to kill him too (12:10). John also says simply that some of them went to the Pharisees, without saying why. It is possible some went in genuine excitement, thinking the authorities would want to know. What the authorities did with the news was not necessarily what the messengers intended, and that is its own small warning about how the machinery of a great wrong is often fed by people who thought they were being helpful.

If miracles do not convince people, what will convince my unbelieving friend? Only God himself, by his Spirit opening the eyes of the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not a reason for despair but for prayer. The Spirit uses means: the word of the gospel, the testimony of what Christ has done, the love of his people, honest answers to honest questions. So keep telling your friend what Christ has done, as the believing mourners did, live in a way that adorns it, and pray specifically that God will give new life. Arguments do not raise the dead. The voice of Christ does, and it is heard through the gospel you speak.

In a sentence. Many who had seen what Jesus did believed in him, but some went and reported it to the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. Miracles do not create faith by themselves. Pray for the Spirit to open hearts as you tell what Christ has done. And when you pass on news about someone, ask what will be done with it.

For worship. The same sun that softens wax hardens clay, and the same sign that brought some to faith drove others to the council. But nothing that men did with the news could undo the fact. Lazarus was alive, and the Lord of life was walking toward Jerusalem. He works faith in whom he will, and he is not defeated by those who refuse it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council. The council (synedrion), the Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish court of seventy-one members, led by the high priest. Chief priests, mostly Sadducees, and Pharisees did not usually agree on much; they agree on this.

And said, What are we to do? There is exasperation in their question. The council has been convened because something has got out of hand.

For this man performs many signs. They do not deny the miracles. They cannot. In closed session, among themselves, with no crowd to satisfy, the highest court in Israel states as a fact that the miracles are real. Everything they do from here is done with that on the record. The problem was never the evidence.

If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him. Their fear is his popularity. And they are describing, as the disaster to be prevented, the exact outcome the Gospel was written to produce. John’s stated purpose is that his readers may believe (20:31). The council’s stated fear is that everyone will. The two sentences are the same sentence, spoken from opposite sides of the same fact.

And the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation. “Our place” means the temple, and perhaps their own positions. The leaders feared that a messianic movement would bring Roman reprisals. The Romans allowed Jewish self-rule as long as there was order, and a popular messianic uprising could end it. It is not a stupid fear; it had happened before and would happen again. And the terrible irony is that they were right about the outcome and wrong about the cause. They killed Jesus to save the temple and the nation, and in AD 70 the Romans came and destroyed both. And listen to the pronouns: our place, our nation. Not God’s house. Theirs. The whole failure is audible in a possessive.

Can churches fall into the same trap? Yes, and often. Whenever a church or ministry protects its reputation, its building, its income or its leaders at the cost of truth, it is speaking the council’s language. The worst form is when abuse is hidden to protect the institution. That is never acceptable: victims must be heard and protected, wrongdoing reported to the proper authorities, and the truth told, whatever it costs the church’s name. The church belongs to Christ, not to us, and he does not need us to protect his reputation by sin. A church that loses its place for the sake of righteousness has lost nothing.

In a sentence. The chief priests and Pharisees called the council, worried that if Jesus kept doing signs everyone would believe, and the Romans would destroy the temple and the nation.

On a Tuesday. Fear for your position can make you oppose God. Hold your place loosely. Ask what you are protecting most anxiously: a role, a reputation, a comfortable arrangement. Is it yours, or his?

For worship. The council feared that everyone would believe in him, and their fear has been coming true for two thousand years. They tried to protect their place by removing the true temple, and God tore their curtain in two and built a temple of living stones that no army can burn. The Lord laughs at the counsels of the nations (Psalm 2:4), and turns the plots of his enemies into the salvation of the world.
verseByVerse.note: “Our place” means the temple. The leaders feared a messianic movement would bring Roman retaliation — as happened in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”

But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long term, kept in office by the Romans, which tells you he was good at exactly this. His father-in-law Annas had been high priest before him and was still powerful (18:13). A bone box inscribed with the name of Joseph son of Caiaphas was found in Jerusalem in 1990. And John’s phrase “that year” has puzzled readers, since the office was not annual. John says it three times (here, v. 51, and 18:13), and the sense is almost certainly not that it rotated but that it was that year, the year everything turned on. A modern writer would say: the man who happened to be high priest in the year it happened.

Said to them, You know nothing at all. Rude and arrogant, in the Sadducee style. He opens with contempt for his own council.

Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish. Political calculation: sacrifice one to save many. Cold, cynical and unjust. He means: kill Jesus before the Romans kill us all. And it should be given its full ugliness. It is not a legal argument, and Caiaphas does not pretend it is. Nobody at that table asks whether the man is guilty of anything. The question of Jesus’ innocence never arises in the entire discussion. It is the oldest political arithmetic there is: an acceptable cost, a regrettable necessity, one life against many. It is always framed as responsibility, and it is always somebody else who pays.

For the people. Notice the preposition, because John is about to build on it. One man should die hyper, on behalf of, in place of, the people. It is the exact word Jesus used of himself in chapter 10, of the shepherd laying down his life for the sheep (10:11), and a word Paul often uses of the atonement. The high priest of Israel, arguing for a judicial murder, reaches instinctively for the vocabulary of substitutionary sacrifice. He is a priest. It is the language he has.

In a sentence. Caiaphas, the high priest that year, told the council they knew nothing, and that it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish.

On a Tuesday. Notice when you are tempted to reason like Caiaphas: someone else can pay so that I am spared, so that the project goes ahead, so that the peace is kept. Expediency that sacrifices the innocent is never wisdom.

For worship. A wicked man spoke the gospel without knowing it: one man died for the people. What Caiaphas meant as murder, God meant as mercy. The innocent one did die for the guilty many, not to save a nation from Rome but to save a people from sin and death and the wrath of God. The arithmetic of heaven was the opposite of the council’s: not one sacrificed unwillingly for the comfort of the powerful, but one offering himself willingly for the life of the helpless.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; “that year” means that fateful year.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.

He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied. John’s note is one of the boldest in the New Testament. He is claiming that God spoke through a man who was at that moment arranging a murder, and not despite his office but through it. God spoke through Caiaphas without his knowing it, as he spoke through Balaam (Numbers 23–24). The high priest was traditionally linked with God’s guidance (the Urim and Thummim, Exodus 28:30). His function was to speak for God to the people and for the people to God, and on the one occasion in the Gospels when Caiaphas exercises it, he does so accurately and without the faintest idea what he is saying. That does not make Caiaphas a good man or excuse anything. It says that God’s purposes are not hostage to the character of the people through whom they run. God can speak even through wicked men, and overrule their evil for good (Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27–28).

That Jesus would die for the nation. “For” (hyper): on behalf of, in place of. Caiaphas meant a political substitute. God meant a saving substitute. This is penal substitution: one dies in the place of the many.

And not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. John adds the wider meaning, and finishes the sentence Caiaphas started. Caiaphas said the nation, meant the Jewish nation, and meant saving it from Rome. John says: not the nation only, and not from Rome, and the gathering runs to the ends of the earth. “The children of God scattered abroad” are the elect among the Gentiles, the other sheep of 10:16. They are already called children of God before they are gathered, because God has chosen them. Christ’s death gathers them into one people. His death is not a general provision, but a purposeful gathering of God’s children. And notice the verb, gather into one. The scattering is what sin did at Babel and what exile did to Israel; the gathering is what the cross undoes. So the sentence that condemned him to death is, read properly, the announcement of what his death would achieve. The high priest of the old covenant pronounced the terms of the new one, out loud, in council, and voted for it.

Does God still speak through people like this today? God is sovereign over every word spoken by every human being, and he can overrule even the words of unbelievers for his purposes. But this was a unique moment, tied to the office of high priest at the climax of redemption. It does not mean we should look for new revelations from God in the words of the people around us. God’s revelation is complete in his Son and his written word (Hebrews 1:1–2; Westminster 1.1, 1.6). What this verse teaches us is not to seek new messages, but to trust that no plot, no wicked decision and no cynical politician is outside his control.

In a sentence. Caiaphas did not speak on his own, but as high priest he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for it, but to gather into one the scattered children of God.

On a Tuesday. When evil people seem to be in control, at work, in politics, in the world’s headlines, remember Caiaphas. God was not absent from that council room. He was steering every word toward the cross and the salvation of his people.

For worship. Christ died to gather God’s scattered children into one family. If you are in Christ, you were one of them, a child of God before you knew it, scattered among the nations, called home by the death of the one who died in your place. The Lord who turned a murderer’s counsel into a prophecy of grace is the Lord who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). Not one of his children will be left scattered.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.

So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. John dates it. There had been hostility for two years and stones twice, but the decision is taken here, in a room, as a formal resolution of the council, and everything from this point is the working out of it. And what turned them was not a blasphemy. It was a resurrection. The giving of life to Lazarus seals Jesus’ death. The last straw was an act of pure kindness to a family in Bethany.

Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews. His hour is close, but not yet. The phrase is worth keeping, because it reverses everything so far. He has taught in the temple treasury, cried out on the last day of a feast, and answered his enemies in Solomon’s colonnade. From here to the entry into Jerusalem, he moves quietly. It is the first time in the Gospel that his public ministry has an after. And this is not fear. He has walked into Judea twice knowing what was waiting, and he will walk in again soon and let them take him. What he will not do is let them set the date. There is a Passover coming, and he intends to die at it, and not before.

But went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim. The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness that drops toward the Jordan valley, perhaps modern et-Taiyibeh, about fifteen miles away (2 Chronicles 13:19). John notes the wilderness deliberately. It is where the Baptist worked, and where Israel was formed before the great crossing.

And there he stayed with the disciples. A quiet time with his disciples before the end. Not preaching, not travelling, not doing anything John thinks worth recording. Before the last week, a stretch of quiet, in a small town on the edge of the desert, with twelve men who did not know what was coming, and one who did.

In a sentence. From that day the leaders plotted to kill Jesus, so he no longer moved openly among them but went to Ephraim near the wilderness and stayed there with his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Jesus took time away with his disciples before the storm. Make room for quiet with him before hard seasons. If you can see a difficult stretch ahead, do not fill the days before it with noise. Spend them with him and with his people.

For worship. The decision to kill him was taken because he gave a man back his life, and he did not run from it. He withdrew, not to escape the cross, but to arrive at it on his Father’s day. His enemies held a council; he held the timetable. And in the quiet weeks at Ephraim, with the warrant already written, the Lamb of God was preparing his friends for the night when he would give himself up for them.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”

Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. The third Passover in John (2:13; 6:4), the one at which Jesus will die as the true Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36). The feast that remembered the lamb whose blood saved Israel in Egypt is the feast at which the Lamb of God will be slain.

And many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. The purification John mentions was a real and demanding business. Pilgrims came up early, a week or more, because anyone who had become ceremonially unclean needed time to be cleansed before he could eat the Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18). Contact with a corpse was the commonest cause, and the ritual took seven days (Numbers 19:11–12). So Jerusalem in these days is full of people washing themselves clean in order to be fit for a meal about a lamb. And John has just spent forty-four verses on a man four days dead who walked out of a tomb, and now he shows us a city preoccupied with the defilement that comes from touching a corpse. He does not comment. He simply puts the two things side by side. The irony: they purify themselves for a feast at which they will kill the Lamb who alone can make them clean.

They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all? The Greek expects that he will not. Surely he will not dare? They are speculating about a celebrity: will he risk it, now there is a warrant out? It is the talk of a crowd with time to fill while they wait for the festival. They are not asking whether he is the Christ. They are asking whether he will turn up. He will come, within the week, on a donkey, with people shouting, and he will come precisely in order to be arrested, which is the one possibility nobody standing in that temple has considered. Days later they will be cutting branches and shouting Hosanna, and five days after that a crowd in the same city will shout for his death. The distance between those two noises is very short.

How am I made clean to come to God? Not by rituals, effort or a week of religious preparation. The pilgrims’ washings could only deal with outward defilement, and only for a time. The uncleanness that keeps us from God is sin, and only one thing removes it: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). You come to God clean not because you have prepared yourself well, but because Christ the Lamb was sacrificed for you. So come now, as you are, trusting him. Then, as one already washed, you will want to put away whatever defiles, out of love and not to earn your place.

In a sentence. As Passover approached, many came early to Jerusalem to purify themselves, and they looked for Jesus in the temple, wondering whether he would come to the feast at all.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether you are trying to make yourself fit for God by your own efforts: a good week, a better mood, a cleaner record. Stop, and come to him through the Lamb who has already made you clean.

For worship. He did come. The Lamb came to the feast to be sacrificed for us. While the crowds washed their hands and wondered whether he would dare, he was already on his way, not as a celebrity but as the sacrifice. Every Passover lamb since Egypt had pointed to this week. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), and by his blood we are made clean for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.

Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know. The chapter that began with a private message from two sisters ends with a public order for an arrest. Jesus is now a wanted man. Anyone who knows must inform. The authorities cannot find him, so they enlist the city. Anyone who has lived where that instruction is issued knows what it does to ordinary life: it makes every neighbour a possible informer, and it works. And in the event it did work. They did not need the general public in the end; they needed one man who already knew where he would be, and he was inside the twelve. This sets the scene for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3). John has laid the warrant on the table two chapters before he collects it.

So that they might arrest him. The net is closing. But the one they plan to arrest is the one who has authority to lay down his life (10:18). The last words of the chapter are arrest him. The attempt has been made four times already in this Gospel and failed every time (7:30, 44; 8:20; 10:39). John has been keeping count. The next attempt will succeed, and when it comes it will be because he walks out of a garden and asks the soldiers whom they are looking for (18:4–8).

The cost of Bethany. What is worth holding, at the end of a chapter about a man who walked out of a grave, is the shape of what happens next. The one who called Lazarus by name and gave him back to his sisters is now a wanted man, because he did it. He knew that when he set out. Thomas knew something like it and said so. The whole journey to Bethany was made on those terms: he raised his friend from the dead, and it cost him his life. The arithmetic was never in doubt to anybody except the disciples, who thought they were going to visit a sick man.

In a sentence. The chief priests and Pharisees had ordered that anyone who knew where Jesus was should report it, so that they could arrest him.

On a Tuesday. When the world seems to close in, remember that the Lord of your life is not at the mercy of his enemies. He knew where every road led, and walked it for you.

For worship. They issued a warrant for the arrest of the resurrection and the life. They thought they were hunting him, and all the while he was coming to them, on his own day, to give himself up. The life of Lazarus was bought with the life of Jesus, and so was ours. He gave life to his friend knowing it would cost him his own, and he counted the cost and paid it gladly. Greater love has no one than this (15:13).

It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, falls ill, and the sisters send word to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” Because he loves them, Jesus waits two more days, then returns to Judea despite the danger, telling the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he is going to wake him. Thomas gloomily urges the others to go and die with him. By the time they arrive, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus with grief and faith mixed; he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she confesses him the Christ, the Son of God. Mary falls at his feet weeping, and Jesus, deeply moved and troubled, weeps too. At the tomb he orders the stone removed, prays aloud to his Father, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man walks out still bound in grave-clothes.

Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees, and the Sanhedrin meets in alarm: if Jesus goes on like this, the Romans will destroy the temple and the nation. The high priest Caiaphas declares that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. John comments that, without knowing it, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God. From that day they plan to kill him. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim, and as Passover approaches the crowds wonder whether he will dare to come to the feast. The one who gives life will give his own life, so that the dead may live.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus’ honour in Bethany, with Martha serving and Lazarus at table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with a pound of expensive nard and wipes them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance. Judas, the future betrayer and a thief who pilfers from the common purse, protests that it could have been sold for the poor. Jesus defends her: she has kept it for his burial, and they will always have the poor, but not always him. Crowds come to see Jesus and the risen Lazarus, and the chief priests resolve to kill Lazarus too. Next day festival crowds carry palm branches out to meet Jesus, hailing him as the blessed King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey as the prophet foretold, though the disciples grasp this only later. Witnesses of Lazarus’s raising spread the news, drawing more people, and the Pharisees despair that the whole world is following him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary's extravagance is the gospel's aesthetic: 'she has done a beautiful thing' (Matt. 26:10). The ointment worth a year's wages poured out on Jesus is the only appropriate response to the one who will pour out his life for the world. Judas' objection — it should have been sold and given to the poor — sounds pious but is calculated. He uses the language of charity to mask the language of control. The contrast between Mary's love and Judas' calculation is the contrast between authentic discipleship and the discipleship that has never really left the world's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: The triumphal entry is at once a royal procession and a misunderstood one. The crowd hails Jesus as king; they are right about the title and wrong about what it means. They expect a Davidic warrior-king who will restore national sovereignty; Jesus enters on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble king of peace. The disciples do not understand this until after the resurrection (v. 16) — another instance of John's pattern where events are incomprehensible until the Spirit illuminates them in the light of the cross and resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.

Meaning first. John 12 closes the first half of the Gospel, the Book of Signs. Jesus is anointed for burial, enters Jerusalem as king, announces that his hour has come, and makes a last appeal to the crowd. The chapter ends with John’s explanation of Israel’s unbelief and Jesus’ final public words. From chapter 13 on, Jesus speaks only to his disciples, and then goes to the cross. It is a chapter of fragrance and shouting and a seed falling into the ground: a woman pours out a year’s wages on his feet, a city waves palms at him, Greeks ask to see him, and he answers that the hour of his glory is the hour of his death. Everything the signs have pointed to is now about to happen.

Six days before the Passover. Probably the Saturday evening before Passover week, after the Sabbath ended. John has started a clock, and it runs to the end of the book. From here he will date almost everything: the next day (v. 12), before the feast (13:1), the day of Preparation (19:14). Nearly half this Gospel covers one week. Time is now counted in days.

Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. The word “therefore” is worth catching. It reaches back to the last verse of chapter 11: the order that anyone who knew where he was should report it. He comes to Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, within an hour’s walk of men with a warrant and a decision on the record, knowing they are looking for him. And John reminds us of the miracle that has put Jesus under sentence of death.

So they gave a dinner for him there. Mark and Matthew place it in the house of Simon the leper (Mark 14:3), perhaps a friend of the family, perhaps a man Jesus had healed. A dinner of gratitude, in the village of resurrection, at the last resting place before Jerusalem.

Martha served. Martha is still serving (Luke 10:40), now without complaint. The verb is diakoneō, from which the church gets its word deacon, and it is exactly what Luke has her doing in the one other scene we have of that house. Her brother has come back from the dead, and she is in the kitchen. Some read that as a failure to have learned anything. It reads better as a woman doing what she is good at, for the man who gave her brother back. Service offered in love is worship too.

And Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table. This is the detail that ought to stop a reader. Diners reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, with feet stretched out behind. A man who had been dead four days and came out of a cave still wrapped is at dinner, on his elbow, in the ordinary posture, eating. Lazarus, once dead, now eating: proof that he is truly alive. John does not describe how he looked or what he said. He puts him at the table like anybody else. There is something in that worth having about resurrection. It does not produce a spectacle or a ghost. It produces a man having supper with his sisters. And it is a small picture of what is coming: the household of the raised, eating with the one who will himself die and rise.

Did Jesus really spend his last week at dinners? Yes, among other things, and it is not a waste. He taught in the temple, wept over the city, washed feet, prayed in the garden; and he also ate with friends. Table fellowship runs all through the Gospels, and his last free evening before the arrest was spent at a meal (13:1–2). Christians sometimes feel that only overtly religious activity counts. But eating together in gratitude, with Christ honoured at the table, is part of the life of his people, and a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

In a sentence. Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where they gave a dinner for him, with Martha serving and Lazarus at the table.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent his last week among friends at a table. Fellowship is not a waste of time. It is a gift. Invite someone to your table this week, and let the meal be a thanksgiving.

For worship. With a warrant out for his arrest and a cross six days away, the Lord of life sat at supper with a man he had raised from the dead. He was not hiding and he was not hurried. And the table at Bethany is a promise. One day all who have been raised by him will recline with him, the dead made alive and eating, in his Father’s house, and he himself will serve them (Luke 12:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,

Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard. The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces or 327 grams. Nard was an aromatic oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas, imported from India, and it was very costly. “Pure” (pistikēs) may mean genuine, unadulterated. This may have been a family treasure, perhaps put by for her own burial or her dowry. It is worth, as Judas will calculate in a moment, about a year’s wages.

And anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. Anointing the head honoured a king; anointing the feet was the act of the humblest servant. And a respectable woman did not let down her hair in public. Mary forgets her dignity in her devotion. She gives the most precious thing she owns, in the lowliest way, at the cost of her reputation, and she does it without a word. It is where she always is: at his feet, listening (Luke 10:39), grieving (11:32), and now worshipping.

Is this the same anointing as in Matthew and Mark? Yes, one supper, and the differences settle without strain. There the woman is unnamed and anoints his head (Mark 14:3); John has the feet. A pound of nard is far more than is needed for either, and Mark describes her breaking the flask and pouring it out; a woman emptying a jar that size over a reclining man will reach both ends of him. She probably did both, and each writer keeps what struck him; John remembers the hair. The host is Simon the leper, and Martha serving fits perfectly well; John says Lazarus was one of those reclining at table, a guest rather than the householder. The objectors are some in Mark and the disciples in Matthew, while John names the one who started it, as he alone names Peter with the sword and Malchus who lost an ear. And the dates measure different things. John’s six days marks the arrival at Bethany; Mark’s two days (Mark 14:1) dates the chief priests’ plotting, and he tells the anointing there because Judas’s betrayal follows from it. This is not the sinful woman of Luke 7, which was an earlier and different anointing in Galilee.

The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. An eyewitness detail: John was in the room, and he remembered the smell. Grace has that quality. It cannot be contained, and it spreads beyond the person who offers it. Some see a picture: her devotion fills the house, and the story fills the world. Matthew and Mark both record a promise Jesus made about this woman, that wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her (Mark 14:9). John does not record the promise. He simply keeps it.

But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said. The contrast is deliberate and immediate. John tells us who Judas is before we hear what he says. Mary gives everything; Judas will sell Jesus for silver. The fragrance of the costliest love and the calculation of the coldest heart are in the same room, at the same table.

What would extravagant love for Christ look like for me? Rarely a jar of nard, but always something that costs. It might be time given when you have little, money given beyond what is sensible, a reputation risked by being openly his, or a long, quiet service no one sees. The mark of Mary’s act is not its size but its direction: it was all for him, and it was not calculated. Ask what you are keeping back because it is too precious, and whether he is worth more. He is the only one who has ever deserved everything, and the only one who gave everything first.

In a sentence. Mary anointed Jesus’ feet with a pound of costly nard and wiped them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance, but Judas, who would betray him, objected.

On a Tuesday. Nothing is too costly to pour out for Christ. Before the week is out, do one thing for him that is not efficient, not calculated, and not seen, simply because he is worthy.

For worship. Mary broke her treasure over the feet of the one who would soon break his body for her. Her nard filled a house; his love fills the world. She gave a year’s wages; he gave himself. Every act of extravagant love ever offered to him is only the echo of his far greater extravagance toward us, and he receives our small offerings as though they were great, because he loves the givers.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.

Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor? The sum is worth converting. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred, once Sabbaths and feasts are taken out, is about a year’s pay for a labourer. So the question is not trivial, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. A year’s income has just been poured onto somebody’s feet and cannot be recovered. The objection sounds pious. Mark says some of the disciples joined in (Mark 14:4); Judas started it. And his arithmetic is correct. If his motive had been what he said it was, his objection would have been a fair one.

He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. John knows what was in his heart, and it is worth noticing how much he knows.

And having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it. “Moneybag” (glōssokomon) was originally a case for the mouthpieces of flutes, then any small box: here the common purse of Jesus and the disciples, from which the poor were helped (13:29). Judas was the treasurer, and he stole from it. “Used to help himself” is continuous: not once, but habitually, over a long time. Love of money opened the door to his betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15; 1 Timothy 6:10).

The disguise of a good cause. The shape of the objection is a permanent shape. Judas does not argue for theft. He argues for the poor. The cover story is not merely respectable; it sounds more obviously righteous than what Mary has just done, and anybody in that room who had not read John’s comment would have thought him the more spiritual man at the table. That is the warning. A concern for the poor can be perfectly genuine, and it can also be the most effective disguise, and from outside the two cannot be told apart. The only person in the room who could tell was the one being anointed.

Why did Jesus choose Judas, and let him keep the money? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (6:64, 70–71), and nothing suggests the theft was hidden from the one who knew what was in man (2:25). He chose Judas so that Scripture would be fulfilled (13:18), and he gave him every privilege of an apostle for three years: his teaching, his miracles, his friendship, his trust. That is the solemn lesson. Judas was not kept out; he was kept close and loved, and he chose silver. Nearness to Jesus, even a ministry in his name, does not save anyone who keeps his heart for something else. And Jesus’ patience with him is a picture of the long patience God shows to every sinner.

How do I guard against the love of money? Give regularly and generously, so that money learns who is master (2 Corinthians 9:6–8). Be open and accountable with money that is not yours: in a church, a charity or a business, never handle it alone. Notice when you begin to justify small dishonesties. Be content with what you have, because he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). And treasure Christ. The cure for loving money is not merely having less of it but loving him more.

In a sentence. Judas asked why the ointment was not sold for a year’s wages and given to the poor, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief who stole from the common purse.

On a Tuesday. Beware of criticising others’ devotion with pious words. Before you object to how someone else gives to Christ, ask what is in your own heart. And beware the love of money: it made a thief of an apostle.

For worship. The Lord who knew what was in the bag let Judas carry it for three years. He fed the thief, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden (Matthew 26:50). There has never been a patience like his. And the one Judas sold for thirty pieces of silver became the treasure of the poor, for though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”

Jesus said, Leave her alone. Jesus defends her, with a directness that is itself an act of protective love. Mary has said nothing, and he speaks for her. He always speaks for those who are criticised for loving him too much.

So that she may keep it for the day of my burial. Bodies were anointed with spices for burial. The Greek is genuinely difficult, since the ointment has already been poured out and there is nothing left to keep. The best sense is probably that she had been keeping it, that this jar had been put by, and that Jesus is saying she has spent it on the right day. Either way, Jesus sees her act as preparing his body for death. In six days he will die, be taken down in a hurry, and be buried before sunset. Nicodemus will bring spices (19:39–40), but to a body already dead. Mary does it six days early, while he can still smell it. Did Mary understand that he would die? Perhaps more than the disciples did. She who sat at his feet may have heard what they missed.

For the poor you always have with you. This half verse has done more damage than almost any sentence Jesus spoke. It is quoted, regularly and confidently, as a reason not to bother: a shrug from Christ himself, proof that poverty is permanent and efforts against it are naive. The sentence is a quotation, and the whole trouble is that the rest of it is left off. He is citing Deuteronomy 15:11: for there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. The permanence of poverty is not the conclusion. It is the premise, and the conclusion drawn from it, in the same breath, is a command to open your hand. Every Jew at that table knew the rest of the verse. So the sentence means the opposite of the way it is often used. Jesus is not dismissing the poor. There will always be time to help them, and his people must (Galatians 2:10).

But you do not always have me. This was a unique moment, one week in human history in which a woman could anoint him for burial. In a few days he would be gone. Devotion to Christ himself comes first; care for the poor flows from it. And notice who raised the objection: Judas had every day of three years to open his hand to the poor, and used the box to fill his own.

So should churches spend money on beauty and worship rather than the poor? This verse does not settle that by making the poor unimportant, nor does it license luxury. Mary’s act was unique, a gift to Christ in person before his burial. The lasting principles are these. Christ himself is worthy of our best, and worship is not wasted when it costs. Care for the poor is commanded and must never be neglected; the early church organised it from the start (Acts 6:1–6). The two are not rivals: those who love Christ most will be most generous to the poor, because he is found among them (Matthew 25:40). Be suspicious of any argument, for spending or for saving, that happens to serve the arguer’s own comfort.

In a sentence. Jesus told Judas to leave her alone, for she was keeping it for his burial, and they would always have the poor, but not always him.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone whose devotion to Christ you have thought excessive? Leave her alone. And open your hand to someone in need this week: not instead of loving Christ, but because you do.

For worship. Worship and mercy are not rivals. But worship comes first, and the love that pours itself out on Christ will pour itself out on the poor. He who defended Mary at the table was himself about to be poured out, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). Her nard prepared his body for the grave; his body, given for us, prepared the way out of ours.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus. Lazarus has become a living proof, a walking sign. They wanted to look at the evidence, which is a very human and entirely reasonable thing to want.

So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well. One of the darkest sentences in the New Testament, and nearly comic in its futility. They are proposing to kill a man who has already been dead once, and got up. Whatever they had learned from the events at Bethany, it was not that the man was hard to bury. It shows the depth of their hardness. The chief priests were Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), and a resurrected man was an embarrassment. Rather than believe the evidence, they plot to destroy it. When testimony cannot be refuted, the remaining option is to remove the witness, and every persecuting authority since has reached the same conclusion by the same route.

Because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus. “Going away” means leaving the authorities’ side. And notice what the problem is. It is not that Lazarus is preaching. There is not a word recorded from him anywhere in this Gospel; he says nothing, before or after. The problem is that he exists.

I have no dramatic story, so do I have a testimony? Yes. Lazarus’s entire testimony was that he was alive and people could see him at dinner, and it drew crowds to Christ. Yours is the same in kind: you were dead in sin and are now alive to God (Ephesians 2:4–5), whether your conversion was sudden or so gradual you cannot date it. The evidence is your life now: a love for Christ you did not have by nature, a fight against sin, a hope that death cannot shake. You do not need to have been a criminal or an addict. You need only to say, truthfully and simply, what he has done for you, and let your changed life back it up.

In a sentence. Crowds came to see Jesus and Lazarus, so the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too, since because of him many were leaving and believing in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. A changed life is the most powerful testimony. It may also be the most opposed. Do not be surprised if being visibly alive in Christ makes some people uncomfortable, and do not hide it.

For worship. They plotted to kill Lazarus, but they could not undo the resurrection. The man was alive because the Lord of life had spoken, and no council could reverse that word. And the one who raised him would soon go into death himself and come out of it never to die again, so that every Lazarus in every generation might live for ever beyond the reach of every plot.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,

The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. The next day is Palm Sunday. Word travels fast in a city full of pilgrims who have been asking about him (11:56).

So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. Two details in what the crowd does are more pointed than they look. The first is the palms. John is the only Gospel writer who mentions them, and they were not general festive decoration; they were a political symbol. Palm branches had become a sign of national victory ever since the Maccabees: when Simon retook the citadel in Jerusalem the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7), and the palm appeared on Jewish coins of the revolts against Rome. Waving them at a man entering the capital was roughly what waving a national flag at a returning general would be. And going out to meet him (hypantēsis) was how cities greeted a visiting king or conqueror.

Crying out, Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. “Hosanna” is Hebrew for save us now (Psalm 118:25). By this time it had become a shout of praise, rather as God save the King is a shout of loyalty more than a prayer, but its meaning is a cry for salvation. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” is from Psalm 118:26, one of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover and the Feast of Booths, a pilgrim psalm of welcome. Every pilgrim had it by heart.

Even the King of Israel! The crowd adds this title, and it is not in the psalm. That is the crowd’s own contribution, and it is the whole misunderstanding in a phrase. The psalm is about pilgrims arriving at the temple. They have turned it into a coronation, and supplied the title themselves. They are hailing a national liberator, like the Maccabees. Jesus is king, but not the kind they expect (6:15; 18:36).

And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written. The other Gospels give the details of how he found it (Mark 11:1–7). Jesus acts deliberately. And the donkey is the argument. He does not silence the crowd, correct the psalm or refuse the shouting. He finds an animal and sits on it. A king coming to a city on a warhorse is coming to take it; a king on a donkey has come in peace. He lets them crown him, and quietly declines the kingdom they have in mind. Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21:2–7), while Mark, Luke and John mention one animal. Matthew names both because Zechariah’s prophecy names both; the others mention only the one Jesus rode. To mention more is not to contradict.

Was this the same crowd that shouted Crucify him a few days later? Probably not entirely. The crowd on the road was largely pilgrims and the Galileans and Bethany witnesses who had seen his works; the crowd before Pilate was gathered early in the morning in the city, stirred up by the chief priests (Mark 15:11). But some may well have been in both, and the point stands: popular enthusiasm is fickle. People who wanted a king on their own terms turned against him when he would not be that king. It is a warning against a faith that follows Jesus only while he seems to be giving us what we want.

In a sentence. The next day, hearing Jesus was coming, the crowd went out with palm branches shouting Hosanna and hailing him as the King of Israel, and Jesus found a young donkey and rode on it, as Scripture says.

On a Tuesday. Hosanna means save us now. When you praise Jesus as King this week, ask whether you want him as he is, the humble king who comes to save from sin, or as you would like him to be.

For worship. Hosanna: save us now. Make that cry your praise and your prayer. The crowd shouted for a king who would save them from Rome, and he rode on into the city to save them from something far worse. He took the cry seriously. Within the week he answered it, not by taking a throne but by going to a cross, and every Hosanna since has been answered by his blood.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!” His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.

Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt! From Zechariah 9:9, combined perhaps with Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16 (fear not). “Daughter of Zion” is Jerusalem. There is a small change worth noticing. Zechariah begins, rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! John writes, fear not. He has swapped the opening for a phrase that runs through Isaiah and Zephaniah, the standard word to a frightened Israel. That changes the register of the whole entry. The crowd is exultant and does not need telling to rejoice; they are already doing it, loudly, and about the wrong thing. What they will need in five days is the other sentence.

A king of peace. A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Zechariah goes on to say that this king will cut off the chariot and the war horse and speak peace to the nations, and his rule shall be from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). Jesus corrects the crowd’s hopes by his choice of mount. He is king, but humble, bringing peace, not a sword.

His disciples did not understand these things at first. An honest admission, and one of the most quietly generous in the Gospel. They were in the procession. They had presumably fetched the animal; the other Gospels say Jesus sent two of them for it. They walked into Jerusalem in the middle of the noise, and John says plainly that none of it meant anything to them at the time.

But when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him. After the resurrection and ascension, and with the Spirit’s help (14:26), they understood the Scriptures (2:22). The whole Old Testament became clear in the light of Christ (Luke 24:27, 45). Understanding came later, and it came as memory: the same events, sitting still, suddenly readable. Understanding was not a condition of being in the procession. The disciples’ confusion did not stop the donkey being the right donkey.

How do we know the apostles did not simply read prophecy into the events afterwards? Because they tell us honestly when they understood, and what they record does not flatter them. Inventors would have made themselves wise at the time. Many of the fulfilments were outside anyone’s control: the place of birth, the manner of death, the piercing, the grave. And Jesus himself acted deliberately to fulfil Scripture, as here, showing that he understood his mission in its light. Above all, the resurrection is the key that opened the Old Testament to them, and the resurrection is the best-attested event of the ancient world. The apostles did not create the pattern. They discovered it, once the risen Lord explained it.

In a sentence. As Zechariah foretold, Zion’s king came humbly on a donkey’s colt, and the disciples did not understand this until Jesus was glorified, when they remembered what had been written and done.

On a Tuesday. Some things in your life you will only understand later. Trust Christ now; the meaning will come. And if you are in the middle of something you cannot read, remember that the disciples walked through a fulfilled prophecy without knowing it.

For worship. The King of the universe came into his capital on a borrowed donkey, and the first word of his welcome was fear not. He comes to his people not to terrify but to save, not with chariots but with peace. And the Spirit he sent has opened our eyes, as he opened theirs, to see in the whole of Scripture the shape of one humble, glorious King.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.

The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The tense is doing work: they continued to bear witness, an ongoing action. They had not stopped talking about it. Weeks after the event, the people who had stood outside that cave were still telling anyone who would listen.

The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign. John connects the triumphal entry directly to Lazarus. The crowd did not come out simply because a famous teacher was approaching. The palm branches are downstream of Lazarus. The whole entry, the shouting, the psalm, the improvised coronation, was generated by a resurrection in a village two miles away. That explains the council’s panic in the next verse. They had already worked out that Lazarus was the problem (v. 10). Here is the demonstration: one man alive at a dinner table produced a crowd large enough to fill the road into Jerusalem.

Two crowds. There are two crowds here: one from Bethany, telling what they saw, and one from Jerusalem, coming out to see. Verse 17 is the people who were there; verse 18 is the people who heard them and came. Nobody in verse 18 saw anything. They acted on the word of witnesses, and they were right to. That is the ordinary way almost every Christian who has ever lived came to faith: not by seeing, but by believing people who did. And it is exactly what Jesus will say to Thomas at the end of the book: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29).

Is believing on the testimony of others really enough? Yes, when the testimony is true and comes from God. Most of what any of us know about history, we know from witnesses. The apostles were eyewitnesses who told what they had seen and heard (1 John 1:1–3), wrote it down, and suffered for it. Their testimony is preserved for us in Scripture, and the Holy Spirit himself bears witness through it to our hearts (Westminster 1.5). Faith is not believing without evidence. It is trusting God’s own testimony, delivered through those he chose, about his Son.

In a sentence. Those who had seen Lazarus raised kept testifying, and that was why the crowd came out to meet Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Keep telling what you have seen Christ do. Your witness is one link in a chain that began outside a cave in Bethany. Someone told you. Tell someone else.

For worship. The chain of witness that began at Lazarus’s tomb has never been broken.
