From Bethany to Jerusalem, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, from the apostles to us, the news has run that Jesus raises the dead. Keep telling what you have seen Christ do. Your witness draws others to him, and he is the one they will find at the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”

So the Pharisees said to one another, You see that you are gaining nothing. Frustration, and it is said by Pharisees to one another, which means it is internal recrimination. Somebody at that meeting is being blamed. They have had a warrant out for days (11:57), they have taken a formal decision to kill him (11:53), they have added Lazarus to the list (12:10), and a crowd has just carried him into the city shouting a coronation psalm. The policy is not working, and they are turning on each other.

Look, the world has gone after him. An exaggeration, but a prophetic one. They mean it as despair: everybody, the whole town, we have lost the room. And John, who has been waiting for this, opens the very next verse: now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. The world indeed: not the crowd from Bethany, not the pilgrims from Galilee, but Gentiles, outsiders to the covenant. So the Pharisees, complaining bitterly and using the biggest word they can find, have accidentally announced the programme. Like Caiaphas, they speak more truly than they know (11:50–51). His enemies keep saying true things in the wrong tone.

A second irony. The Pharisees think the crowd’s enthusiasm is their defeat. In five days that same city will be shouting for a crucifixion, and the Pharisees will have won everything they wanted. And the world will go after him anyway, by exactly the route they arranged.

Is the world really going after him today? More than ever before in history. The church that began with a handful of believers in Jerusalem is now found in almost every nation on earth, and in many places it is growing fastest among the poor and the persecuted. That is not a reason for pride or complacency; there are still many peoples with no church at all. But it is the fulfilment of what the Pharisees feared and what Jesus promised: people from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 5:9).

In a sentence. The Pharisees told one another they were getting nowhere, for the whole world had gone after Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The world has gone after him, from every nation. You are part of that crowd. Pray this week for one nation where the church is small or suffering.

For worship. His enemies said in despair what heaven says in joy: the world has gone after him. No warrant, no council, no cross could stop it. The plotting of his enemies became the road by which he drew the nations, and he is drawing them still. The Lamb who was slain is worthy, for by his blood he ransomed people for God from every nation (Revelation 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some Greeks who have come to worship at the feast ask Philip to let them see Jesus. When Philip and Andrew tell him, Jesus declares that the hour for the Son of Man’s glory has come. A grain of wheat stays alone unless it falls into the ground and dies; then it yields a great harvest. Whoever clings to life loses it, and whoever lets go of it in this world keeps it for eternity. His servants must follow him, and the Father will honour them. His soul is troubled, yet he will not ask to be spared this hour, for it is why he came; he prays that the Father will glorify his name. A voice from heaven replies that it has and will again. Some hear thunder, others an angel. Jesus says the voice was for them: now this world is judged, its ruler is driven out, and when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself, meaning the death he would die. The crowd asks how the Messiah, who remains for ever, can be lifted up, and who this Son of Man is. Jesus urges them to walk in the light while they have it and become children of light, then hides from them. Despite all his signs they do not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about unbelief and hardened hearts; Isaiah said this because he saw Jesus’ glory. Even many leaders believe but keep quiet for fear of expulsion, preferring human praise to God’s. Jesus cries out that to believe in him is to believe in the one who sent him; he came as light so that believers need not stay in darkness. He does not judge those who reject his words now, for he came to save; but his word will judge them on the last day, for he speaks what the Father commanded, and the Father’s command is eternal life.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is the theological center of John's gospel — referenced as 'not yet come' repeatedly throughout the narrative (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), now announced as arrived (v. 23). The hour is the cross-resurrection-ascension event, the moment when the Son of Man is simultaneously lifted up in humiliation and glorified in triumph. The cross is not the Father's defeat but his decisive victory; it is not the Son's shame but his glory. This is the theology that has to be maintained against every attempt to split the crucifixion from the resurrection: both are the one event called 'the hour.'
verseByVerse.examples: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is the law of the kingdom: life through death, fruitfulness through sacrifice. Jesus applies it first to himself and then to his disciples. The disciple who 'hates his life in this world' — who does not cling to temporal existence at the cost of eternal loyalty — will find life preserved in ways that the self-preserver never can. The call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death.

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”

Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. Who these men were is worth getting right. John calls them Greeks: Gentiles by birth, not Greek-speaking Jews up for the feast. They are outsiders. They had come to worship at the feast, which places them among the God-fearers: Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel and kept his moral law without becoming full converts, like Cornelius (Acts 10:2; 17:4). They came to the feasts and worshipped in the Court of the Gentiles. And there was a wall for them. The temple’s outer court was as far as a Gentile could go, and stone notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who passed the barrier had only himself to blame for the death that followed. Two of those inscriptions have been dug up. So these men have travelled to a feast at a temple they are forbidden to enter, to worship a God who has told them, in writing, where to stop. That is the position from which they ask their question. Their coming fulfils the Pharisees’ complaint: the world goes after him.

So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee. Philip has a Greek name, and Bethsaida was a mixed border town near Gentile areas, where Greek would have been spoken daily. They picked the man most likely to understand them, which suggests they had thought about it.

And asked him, Sir, we wish to see Jesus. A request carved on the inside of many pulpits, where only the preacher can see it. It is worth taking at face value first. They are not asking for a doctrine or a debate. They want to see him, which here means to meet him, to come to know him. It is the least sophisticated request in the chapter and, as it turns out, the one that brings the hour. The Gentiles are asking for Jesus. It is the sign that his hour has come.

What does it mean to see Jesus today? Not a vision, but to know him truly by faith. We see him in the Gospels, where his words and works are written so that we may believe (20:31). We see him in the preaching of his word, when Christ is set before us as crucified (Galatians 3:1). We see him in the Lord’s Supper, which proclaims his death until he comes. And we see something of him in his people, when they love one another as he loved them (13:35). One day we shall see him face to face (1 John 3:2). Until then, every Sunday ought to answer this request.

In a sentence. Some Greeks who had come to worship at the feast came to Philip from Bethsaida and asked to see Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you go to church, go with this request in your heart: Sir, we wish to see Jesus. And if you ever teach or preach, remember that this is what people have come for.

For worship. Sir, we wish to see Jesus. Let that be the cry of every person who comes to church, and the aim of every preacher. These men stood outside a wall that told them where to stop, and asked for the one who would break it down. He did not leave them outside. Through his death the dividing wall of hostility fell (Ephesians 2:14), and the outsiders were brought near. We were those Greeks, and he let us see him.
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. Watch what Philip does, because it is oddly hesitant. He does not take them to Jesus. He goes and tells Andrew, and then the two of them go together. Philip is the man who did the arithmetic on the loaves and concluded it could not be done (6:7). Andrew is the man who brought the boy with the lunch anyway (6:8–9), and who brought his brother Peter in the first place (1:41). It is the same pair doing the same thing: Philip hesitates; Andrew brings people to Jesus again. Why the hesitation? Almost certainly because they were Gentiles, and there was no procedure for this. Jesus had said he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel (Matthew 15:24). Philip is not being obstructive. He does not know whether it is allowed.

And Jesus answered them, The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. The answer does not mention the Greeks at all, and it is the pivot of the entire Gospel. Jesus’ hour in John is the time of his death and glorification. Three times John has told us it had not yet come: at Cana (2:4), at the feast when no one laid a hand on him (7:30), in the treasury (8:20). The clock has been running under this book since the second chapter, and now it strikes. What made it strike was not the arrest, the plot or the entry into Jerusalem. It was a handful of foreigners asking to see him. Why? Because the Gentiles can only truly see him through his death, when he is lifted up and draws all people (v. 32). The only way the world gets in is through what is about to happen.

The Son of Man. Notice the title. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is given dominion over all peoples, nations and languages (Daniel 7:13–14). Greeks ask for him, and he answers with the title that has the nations written into it.

The cross is the glory. “Glorified” in John means the cross, resurrection and return to the Father, seen as one. The cross is not a defeat followed by glory; the cross is itself the glory. It is where the love of God, the justice of God, the wisdom of God and the power of God are all shown most fully, and so it is where God is seen as he is.

How can a crucifixion be glorious? Because glory in Scripture is the shining out of who God is, and nowhere does that shine more brightly than at the cross. There we see his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself for his enemies; and his power, which turns the worst crime in history into the salvation of the world. A crucifixion was meant to be the most shameful death imaginable. God made it the place where he is most honoured. That is why Paul could say, far be it from me to boast except in the cross (Galatians 6:14).

In a sentence. Philip and Andrew told Jesus, and he answered that the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure whether someone is welcome at Jesus’ feet, do what Andrew did: bring them anyway. And when you think of glory, think first of the cross.

For worship. The hour of his glory was the hour of his death. See the glory of God in the cross. For three years the clock had said not yet, and when the nations came knocking it struck. The Son of Man went to his throne by way of a gibbet, and the dominion promised to him over every people was bought with his blood.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.

Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone. He answers a request from Gentiles with a fact about farming, and it takes a moment to see why it is the answer. They want to see him. He tells them what it will cost to be seen. A seed kept in a jar stays exactly what it is. It remains alone, which is the word he uses, an odd word for a seed and the right word for him. Planted in the ground, it dies as a seed, and from it a plant grows with many seeds. Jesus’ death is like that. If he did not die, he would remain alone. Through his death comes a great harvest of people from every nation, including the Greeks who have just asked to see him. There is no route by which those Greeks get in except the one he is about to take: not by his teaching more clearly, not by his living longer, not by a change of rules about the outer court. The wall comes down because the seed goes into the ground.

But if it dies, it bears much fruit. The cross is the way to fruitfulness. Life comes out of death. And the picture is not decoration. It is what happens in a field: the seed must truly be lost, must stop being retrievable, before anything comes up. He is telling them plainly that he is going to die, in the gentlest image available, days before it happens.

Whoever loves his life loses it. The principle applies to his followers too (Mark 8:35). “Life” here is psychē: the self, one’s earthly life. Clinging to your life, living for yourself, is the way to lose everything.

And whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. This needs a guard, because read flatly it has done harm. “Hates” is a Hebrew way of saying loves less, prefers something else. Jesus says a disciple must hate his father and mother (Luke 14:26), and God says through Malachi, Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (Malachi 1:2–3), where the sense is choosing and setting aside rather than malice. So this is not self-loathing, and it is not an instruction to despise one’s own existence, which some devout people have taken it to be, with miserable results. It is about ranking: putting Christ above self. The man who holds his life as the thing that must be preserved at all costs will find it was not preservable; the man who holds it loosely, because something matters more, gets it back. Those who give up their lives for him find true life. And it is not a single act of renunciation performed once at conversion, but a way of holding things.

What does falling into the ground look like in ordinary life? Usually not martyrdom, but many small deaths. It is giving up the evening you wanted for someone who needs you. It is letting go of a grudge you had every right to hold. It is choosing obedience when it costs a promotion, a friendship or your reputation. It is pouring years into children, a church or a neighbour without seeing the fruit. Each feels like loss, and each is a seed. And here is a plain test: ask what you would be unable to obey God about, if he asked. Not what you would find hard; what is genuinely not on the table. Whatever that is, it is the part of your life you are still loving in the sense this verse means.

In a sentence. Jesus said a grain of wheat remains alone unless it falls into the earth and dies, but if it dies it bears much fruit; whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates it in this world will keep it for eternal life.

On a Tuesday. What are you clinging to? Plant it, let it die for Christ’s sake, and see what fruit he brings.

For worship. The grain of wheat fell into the ground outside Jerusalem and lay there three days, and from it has come a harvest that fills the earth. Every believer in every nation is fruit from that one seed. He would not remain alone. He chose to die rather than to be without us, and he has never been alone since, for he is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.

If anyone serves me, he must follow me. Serving Christ means following him, even on the road of the grain of wheat. Discipleship is not admiration from a distance.

And where I am, there will my servant be also. Where he goes, through death to glory, his servants go too (14:3; 17:24). It sounds like a promise about heaven, and it is; but in this context it is first of all a promise about the road. The place he is going in a few days is a cross.

If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. The Father honours those who serve his Son. Not human glory, but the Father’s approval. That is precisely the honour the authorities in verse 43 would refuse to be paid in.

Now is my soul troubled. This is John’s Gethsemane, and it should be named as such, because it is easy to miss that he has one. John records no agony in the garden, no let this cup pass, no sleeping disciples; when we reach the garden in chapter 18, Jesus walks out to meet the soldiers. Readers have sometimes concluded that John’s Jesus is too serene to struggle. He is not. The struggle is here, in public, days early. “Troubled” (tetaraktai) means agitated, shaken, like water stirred up; John has used it of Jesus at the tomb (11:33) and will use it at the supper (13:21). Jesus is truly human and feels the horror of what lies ahead: not just physical death, but bearing the wrath of God against sin (Mark 14:34).

And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? The sentence is the whole of Gethsemane compressed. The Greek can be punctuated as a question he considers and rejects, or as a real prayer answered by himself in the next breath. Either way the content is the same as in the garden: a genuine recoil, and a genuine refusal to act on it.

But for this purpose I have come to this hour. He came for this. The whole of his life led to this hour. And he does not hide the struggle. He is standing among Greeks, disciples and a crowd, and he says out loud that his soul is in turmoil. There is no attempt to present a settled face. That is worth a great deal to anyone who has assumed that faith means calm, or that being troubled about something God has clearly appointed is itself a failure. Here is the Son of God, entirely certain of the Father’s will, entirely committed to it, and churned up about it, and the trouble does not weaken his obedience by a syllable.

Is it a sin to feel troubled about what God is asking of me? No. Jesus was troubled, and he never sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Feelings of dread, grief or fear in the face of suffering are part of being human in a fallen world. What matters is what you do with them. Jesus brought his trouble to the Father in prayer, named it honestly, and then chose the Father’s glory over his own escape. You may do the same: tell God exactly how you feel, ask for help, and then say, for this purpose I am here. Obedience does not require that you stop feeling. It requires that you keep going.

In a sentence. Jesus said that his servant must follow him, and will be where he is and be honoured by the Father; and then said his soul was troubled, but he would not ask to be saved from this hour, for this was why he had come.

On a Tuesday. If your soul is troubled this week about something you know God has asked of you, say so to him, as Jesus did. Then take the next step anyway.

For worship. He was troubled, and still he went to the cross for us. His resolve is our salvation. The Son of God felt the full horror of the cup and did not put it down. He could have prayed to be saved from that hour, and the Father would have heard him. He chose instead to be the one who saves us from ours.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”

Father, glorify your name. This is his prayer instead: not save me, but glorify your name. Like your will be done in Gethsemane. He has just said his soul is churning, and the request he settles on has nothing about himself in it at all. Not even give me strength, which is what any of us would have asked for. The glory of God matters more to Jesus than his own escape from suffering.

Then a voice came from heaven. The third time in the Gospels that the Father speaks from heaven, after the baptism (Mark 1:11) and the transfiguration (Mark 9:7). And it is the only one John records. He has no baptism scene and no transfiguration, so this is the single occasion in the fourth Gospel on which the Father speaks aloud. John saved it for here.

I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again. He has glorified it in Jesus’ life and signs; he will glorify it again in Jesus’ death and resurrection. Past and future, and nothing in the present, which is exactly right, since the present is the hour itself. The Father is saying: everything up to now, and everything about to happen, are the same work.

The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, An angel has spoken to him. Some heard only noise; others knew it was speech, but not whose. Compare Paul’s companions on the Damascus road (Acts 9:7; 22:9). In the Old Testament, God’s voice is likened to thunder (Psalm 29:3; Exodus 19:19). And this is one of the shrewdest observations in the New Testament. Nobody in the crowd reports hearing words. That is not a comment on their hearing but on what happens when God speaks into a crowd that is not listening for him. The sound was real; everybody agreed something had happened. What they could not do was receive it as address. So it became weather, or at best a phenomenon, impressive, safely categorised, requiring nothing. That is still the commonest response to God, and it is not usually denial. It is reclassification. Something happens that does not fit, and the mind files it under coincidence or psychology or atmosphere, and the label does the work that unbelief used to do openly.

Should I expect God to speak to me with an audible voice? No; that is not how he has promised to guide us. The voice from heaven was a rare act at the climax of redemption, to confirm the Son before the cross. God has now spoken to us fully in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and his word is written in Scripture, which is complete and sufficient for all we need for salvation and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Westminster 1.6). The Spirit speaks to us through that word, opening it to our hearts. So when you want to hear God, open the Bible. And when he speaks there, do not file it as thunder.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed for the Father to glorify his name, and a voice from heaven said he had glorified it and would glorify it again, which some of the crowd took for thunder and others for an angel.

On a Tuesday. When you are troubled, pray as Jesus did: Father, glorify your name. It is a prayer God always answers.

For worship. The Father answered the Son from heaven in the hour of his trouble, and the answer was glory. The name of God was glorified in the life of Jesus and was about to be glorified as never before in his death. Hallowed be your name, we pray, and the cross is the place where it has been hallowed most of all.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.”

Jesus answered, This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Jesus did not need it; he knew the Father’s will, and had said as much at the tomb: I knew that you always hear me (11:42). It was for the crowd, to confirm him. Twice in two chapters he tells a crowd that the visible prayer is for their benefit, and both times he says so openly rather than letting them think they are overhearing something private.

Now is the judgment of this world. Not at the end of history: now. At the cross, the world is judged. Its verdict on Jesus is overturned by God, and the world’s sin is exposed and condemned. The trial in which the world condemns Jesus is the trial in which the world is condemned. Both verdicts are handed down in the same week.

Now will the ruler of this world be cast out. “The ruler of this world” is Satan (14:30; 16:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4). The verb is ekballō, the ordinary word for throwing something out, and the word used all through the Gospels for casting out demons: the exorcist’s word, applied to the chief of them. At the cross, he is cast out, dethroned. How? By the cross Christ removed the ground of Satan’s accusation, our sin (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15; Revelation 12:9–11). Through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, and delivered all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. Satan still works, but he is a defeated enemy.

The enemy’s own plan. It is easy to keep the cross entirely in the register of forgiveness and miss the other half. Something was defeated at Calvary. The enemy arranged that execution. He entered Judas (13:27), and he got exactly what he wanted, and it turned out to be the means of his eviction. It is the oldest pattern in Scripture, the thing meant for harm becoming the thing that saves, and here it is at full scale.

Where Christians differ: the binding of Satan. Premillennial Christians often teach that Satan will be bound only in a future thousand-year reign after Christ’s return. Verdict: Jesus says Satan is cast out “now,” at the cross. Revelation 20’s binding of Satan describes this present age, in which he can no longer deceive the nations or stop the gospel going to them (Matthew 12:29). This is the amillennial view: the thousand years are the gospel age between Christ’s first and second comings.

If Satan has been cast out, why is there still so much evil, and why am I still tempted? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. Think of a war in which the decisive battle has been won, but the enemy’s forces still fight on in pockets until the final surrender. Satan is still a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), still tempting and accusing, and the world still lies under his influence (1 John 5:19). But he cannot stop the gospel, cannot snatch a single sheep from Christ’s hand (10:28), and cannot condemn anyone for whom Christ died (Romans 8:33–34). So resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the outcome is settled. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20).

In a sentence. Jesus said the voice came for their sake, and now was the judgment of the world and the casting out of its ruler.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes this week, remember who you are dealing with: a defeated enemy. Do not argue with him. Resist him in Christ’s name, and he will flee (James 4:7).

For worship. At the cross, the devil was cast out. You serve a conquering King. The ruler of this world thought he had the Son of God at his mercy, and in the very hour of his apparent triumph he was thrown down. The Lamb overcame him, and so do all who belong to the Lamb, by his blood and by the word of their testimony (Revelation 12:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.

And I, when I am lifted up from the earth. This is the third and last of the lifted up sayings in John (3:14; 8:28). In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation. It is used in Scripture of raising someone to honour: Isaiah’s Servant shall be high and lifted up (Isaiah 52:13). And it is also, brutally and literally, what happened to him: a man raised off the ground on a beam. He will be lifted up on the cross, and that lifting up will be his exaltation. The two meanings are one movement.

Will draw all people to myself. “Draw” (helkō) is the same verb as 6:44, no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him: an effective pulling. It is a strong word, used of hauling a net (21:6) and drawing a sword (18:10). And “all people” is, in the Greek, simply all; the word people is supplied by translators. In context, the Greeks have just asked to see him. Through the cross, Jesus will draw people from every nation, not only Jews. This is the answer to their request. And notice where the drawing power lies. Not in his teaching, which they had had for three years, and not in his miracles, which the council admitted and used against him. In the cross. The thing that draws is a man being executed, and it is at his most powerless that he says he will pull the world in.

He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die. Crucifixion: lifted up from the earth on a cross. John stops to explain, the only time he does so with these sayings, which settles the meaning without cancelling the other. The exaltation and the execution are one event.

Where Christians differ: does Christ draw every person? Some take “all people” to mean every individual, drawn with a resistible grace. Verdict: in 6:44 the one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. If every person were drawn in that sense, every person would be saved, which Scripture denies. Here, “all people” means all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews, as the context of the Greeks shows (compare 11:52). The cross draws, effectively, people from every nation.

Does this mean everyone will finally be saved? No. Some have read all as a promise of universal salvation, but this same Gospel records that many turned back (6:66), that some will die in their sins (8:24), and that the word Jesus spoke will judge on the last day (12:48). John does not contradict himself a few verses apart. The barrier between Jew and Gentile is down, and the cross now draws from every nation on earth. It is the same promise as the other sheep of chapter 10, and the one flock. Everyone who comes to him is drawn, and everyone who is drawn will come.

In a sentence. Jesus said that when he is lifted up from the earth he will draw all people to himself, which showed the kind of death he would die.

On a Tuesday. Christ lifted up still draws people from every nation. Lift him up in your speech and your life. When you talk about your faith, talk about the cross.

For worship. Christ lifted up still draws people from every nation. The cross was meant to repel, to shame a man before the world, and it has become the strongest pull on the human heart in history. He was lifted up to die, and he was lifted up to reign, and from that throne he is drawing to himself a people no one can number.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.”

So the crowd answered him, We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. Their objection is serious and deserves to be stated properly. “The Law” here is the Old Testament. They are right, and they can cite it. The promise to David was of a throne established for ever (Psalm 89:36–37); Isaiah’s child would reign from this time forth and for evermore (Isaiah 9:7); Ezekiel’s David would be prince for ever (Ezekiel 37:25); Daniel’s son of man received a dominion that would not pass away (Daniel 7:14). The Messiah’s kingdom is everlasting. True, but they could not imagine that he would reach it through death.

How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? They understand lifted up as death. A dying Messiah made no sense to them; it was exactly the objection Paul would meet for the rest of his life: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Who is this Son of Man? The honest question. They do not know who he is talking about. They have noticed that he has quietly changed the title. They said the Christ; he said the Son of Man; and they want to know whether these are the same person.

So Jesus said to them, The light is among you for a little while longer. Jesus does not argue. He warns. The time is short. It is the last exchange of his public ministry, and he lets a fair theological difficulty go unresolved. The little while is about four days. He is not refusing to answer from impatience. He is telling them that the season for standing about asking questions is nearly over, and the light will shortly go out of the street. The urgent thing is not to resolve the puzzle. It is to walk while there is enough light to see by. That is not hostility to thinking, and it should not be used as an excuse for it. He answered questions for three years. It is a statement about a particular moment, and about the fact that understanding can always be postponed, and daylight cannot.

Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. “Overtake” (katalabē) is the same word as 1:5, where the darkness has not overcome the light. Now the darkness will overtake those who refuse the light.

The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going. Life without Christ is aimless.

Is it wrong to have unanswered questions before I believe? No. Honest questions are not sin, and many believers carry some for years. But do not make every question a condition of coming to Christ. The crowd’s question had a real answer, the Messiah would reign for ever by dying and rising, but they would only see it if they walked in the light they had. Faith often works that way: you trust what you can see of Christ now, and understanding grows as you follow. Waiting to have everything solved first is itself a choice, and the light does not wait.

In a sentence. The crowd objected that the Christ would remain for ever, so how could the Son of Man be lifted up, and who was he? Jesus warned them that the light was with them only a little longer, and they should walk in it before darkness overtook them.

On a Tuesday. The light will not always be offered. If you have not come to Christ, come now. And if you have, do not postpone the obedience you already understand while you wait for answers to questions you do not.

For worship. The Christ does remain for ever, and he remains because he was lifted up. He went down into death and rose to an everlasting throne, and both the cross and the crown belong to the one Son of Man. The light that was among them for a little while is the light that now shines for ever, and the darkness has not overcome it.

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,

While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light. “Sons of light” is a Hebrew way of saying people who belong to the light and share its character (Luke 16:8; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). Believing makes you a child of the light. Not merely lit up, but given the family likeness. It echoes the prologue, where those who received him were given the right to become children of God (1:12). The offer standing at the close of the public ministry is the one made at the beginning.

When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. His last public appeal. The light withdraws. That is the last thing Jesus does in front of a crowd in this Gospel. Everything after it is private: the supper, the disciples, the arrest, the trials. He has been teaching in public for three years, and it stops here, in the middle of a street, with a warning about walking while the light lasts, and then he is gone. John used the same phrase at the end of chapter 8 (8:59), and both times it follows a moment when the light was offered and refused. There is nothing dramatic about the exit. He simply stops being available.

Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him. John now explains the great mystery of the Gospel: why did Israel, God’s own people, reject their Messiah? The signs were many and clear. Water into wine, an official’s son healed at a distance, a man off his mat after thirty-eight years, five thousand fed, a walk on the sea, a beggar born blind, and a man four days dead walking out of a cave. And the verdict on the whole series is they still did not believe. It is a devastating sentence to write about the ministry of the Son of God, and John writes it flatly. It disposes, permanently, of the notion that people’s failure to believe is a failure of evidence or presentation. Nobody has ever had better material, and the material was not the problem.

Can a person put off believing for too long? Yes, and this verse is a solemn warning. The light was among them, and then it withdrew. Scripture urges, now is the favourable time; now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), because no one is promised tomorrow, and a heart that keeps refusing grows harder. But if you are concerned about your soul and want to come to Christ, that very desire shows the light has not left you. No one who comes to him is turned away (6:37). The danger is not for those who are anxious to come, but for those who are content to wait.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to believe in the light while they had it, then withdrew and hid himself, and though he had done so many signs, they still did not believe.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, you are a child of light. Live as one: honest, open, without hidden corners, so that the family likeness can be seen.

For worship. The light withdrew from a city that would not have it, and went on toward the cross for the very people who had refused it. He who hid himself from the crowd did not hide himself from the Father’s purpose. And to everyone who believes he still gives the right to become a child of light, sharing the likeness of the one who is light, and in whom is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5).

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,

So that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. Their unbelief was foretold. It did not take God by surprise; it was part of his plan. John reaches for Isaiah twice to explain what he has just reported, and it matters which parts of Isaiah he takes.

Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? From Isaiah 53:1, the opening line of the great Suffering Servant passage: the chapter about the man despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter. The prophet asks who has believed the message about the Servant, and the question has an answer built into it: almost nobody. The prophet who was given the fullest description of the cross in the Old Testament opens it by asking who will accept the report. And the answer, seven centuries later, is a rejected Messiah walking away from a crowd. So the unbelief is not a surprise, and it is not a defeat. It was written into the very passage that describes the whole work. “The arm of the Lord” is God’s power in salvation, revealed in Christ’s signs and in his cross.

Therefore they could not believe. Not merely did not, but could not. Their unbelief has become an inability. It is the hardest phrase in the chapter, and it should not be softened, but it should be read in order. Verse 37 says they did not believe though they had seen everything. Verse 39 says that at a certain point they could not. The inability follows the refusal; it does not come before it. That is the consistent biblical pattern. Pharaoh hardened his own heart through several plagues before Exodus says that God hardened it. Romans 1 says three times that God gave them up, to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). The judgment is that a man is finally given what he has been insisting on. Why could they not? The next quotation explains.

Does this mean God stops people who want to believe? No. Nobody in Scripture is ever shown wanting to come to God and being refused. Behind all human unbelief lies the fallen heart, which does not want God (3:19–20); and God in his justice may confirm a person in the refusal he has chosen. But he never turns away a sinner who seeks him. If you want Christ, that desire is itself evidence of God’s grace at work in you, not of his rejection. Come to him. The doctrine of hardening is a warning to the careless, not a threat to the seeking.

In a sentence. Their unbelief fulfilled Isaiah’s words asking who had believed the message and to whom the Lord’s arm had been revealed, and so they could not believe, because Isaiah also said...

On a Tuesday. Do not treat God’s patience as permission to keep refusing what you know. Respond to the light you have today, while your heart is still soft enough to hear.

For worship. The arm of the Lord was revealed in the crucified Servant. If you believe, it was revealed to you. What grace. Isaiah saw it coming and asked who would believe; and against all the unbelief of the world, God has opened the eyes of a multitude to see his strong arm in the weakness of a cross. You did not find it yourself. It was revealed.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.” Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.

He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. From Isaiah 6:10, quoted freely. When Isaiah was called, God told him his preaching would harden Israel. It is the bleakest commission given to any prophet: go and preach, and the preaching will close their eyes. This passage is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts (Mark 4:12; Acts 28:26–27) to explain Israel’s unbelief.

Lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them. Hardening is God’s judgment on persistent unbelief. They first refused to believe (v. 37); then God gave them over to their refusal (Romans 1:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:11). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility stand together. They would not; therefore they could not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the author of sin or that they were innocent victims. They had seen and rejected the light (v. 37). Nor does it mean all Israel is hardened for ever: Paul says a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25), and many Jews have believed and will believe.

How far does God’s hand reach in hardening? Some read hardening only as God giving people over to the unbelief they have already chosen, as with Pharaoh. Others, with Romans 9:17–24, see God’s sovereign purpose behind the hardening itself. Scripture holds both: God hardens, and those hardened are responsible, for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God (v. 43). He never hardens a heart that is seeking him.

Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him. This ought to stop a reader cold. Isaiah 6 is the great vision every reader of the Old Testament knows: the year King Uzziah died, the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, his train filling the temple, the seraphim crying, holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts (Isaiah 6:1–5). And John says that glory was Christ’s. The him in the sentence is Jesus. The Lord whom Isaiah saw on the throne was the Son. Isaiah 6:5 says the prophet saw the King, the LORD of hosts: the covenant name, the God of Israel. John says he saw Christ. This is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is the Lord of the Old Testament, Yahweh himself, and it is made in a subordinate clause. There is no way to hold both Isaiah and John together except the one the church confessed in its creeds.

High and lifted up. There is something further. Isaiah saw him high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1), and lifted up is the very phrase Jesus has used of himself three times in this Gospel, most recently nine verses ago, with John’s note that it meant the manner of his death. The throne Isaiah saw and the cross John is walking toward are described with the same language. The glory the seraphim could not look at is the glory of a man on a Roman cross outside a city wall, and this Gospel has been saying so since the prologue: we have seen his glory (1:14).

Has God then rejected the Jewish people? No. Paul answers that question directly: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Romans 11:1). There has always been a remnant chosen by grace, and Paul himself was one. Christians hold different views on how Romans 11:25–26 will be fulfilled: some expect a large turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, others read all Israel as the full number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles together. But all agree that God’s promises do not fail, that Jewish people are saved in the same way as everyone else, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians owe them love, humility and the gospel, never contempt.

Could I be hardened? If you are worried that you might be, that very worry is a sign you are not. Hardened hearts are not anxious about God; they are indifferent. The warning is real, and it is for anyone who has heard the gospel many times and keeps saying not yet. But it is answered in the same way it always has been: turn to Christ today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13–15). He has never refused anyone who came.

In a sentence. Isaiah said God had blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts so that they would not see, understand, turn and be healed, and he said this because he saw Christ’s glory and spoke of him.

On a Tuesday. When you sing holy, holy, holy this Sunday, remember whose glory Isaiah saw. You are singing to Jesus.

For worship. The Lord high and lifted up whom Isaiah saw is Jesus. Holy, holy, holy is he. The seraphim covered their faces before him, and he came down from that throne to be lifted up on a cross, so that unclean lips like Isaiah’s and ours could be touched with the coal from the altar and made clean (Isaiah 6:6–7). The whole earth is full of his glory, and the fullest glory of all is the crucified King.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.

Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him. Not all rejected him. Some of the rulers believed, and John uses his full phrase, believed in him; by his own vocabulary these are not mere admirers. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers (19:38–39).

But for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it. Belief without confession. They were afraid.

So that they would not be put out of the synagogue. The same threat as 9:22. The beggar had little to lose; they had a great deal.

For they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God. “Glory” (doxa) here means honour, approval, reputation. There is a play on Isaiah’s glory in verse 41: Isaiah saw the glory of God; they preferred human glory. The root of their silence was not fear alone but love of human approval. Jesus had made the same charge earlier: how can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? (5:44). So this is not chiefly about cowardice. It is about which currency a man is being paid in. Some of these authorities were formidable people. They had simply arranged their lives around a kind of approval that Jesus was about to cost them.

Is this saving faith? Jesus said that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and that confession with the mouth goes with true belief (Romans 10:9–10). Their faith is at best weak and immature, at worst not real. Joseph and Nicodemus later came out into the open.

Am I saved if I have kept my faith secret? This needs care, because there is a way of preaching these verses that produces despair in exactly the wrong people. Notice who John places in this category elsewhere. Nicodemus came at night, and the same book puts him at the cross with about seventy-five pounds of spices (19:39). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (19:38), and it was he who went to Pilate and asked for the body when the twelve had scattered. Both men belong to this verse’s category. Both came through. John records the failure and then records what became of them, which is his way of saying that a hidden faith is a dangerous condition, not a settled verdict. If you are hiding your faith, do not conclude you are lost. Conclude that you must come out, and ask Christ for the courage he gave those two men. Start with one person this week.

Naming the cost. Here is a test more useful than resolving to be braver. Ask what specifically would be lost: name it precisely, not people might think less of me, but the actual thing, the promotion, the friendship, the family meal, the standing in a particular room. Then ask what it is worth, and whose opinion is being bought with it. The men in verse 42 never did that sum out loud. That is why the verse can describe them as believers and still be about their loss.

In a sentence. Even so, many of the rulers believed, but for fear of the Pharisees they kept quiet so as not to be expelled from the synagogue, because they loved human praise more than God’s.

On a Tuesday. Whose approval do you crave most? Choose the glory that comes from God. Think of one place where you have kept quiet about Christ, and ask him for an opportunity to speak there.

For worship. The glory that comes from God is worth more than every human honour put together, and it is freely given to those who are his. One day the Father will honour all who served his Son (v. 26). And the Son was not ashamed of us: he was despised and rejected by men, and endured the cross, despising its shame, so that we might share his glory (Hebrews 12:2). The praise of men fades. His well done lasts for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.”

And Jesus cried out and said. The verb should be heard. It is a shout, the same register as the cry at the tomb and on the last day of the feast (7:37). These are not quiet closing remarks; the last public words of the ministry are given at full voice. And their position is unusual. He hid himself in verse 36; John gave his verdict in verses 37–43; and now, with no sign of a new scene, Jesus speaks again. These final verses (vv. 44–50) are a summary of Jesus’ public teaching, perhaps spoken earlier, placed here as his last word to the world. A summary shows what the author thinks the whole was about.

Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. Read flatly that is nearly a denial, and it means the opposite. Not that faith in Jesus is wrong, but that it does not stop with him: it reaches the Father. To trust Jesus is to trust God. Nobody who comes to him stops at him, because faith in Jesus is not a dead end but a window. Look at him, and what you see is the Father.

And whoever sees me sees him who sent me. Jesus is the perfect revelation of the Father (1:18; 14:9). There is no hidden God behind Jesus who is different from him. That answers a suspicion that has followed Christianity from the beginning: that Christians have become attached to a human figure and lost God somewhere behind him. The prologue said, no one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (1:18). Here is the same claim in the first person, at the end, as the door closes on the public ministry.

Do other religions worship the same God, just without Jesus? No, not according to Jesus. If to see him is to see the Father, then to reject him is to reject the Father; whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (5:23). People of other faiths may truly know that God exists and that they are accountable to him (Romans 1:19–20), and they are to be treated with respect and love. But the God who is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is known and worshipped truly only through his Son (14:6). That is why we share the gospel with them.

In a sentence. Jesus cried out that whoever believes in him believes in the one who sent him, and whoever sees him sees the one who sent him.

On a Tuesday. When you wonder what God is like, how he feels about you, whether he can be trusted, do not guess. Look at Jesus in the Gospels this week. That is the Father’s face.

For worship. When you look at Jesus, you see God. There is no other face of God than his. The one who wept at Lazarus’s grave, washed his disciples’ feet and died for his enemies is not a softer image of a harder God. He is the exact imprint of the Father’s nature (Hebrews 1:3). The heart of God is the heart of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.

I have come into the world as light. The theme of 1:4–9 and 8:12. The prologue said it about him: the true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world (1:9). Chapter 8 had him say it in the temple beside the great lamps of the feast. Chapter 9 had him prove it with mud. And here, in the last thing he says in public, he says it once more, and adds what it is for.

So that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. “Remain” implies that everyone starts in darkness. Not may escape the darkness, but may not remain in it: it assumes where everybody begins. Faith brings us out.

If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. Not now, at his first coming.

For I did not come to judge the world but to save the world. The purpose of his first coming was salvation (3:17). Judgment will come at his second coming (5:22, 27). This is 3:17 again, almost word for word, and it stands at both ends of the public ministry like a pair of brackets. Whatever else is said about judgment in between, and a great deal is, including for judgment I came into this world (9:39), the purpose of his coming never changes.

So does Jesus judge or not? Both, in different senses. He did not come the first time to condemn; he came to save, and anyone who comes to him finds mercy. Yet his coming inevitably divides, because light exposes darkness (3:19–21; 9:39), and on the last day he will sit as judge of all (5:22, 27). The way the two fit is in the next verse. He does not need to pronounce a new sentence on those who reject him; the word they refused will itself be the standard. The purpose of his coming is salvation. Judgment is the consequence of refusing it.

In a sentence. Jesus said he came as light so that believers would not remain in darkness, and he did not judge those who heard and did not keep his words, for he came not to judge but to save the world.

On a Tuesday. Christ came to save you, not to condemn you. Come into his light. Bring him the thing you have been keeping in the dark, and let him deal with it in mercy.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth came first as a Saviour. He had every right to come in judgment, and he came instead as light, to find the lost, to open blind eyes, to lift the dead. Everyone who has come out of darkness into his marvellous light owes it to this: that he did not come to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him (3:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak.

The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge. Rejection has consequences. There is a judge. The phrase “the one who rejects me” means setting aside, disregarding, rather than arguing against. That fits the chapter. Nobody in John 12 has refuted Jesus. The council admitted the signs, the crowd could not answer the donkey, and the authorities in verse 42 actually believed. What the chapter describes is not defeat by argument but a decision to set the whole thing aside and get on with life. That is how most rejection of Christ happens, then and now. Not a conclusion reached. A subject dropped.

The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. His words themselves will be the evidence. Those who heard and rejected them will be judged by them. There is something worth sitting with in the idea that a word is the judge. Nobody will stand before a judge with private information, hidden criteria or an uncertain temper. The standard on the last day is a set of sentences that were spoken publicly, in Galilee and Jerusalem, before crowds, and written down, and have been available ever since in almost every language on earth. There will be no surprises about the criteria. To hear the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility (Matthew 11:20–24; Hebrews 2:1–3). The gospel is never neutral once it has been heard. It arrives as an offer, and it stays as a standard.

For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what to say and what to speak. His words are the Father’s words, which is why rejecting them is so serious. The two verbs are slightly different, roughly the content and the delivery. He claims that neither the substance nor the manner was his own invention. It is a strange thing to be the last claim of a public ministry. A teacher’s closing statement is usually about what he has taught. His is that none of it was his own. And so to refuse his words is not to disagree with a Galilean rabbi. It is to have been handed, by the Father through the Son, a commandment whose content is eternal life, and to have put it down.

What about those who never heard Christ’s words? They will not be judged for rejecting a message they never received. God judges each person justly, by the light he was actually given, and every person has some light: the witness of creation and of conscience, enough to leave them without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). But that light cannot save, because salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–14). Infants who die in infancy and are elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). For everyone else, this is why the church sends missionaries: so that those who have never heard may hear the words that give life.

In a sentence. Jesus said that whoever rejects him and his words has a judge, for his word will judge him on the last day, since he did not speak on his own but as the Father commanded.

On a Tuesday. You have heard his words, many times. Do not let them become a subject you have quietly dropped. Take one of them this week and do it.

For worship. The words that save us now will judge the world on the last day. Receive them gladly. They are the Father’s own words, given to the Son and given by the Son to us, and they have not changed in two thousand years. The same word that will stand as a witness against those who refuse it stands as a pardon for all who receive it, and the Judge who spoke it is the Saviour who died to make it good.

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.

And I know that his commandment is eternal life. The Father’s command to the Son, and through the Son to the world, leads to eternal life. The phrase repays a long look. Not his commandment leads to eternal life, which is what we might expect. The commandment is life. What the Father told the Son to say is not a set of instructions with life attached at the far end as a reward. The words are the thing itself, as he said in Capernaum when the crowd was leaving: the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (6:63). So the public ministry ends where the prologue began: in him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4).

What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me. Jesus’ last public words in John: complete obedience to the Father. From here, he turns to his own (13:1). Nothing more will be said to the world in this Gospel. From the next verse he is alone with the twelve in a room with a basin of water, and the only people who will hear him speak in public again are Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate and a few soldiers.

Three years of speaking. He talked to anybody for three years: crowds who wanted bread, a woman at a well at noon, a teacher who came by night, men who picked up stones twice, a beggar nobody had ever addressed by name. He answered questions from people arguing in bad faith and from people who did not understand a word he said, and he went on doing it until days before he died. And the last thing he says to all of them, at the top of his voice, is that the message was never his own, and that its content is life.

How do I read Jesus’ words so that they give me life? Read them as the Father’s words to you, not as information about the past. Read slowly, a passage at a time, asking what it shows you of Christ and what it asks of you. Read with prayer, asking the Spirit who inspired them to open them to you (14:26). Read with others, in your church, where the word is preached and taught. And obey what you understand; the words of Christ give life to those who keep them, not to those who only admire them (8:51). Life does not come from the reading as a technique. It comes from the living Christ who speaks through what is read.

In a sentence. Jesus said he knew the Father’s command is eternal life, and so he speaks just as the Father has told him.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s words are eternal life. Read them today as if your life depended on them, for it does.

For worship. The last public word of the Son of God was a word about life. After three years of signs and refusals, of bread and stones and tears, he cried out that the Father’s commandment is eternal life, and he went from that street to give it, at the cost of his own. Every word he spoke was the Father’s word, and every word was for us. Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life (6:68).

Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.<sup>3</sup>Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.<sup>4</sup>But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,<sup>5</sup>“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”<sup>6</sup>He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.<sup>8</sup>For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”<sup>9</sup>When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.<sup>10</sup>So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well,<sup>11</sup>because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.<sup>12</sup>The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”<sup>14</sup>And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,<sup>15</sup>“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!”<sup>16</sup>His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.<sup>17</sup>The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness.<sup>18</sup>The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.<sup>19</sup>So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”<sup>20</sup>Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.<sup>21</sup>So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”<sup>22</sup>Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.<sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.<sup>25</sup>Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.<sup>26</sup>If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.<sup>27</sup>“Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ’Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.<sup>28</sup>Father, glorify your name.“ Then a voice came from heaven: ”I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”<sup>29</sup>The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”<sup>30</sup>Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine.<sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.<sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”<sup>33</sup>He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>34</sup>So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”<sup>35</sup>So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.<sup>36</sup>While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them.<sup>37</sup>Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,<sup>38</sup>so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”<sup>39</sup>Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,<sup>40</sup>“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”<sup>41</sup>Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.<sup>42</sup>Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;<sup>43</sup>for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.<sup>44</sup>And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.<sup>45</sup>And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.<sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.<sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.<sup>48</sup>The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.<sup>49</sup>For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak.<sup>50</sup>And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 closes the first half of John’s Gospel, the “book of signs”, and opens the way to the cross. Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus at the table, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas, a thief, complains about the waste; Jesus defends her: she has kept it for the day of his burial. The next day crowds wave palm branches and hail Jesus as the King of Israel as he rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey, fulfilling Zechariah. The Pharisees despair: “the world has gone after him.”

Then some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Like a grain of wheat he must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit; whoever loves his life will lose it. His soul is troubled, but he will not ask to be saved from this hour; instead he prays, “Father, glorify your name,” and a voice from heaven answers. Lifted up from the earth, he will draw all people to himself, and the ruler of this world will be cast out. John then sums up Jesus’ public ministry: despite all his signs, most did not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts; even among the leaders some believed secretly but would not confess him, loving human glory more than God’s. Jesus’ final public appeal follows: he has come as light into the world, and his word will judge those who reject it on the last day.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Just before Passover, knowing his hour has come to return to the Father, Jesus shows the full extent of his love for his own. At supper, with Judas already moved by the devil to betray him, Jesus, conscious of his authority and his origin and destiny in God, lays aside his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes the disciples’ feet. Peter protests and is told he will understand later; when he refuses, Jesus warns that without this washing Peter has no share in him. Peter then asks for a complete wash, but Jesus says the one already bathed needs only his feet cleaned; they are clean, except one. Back at table, Jesus explains that as their Lord and Teacher he has given them an example: they must wash each other’s feet, for no servant outranks his master, and blessing lies in doing it. He knows whom he chose, yet Scripture foretold that a companion at his table would turn against him. He tells them in advance so that they will believe. To receive his messengers is to receive him and the Father who sent him.
verseByVerse.theology: The foot washing is simultaneously a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (you need to have your feet washed to have a part in me). Peter's characteristic resistance — then misunderstanding, then over-correction — clarifies both aspects: the washing Jesus gives is not merely a lesson in humility but the cleansing that makes fellowship with him possible. The once-washed disciple needs only the cleaning of feet — the ongoing renewal of those already justified, not re-justification. This is the distinction between initial cleansing (bath) and ongoing renewal (feet-washing): the one already clean needs only this.
verseByVerse.examples: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (v. 13). The authority of the foot-washing is its own argument. Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (v. 3-4). The servant heart flows from the secure identity: those who are anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know their position in Christ serve without self-protection. Genuine servanthood is not self-abasement but the overflow of a heart that has been secured by the Father's love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,

Meaning first. The second half of John’s Gospel begins here. John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17), far more than the other Gospels give it. Jesus washes his disciples’ feet, exposes the betrayer, gives the new commandment, and then teaches them about his going, the Spirit, and the life of union with him, before praying for them. John does not describe the institution of the Lord’s Supper, which the other Gospels and Paul had already recorded (1 Corinthians 11:23–26).
