He gives us what they left out: the Lord of glory on the floor with a towel round his waist, and the love that put him there.

The setting. It is Thursday evening in Jerusalem, in an upper room, at the Passover season. The lambs are about to be slaughtered, and the true Passover Lamb is hosting his final meal. Before the sun sets again he will be dead and buried. Everything John records from here to the end of chapter 17 is said in a few hours, to men who will all run away before morning.

Now before the Feast of the Passover. A question arises as the chapter opens, and it is the kind a reader notices and then cannot un-notice. John says this happened before the Feast, later says the authorities avoided the governor’s headquarters so that they might eat the Passover (18:28), and calls the day of the crucifixion the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14). Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper plainly as the Passover meal itself. So did Jesus die on the day the lambs were killed, or the day after eating the lamb with his disciples?

Is there a contradiction about the date? The tension is real, but it is smaller than it looks, and most of it dissolves in the wording. The word rendered Preparation is the ordinary Greek term for Friday; it is still the word for Friday in Greek today. So the day of Preparation of the Passover most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. And Passover was used loosely for the whole seven-day festival, so to eat the Passover at 18:28 can easily mean the festival meals that followed. Read that way, John and the others agree: the supper was the Passover meal, and Jesus was crucified on the Friday of the feast. A second solution has long been offered, that different groups reckoned the feast a day apart. Either resolution serves. What should not be said is that John invented a date to make a point. He did not need to. Jesus really did die at Passover, and John’s great theme, behold the Lamb of God, was handed to him by the calendar, not the other way round.

Where is the bread and the cup? All three of the other Gospels record the institution of the Lord’s Supper at this table, and Paul had already written it down for the Corinthians. John gives us a basin and a towel instead. The most likely reason is the one that explains much else in this Gospel: John writes last, with the other accounts long in circulation and the church keeping the Supper for sixty years. He does not repeat what everyone has; he supplies what is missing. And he had already given the meaning of that meal at length in chapter 6: the bread that came down from heaven, the flesh given for the life of the world. Having taught what the Supper means, he gives us here what the Supper requires.

When Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father. All through the Gospel the hour has not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now it has. And John’s word for his death is gentle: a departure, a passing over (metabē), out of this world to the Father. It is fitting at Passover, the feast of the night when the LORD passed over. For Jesus the cross is not the end of a road but a doorway home, and he walks toward it knowing exactly where it leads.

Having loved his own who were in the world. One phrase here reaches all the way back to the prologue and is easy to walk past. The word for his own is idios, and John used it in his opening paragraph, twice in one sentence, in the saddest verse of the Gospel: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). There he had his own and they turned him away. Here, twelve chapters later, on the last night, he has his own again, eleven men in a room and one who is leaving, and this time the sentence ends differently. His own are those the Father gave him (10:3–4; 17:6), the sheep he calls by name.

He loved them to the end. The Greek eis telos can mean to the end of his life, and to the uttermost, completely. John will not decide between duration and degree, because both are true: to the last minute, and to the last inch. The cross is the temporal end of his earthly life and the absolute limit of love’s self-giving. His love would not stop, and it held nothing back. Everything in chapters 13–17 is an expression of this love, and so is the cross that follows them.

When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him. This sets the temperature of the room. The decision has been taken. Whatever conversation happened with the chief priests has already happened, and the money is already agreed (Mark 14:10–11). So the man whose feet are about to be washed has, at that moment, an arrangement in place. He is not being tempted; he is executing. The devil planted the idea, and Judas welcomed it. And John does not tell us this afterwards, as an explanation of how things went wrong. He tells us at the top, before the basin comes out, so that the reader watches the whole washing knowing. Love and treachery sit side by side at one table, and Jesus knows it all and washes Judas’s feet anyway.

Does to the end mean Jesus’ love for me could still run out? No; it means the opposite. To the end is the measure of a love that has already been tested at its worst point and held. It held when one of the Twelve was selling him, when Peter was about to deny him, when all of them were about to run. If it did not fail them that night, it will not fail you on yours. Jesus himself says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (10:28), and Paul that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39). The question to ask is not whether his love will last, but whether you are one of his own, and the mark of his own is that they hear his voice and follow him.

In a sentence. Before Passover, knowing his hour had come to go to the Father, Jesus loved his own to the end, and during supper, when the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart to betray him...

On a Tuesday. Notice where your love for people has a quiet stopping point: the colleague who let you down once, the relative you have privately written off, the friend whose need comes at a bad time. Ask what it would look like to love one of them past the point where you usually stop. Not with a feeling, but with one concrete act this week that costs you something. You will not love to the uttermost. But you can love one step further than you did, because you have been loved all the way.

For worship. He came to his own and his own did not receive him, and on the last night he loved his own to the end anyway. He knew the hour, the betrayer and the cost, and he did not withdraw one degree of his love. This is the Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, the Lamb who walks to the altar on his own feet, the Son going home to the Father by way of the cross. If you are his, you were in that room in his heart, and his love for you has no end, because it was given to the uttermost before you ever asked for it.
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.

Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands. The sentence is built to make one contrast, and it is worth slowing down for. John gives him the largest possible credentials in the same breath: everything handed over (3:35), come from God, going to God. Total authority, known origin, certain destination. And the next thing those hands do is pick up a towel. The hands into which the Father has given the universe are the hands that will wash dirty feet. Jesus does not stoop because he has forgotten who he is. He stoops because he knows exactly who he is.

And that he had come from God and was going back to God. Secure in his origin and his destiny, he is free to serve. The sequence is crucial. Because Jesus knows his authority and his security, he can serve without self-protection. The servant heart flows from the secure identity; those who are uncertain of their status cannot truly serve, because service threatens what they are still trying to establish.

Rose from supper. In the middle of the meal. Not before it, when washing would have been expected and a servant would have done it at the door. Nobody had done it, and the meal had gone on with dirty feet. Luke tells us what the Twelve had been doing over supper: arguing about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24). So Jesus gets up in the middle of the argument.

He laid aside his outer garments. The verb is the one to catch. He laid aside (tithēmi) is the identical word he used repeatedly in chapter 10 about his life: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; I lay it down of my own accord (10:11, 15, 17, 18). And in verse 12 he will take his garments again, with the verb of taking his life up again. He lays aside his clothes as he will lay down his life, and he will put them on again as he will take his life up again. The footwashing is the crucifixion in miniature, acted out at a supper table hours before it happens. And behind it lies the whole movement of the incarnation: he who was in the form of God emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:6–8).

And taking a towel, tied it around his waist. What he is doing is dressing as a slave. He is now, visibly, in the costume of the lowest person in the household. Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; even Jewish slaves were often not required to do it. Roads were dusty, people wore sandals, and feet were filthy. No disciple had done it.

Where does the freedom to serve come from? Not from thinking little of yourself. The man in this verse knows exactly who he is; John has just told us in the most extravagant terms available, and that is given as the reason he can kneel. Nobody who is still trying to establish his position can afford to take the towel. Only someone whose position is beyond question has nothing to lose by it. That is why the Christian’s freedom to serve grows out of knowing who he is in Christ: a child of God, forgiven, loved, with his future secure. A man who knows he is accepted by the Father no longer needs the best seat to prove anything.

In a sentence. Knowing that the Father had given him all things, and that he had come from God and was returning to God, Jesus got up from supper, took off his outer garments, and tied a towel around his waist.

On a Tuesday. You will never be too important for the towel. The one with all things in his hands picked it up. Notice the jobs you quietly regard as beneath you, the tasks you leave because someone less busy or less senior will surely do them. Pick one up today without mentioning it. And when you feel the reluctance, ask what it is protecting: usually it is a sense of position that Christ has already made unnecessary.

For worship. The hands that flung the stars into space and hold all things together tied a towel round his waist. He did not cling to his rights; he laid them aside as he would lay aside his life, and took them up again only after the work was done. The Lord of all became the servant of all, not because he lost sight of his glory, but because this is what his glory is like. There is no other God who kneels, and this one knelt for us.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”

Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet. The details are slow and deliberate, as if an eyewitness remembered every movement: the water poured, the basin, the washing, the drying with the towel he was wearing. It has to be said how far down this was, because modern readers hear footwashing as a quaint courtesy rather than the thing it was. Roads were dust or mud; people wore open sandals; the same streets carried animals. Feet arriving at a house were genuinely filthy, and washing them was the job at the bottom of the household list. The rabbinic material is explicit that a Jewish slave could not be required to do it. There were rabbis who said a disciple should do anything for his teacher except loosen his sandal.

Thirteen men, one basin. So there was a basin and a jug in that room, and there had been all evening, and nobody had touched them. Thirteen men, one basin, and a dispute about rank. Then the Lord of glory kneels at each pair of feet in turn.

He came to Simon Peter. Which implies others first. John does not say in what order he went round, and Peter’s objection comes partway through. Whatever the sequence, at some point in that circuit he knelt in front of Judas, and Judas put his feet in the water, and neither of them said anything that John thought worth recording.

Lord, do you wash my feet? In Greek the words you and my stand side by side for emphasis: Lord, you, my feet? Peter is shocked, and his objection is not false modesty. He is registering that the universe is the wrong way up. And he is right, which is what makes him wrong. Everything Peter’s instinct is protecting is true: this is the Lord, and lords do not wash feet. What he cannot yet accommodate is a Lord who does, and within a day he will have to accommodate a Lord who is executed, which is the same problem at full scale. Peter’s difficulty at the basin and his difficulty at the cross are one difficulty. The one who should be served serves; the one whose feet should be washed washes. The incarnation and the atonement are both versions of the same reversal.

Why did Jesus wash Judas’s feet if he knew? Because his love is not a reward for loyalty. He washed the feet of a man he knew had already sold him, and the knowledge did not change the service by one degree. It was a real kindness and, as the morsel will be in verse 26, a real appeal, though it was refused. It also shows the disciples, and us, that the command to wash one another’s feet reaches even those who will wrong us (Luke 6:27–28). It does not mean Judas was cleansed; verse 10 says plainly he was not. Outward kindness from Christ is not the same as inward cleansing by Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus poured water into a basin and began washing and drying the disciples’ feet, and when he came to Peter, Peter asked whether he, the Lord, would wash his feet.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your life whose feet you would least like to wash: the one who has used you, or criticised you, or simply wearies you. What would a hidden act of kindness toward that person look like this week? Not a gesture to make a point, but something done quietly and well, as Jesus did it for Judas without a word.

For worship. Stand amazed with Peter. The Lord of glory kneels on a stone floor before sinners, with dust and water on his hands, and moves from one pair of feet to the next, including the feet that would walk out into the night to sell him. Peter was right that the picture is upside down. It is upside down because grace is upside down: the Holy One serving the unholy, the Master washing the servants, the Judge kneeling before the guilty to make them clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.” Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”

What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand. This is a promise worth keeping for a dark stretch. He does not explain. He could have; the explanation comes ten verses later. Instead he asks Peter to let him proceed without it. The understanding is promised, and it is promised for later: after the cross and resurrection, when the Spirit would bring these things to mind (12:16; 14:26), Peter would see that this washing pointed to Jesus’ death for him.

Living in the not yet. That is the position a good deal of the Christian life is lived from. Something is being done that does not make sense while it is happening, and the assurance offered is not an account of it but a person’s word that it will make sense in retrospect. John himself is the proof: he is writing this sixty years afterwards, and the afterward arrived.

You shall never wash my feet. The Greek is as absolute as English can make it: a double negative with an eternal future (ou mē … eis ton aiōna), you shall never, to eternity, wash my feet. He is not hesitating. He is forbidding. It is Peter’s pride dressed up as humility. He would rather serve than be served. But refusing grace is not humility.

If I do not wash you, you have no share with me. The sharpest sentence in the chapter. The word is meros: a portion, a part, an allotted share, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for a tribe’s inheritance in the land. No part in me. No inheritance. The washing now clearly means more than feet. Unless Christ cleanses us from sin, we have no part in him or his kingdom. Salvation begins with letting Christ do for us what we cannot do for ourselves. Which turns the whole exchange: Peter thinks he is defending his master’s dignity, and he is in fact refusing his own salvation, and the two look identical from inside.

The refusal that looks like reverence. Here is the test, and it catches a particular kind of good person. There is a refusal of grace that presents as humility: I could not ask that, others need it more, I will manage. It can be indistinguishable from reverence. The way to tell them apart is to ask what it protects. Reverence protects God’s honour. This protects a self-image in which one does not need to be carried, and it will keep a man out of the kingdom while he is being admired for it. I am not worthy can be a deeper refusal than I do not need it.

What if I feel too dirty or too unworthy to come to Christ? Then you are exactly the person he washes. The basin is for dirty feet; clean ones do not need it. Feeling unworthy is not the obstacle. The obstacle is refusing to let him do what only he can do. You do not clean yourself up first and then present yourself. You come as you are, put your feet in the water, so to speak, and let him wash you: that is what faith is. His word to Peter is his word to you: unless he washes you, you have no part with him, and if he washes you, you are completely clean (v. 10).

In a sentence. Jesus told Peter he would understand later, and when Peter refused to let him wash his feet, Jesus said that unless he washed him, Peter would have no share with him.

On a Tuesday. Let Christ serve you. The hardest humility is accepting grace you cannot repay. Notice also how you receive help from other people: the meal brought when you are ill, the offer to cover a shift, the gift you cannot return. If you always deflect, ask whether something in you would rather be the giver because giving keeps you in control. Receive one kindness this week simply, with thanks.

For worship. He will not be refused, because his love will not leave us dirty. He stands with the basin and the towel, and says to the proudest of his friends that without his washing there is no share in him at all. And then he goes to the cross to make the washing real. Every part we have in Christ, every inheritance and every hope, comes to us by his hands and none by ours. Blessed be the Lord who insists on serving us.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!” Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”

Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head! Peter swings to the opposite extreme in a single verse, and it is entirely in character: if this is the condition, wash all of me. If washing means belonging to Jesus, then wash everything. Impulsive, but full of love. He is wrong twice in ninety seconds, in opposite directions, and both times because he is trying to control the terms. First he will have none of it; then he will have more than is offered. What he never does is simply put his feet in the water.

The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. Jesus’ answer turns on two Greek verbs that English flattens into one. The one who has bathed (louō, to wash the whole body) does not need to wash (niptō, to wash a part). The picture is ordinary domestic life. Guests bathed at home before a banquet and then walked to the house through the streets, and by the time they arrived only their feet needed attention. Nobody had a second bath at the door. So: one bath, many footwashings.

Justification once, cleansing daily. That is the whole of the Christian doctrine of assurance and confession in a household image. The one who has been cleansed by Christ once for all, in justification and regeneration (Titus 3:5), does not need to be saved again. The justification is not renewed each time it is damaged, because it was never resting on the walking. And yet the walking does soil, daily and genuinely, and the feet do need washing (1 John 1:7–9), and pretending otherwise is not faith but grubbiness. Justification happens once; confession and forgiveness go on.

A textual note. Some early manuscripts lack the words except for his feet, and a footnote may appear in a modern Bible. The shorter reading gives essentially the same sense, that the bathed man does not need washing, and the distinction between the bath and the feet is carried by the two verbs regardless.

And you are clean, but not every one of you. The sentence darkens the room again. The disciples are clean, cleansed by the word he has spoken to them (15:3). But not all. Twelve pairs of feet have been washed. Eleven men are clean. The washing was identical and the outcome was not.

When I sin as a Christian, do I need to be saved all over again? No. If you have truly trusted Christ, you have had the bath, and you are completely clean in God’s sight; your standing as his child does not lapse every time you fall. What you need is the footwashing: to bring that sin to him in honest confession, trust that he forgives it (1 John 1:9), and get up and walk on. A believer who keeps asking to be saved again is like Peter asking for his head to be washed, and the answer is the same: you are clean. But a believer who never confesses is walking about with dirty feet. Both the once-for-all and the daily belong to the Christian life.

In a sentence. Peter asked Jesus to wash his hands and head too, but Jesus said that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, being completely clean, and they were clean, though not all of them.

On a Tuesday. At the end of today, before you sleep, bring Christ the dust of this one day: the sharp word, the neglected duty, the private indulgence. Name each specifically, thank him that you are already bathed, and receive his washing for the feet. Then sleep as a clean child, not as a defendant awaiting trial.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you are completely clean, not partly, not provisionally, but completely, by the blood of the one who washed you once for all. And still he stoops each day with the basin, because he will not have his people walk about soiled. Once for all and every day: the finished work and the faithful High Priest. Bring him the dust of today, and he will wash it.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.” When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?”

For he knew who was to betray him. This verse should not be smoothed over. It is placed here, after the washing, so that the reader is told twice, at verse 2 and again at verse 11, that nothing about Judas was hidden. There is no possibility of reading this chapter as a story about a man who was fooled. Judas had his feet washed, but was not clean. Outward contact with Jesus does not make a person clean. Only faith joins a person to him.

The warning of the means of grace. Judas received the footwashing along with the eleven, but without the cleansing it signified. External participation in the means of grace, baptism, the Lord’s Supper, the ministry of the word, does not by itself produce inward cleansing. They are genuine means by which God blesses his people, but they bless through faith, not apart from it. A person can sit under the word, take the bread, and be baptised, and still be Judas.

When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place. The two verbs of verse 12 close the loop that verse 4 opened. He took (elaben) his garments, the verb of taking up his life again (10:17–18). Laid aside, taken up. He has acted out the whole thing at the table: the descent from his place at the meal to the floor, and the return. After the cross come the resurrection and the return to his place at the Father’s side.

Do you understand what I have done to you? Having done it, he asks a question rather than delivering a lesson. Note the order, because it is his method throughout this Gospel and it is the reverse of ours. The sign comes first and the explanation second. He turned water into wine before anyone knew what to make of it, fed five thousand before the discourse about bread, healed the blind man before he explained anything. Here he washes twelve pairs of feet in silence, dresses, sits down, and then asks what they made of it. And the answer at that moment was almost certainly no; verse 7 has already said so. He asks anyway, not to expose them but to begin the explanation, which is the next thing he does: a second meaning, an example.

Can a person go to church, be baptised and take communion, and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and Judas is the warning. He was chosen as an apostle, lived with Jesus for three years, preached, saw miracles, and had his feet washed by the Son of God, and he was not clean. This is not said to make sincere believers anxious, but to stop anyone resting on outward things. The question is not whether you have been near Jesus but whether you have trusted him. If you have come to him as a sinner and rest on him alone, the outward signs are real blessings to you. If you have not, no amount of religious contact will substitute. Come to him today.

In a sentence. Because Jesus knew who would betray him, he said not all were clean; and after washing their feet and returning to his place, he asked if they understood what he had done.

On a Tuesday. Being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. Judas sat at the table and was washed, and was lost. Ask yourself honestly where your confidence rests: on your attendance, your upbringing, your service, or on Christ himself. Then thank God for every means of grace in your week, and use them as places to meet him, not as tokens to show him.

For worship. He knew. He knew who would betray him and he knelt anyway; he knew the whole cost of the cross and laid down his life anyway; and having done it, he took it up again and sat down in his place. Nothing about us takes him by surprise, and nothing in us made him withdraw. Glory to the Saviour who stooped with full knowledge, and rose to his throne with the work complete.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. Jesus does not modestly disclaim the titles. He takes them without a flicker. There is no self-deprecation anywhere in this passage, no protest at being called that. The man who has just been on the floor with the towel claims both titles in front of twelve witnesses. His service does not lessen his authority; it shows what kind of Lord he is.

Your Lord and Teacher. The order of the titles in verse 13 is worth noticing, because he reverses it in verse 14. They call him Teacher and Lord; he says your Lord and Teacher, putting the greater first for the argument he is about to make.

If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. The argument goes from greater to lesser. If the Lord serves, how much more should the servants. Ought (opheilete) is a word of obligation, the language of a debt owed. The way Jesus loves is the way his people are to love: the voluntary downward movement of serving those who cannot repay.

Where Christians differ: is footwashing an ordinance? Some churches practise footwashing as a regular ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and they are not being silly: the sentence says you also ought to wash one another’s feet. Verdict: Jesus calls it an example (v. 15), not a sacrament. The apostles never practised or commanded it as a church rite; in 1 Timothy 5:10 it appears as an act of humble hospitality. The command is to do the humble, menial, loving service that meets real needs, whatever form that takes today. A literal footwashing can be a moving act, but the point is the lowly love behind it.

The harder obedience. Where a church washes feet, it is obeying the surface of the text, and no harm is done. Where a church does not, it is under exactly the same obligation and has a harder time discharging it, because the substance is not a ritual with a towel but the willingness to do, for one another, the job nobody wants. That is the more searching form of the command. A footwashing service can be got through in twenty minutes once a year. What he is describing has no fixed occasion and no end.

What does washing one another’s feet look like today? It looks like doing the needed thing nobody notices or wants. Cleaning up after the church meal. Visiting the elderly member who repeats herself. Changing the nappy, sitting with the dying, driving the person without a car, doing the paperwork for the widow, listening to the same trouble for the fifth time. It includes the humbler work of forgiving, of bearing with someone’s faults, and of gently helping a brother with his sin (Galatians 6:1–2). The mark of footwashing is that it is beneath your dignity and meets a real need.

In a sentence. Jesus said that they were right to call him Teacher and Lord, and if he, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, they should wash one another’s feet.

On a Tuesday. What is the lowest, dirtiest job no one wants to do in your home, church or workplace? That is your towel today. Do it, and do not let anyone know you were the one.

For worship. The Lord whom angels worship and the Teacher whose word is truth knelt on the floor and washed his servants. He did not stop being Lord to do it; he showed us that the Lord of heaven is the one who serves. We owe him everything, and he has turned our debt into the privilege of serving one another in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

For I have given you an example. The word is hypodeigma: a pattern, a specimen, a model laid down to be copied (1 Peter 2:21). The footwashing is not a unique act to be admired from a distance, but a pattern of loving service to be lived out in the community of disciples.

That you also should do just as I have done to you. What is to be copied is stated more precisely than we usually notice. Not something vaguely similar in spirit. The measure of the imitation is the original act, and the original act was performed by somebody with all things in his hands, for people who were arguing about rank, including one who was selling him. That is why this cannot be reduced to a general disposition toward helpfulness. The pattern has specifications: it is voluntary, it is downward, it is done for people who will not repay it, and at least one of the recipients does not deserve it.

A servant is not greater than his master. If the master is not too proud to wash feet, the servant cannot be. The hierarchy of dignity that the world constructs is inverted in the kingdom: the greatest serves, the first becomes last, the Lord takes the towel. And this proverb comes back later in the farewell discourse with the comfort taken out of it. In chapter 15 the same sentence will mean that if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (15:20). The proverb cuts twice: it puts a limit on how high a disciple can hold himself, and a floor under how much he can expect to be spared.

Nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. The word for messenger is apostolos, apostle, and this is the only time the word occurs in John’s Gospel: in a sentence about not being above the job. It cuts against a particular danger in Christian service: the servant who begins to think the work is his. Everything an apostle has, the message, the authority, the commission, arrived from somewhere else. A man carrying a letter is not the author of it, and the moment he starts behaving as though he were, he has misunderstood his own position in a way that will eventually show.

Am I meant to copy everything Jesus did? Not everything. Some of what he did belongs to him alone: he alone died for sins, rose from the dead, and is Lord. We follow him as servants, not as substitutes. But in his humility, his love and his patience toward the undeserving, he is meant to be copied, and the footwashing is given precisely as that kind of example. Peter says Christ left us an example so that we might follow in his steps, and in the same breath says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:21–24). He is first our Saviour, and then our pattern.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had given them an example to follow, for a servant is not greater than his master, nor a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in church in any visible way, preaching, leading, teaching, organising, ask whether you have begun to think of the work as yours. One test: how do you feel when someone else gets the credit, or when your role is changed without your being consulted? The servant carries the master’s letter; he does not need his own name on it.

For worship. Christ is our pattern as well as our Saviour, and he is our pattern only because he is first our Saviour. He did not lay a burden on us and walk away; he went first, down to the floor and down to the grave, and every step we take after him is a step on ground he has already walked. The Sent One of the Father sends us, and his sending is our dignity.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ‘He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’

If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. One of the most exposed sentences in the Gospel. Two conditions, and the blessing hangs on the second. Knowing is assumed: he has just explained it, and they cannot claim ignorance. What is not assumed is the doing, and the blessing is attached there (James 1:22–25). It is worth pausing on how uncomfortable that is for a commentary and for anyone reading one. Every commentary ever written, this one included, is on the wrong side of that sentence. Knowledge about footwashing is not the blessing. The verse distinguishes between the two and places the happiness on the far side of the gap.

I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. Jesus chose the Twelve, including Judas (6:70). But here whom I have chosen probably means chosen for salvation: he knows his own, and he knows Judas is not among them. His choosing of Judas was not ignorance; it was in sovereign purpose, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me. From Psalm 41:9, where David laments a close friend’s betrayal, probably Ahithophel, his counsellor, who went over to Absalom and later hanged himself, as Judas would (2 Samuel 15–17). David wrote it about his own betrayal; Jesus quotes it about a man sitting at the table with bread in his hand. To eat someone’s bread was to bind yourself in friendship. Lifting the heel is a picture of treachery: what a horse does before it kicks, or showing someone the sole of one’s foot, a deep insult in the East. Judas would betray the friend who had just fed him and washed his feet.

What he leaves out. The psalm says my close friend in whom I trusted, and Jesus drops that clause. He could not say it. He had known from the beginning who would betray him (6:64). That is its own kind of loneliness, and it is worth naming. He was betrayed by someone he had not trusted, and had kept beside him anyway for three years, and had just washed.

Was Judas, then, chosen to be lost and so less guilty? Jesus chose him to be an apostle (6:70), not to be saved. Judas acted willingly, for money, and was fully responsible; Scripture foretold his act but did not force it (Acts 1:16). Jesus said it would have been better for that man not to have been born (Matthew 26:24). God’s sovereignty and Judas’s guilt stand side by side, as they do at the cross itself (Acts 2:23).

Could I turn out to be a Judas? If you are asking that question with fear and longing to be true to Christ, it is very unlikely you are. Judas was not a tender believer who fell; he was a thief all along (12:6), and he never showed grief over his sin before Christ, only remorse that ended in despair. The warning is for those who are comfortable near Jesus without loving him. If you hate your sin, run to Christ with it, and want him more than what he gives, those are the marks of the Spirit’s work, and the one who began that work will finish it (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. Jesus said they would be blessed if they did what they knew, but he was not speaking of all of them, for he knew whom he had chosen, and Scripture would be fulfilled that one who ate his bread would turn against him.

On a Tuesday. Knowing about service is easy. Doing it is the blessing. Choose one thing you already know you should do, a letter of thanks, an apology, a visit, a gift, and do it before the week is out. Do one hidden act of service today, and let the doing, not the reading, be where you look for blessing.

For worship. He knew whom he had chosen, and he loved them. He knew who would lift the heel against him, and he still fed him and washed his feet. Even the treachery of a friend was written beforehand and woven into God’s purpose, so that the greatest evil ever committed became the means of the greatest good. The Lord who reigns over betrayal can be trusted with every wound you carry.
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.

I am telling you this now, before it takes place. The reason he tells them in advance is pastoral rather than merely predictive. Think about what the betrayal would otherwise have done to them. One of the Twelve, hand-picked, sells him, and if that had come without warning, the obvious conclusion is that Jesus had been taken in. A man who cannot see through his own treasurer is not the Son of God. So the announcement is protective work done in advance. When it happens, the disciples will have two readings to choose between, and he has given them the true one before the event, so that the thing which looks most like a failure of his judgement becomes evidence of the opposite.

That when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Again I am (egō eimi), the words of 8:24 and 8:28. The God of Isaiah declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10; 48:5), and Isaiah 43:10 is closely echoed: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Only God knows the future. Jesus’ prediction proves that he is the I AM. The claim is laid down once more, at supper, attached to a warning about a friend. This is the function of prophecy in John’s Gospel: not to satisfy curiosity about the future but to strengthen faith when the future arrives.

Whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. This looks like a change of subject and is not. He has been talking about a man who was sent and went wrong. Now he tells the other eleven what it will mean when they are sent. The chain runs unbroken from the Father through the Son to them, and how people treat them is how they are treating him, and the Father (Matthew 10:40). Even after Judas’s betrayal, the apostles’ mission stands. Their authority comes from Christ, and Christ’s from the Father.

The dignity conferred. It is an extraordinary weight to place on eleven fishermen and tradesmen, and it is placed on them the same night one of their number sells him and another denies him and all of them run. He does not wait until they have proved reliable.

How do I receive the ones Jesus sends today? The apostles were sent once, and their message now stands written in the New Testament; to receive their word is to receive Christ, and to reject it is to reject him. So the first application is to receive the apostolic Scriptures as the very word of the Lord. The principle reaches further, in a secondary way: those who faithfully bring that word to you, your pastor, a missionary, a friend who shares the gospel, are to be welcomed for the sake of the one whose message they carry, not for their eloquence (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

In a sentence. Jesus told them this before it happened so that when it did they would believe that he is the I AM, and that whoever receives those he sends receives him and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. When something happens in your life that seems to say God has lost control, a betrayal, a diagnosis, a collapse, go back to what he has already told you: that in this world you will have trouble, that he works all things for good to those who love him, that he will never leave you. Read one of those promises today, before the trouble comes, so that when it comes you remember he told you beforehand.

For worship. Nothing takes Christ by surprise, not even betrayal. He is the I AM who declares the end from the beginning, and he told his friends in advance so that the darkest event of the night would become a reason to believe in him. The Father sent the Son, and the Son sends his servants, and the whole chain is held in sovereign hands. Rest in his foreknowledge; it is the foreknowledge of the one who loves you to the end.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Troubled in spirit, Jesus announces that one of them will betray him, and the bewildered disciples look at one another. At Peter’s signal, the disciple Jesus loves, reclining beside him, asks who it is. Jesus answers that it is the one to whom he gives the dipped morsel, and he hands it to Judas. Satan enters Judas, and Jesus tells him to act quickly; the others assume he is being sent on an errand with the common purse. Judas goes out into the night. Then Jesus says that the Son of Man is now glorified, and God in him. He will soon leave them, and they cannot follow yet. He gives them a new command, to love one another as he has loved them, the mark by which all will recognise his disciples. When Peter insists he will follow even to death, Jesus predicts that before the rooster crows Peter will disown him three times.
verseByVerse.theology: Love one another as I have loved you is the social ethics of the atonement made into community commandment. The 'as I have loved you' is the measure and the model: not abstract love or sentiment, but the costly, self-giving, foot-washing, cross-bearing love that Jesus has just demonstrated and is about to complete. This is a new commandment not because love was absent from the Mosaic law (Lev. 19:18) but because the standard is new: as I have loved you is qualitatively greater than 'as yourself.' The measure of Christian community love is the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter's denial is embedded within Peter's most confident declaration. He will not only follow Jesus but lay down his life for him. Jesus accepts neither the protest nor the probability: Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you — the triple denial will come before morning. Jesus does not shame Peter but tells the truth that Peter needs to hear: his fidelity rests on a foundation Peter has not yet tested. The testing will come, the failure will happen, and the restoration that follows (ch. 21) will be built on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.

Jesus was troubled in his spirit. This is the third time John uses this verb of him, and the three occurrences map the whole approach of the cross. At the tomb of Lazarus he was greatly troubled (11:33). In the temple courts, when the Greeks came: now is my soul troubled (12:27). And now, at the table, troubled in his spirit. Each time it is agitation, churning, and each time it is provoked by death: somebody else’s, then his own, and now the man who will arrange it. Betrayal by a friend cut deep. The Son of God was not serene in the sense of untouched; he felt it.

And testified. A solemn declaration, the language of a witness on oath. What he is about to say is not a guess or a mood but testimony.

One of you will betray me. One of the Twelve. The betrayer is not a stranger but a companion of the table.

The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke. What is remarkable is this verse rather than the one before. He says one of you will betray me, and eleven men look at each other with no idea who is meant. Judas had been the treasurer for years. He had been stealing from the bag the whole time (12:6). He had gone to the chief priests, taken money, and come back to supper. And not one of the men who had lived on the road with him, slept in the same rooms, and eaten every meal with him, had the faintest suspicion. He had hidden his heart perfectly.

Is it I? Matthew and Mark record that they each asked, Is it I? (Mark 14:19), which is the other half of the same fact. Nobody could point at Judas, and every one of them was uncertain enough about himself to ask. That is worth having in both directions. A man can be indistinguishable from a disciple for years, not by clever acting but by doing the same things and going to the same places, and be nothing of the kind. And the disciples’ instinct, when told there was a traitor at the table, was to look inward rather than around the room. It is the healthier reflex, a healthy self-suspicion, and the one Judas never had.

Is it wrong for Jesus to be troubled, if he is God? No. He is truly God and truly man, and as man he had a real human soul that could be grieved, shaken and pained, without any sin (Hebrews 4:15). His trouble was not doubt or panic; it was the holy grief of a pure heart facing treachery and death. That is a great comfort. When you are troubled by betrayal or loss, you are not praying to a Saviour who cannot understand. He has been there, at a table with a friend who had sold him.

In a sentence. Deeply troubled, Jesus solemnly declared that one of them would betray him, and the disciples looked at one another, not knowing whom he meant.

On a Tuesday. Judas seemed no different from the others. Examine your own heart before you suspect others’. When you hear a sermon about a sin, resist the instinct to think of who needed to hear it. Ask first: Lord, is it I?

For worship. The Son of God was troubled in spirit for us. He did not face the betrayal untouched; he felt the full weight of a friend’s treachery and went on loving. He is the High Priest who sympathises with our weakness, because he has sat where we sit and been wounded where we are wounded, and he did not sin.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.

One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. The first appearance of the disciple whom Jesus loved, a title that will recur and never be attached to a name. He is at the supper, at the cross (19:26), at the empty tomb (20:2), on the beach (21:7, 20), and named at the end as the one who wrote these things (21:24). He is almost certainly John, son of Zebedee, as early church tradition says, and nothing in the book contradicts it. Note the modesty of the arrangement. He never uses his own name. What he does record about himself is that he was loved, which is either the most self-effacing or the most confident thing a writer could say, and probably both. He describes himself not by his love for Jesus but by Jesus’ love for him. Not that Jesus did not love the others, but John marvels that he was loved.

Was reclining at table at Jesus’ side. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, so the man to the host’s right had his head near the host’s chest and could lean back to speak privately. The ESV margin gives the Greek as in the bosom of Jesus. And the last time John wrote those words was in the prologue’s final sentence, about the Son: the only God, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (1:18), where the Greek has in the bosom of the Father. Same phrase. So the Gospel’s opening picture of the Son against the Father’s heart is reproduced at the supper table, with a man in the Son’s place, and the man is the one who will write it all down. He tells us who Jesus is because he was lying against him when he found out.

So Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking. Peter was further away and could not ask quietly. He cannot get at the information himself, so he signals to the man who can. It is characteristic of the pair throughout this Gospel. Peter acts; John sees. Peter, who will soon fail most visibly, organises the inquiry; John, who will stand at the cross, is already in the place of intimate witness.

Did Jesus have favourites? Not in any sense that slights the others. He loved all his own to the end (v. 1), and he died for each. John’s title is not a claim that he was loved more but a confession of wonder that he was loved at all, and every believer may say the same of himself: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Jesus did have friendships of different closeness, as any true man does: the Twelve, then Peter, James and John, then John. Closeness in friendship is not partiality in salvation.

In a sentence. The disciple Jesus loved was reclining next to him, so Peter signalled to him to ask Jesus who he meant.

On a Tuesday. How would you describe yourself, if you had to do it in one phrase? By your work, your failures, your service, your opinions? Try John’s way. Begin today by saying to yourself, before anything else: I am one whom Jesus loves. Then go into the day as that person.

For worship. As the Son rests in the bosom of the Father, so the beloved disciple rested against the Son, and so every believer is held near the heart of Christ. The eternal love between the Father and the Son has opened to take in sinners. Think of yourself as John did: the one whom Jesus loves. It is true of every believer, and it is the best thing that will ever be said about you.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.

Leaning back against Jesus. He leans back to whisper, and asks the question Peter wanted asked: Lord, who is it?

It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it. Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour, a special gesture of friendship from the host. Bread was dipped into a common dish, perhaps of bitter herbs or sauce, and given to a particular guest: a host singling somebody out for favour, the equivalent of serving him first. There are cultures where it is still done. So the morsel itself is not a mark of guilt.

The seating plan. There is something here that most readers never see, and it changes the scene. The place of highest honour at such a meal was immediately beside the host, close enough that he could reach it without effort. The beloved disciple is on Jesus’ right, since he leans back against his chest to ask. And Jesus hands the morsel to Judas without any indication of getting up or passing it along. That puts Judas within arm’s reach on the other side, perhaps in the place of honour. Whether or not the seating was deliberate, it means the two men closest to Jesus at that supper may well have been the disciple he loved and the man who had already sold him, one on each side.

So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. A final offer of love. Even now, Jesus reaches out to him. The identification of the betrayer is made by an act of hospitality. Nobody else at the table registers it as an accusation, which is exactly why they do not understand what has happened when Judas leaves. Only John knew the meaning of the gesture. All the others saw was a kindness. Consider what that gesture was. Jesus knew everything, the arrangement, the money, the hour, and what he does with the knowledge is offer the man the best piece of bread. There is no scene, no denunciation, no naming to the room. Eleven men go on eating. It is the last thing he ever gives him.

Was Judas present for the Lord’s Supper? Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the cup (Luke 22:21), while Matthew and Mark place it before, and John has Judas leave right after the morsel. Luke often arranges events by topic rather than strict order, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the bread and cup were shared.

Grace offered and refused. The bread given and received could have been a token of friendship restored. Judas receives the morsel that names him, and it seals him instead. Grace offered and refused becomes the occasion of judgement.

In a sentence. The disciple leaned back and asked Jesus who it was, and Jesus said it was the one to whom he would give the dipped morsel, and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.

On a Tuesday. Jesus honoured his betrayer to the end. Love your enemies, and keep offering kindness to those who wrong you. Is there someone you need to confront? You may still have to, but notice how Jesus did it: privately, without humiliating him before the room, and with an open hand. Ask whether your way of dealing with the person who has wronged you leaves the door open for him to come back.

For worship. With every reason to denounce, he gave bread. With the betrayer at arm’s length, he offered honour. This is the heart of the Lord we serve: slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, holding out kindness to the last moment to those who are already turning away. If he did that for Judas, how sure may his own be of his tenderness toward them.
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.” Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.

Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. It is the only time John uses the name Satan in the whole Gospel, and the timing is exact: after the morsel. The last kindness offered was the point at which the door closed. That is a solemn thing, and it should not be softened. Grace refused does not leave a man where it found him. Verse 2 said the devil had already put the idea into his heart; verse 27 says he entered (Luke 22:3). Between those two is a washing and a piece of bread, both received, neither of them opening anything. Refused love hardens. Judas is not a puppet; he chose, and his choice gave Satan entry.

What you are going to do, do quickly. Hear how strange it is. Not do not. Not a plea, not a warning, not even a rebuke. A release, with the timing attached. Jesus is in control: he sets the timing of his own betrayal. Judas thinks he is running an operation. He has chosen his moment, kept his own counsel, and fooled eleven men. And the man he is selling tells him to get on with it, and he goes when he is told, and the arrest happens on the night Jesus intends to die rather than any of the several other nights available.

Not permission, but enough. This command is not permission, and it is not encouragement, and it should not be read as either. It is the last word Jesus ever speaks to Judas, and it is a dismissal from the room: the point at which a man who has decided is allowed to go and do it. There is nothing in it of go ahead. There is a great deal in it of enough. God does not compel anybody’s betrayal. But there comes a moment when he stops restraining it, and this verse is what that sounds like.

Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him. Even John did not yet put it together. John says so twice, here and in the next verse, and it is characteristic: the most decisive moment of the evening passes in front of eleven witnesses and registers as nothing. The cross is not understood until the Spirit interprets it in the light of the resurrection.

Can a Christian be possessed by Satan like Judas? No. A true believer belongs to Christ and is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt, accuse and harass a Christian, and a Christian can give him a foothold by sin (Ephesians 4:27), but he cannot own one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never a believer (6:64, 70); he was a man who had kept company with Jesus while his heart belonged elsewhere. The way to resist the devil is to submit to God and to keep near to Christ (James 4:7–8), not to live in fear.

In a sentence. When Judas took the morsel, Satan entered him, and Jesus told him to do quickly what he was going to do, though no one at the table understood why.

On a Tuesday. If there is a sin you keep hearing warnings about and keep putting off dealing with, take this verse seriously. Every refusal of grace makes the next refusal easier. Deal with it today: confess it to God, tell a trusted Christian friend, and remove what feeds it.

For worship. Even the hour of betrayal was under Christ’s command. Satan entered Judas, and still it was Jesus who said when. The prince of darkness thought he was striking the decisive blow, and he was carrying out the plan by which he himself would be cast out (12:31). Nothing in your life is out of his hands, not even the worst that others intend against you.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.

Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag. He was the treasurer (12:6). The disciples’ two guesses show how completely normal Judas seemed.

Jesus was telling him, Buy what we need for the feast. For the rest of the Passover festival, perhaps. That was the sort of errand the man with the bag would ordinarily be sent out to do.

Or that he should give something to the poor. Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom, and Jesus’ group gave regularly. It is the very cause Judas had championed so publicly over Mary’s ointment (12:5). Nobody thinks anything is wrong. The treasurer has been sent on an errand at night, which is odd but not sinister, and eleven men return to their supper. That is how betrayal generally leaves a room: not with a slammed door but with a plausible explanation that everybody accepts because they have no reason not to. The forces of darkness always have their cover story.

So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. He leaves the light. He gets up from a table where the Light of the world is sitting, walks to the door, and goes out.

And it was night. Four words in Greek, the darkest in the Gospel, and John puts them at the end of the sentence where they cannot be missed. It is a statement of fact: it was after sundown, and the meal was a night meal. But John does not write about darkness by accident. He opened the book with it: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). Nicodemus came by night. People loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (3:19). Jesus had said on the way to Bethany that if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him (11:10; 12:35). Note that John does not say he went out into the night. He says he went out, and it was night. The clause is left standing on its own, without comment, and it is the last thing said about Judas before the arrest. He went out into night, and night went into him.

Is it ever too late to come back? For anyone who wants to come back, no. Judas did not go out because the door was locked against him; he went out because he chose the dark, and he never came back to Christ even when remorse came (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter fell that same night and wept and was restored. The difference is not the size of the sin but where each man went with it. If you feel the pull to return to Christ, that pull is grace, and he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37).

In a sentence. Some thought Jesus was telling Judas, the treasurer, to buy supplies or give to the poor, but he took the bread, went out at once, and it was night.

On a Tuesday. To leave Christ is to walk into the night. Stay near the light. Notice the plausible explanations you give for drifting: busy season, the church has problems, I am tired. Some of them may be true. But ask which way the door you are walking through faces.

For worship. The Light of the world sat at the table, and the darkness could not overcome it, though a man walked out into the night to bring it down. In a few hours the sun itself would be darkened over the cross, and on the third day the light would rise again never to set. For all his own, the night is not the last word: the Lamb is the lamp of the city where there is no night (Revelation 21:23–25).
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.”

When he had gone out. The first words matter. Not before. The betrayer gone, the events are set in motion. The great discourse of chapters 14 to 17, the vine, the Spirit, the peace, the prayer, begins the moment the door shuts behind Judas. What follows is said to eleven men, and nothing in it was said in his hearing.

Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. What Jesus says at that moment is astonishing, because the situation has just become irreversible: the betrayer is on his way to the chief priests, and the machinery is running. Now. Not on the third day, and not at the ascension; now, with the arrest a few hours off and the trial and the flogging and the nails between here and there. With Judas gone the cross is certain, and Jesus speaks of it as already done. He greets the beginning of the worst night in history by announcing that his glory has started.

Glorified, five times. The verb appears five times in two verses, and the movement in it is mutual: the Son is glorified, God is glorified in him, God will glorify the Son in himself, and at once. Father and Son passing glory back and forth across the cross. The cross is the glory of the Son: there his love, obedience and holiness shine most brightly. And it is the glory of the Father: there God’s justice and mercy are both displayed, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

The dying itself is the glory. This is worth stating plainly, because it is the thing most people find hardest to hold about the crucifixion. It is not only that the cross was terrible and God brought good out of it afterwards, though that is true as far as it goes. The claim here is stronger: that the dying itself is the glory, that if you want to know what the weight and beauty of God look like, the answer is a man on a Roman cross taking what he did not owe. Anywhere else, glory means the absence of humiliation. Here it is the same event.

If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once. The Father will respond by glorifying the Son in his own presence: the resurrection and ascension. At once means very soon; the resurrection is three days away. The certainty of the vindication is already present in the announcement.

How can a death be glorious? Glory in the Bible is the shining out of what God is. At the cross more of God is seen than anywhere else: his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself in his Son; his wisdom, which saves sinners without compromising his righteousness; and his power, which turns the devil’s victory into his defeat. The cross is ugly as a human deed and glorious as a divine one. That is why Christians sing about it and Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).

In a sentence. When Judas had gone, Jesus said the Son of Man was now glorified, and God was glorified in him, and God would glorify him in himself, at once.

On a Tuesday. When you meet your own small humiliations this week, the unnoticed work, the misunderstood motive, the slight from a colleague, remember that God’s glory was revealed in the lowest place. You do not need to be noticed to glorify God; you need to be faithful where he has put you.

For worship. Look at the cross and see the glory of God. Nowhere does it shine more brightly. The Father and the Son glorify one another in the hour of darkness: the Son by perfect obedience to the Father’s saving will, the Father by raising and exalting the Son. And all of it for sinners, so that the glory of God might be seen in the face of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ‘Where I am going you cannot come.’ A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.

Little children. A tender word (teknia), like a father about to leave his children. He has never called them that before, and he will not again in this Gospel: one occurrence, here, in the first sentence after Judas leaves. It is the sort of word an old man uses, and John himself will use it seven times in his first letter, sixty years later, evidently having kept it.

Yet a little while I am with you. A few hours.

Where I am going you cannot come. The hardest thing he has said to them, and he points out that he has said it before, to the men who wanted him dead (7:34; 8:21). The same sentence, now turned to his friends, with the difference that for them it is temporary: not yet (v. 36).

A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. And into the announcement of separation comes the commandment. The obvious question is what is new about it. Loving one another is not an innovation; Leviticus 19:18 had said you shall love your neighbour as yourself, and Jesus had already called it the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:39). What is new? The new standard: as I have loved you, the love that washes feet and lays down its life. The new community: a family of disciples bound to one another in Christ. And the new covenant, of which this is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). The Latin for commandment, mandatum, gives us the name Maundy Thursday.

Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. The newness is in the standard, and it is in these words at the centre. Leviticus gave a measure that everybody carries with them: as yourself. It is a real standard and a demanding one, and it has the advantage of being always available for comparison. What replaces it here is a measure outside the self altogether, one that has just been demonstrated on the floor with a basin, and will be demonstrated again tomorrow afternoon.

Impossible on purpose. That raises the bar past anything achievable by effort. As yourself can be attempted. As I have loved you cannot be attempted at all in the ordinary sense; it can only be received first and then passed on, which is why the vine comes in chapter 15 and the Spirit in chapter 14. His love is both the pattern and the power for ours: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). The commandment is impossible on purpose, and the rest of the discourse is the provision for it.

Does one another mean only Christians? In this verse, yes: Jesus is speaking of the love of his disciples for each other, the family love of the church. Elsewhere he commands love for neighbours and even enemies (Luke 6:27–36; 10:25–37), so this is not permission to love Christians only. But there is a particular, covenant love owed within the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), and it is this love that the world is meant to see (v. 35). In practice that means the hardest test is often not the stranger but the fellow member you find difficult.

In a sentence. Jesus told his little children he would be with them only a little longer, and they could not come where he was going, and gave them a new commandment, to love one another as he had loved them.

On a Tuesday. Measure your love for other Christians against his love for you. Then ask him for more. Pick one believer you find hard to love and ask: what would the love that washes feet look like toward him this week? Pray for him by name first, and then do one thing.

For worship. He called them little children on the night he left them, and he gave them his love as their law. The Lord who commanded love first poured it out, so that his commandment is not a weight but a gift: the very love with which he loved us, living on in his people. The law of the new covenant is written in his blood and in our hearts, and it is love.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”

By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. He names the badge, and it is worth noticing what he did not choose. Not doctrine, though he cared enormously about truth and this Gospel is the most doctrinally dense of the four. Not moral rigour. Not miracles, though there had been plenty and there would be more. Not numbers, not buildings, not learning, not zeal. The mark of a Christian community before the watching world is not first its doctrine, buildings or programmes, but its love. And the test he sets is one an outsider can apply without any theological equipment at all. That is the force of all people. He is handing the world a criterion and inviting it to use it.

Vindication and humiliation. This has been historically both the church’s great vindication and its great humiliation, and honesty requires saying both. The second-century writer Tertullian reported pagans saying of Christians, see how they love one another, and the early church’s care for its poor and its plague victims was noticed across the empire and is one reason it grew. The same church has produced schisms, wars, and congregations where the coldness is obvious to any visitor within ten minutes. He knew what he was risking. The sentence hands unbelievers a fair objection whenever the love is not there, and he said it anyway. The world can argue with theology; it has no argument against a community that genuinely loves the unlovable, forgives the unforgivable, and serves the unworthy. This is the church’s great apologetic.

Does this mean doctrine matters less than love? No. The same Lord who said this prays in chapter 17 that his people be sanctified in the truth, and John’s letters insist that love and truth belong together (2 John 1–6). Love without truth is not Christ’s love, because he loved us by telling us the truth and dying for it. But truth without love fails the very test he gives the world. The answer is not to choose but to hold both: to be as careful with one another’s souls as with one another’s doctrine.

Lord, where are you going? Peter, who has not been listening to any of it. Jesus has just given the new commandment, and Peter skips over it to ask about Jesus’ departure. He is still back at verse 33.

Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward. The answer is gentler than his interruption deserves. Not a refusal; a postponement, and a promise. What Peter cannot do tonight he will do later: in death, as a martyr (21:18–19), and into glory. The cross that separates them now will be the path Peter himself eventually walks, and John will collect on the promise in the last chapter.

In a sentence. Jesus said all people would know they were his disciples by their love for one another, and when Peter asked where he was going, said Peter could not follow now, but would later.

On a Tuesday. If an unbeliever visited your church next Sunday and stayed for the coffee, what would he conclude about how you love one another? Ask what you could do to change the answer. Speak to someone standing alone. Ask a newcomer home. Settle the quarrel you have been nursing with a fellow member.

For worship. Let the world see Christ in your love for his people.
