The love that knelt with a towel and hung on a cross is meant to be visible in ordinary congregations, among ordinary sinners, because he loved them first. And the promise to Peter is his promise to all his own: you cannot follow now, but you will follow afterward, into the Father’s house.

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.”

Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you. Peter’s promise uses the exact words Jesus has used of himself: lay down (tithēmi), the verb from the good shepherd (10:11, 15), the verb from laying aside the garments at the start of this evening. He has been listening to the shepherd language and has taken it on himself. And he means it. That has to be said clearly, because Peter is usually treated as a braggart here and he is not. Within a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed band in the dark (18:10), which is not the act of a coward. He was willing to die. What he was not able to do was survive a servant girl’s question by a fire. He does not know his own weakness.

Failing where we did not brace. That is a real thing about human courage. Most people who fail do not fail at the point they had braced for. Peter had prepared himself for a fight and was undone by a conversation.

Will you lay down your life for me? Gently, Jesus echoes his words back to him as a question. The irony: Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus; in fact, Jesus will lay down his life for Peter (10:11).

Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times. Before dawn. Roosters crowed in the early morning, and the Romans called the watch from midnight to three cockcrow. Peter’s denials follow in 18:15–27. And the specificity is the mercy. A general warning that he would fail would have been forgotten or argued with. What he gives Peter is a marker so precise that when it happens there can be no doubt it was foreseen. Luke records the moment it lands, when the rooster crows and the Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

Two failures, two endings. Those tears are the beginning of the restoration, and they were made possible by this verse. Judas also failed that night, and the warnings he had been given did not bring him back; he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). The difference between the two men is not the size of the sin. It is that one of them had been prayed for (Luke 22:32), and had been told in advance, and therefore knew at the worst moment of his life that he had not surprised the Lord who had washed his feet. Jesus does not give up on him. He restores him with three questions by the lake (21:15–17).

What if I have failed Christ badly, after promising him much? Then Peter is your brother. He made the boldest promise in the room and broke it three times within hours, with curses. Jesus knew it would happen, loved him through it, prayed that his faith would not fail, and went looking for him after the resurrection. Your failure does not surprise Christ, and it does not cancel his love. Do what Peter did: weep over it honestly, do not run from him as Judas did, and let him restore you. Then, like Peter, strengthen your brothers out of what you have learned (Luke 22:32).

In a sentence. Peter asked why he could not follow now and promised to die for Jesus, and Jesus asked if he really would, and said that before the rooster crowed Peter would deny him three times.

On a Tuesday. Do not trust your own strength. Trust the one who laid down his life for you, and who keeps you even when you fail. Notice where you are confident you could never fall, and pray there especially. And when you do fail, go back to Christ quickly, before the night closes in.

For worship. He knew exactly what every one of them was about to do, Judas going out into the night, Peter by the fire, the rest scattering, and knowing it, he had already knelt down and washed all twenty-four feet. Peter promised to lay down his life for his Lord; his Lord laid down his life for Peter, and then came back to find him. Our hold on Christ fails within hours. His hold on us does not fail at all.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.<sup>2</sup>During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,<sup>3</sup>Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God,<sup>4</sup>rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.<sup>5</sup>Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.<sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”<sup>7</sup>Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”<sup>8</sup>Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”<sup>9</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”<sup>11</sup>For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”<sup>12</sup>When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?<sup>13</sup>You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am.<sup>14</sup>If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.<sup>15</sup>For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.<sup>16</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.<sup>17</sup>If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.<sup>18</sup>I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”<sup>28</sup>Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.<sup>29</sup>Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.<sup>30</sup>So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.<sup>31</sup>When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.<sup>32</sup>If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.<sup>33</sup>Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.overview:
With chapter 13 the “book of glory” begins. The public ministry is over; for five chapters Jesus is alone with his disciples on the night before he dies, in what is often called the Upper Room or Farewell Discourse (13–17). John opens it with a sentence that sums up the cross: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rises from supper, ties a towel round his waist and washes his disciples’ feet, the task of a slave. Peter protests, then asks to be washed all over; Jesus explains that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, and that unless he washes Peter, Peter has no share with him. He tells them he has given them an example: as their Lord and Teacher has served them, they must serve one another.

Then Jesus, troubled, announces that one of them will betray him. At Peter’s prompting the disciple whom Jesus loved asks who it is; Jesus gives a morsel of bread to Judas, Satan enters him, and Judas goes out: “and it was night.” With the betrayer gone, Jesus speaks of his glorification and gives his disciples a new commandment: to love one another as he has loved them, so that all people will know they are his disciples. When Peter vows to lay down his life for him, Jesus foretells that before the rooster crows Peter will deny him three times. The chapter holds together the humility of Christ, the treachery of a friend, the weakness of the boldest disciple, and a love that does not let go.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calms his troubled disciples: as they trust God, they should trust him. In his Father’s house there is ample room, and he goes to prepare a place and will return to take them to himself. Thomas protests that they do not know the way; Jesus replies that he is the way, the truth and the life, the only route to the Father. To know him is to know the Father. When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father, for the Father lives in him and does his works through him. Believers will do the same works and greater, because he is going to the Father, and he will do whatever they ask in his name for the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a way to the Father, it is real, it is accessible, it is Jesus. Exclusivity: this is the only way, and all other paths are paths that do not lead to the Father. The exclusivity is not arrogance; it is the necessary consequence of the incarnation. If God has come in one place, in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home. The scandal of particularity cannot be removed without removing the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula attached to the end of requests; it is prayer aligned with his character, his purposes, and his glory. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as he would ask, for what he would ask for, in the way that honors the Father through the Son. This is why prayer in Jesus' name is effective: it brings human desire into alignment with divine will, and divine will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?

Meaning first. John 14 is Jesus’ comfort to frightened disciples. He has just told them he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him. Now he tells them why they need not be troubled: he is going to prepare a place for them, he is the way to the Father, he will send the Spirit, and he gives them his peace. It is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible, read at countless funerals, and it was first spoken by a man on the last night of his life to the friends he was about to die for.

The setting. The meal is over, Judas has gone out into the night, and eleven men remain in the upper room. Peter has just been told he will deny his Lord three times before dawn. There is no break between 13:38 and 14:1; the comfort comes straight after the warning, to the man who will fail and to the others who will scatter.

Let not your hearts be troubled. The verb in the first sentence is one this Gospel has been using carefully, and it changes the weight of the command entirely. Troubled (tarassesthō) means stirred up, agitated, churned. John has used the word three times already, and every time the subject was Jesus. He was greatly troubled at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33). Now is my soul troubled, in the temple, when the Greeks came (12:27). And troubled in his spirit, at this table, an hour ago, when he named his betrayer (13:21). So this is not a man telling frightened people to pull themselves together. It is the only person in the room who has been visibly shaken three times in three chapters, telling them not to be, and he knows precisely what he is asking, because he has just done it himself and will do it again in a garden before dawn. He was troubled so that they need not be.

Hearts, and one heart. Your hearts is plural, but heart in Greek is singular: the shared heart of the group, one heart in eleven men. The command does not forbid the feeling. It forbids letting it settle in and take charge.

Believe in God; believe also in me. The remedy he gives is not an explanation. It is two imperatives with an astonishing claim buried in the second. The Greek can be read as commands or statements; most likely, keep trusting God, and keep trusting me. But whichever way it is taken, the structure is the same: whatever trust they place in God, place the identical trust in the man sitting opposite them. Nobody in Israel could have said that sentence and remained a faithful Jew, unless it was true. No mere man could say this.

In my Father’s house are many rooms. One word here deserves the reader’s attention. The rooms are monai, dwelling places, and the noun comes straight from menō, the abiding word that will run through the whole of chapter 15. A monē is a staying place, somewhere one remains. The old translation mansions is not a mistranslation so much as a word that has drifted; it came from the Latin mansiones, which meant dwellings or stopping places. What the text says is not that there are grand apartments but that there is room to stay, permanently, in the Father’s house. The picture is of a great family house with room for all the children, and the emphasis falls on many. There is no shortage. There is room for all the Father has given the Son.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you. Either way, the point is that Jesus would never mislead them. He is going ahead to make ready. The cross is the preparation; the resurrection and ascension complete it.

How can I stop my heart being troubled? Not by pretending the trouble is not there. Jesus does not tell the disciples that nothing bad is coming; the worst night in history is a few hours away. He gives them something to do with the trouble: trust God, and trust him. In practice that means taking the specific thing that troubles you and placing it, in prayer, in the hands of the God who has shown his heart in Jesus. It means reminding yourself of what he has promised, a room, his return, his presence, his peace, and saying them back to him. The feelings may not go at once. But a troubled heart that keeps turning to Christ is already obeying this verse.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to be troubled, but to trust God and him, for there are many rooms in his Father’s house, and he is going to prepare a place for them.

On a Tuesday. When anxiety rises today, the bill, the test result, the child who will not speak to you, stop and say this verse aloud, slowly. Then name what is troubling you and say: I trust you with this, Lord Jesus. Do it as many times as the trouble returns.

For worship. The one who would be troubled in Gethsemane spoke peace to troubled men. He asked them to trust him as they trusted God, because he is God, and then went to prepare their room at the cost of his own life. There is a room in the Father’s house with your name on it, and Christ himself has gone to make it ready. The house is large, the Father is welcoming, and the Son is the way in.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going.

And if I go and prepare a place for you. How does he prepare it? By his death, resurrection and ascension he opens the way into the Father’s presence, entering as our forerunner behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20; 9:24). The place is prepared by the cross.

I will come again and will take you to myself. The promise has been read four ways, and it is worth knowing which is likely, because a good deal of comfort depends on it. Some have taken it of the resurrection, which is three days off; some of Pentecost; some of his coming to each believer at death; and most, rightly, of his visible return at the end of the age (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The reason the last is best is the second half of the sentence: that where I am you may be also. The resurrection appearances did not accomplish that; he left again. Pentecost did not, in the sense meant here. What is being described is a fetching, and a permanent one.

Take you to myself. The verb is domestic rather than judicial: paralambanō, to take somebody along with you, to receive them to yourself. It is the word for collecting a person, not summoning him. That is worth setting against the way the second coming is usually pictured. Most of the imagery that has attached itself to it, the trumpet, the sky splitting, the judgement seat, is genuinely biblical, and it is not what Jesus reaches for at a supper table with frightened men. What he says is: I am going to get a room ready, and then I am coming back for you personally.

That where I am you may be also. Note the purpose clause, because it is the whole point and it is easy to slide past. Not that you may be in a good place. Not that you may be comfortable at last. That where I am you may be also. Heaven is defined here entirely by a location relative to a person. Whatever else is true of it, and Scripture says a great deal elsewhere about a body, a city and a new earth, the reason given for the whole operation is that he wants them where he is (17:24; Philippians 1:23). The heart of heaven is not the place but the person.

Where Christians differ: the coming again and the rapture. Dispensationalists see this as a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation, distinct from Christ’s visible return. Verdict: Scripture speaks of one return of Christ, visible, glorious, and final, at which the dead are raised, believers caught up to meet him, and the world judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). There is no secret rapture. The Lord comes once, and takes his people to be with him for ever.

And you know the way to where I am going. The sentence that provokes Thomas. Jesus says they know it. Thomas is about to say flatly that they do not. Both are true, which is the point of the exchange: they had been walking the way for three years without ever having heard it named. They know him, and he is the way (v. 6).

What happens to a Christian who dies before Jesus comes back? He goes at once to be with Christ. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no sleep of the soul in between and no purgatory; the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received into heaven at death, while the body rests in the grave until the resurrection (Westminster 32.1). Then, when Christ returns, the dead in Christ will be raised with glorified bodies, and all his people together will be with him for ever. So this promise holds for those who have already died: he will come for them too.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he went to prepare a place for them, he would come again and take them to himself, so that they would be where he is, and they knew the way.

On a Tuesday. Heaven is where Jesus is. The best thing about it is him. Ask yourself honestly what you look forward to about heaven. If the answer is mostly rest, reunion or relief, those are good gifts, but let them lead you to the Giver. Spend five minutes today telling Christ that you long to be with him, and ask him to make that longing true.

For worship. The Lord of glory has gone ahead to make ready, and he will not send for us; he will come himself. He will take us to himself, as a bridegroom takes his bride home, and where he is we will be. All the comfort of heaven is gathered up in that one promise: with him, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way? Give Thomas his due first. Honest Thomas (11:16; 20:25) is the only man in the room honest enough to say he is lost, and his question produces the most quoted sentence in the Gospel. He does not pretend to understand. Bewildered people who admit it out loud have done the church more good than confident people who do not.

I am the way, and the truth, and the life. This is the sixth of Jesus’ great I am sayings in John, and the most comprehensive. Note the three definite articles, which English keeps but rushes past: the way, the truth, the life. Not a way, not one truth among others. And not I show the way, but I am the way. Jesus does not point to a road; he is the road. The truth: he is the reality of God revealed (1:14, 17), not merely accurate information but God as he is. The life: he is the source of eternal life (1:4; 11:25), the life of God shared with humanity, beginning now and continuing for ever.

The way is the main idea. The three are not a list of separate titles. The second two explain the first: he is the way because he is the truth about God and the life of God. A road that does not correspond to reality leads nowhere, and a road that cannot carry you alive is no use either.

No one comes to the Father except through me. Now the hard half, and it should be met directly rather than managed, because it is the sentence that makes Christianity intolerable to a great many decent people. One of the most exclusive statements in Scripture: there are not many ways to God; there is one, Jesus Christ (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). Three things need saying. The first is that the offence is not removable. Every attempt to soften this into Jesus is the way for Christians founders on the grammar. He is not describing a preference. If it is not true it is monstrous, and if it is true it is the best news there has ever been, and there is no third position.

Not a boast. The second is that the exclusivity is not a boast about the people who hold it. Christians have used this verse to feel superior, and that is a straightforward abuse of it. What the sentence says is that there is one bridge. It says nothing whatever about the merit of the people crossing it, and the whole of this Gospel has been at pains to establish that they have none.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways to God? Many today hold that all religions lead to God (pluralism), or that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him, by following the light they have (inclusivism). Verdict: no one leaves no exceptions, and Acts 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must send missionaries. It is not arrogance to say this; it is what Jesus himself said. And the way is open to anyone, from any background, who comes through him.

What about those who never heard? This is the question everybody actually wants answered. No one is saved except through Christ, and no one comes to the Father but through him. Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light of creation and conscience they did have (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12–16). Some Christians hope that God may save people who respond to that light without knowing Christ; but Scripture never promises it, and Paul’s argument is that faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). Infants dying in infancy, and those unable to understand, are a different case: the elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases, and there we may rest in the mercy of the Judge of all the earth who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). The right response to this question is not speculation but sending.

An answer to a frightened man. Notice what the sentence is doing where it stands. It is not a boundary marker put up against outsiders. It is an answer to a frightened disciple asking how to get home, and the answer is that the way is not a map or a technique or a standard, but the man who is talking to him.

In a sentence. When Thomas said they did not know where he was going or the way, Jesus answered that he is the way, the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through him.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who is trying to reach God by another road: good works, another religion, spirituality without Christ, or simply hoping it will be all right? Pray for them by name today. And if the opportunity comes, tell them gently and plainly that Jesus said he is the way, and that the way is open to them.

For worship. Christ is not one way among many. He is the way, and the door is wide open. He is the truth in a world of half-truths and lies, and the life in a world under death. He did not hand us a map and leave; he took our hand and became the road himself, laid down through his own body to the Father’s house. Blessed be the Way who comes to the lost and carries them home.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him. Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (8:19). There is no separate route to God behind him.

From now on you do know him and have seen him. A promise easy to miss under Philip’s interruption. From now on: from the coming hour of the cross and resurrection. Something changes tonight, not in what is available to be seen, which has been standing in front of them since Cana, but in their capacity to see it. The Spirit is promised nine verses later, and chapter 16 will say that the disciples cannot bear things now which they will grasp afterwards. That is worth having for anyone who has read the Gospels a long time and found them flat. The problem is not usually the light.

Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. Philip’s request is the oldest and best request in the Bible, and he does not know whose words he is borrowing. Moses had asked it: please show me your glory (Exodus 33:18). He was refused, told he could not see God’s face and live, hidden in a cleft of rock while the glory passed, and permitted to see only the back. It is the great unanswered petition of the Old Testament. Now a man from Bethsaida asks the same thing, and adds that it would be enough. He is right about that. If a man could see God, nothing else would be needed, ever again. And the answer he gets is not a refusal. It is that the request has been granted for three years and he has not noticed.

What Philip assumes. His request assumes that the Father is somewhere else, and that Jesus might be able to arrange an introduction. That is the natural religious instinct: the visible teacher is a means of access to the invisible God behind him. Everything in this Gospel has been dismantling it, and here it is again, in the mouth of a man who has been present for all of it. He means it sincerely. But he does not realise the Father has been in front of him all along.

Will I ever see God? Yes. Scripture promises that the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and that his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4). That sight will come in glory, when we see Christ as he is and are made like him (1 John 3:2). Now we see by faith, through the Son whom the Scriptures show us. But the God you will one day see face to face is not a stranger behind Jesus; he is the Father whose heart you have already seen in the Son. Seeing God in glory will not be meeting someone new, but seeing fully the One you have known.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they had known him, they would have known his Father, and from now on they did, and Philip asked him to show them the Father, which would be enough.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a vision. You have Jesus. To know him is to know God. If you long for a clearer sense of God, do not look for an experience beyond Christ; open one of the Gospels and read slowly, asking at each scene: what does this show me of the Father?

For worship. The prayer Moses could not have answered on the mountain was answered at a supper table. The glory he was hidden from in the rock now sat at meat with fishermen and washed their feet. God has shown us his face, and it is the face of Jesus Christ. What was refused to the greatest of the prophets has been given to the least of the believers, and it is enough.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.

Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? A gentle rebuke, with a hint of sadness. Three years together. There is no rebuke in it of the sharp kind: this is the sentence of somebody who is disappointed rather than angry, and it is one of the very few places where we are allowed to hear what it cost him to be misunderstood by his friends for three years.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. There is no larger sentence in the Bible about the knowledge of God, and it is worth stating exactly what it does and does not claim. It does not say Jesus is the Father. John has been careful about that since the first verse of the book, where the Word was with God and was God; they are distinct persons. It does not say Jesus merely resembles the Father, or represents him well, or teaches accurately about him. It says that looking at the one is seeing the other. Jesus is the image of the invisible God, the exact imprint of his nature (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). The Father is fully revealed in the Son.

No God behind Jesus. That settles something that would otherwise remain permanently open. There is a suspicion, very old and still current, that behind the kindness of Jesus stands a different sort of God: sterner, more remote, harder to please. It survives in people who are perfectly orthodox on paper. They trust Christ and are afraid of God, and they would not put it that way, but it governs how they pray. This verse forbids it. There is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him. Do you want to know what God is like? Look at Jesus: his compassion, his holiness, his tears at the tomb, his anger in the temple, his hands washing feet, his body on the cross. The face that wept at a grave, and knelt with a towel, and did not break a bruised reed, is the face.

Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The mutual indwelling (10:38), later called by the church the perichoresis of the persons, is not offered as a speculation but as the reason his words and works are what they are.

The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works. His words and works are the Father’s words and works. Note the odd division of labour: the words he speaks are not on his own authority, and the works are the Father’s, done through him. He claims almost nothing for himself in a sentence that claims everything. The miracles are not independent demonstrations but the Father’s acts performed through the Son.

But is the God of the Old Testament not harsher than Jesus? No; he is the same God, and Jesus himself said so. The God who thundered at Sinai is the God who proclaimed his name as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6), and Jesus is the full showing of that name. And the Jesus of the Gospels is not soft: he drove traders from the temple, pronounced woes on hypocrites, and spoke more about hell than anyone else in Scripture. Holiness and love meet in both Testaments, and they meet perfectly in Christ, and supremely at the cross. Read the Old Testament through him, and the one God comes into focus.

In a sentence. Jesus asked Philip whether he still did not know him after so long, for whoever has seen him has seen the Father, since he is in the Father and the Father in him, doing his works.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is worth running slowly. Picture God. Not the doctrine: the picture that comes up unbidden when you pray badly, or when you have failed. If what appears is a face that is disappointed, or cold, or busy elsewhere, then something other than this verse is furnishing the image, and it needs correcting from a Gospel rather than from experience. Read one Gospel scene today and let it redraw the picture.

For worship. When you see Jesus, you see God. Look long at him. The Father is not a hidden stranger behind the Son; the eternal Son has made him known, full of grace and truth. The face that turned toward lepers, sinners and thieves, the face set like flint toward Jerusalem, the face spat on and bruised, is the face of God toward us. There is no darker God behind him. In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.

Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me. Believe his word. That is the first and best ground of faith: his own testimony about himself.

Or else believe on account of the works themselves. And if not, believe the evidence of his works. He meets weak faith where it is, and gives it something to hold.

Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do. Believers will continue Jesus’ work. Whoever believes: not the apostles only, not the specially gifted.

And greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father. This promise needs working through carefully, because it is claimed far too much and believed far too little, and both errors do damage. Start with what it cannot mean. It cannot mean more impressive miracles. Nobody in Acts or since has fed five thousand from a boy’s lunch, walked on a lake, or called a man four days dead out of a cave. If greater means more spectacular, the promise failed immediately and has been failing ever since. And Jesus supplies the reason himself, in the clause attached: because I am going to the Father. Whatever the greatness consists of, it is unlocked by his departure. So it is not a promise about the disciples’ capacities at all. It is a promise about what becomes possible once the ascension has happened and the Spirit has come (16:7).

Greater in scope. Jesus in his earthly ministry was one man, in one province, speaking to whatever village his feet reached. Within thirty years of that supper the message was in Rome. Within three centuries it was across the empire. He is describing a work that would go where he did not go in the flesh, through people who could be in a hundred places at once because there were a hundred of them.

Greater in effect. On the day of Pentecost Peter preached one sermon and three thousand people were converted, more than in the whole of Jesus’ earthly ministry, and the gospel went to the nations. Nothing like that happened in his ministry. His greatest single day ended with a crowd trying to make him king and, by the following day, many walking away. Why? Because the cross had not happened yet. Peter could preach a finished atonement and a risen Lord; Jesus in the days of his flesh preached a coming one. The disciples’ sermons were greater in the only sense that finally matters: they could tell people the thing had been done. They belong to the new age, the age of the Spirit, after the cross.

Where Christians differ: greater works and miracles. Some take this as a promise that every believer can do greater miracles than Jesus. Verdict: no believer has ever done greater miracles than Jesus; the promise must mean something else. The greater works are the saving works of the Spirit through the gospel, bringing people from death to life. Miraculous sign gifts accompanied the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and ceased with the apostolic age. But the greatest work, new birth, goes on wherever the gospel is preached.

Both guards. Against the overreach: this verse does not license a Christian to expect that he will personally do more remarkable things than Jesus did, and preachers who have promised congregations that have left a trail of disappointed and ashamed people behind them. Against the deflation: it is a promise, not a metaphor, and it was fulfilled in things that actually happened in public. The ordinary Christian who says something true about Christ to somebody who then believes it has taken part in a work that Jesus, in the days of his flesh, did not do in that way, because the ground of it was not yet laid. And the work is still his: it is the risen Christ, working by his Spirit through his people, who saves.

Can I do greater works if I am not a preacher? Yes, because the greater works are not about platform but about the gospel reaching people. The mother teaching her children the faith, the friend who invites a colleague to church, the believer who gives so a missionary can go, the church member who prays for the lost by name: all of these share in the work of bringing people from death to life. The power is not in you but in the Spirit Christ sends, and in the word. You are not asked to be impressive; you are asked to be a faithful witness.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to believe him, or at least his works, and said that whoever believes in him will do his works, and greater works, because he is going to the Father.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel and someone is born again, that is a greater work than healing a body. Take part in it. Think of one person you could speak to about Christ this week, and pray for the opening. Then, when it comes, say one true thing about him.

For worship. He went to the Father, and from the throne he poured out the Spirit, and the gospel that began in one province ran to the ends of the earth. Every conversion since Pentecost is a work of the ascended Christ, and a greater work than the raising of a body, because it is the raising of a soul from death to everlasting life. Glory to the Lord who works from heaven through the weakest of his servants.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.

Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do. This is the most quoted and most quietly resented promise in the New Testament, and it needs to be met head-on, because there is a person reading it who prayed for something enormous and did not get it. Read as a blank cheque, the sentence is falsified by the life of every Christian who has ever lived, including the men it was spoken to. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked that, if it were possible, the cup might pass, and drank it. Every one of the eleven at that table prayed for things they did not receive, and most of them died violently. So either the promise is false, or it means something other than the flat reading. And the qualification is not hidden in the small print; it is in the middle of the sentence.

In my name. In the ancient world a person’s name stood for his character and authority; to act in someone’s name was to act as his representative, within his commission. An ambassador can commit his government to anything the government would want and nothing it would not. So praying in Jesus’ name means praying as his representatives, according to his will and for his glory (1 John 5:14). It is not a magic formula added to the end of a prayer. To pray in Jesus’ name is to come to the Father on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, and to ask what he would ask.

That the Father may be glorified in the Son. The purpose of prayer is the Father’s glory, and it comes immediately as the boundary. It is stated openly rather than concealed. The promise is unlimited within it and does not exist outside it. Prayer in Jesus’ name is not a formula but an alignment: an invitation into the Son’s own posture before the Father, always seeking the Father’s glory.

If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it. Ask me: prayer to Jesus himself, as well as to the Father. A modern Bible may footnote it, since some manuscripts omit the word me. If it stands, it is remarkable: prayer directed to Jesus, said by Jesus, at a table with Jews who prayed only to God. Prayer to Christ is right, because he is God (Acts 7:59).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can get anything we want by saying in Jesus’ name. Prayer in his name is prayer shaped by his will and aimed at the Father’s glory.

What about the good prayer that was refused? Something must be said to the person for whom all that is cold comfort, because the honest difficulty is not the greedy prayer. It is the prayer that was plainly good, healing for a child, a marriage saved, a friend brought to faith, that was refused, when the sufferer knows perfectly well it was the kind of thing the Father is glorified by. Two things are true. The first is that Scripture never explains each case. There is no verse that accounts for why one good prayer is answered and another is not, and any commentary that produces a formula is selling something. The second is that the New Testament everywhere assumes the refusals are not indifference. The same Gospel has a man deliberately waiting two days while his friend died (11:6), and the family got more than they asked for and nothing like what they wanted at the time. A refused prayer is heard by a Father who is working a greater good than we can see (Romans 8:28), and who will one day show us why.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that whatever they asked in his name he would do, so that the Father would be glorified in the Son.

On a Tuesday. Take one thing you are praying for and ask: would Jesus ask for this? How would it glorify the Father? You may find the prayer changes shape, or you may find you can pray it with new boldness. Then pray boldly in Jesus’ name, and leave the answer with him.

For worship. The Son who always did what pleased the Father has opened his own access to us, and invites us to come in his name. We do not approach the throne on our own credit, but on his, and he has never been refused. And the Father who answers is glorified in the Son, so that every true prayer and every answer turns at last into praise. Blessed be the God who hears.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for Jesus shows itself in obeying him. He will ask the Father to give them another Helper, the Spirit of truth, who will stay with them for ever. The world cannot receive him, but they know him, for he lives with them and will be in them. Jesus will not leave them orphaned; he will come to them. Soon the world will not see him, but they will, and because he lives, they will live. Then they will know that he is in the Father, they in him and he in them. Whoever keeps his commands loves him and will be loved by the Father, and Jesus will show himself to them. Judas (not Iscariot) asks why he will reveal himself to them and not the world. Jesus replies that he and the Father will come and make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word. The Spirit, sent in his name, will teach them everything and remind them of all he said. He leaves them his peace, unlike the world’s, so they need not be troubled or afraid. If they loved him, they would be glad he is going to the Father, who is greater than he. He tells them now so they will believe when it happens. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no hold on him; he goes to show the world that he loves the Father and does what he commands. Then he tells them to get up and leave.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (Parakletos — Advocate, Comforter, Counselor) is described with four characteristics in the farewell discourse: he is the Spirit of truth (14:17), the Holy Spirit who teaches and reminds (14:26), the Spirit who testifies about Jesus (15:26), and the one who convicts the world (16:8). Each characteristic is an aspect of the single mission: to continue and apply what Jesus accomplished. The Spirit does not bring new revelation beyond Jesus but illuminates everything Jesus said and did, making it present and personal to each generation of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: My peace I give to you: not as the world gives. The world's peace is the absence of conflict, the management of anxiety, the temporary resolution of problems. Jesus' peace is an interior stability that coexists with external trouble — the shalom of the covenant, the wholeness that comes from being right with God and secure in his love. Not as the world gives: the two kinds of peace are not on the same spectrum; one is the presence of order, the other is the presence of God. The disciples will need this peace before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,

If you love me, you will keep my commandments. This sets the relation between love and obedience in an order worth getting right, because reversed it becomes a machine for producing anxiety. He does not say keep my commandments and that will prove you love me, which is how it is often heard. It is a plain future: if you love me, you will keep my commandments. It is a statement about what love does, not a test love must pass. Love shows itself in obedience (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3). Not obedience to earn love, but obedience as the fruit of love. Keep (tērēsete) means guard, treasure, obey. The Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create.

And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper. The word for what he promises has no good English equivalent, which is why translations disagree: Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Counsellor; some simply transliterate it, Paraclete. The ESV notes that Helper can also be rendered Advocate or Counselor. Paraklētos means, literally, one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was a legal term: the friend you brought to court with you, not so much a hired advocate as somebody of standing who stood at your side and spoke for you. So he is someone who comes to stand with you, to help, comfort, plead for you and speak for you. Comforter is Wycliffe’s word and it has weakened badly; it meant strengthener, from the Latin fortis, not somebody who soothes.

Another. The word is allon: another of the same kind. Jesus has been their Helper; the Spirit will be another like him. John will call Jesus himself a paraklētos in his first letter, using the same word (1 John 2:1), which confirms the reading: the Spirit is the second one because Jesus was the first. So the promise is not a substitute of a lesser order. It is: you are losing me, and you are getting one exactly like me. This also shows that the Spirit is a person, not a force: Jesus would not compare himself to a power. And note the Trinity: the Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes.

To be with you forever. The phrase quietly outdoes everything they have had so far. They had Jesus in the flesh for three years and are losing him tonight. Unlike his earthly presence, which is about to end, the Spirit will never leave them. What is coming has no term on it at all.

What if I do not feel that I love Jesus enough to obey him? Then start where the love starts: not with your love for him, but his for you. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ grows as you look at what he has done, so read the Gospels, sit at the cross, and remember your forgiveness. Then obey in the small thing in front of you, even without strong feeling. Obedience is often how love is learned, as a child learns love for a parent partly by trusting and doing what he says. And the Helper is given precisely because you cannot do this alone. Ask him for love, and he gives it (Romans 5:5).

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they loved him they would keep his commandments, and he would ask the Father, who would give them another Helper to be with them for ever.

On a Tuesday. You are never alone. The Helper is beside you, and in you, today and for ever. Before a hard conversation, a difficult task, or a temptation you know is coming, pause and ask the Spirit to stand with you and give you words and strength. Then go in, not alone.

For worship. The Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes: the whole Trinity bends toward eleven frightened men, and toward every believer since. We have not lost Christ; we have been given another like him, who will never be taken from us. Glory to the Father who gives, the Son who asks, and the Spirit who stays.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.

Even the Spirit of truth. He is the Spirit who brings and teaches the truth, and the truth is Christ (15:26; 16:13).

Whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. The unbelieving world has no capacity to receive him (1 Corinthians 2:14). The natural mind cannot recognise the Spirit, because spiritual sight requires the new birth he creates.

You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. Two prepositions do all the work, and the shift between them marks the change of an age. With you now, in the person of Jesus and his ministry; in you after Pentecost, dwelling within. Alongside, and then inside. The Spirit had always been at work: he came upon judges and prophets and kings, and rested on Jesus without measure. But in the old covenant he came and went, and came on particular people for particular tasks. What is promised here is permanent residence in ordinary believers, which is precisely what Ezekiel and Joel had said would mark the last days (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28–29). The ESV notes that some manuscripts read and is in you. The difference is small; the future reading fits the context of Jesus’ promise better.

I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you. The word is more specific than most readers realise. Orphans (orphanous) means bereaved children, and disciples whose teacher had died were sometimes called orphans. So he is naming exactly what they are about to be, and denying it. By tomorrow evening they will look, to anybody watching, precisely like a school whose master has been executed: leaderless, frightened, with nothing to do but go home. He tells them in advance that the appearance will be false.

I will come to you. The promise is not I will send help. It is I will come to you: in the resurrection appearances (v. 19), and by the Spirit, who brings Christ’s own presence (v. 23). The coming of the Spirit is the coming of Christ himself to his people, by another route.

For the one who has lost the person who explained things. There is a particular loneliness that belongs to people who have lost the one who made the world make sense: a parent, a mentor, a pastor. This verse was spoken to eleven men about to be exactly that, by the man they were about to lose, and what he promised was not a replacement but his own return.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Not chiefly by unusual feelings, but by what he does. The Spirit makes you confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), makes you cry out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), makes you love Christ and his people, gives you a hatred of your sin and a desire to be holy, and opens the Scriptures to you so that they speak. If you have trusted Christ, the Spirit dwells in you, for anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). You do not have to earn a second gift; you have been given the Helper.

In a sentence. The Helper is the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, but whom the disciples know, for he is with them and will be in them; Jesus will not leave them orphans but will come to them.

On a Tuesday. When you feel abandoned, by friends, by circumstances, or by your own sense of God’s presence, say this verse back to him: you said you would not leave me as an orphan. Then do one thing a child of a present Father would do: pray, open his word, or go to his people.

For worship. You are not an orphan. Christ has come to you by his Spirit. The world cannot see him, but the weakest believer knows him, because he has made his dwelling within. The promise of the prophets has come true in ordinary people: God not only with us but in us, for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.

Yet a little while and the world will see me no more. After his death the world will not see him again until he returns.

But you will see me. In the resurrection appearances, and by faith.

Because I live, you also will live. Seven words carry the whole Christian hope. Note the grammar. It is not if; the ground is stated as a fact, and the consequence follows from it and not from anything about the disciples. I live is present tense: he is the living one, even facing death. Their living depends wholly on his. His resurrection life is the source and guarantee of theirs, both now in the new birth and at the last in the resurrection of their bodies. Paul says the same thing in a sentence that is unanswerable if this one is true: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Where assurance rests. That is where a Christian’s assurance finally rests, and it is worth saying plainly, because most of us look in the wrong place for it. The question is not whether my faith is strong enough to survive, or whether my grip will hold. It is whether he is alive. If the answer to that is yes, the rest follows by the logic of this verse, and the strength of my grip is not what holds me.

In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. That day is the day of resurrection and Pentecost. Three circles of union, and the order repays attention. The chain runs from the life of God outward. First the relation that has always existed, between Father and Son. Then the believer placed inside the Son. Then the Son placed inside the believer. It is not merely a comparison, as if your union with me will be a bit like mine with the Father, but a series of nested indwellings, and the outermost is God’s own. Union with Christ is the heart of the Christian life. We are drawn into the fellowship of the Trinity (17:21–23). And it will be known only in that day: not tonight, and not by argument. They will find it out afterwards, when the Spirit comes and the whole evening becomes clear.

What does it mean to be in Christ? It means that by faith, through the Spirit, you are joined to him so closely that what is true of him becomes true of you. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness as your righteousness, his life as your life, his Father as your Father (Romans 6:4–11; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a feeling, though it brings feelings; it is a fact God has made. Every blessing of salvation comes to you in him (Ephesians 1:3). And because it is his work, it does not come undone. The branch does not hold the vine; the vine holds the branch.

In a sentence. Jesus said that soon the world would not see him, but they would, and because he lives they would live, and on that day they would know that he is in the Father, they in him, and he in them.

On a Tuesday. Because he lives, you will live. Nothing can break that link. When you think of your own death, or stand at the grave of a believer, say these words. Then go about today’s work as someone whose life is hidden with Christ in God and cannot be lost.

For worship. He lives, and therefore we live. Death had no claim on him and will not keep those who are in him. The Son is in the Father, we are in the Son, and the Son is in us: we have been taken up into the life and love of the eternal God. Glory to the living one, who died and is alive for evermore, and holds the keys of death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him. Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”

Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. Having them, knowing them, and keeping them, doing them. Love for Christ is not sentiment but allegiance expressed in the pattern of a life.

And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him. The chain of love here does not run the way religion expects. Read carelessly it is a transaction: love him, and God will love you back. It cannot be, because the same Gospel has already said the Father loved the world first (3:16), and John’s letter will make it explicit: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). What is described is not the beginning of the Father’s love but its answering movement. Not that the Father’s love is earned, but that those who love Christ experience the Father’s love in a special, intimate way. Somebody who has come to love Christ finds himself inside the flow of a love that was there before he arrived, and now comes toward him in a particular and personal way. Not a reward for loving; a response within a relationship that God started.

And manifest myself to him. The verb is the one to catch. Manifest (emphanisō) means reveal, make visible, show plainly. Jesus makes himself known to those who love him. It is a promise of something experienced rather than merely believed, and it is the reason Judas asks his question.

Judas (not Iscariot). This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark’s lists (Luke 6:16; Matthew 10:3). John’s parenthesis is one of the small human touches in this Gospel. By the time John is writing, the name has become unusable. Sixty years on he still cannot let it stand without the note: a small mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else.

Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world? He is not being slow. He expects the Messiah to show himself publicly to the world. If the Messiah is going to make himself plainly visible, surely that is a public event; the whole point of the messianic hope was a disclosure the nations could not miss. Why only to them?

Why does Jesus seem more real to some Christians than to me? Part of the answer is in this verse: he shows himself to those who love him and keep his word. Closeness to Christ grows along the path of obedience and his word, not by waiting for a special experience. Where there is unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture, or a divided heart, the sense of his presence often fades. But not every dry season is caused by sin; godly believers have walked through long stretches of darkness while trusting him (Isaiah 50:10). Keep reading, keep praying, keep obeying, and keep company with his people. He has promised to make himself known, and he keeps his promises.

In a sentence. Jesus said that whoever keeps his commandments loves him and will be loved by the Father, and he will reveal himself to him, and Judas (not Iscariot) asked why he would reveal himself to them and not to the world.

On a Tuesday. Choose one command of Christ you know you have been slow to keep: forgiving someone, speaking truthfully, being generous, guarding your eyes. Keep it today, deliberately, as an act of love for him. Love him, and he will make himself more and more real to you.

For worship. The Father who loved us before we loved him delights to pour out his love on those who love his Son. And the Son, who could have shown himself in blazing glory to the world, chooses to show himself quietly to those who love him. Christ shows himself to those who love him; that is the sweetest secret of the Christian life.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.

If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. Jesus answers Judas indirectly. He reveals himself to those who love him and keep his word; the world neither loves nor obeys. Note the condition, repeated for the third time in this chapter. He will not stop saying it. Whatever else this indwelling is, it is not available to mere admiration.

And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. One word in this verse turns the whole chapter round, and it is invisible in English. Home is monē: the same noun, in the singular, that stood in verse 2, in my Father’s house are many rooms. So the chapter has two dwelling places in it, and they point in opposite directions. In verse 2 he goes away to prepare a monē for us in his Father’s house. In verse 23 he and the Father come and make a monē with us. Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for us in the Father’s house; meanwhile the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling in us.

The answer to Judas. That is a far better answer to Judas’s question than a discussion of visibility would have been. How will he manifest himself to us and not to the world? By moving in. The disclosure is not a display the nations could photograph; it is the Father and the Son taking up residence in a person, which is a thing only that person and God can know.

We. Father and Son together, by the Spirit. In the same discourse the Spirit is given to be with them for ever (v. 16) and to be in them (v. 17). All three, in the same chapter, described as taking up residence in ordinary people. The whole Trinity dwells in the believer. Every believer is a temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19).

The dwelling moves into people. This is the fulfilment of the promise that ran through the whole Old Testament. God dwelt in a tent, and then in a temple, and the glory departed from it in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 10). John said at the start of this Gospel that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (1:14). Now the dwelling moves again, into people.

Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me. The other side. To reject Christ’s word is to reject the Father’s. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as its source.

If God lives in me, why do I still sin so much? Because the house is being renovated while he lives in it. God does not wait for a believer to be perfect before he moves in; he moves in to make him holy. His presence is the reason you now hate your sin and fight it, which you did not before. Your body is his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), so sin is now a grief to him (Ephesians 4:30), and that should make you serious. But it is not a reason to doubt that he dwells in you. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. Jesus answered that whoever loves him keeps his word, and the Father will love him, and they will come and make their home with him; whoever does not love him does not keep his words, which are the Father’s.

On a Tuesday. God makes his home in you. Keep the house ready for such guests. Ask what in your life you would be ashamed for the Father and the Son to see: the screen, the grudge, the habit. Clear one room today, not to earn his presence but because he is already there.

For worship. The God whom heaven cannot contain has chosen to make his home in sinners who love his Son. While Christ prepares our room in the Father’s house, the Father and the Son take up their room in us. One day we will go to live with him; already he has come to live with us. Glory to the God who dwells with the humble and contrite.

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.

These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. They have heard much they do not yet understand.

But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name. This is the first time in the Gospel that the full title the Holy Spirit appears in Jesus’ own teaching. The Father sends him in the Son’s name: as the Son’s representative, to continue his work.

He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you. The two verbs are worth separating, because they do different jobs. The second is the more remarkable and the more consequential. It is a promise about memory, made to men who had spent three years misunderstanding almost everything they were told, and whose recollection was about to be the only record there would ever be. Think about the position they were in. Nothing had been written down. The teaching of Jesus existed, at that moment, inside the heads of eleven frightened men, several of whom had already shown that they could not follow a metaphor. Within a few decades they would need to hand on that teaching accurately to churches all round the Mediterranean, and eventually into books.

The promise that grounds the New Testament. This is a promise especially to the apostles. The Spirit would remind them of all Jesus said, and teach them its meaning. This is the basis of the New Testament: the Gospels were written by men whom the Spirit helped to remember, by the Spirit’s work of inspiration (2 Peter 1:21), and the letters by men whom he taught. We have the apostles’ testimony in Scripture because of this promise. And John, writing decades later, is the standing exhibit: he reproduces long discourses, exact phrases, the fragrance of the ointment, the number of the water jars, the seating at a supper. Either he had a remarkable memory, or this promise was kept, and there is no reason it cannot be both.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit’s teaching today. Some claim the Spirit gives new revelation today, beyond Scripture. Verdict: the promise is first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament, which is complete and sufficient (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Spirit still teaches every believer, not by new revelation, but by illuminating the Scripture he inspired. The canon is closed; the Spirit opens our eyes to it.

The boundary. Note it, because it is important and often ignored. The Spirit does not bring new material. Everything in the two verbs is tethered to what Jesus said: teaching all things, and reminding of all that I have said to you. Every claim to fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts what is in these books has this verse standing against it. That cuts against a particular kind of enthusiasm, and also against a particular kind of dryness. The Spirit is not a source of information beyond Christ. Nor is he an idea; his work is to make what Christ said land in a person who has read it many times without it moving anything.

Does the Spirit still guide me personally? Yes, but through his word, not beside it. He gives wisdom as you study Scripture, pray and take counsel (James 1:5); he brings to mind what you have read when you need it; he convicts, comforts and directs your heart along the lines Scripture has drawn. What you should not do is treat impressions, dreams or inner nudges as new words from God that bind you or others. Test every impression by Scripture, and where Scripture leaves a choice open, choose wisely and in faith, trusting God’s providence. A feeling may be from the Spirit, but only the Bible is certainly from him.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he had spoken these things while still with them, but the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send in his name, would teach them all things and remind them of everything he had said.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible today, pray a short prayer: Holy Spirit, teach me, and bring Christ’s words to life in me. Then read slowly, and carry one verse with you through the day.

For worship. Thank God for the New Testament, the Spirit’s gift through the apostles. The words that fell on the ears of eleven frightened men were not lost; the Spirit kept them, taught them, and wrote them for us, so that we hold in our hands what Jesus said on the night he was betrayed. The same Spirit opens our eyes to see in those words the glory of Christ. Blessed be the God who speaks, and keeps his word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, ‘I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Peace (shalom) was simply how a Jew said goodbye: the everyday greeting and farewell, what you said at a door, and it still is. So the sentence begins as the most ordinary farewell in the language, and he then takes it apart in the next clause. Jesus gives far more than a greeting. And the word he uses is worth noticing: leave is what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate, and this is what is in it. It is his last will and testament: what he leaves them. His peace is wholeness, right relationship with God, the calm that comes from reconciliation (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7), bought at the cross by the one who bequeaths it.

Not as the world gives do I give to you. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble, and it does not last. The world’s shalom at a doorway is a wish. It commits the speaker to nothing, costs nothing, and secures nothing, which is exactly what our own take care and all the best amount to. He is distinguishing a bequest from a pleasantry. And shalom is not the absence of trouble; it is wholeness, everything in its right relation, and it is perfectly compatible with a storm outside. What he is bequeathing is not a quiet life. Within a few hours the men receiving it will scatter into the dark, and by the end of their lives most of them will have been killed. So it cannot mean circumstances. It means that the thing which makes a person whole, being right with God, has been settled elsewhere and cannot be reached by circumstances. Christ’s peace holds in the middle of trouble (16:33).

Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. The chapter returns to its start. The first half is verse 1 word for word; the second is new. He has been talking for a whole chapter and the fear is still in the room, so he says it again, and adds the word for what they are actually feeling.

If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father. His going is gain for him: return to glory.

For the Father is greater than I. How can this be, if the Son is equal with God (5:18; 10:30)? Not greater in nature or being, but greater in position: in his incarnation and earthly mission, the Son took the role of a servant, and the Father sent him. Now he returns to the glory he had with the Father (17:5). The Son is equal in essence, but submits in role.

Where Christians differ. Arians in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, cite this verse to show that the Son is a lesser being. Verdict: the same Gospel calls him God (1:1; 20:28). This verse speaks of his incarnate state, as the one sent; greater refers to role and position, not essence.
