A son can be equal to his father in nature and still honour his father as the head of the house. Athanasius and the Nicene Creed held both truths together.

Four answers to the Arian reading. This sentence has done more service in the denial of Christ’s deity than any other in the Gospel. It was an anchor text of Arius, whose teaching the Council of Nicaea was called to answer, and it is the verse a Jehovah’s Witness is most likely to open at your door. Four things answer it. First, look at what the sentence is for. It is not a concession wrung out of him in debate; it is a reason he gives his friends to be glad. Nobody offers a confession of inferiority as consolation. Second, the word is greater, not better. Greater is the language of position: a king is greater than his son without being more human than he is. Third, and this is decisive, consider who wrote it down. The same man in the same book tells us the Word was God (1:1), that Jesus said I and the Father are one (10:30) and before Abraham was, I am (8:58), and closes with Thomas saying to him, my Lord and my God, uncorrected (20:28). A sentence must be read inside the book it belongs to. Fourth, remember where he is standing. He is hours from the cross, having taken the form of a servant, the one whom Paul describes as being in the form of God and not counting equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6–7). A man on his way to be crucified saying the Father is greater is telling you where he has placed himself, not what he is. The old answer remains the best one: greater in office, equal in nature. And notice the tenderness of it. He is not lecturing them about the Trinity. He is telling frightened men that where he is going is better, and that if they loved him they would be glad for him.

How do I keep Christ’s peace when life is falling apart? By remembering where it is kept. His peace does not live in your circumstances, so circumstances cannot take it; it lives in your standing with God, which he has settled by his blood. When fear rises, bring it to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Fill your mind with what is true. Keep company with believers. And do not mistake feeling shaken for having lost his peace: Jesus himself was troubled in spirit while perfectly at peace with the Father. The storm may be loud; the anchor still holds.

In a sentence. Jesus gave them his peace, unlike the world’s, telling them not to be troubled or afraid, and that if they loved him they would rejoice that he was going to the Father, who is greater than he.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s peace does not depend on your circumstances. Receive it today, in the middle of whatever troubles you. When you say goodbye to someone today, notice how empty our ordinary farewells are, and thank Christ that his farewell was a gift that cost him his life.

For worship. He made his will on the night before he died, and he left us his peace. No thief can steal it and no storm can reach it, because it was purchased by his blood and kept in the Father’s hands. And he went home to the Father, the glory he had before the world was, not as a lesser being returning to his superior, but as the eternal Son returning to the Father’s side with his work done. Rejoice with him, as he asked his friends to do.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,

And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. As in 13:19. His foreknowledge will strengthen their faith. The disciples will endure the passion with greater faith because they remember these words.

I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. Satan comes through Judas and the soldiers (13:27; 18:3), through the temple police and the cohort with lanterns.

He has no claim on me. Literally, in me he has nothing. It is a picture from a search. The enemy is arriving, and he will go over this man and find nothing belonging to him: no handhold, no debt, no compromise, no old arrangement he can call in. Satan has no hold on Jesus, no foothold of sin, no legal claim. Jesus is sinless. That is the claim of sinlessness stated in its most practical form, and it is what makes the next three days work.

The sting with nothing to inject. Everyone else who has ever died had something in them that death could rightly claim. Hebrews describes the devil as the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and Paul puts the mechanism plainly: the sting of death is sin (1 Corinthians 15:56). The devil has a claim on every sinner, for the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). On Jesus he has none. So Jesus does not die because Satan has power over him, but freely, for love of the Father. When they come for him in the garden, they are arresting a man over whom they have no rights whatever, and he goes anyway.

Does the devil have a claim on me? If you are in Christ, no. His accusations are real, and some of them are true, but they have no legal force, because Christ has paid the debt in full and cancelled the record that stood against you, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). When the accuser reminds you of your sins, agree that they were real, and then point him to the cross where they were punished. He has nothing in Christ, and you are in Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them beforehand so that they would believe, and he would not talk much more, for the ruler of this world was coming, but had no claim on him.

On a Tuesday. When guilt over a forgiven sin comes back at you today, answer it with Scripture, not feelings: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Say it aloud if you need to.

For worship. The devil had no claim on Christ. Because Christ is yours, the devil has no claim on you either (Romans 8:33–34). The spotless Lamb walked into the enemy’s hour with nothing in him for the enemy to seize, and laid down his life of his own accord. The sinless one bore our sins, so that the accuser would have nothing left to say.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.

But I do as the Father has commanded me. Jesus goes to the cross in obedience to the Father. The voluntary obedience of the Son is the world’s lesson in what love for the Father looks like.

So that the world may know that I love the Father. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus says in so many words that he loves the Father. The cross is the proof. That is a startling reason to give for a crucifixion, and it is the one he gives. The cross is many things at once, a ransom, a substitution, a victory, and here, at the door of the room, he names it as a demonstration of his love for his Father, put on where the world can see it. It is the supreme display of the love of the Son for the Father, the love that is at the foundation of all things.

Rise, let us go from here. There is a real puzzle here, and it is better faced than ignored, since any attentive reader trips over it. Three more chapters of discourse follow before anybody actually leaves. Chapter 18:1 says that when Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way to the garden, perhaps passing the vines on the slopes or the golden vine on the temple gate (15:1). Others think they rose but lingered, which is exactly what happens when people are about to part. Either is possible. What should not be said is that this is a seam left by clumsy editing that nobody noticed. The man who wrote this Gospel could have removed a few words if he had wanted to. He left them.

Not the words of a victim. Rise is the ordinary word for getting up. Let us go. Not they are coming for me, not it is time to hide. He is the one who ends the meal, opens the door, and sets off toward the garden where he knows Judas will bring the soldiers, because he told him to go and do it quickly. Nobody comes to get him. He goes. The Son goes forward in love, not under compulsion.

Why did Jesus have to obey the Father, if he is equal with him? Because in the plan of salvation the Son freely took the place of the servant, as the second Adam who would obey where the first disobeyed (Romans 5:19). His obedience is not the obedience of an inferior being but the willing obedience of a Son who shares the Father’s will and delights in it. And it was for us: his perfect obedience in life and death is counted to everyone who trusts him. When you obey God, you are not earning his favour; you are walking in the steps of the Son whose obedience has already won it for you.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would do as the Father commanded, so the world would know he loves the Father, and told them to get up and leave.

On a Tuesday. Love for God shows itself in obedience, even costly obedience. Rise, and go where he sends you. Is there a step of obedience you have been putting off because you know it will cost you? Take it today, and do it out of love for the Father, as Christ did.

For worship. Nobody dragged him to the cross. He rose from the table, opened the door, and walked out into the night toward the garden, because he loved the Father and loved his own. The love between the Father and the Son, from all eternity, was displayed before the world on a Roman gallows. Rise, let us go: the Captain of our salvation leads the way, and we follow him home.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?<sup>3</sup>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.<sup>4</sup>And you know the way to where I am going.”<sup>5</sup>Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.<sup>7</sup>If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him.”<sup>8</sup>Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”<sup>9</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ’Show us the Father’?<sup>10</sup>Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.<sup>11</sup>Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves.<sup>12</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.<sup>13</sup>Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.<sup>14</sup>If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.<sup>15</sup>“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.<sup>16</sup>And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,<sup>17</sup>even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.<sup>18</sup>“I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.<sup>19</sup>Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.<sup>20</sup>In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.<sup>21</sup>Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”<sup>22</sup>Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.<sup>24</sup>Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.<sup>28</sup>You heard me say to you, ’I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.<sup>29</sup>And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe.<sup>30</sup>I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him. Into their fear he speaks some of the most comforting words in Scripture: “Let not your hearts be troubled.” He is going to prepare a place for them in his Father’s house and will come again to take them to himself. When Thomas asks the way, Jesus answers, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus replies that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Those who believe will do greater works, because he is going to the Father, and whatever they ask in his name he will do.

The second half of the chapter introduces the Holy Spirit as “another Helper”, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them for ever and in them. Jesus will not leave them as orphans; he will come to them, and he and the Father will make their home with those who love him and keep his word. The Spirit will teach them all things and remind them of everything Jesus said, the promise that underlies the writing of the New Testament. He leaves them his peace, not as the world gives. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no claim on him; Jesus goes to the cross so that the world may know that he loves the Father. Here the doctrine of the Trinity is not argued but lived: the Father sends, the Son goes and prays, the Spirit comes, and all three make their home with the believer.

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls himself the true vine, with his Father as the gardener who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones to make them more productive. The disciples are already made clean by his word. They must stay joined to him, for no branch bears fruit cut off from the vine, and without him they can achieve nothing; branches that do not remain are thrown out to wither and burn. If his words remain in them, their prayers will be answered, and their abundant fruit will glorify the Father and prove them disciples. He has loved them as the Father loves him, and they remain in his love by obeying him, as he obeys the Father, so that his joy may fill them. His command is that they love one another as he has loved them; the highest love gives its life for friends. They are his friends, not mere servants, for he has shared with them all he heard from the Father. He chose them, not they him, and appointed them to bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the true vine: Israel was the vine God planted (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7; Jer. 2:21; Ezek. 15; Hos. 10:1). Israel repeatedly failed as the vine. Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be — the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who bears fruit that lasts. The disciples are branches in this vine: their fruitfulness is entirely dependent on their connection to Jesus. Apart from me you can do nothing is the Reformed doctrine of total human dependence stated for the community of disciples. The branch does not produce fruit; it bears fruit — the distinction between human effort and Spirit-mediated connection.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16): the elective basis of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make the disciples passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative, the foundation, and the guarantee of fruitfulness reside in the one who chose, not in those who were chosen. Whatever fruit the Christian life produces is the fruit of the Vine, borne through the branches who abide.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.

Meaning first. John 15 teaches what life in Christ looks like after he has gone. First, the vine and the branches: union with Christ, from which all fruit flows (vv. 1–17). Then the world’s hatred, which his people must expect (vv. 18–27). Abiding in Christ, loving one another, and bearing witness in a hostile world: that is the Christian life. And underneath all of it is the vine himself, the true Israel, through whom the life of God flows into ordinary people and makes them fruitful.

The setting. Jesus has just said, Rise, let us go from here (14:31). He may be speaking these words in the upper room as they gather themselves to leave, or on the walk through the city and down toward the Kidron valley, past vineyards and perhaps past the temple. It is the last hours before his arrest, and Judas has gone out to fetch the soldiers.

I am the true vine. The seventh and last of the great I am sayings in John. The force of true only lands once you know what the vine had always meant, and the record is uniformly grim. The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; Hosea 10:1). Every substantial vine passage in the Old Testament is a passage about failure. Isaiah’s song describes a vineyard dug, cleared, planted with choice vines, given a tower and a winepress, and the owner looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2), and the vineyard is laid waste. Jeremiah: God had planted Israel a choice vine, wholly of pure seed, and it had turned degenerate (Jeremiah 2:21). Ezekiel devotes a whole chapter to pointing out that vine wood is useless for anything but burning (Ezekiel 15). Hosea: Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit for itself (Hosea 10:1). Psalm 80 is the one prayer among them, and even it is a lament over a vine whose walls are broken down. So when a Jew heard vine, he heard a story that had gone wrong: the standing image for a people planted with every advantage who produced nothing worth picking.

True, not derivative. The word alēthinē does not mean truthful. It means real as against derivative: the genuine article of which the others were copies, the same word John used of the true light (1:9) and the true bread (6:32). So the claim is: everything that vine was meant to be and never was, I am. Israel was meant to be God’s fruitful vine, and failed. Jesus is the true vine: the real Israel, the faithful Son, the one who bears the fruit Israel did not. To belong to God’s people is to be joined to him. It is a claim to be Israel.

The golden vine. There is also the possibility that they could see one. Josephus describes a vine of gold above the entrance to the temple sanctuary, with clusters as tall as a man, and the Mishnah adds that worshippers gave golden leaves and grapes to hang on it as offerings. If chapter 14 ended with them leaving the room, the road to the Kidron may have run within sight of the temple. It cannot be proved, and it does not need to be; but a man saying I am the true vine under a golden one worth a fortune would not have needed to explain himself.

And my Father is the vinedresser. Vinedresser (geōrgos) means farmer, gardener. The Father tends the vine. Nothing happens to the branches by accident; every cut is made by the Father’s hand.

Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. Who are these fruitless branches in the vine? In context, Judas is the clearest example: outwardly attached to Christ, a disciple, but never truly united to him by faith. Some take takes away (airei) as lifts up, as a vinedresser lifts trailing branches off the ground; but v. 6 makes clear that fruitless branches are removed and burned. It is an attractive reading, and it is probably wrong: verse 6 describes the same kind of branch being thrown out, withering, gathered and burned, which is not what happens to a branch that has been tied up.

Can a believer be cut off? The branch taken away is one that bears no fruit at all, and v. 6 shows what becomes of it. It was attached to the vine outwardly, but never drew life from it; it is a professing, not a living, branch (compare 1 John 2:19).

And every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. Prunes (kathairei) means cleans, cuts back: a play on words with clean in v. 3. Pruning hurts, but it makes a vine more fruitful. The Father uses trials, discipline and his word to cut away what hinders fruit (Hebrews 12:5–11). And this second knife is the important one, because it falls on the healthy branch. Both branches feel a blade. The difference is what it is for. The pruning is not punishment but cultivation. God sometimes cuts away what is good to produce what is better, and removes what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful.

How do I know whether I am being pruned or punished? If you belong to Christ, the Father’s knife on your life is never punishment in the sense of paying for your sins, because Christ has borne that punishment in full (Romans 8:1). What you experience is a Father’s discipline, which is always for your good, that you may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sometimes he removes a sin; sometimes he removes a comfort, a plan, a reputation, or even a good thing that had become too large in your heart. You may not know the precise reason for each cut. You can know the purpose: more fruit, more likeness to Christ, more joy in him. Ask him what he is teaching you, and trust the hand that holds the knife.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes every branch in him that bears no fruit and prunes every fruitful branch so that it bears more.

On a Tuesday. If you are being pruned, it means you are bearing fruit, and the Father wants more. Trust the gardener’s knife. Think of the loss or difficulty that has hurt most this year, and ask the Father, not why, but what fruit he means to grow from it. Then tell him you trust his hands.

For worship. Where Israel failed, Christ stands as the true vine, faithful in every root and branch, bearing the fruit God looked for and never found. And the Father who tends him tends us, with a gardener’s patience and a Father’s love. No cut is careless, no season is wasted, and no living branch is ever thrown away. Blessed be the Vine who gives life, and the Vinedresser who makes us fruitful.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.

Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Clean (katharoi): the eleven have been cleansed by receiving his word in faith (13:10). Judas has gone. And there is a piece of wordplay between verses 2 and 3 that no English version can carry, and it changes the tone of the pruning. He prunes it, kathairei. Already you are clean, katharoi. Same root. The verb for what the vinedresser does to a branch is the verb for making something clean, and John puts the two words in consecutive sentences. So the pruning is not primarily about productivity, as a modern reader assumes. It is cleansing. The blade takes off what is diseased or dead or simply in the way, and what is left is clean.

The knife is the word. The instrument is named: because of the word that I have spoken to you. The knife is what he says. That is worth pausing on, because it locates the pruning somewhere unexpected: not only in circumstances, though God certainly uses those, but in the word landing on a person and taking something off him (Hebrews 4:12).

Abide in me, and I in you. Now the command, and it is the keyword of the chapter. Abide (menō) appears again and again in vv. 1–10; nothing else in the discourse is repeated at that rate. It means remain, stay, live in. It is both a command and a promise. The believer is already in Christ; now he must stay there, living in conscious dependence on him. And Christ lives in him.

What abide means. It has to be made concrete, because abide in Christ is one of those phrases that gets preached warmly and leaves people with nothing to do on Monday. Start with what the word means. It is not a mystical exercise. Menō is the ordinary word for staying: the disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed with him (1:38–39); he stayed two days in Samaria (4:40); he remained beyond the Jordan (10:40). It means to go on being where you already are. That is the first thing to say, and it is a relief. The command is not get in. The branches are already in the vine; he says so in the same breath. The command is: do not go anywhere.

How do we abide? The chapter supplies the content rather than leaving it vague. By keeping his word in us (v. 7): Scripture staying resident rather than visited. By resting in his love (v. 9): staying inside his love rather than trying to earn it. By keeping his commandments (v. 10): doing what he said. And by prayer, which runs through all three. So abiding turns out to consist of ordinary things done continuously. Nothing there requires a special temperament or technique. It is the difference between a branch attached to a vine and a branch lying on the ground, and the branch does not achieve it. It simply does not detach.

As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you. A branch does not produce fruit by effort. It bears fruit by staying connected to the life of the vine. All fruit comes from the life of Christ flowing through us. This is the dependence that pride always resists and grace always establishes.

What does abiding look like on a busy day with no time for long devotions? It looks like staying turned toward Christ in the ordinary hours. Begin the day with even a few verses, read with attention, and carry one with you. Speak to him briefly and often: before the meeting, in the queue, when you are tempted, when you are glad. Obey him in the small next thing. Remember, when guilt or worry rises, that you are loved and forgiven in him. Abiding is not measured by the length of your quiet time but by whether you are depending on him or on yourself. Longer times with the Scriptures and prayer feed it, and you should make room for them, but a branch abides all day, not only in the morning.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples they were already clean by his word, and must abide in him as he in them, for no branch can bear fruit unless it remains in the vine.

On a Tuesday. Choose one verse from this chapter and write it somewhere you will see it repeatedly today. Each time you see it, turn your heart back to Christ for a moment. That is abiding: staying where you are, in him, on purpose.

For worship. You do not have to manufacture fruit. Stay close to Christ, and his life will bear it in you. He has already made you clean by his word, and he holds you in himself as surely as the vine holds the branch. All the life is his, all the fruit is his, and all the glory is his, and he shares it with branches that could produce nothing on their own.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.

I am the vine; you are the branches. Simple and clear. He says it again, plainly, so that no one can miss who is which.

Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit. Much fruit: not a little, but abundant. What is the fruit? Christlike character, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience (v. 10); love (v. 12); joy (v. 11); answered prayer (v. 7); and people brought to Christ (4:36; Romans 1:13).

For apart from me you can do nothing. The most absolute statement of dependence in the Gospel. Not a little, not very much: nothing of spiritual value. The branch that is separated from the vine does not produce diminished fruit; it produces no fruit at all. A humbling truth: all our gifts, efforts and plans produce nothing that lasts without him. And an encouraging one: with him, everything he calls us to is possible (Philippians 4:13). Apart from me you can do nothing means, from the other side, with me, everything.

If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers. Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned (Ezekiel 15:2–5). It is good for nothing else.

And the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned. A picture of final judgement (Matthew 13:40–42). This is not casual language. It describes the end of the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection, finally revealed and removed.

Can a branch in Christ be cut off and burned? That answer should not be given quickly, because the words are severe and a reader may be frightened by them, and the difficulty is real. Verse 2 says every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. In me. How can a branch be in Christ and be cut off and burned, when the same Lord said five chapters earlier that no one is able to snatch them out of his Father’s hand (10:29)?

The vine was always mixed. The picture itself supplies the answer. The vine is an image lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where the vine is Israel: a nation full of people who belonged to the covenant community outwardly, carried its sign in their bodies, kept its feasts, and were not the true people of God at all. That is precisely Isaiah’s complaint: he looked for grapes and it yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). To be a branch on that vine never guaranteed life in it. And notice who Jesus is speaking to. He is in a room with the Twelve, and one of them has just gone out into the night to sell him (13:30). Judas was a branch in every visible sense, called, trusted with the common purse, and he bore nothing, because there was nothing in him to bear with. John gives us the category plainly in his letter: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19).

No sheep prised from his hand. So the two sayings stand together without strain. The fruitless branch is not a sheep prised out of the Shepherd’s hand; it is a branch tied on to the vine that never drew a drop of sap from it. Union with Christ that is real produces fruit, always, however slowly and however little: that is what the passage means by fruit, not a level of achievement but evidence of life.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this to teach that genuine Christians can lose their salvation if they stop abiding. Verdict: the branches that are burned are those who “do not abide,” like Judas: outwardly attached, never inwardly united. True abiding is the mark of true disciples (8:31), and Jesus has promised that his sheep will never perish (10:28). The warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people abiding. It calls us to examine whether our union with Christ is real, not to fear that the Father will drop his own.

The Arminian reading. Arminian Christians read this verse as a warning that a true believer can fail to abide and be cut off and lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6; Galatians 5:4). The warning is real and must be heeded. But Jesus has already said of his sheep that they will never perish (10:28), and a branch that bears no fruit at all shows that it never drew life from the vine. The more likely reading is that the burned branches are those who seemed to belong to Christ but never did, like Judas, and that the warning is one of the means by which Christ keeps the true branches abiding.

If this frightens you. And to the person genuinely alarmed by this verse, one thing more. Ask yourself why you are alarmed. A dead branch does not lie awake fearing that it is fruitless; it feels nothing at all, which is the whole trouble with it. The very desire to abide is sap moving. Christ did not tell his friends this to leave them measuring themselves for the fire; the command in the passage is not examine yourself but abide in me, and abiding is not an achievement to be pulled off. It is a staying put. Stay where you are, in him, and the fruit is his business, not yours.

How much fruit must I see to be sure I am a true branch? There is no quota. Jesus speaks of fruit, more fruit and much fruit (vv. 2, 5), which means growth, not a fixed measure. Look for the kind of thing the chapter names, not for impressive results: a real love for Christ and his word, a hatred of your sin and a willingness to fight it, love for his people, and some desire that others know him. Those may be small and mixed with much weakness, but they are signs of sap. And do not base your assurance chiefly on your fruit. Base it on Christ’s promise to keep his sheep, and on the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16); then let the fruit confirm what the promise declares.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the vine and they the branches, and whoever abides in him bears much fruit, for without him they can do nothing, but whoever does not abide is thrown away like a branch, withers, and is burned.

On a Tuesday. Start your day with this: apart from him I can do nothing. Then ask him to work through you. Before each significant task today, the email, the meeting, the meal with your family, pray in one sentence: Lord, I can do nothing of value here without you; work through me.

For worship. The Vine does not let go of his living branches. He holds them with the same hand that holds the sheep, and no one can snatch them out. The warning that sobers us is the very voice that keeps us, calling us to stay where we are, in him. Apart from him we can do nothing; in him we bear fruit that lasts. Glory to the faithful Vine, who keeps all whom the Father has given him.
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.

If you abide in me, and my words abide in you. Abiding in Christ goes with his words abiding in us. You cannot abide in him while ignoring his word. Scripture filling the mind and heart is how Christ dwells richly in us (Colossians 3:16). Two directions of abiding: in the person of Christ and in the word of Christ.

Ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. The promise has a condition. When Christ’s words fill us, our wishes are shaped by his will. Then we ask what he wants to give. This is the third prayer promise in two chapters, and the conditions are worth laying side by side, because they accumulate rather than repeat. At 14:13–14 it was whatever you ask in my name. Here: if you abide in me, and my words abide in you. At verse 16 it will be tied to being chosen and sent. So the promise is never bare. Each statement of it carries a boundary, and the boundary here is the most searching of them: not a formula appended to a request but a condition about where the person praying is living.

The prayers change before the answers do. Notice the mechanism, because it explains why the promise is not reckless. A person saturated in what Christ said begins, over time, to want different things. That is why ask whatever you wish can be said without qualification after that clause: the wishing itself has been under instruction. And that is also the answer to the suspicion that this is a trick, that God grants only what he was going to do anyway, so the promise is empty. It is not empty; it is a description of what happens to desire when somebody lives close to Christ for a long time. The wishes are genuinely the person’s own. They have simply stopped being arbitrary.

By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit. The goal of fruit-bearing is the Father’s glory (Matthew 5:16). The church’s calling to bear much fruit is not self-promotion but the honour of the Father. The vine’s purpose is the vinedresser’s glory.

And so prove to be my disciples. Prove to be (genēsthe) means become, show yourselves to be; more literally, and become my disciples. Discipleship is treated as something one grows into rather than only a status secured at the start. Fruit is the evidence of discipleship, not its cause. The fruit does not earn the title. It is how the title becomes visible.

How can I let Christ’s words abide in me, if I struggle to read the Bible? Start small and steady rather than large and occasional. Read a short passage, perhaps a few verses of a Gospel, at the same time each day. Read it twice, slowly, and ask: what does this show me of Christ, and what does it ask of me? Choose one sentence to carry with you, and say it to yourself during the day. Listen carefully to the preaching on Sunday and talk about it afterwards. Learn a verse by heart each week. If reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud. The aim is not to finish a plan but to let his words take up residence.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they abide in him and his words abide in them, they may ask what they wish and it will be done, for the Father is glorified when they bear much fruit and so show themselves to be his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray today, read a few verses of Scripture and let them shape what you ask. Pray those words back to God, turning his promises into requests. Notice how different your prayers become when his words are in them.

For worship. Fill your heart with his words, and your prayers will be shaped by his will. Then ask boldly. The God who speaks invites us to answer him in his own words, and he delights to grant what his words have taught us to desire. The Father is glorified in fruitful branches, and the fruit is from the Vine, so that all the glory returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.

As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. The comparison is the largest in the chapter, and it is easy to read past as a pleasantry. The measure of Christ’s love for us is the Father’s love for him: eternal, infinite, perfect. The measure is not a great deal, or more than you know. The measure is the love within the Godhead, the love the Father has had for the Son from before the foundation of the world, which chapter 17 will say in so many words (17:24). That is the quantity being reported. Breathtaking.

Abide in my love. Live in it. Make his love your home. Do not wander out into doubt or self-reliance. The phrase needs unpacking, because it can be heard as a threat: stay in it or you will fall out of it. Read it against the picture. A branch does not generate the sap; it lives in a supply that is already flowing. Abiding in his love is not maintaining his affection at a certain level, which is impossible and was never asked; it is remaining inside something that is there whether one feels it or not.

If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love. Obedience is how we stay in his love, not to earn it but to enjoy it. As a child who disobeys does not stop being loved, but loses the sense of closeness. Now the guard, because this sentence has produced a great deal of misery. It does not say obedience purchases the love. The clause that follows settles it.

Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love. Jesus is the model. His obedience and the Father’s love went together. Nobody supposes the Son earns the Father’s love by good behaviour. His obedience is the form of a love that was never in question, and the disciples’ obedience is being described in the same way. Obedience is love’s response, not love’s price.

Does God love me less when I disobey? No. His love for his children rests on Christ, not on their performance, and it does not rise and fall with your week (Romans 8:38–39). But your enjoyment of his love can be clouded by sin, as a child who has disobeyed may avoid his father’s eyes even while his father loves him as much as ever. The way back is not to make up for it first, but to come home: confess, receive his forgiveness, and walk with him again. You do not obey to get into his love; you obey because you are in it, and obedience keeps you in the warmth of it.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he loves them as the Father loves him, and they should abide in his love by keeping his commandments, as he has kept his Father’s and abides in his love.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test. Ask what happens inside you after a bad week: whether you approach God expecting the temperature to have dropped. If the answer is yes, then something is being treated as a wage that this verse treats as a home. Christ loves you as the Father loves him. Live there today.

For worship. The love that has flowed between the Father and the Son from all eternity has been turned toward us. We are loved with the love the Father has for his only Son, and that love will not run dry, because it springs from God himself. Nothing we do began it, and nothing can exhaust it. Let the heart rest there, and be glad.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.

These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. Stop at the word and at when it was said, because both are extraordinary. My joy: not joy in general, and not the disciples’ cheerfulness, but a joy that belongs to him and is being transferred. His joy is the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing his will. And the man saying it will be arrested within a few hours and dead by tomorrow afternoon. He knows it; he has been telling them so all evening. On the night before the cross, Jesus speaks of joy. That means the joy he proposes to hand over is not a mood produced by favourable circumstances, because his circumstances at that moment were the worst ever arranged for anybody. Hebrews describes the same thing from the far side: for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2).

Full. A container word: filled up, brought to the brim. It is what John says elsewhere: we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete (1 John 1:4). He wants us to share his joy, and to be full of it. The Christian life is not grim duty. Obedience and joy go together.

For the believer who does not feel joyful. Now the pastoral half, because there is a reader for whom this verse is an accusation. Christians are frequently told they ought to be joyful, and the ones who are not conclude that something is defective in them, which is often untrue and always unhelpful, particularly for people whose flatness is a matter of temperament, exhaustion or illness rather than of the soul. Notice therefore where the joy is located. It is his, and it is in them, and it arrives by the route the whole chapter has been describing: abiding. It is not summoned up. It is a by-product of staying attached to a vine, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful. Several of the most joyful Christians who ever lived were also, by any modern measure, depressed men. And the location of the sentence tells against the sunny reading. This is not said at a wedding. It is said in a room somebody has just walked out of to fetch soldiers.

How can I have joy and sorrow at the same time? Because Christian joy is deeper than mood. Paul describes himself as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Joy in this sense is the settled gladness of knowing that you are loved by God, forgiven in Christ, and kept for glory, and it can sit underneath real grief like the deep water under a stormy surface. You do not have to pretend to be happy at a graveside or in a hospital ward. You can weep, and still know that the One who loves you is risen and that the end of the story is good. That is his joy in you.

This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. The new commandment of 13:34, repeated. The vine and the branches now become the basis for life together: branches in the same vine are branches in relationship with each other. The love of Christ for the disciples becomes the measure of their love for one another.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them these things so that his joy would be in them and their joy would be full, and his commandment was that they love one another as he loved them.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of five things that are true of you in Christ, whatever your feelings today: forgiven, loved, adopted, kept, heading home. Read it slowly and thank him for each. Then do one loving act for another believer, because joy and love grow on the same branch.

For worship. On the night of his betrayal, with the cross before him, the Son of God spoke of his joy, and wanted it in us. His joy did not depend on comfort; it was the joy of the Son in the Father, set before him beyond the cross. Christ wants your joy to be full, and he has gone through death to make sure that one day it will be, brim full, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you.

Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. This sentence is carved on war memorials all over the world, and it belongs there. A man who dies to bring his friends out is doing something Christ himself calls the greatest love there is, and no Christian should be grudging about it. It is the highest human love: to die for someone else. Jesus is about to do it.

Greater than the greatest. But the verse says something the memorials cannot. He is defining the ceiling of human love and then going beyond it the following afternoon. Paul makes the point explicitly: one will scarcely die for a righteous person, but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:7–8), and a few lines later, while we were enemies (5:10). So the soldier’s love is the highest thing on the human scale, and Christ exceeds it, because his friends at that moment were not behaving like friends. One had sold him, one would deny him three times before dawn, and the rest would run. He calls them friends anyway, and the word is not sentimental: philoi, from the affectionate verb, the same root as the word the sisters used of Lazarus, he whom you love (11:3). His love is greater than the greatest love.

You are my friends if you do what I command you. The condition reads awkwardly, and it sounds like a friendship on probation. The next verse forbids that reading. He does not say you will become my friends if. He has already called them friends and is about to say so again (v. 15). What the conditional does is describe the shape of the friendship rather than set its price: friends of this particular friend are people who do what he says, because of who he is. Not that obedience makes us his friends, but that it shows we are.

He goes first. A command has been given by somebody who is about to obey a harder one. He is not asking them to do anything he is unwilling to do first.

Can I really call Jesus my friend? Yes, and with wonder, because he calls you that first. Friendship with Christ does not make him less than Lord; you are friends of the King, not his equals. So the friendship is full of reverence as well as warmth. But it is real: he has laid down his life for you, he has told you the Father’s plans, he hears you, he is for you. You may speak to him with the openness of a friend, bring him your troubles without performance, and trust his loyalty when you feel least loyal yourself. What a friend we have in Jesus is sentimental only if it forgets the cross; remembered there, it is the plain truth.

In a sentence. Jesus said there is no greater love than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends, and they are his friends if they do what he commands.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church needs a friend who will lay something down for them: time, comfort, convenience, money? Lay one thing down for that person this week, quietly, for Christ’s sake.

For worship. He laid down his life for his friends, and he calls you his friend. What love. He died for those who were failing him at that very hour, and called them friends while they were still running. The love that went beyond the highest human love has found us, and it will never let us go.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.

No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing. Weigh what has just happened, because it is one of the most startling sentences in the Bible and familiarity has worn it smooth. Every great figure of the Old Testament is a servant. It is the title of honour: Moses my servant, David my servant, Israel my servant, and the prophets my servants. To be called the servant of the LORD was the highest thing a Jew could aspire to. And he takes it off them. And the reason is precise rather than sentimental: a slave just obeys orders without explanation. He is told what to do and not why; the plan is not his business.

But I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. In the whole Old Testament two men are called the friend of God. Abraham (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; taken up in James 2:23). And Moses, to whom the LORD spoke face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). Two, in two thousand years. God shared his plans with them (Genesis 18:17). Now Jesus calls all his disciples friends, because he has shared the Father’s plans. So the promotion is a promotion in disclosure. They have not been given easier commands; they have been given the reasons. And that has been happening all evening: he has told them about the Father’s house, the Spirit, the world’s hatred, his own death and return, none of which they needed to know merely in order to obey. They are still his servants (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but more than servants: trusted friends.

All, and yet more to come. Jesus says he has made known all that he has heard from his Father, yet soon says he still has many things to say to them, but they cannot bear them now (16:12). He has told them all they need as his friends; the rest the Spirit will bring out after his glory, through the apostles (16:13).

You did not choose me, but I chose you. This inverts the ordinary practice of the world they lived in. In that culture, disciples chose their rabbi. A young man picked the teacher whose yoke he wanted to take, applied himself, and hoped to be accepted. Everybody at that table would have expected discipleship to work that way, and several of them had first followed John the Baptist. Jesus reverses it. He chose them.

Is I chose you about salvation, or about the apostles’ office? In the first place it is the choosing of the Eleven for their mission, that you should go and bear fruit; Judas, too, was chosen as an apostle (6:70). But it rests on the same truth that runs through John, that those who come to Christ come because the Father gave them and drew them (6:37, 44). So it is rightly applied to every believer: our faith began with his choice. It reflects the deeper truth of election to salvation (13:18; 17:6; Ephesians 1:4). Our salvation starts with his choice, not ours. We chose him only because he first chose us.

Does election make my choice meaningless? No. You really did repent and believe; no one did it for you, and it was truly your act. Election explains why you did. Left to ourselves we would never have chosen him (6:44), so behind your choosing lies his, which made it possible and certain. That does not make you a puppet; it makes you a rescued sinner. And it brings two great gifts: humility, because you cannot boast about having chosen well, and security, because what began with his choice does not depend on the strength of yours.

And appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide. Chosen for a purpose: to go and bear lasting fruit, in lives changed by the gospel. The purpose is not privilege. It is a calling. Election in this verse runs straight out into mission, and the last word about the fruit is the chapter’s keyword, abide. Fruit that stays.

So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you. Prayer is connected with fruitful mission. Those whom he has chosen and sent pray in his name, and the Father answers them.

In a sentence. Jesus said he no longer calls them servants but friends, for he has told them all the Father told him, and they did not choose him but he chose and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit, so that the Father will give them whatever they ask in his name.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s friend, chosen by him. Live today as one entrusted with his purposes. Ask yourself: what fruit that lasts could I invest in today? A conversation about Christ, time with a younger believer, prayer for a missionary, teaching your children. Do one of them.

For worship. Two men in the Old Testament were called the friend of God, and now the Son calls every one of his people friends. He chose us before we chose him, opened to us the counsels of the Father, and sent us out to bear fruit that will outlast the world. We did not find him; he found us. Glory to the electing love that will not let its chosen go.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I command you, so that you will love one another.

These things I command you, so that you will love one another. One sentence, and it is doing a specific job: it closes the first half of the chapter by naming what all of it was for. These things reaches back over everything since verse 1: the vine, the pruning, the abiding, the joy, the friendship, the choosing. All of it is now said to have been aimed at a single outcome, and the outcome is love among his people. Everything he has commanded, abiding, obeying, bearing fruit, has love as its goal. It is the third time in this chapter (vv. 12, 17) and the theme of the whole discourse. The world will hate them (v. 18); they must love one another.

Not where we would have put the emphasis. That is worth stopping on, because it is not where any of us would have put it. Given a discourse on union with Christ, most preachers land on the upward direction: know him better, depend on him more, pray with confidence. Those are all in the passage. And he says the point of the whole thing is that they should love each other. Good doctrine always runs out into love: election produces humility, grace produces gratitude, and both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen.

An expected result. Note the grammar: so that you will love one another. It is put as an expected result of the teaching taking hold, which fits the vine: fruit is not extracted from a branch by exhortation.

To these men, that night. There is a reason this needed saying to these particular men. They had spent the meal arguing about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), and within hours they would all abandon him and then spend the weekend locked in a room together, with Peter’s failure in the middle of it. The community he is commanding to love one another was, on the available evidence, not good at it. He gives the command anyway, to them, that night. And it is the third time he has issued it in three chapters: a new commandment at 13:34, this is my commandment at 15:12, and now again here. Three times in one evening, to eleven men, about the same thing. Whatever else he wanted them to carry out of that room, this is what he thought needed saying repeatedly.

What if the Christian I find hardest to love has really wronged me? Then love will look like forgiveness, and forgiveness is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It means you do not hold it against him or seek to pay him back, because Christ has not held your sins against you (Ephesians 4:32). It may mean a hard conversation (Matthew 18:15), and where there is abuse or danger it means protection and, where needed, the involvement of church leaders and the authorities; love never requires you to stay in harm’s way. But it does mean praying for him, refusing bitterness, and being ready for reconciliation when there is repentance. Ask Christ for his love, because yours will run out.

In a sentence. Jesus said he commanded these things so that they would love one another.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last disagreement you had with a fellow believer. Is anything still unresolved? Take a step toward peace this week: a message, a call, an apology for your part, a prayer for his good.

For worship. All Christ’s commands lead to love. Ask yourself today: whom can I love as he loves me? The Vine pours his life into every branch alike, and the branches that share one sap are meant to share one love. He commanded it three times on the night of his betrayal, to men who would fail him, and by his Spirit he made them a family. He is doing the same with us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the world hates them, they should remember it hated Jesus first. If they belonged to the world, it would love them, but because he chose them out of it, it hates them. No servant is greater than his master: those who persecuted him will persecute them, and those who kept his word will keep theirs. All this will happen because of his name, for they do not know the one who sent him. Had he not come and spoken, they would not be guilty, but now they have no excuse; to hate him is to hate his Father. Had he not done works no one else did, they would not be guilty, but they have seen and hated both him and the Father, fulfilling the words of their law that they hated him without cause. But when the Helper comes, the Spirit of truth whom Jesus will send from the Father, he will testify about Jesus, and the disciples must testify too, for they have been with him from the start.
verseByVerse.theology: The world's hatred of the church is not an accident to be explained away but a structural feature of the relationship between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy or cultural accommodation will eliminate the hatred; he promises that the Spirit will sustain the witnesses through it. The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (v. 26) — a phrase that has generated centuries of debate about the procession of the Spirit — testifies about Jesus, and the disciples testify because they have been with Jesus from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). The disciple is not above the master. This is simultaneously warning and honor: to be persecuted for Christ is to share in Christ's experience, to enter the fellowship of his sufferings. The church that is never persecuted has either been culturally absorbed to the point of invisibility or is living in an extraordinarily tolerant society — possibly both. The cross-bearing disciple should expect the world's hostility as confirmation, not contradiction, of authentic discipleship.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.

If the world hates you. The first thing to notice is the change of subject, and it is abrupt. Seventeen verses about a vine, love, joy and friendship, and then, without a pause, hatred. From love (vv. 9–17) to hatred (vv. 18–25): the contrast is deliberate. The community that has just been commanded to love one another is going to need to, because nobody outside it will. The world in John is humanity in rebellion against God. And the word is not dislike. Miseō is hatred, and it appears again and again in these verses. He is not warning them about awkwardness at parties.

Know that it has hated me before it hated you. The world’s hatred is first directed at Christ. Disciples share in what he suffered (1 Peter 4:12–14). Their persecution is not unique but a sharing: they share in his experience because they share his name.

If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own. The world loves its own kind. The logic is oddly comforting once it is seen. The hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the disciples; it is evidence that they no longer belong to the system that is doing the hating. Belonging elsewhere is the whole cause.

But because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Christ’s choice took them out of the world. They now belong to another kingdom (17:14–16), called to different loyalties and marked by a different love. The world senses the difference and resents it. Their chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger.

Two guards. This passage is misused in both directions, and the damage is real. The first guard is against manufacturing persecution. There is a habit of treating any friction as persecution and wearing it as proof of faithfulness, and a great deal of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is not persecution but the ordinary consequence of being rude, ill-informed or needlessly provocative. Peter drew the line himself: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Peter 4:15). Being disliked for being disagreeable is not sharing in the sufferings of Christ. The second guard is against the opposite error, which is commoner in the West. This passage is not hypothetical, and it is not history. Many Christians are under real pressure today, imprisoned, dispossessed, killed, and a church that reads verse 18 as a metaphor for social awkwardness has quietly excluded much of its own family from the conversation. The honest position for a comfortable believer is neither to invent a persecution nor to conclude the verse is spent. It is to notice that Jesus said if, to pray for the persecuted church, and to ask what it means that the answer, in his own case, is mostly no.

Should I try to be liked by unbelievers, or expect to be hated? Neither as a goal. Aim to be faithful to Christ and kind to people, and leave the reaction to God. Scripture tells us to live such good lives among unbelievers that they may see our good deeds (1 Peter 2:12), to be wise toward outsiders and gracious in speech (Colossians 4:5–6), and to live peaceably with all as far as it depends on us (Romans 12:18). Many unbelievers will respect, even love, a gentle and honest Christian. But when faithfulness to Christ costs you their approval, do not trade him for it. Being hated is not a mark of holiness in itself; being hated for his name is.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if the world hates them, it hated him first, and it would love them if they belonged to it, but it hates them because he chose them out of the world.

On a Tuesday. Do not be surprised when the world resents your faith. It means you belong to Christ. Pray today, by name if you can, for a persecuted believer or church somewhere in the world. And ask whether any of the friction you feel is your fault rather than his name; if so, put it right.

For worship. He was hated first, and he bore it to the cross. And he chose us out of the world, so that we belong to him and not to the system that crucified him. The world’s hatred cannot reach the love that chose us; it can only confirm whose we are. Blessed be the Lord who suffered before us, and goes with us when we suffer for his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember the word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.

A servant is not greater than his master. Jesus says, remember the word that I said to you, and the word he tells them to remember is one he said earlier that evening, at the basin (13:16). There it was an argument for washing feet: if the master takes the towel, no servant is above it. Here the identical sentence is turned over, and the other edge is out: if the master is hunted, no servant should expect to be exempt. He said this in 13:16 about serving; now it applies to suffering. The same proverb produces humility in one direction and realism in the other, and John is the only evangelist who records both uses.

If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. The church shares her Lord’s experience (Acts 9:4; 2 Timothy 3:12). The world’s treatment of the disciples mirrors its treatment of Jesus because it sees in them something of him.

If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. A clause that is easy to skip and should not be. The parallel runs both ways. Some will receive their message, as some received his. The verse is not a prediction of universal hostility; it is a prediction that the disciples’ reception will mirror his, and his was mixed. Crowds followed him for three years. A Samaritan village believed. Some of the authorities believed and would not say so. That is worth having, because the passage is often read as though the church should expect nothing but rejection, and that is not what it says. It says the reception will be his reception, and his reception included Nicodemus and Nathanael and a beggar who worshipped in the street.

But all these things they will do to you on account of my name. Because they belong to him. Persecution of the church is ultimately directed at Christ, as the risen Lord asked Saul why he was persecuting him (Acts 9:4).

Because they do not know him who sent me. The root cause is ignorance of the true God (16:3). The hostility is not fundamentally about the disciples, or their manner, or their politics. It is about the Father, whom the world does not know, which means the disciples are not really the target. They are being hit by something aimed past them. And the ignorance is not innocent: they have had the opportunity to know and refused.

How should I respond when I am treated badly for being a Christian? Remember that you are sharing your Master’s lot, and that it is an honour (Acts 5:41; Matthew 5:11–12). Do not repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but bless (1 Peter 3:9). Pray for those who mistreat you, as Jesus did on the cross. Speak the truth gently and stand firm without bitterness. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul did (Acts 22:25). And keep on with the work: some who now oppose you may later keep the word, as Saul of Tarsus did.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that a servant is not greater than his master, so if they persecuted him they would persecute them, and those who kept his word would keep theirs, all because of his name, for they do not know the Father.

On a Tuesday. If you have been mocked or sidelined this year for your faith, thank God that you were counted worthy to share in the lot of your Lord. Then pray for the person by name, and look for a way to do him good.

For worship. To suffer for his name is to be counted with him (Acts 5:41). The Master went before his servants into hatred, and he goes with them still. And the same word that is rejected by some is kept by others, so that through the sufferings of his people the gospel runs on. Glory to the Lord whose name is worth every loss.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also.

If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin. The sentence needs care, because read flatly it says something Scripture denies everywhere else. He cannot mean they would have been innocent. Paul spends three chapters establishing that the whole world is guilty before God (Romans 1–3), and John himself has already had Jesus say that people loved the darkness rather than the light (3:19). What is meant is the specific sin the chapter is about: rejecting God’s Son with the evidence in front of them. That sin was not available before he arrived. A man cannot refuse a person he has never met. Not that they would be sinless, but that they would not be guilty of this sin.

Responsibility tracks light. The principle underneath runs right through the Bible: privilege increases responsibility (9:41; Luke 12:47–48). The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it receives the heavier beating, and that means the position of the well-informed is more dangerous, not safer. A person who has grown up hearing the gospel, who owns several Bibles and can predict the sermon, is in this verse’s territory. The excuse of not knowing is gone. That is not a comfortable thing to say to a religious reader, and it is the plain sense of the passage.

But now they have no excuse for their sin. Excuse (prophasin) means pretext, cover, a cloak: the plausible cover story. They have heard him clearly. The image is of something pulled away. What his coming did was not to create the guilt but to remove the covering that had made it deniable.

Whoever hates me hates my Father also. There is no loving the Father while hating the Son (5:23; 1 John 2:23). It is the same claim as 14:9 turned round. If seeing him is seeing the Father, then hating him is hating the Father; the identification does not work in one direction only. And it closes off a very common position, held sincerely by a great many people: that one may honour God and set Jesus to one side as a good man about whom the church has exaggerated. This verse says the arrangement does not exist. There is no God available behind Christ to be respected while Christ is declined.

What about religious people who worship God but reject Jesus? This verse speaks to them with great seriousness and great love. Many sincerely believe they honour God while rejecting Jesus as the Son. But Jesus says that the Father and the Son cannot be separated: to refuse the Son is to refuse the Father who sent him (5:23). That is why Christians must lovingly and humbly tell their Jewish, Muslim and other religious neighbours about Christ, not to win an argument but because there is no other way to the God they seek. We should honour their sincerity and their questions, and never despise them, while still saying plainly who Jesus is.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he had not come and spoken, they would not have this guilt, but now they have no excuse, for whoever hates him hates the Father too.

On a Tuesday. If you have heard of Christ, you have no excuse. Respond to him. If you have grown up in church, ask honestly whether you have ever personally come to Christ, or only been near him. If you have, thank God for the light you were given, and ask what he wants you to do with it this week.

For worship. The Son came and spoke, and the light shone so clearly that no cloak was left for sin. That is a terrible thing for those who refuse him, and a wonderful thing for those who receive him: the God who was hidden has spoken plainly in his Son. To love the Son is to love the Father, and to be loved by both. Glory to the God who would not leave us without a word.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without a cause.’

If I had not done among them the works that no one else did. The escalation matters: not works in general, but the works that no one else did. His works were unique (9:32). He is claiming a category of evidence nobody else had ever produced, which the previous chapters have set out at length, and which the council itself conceded in closed session (11:47).

But now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. Seeing and hating: the clearest evidence of the depth of sin. When perfect goodness came among them, the world’s enmity against God became fully visible.

They hated me without a cause. The word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled. Their Law here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms. The words come from Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, laments of David hated by enemies without reason. David’s greater Son suffered the same, perfectly innocent. Psalm 69 is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, and it is often applied to Jesus: it supplies the zeal for the house that consumed him (2:17), the sour wine offered on the cross (19:28–29), the reproaches that fell on him (Romans 15:3), and this line. David wrote it out of an experience of being hated for no reason he could identify, and it turned out to be a description of somebody else. Even their hatred fulfilled Scripture.
