Their Law. He has used the phrase before (8:17; 10:34), and it is not a repudiation of Scripture. He is quoting it as authoritative, which is the point: the court’s own law testifies against the verdict.

Without a cause, and as a gift. There is a word in the quotation that does more work than it looks. Without a cause is dōrean. It means gratuitously, as a free gift, for nothing. The same word appears in Romans 3:24: we are justified by his grace as a gift, dōrean, freely, for nothing. So the two great gratuitous acts in the story are described with the identical word. The world’s hatred of Christ was unearned, and the sinner’s acquittal is unearned, and they meet at the same cross. He received hatred he had done nothing to deserve; the people who hated him receive a righteousness they have done nothing to deserve.

Why would anyone hate Jesus? Because his light exposes what we love in the dark (3:19–20). He was kind, but he was also holy, and his holiness told people the truth about themselves. He claimed authority over their lives, their religion and their future. He would not be used. People who wanted a different kind of God found in him the real one, and resisted. The same thing happens in every heart before the Spirit changes it: we may admire Jesus at a distance, but when he comes close and claims us, the natural heart pushes him away. That is why new birth is necessary (3:3).

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he had not done unique works among them they would not be guilty, but they had seen and hated both him and his Father, fulfilling the Scripture that they hated him without cause.

On a Tuesday. When you are treated unfairly today, remember that the Lord was hated without cause, and was silent like a lamb. Then remember that you were loved without cause, and let that shape how you answer.

For worship. Christ was hated without cause, and loved us without cause. Marvel at his grace. The same word marks both: the world’s hatred freely given, and God’s righteousness freely given. At the cross they meet, and the free gift wins. He bore the gratuitous hatred so that we might receive the gratuitous grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.

But when the Helper comes. The ESV notes that Helper can also be rendered Advocate or Counselor. In a hostile world, the Spirit is our advocate. He stands alongside the persecuted church and speaks for Christ.

Whom I will send to you from the Father. The Son sends the Spirit; in 14:16, 26, the Father sends him. Both send.

The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father. Proceeds (ekporeuetai) means goes out from, comes forth. Most take this to describe the Spirit’s mission, his being sent out into the world. Theologians have also seen in it his eternal relationship to the Father.

The phrase that divided the church. A reader may want to know what actually happened. The Nicene Creed, as agreed in the fourth century, said the Spirit proceeds from the Father, which is this verse. Western churches later added and the Son, in Latin filioque, and by 1054 it was among the causes of the split between East and West. What is worth knowing is that this single verse contains both halves of the argument. The Spirit proceeds from the Father, and in the same sentence Jesus says whom I will send to you from the Father. The East protects the Father as the single source within the Godhead; the West protects the Son’s full involvement. Both are defending something the verse says. And on Easter evening the risen Son will breathe on the disciples and say, receive the Holy Spirit (20:22).

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit proceed from the Son? The Western church added to the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque). The Eastern Orthodox church rejected the addition, and it was a major cause of the split of 1054. Verdict: the Western confession, held by the Reformed churches (Westminster 2.3), is right in substance: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), and the Son sends him, as here. Yet the matter is subtle, and should be held humbly, with respect for Eastern brothers and sisters who confess the same Trinity.

He will bear witness about me. The Spirit’s great work is to point to Christ (16:14). He does not draw attention to himself; he is the floodlight that shines on the Son.

And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. The Spirit and the apostles bear witness together. Two witnesses, which is the requirement of the law that has run through this whole Gospel (8:17). And the qualification given for the human half is purely factual: because you have been with me from the beginning. Not because they are eloquent or brave, neither of which they were about to prove. Because they were there. The apostles were eyewitnesses from the beginning of his ministry (Acts 1:21–22). Their witness, preserved in Scripture, is the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). And the Spirit still bears witness through every believer who speaks of Christ.

The pressure taken off. That is the shape of Christian testimony still, and it takes the pressure off in a useful way. The Spirit’s witness is the one that convinces; the disciples’ job is to say what they saw. Nobody in this verse is asked to produce faith in anybody. And the last phrase is worth holding against what is about to happen. You have been with me from the beginning: said to eleven men who would, before the night was over, all be somewhere else. He sent them anyway.

I was not an eyewitness, so how can I bear witness? By passing on faithfully what the eyewitnesses saw, and by telling what Christ has done for you. The apostles’ testimony is written down for you (20:31; 1 John 1:1–3), so you do not need to invent anything; you point people to it. And you can say, as the healed blind man did, what you know: I was blind, now I see (9:25). The Spirit uses that ordinary testimony. You are not responsible for convincing anyone. You are responsible for being honest and clear about Jesus, and leaving the convincing to the Spirit who loves to glorify him.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Helper, the Spirit of truth, whom he would send from the Father and who comes from the Father, would bear witness about him, and they also would bear witness, having been with him from the beginning.

On a Tuesday. Pray this morning for one opportunity to speak of Christ, and ask the Spirit to go before you. When the moment comes, say simply what he means to you, or point to something he said. Then trust the Spirit with the rest.

For worship. When you speak of Christ, you never speak alone. The Spirit bears witness with you. The Father sends, the Son sends, and the Spirit comes forth to make the Son known, so that the whole Trinity is at work whenever a believer speaks the name of Jesus. Eleven frightened men were sent with that witness, and the world has never silenced it. Glory to the Spirit of truth, who will not let Christ be forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
In the Old Testament Israel was God’s vine, planted and tended by him but so often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21). Jesus now says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” His disciples are the branches. Fruitless branches are removed; fruitful ones are pruned to bear more. The secret of fruitfulness is to abide in him, to remain joined to him by faith, his words living in them, as he lives in them: apart from him they can do nothing. Abiding means remaining in his love by keeping his commandments, the chief of which is to love one another as he has loved them, with the greatest love of all, laying down one’s life for one’s friends. He calls them no longer servants but friends, because he has made known to them all he heard from the Father. They did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit.

The second half turns from love within the church to hatred from the world. If the world hates them, it hated him first; a servant is not greater than his master. Their hatred is without excuse, since Jesus spoke and did works no one else did, and it fulfils the psalm, “They hated me without a cause.” Yet the disciples will not be alone: the Helper, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, will bear witness about Jesus, and they too will bear witness, because they have been with him from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus forewarns the disciples so that persecution will not make them fall: they will be thrown out of synagogues, and their killers will think it service to God, not knowing the Father or the Son. Grief has filled them at the news of his departure, but his going is for their good, since only then will he send the Helper. The Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, shown in its unbelief; about righteousness, proved by Jesus’ return to the Father; and about judgment, for the world’s ruler is condemned. There is more Jesus could tell them, more than they can now bear, but the Spirit of truth will lead them into all truth, speaking what he hears, revealing what is to come, and glorifying Jesus by making known what belongs to him, which is all that the Father has. Soon they will not see him, and soon after they will see him again.
verseByVerse.theology: The conviction work of the Spirit operates on three fronts: sin (the world's refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (the vindication of Jesus in his ascension to the Father), and judgment (the condemnation of the ruler of this world at the cross). This Trinitarian work of conviction is not coercive but illuminating — the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about the world's condition, about Jesus' identity, and about the decisive verdict already rendered at Calvary. Evangelism that presents the gospel as optional enhancement rather than rescue from genuine condemnation has not yet let the Spirit do his convicting work.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all truth (v. 13): the Spirit's hermeneutical function is ongoing, not merely the initial inspiration of the apostolic witness. The community that has the Spirit has access to the interpretive presence of the one who knows the mind of God (1 Cor. 2:10-11). This does not mean every Christian's interpretation is equally valid; it means that the Spirit-guided community reading the Spirit-inspired text under the guidance of the Spirit through his word can arrive at the truth Jesus promised. The church's theology is a work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.

Meaning first. John 16 completes Jesus’ farewell teaching. He warns of persecution, explains why his going is good for them, describes the Spirit’s work in the world and in the church, and promises that their sorrow will turn to joy. It ends with one of the great promises of Scripture: I have overcome the world. Spoken on the last free evening of his life, to men about to scatter, it is the voice of a Victor who has not yet fought and has never doubted the outcome.

The setting. The words follow straight on from the end of chapter 15, where Jesus warned that the world would hate his disciples. It is late on Thursday night, and he is either still in the upper room or on the way to the Kidron valley. Within hours he will be arrested, and these men will be asked whether they know him.

I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. Two words in this passage deserve the reader’s attention, and the second is genuinely chilling. The first is falling away (skandalisthēte): to be tripped, to stumble over something in the road. It is not the word for formally renouncing the faith. The picture is of a man walking who catches his foot on an obstacle he did not see, and the obstacle Jesus has in mind is persecution arriving without warning. Forewarned is forearmed. Persecution will not shake those who expected it.

The stumbling-block placed in view. That explains the purpose of the whole passage, and it is worth stating, because it looks at first like a discouraging thing to say to frightened men. He is removing a stumbling-block by putting it in the road ahead of them where they can see it. Suffering that has been predicted by the one you are following is a different experience from suffering that seems to prove he was not in control. Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps his people.

They will put you out of the synagogues. As had already happened to the man born blind (9:22, 34). For a Jew of that day, it meant being cut off from community, worship, family and livelihood.

Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God. The English softens the word. Service (latreia) is not general service but worship, religious duty, the technical term for what went on in the temple. Paul uses it of presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice, your spiritual worship (Romans 12:1). So what is predicted is not that religious people will do something violent and afterwards justify it. It is that the killing will be performed as an act of worship, offered up like a sacrifice, by men who go home afterwards believing they have pleased God. Religious zeal without the knowledge of God can become murderous. Stephen was the first to die this way (Acts 7:58–60).

The case study who became an apostle. The case study was sitting in the early church, writing letters. Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God. He says of himself that he was convinced he ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 26:9–11), that he had been extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:13–14), and he hunted Christians sincerely. That is the hope buried inside the warning, and it should not be missed. The first man to fulfil this prophecy on a large scale ended up writing a large part of the New Testament. Nothing in verse 2 puts a person beyond the reach of grace.

Why does God let his people be persecuted at all? Scripture does not give a complete explanation, but it gives enough to trust him. Suffering for Christ joins us to him and makes us share his path (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13). It purifies faith like fire refining gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It bears witness to the world, as the blood of martyrs has so often been seed for the church. And it is temporary, while the glory to come is eternal and far outweighs it (Romans 8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). None of this makes persecution good in itself. But God never wastes the sufferings of his people, and he holds the persecutors, too, in his hand.

In a sentence. Jesus said he told them these things to keep them from stumbling, for they would be expelled from synagogues, and the time was coming when those who killed them would think they were serving God.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shaken when opposition comes in religious dress. Jesus told us it would. And pray today for someone who opposes the gospel fiercely. Saul of Tarsus was such a man, and God made him an apostle.

For worship. The Lord who warned his friends before the storm is the Lord who rules the storm. He did not leave them to be surprised, and he does not leave us. And the grace that turned Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle is still at work: the same Christ who was hated by zealous men is mighty to save them. Glory to the Shepherd who walks ahead, and to the grace that reaches the worst of sinners.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.

And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. The diagnosis is the most important sentence in the passage, and it should be stated flatly: religious violence is not caused by too much God but by not knowing him. The root of persecution is ignorance of God (15:21). That cuts against the standard modern account, which holds that strong religious conviction is itself the danger and that the cure is holding beliefs more loosely. Jesus says the opposite. The men who will kill his followers as an act of worship are not people who know God too well. They do not know him at all, and their zeal is the evidence of it.

A usable test. It gives a Christian a test, which is more than most explanations of religious violence provide. Any conviction that makes a person willing to destroy someone in God’s name has, by that fact, revealed itself as ignorance of the God who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy. Those who truly know the Father, who loves the world and gave his Son, cannot persecute those who bear the Son’s name.

But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. Their hour: the hour of the persecutors. Remembering his words will steady them. When the persecution comes, the memory of these words produces not despair but confirming faith: this is what he said would happen, and it is happening, therefore he is true.

I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you. A small window into how he had handled them for three years. While he was with them, the hostility was aimed at him. Now it will turn on them. He had known all of this from the start and had not told them. Not because it was untrue, and not to shield them from reality, since he tells them now, but because there had been no need while he was there to absorb it. The warnings come out on the last night, when they are about to be needed. That is worth knowing about God’s dealings generally. There is information he holds back, and the holding back is not deception. It is timing.

Does this mean every religious person who opposes Christians does not know God? It means that no one who truly knows the Father will persecute those who belong to his Son. People may disagree with Christians, even sharply, for many reasons, and many in other religions are sincere and morally serious. But Jesus says the deepest reason for hostility toward him and his people is not knowing the Father as he has revealed himself in the Son. That is a reason for compassion, not contempt: they need what we have been given, the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And Christians must apply the test to themselves first: the church has sometimes persecuted in God’s name, and every time it did, it was failing to know him.

In a sentence. Jesus said they would do this because they did not know the Father or him, and he told them so that they would remember when it came, having not said it before because he was with them.

On a Tuesday. When you face opposition, recall a promise or warning of Christ that fits it, and say it to yourself: he told me this would happen. Then let the remembered word steady you.

For worship. Christ shielded his disciples while he was with them. He shields us still, by his word and Spirit. He took the world’s hostility on himself, and he measures out to his people what they can bear, when they can bear it. The God who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy is the God we know and worship.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.

But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, Where are you going? The apparent contradiction should be dealt with directly, because a careful reader trips on it. Peter had asked precisely that three chapters earlier: Lord, where are you going? (13:36). Thomas had asked something very close (14:5). The resolution is in what is happening in the room: none of you asks me, now, at this moment. Peter asked earlier and did not want the answer; he immediately turned the conversation to his own loyalty. They had asked only about the separation, not about where he was going and why it would be good. Nobody is asking now, and verse 6 says why. They are thinking only of their loss.

Because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. That is a real observation about grief, and it is worth pausing on. Sorrow does not usually make people curious. It closes the questions down. These men have stopped enquiring where he is going because they have absorbed only the one fact, that he is going, and it has filled up all the available room. The verb is exact: sorrow has filled the heart. Not touched, not troubled. Filled, like a vessel with nothing left over. Grief has crowded out understanding.

What Jesus does not do with it. He does not tell them to stop being sad, or explain that their sorrow is misplaced, or hurry past it. He names it, because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart, and he takes responsibility for having caused it. Then he begins, slowly, to give them the one thing that will eventually turn it round, which is not an argument but a fact about the Spirit.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve deeply? No. Jesus did not rebuke these men for their sorrow, and he himself wept at a grave (11:35). Christians grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love feeling the weight of loss, and the Psalms give us words for it. What faith adds is not the removal of sorrow but a window in it: the knowledge that God is doing something we cannot yet see, and that the story does not end here. So grieve honestly, bring your grief to the Lord, and let others carry it with you. In time, ask him to show you what he is doing.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he was going to the one who sent him, and none of them asked where, because sorrow had filled their hearts.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a gentle one. In a season of grief, notice which questions have gone quiet: the curiosity about what God is doing, the interest in anything beyond the loss. Their absence is not sin and does not need repenting of. But it is worth knowing that it happens, because the disciples in this room were not rebuked for it, and because the answer came from outside them. Sorrow can make us forget to ask what God is doing. Lift your eyes from your loss to his purpose.

For worship. The Man of Sorrows sat with sorrowing men and did not hurry them. He named their grief and took its weight, and then he pointed them beyond it, to the Father and to the Spirit who would come. He is the same with us: patient with our tears, and already at work on the joy that will one day fill the room where sorrow now sits.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:

It is to your advantage that I go away. A startling statement, and the most counterintuitive sentence of the farewell discourse. Better for them that Jesus leave? Yes. One verbal detail here is remarkable and easy to miss. The verb is sympherei: it is expedient, it is better for you. It is the same word Caiaphas used: it is better for you that one man should die for the people (11:50), and John made a point of telling us that the high priest prophesied without knowing it. So the word runs twice through this Gospel, once in a council chamber as cold political arithmetic and once in an upper room as the tenderest thing anybody has ever said to frightened friends. Caiaphas meant: better for us that he dies. Jesus means: better for you that I go. The same calculation, and the difference is everything.

For if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. Why could the Spirit not come while Jesus was here? The passage gives one reason directly and implies another. Directly: the Spirit is sent by the glorified Son, and John has already told us that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The order of salvation history is the cross, resurrection and ascension first; then Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The Spirit applies the finished work of the cross, which had to be completed first. There was nothing to apply until the work was done.

A distribution of his presence. Implied, and this is the part that touches the disciples’ grief: a body is in one place. For three years, being near Jesus meant being in the same room as Jesus. While on earth he was in one place at a time. The Spirit is with every believer everywhere, always, and within them. What is coming is not a replacement for his presence but a distribution of it: with them, and in them, and everywhere at once. That is why the sentence is not a consolation prize dressed up. He is not saying you will manage. He is saying the arrangement they are grieving the loss of was the inferior one.

Did Old Testament believers not have the Spirit? They did: David prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Psalm 51:11), and they too were born of God (3:10). What came at Pentecost was the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, dwelling in them permanently, on the ground of Christ’s finished work. That is what Jesus means: the Spirit as the promised gift of the new covenant could not come until he had gone.

And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment. Convict (elenxei) means expose, prove guilty, bring to conviction. It is a courtroom word: to cross-examine, to bring to light, to prove a case. The Spirit acts like a prosecutor in a courtroom, proving the world wrong on three counts. The world thinks it has judged Jesus; the Spirit turns the case around.

Would it not be better to have Jesus here in person? It feels that way, and Jesus says plainly that it is not. If he were here in the flesh, he could be in only one place; you might live your whole life without getting near him. By the Spirit he is with every believer, in every place, at every hour, and not beside you only but within you. The disciples who walked with him in Galilee often misunderstood him; after Pentecost the same men understood and preached with boldness. You are not a second-class Christian for living after the ascension. You live in the age Jesus called better.

In a sentence. Jesus said it was good for them that he was going away, for otherwise the Helper would not come, but he would send him, and the Spirit would convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgment.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever wished you had lived in the time of Jesus, turn the wish into thanks. Thank him today that by his Spirit he is nearer to you than he was to the crowds in Galilee, and ask the Spirit to make that nearness real to you.

For worship. You are better off with the Spirit than the disciples were with Jesus in Galilee. Live in that privilege. The Son went away to the cross and to the throne, and from the throne he sent the Spirit, so that his presence now fills the whole church and every believer in it. What Caiaphas meant as murder God meant as salvation, and what the disciples felt as loss God meant as gain. Blessed be the Lord who goes away in order to come nearer.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;

Not making people feel bad. Start with the verb of verse 8, because the English has drifted and the drift causes real damage. Convict does not mean to make somebody feel bad. That distinction is worth having very clearly, because many Christians confuse the Spirit’s work with something else entirely, and the confusion is destructive. What the Spirit does is show a person what is true. What the accuser does is press a person about what he is. The one produces clarity and moves toward a remedy; the other produces a fog of general unworthiness and moves nowhere at all.

Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me. Not concerning sins, plural, catalogued. The root, singular. The world’s great sin is not first its immorality, but unbelief: rejecting Christ (3:18–19). The Spirit shows people that their refusal of Christ is sin, and the root of all their sins. Every other sin is fruit of this tree. The Spirit’s first move is not to make the world ashamed of its behaviour but to expose what is underneath it. This is how conviction began at Pentecost: “cut to the heart” over the one they crucified (Acts 2:36–37).

Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father. This is the difficult clause, and it repays the work. A man was tried, convicted, and executed as a blasphemer and a criminal. The world thought Jesus was a sinner, rightly executed. On the world’s verdict he was guilty. The ascension is the appeal court: the Father receives him, which is a public overturning of the sentence. His return to the Father, in resurrection and ascension, proves that he was righteous (Acts 2:24, 32–36; 1 Timothy 3:16). So the Spirit convinces people that Jesus was in the right, that the standard of righteousness the world applied was itself the thing on trial, and that their own righteousness is worthless. And the righteousness of Christ, now accepted in heaven, is the righteousness God gives to all who believe (Romans 3:21–22).

And you will see me no longer. He will not be visible on earth. And the phrase belongs to the argument. The vindication is invisible. Nobody watched the Father receive him. The Spirit’s work is to convince the world of a verdict handed down out of sight.

How can I tell the Spirit’s conviction from false guilt? Here is the test, and it is practical. Conviction from the Spirit is specific: it names a thing, and it can be dealt with, and there is a door out of it marked with the name of Christ. The other kind is vague, cumulative, and always about the whole self rather than an act, and it never once suggests anything to do. If what you are hearing has no exit, it is not this verse. When the Spirit convicts, he leads you to confess and to trust Christ’s blood (1 John 1:9), and then he lifts the burden. When the accuser speaks, he tells you that you are beyond help. Answer him with the cross.

In a sentence. The Spirit would convict the world of sin, because it does not believe in Jesus, and of righteousness, because he is going to the Father, where they will see him no more.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Spirit to convict your friends of the sin of unbelief. Only he can. And if you are carrying a vague guilt today, ask the Spirit to show you specifically what is wrong, confess it, and receive Christ’s forgiveness. If he shows you nothing specific, refuse the fog and rest in Christ’s righteousness.

For worship. The world condemned the Righteous One, and the Father reversed the verdict, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand. Now the Spirit carries that verdict into human hearts, showing sinners their unbelief and showing them the righteousness that is not theirs but Christ’s, given freely. The Judge who was judged is the righteousness of all who believe in him.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.

Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. The third count completes the courtroom scene, and the tense is what matters: the ruler of this world is judged, already. Said before the cross, about the cross. The world judged Jesus at the cross, but in fact it was Satan who was judged there (12:31). The Spirit is not prosecuting an open case. He is publishing a verdict already entered. That is worth knowing when the world looks as though the enemy is winning, which it frequently does: the question of who governs was settled on a Friday afternoon and nothing since has reopened it. Satan’s defeat proves that judgement is real and coming for all who side with him. The Spirit convinces people that the world’s verdicts are wrong and God’s judgement is certain (Acts 17:31).

I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. The word is bear, to carry a weight. It is not only that they would fail to understand; it is that they could not hold it. He has more to say, it is true, it would be good for them eventually, and he stops, because there is a limit to what people can carry on a given night, and he can see where theirs is. They are not ready. The Spirit will teach them later. This is why the New Testament contains more than the Gospels: the apostles’ letters unfold what Jesus began to teach.

Measured to our strength. Consider what that means about the God who deals with us. He is not indifferent to capacity. There is truth he has and withholds, and the withholding is not evasion but mercy, timed to what a person can lift. Here is the comfort in it, and it runs the opposite way to how this is usually felt. Most Christians at some point suspect that God is expecting more of them than they can manage. This verse has him doing the arithmetic in the other direction: measuring what he says against what they can carry, and stopping short. And he does not say they will never hear it. The Spirit will bring it, later, when the weight can be borne. Nothing is being permanently withheld; it is being postponed to a point where it will help rather than crush.

If Satan is already judged, why is there still so much evil? Because his sentence has been passed but not yet fully carried out. At the cross Christ disarmed him and broke his claim on God’s people (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15), and the gospel now goes out to the nations, freeing his captives. He still prowls like a lion (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, and his time is short. At Christ’s return the sentence will be executed in full, and he will be cast out for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the verdict and the execution. That is why we fight, and why we fight without fear.

In a sentence. The Spirit would convict the world of judgement, because its ruler has been judged; and Jesus said he had more to tell them, but they could not bear it yet.

On a Tuesday. If you feel overwhelmed by what you do not understand in the Bible or in your life, take comfort: Christ measures what he gives to what you can carry. Ask him for today’s portion, and trust him with the rest.

For worship. Satan is judged. Every enemy of God’s people is already condemned. Rejoice. The prince of this world was cast out at the very cross where he thought he had won, and his sentence stands. And the Victor is gentle: he does not lay on his people more than they can carry, but feeds them truth as they are able to bear it. Mighty to defeat the devil, tender toward the weak: that is our Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.

When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth. A promise first to the apostles. The verb is worth having: guide (hodēgēsei), from the word for a road. It means to lead somebody along a way, and it is what a guide does for a traveller who does not know the country. All the truth means everything they need about Christ and the gospel: not all truth about everything, chemistry or astronomy, but the truth about God, salvation and the meaning of Jesus. This was fulfilled in the writing of the New Testament. It is why we can trust the apostles’ teaching as God’s word.

A guide does not invent the terrain. That sets a boundary this verse badly needs, because he will guide you into all the truth has been claimed by every movement that ever wanted to add something to Scripture. A guide does not invent the terrain. He takes people over ground that is already there.

For he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak. Jesus states the limit himself. The Spirit does not bring a different message from the Son, any more than the Son brought a different message from the Father. He is not a second source. He reports.

And he will declare to you the things that are to come. Including the things of the new age: the meaning of the cross, the life of the church, the future hope (as in Revelation). These words should not be inflated. It is not a promise of prediction to individual believers about their own futures. Read alongside the rest of the New Testament it most naturally means the things the apostles would be given to understand and write: the meaning of the cross, the shape of the age, the end.

He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you. The Spirit’s great purpose is to glorify Christ. He shines the spotlight on Jesus, not on himself. This is the single best test of any spiritual claim ever made, and it should be kept ready to hand. It is the Spirit’s stated job description, given by the Son, on the last night. So the question to ask of any teaching, experience, movement or manifestation that claims the Spirit is not whether it is impressive, or emotional, or accompanied by power. It is simpler and much harder to fake: does it make much of Christ? Does it end up with people thinking more of Jesus Christ?

The Spirit who stands out of the light. A great deal that has gone under the Spirit’s name over the centuries fails that test on its own terms, because the attention settles on the phenomenon, or on the man producing it, or on the Spirit himself as the object of interest. The Spirit does not seek his own glory, which is a striking thing to notice about the third person of the Trinity: he is the one who habitually stands slightly out of the light and points.

Is this a promise to every believer, or to the apostles? In the first place it is to the apostles, who received the Spirit’s guidance into all truth and wrote it down in the New Testament. Believers today share in the promise through their word, as the Spirit opens our eyes to it (1 Corinthians 2:12–13). It is not a promise of new revelation beyond Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every Christian will receive infallible guidance into all truth, or that new revelation continues today. The apostles received it, and wrote it down. The Spirit now illuminates that word for us (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).

If the Spirit guides into truth, why do Christians disagree? Because the Spirit’s guidance into all the truth was given infallibly to the apostles, and what he gave them is in Scripture without error. Our reading of it is not infallible. We are sinners, limited in knowledge, shaped by our backgrounds, and sometimes stubborn. Where Scripture is clear, on Christ, the gospel and the way of salvation, true believers broadly agree, and that agreement is itself the Spirit’s work. Where we differ, the remedy is to go back humbly to the text, to pray, to listen to the church’s wiser teachers, and to love those with whom we disagree. The Bible is the judge, not our impressions.

In a sentence. Jesus said the Spirit of truth would guide them into all the truth, speaking only what he hears, declaring what is to come, and glorifying Christ by making known what is his.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture, ask the Spirit to show you Christ. That is his delight. And when you hear a sermon, read a book, or attend a conference that claims the Spirit, ask afterwards: am I thinking more of Jesus? Let that be your test.

For worship. The Spirit of truth led the apostles into all the truth, and they wrote it down for us, so that we hold in our hands what the Spirit heard and spoke. And his great delight is to take what is Christ’s and show it to us, until our hearts burn with the glory of the Son. Blessed be the self-forgetting Spirit, who points always away from himself to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.

All that the Father has is mine. Stop on that, because it is one of the largest claims in the Gospel, and it is dropped in almost casually as the reason for something else. A stunning claim. Not all that the Father has given me, which would be the language of a servant entrusted with an estate. All that the Father has. Without limit and without qualification. Everything the Father has belongs to the Son. No creature could say it. The Father, the Son and the Spirit share all things (17:10).

Therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. The logic of the sentence is the point. The Spirit takes from the Son, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, so what the Spirit brings to the church is drawn from the whole wealth of God. There is no smaller supply reserved for people at this end of the chain. The Spirit takes from the Son what belongs to the Father, and gives it to us: the Trinity working together for our salvation.

A little while, and you will see me no longer. His death, in a few hours. The riddle that is about to occupy the disciples for four verses.

And again a little while, and you will see me. His resurrection, three days later. Some also see a reference to his second coming. The two little whiles are not the same length. The first is less than a day. The second is three days, and behind it, arguably, the whole age of the church, since the seeing that began on Easter has not ended. That elasticity is not a trick. It is how the New Testament always speaks about the interval: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay (Hebrews 10:37), written two thousand years ago.

What does it mean for me that all the Father has belongs to Christ? It means that in Christ you lack nothing that you truly need. Every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places is yours in him (Ephesians 1:3); his righteousness, his sonship, his inheritance, his access to the Father are shared with you. Paul could say that all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). When you feel spiritually poor, the remedy is not to look for some other source, a technique or an experience, but to look to Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Spirit’s work is to show you what is already yours.

In a sentence. Jesus said that all the Father has is his, so the Spirit would take what is his and declare it to them, and in a little while they would not see him, and then in a little while they would.

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of what is yours in Christ: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the Father’s love, eternal life, a future inheritance. Read it as a statement of your wealth, and thank God for each item.

For worship. All the riches of God belong to Christ, and through the Spirit he shares them with you. The Father gives all to the Son, the Son opens his treasury, and the Spirit carries its riches to the poorest believer. There is no lesser God at our end of the chain, and no smaller portion. In Christ we have all, because in him we have God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Puzzled, the disciples ask one another what he means by “a little while” and “going to the Father”. Knowing their question, Jesus tells them they will weep and mourn while the world rejoices, but their grief will become joy, like a woman whose pain in labour is forgotten in the joy of a new child. They grieve now, but he will see them again, and their joy no one will take away. In that day they will not need to ask him; the Father will give them whatever they ask in his name. Until now they have asked nothing in his name; they should ask and receive, so that their joy may be complete. He has spoken in figures, but soon he will speak plainly about the Father. They will ask in his name, not because he must plead for them, but because the Father himself loves them for loving and trusting his Son. He came from the Father into the world and is now leaving it to return. The disciples say that now he speaks plainly, and they believe he came from God. Jesus asks whether they really believe now. The hour has come when they will scatter, each to his home, and leave him alone; yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. He has told them this so that in him they may have peace. In the world they will face trouble, but they should take courage: he has conquered the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chapter's second half turns on a claim about time. Everything Jesus promises here is stated as though it has already happened: the sorrow will turn into joy, the ruler of this world is judged, and — in the last verse — I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The disciples are being taught to live inside an outcome that is settled but not yet visible, which is the permanent situation of the church.

This is why the childbirth image governs the section. It is not a picture of pain compensated afterwards by an unrelated good, which is how providence is usually consoled about. It is a picture of pain that turns out to have been productive — the same event, read from the far end, carrying a meaning it could not disclose at the time. Applied to the cross, this is the interpretive key to the whole Gospel: the worst thing that ever happened is the thing the church sings about, and nothing had to be deleted for that to be true.

And the prayer promise sits in the middle of it for a reason. Prayer in the name of Jesus is not a technique for extracting outcomes; it is the practice of people who believe the outcome is already secured and are asking to be brought into line with it. Its stated end in verse 24 is not acquisition but fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) is the sentence to set against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. Not may, not could — will, spoken by the one person entitled to say it, on the last free evening of his life. And it stands beside in me you may have peace without contradiction, because the two prepositions name two locations and a believer is in both at once. That is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

The pastoral use of verse 22 is worth naming: no one will take your joy from you is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy in this passage is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is precisely why it cannot be confiscated — nobody can reach the thing it depends on.

And verse 12 — you cannot bear them now — is the answer to the reader who suspects God is asking more than can be carried. Here is the Son measuring what he says against what eleven exhausted men can hold, and stopping short, on the one night when he had most to say and least time to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ‘A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ‘because I am going to the Father’?” So they were saying, “What does he mean by ‘a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”

What is this that he says to us? The disciples are puzzled, and whisper among themselves. These two verses are worth reading aloud, because John has recorded something almost comic and entirely human. They repeat the riddle back to each other, word for word, as though saying it again might help. They add the other thing he said, about going to the Father, in case it is a clue.

What does he mean by a little while? We do not know what he is talking about. And then they give up. An honest admission of confusion. The repetition of the phrase shows how much it bothered them. They could not imagine death and resurrection. And notice that they do not ask him. He is sitting there. They discuss it among themselves in what must have been an audible mutter, and the next verse says he knew they wanted to ask, which means nobody did. Why not? Probably the same reason anybody sits on a question in a room where the mood has turned: it has been a long evening, they have already been told one of them is a traitor and that Peter will deny him, and asking would mean admitting in front of the others that they had not followed.

They had understood almost nothing. It is worth saying to whoever needs it that this is the last night, these are the eleven, and they have understood almost nothing. Not the footwashing, not the betrayal, not the vine, not the going away. Three years of the best teaching that has ever been given, delivered by the Son of God in person, and on the final evening they are muttering to each other that they cannot make out what he means. That puts the ordinary Christian experience of not understanding into a more forgiving light. Whatever is required to follow him, comprehension on the night is evidently not it. What changed these men was not a better explanation. It was Easter, and then the Spirit, and both were entirely outside their control.

John’s own name inside it. There is also a small mercy in the way John has recorded it. He was in that room. He is one of the men muttering, and when he came to write the account decades later he could have left this out, or tidied it, or given himself a better line. Instead he preserves the exchange in full, including the flat admission at the end, in the first person plural, with himself inside it: we do not know what he is talking about.

Is it wrong to have doubts and questions about the faith? Questions are not the same as unbelief. These men loved Jesus and were confused, and he did not reject them for it. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to meet him (20:27). The Psalms are full of honest questions put to God. What matters is where you take them. Bring them to Christ in prayer, to his word, and to mature believers, rather than nursing them in private or letting them harden into a reason to walk away. Some questions will be answered as you grow; some will wait for glory. Faith is not the absence of questions but trust in the Lord while you ask them.

In a sentence. Some disciples asked one another what Jesus meant by a little while and not seeing him, and seeing him again, and going to the Father, admitting they did not understand.

On a Tuesday. It is fine to admit you do not understand. Bring your questions to Jesus, as they eventually did. Write down one thing in Scripture that puzzles you, pray about it, and ask your pastor or a mature Christian friend this week.

For worship. The Lord bore with men who understood almost nothing on the last night, and he made them the foundation of his church. He did not wait for their comprehension before he loved them, died for them, and sent them. The same patient Teacher bears with our slowness, and by his Spirit he will make plain in his time what is dark to us now.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ‘A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.

Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him. He knows their hearts. They had said nothing to him. He answers the question they did not put. And what he gives them is not the explanation they were after. They wanted the timetable decoded: what does a little while mean? He tells them instead what it is going to feel like, which is the thing they will actually need.

You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. The verbs are worth separating. You will weep: the ordinary word for shedding tears. And lament: formal mourning, the sound made at a funeral, wailing. But the world will rejoice. At the cross the disciples will mourn while his enemies celebrate. Those are not the same activity in different moods; they are two rooms on the same afternoon, and one of them is celebrating. That is the hardest thing about the cross for the people who loved him, and it is worth naming. It was not only grief. It was grief while other people were pleased.

You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy. The preposition is everything. Not will be followed by. Not will be replaced with. Not replaced by joy, but turned into joy. The sorrow itself becomes the joy, which is exactly what happened, because the thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since. The very thing that causes their sorrow, his death, will become the source of their joy. The cross, their grief, becomes their glory (Galatians 6:14). Nothing was deleted. The same event changed meaning.

A better promise. That is a different promise from the one people usually hear, and a better one. It does not say the bad thing will be compensated for later by a good thing. It says the bad thing is going to turn out to have been the good thing, seen from the wrong end. And notice that he does not tell them the sorrow will be short. He tells them it will be real, that the world will be enjoying itself while they endure it, and that it is going to change into something else. That is a more useful thing to know in advance than a timetable would have been. The disciples on the Saturday did not need to be told how many hours were left; they needed to have been told that what they were feeling was not the end of the story, by somebody who had known it would happen.

Does this mean every sorrow of mine will become joy? For the believer, yes, in God’s time, though not always in the way or on the timetable we would choose. God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (8:18). Some sorrows are turned within this life: a loss that later bears fruit, a trial that deepens faith. Others will be turned only when Christ returns and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). But nothing a Christian suffers is wasted or final. The cross is the proof: if God could turn that into joy, he can turn yours.

In a sentence. Jesus knew what they wanted to ask, and solemnly told them they would weep while the world rejoiced, but their sorrow would turn into joy.

On a Tuesday. Name a sorrow you are carrying. Do not pretend it is small. Then tell the Lord that you trust him to turn it into joy, in his way and his time, and ask him for strength to wait.

For worship. What brings you sorrow now, God can turn into joy. He did it at the cross. The darkest afternoon in history, when the world laughed and the disciples wept, became the source of the church’s everlasting song. The God who did that is the God who holds your grief, and his specialty is turning it into joy.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.

When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come. One detail in the image is more deliberate than it looks. Because her hour has come: that is his word. It has been running through this Gospel since Cana, my hour has not yet come, and it has meant, almost throughout, the cross. He now puts it in the mouth of a woman in labour, the one place where it is used of ordinary human anguish. It is a picture used often in the Old Testament for the pains that come before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Her pain is real and intense. But it leads to new life.

The pain is the way the joy arrives. The image is chosen with great care, because it is not the obvious one. He could have said the sorrow passes, as weather passes. He could have said it is worth it, as a price is worth paying. Childbirth says something neither of those says: that the pain is not incidental to the joy but is the way the joy arrives. Nobody gets the child by another route. The cross is the birth pang of the new creation.

But when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. The joy outweighs the pain. The clause about forgetting deserves honesty, because it can be overstated. No mother forgets that labour hurt. What is meant is that the pain stops being the thing the day is about. It is still in the account, and it has ceased to be the headline, displaced by something in the room that was not there before.

So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice. I will see you: he will come to them in the resurrection (20:20). Notice the direction. Not you will see me, which is what verse 16 promised and what they were arguing about. He will see them. The joy is grounded in his looking at them, not in their managing to catch sight of him.

And no one will take your joy from you. Not nothing: no one. It names a person rather than a circumstance, which is fitting in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged. There is someone whose business is taking things from Christians, and this is on the list of what he cannot reach. Joy grounded in the risen Christ cannot be taken away by persecution, loss or death. The apostles rejoiced after being flogged (Acts 5:41). Circumstantial joy can be taken; the joy rooted in the resurrection cannot be extinguished by any power in heaven or earth. This joy is permanent.

But I have lost my joy; was it taken? The joy itself, rooted in the risen Christ, cannot be taken, but your sense of it can be clouded: by sin, by sorrow, by exhaustion, by illness, by spiritual attack. David prayed, restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12), which shows that a true believer can lose the feeling and still have the salvation. Go back to the source. Confess any known sin. Rest your body if it is worn out. Get help if you are ill. Look again at the risen Christ in the Gospels, and keep company with his people. The joy has not been stolen; it is waiting where it always was, in him.

In a sentence. Jesus compared their sorrow to a woman in labour, who forgets the anguish for joy once her baby is born, and said that he would see them again, and they would rejoice with a joy no one could take away.

On a Tuesday. No one can take your joy in the risen Christ. Not your boss, your illness, or your enemies. When something threatens to steal your peace today, say quietly: no one will take my joy from me, because Jesus lives.

For worship. The cross was the labour pain of a new world, and on the third day the joy was born. The risen Lord came and looked at his friends, and their hearts rejoiced. He looks on us with the same face, and the joy he gives is kept beyond the reach of every thief. Glory to the Lord whose agony brought forth everlasting joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.

In that day you will ask nothing of me. That day: after the resurrection. There is a small verbal fact here that clears up an apparent oddity, and it is invisible in English, because we use one word for two things. Ask nothing of me is erōtaō, which is to ask a question, as in v. 19. It is what the disciples have been doing all evening: Peter asking where he is going, Thomas asking about the way, Philip asking to see the Father, the whole group muttering about a little while. They will no longer be confused, because the Spirit will teach them.

Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. And that ask is aiteō: to make a request, to petition. So the sentence is not saying that prayer to Jesus will cease. It is saying the questions will stop, because the thing that has confused them all night will have happened and be plain. The interrogation ends; the asking begins. That is a good description of what the resurrection did to these men. There is little record after Easter of the disciples asking Jesus what he meant. They ask about the timing of the kingdom once, are told it is not for them to know, and then they go and preach (Acts 1:6–8). A new way of prayer opens: directly to the Father, in the name of the Son.

Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Prayer in Jesus’ name is new, made possible by his death and exaltation as our mediator (Hebrews 4:14–16). The disciples had prayed, but not yet on the ground of the Son’s completed work.

Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full. Answered prayer fills our joy. Prayer is presented not as a duty but as the pathway to the full joy Jesus has been promising throughout this discourse.

At full stretch. The promise stands here at full stretch, and it has to be handled honestly, because every Christian who has prayed for long has asked and not received. A parent prays for a dying child. A wife prays for twenty years for a husband who never turns. To leave the sentence unqualified is to hand such people either a false hope or a private verdict on their own faith, and neither is what Jesus is doing on the last night of his life.

Not a formula. Two things keep the promise from becoming a formula. The first was said at 14:13 and is worth holding on to: in my name is not an incantation attached to the end of a request. A name stands for a character and an authority, so to ask in his name is to ask as his representative, for what he himself would ask. John states the qualifier plainly when he comes to write his letter: this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). The promise is not that God will do our will if we invoke the right name, but that he will not refuse his own.

The prayer he did not press. The second is that Jesus had prayed such a prayer himself, and John recorded it four chapters back. Standing before the cross he said, now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour? And then he answered his own question: but for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). He raises the request and declines to press it, because there was something he wanted more. That is what praying in his name looks like from the inside, and it is why the promise is safe. The Father did not save him from that hour, and the whole world was saved through it.

The stated end is joy. So notice what this verse actually guarantees, because it is easy to misread as a guarantee of acquisition. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full. The stated end is joy, not delivery of goods. Some prayers God grants outright; some he answers with something better than we had the wit to ask for; and some he answers with himself, which is why saints who received almost nothing they asked for have so often been the gladdest people in the room. The prayer that goes unanswered in the form we wanted has not fallen to the ground. It has been taken up by a Father who is committed to the fullness of our joy and not merely to the shortening of our discomfort.

How do I pray in Jesus’ name in practice? Come to the Father as his child because of Christ, not because of your own record. Bring what is on your heart honestly; you do not have to tidy it first. Ask yourself whether what you are asking fits what Jesus loves and what Scripture promises, and let that shape your request. Pray for his kingdom and his glory first, as he taught in the Lord’s Prayer, and then for your daily needs without embarrassment. End with in Jesus’ name, not as a password but as a confession: I come only through him. Then trust the Father with the answer.

In a sentence. Jesus said that in that day they would no longer question him, and whatever they asked the Father in his name, the Father would give, for they had not yet asked in his name, but should ask and receive so that their joy would be full.

On a Tuesday. Take the prayer you have prayed longest without an answer. Bring it to the Father again today, in Jesus’ name, and add: but above all, Father, glorify your name, and fill my joy in you. Then leave it with him.

For worship. You can go straight to the Father in Jesus’ name. Use that privilege today. The Son who did not press his own prayer to be spared the hour went through the hour, and by it opened the door of prayer to us for ever. The Father hears in his name, and the end of all his answering is our full joy. Blessed be the God who gives, and gives himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;

I have said these things to you in figures of speech. Figures of speech (paroimiai) are veiled sayings, pictures: the same word John used of the shepherd discourse that nobody followed (10:6). The vine, the woman in labour, the house with many rooms, the shepherd, the bread, the water: figures that point beyond themselves.

The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. After the resurrection, through the Spirit. Verse 25 says from the other side what verse 23 said: the hour is coming when the meaning will be plain.

In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf. The delicate clause. It sounds at first like a withdrawal of the intercession, and it is not. Hebrews says he always lives to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25), Paul that he is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:34), and John’s own letter calls him our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Not that Jesus stops interceding, but that they do not need to think of the Father as reluctant, needing to be persuaded by the Son. What he is dismantling is a picture: the idea of a Son who has to work on a Father, of prayer as something extracted by a sympathetic mediator from a reluctant judge. The Son’s mediation is not distance but access; the name of Jesus opens the door, and does not stand between the one praying and the Father. The next verse says exactly why that picture is wrong: the Father himself loves them (v. 27).

If the Father loves me, why do I need Jesus as mediator at all? Because the Father’s love for sinners is holy love. He loves us, and he will not pretend our sin is nothing. In Christ, love found a way to be just and to justify (Romans 3:26): the Father gave the Son, and the Son bore our sins, so that we could come near. Christ’s mediation is not the cause of the Father’s love but its gift. The Son did not die to make the Father love us; the Father sent the Son because he already loved us (3:16). So we need Jesus, and we need not fear the Father. Through the one we come confidently to the other.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had spoken in figures, but would soon speak plainly about the Father, and they would ask in his name, without needing him to persuade the Father for them.

On a Tuesday. The Father does not need persuading to love you. Pray with confidence. Notice if you tend to pray to Jesus but avoid addressing the Father, as though he were sterner. Today, begin your prayer with Father, and speak to him as a loved child.

For worship. The Son speaks plainly now, and what he tells us is the Father. There is no reluctant Judge behind a kind Mediator; there is a Father who loved us enough to give his Son, and a Son who loved us enough to come, and the Spirit who brings us home. The door of the Father’s house is open, and the Son himself has opened it.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.

For the Father himself loves you. The emphatic himself is doing deliberate work. Not because Jesus asks him to. Not the Father will be persuaded to love you. The Father, himself, loves them: independently, directly, without anything having to be arranged. Loves here is phileō, the warm love of friendship and family. The Father is not a stern judge whom the kind Son must soften. The Father sent the Son because he loved the world (3:16).

The commonest distortion. This is the correction of the commonest distortion in the Christian imagination, and it is worth naming plainly, because it survives in people who would deny holding it. The picture runs: the Father is holy and severe, the Son is warm and merciful, and Christian safety consists of the Son standing between us and him. It is a picture with no basis in this Gospel, and it makes prayer into a kind of legal manoeuvre. Here the Son takes it apart in one sentence. There is nobody to be got round. The Father does not need talking into it.

Because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. Their love and faith are the evidence that they belong to the Father’s family, and themselves the fruit of his love.

Does the Father’s love, then, depend on ours? No. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus is speaking of the Father’s fatherly delight and fellowship with those who love his Son (compare 14:21, 23), not of the love that chose them before they loved. Their love for Jesus is itself the fruit of God’s love, and the Father rejoices in it.

I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father. The whole of Jesus’ mission in one sentence, and John has been building to it since chapter 1. Four movements. I came from the Father: his pre-existence with the Father. And have come into the world: the incarnation. And now I am leaving the world: the cross. And going to the Father: the resurrection and ascension. Coming down and going back. It is a creed before there were creeds, said conversationally at a supper table, and the disciples’ response in the next verse is the first sign all evening that something has got through.

How can I believe the Father loves me when I feel so far from him? Look not first at your feelings but at what he has done. The Father sent his Son into the world for you; that is how you know the love of God (1 John 4:9–10). He has given you his Spirit, who cries Abba, Father, in your heart (Galatians 4:6), even when your own voice is weak. He has adopted you, and a father does not disown his child on a bad day. Feelings of distance are real and painful, and the Psalms are full of them, but they are not the measure of his love. The cross is.
