Speak to him as Father even when it feels hollow, and let his word, not your mood, tell you who you are.

In a sentence. Jesus said the Father himself loves them because they have loved him and believed he came from God, for he came from the Father into the world, and was now leaving the world and going to the Father.

On a Tuesday. Write on a card: The Father himself loves me (John 16:27). Put it where you will see it when you are most likely to feel condemned or forgotten, and read it every time.

For worship. The Father himself loves you. Let that sink in. The Son came down from the Father’s side into our world, walked our roads, went to our cross, and returned to the Father, all to bring us into the love that was there before the world began. There is no one to be got round and no one to be persuaded. The heart of God is open, and it is the heart of a Father.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”

His disciples said, Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! There is something touching and slightly absurd about this, and John does not spare them. They think they finally understand. They say it after a sentence about coming from the Father and going to the Father, which is arguably no plainer than anything else he has said that evening. They have not solved the riddle. Something has simply landed, and the relief in their voices is audible.

Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you. Notice what they seize on as the ground of their faith. He has answered the question they had not asked aloud (v. 19). He knows their thoughts. What has impressed them is that incident, where he read the room. That is what has convinced them: not the vine, not the Spirit, not the four-stage summary of his descent and return, but a display of knowing what they were thinking. It is a real thing to have noticed, and it is a very small basis for what is coming.

This is why we believe that you came from God. A real confession, but their confidence is ahead of their understanding. They will be tested within hours. The clarity they feel is real but not yet tested; the faith they express is genuine but not yet refined by the fire of the passion. The distance between expressed faith and proven faith is always the cross.

Lighter than it feels. The pattern is universal and mostly harmless until it is tested. Faith attaches itself to the evidence that happens to be in front of it: an answered prayer, a coincidence too neat to dismiss, a sermon that seemed addressed to one person in the room. None of that is false. It is simply lighter than it feels, and the weight it will have to carry is not known in advance. Jesus does not disparage their confession. He asks one question about it, and then tells them what will happen before dawn.

Is my faith real if it is weak and untested? Yes. These men truly believed, and Jesus prayed for them as those the Father had given him (17:6–8). Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because it is the Saviour who saves, not the strength of the faith. But faith grows by being tested, and God will test it, not to break it but to deepen it (1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:2–4). So do not despise your faith for being small, and do not trust it for being fervent. Trust Christ, and let him strengthen it through the trials he sends.

In a sentence. His disciples said he was now speaking plainly, and they knew that he knew all things, and so they believed he came from God.

On a Tuesday. Faith is real even when it is immature. But do not mistake a moment of clarity for strength to stand. After a spiritual high, a moving service, a powerful answer to prayer, ask Christ to root your faith deeper, in his word and his promises, so that it holds when the feeling fades.

For worship. The Lord received the stumbling confession of eleven men who would run away within hours, and he did not despise it. He knew how small their faith was, and he went to the cross to save them anyway, and made their faith strong after Easter. He treats our faith the same way: he will not break the bruised reed or quench the smouldering wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.

Do you now believe? The Greek can be read as a question or a flat statement, so now you believe, and either way there is no mockery in it. Not doubting their faith, but warning them of its weakness. He does not say they are wrong. He says what their believing is about to do.

Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home. The prediction is drawn from Scripture. You will be scattered is the language of Zechariah: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zechariah 13:7), which Matthew and Mark record him quoting that same night (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27, 50). He has spent chapter 10 as the good shepherd. Now the shepherd tells the flock what is about to happen to them when he is struck. And the detail is what makes it hurt: each to his own home. Not a heroic collapse. They will simply go back to where they came from, individually, the way people do when something ends.

And will leave me alone. All of them would run. The specificity of the prediction is its own kind of mercy: Jesus is not surprised by their failure; he has accounted for it in advance.

Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me. The Father never leaves him (8:29). This sentence has to be handled with great care, because it stands a few hours from a cry that appears to contradict it. What then of his cry from the cross that God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34)? Both are true, and the church has always held them together rather than choosing. There the Son bore the Father’s judgement against our sin, and experienced the loss of the Father’s comforting presence. The abandonment at Golgotha is real: it is the sin-bearing, the cup, the thing he asked to be spared. Yet even there the Father’s love for the Son never ceased, and the unity of the Trinity was never broken. It is the Son experiencing, in our place, the one thing he had never known. Jesus could still say my God and, at the end, Father, into your hands (Luke 23:46).

Why the words here are not made false. The words here are not made false by the words there. He is telling them, on the Thursday, that the Father is with him. What happens on the Friday is the specific, temporary, substitutionary exception, and it fell on him precisely so that it would never fall on them.

What if I feel completely alone? Then you are in the place where Jesus has been, and where he has promised to meet you. He knows what it is to have every friend go home. And he knows, in a way nobody else ever will, what it is to bear the Father’s turning away, which means that the promise I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5) is not a slogan. It cost something to be able to say it. If you are in Christ, the Father is with you as he was with his Son, and he will never forsake you, because the forsaking was borne for you. Tell him how alone you feel. Then reach out to his people; loneliness often lies to us about who would gladly come.

In a sentence. Jesus asked if they now believed, warning that the hour had come when they would scatter and leave him alone, though he would not be alone, for the Father was with him.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church who may feel alone: a widow, a single parent, a student far from home, a member who has stopped coming. Contact one of them this week. You may be the way the Father says, I am with you.

For worship. When everyone else leaves, the Father remains. That was true for Christ, and in him it is true for you. He was left alone by his friends and bore the Father’s wrath for our sins, so that no believer would ever be forsaken by God. The Shepherd was struck and the sheep scattered, and then he gathered them again, every one. Glory to the Lord who was forsaken that we might never be.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.

I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. Take the verse in three parts, because it is built as a hinge and each part turns on the one before. The purpose of the whole farewell discourse is peace. Not in circumstances, but in me. The location is stated first, and it is not a place or a circumstance. Peace is available in a person, which is the same preposition the vine chapter has been using, and it means the peace does not depend on the state of the world outside, because it is not stored there. Peace is found in union with Christ.

In the world you will have tribulation. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, distress, affliction: the same word used of the woman in labour twelve verses ago. And the verb is not conditional. Not might, but will. Not may, not could. The Christian life is not trouble-free (Acts 14:22). It is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for correcting expectations, and it is spoken by the one person entitled to say it.

Two locations. Notice the two prepositions side by side. In me, peace. In the world, tribulation. Both are true at the same time and of the same people, which is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon. It is not a contradiction. It is two locations, and a believer is in both at once.

But take heart; I have overcome the world. Take heart (tharseite) means be courageous. And the tense is the thing. I have overcome (nenikēka) is perfect tense: a completed victory with lasting effect. Not I will overcome. Not I am overcoming. He says it is done, and he says it before the arrest, before the trial, before the nails, on the last free evening of his life, to men who are within hours of running away. Jesus says it on the eve of the cross, as if the battle is already won. And it is. By the cross and resurrection he has defeated sin, death and Satan. The verb is the ordinary word for winning, the root behind nikē, victory. John will use its noun in his letter: this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). His people share in his victory (1 John 5:4–5; Revelation 3:21).

The order of the verse. So the arithmetic of the verse is this. The trouble is guaranteed, the peace is available, and the outcome was settled before the fight started. That is the order, and it is not the order anybody would have chosen. He does not remove the tribulation, and he does not promise to. He tells them where the peace is kept and who has already won.

Before the prayer. It is worth saying, finally, what this sentence is not. It is not merely a slogan for getting through a difficult week, though it has carried a great many people through a great many of those. It is the last thing he says to his friends before he lifts his eyes to heaven: the closing sentence of four chapters of farewell, and the next words out of his mouth are a prayer. He had overcome nothing yet, by any measure available that evening. The crowds were gone, the traitor was out arranging the arrest, the eleven were about to scatter to their own homes, and the man himself would be dead within a day. And he says it in the perfect tense. Finished, standing, done, with the whole of it still in front of him, because he had never once been in any doubt about how it ends.

If Jesus has overcome the world, why do I keep losing? Because the victory is his before it is yours, and you are living in the time between the decisive battle and the final peace. The world still presses, sin still wounds, and you will sometimes fall. But the outcome is not in doubt, because it does not rest on your strength but on what he has already done. Your faith joins you to the Victor (1 John 5:4–5), and he will finish the work he began. So fight, but fight from victory, not for it. When you fall, get up in his strength, not yours. The last chapter is already written, and in it the Lamb has conquered.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them these things so that they would have peace in him, for in the world they would have trouble, but they should take heart, because he has overcome the world.

On a Tuesday. Trouble will come today. Take heart: Christ has already overcome the world. When it comes, say both halves of the verse: in the world I have tribulation; in him I have peace. Then do the next right thing with courage.

For worship. On the night before he died, with the cross still ahead, the Son of God spoke in the perfect tense: I have overcome. He knew the end from the beginning, and the end is his. Sin, death and the devil are beaten foes, and the world that crucified him is conquered by the love that went to the cross. We walk through tribulation inside a victory already won. Take heart, and worship the Overcomer.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world

Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.<sup>3</sup>And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me.<sup>4</sup>But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. “I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.<sup>5</sup>But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ’Where are you going?’<sup>6</sup>But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.<sup>8</sup>And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:<sup>9</sup>concerning sin, because they do not believe in me;<sup>10</sup>concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;<sup>11</sup>concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged.<sup>12</sup>“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.<sup>13</sup>When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.<sup>14</sup>He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>15</sup>All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>16</sup>“A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.”<sup>17</sup>So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ’A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ’because I am going to the Father’?”<sup>18</sup>So they were saying, “What does he mean by ’a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”<sup>19</sup>Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ’A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’?<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.<sup>21</sup>When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.<sup>22</sup>So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.<sup>23</sup>In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you.<sup>24</sup>Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.<sup>25</sup>“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.<sup>26</sup>In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;<sup>27</sup>for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.<sup>28</sup>I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”<sup>29</sup>His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech!<sup>30</sup>Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”<sup>31</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?<sup>32</sup>Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly so that they will not fall away when persecution comes: they will be expelled from synagogues, and some will kill them thinking they are serving God. Sorrow fills their hearts at his going, but he tells them it is for their good, for unless he goes the Helper will not come. When the Spirit comes he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment: sin, because they do not believe in Jesus; righteousness, because Jesus goes to the Father and is vindicated; judgment, because the ruler of this world is condemned. The Spirit of truth will guide the apostles into all the truth, declaring what is to come and glorifying Christ by taking what is his and making it known.

Then Jesus speaks of “a little while”: a little while and they will not see him, and again a little while and they will see him. The disciples are puzzled. He explains with the picture of a woman in labour, whose anguish gives way to joy when the child is born: they will grieve while the world rejoices, but he will see them again, and no one will take their joy from them. In that day they will pray to the Father in his name and receive, so that their joy may be full, for the Father himself loves them. When the disciples declare that now they understand and believe, Jesus warns that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone, yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. His last words before his prayer are a promise for every age: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Raising his eyes to heaven, Jesus asks the Father to glorify the Son now that the hour has come, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. That life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Having finished his work on earth, Jesus asks for the glory he shared with the Father before creation. He has revealed the Father to those given him out of the world, and they have received his words and believed. He prays for them, not for the world: that the holy Father would keep them in his name and make them one; he has kept them, and none is lost except the son of destruction. The world hates them, but he asks not that they be removed from it, but guarded from the evil one, set apart by the truth of God’s word, and sent as he was sent; for them he consecrates himself. He prays too for all who will believe through their message, that they may be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world may believe and know the Father’s love. He longs for them to be with him and see his glory, and promises to keep making the Father known, so that the Father’s love and the Son himself may be in them.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it parallels the High Priest's prayer on the Day of Atonement — the one moment in the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is simultaneously the priest and the sacrifice; he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he prays for. His prayer for their sanctification (v. 17), protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), and unity (v. 21-23) is the charter of the church's life.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian unity of Father and Son. This is not organizational uniformity or ecclesiastical merger but the living unity of love, shared purpose, and mutual indwelling. The church's unity is the Father's means of witnessing to the world (v. 21, 23): the divided church contradicts its own evangelistic witness. The prayer for unity is also the prayer for effective mission — they are inseparable in Jesus' own intercession.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.

Meaning first. John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays as the great High Priest for his people before offering himself as their sacrifice. Like the high priest who carried the names of the tribes on his heart into the holy place (Exodus 28:29), Jesus carries his people before the Father. He prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through them (vv. 20–26). It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us overhear the conversation within the Trinity. The upper room discourse of chapters 13 to 16 has ended; within the hour he will cross the Kidron into the garden and be arrested. What he does with the last quiet he has is pray, out loud, where eleven frightened men can hear every word.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. Begin with the posture, because John records it and it is not what most readers picture. Eyes open, head up, looking. That was the ordinary Jewish attitude in prayer, standing, face raised, hands often spread, and the bowed head and closed eyes we default to are a later Christian habit, not a biblical instruction. He did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). It changes the scene. This is not a man with his face in his hands. It is a man looking his Father in the face on the last evening of his life.

The Son who looks up and the sinner who cannot. Set beside him the one man in the Gospels who could not do it: the tax collector in the parable, who would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast (Luke 18:13). Both were heard. There is no single correct posture in Scripture. There is a Son who looks up because he has every right to, and a sinner who cannot because he has none, and the Father receives them both, the second because of the first.

Father. The address will repeat. Six times in this prayer he says it, and twice with an adjective: Holy Father at verse 11 and righteous Father at verse 25, forms of address found nowhere else in the Bible. He is not reaching for formality. He is using the family word, the one he taught his disciples to use, and qualifying it only where the petition needs it.

Father, the hour has come. The hour so long awaited closes a thread that has run the whole length of the book. Three times it was not yet: at Cana to his mother (2:4), and twice when men tried to seize him and could not (7:30; 8:20). Then, from the arrival of the Greeks onward, it has come (12:23, 27; 13:1; and here). For three years the not-yet was a protection; no hand could touch him before his Father’s time. It has now expired, by his own announcement, and the first thing he does with the news is pray.

Glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you. Not a selfish prayer. The Son asks to be glorified in his death, resurrection and exaltation, so that he can glorify the Father. Their glory is one. And notice where he expects the glorifying to begin: not on a throne but on a cross. In this Gospel the lifting up on the cross is the beginning of the lifting up to glory (3:14; 12:32–33). The Father’s glory is the shining out of who he is, and nowhere does he show what he is more fully than in the hour when he gives his Son for sinners. The Son is asking to be the place where that is seen.

Since you have given him authority over all flesh. “All flesh”: all humanity. The Son has authority over every person (Matthew 28:18). The man about to be bound and led from court to court is the one to whom every human being in those courts already answers.

To give eternal life to all whom you have given him. The phrase “given me” appears seven times in this prayer (vv. 2, 6 twice, 9, 11, 12, 24). The Father has given a people to the Son, and the Son gives them eternal life. His authority is universal; his saving gift is particular. This is the covenant of redemption: the Father’s gift of a people to the Son, made before the world began (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4). Some read given as those the Father foresaw would believe. But Jesus will say, I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me (v. 9), which shows that the giving is the Father’s choice, not merely his foresight. And none of those given will fail to receive what the Son was given authority to give (6:37–39).

If some are given, can I know whether I am one of them? You do not find out by looking into the secret counsel of God; you find out by coming to Christ. The same Jesus who spoke of those the Father gives him said in the same breath, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (6:37). The giving is the hidden root; the coming is the visible fruit. Nobody has ever come to Christ and been turned away because his name was missing from a list. If you are coming to him, trusting him, wanting him, that is how the Father’s gift shows itself in a human life. Election is not a wall to keep anyone out. It is the reason anyone comes in at all.

In a sentence. Jesus looked up and prayed that the Father would glorify the Son in this hour, so that the Son might glorify him, since the Father had given him authority over all people to give eternal life to all the Father had given him.

On a Tuesday. Pray with your eyes on the Father, not on yourself. Before you bring him a list, say his name the way a child does, and remember who taught you to say it. Then, when the hour you have been dreading arrives, a diagnosis, a hard conversation, a day you cannot avoid, do what Jesus did with his: speak to your Father first, and ask that he be glorified in it.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you were the Father’s gift to the Son. Before there was a world, the Father chose a people and gave them to his Son as a love-gift, and the Son received them, and on the night before he died he named the gift aloud in prayer. He holds authority over every human being who has ever lived, and he uses it to give life. Blessed be the Father who gave, and the Son who received, and who will not lose one of those he was given.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.

And this is eternal life, that they know you. Verse 3 is the nearest thing to a definition of eternal life anywhere in Scripture, and it is not the definition most people carry. Not: eternal life is living for ever. Not: eternal life is going to heaven when you die. Both of those are true, and neither is what he says. Eternal life is knowing, and the verb (ginōskō), in this Gospel and in the Old Testament behind it, means the knowledge of a person rather than of a subject. “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). It is the word for a husband knowing his wife, for God knowing his people, for the new covenant promise that they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

Eternal life has already begun. That has two consequences, and both matter. The first is that eternal life has already started for anyone who has it. If it were duration, it would begin at death. Because it is a relationship, it begins when the relationship does, the moment we come to know God, and dying does not interrupt it. That is precisely what he told Martha at the tomb: everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die (11:25–26). It grows for ever, but it does not wait.

What makes eternal life eternal. The second consequence is more searching. Endless existence without God would not be eternal life at all. Suppose a person were granted unlimited time, health restored, every faculty intact, and God were simply absent. That is not the offer being described here, and on this verse’s terms it would not be life. What makes eternal life eternal is not the length of it but who is in it. Heaven without God would be a long exile; a cell with God in it is already the beginning of heaven.

The only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Knowing God and knowing Christ go together. This verse is sometimes used against the deity of Christ, as though the only true God excluded Jesus, and the argument deserves an answer rather than a dismissal. Notice what the sentence actually does. It makes knowing Jesus Christ part of the definition of eternal life, standing in the same clause and joined by and to knowing the only true God. No monotheist would put a creature there. He does not deny his own deity by calling the Father the only true God; he denies the idols. The Son is included within the one true God (1:1). And John, who wrote this sentence, wrote in his letter of the Son: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), using the same two words. The verse distinguishes the Father from the Son, which orthodoxy has always done. It does not divide them.

Jesus Christ. One curiosity worth flagging honestly: this is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus uses the full name Jesus Christ of himself. Some think John has phrased his Lord’s words for readers a generation later, which would be in keeping with how he writes. Nothing turns on it either way; the words are the true Word of God as John was moved to record them.

I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do. “Accomplished” (teleiōsas): completed, finished. Jesus speaks of the cross as already done. On it he will cry, “It is finished” (19:30), the same root word. He speaks from the threshold of the cross as though it were behind him, because his obedience was already settled: there was no part of the Father’s will he would leave undone. And look at what he claims. Every word, every sign, every hour of thirty-odd years, offered to the Father without a single failure. No other human being has ever been able to say, I glorified you on earth, without needing to add a confession.

How do I actually get to know God better? The same way you come to know anyone: by listening to him, speaking with him, and spending time in his company. He speaks in Scripture, so read it not only to learn facts but to meet him; ask as you read, what does this show me of God and of Christ? Speak to him in prayer, honestly, as a child does. Meet him with his people at his table and under his preached word. And obey what you learn, because Jesus said the one who keeps his commands is the one to whom he shows himself (14:21). Knowledge of God grows slowly, like a friendship, and it grows most in the hard seasons when he is all you have.

In a sentence. Jesus said eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, and that he had glorified the Father on earth by finishing the work he gave him.

On a Tuesday. Eternal life is knowing God, so ask yourself whether you know him better this year than last. Not whether you know more about him, but whether you know him. Give him ten unhurried minutes today with a Gospel open, and ask, Lord, show me yourself. And when you are tempted to measure your life by its achievements, remember that the one thing that will last for ever is the friendship God has begun with you.

For worship. The God who made galaxies has made himself knowable, and the knowing of him is life itself. He did not leave us to guess at him. He sent his Son, who could say on the last night that he had glorified the Father in every hour of his life and left nothing of his work unfinished. Christ’s finished work is the ground of our knowing; his perfect obedience is credited to people whose obedience is full of holes. And the life he gives does not wait for death to begin. It has already begun in everyone who knows him, and it will never end, because the one we know will never end.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

Glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. Weigh what is being asked in verse 5, because it is one of the boldest sentences in the Bible and it is said as a request. No prophet ever prayed anything remotely like it. Moses asked to see God’s glory; this is a man asking for his own back. And the claim inside the request is the whole of the Prologue in a single clause: he had glory, with the Father, before there was a world to have it in. It is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s eternal pre-existence. God says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). So the Son is not another; he is God.

With you. Note the preposition. It is the same thought as 1:1, the Word was with God. Not glory God gave him at some point, but glory possessed alongside the Father when nothing else existed. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem. He came from somewhere, and he is about to go back.

The glory set down. This locates the incarnation exactly. Something was set down. In the incarnation he veiled that glory: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). This prayer is the same fact from the inside: a man asking to be given back what he had before, having spent some thirty years without its outward splendour. And he asks to return to it now in his human nature as well. The one who goes back to the Father’s presence goes back with hands that were pierced and a body that was raised. Our flesh has entered that glory in him.

Did Jesus stop being God when he laid his glory aside? No. He did not lay aside his deity; he laid aside the open display of it. He remained what he always was while becoming what he was not, a man. The emptying of Philippians 2 is explained by the next words, taking the form of a servant: he emptied himself by adding, not by subtracting. So even in the manger and on the cross he was the eternal Son, upholding all things (Hebrews 1:3). The glory was hidden, as the sun is hidden behind cloud. At times it broke through, at Cana, on the mountain, at the tomb of Lazarus. Here he asks for the cloud to be taken away.

I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. “Your name”: God’s character, all that he is. Jesus has revealed the Father to his disciples (1:18). The whole ministry of Jesus, teaching, signs, foot-washing and finally the cross, is the disclosure of the Father’s name. If you want to know what God is like, you do not guess; you look at Jesus.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me. They belonged to the Father before they belonged to the Son. Chosen before they came (6:37; Ephesians 1:4). They are not first the Son’s and then the Father’s; they are first the Father’s and then, by gift, the Son’s. Election is the Father’s prior claim on the people the Son will redeem.

And they have kept your word. One phrase here is startlingly generous. Look at who he is talking about. Eleven men who have understood very little all evening, who argued that same night about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), who are within an hour of running into the dark, and one of whom will deny knowing him three times before the cock crows. And this is his report to his Father about them. Not they are trying. Not they will improve. They have kept your word. Despite all their weakness and the coming failures of that night, Jesus speaks well of them. He sees their faith as genuine.

How he measures his people. Think of what an honest assessment of your own discipleship would sound like, the version you would give if pressed, with the failures included. Now notice that Jesus, praying to the Father about men whose failures were about to become proverbial, did not give that assessment. He is not blind, and he is not flattering. He is describing them as what they had become by receiving his word, which is a different measurement from the one we habitually run on ourselves.

Does this mean my sin does not matter to him? No. He grieves over it and he will deal with it; three days later he will restore Peter by name, and it will hurt (21:15–17). But he does not define his people by their failures. He defines them by what grace has made them: people who have received his word and are his. That should make you more serious about sin, not less, because you are being treated as something better than your worst nights. And it should silence the voice that tells you that your stumbles prove you were never his.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the Father to glorify him with the glory he had with him before the world existed, and said he had revealed the Father’s name to those the Father gave him from the world, who were his and had kept his word.

On a Tuesday. When you pray about your failures, confess them plainly; and then listen to how your High Priest speaks of you to the Father. When you speak to other believers about their failures, ask whether you sound like him. A church in which people describe each other as Jesus described the eleven is a church in which the weak grow strong.

For worship. The one who prayed for you shared the Father’s glory before the world began. Before the first star burned, the Son was face to face with the Father in a glory no creature had seen. He laid the display of it aside to be born in a stable and to die on a cross, and now he has taken it up again with our nature joined to him for ever. And this Lord of glory still speaks well of his weak disciples. He looks at men about to run away and says to his Father, they have kept your word. Such is the kindness of the one who holds all glory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.

Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. They recognise that Jesus’ words and works come from the Father. Everything: the teaching, the signs, the authority, the men themselves. Nothing in the ministry of Jesus originated with him considered apart from the Father, and the disciples have finally grasped it, on the last night, about an hour before their nerve fails them.

For I have given them the words that you gave me. The chain of revelation: Father to Son, Son to disciples, and through them to us. There are four verbs in these two verses, laid out as a sequence: I have given them the words, they have received them, they have come to know, they have believed. Given, received, known, believed. That is the whole mechanism of Christian faith in one sentence. Only the first is God’s action in the grammar, though the whole prayer has been saying that the rest are his doing too.

And they have received them. Faith begins by receiving God’s word. Not by inventing it, not by improving it, but by taking what is handed over. The word elabon is the word for taking something into your hands. A gift is not earned, and it is not worked out; it is received.

And have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me. Knowing and believing together. The central truth of the Gospel: Jesus came from God. And the order is instructive. Knowing comes before believing here, which is not how we usually put it. But look at what is known and what is believed. They came to know that I came from you: his origin. They believed that you sent me: his commission. The recognition of who he is precedes the trust in what he was sent to do, and both rest on words that were handed over rather than worked out.

Two errors corrected at once. Faith is not a leap made in the absence of content; there are words here, given and received, and a person to be known. And it is not a conclusion reached by unaided reasoning either, since the words came from outside, from the Father through the Son. Christian faith is neither blind nor self-made. It is the open-eyed reception of what God has said.

A report credited in full. There is a quiet dignity in how he reports it to the Father. He does not say they have begun to understand, or they are nearly there. He says they know, they have received, they have come to know, they have believed: four completed actions, credited in full. He knew what the next few hours would show, and he still said it.

My faith feels nothing like as solid as that. Does it count? Yes. The disciples’ faith that night was real, and within an hour it was shaking badly. Jesus called it faith anyway, because faith is measured by its object, not by its strength. A trembling hand that grasps a strong rope is as safe as a steady one. If you have received his words as true, if you believe that Jesus came from God and that the Father sent him to save sinners, you have the faith this verse describes, however weak it feels. Feed it with the same words that created it, and ask him, as a father once did, to help your unbelief (Mark 9:24).

In a sentence. Jesus said the disciples now knew that everything he had came from the Father, because he gave them the Father’s words, and they received them, knew he came from the Father, and believed the Father sent him.

On a Tuesday. Receive God’s words as the disciples did. Faith grows by hearing. When doubts come, do not first look inward to test the strength of your faith; look outward to the words that were given, and read them again. Ask of today’s reading not only what you should do, but who Jesus is and where he came from. Faith that is fed on him grows; faith that is fed on itself starves.

For worship. The Father spoke to the Son, the Son spoke to fishermen, and the fishermen spoke to the world, and the word has reached us intact. God did not leave his people to climb up to him by speculation. He came down with words, and put them into hands that could receive them. And the Son, presenting his disciples to his Father, credits them with everything grace had done in them. Blessed be the God who speaks, and the Son who gives his Father’s words to beggars and calls their trembling reception faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.

I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world. It is the coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter in the Bible, and people are genuinely troubled by it, so it should not be hurried past. Jesus’ high priestly intercession here is particular: for those the Father has given him. That does not mean he never prayed for unbelievers (Luke 23:34), or that we should not (1 Timothy 2:1). But his intercession as High Priest, which secures salvation, is for his own (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). His sacrifice and his intercession have the same scope. He prays for those for whom he dies, and he dies for those for whom he prays. This is one of the strongest supports for definite atonement.

What the sentence is. Three things help. The first is simply what the sentence is: a statement about the scope of this petition, not about the heart of the one praying. He is asking for something specific, that these men be kept, and that what he is about to do for them be applied to them, and the world that is rejecting him cannot be the subject of that request. One does not pray for the fire and for the house in the same sentence.

The world in the same prayer. The second is that the same prayer turns to the world twice, a few verses on: so that the world may believe that you have sent me (v. 21); so that the world may know (v. 23). The unity he asks for is asked for the world’s sake. A man indifferent to the world does not make its persuasion the goal of his petition for the church. He prays for his church in order to reach the world.

Father, forgive them. The third is the plainest. Within hours the man who said I am not praying for the world would be praying, out loud, from a cross, for the men driving the nails: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). That is not indifference. So what the verse does say, and it does say it, is that there is a particular intercession which has a particular object, and the object is the people the Father gave him. This is the High Priest with the names on his breastplate. He is not praying generically. He is praying for named individuals, and the naming is the comfort rather than the offence.

But for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. Again the Father’s gift. He pleads for them on the ground that they belong to the Father. The argument is the argument of a son to a father: these are yours; take care of what is yours.

All mine are yours, and yours are mine. Then the clause that sounds like accounting and is not. Any of us could say the first half. Everything I have is God’s: that is ordinary piety, and it is true. Nobody else can say the second half. Yours are mine is a claim to hold the Father’s property as one’s own (16:15). Luther is said to have observed that no creature could utter it. It is the language of perfect equality, spoken quietly as a matter of course.

And I am glorified in them. Christ is glorified in his people, weak as they are. Their existence is his ongoing glory: an exhibition of what grace produces in those who receive it. The eleven are not much to look at tonight, and he says he is glorified in them anyway, as a craftsman is honoured by the work still on his bench.

Is Jesus praying for me now? Yes, if you are his. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and Paul names it as one of the reasons no one can condemn us: Christ Jesus is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:34). His intercession is not a nervous pleading with a reluctant Father; it is the risen Son presenting his finished sacrifice for the people it was offered for, and asking for what it purchased. It is never refused. On the days you cannot pray, he is not silent.

Then should I pray only for Christians? No. The Son’s high priestly intercession is unique to him, and it is not our pattern for every prayer. We are told to pray for all people, kings and those in authority included (1 Timothy 2:1–4), to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), and to plead for the lost as Paul did for Israel (Romans 10:1). We do not know who the Father has given to the Son, so we pray for everyone and preach to everyone, trusting that he will call his own through those prayers and that preaching.

In a sentence. Jesus said he was praying not for the world but for those the Father had given him, who were the Father’s, for all that is his is the Father’s and all the Father’s is his, and he is glorified in them.

On a Tuesday. Write down three people you know who belong to Christ and are struggling, and pray for them by name today, specifically, as he does. Then write down one person who does not yet know him and pray for that person too. You will be imitating your Lord in both: his intercession for his own, and his prayer from the cross for those who did not know what they were doing.

For worship. Christ prays for his own, and his prayers are always answered. He prays for you now. The High Priest of the new covenant does not carry a vague concern for humanity into the holy place; he carries names, and among them is yours, written on his heart before the world began. All that the Father has is his, and all that he has he spends on the people he was given. Nothing he asks for them is ever refused, because nothing he asks for them was not first paid for with his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world. He speaks as if already gone. They will remain in a hostile world, and he knows exactly what that will cost them. Everything he asks in the next verses is asked with that picture before him: his friends left behind, in enemy country.

Holy Father, keep them in your name. “Holy Father”: the form occurs only here in the Bible. He has been saying Father all evening. Here, and only here, he adds holy, and the reason is in the petition attached: he is asking that these men be kept in a world that is unholy, and that they be made one. Holiness and fatherhood together: the God who is utterly set apart from all evil is the God who holds his children close. “Keep” (tērēson): guard, protect, preserve. “In your name”: by the power of who you are, and in loyalty to your revealed character. His first request for them is preservation. This is the basis of their perseverance.

Which you have given me. The Father has given the Son his name: the divine name (Philippians 2:9–11). The Son keeps his people by the same name in which he reveals the Father, the name above every name.

That they may be one, even as we are one. The goal of their preservation: unity, modelled on the Trinity. Not organisational sameness, but the unity of shared life, love and purpose that the Father and Son have always had.

I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction. There is a wordplay here that no English version can show, and it is the sharpest thing in the passage. Not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction: apōleto and apōleias, the same root twice in one clause. Not one was lost except the son of lostness. The man is named by the very thing that did not happen to anybody else. “Son of destruction” is a Hebrew way of describing one who belongs to destruction and is destined for it; the phrase turns up once more in the New Testament, for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). It is Judas. He was never one of those truly given; he was lost because he never truly belonged (6:64, 70).

That the Scripture might be fulfilled. His loss fulfilled Scripture (Psalm 41:9; 13:18). The Scripture Jesus means is probably the psalm he quoted of Judas the night before: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Peter later applies another psalm to him: “Let another take his office” (Acts 1:20; Psalm 109:8). Jesus did not fail to keep him; Judas’s end shows his own guilt and God’s sovereign purpose, both together.

Was Judas free? The hard question must not be dodged. Two things have to be held, and the New Testament holds them both without visible strain. Judas is never once described as a victim. He is called a thief who helped himself to the money bag (12:6), Satan enters him after he takes the morsel (13:27), and Peter says he turned aside to go to his own place (Acts 1:25): his own, chosen, fitting. Nothing in any account treats him as a man who wanted otherwise. And equally, Scripture had said it would happen, and Peter at Pentecost says the whole event went forward according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, in the same breath as you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). What Scripture never does is derive one from the other. It does not say Judas betrayed him because it was written; it says it was written, and he did it, and both are true. Anyone who claims to have resolved that has almost certainly done so by quietly dropping one half.

Could I turn out to be a Judas? The verse is not given to help us classify anybody, still less to frighten the trembling. It is given to explain why the keeping did not fail: I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost. The exception is the man who was never inside the guarding in the first place. Judas loved money, kept his heart closed, and never came to Jesus in sorrow; even his remorse took him away from Christ rather than to him (Matthew 27:3–5). If you fear that you might be a hypocrite and run to Christ with that fear, you are doing the one thing Judas never did. The sheep who worry that they are goats are seldom goats. Bring your fear to the Shepherd, and let his keeping be your confidence.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that the Holy Father would keep his disciples in his name and make them one as they are one, for while he was with them he kept them, and none was lost except the son of destruction, as Scripture foretold.

On a Tuesday. The Holy Father keeps you. Your security rests on his name, not on your strength. When you feel your grip on God loosening, in illness, in temptation, in a long dry season, pray the words Jesus prayed: Holy Father, keep me in your name. You will be asking for something the Son has already asked for you, and the Father does not refuse his Son.

For worship. The Good Shepherd kept every one of his flock through three years in a dangerous country, and he did not lose one whom the Father had given him. Now he hands them over to his Father’s keeping, and the Father is holier and stronger than any enemy. Our perseverance is not the story of how tightly we held on. It is the story of a Father who keeps, and a Son who guards, and a name that has never once failed those who are kept in it. No one will snatch them out of his hand (10:28–29).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

That they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. Notice the reason he gives for having said any of it out loud: these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. He is praying. They are listening. And he says he is praying audibly, in their hearing, for their sake, so that they will have his joy (15:11). That is a strange and moving thing to realise about this chapter. It is a genuine prayer, addressed to the Father throughout, and it is also being said where eleven frightened men can hear every word. He wanted them to overhear it.

Overheard love. Consider the difference between somebody telling you that they value you, and overhearing them say it to a third party when they did not know you were listening. The second is the one that lands. This prayer was spoken so that it would land that way. Everything in it about their being given to him, kept, guarded, loved and sent, they heard him say to his Father, and they were meant to spend the rest of their lives remembering what he said about them when he was talking to God. John did remember, and wrote it down, so that we could overhear it too.

My joy. This is the third time joy has come up in about an hour (15:11; 16:24; and here). He keeps returning to it on the worst night of his life, which tells you what he thought his friends were going to need. And it is his joy he gives: not a mood they must manufacture, but the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing the Father’s will. That joy did not leave him in the garden. It was the joy set before him for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

I have given them your word, and the world has hated them. The sober half. The word they received sets them apart, and draws the world’s hatred. He does not pray it away. He states it as the present condition, has hated, already, before the arrest, and moves straight on to what he will ask instead.

Because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Their origin is now from above, like his (3:3). The new birth has made them citizens of another country, and the world can sense it. They are hated not because they are odd but because they belong to the one the world rejected.

Why does the world hate Christians, and what if I am not hated? The world’s hatred is first a hatred of Christ, and it falls on his people because they carry his word (15:18–20). It does not always look like persecution; often it is scorn, exclusion, or simply being left out. And many Christians in many places live quietly with kind neighbours, which is a mercy to be thankful for, not a sign of failure. But if your faith never costs you anything, it is worth asking whether anyone can see it. Do not court hostility by being unpleasant; Peter says we must suffer for doing good, not for being foolish (1 Peter 4:15–16). Simply be faithful, and let the response be his business.

In a sentence. Jesus said he was speaking this in the world so that they would have his joy in full, and that he had given them the Father’s word, and the world hated them because they, like him, did not belong to it.

On a Tuesday. Read this chapter aloud slowly this week, and as you do, remember that you are overhearing what your Lord says about his people to his Father. Then take the joy he gives into the place where you are least welcome as a Christian: the office where your faith is mocked, the family gathering where it is ignored. Joy is not denial of the hostility; it is a deeper possession that the hostility cannot reach.

For worship. On the night of his betrayal, with the cross before him, the Son of God was thinking about his friends’ joy. He let them overhear his love for them so that their gladness would be full, and the gladness he gave them was his own, the joy he has in the Father from all eternity. Christ’s joy can be yours, even when the world hates you. The world can take a great deal from the people of God, but it cannot reach the joy that lives in the heart of the Son, and that is the joy he has given.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

I do not ask that you take them out of the world. This is the verse that settles what a Christian is supposed to do with the world, and it does it by refusing both of the available shortcuts. The church is not meant to withdraw from the world into isolation. They must stay in it, for their mission (v. 18). The first shortcut is withdrawal: the compound, the Christian bubble, the instinct to arrange a life in which one need never deal with anybody who does not already agree. It is an ancient instinct and it is not wicked; it is usually driven by a genuine desire not to be defiled. He declines to ask for it, and he had the strongest possible reason to want it for men he loved who were about to be hunted.

But that you keep them from the evil one. “The evil one” (tou ponērou): Satan (1 John 5:18–19). Compare deliver us from evil in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13). The danger is not the world itself, but the evil one who works in it. The Father keeps his own from his power. The Greek form is genuinely ambiguous; it could equally be rendered from evil, and translators differ, which is the identical ambiguity in the last line of the Lord’s Prayer and for the same reason. Either way, behind the evil stands the evil one, and the Father’s keeping is the answer to his strategy.

Protection, not exemption. What he asks for is protection rather than exemption. Not that nothing will happen to them: a great deal did, and most of them died for it. But that the one who wants them will not get them. Satan may sift them like wheat (Luke 22:31); he will not keep them. A Christian can lose his job, his health, his life for Christ, and lose nothing that the evil one was after.

The prayer he taught them. This prayer keeps brushing against the one he gave them: a Father addressed, a name made known and honoured, a will done, a keeping from evil, a glory at the end. He taught them to pray it, and here he is doing something very like it himself, on the last night, with the petitions turned toward them.

They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. In the world, but not of it. The second shortcut is assimilation, and this verse blocks it. Staying in the world is not the same as belonging to it. So the position he prays for is the uncomfortable middle, and it is the only one on offer. Fully in, not of. Its practical shape is not withdrawal from the neighbours but a difference in what one is loyal to, which is much harder to arrange and impossible to fake. They are citizens of heaven on embassy in the world.

Where Christians differ: separation from the world. Some Christians have sought holiness by withdrawing from society; others have so blended in that no difference remains. Verdict: Jesus prays for neither. His people are to live in the world, engaged in its life, but distinct in character and loyalty, kept by God from evil. Not monasteries, nor conformity, but holy presence.

So is it wrong to protect my children or avoid certain places? No. Wisdom is not withdrawal. Parents rightly guard young children from what would harm them, and every Christian should flee situations that feed his own particular temptations (2 Timothy 2:22). The question is direction and purpose. Are you sheltering in order to grow strong enough to go out, or hiding so that you never have to? Christian schooling, careful choices about entertainment, a decision not to take a job that would compromise you: none of these is the error Jesus refuses. The error is a life that has no unbelieving friends, no presence among the lost, and no intention of having any. He sends his people in, and he keeps them while they are there.

In a sentence. Jesus asked not that the Father take them out of the world, but that he keep them from the evil one, since they, like him, did not belong to the world.

On a Tuesday. Your workplace is where God wants you. Ask him to keep you from the evil one there. Think of the place where you feel most out of step as a Christian, and instead of planning your exit, ask what it would look like to be present there for Christ this week: honest when others cut corners, kind where others are cruel, unashamed when the subject comes up. Then ask the Father to keep you from the particular evil that place presents.

For worship. The Son who had every reason to ask that his friends be taken out of danger asked instead that they be kept in it, because he loved the world he was sending them to. And the Father has kept them: through arenas and exiles, through two thousand years of hostility, his church has never been taken out of the world and never been swallowed by it. The evil one is strong, but he has never yet taken from the Father one whom the Father was asked to keep. Our safety is not distance from danger. It is the hand of God.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.

Sanctify them in the truth. Two things in verse 17 are sharper than the English suggests. The first is that sanctify is not first a moral word. Hagiazō means to set apart for a purpose: it is what was done to vessels, to a day, to a priest. The moral content follows from the setting apart rather than the other way round: a thing devoted to God must then be fit for him. So to sanctify is both a status (set apart, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and a process (made holy, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). The petition is not first make them better but make them yours, for this work, which is exactly why the next verse is about being sent. Jesus prays that the Father will make them holy, for their mission.

Your word is truth. The second is the grammar of the last clause. Not your word is true, which would be a claim about accuracy, though it is accurate. Your word is truth: a noun, not an adjective. It does not merely correspond to reality; it is the thing reality is measured by. God’s word is the instrument of sanctification. Not contains truth or becomes truth, but is truth. It is the standard of all truth. This is why Scripture is central to the Christian life. We grow in holiness as we are shaped by God’s word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

The answer is a book. The instrument named for the sanctifying is that word. Not an experience, not a technique, not a decision. If a person wants to know what God actually uses to set people apart and make them fit for him, this verse answers in four words. The most common Christian instinct when growth has stalled is to look for a new method or a stronger resolution. This verse points somewhere quieter and more effective, the same place the pruning came from in chapter 15: you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (15:3). The Spirit sanctifies, and the sword he uses is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. The Son’s mission is the pattern for the church’s (20:21). Sent, as he was sent; set apart, as he was set apart. This is the Gospel of John’s version of the Great Commission, often overlooked because it sits inside a prayer, and he will say it to their faces on Easter evening. The comparison is not modest. The pattern for how the church is sent is how the Son was sent, which meant coming all the way in, living among people at their level, and being at their disposal. Of course the church does not atone; that work is his alone. But it goes as he went: humbly, truthfully, and at cost.

What if reading the Bible feels dry? It sometimes will, and the word works anyway. Much of what nourishes us does so without our feeling it; nobody remembers last month’s meals, but they are why you are alive. Keep reading, and read more of it at a time so that you see its shape. Read it with others, ask questions of it, hear it preached, and pray before you open it: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read it to meet Christ, not only to tick a box. And remember that sanctification is the Father’s work in answer to the Son’s prayer. You are not making yourself holy by effort; you are putting yourself where he has promised to work.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that the Father would make them holy by the truth, for his word is truth, and said that as the Father sent him into the world, he has sent them.

On a Tuesday. Choose one verse from your reading this morning and carry it into the day: write it on a card, say it at the moments you are tempted, let it shape one decision. And look at the people around you at work as people to whom you have been sent, as the Son was sent to us. You are not merely employed there. You are there on assignment.

For worship. God has not left his people to grope for holiness in the dark. He has spoken, and his word is truth, the measure of everything else that claims to be true. By that word the Father sets apart sinners for himself and makes them fit for his presence, and he has been doing it in every generation since this prayer was prayed. God’s word is truth. Blessed be the Father who sanctifies, the Son who prayed for it, and the Spirit who wields the word that makes us holy.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,

And for their sake I consecrate myself. Verse 19 has the priest and the sacrifice in one sentence, and the verb is the one from two verses earlier. “Consecrate” (hagiazō) is the same word as sanctify. Jesus was already holy. Here he means he sets himself apart for the sacrifice, as a priest was consecrated and as an offering was consecrated (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). He is both priest and sacrifice, dedicating himself to death for their sake (hyper, on their behalf and in their place). In the Old Testament ritual those were different operations performed by different parties. The priest was consecrated; the animal was consecrated; the priest offered the animal. Here one person does all of it to himself, for other people, the night before it takes effect.

That they also may be sanctified in truth. His self-offering is what makes them holy (Hebrews 10:10, 14). The logic is stated: their being set apart depends on his. He goes first, and what he does to himself is the reason the thing can be done to them at all. We are sanctified by the will of God through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all; by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.

How can my holiness depend on his? Because holiness is first a belonging and only then a likeness. By his death Christ has set you apart for God once and for all; you were washed, you were sanctified (1 Corinthians 6:11). That is finished, and it cannot be undone by a bad week. Out of that settled status comes the daily growth in holiness, as the Spirit uses the word to make you in practice what Christ’s sacrifice has already made you in standing. So you do not fight sin in order to become God’s; you fight it because you already are his, and you fight it with the confidence of someone whose victory was bought before the battle started.

I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. Then verse 20, and the reader should stop here. Now Jesus prays for us. The prayer has been about eleven men in a room. In one sentence it opens out and takes in everybody who would ever come to faith through what those men would go on to say: the whole church, in every century, including whoever is reading this page. Every Christian since the apostles has believed through their word, the gospel they preached and wrote down. If you believe, Jesus prayed for you that night.

Through their word. That is not a devotional flourish; it is what the sentence means. The chain is specified. The eleven spoke, and people believed, and those people spoke, and it has not stopped. Anybody who believes in Christ today believes because that word arrived, by however long a route, and this verse says such a person was in view on the Thursday night. And the word is still theirs: the apostolic word we have in the New Testament, which is why the church has always measured its preaching by Scripture. So everything that follows, the unity, the glory given, being loved as the Son is loved, being with him where he is, is not asked for the apostles alone. It is asked for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

How can he have prayed for me if I did not exist yet? Because he is the eternal Son, and he knew the people the Father had given him before the foundation of the world (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4). He named you in the only way a person can be named who does not yet exist, those who will believe in me, and the Father, who knows every one of them, heard the request as a request for each. And notice that he did not merely foresee you. He prayed for you, and then he went out and made it possible.

In a sentence. Jesus said he consecrated himself for their sake, so that they too would be made holy by the truth, and that he prayed not only for them but for all who would believe in him through their word.

On a Tuesday. Trace the chain that brought the word to you: the person who first told you, the person who told them, the church that sent them. Thank God for them by name. Then ask who is the next link. Somebody will one day believe in Christ through your word, spoken over a kitchen table or written in a message, and that person too is in this prayer.

For worship. Jesus prayed for you, two thousand years ago, on the night before he died. Nobody has ever been prayed for like that. Not only because the requests are large, though they are, but because of when it was said: with the arrest an hour off, in the last quiet he would have, spending it on strangers who had not been born. He knew, in that room, that there would be people twenty centuries later who would come to him because eleven frightened men eventually told somebody. Then he consecrated himself as their sacrifice and walked out into the night. Thank him.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,

That they may all be one. His prayer for future believers: unity. This is the verse on which the whole question of a divided church turns, and three answers have been given to it. Rome reads the prayer as asking for one visible institution under one visible head, and takes the existence of separated churches as the standing wound this prayer was meant to prevent. The ecumenical movement of the last century read it as a mandate to merge structures, and set about doing so. And a good many Protestants have read it as a prayer for an invisible unity only, on the comfortable assumption that since all true believers are already one in Christ, our visible divisions cost nothing.

Just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you. The model of their unity is the unity of the Trinity: distinct persons, perfect oneness of love and life. The prayer itself rules out each of the three readings. Against the single-institution and merger readings, look at the pattern Jesus gives. The unity he asks for is modelled on the life of the Trinity, where the persons are genuinely distinct and the unity is one of love, life and will rather than of administration. Nothing in that picture requires a single earthly organisation, and the apostolic churches of the New Testament were plainly many congregations, not one structure.

That they also may be in us. Not just one with each other, but one in God. Christian unity is rooted in union with the Father and the Son. It is not first something we build but something we are brought into. The unity of believers is a share in the life of God himself, and that is why it is precious and why breaking it is serious.
