So that the world may believe that you have sent me. Unity is a witness. Divided Christians make the gospel hard to believe; loving unity makes it credible. And here is the answer to the invisible-only reading: a unity the world cannot see cannot persuade the world of anything. Whatever this unity is, it must show. Which leaves the harder and better answer. It is not a summons to dissolve our confessions into one institution, and it is not permission to be comfortable about our divisions. It asks for a love between Christians that outsiders can actually observe and cannot account for: believers who honour one another across the lines, refuse to caricature, and are visibly glad of grace wherever it appears (13:35).

Unity and truth in one prayer. One thing more must be said, because it is in the same prayer. Four verses earlier Jesus asked, sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (v. 17). Unity and truth are petitions of one prayer and cannot be traded against each other. A unity bought by agreeing to say less than the gospel says is not the answer to this prayer but a counterfeit of it, and the Reformers, who did not leave lightly, understood that. What is asked here is not that we stop caring what is true. It is that those who hold the truth should stop treating each other as enemies.

The glory that you have given me I have given to them. The glory of the Son, revealed in his life and above all in the cross, he shares with his people. Given: past tense, before the cross, to eleven men who were about to run. Whatever this glory is, it was already theirs while they were behaving at their worst, which rules out reading it as a reward for anything. And the prayer says what it is for in the same breath: that they may be one even as we are one. The glory given is the shared life that produces the unity. Not radiance, not status, not visible splendour, but a share in what the Father and the Son have between them.

What it does not mean. This prayer is not a call for one worldwide church organisation that ignores the truth. The unity Jesus prays for is “in us,” in the truth of the Father and the Son, and among those who “believe in me through their word” (v. 20). Unity apart from apostolic truth is not the unity he prayed for. But neither does it excuse needless division among true believers.

When should I leave a church, and when should I stay? Stay through disagreements over secondary matters, through disappointing preaching, through personalities that grate; those are the very places where the unity Jesus prayed for is proved. Leave, peaceably and without slander, when a church abandons the gospel itself, denies the authority of Scripture, or will not deal with serious sin or abuse, and only after you have raised your concern honestly with its leaders. Even then, do not burn the bridge; you may be leaving brothers and sisters you will spend eternity with. And never leave a church simply to escape a person you have refused to forgive.

Can I be united with Christians whose baptism or church order differs from mine? Yes, in the deepest sense, and in more practical ways than many think. A Baptist and a Presbyterian who both trust Christ alone are already one in the Father and the Son. They may not be able to form one congregation, because each must act on his convictions about baptism with a clean conscience. But they can pray together, honour each other’s ministers, share platforms for the gospel, help each other’s churches in need, and speak of each other with warmth. This app holds believer’s baptism, and holds it alongside a glad affection for paedobaptist brothers who love the same Lord.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that all believers would be one, as the Father and Son are in each other, and that they would be in them, so that the world would believe, and he has given them his glory so that they would be one.

On a Tuesday. Is there a believer you are at odds with? Pursue reconciliation. The world is watching, and Jesus prayed for this. Write the message, make the call, ask the forgiveness, offer the forgiveness. And this week, say something warm and true in public about a church or Christian tradition other than your own. The unity he prayed for is made visible one costly kindness at a time.

For worship. The Father and the Son have dwelt in one another in perfect love from all eternity, and the Son has prayed that we should be brought into that life. The church’s unity is not a committee’s achievement. It is a share in the life of the triune God, given by grace to people who did not deserve it, and every time two estranged believers are reconciled, the world catches a glimpse of what God is like. He has given us his glory. Let the church’s life become the answer to its Saviour’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one. “Perfectly” (teteleiōmenoi): brought to completion. Unity grows towards its goal. It is the same family of words as accomplished in verse 4 and it is finished on the cross. What his finished work secured, his people grow into.

So that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Two clauses in these verses are among the hardest things in the Bible to believe about oneself, and they should be stated as plainly as possible. The first is this one. Not loved them. Not loved them very much. Even as you loved me: the same comparison he used at 15:9, now made to the Father in prayer, which means it is not a figure of speech aimed at encouraging anybody. He is telling the Father what is the case. The Father loves believers as he loves the Son. Not that we are equal to the Son, but that we are loved with the same love, because we are in him.

The measure of the Father’s love. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Most Christians will affirm that God loves them, and most, if pressed, would describe that love as something a good deal cooler than the love of the Father for the Son: a settled goodwill, perhaps a determination to put up with them. This verse forbids it. The measure is not a lot; the measure is the love that has existed between the Father and the Son from before the world was made, and the sentence has no qualifier in it anywhere.

How can God love me like that when I am so sinful? Because he does not love you on the strength of what you are in yourself. He loves you in his Son. You have been united to Christ by faith, clothed in his righteousness, adopted into his sonship (Galatians 4:4–7). When the Father looks at you he sees you in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), and the love that rests on the Son rests on you there. Your sin is real, and it grieves him; but it was laid on Christ and punished in him, so it cannot shut you out of the love that Christ enjoys. You will not feel this every day. It is true every day.

Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am. The second is verse 24, and the verb changes. Everything up to now has been asking. Here: “I desire” (thelō): I will. Not a request but the confident will of the Son, in perfect agreement with the Father. It is the language of a son who knows exactly where he stands, exercising a right. And what he uses it for is not deliverance, or vindication, or a shorter road. He uses it to ask that the people he is leaving should end up where he is. His last request for his people: that they be with him. This is the heart of heaven (14:3).

To see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Heaven is seeing Christ’s glory. This is the second time in this prayer he has looked back before the world existed: first to ask for his glory back (v. 5), now to say why the Father gave it, because you loved me before the foundation of the world. And here is the eternal love within the Trinity: the Father loved the Son before creation. God did not need to create to have someone to love. He is love, from all eternity (1 John 4:8). Before light, before time, before there was anything to be glorified in front of, there was a Father loving a Son, and this prayer asks that a crowd of latecomers be brought in to watch.

What will heaven actually be? Before it is a place of rest or reunion, it is being with Christ and seeing him. Everything else follows from that. The reunions are real, the end of pain is real (Revelation 21:4), the renewed creation is real; but the centre is the face of the Lamb (Revelation 22:4). Paul said to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23), and John said that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). If heaven seems vague or dull to you, it is usually because Christ seems vague to you now. Get to know him here, and you will long to see him there.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that they would be perfectly one, so that the world would know the Father sent him and loved them as he loved him, and willed that those the Father gave him would be with him to see his glory, given in the Father’s love before the world began.

On a Tuesday. Say it to yourself before you get out of bed: the Father loves me as he loves his Son. Then let that settle how you face the day’s small humiliations and fears. A person who knows he is loved like that does not need to win every argument or be noticed in every room. And when you think about dying, think first of whom you will see.

For worship. The Son wills that you be with him and see his glory. It will surely happen. He used the one recorded “I will” of his prayers not to escape the cross but to secure our company. The Father loved the Son before the world was made, and has loved us with that same love in him, and one day the eternal love that was before all things will be the light by which we see everything. We will see the glory of the Son with our own eyes, and we will not grow tired of looking.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.

O righteous Father. “Holy Father” in v. 11, “righteous Father” here: the second and last of the qualified addresses, and again unique in Scripture. The Father is just. He will vindicate the Son and judge the world. He reaches for righteous at the point where he is contrasting the world’s ignorance with his own knowledge and the disciples’ recognition. It is the word for a judge who gets the verdict right, and it is used at the moment when a right verdict is about to be spectacularly withheld by every human court he will stand in before morning. The courts of men will condemn him; the righteous Father will raise him.

Even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. Three groups: the world that does not know God, the Son who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who know that the Son came from him. The only way out of the first group into the third is through the second. Nobody comes to know the Father except through the Son who knows him (Matthew 11:27).

I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known. Through the cross and resurrection, and by the Spirit. Two tenses, and the future is the striking one. He is an hour from arrest and speaks of a work of disclosure that will go on. He said at verse 4 that he had accomplished the work he was given, and here he says the making known continues. Both are true: the accomplishing is the cross, and the disclosing does not stop at the cross. It goes on through the Spirit, through the word, through the preaching of the church, and it is going on now, wherever the gospel is read.

That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them. The prayer ends where all the purposes of God end: the love of the Father for the Son dwelling in believers, and Christ himself dwelling in them. This is salvation’s goal: to be loved with the love that flows between the Father and the Son, for ever. And these are the last words of the prayer, which are also the last words he speaks before the garden. Not that they may know about the love. That the love itself, the actual love of the Father for the Son, should be located inside them.

And I in them. Then four words in English with nothing after them. The prayer ends without a petition. He does not close with a request or a summary; he ends by naming a destination, and the destination is not a place. Four chapters of farewell, a discourse about a vine, a promise of the Spirit, an intercession for the whole church across every century, and the final word is a preposition and a pronoun. In them. That is where all of it was going. Not to a system, not to an institution, not even to heaven considered as a location, but to the Son of God taking up residence in ordinary people.

What does it mean in practice that Christ is in me? It means you are never alone and never left to your own resources. By his Spirit the risen Christ lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). That is why you can love people you could not love by nature, endure what would otherwise crush you, and keep praying when prayer feels empty: the life of Christ is working in you. You will not usually feel it as a sensation. You will see it, over years, in a growing likeness to him and a love for him that was not there before. It is also why you can face death calmly: what is in you cannot die.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed to his righteous Father that, though the world did not know him, he did, and the disciples knew he was sent; he had made the Father’s name known and would continue to, so that the Father’s love for the Son and the Son himself would be in them.

On a Tuesday. When you face something today that you cannot manage, a temptation, a grief, a person, do not first reach for your own strength. Say quietly, Christ is in me, and ask him to live his life through you in that moment. And when you are tempted to think yourself unloved, remember the last words of this prayer: the love with which the Father has loved the Son has been put in you.

For worship. The love of the Father for the Son is in you, and Christ himself is in you. Nothing is greater than this. The eternal love that flowed between the Father and the Son before there was a world has been poured into the hearts of sinners, and the Son of God has made his home in them. He asked for it out loud, where they could hear, and then he stood up and went out across the Kidron to make it possible. The righteous Father heard him, and the prayer that ended with the words in them has been answered in every believer since.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you,<sup>2</sup>since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.<sup>3</sup>And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.<sup>4</sup>I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.<sup>5</sup>And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.<sup>6</sup>“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Before going out to Gethsemane, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. Since the sixteenth century this has been called his “high-priestly prayer”: like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles), and for the people. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us hear the Son speaking to the Father on the night before the cross.

First he prays for himself: the hour has come; may the Father glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. He asks to be restored to the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. Then he prays for his disciples: he has made the Father’s name known to those given him out of the world, and kept them, losing none but the son of destruction. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one, made holy by the truth of God’s word, and sent into the world as he was sent. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their word: that they may be one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world may believe; and that they may be with him where he is, to see his glory and share the Father’s love. Every Christian is named in this prayer, and Christ’s intercession continues for them in heaven (Hebrews 7:25).

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a garden across the Kidron, Judas arrives with soldiers and temple guards. Jesus, knowing what lies ahead, steps forward and identifies himself, and at his “I am he” they fall back to the ground. He secures his disciples’ release, so that none of those given him is lost. When Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, the high priest’s servant, Jesus orders him to put up his sword: he will drink the Father’s cup. Bound, he is taken to Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Another disciple, known to the high priest, gets Peter into the courtyard, where Peter denies to the doorkeeper that he is a disciple and warms himself by the fire. Questioned about his teaching, Jesus says he has taught openly and they should ask those who heard him. An officer strikes him, and Jesus asks for evidence of any wrong he has said. Annas sends him to Caiaphas. Asked twice more, Peter denies Jesus again, and the rooster crows.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he — ego eimi — spoken in the garden, is the same divine Name Jesus has been claiming throughout the gospel. When he says it, the soldiers fall to the ground: the mere self-identification of the Son of God is enough to flatten an armed cohort. Jesus surrenders not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to. This is the theology of the atonement in action: the Lamb who lays down his own life, the Shepherd who gives himself for the sheep. The arrest is simultaneously Jesus' most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter's denial happens at the same fire where the servants are warming themselves — the detail is vivid and specific. He denies knowing Jesus to a slave girl, to bystanders, to a relative of the man whose ear he cut off. Three denials as predicted, completed at the crowing of the rooster. Peter's failure is not moral weakness alone but the collapse of self-confident discipleship — the faith that depends on its own resources rather than on grace. His restoration (ch. 21) will be built on a different foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.

Meaning first. John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus in complete control. He goes out to meet his captors, they fall before him, he protects his disciples, and before Pilate he is the one who judges. Meanwhile Peter denies him three times. The King goes to the cross not as a victim, but as the Lord who lays down his life of his own accord (10:18). Over the next two chapters every human power in Jerusalem will take its turn with him, the temple guard, the high priests, the Roman governor, the soldiers, the crowd, and each will think it is deciding his fate. John wants us to see from the first verse that none of them is.

He went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, on the east side of the city. It was dry most of the year: John calls it a cheimarros, a winter torrent, a stream bed that runs only after rain. There is a tradition, impossible to verify, that the blood of the temple sacrifices was channelled down into it, which at Passover would have been the blood of thousands of lambs. Whether or not that is so, the Lamb of God now crosses it on his way to his own death.

The king who crossed the Kidron weeping. There is an Old Testament scene underneath this crossing, and once it is seen the whole night changes shape. A thousand years earlier another king went out of Jerusalem in the dark, betrayed: “And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron” (2 Samuel 15:23). David is fleeing Absalom, and he goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare. The man who had betrayed him was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, the friend whose advice had been “as if one consulted the word of God” (2 Samuel 16:23). David prayed that his counsel would be turned to foolishness, and when Ahithophel saw that it had been, he set his house in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). A king crossing the Kidron by night, out of Jerusalem, betrayed by a trusted intimate who then hangs himself. It has all happened before, and the Son of David now walks the same ground with the opposite purpose. David went over it to save his life. This King goes over it to lay his down.

Where there was a garden. The other Gospels call it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives. John plainly knows the place, but he alone calls it a garden (kēpos), and he will use the word again: in the place where he was crucified there was a garden (19:41). A garden, where Adam fell; a garden, where the second Adam is arrested; and a garden, where he will be buried and rise. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one, and John has quietly bracketed the passion between two of them.

Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples. Then the detail that hurts. The place was not discovered. It was known, because it was theirs. The place they had gone to be together is the place that made the arrest possible, and the only reason Judas could find him in the dark is that he had been welcome there. That is the pattern of all intimate betrayal: the enemy uses knowledge gained in trust. And Jesus did not hide. He did not change his habits that night or choose a safer olive grove. He went where Judas would find him.

Was it right for Jesus to walk into danger like that? Yes, because his hour had come and his Father had sent him to this. For three years he had withdrawn when men tried to seize him early (7:30; 10:39), because his time was not yet. Now it was, and to avoid the garden would have been to refuse the cup. That is very different from courting danger or despising one’s life. Jesus is not teaching us to put ourselves in harm’s way for the sake of it; ordinary prudence is right for us, as it was for him in the years before. He is showing us a Saviour who laid down his life when it was required, and not one moment before or after.

In a sentence. After praying, Jesus went with his disciples across the Kidron to a garden, which Judas knew, because Jesus often met his disciples there.

On a Tuesday. Think of the places where you have known Christ’s company: a room where you pray, a church where you have been fed, the friendships in which you have opened your heart. If one of them has become the place of a wound, a betrayal in the fellowship, a hurt in the church, remember that your Lord knew that too. He did not stop going to the garden because Judas knew it. Do not abandon the places of fellowship because one person abused them.

For worship. Jesus went to the place where he knew he would be arrested. He went willingly, for you. The Son of David crossed the valley his father had crossed in tears, not fleeing a usurper but going out to meet the cross, and he went to the very spot where the betrayer could find him. Nothing forced him; love led him. The garden where we lost everything is the garden where he gave himself up, so that a third garden could hold an empty tomb.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, “Whom do you seek?”

A band of soldiers. Two things about the arresting party are worth measuring, because both are absurd and the absurdity is the point. The first is the size. The ESV notes that the band of soldiers was a cohort (speira), a tenth of a Roman legion, nominally six hundred men, though a detachment may have been sent. Even a detachment would be a couple of hundred. Their presence shows the Romans were involved from the start; Pilate had already been approached. With them came the temple police (“officers”). A huge force, to arrest one unarmed teacher and eleven followers, in a garden, at night.

With lanterns and torches and weapons. The second is the equipment. It is Passover, which falls at full moon. They have come out on the brightest night of the month, carrying fire, to look for the light of the world, and they will not find him until he steps out and tells them where he is. They come with their little lights to arrest the Light.

Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward. He does not hide or run. He steps forward. Not was found, not was seized: he went out to them. Everything that follows in this Gospel’s account of the passion is governed by that verb. And John pauses to tell us what he knew as he did it: all that would happen to him. Not the general shape of it. All of it: the ropes, the courtyard, the slap, the flogging, the nails, the cross. There is a kind of courage that depends on not knowing quite how bad it will be. This is the other kind, and it is much rarer. He walked out of the trees toward the torches with the whole of the following day already in view.

Whom do you seek? It is the first thing he says in the passion narrative, and it echoes the first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel, what are you seeking?, asked of two men following him (1:38). He will ask it again of Mary at the tomb (20:15). The book opens with him asking what people want, the arrest opens with the same question put to men with weapons, and the resurrection morning opens with it put to a weeping woman. The hunters are asked to name their quarry, as though he were in charge of the proceedings, which he is.

Did Jesus really know everything that would happen? Yes. As the eternal Son he knows all things, and in his human mind he had been given to know his path in detail; he had predicted his betrayal, his handing over to the Gentiles, the mocking, the flogging and the cross (Mark 10:33–34). That is what makes his going forward so astonishing. Nothing took him by surprise. And it is a comfort for us: the Christ who goes before you into your sufferings is not improvising. He knows the road you are on, and he walked a harder one with his eyes open.

In a sentence. Judas came with a detachment of soldiers and temple officers, carrying lanterns, torches and weapons, and Jesus, knowing everything that would happen, stepped forward and asked whom they were looking for.

On a Tuesday. When you know a hard thing is coming, the operation next week, the conversation you have been putting off, the consequence of an old sin, do not hide among the trees and wait to be found. Go forward to meet it, as he did, praying. And ask yourself the question he asked the soldiers: whom am I seeking today? The answer shapes everything else.

For worship. He knew all that would happen to him, and came forward. That is love. Hundreds of armed men came out by torchlight under a Passover moon to take the Light of the world, and he walked out to them before they could look. The whole terrible day lay open before him, every blow and every nail, and he did not step back. He stepped forward. Blessed be the Lamb who went to the altar on his own feet.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.

Jesus of Nazareth. They seek a man from a despised village (1:46). It is the name that will be nailed above his head in three languages (19:19).

I am he. The Greek is barer than the English can be. They say they want Jesus of Nazareth, and he answers with two words: egō eimi. There is no he. The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verses 6 and 8; the pronoun is supplied because English needs it. On one level, it simply means I am the one. But John’s readers have heard Jesus use these words as the divine name (8:24, 28, 58). The sentence he speaks in the dark is grammatically identical to the sentence that made them pick up stones at 8:58, and an echo of what God said out of the bush (Exodus 3:14). And what happens next shows the deeper meaning.

Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. John will not let it pass. He has already said in verse 2 that Judas knew the place; now, in the middle of the sentence about the divine name, he records where the man was standing. Judas has changed sides completely. He was among the soldiers.

They drew back and fell to the ground. At the name of God, the soldiers collapse. A flash of his divine majesty. They could not take him unless he let them. This is the one who has authority to lay down his life (10:18). And when they went down, Judas went down with them.

What the falling is and is not. It is worth being careful. It is not a rescue: nobody is prevented from anything, and within moments he is being tied up. It is not a threat; he does not follow it up. The soldiers get up and do their job. What it is, is a demonstration placed at exactly the point where the reader most needs it. From here to the end of the book, everything done to him is done by other people: he is bound, struck, tried, flogged, sentenced, nailed. John puts one moment at the front of that sequence in which an armed cohort goes over backwards at two words, so that nobody afterwards can say he was overpowered.

Why did they fall? Was it a miracle? John does not explain the mechanism, and we should not invent one. He simply records that when the Son of God spoke his name, armed men could not stand. Some have suggested shock or confusion, but that would not explain why soldiers who had come for this very purpose went down together. The plain sense is that for a moment the majesty of who he is broke through, as it did on the mountain of transfiguration, and creatures fell before their Creator. The day is coming when every knee will bow at that name (Philippians 2:10). In the garden, a few hundred knees bowed early.

In a sentence. When they said they were looking for Jesus of Nazareth, he said “I am he,” and with Judas standing among them, they drew back and fell to the ground.

On a Tuesday. When Christ seems weak in your world, mocked at work, ignored in the news, outvoted in the culture, remember the garden. He has never been overpowered. He has only ever been patient. Let that steady you when you speak of him, and let it humble you when you are tempted to think his cause depends on your cleverness.

For worship. One word from Christ, and an armed cohort falls. He went to the cross not because he was weak, but because he was willing. The great I AM who spoke to Moses from the fire stood among the olive trees in a carpenter’s body, and the soldiers of the strongest empire on earth could not stay on their feet before his name. Then he let them rise and bind him. Majesty that could have scattered them chose to be led away, for us.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go.”

So he asked them again. Whom do you seek? They pick themselves up. He asks again. He is directing his own arrest.

I told you that I am he. The third “I am.” He identifies himself a second time to men who have just been knocked down by the first. There is no hiding and no evasion; he makes their task easy.

So, if you seek me, let these men go. It is a condition. He is negotiating, at the moment of his arrest, with a cohort that has just been knocked off its feet, and the only thing he asks for is that his friends be allowed to walk away. Consider what he does not ask for. Not a hearing. Not fair treatment. Not time. Not that the disciples be permitted to come with him, which is what they had all sworn they wanted a few hours earlier. He uses the one piece of leverage he has to get them out of the garden. The Good Shepherd protects his sheep (10:11–12). He gives himself up so that they go free. A picture of substitution: he is taken; they are released.

And it worked. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. The Romans had every reason to take the lot of them. He had prayed an hour before, out loud where they could hear, that the Father would keep them (17:12). Here he is making it true himself, with soldiers in front of him. The prayer and the answer to the prayer are the same person. He asked the Father to keep them, and then kept them, and the keeping cost him the thing he was keeping them from.

Is this really a picture of the cross? Yes, and John means it to be. The arrest is not the atonement; that happens on the cross, where Jesus bears God’s wrath for sin. But the garden shows its shape in advance: the Shepherd stepping between his sheep and the danger, accepting what was coming for them so that they can go free. At the cross he does the same thing before a far greater judgment. The law’s sentence against his people falls on him, and they are released. Whenever you feel the accusation of your sins, hear him say to it: if you seek me, let these go.

In a sentence. Jesus asked again whom they wanted, and when they said Jesus of Nazareth, he said he had told them he was the one, and if they were looking for him, they should let his disciples go.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you, do not answer it with your record. Answer it with his words in the garden. And when you have the chance to shield someone weaker, a colleague being blamed, a child being mocked, a believer being slandered, step forward as he did, even at cost to yourself. Those who have been released by a substitute should be quick to stand in the gap for others.

For worship. “Take me, let them go.” That is what Christ said for you at the cross. With soldiers around him and the cross before him, his one demand was for the safety of his friends, and he got it, and they walked out of the garden alive while he was led away bound. He is still that Shepherd. Not one of his sheep is taken while he stands between them and the danger, and he will stand there for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.” Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)

This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken. Jesus’ words are fulfilled like Scripture, because they are Scripture. The word is from 17:12 (and 6:39): of those whom you gave me I have lost not one. Their physical rescue here is a sign of his keeping them for eternal life. John applies a saying about eternal security to a matter of physical safety on one particular night. That is not a misapplication; it is a window. The man who will not let them be arrested in a garden is the same man who will not let them be lost at the end, and the second promise is made credible by watching him keep the first.

Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it. Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant. Peter acts as he promised (13:37), bravely and foolishly, against a cohort. And it is worth being fair to him before drawing the lesson. He was outnumbered several hundred to one. He had been told an hour earlier that he would deny his master before dawn and had flatly contradicted it. He drew anyway. Whatever else this is, it is not cowardice, and the same man will be denying everything within the hour, which tells you something uncomfortable about how little courage in one form predicts courage in another.

And struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. Probably aiming for his head; if his aim had been better he would have killed him. Luke, who was a doctor, tells us that Jesus touched the ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). It was his last miracle before the cross, and it was performed on an enemy, to repair damage done by a disciple.

The servant’s name was Malchus. An eyewitness detail. John knew the high priest’s household (v. 15). The other three Gospels say only that one of those who stood by struck the servant of the high priest. John writes last, probably a generation later, when the man who assaulted the high priest’s household, and the servant who could identify him, were both beyond the reach of anybody who might have made trouble.

What Peter got wrong. Peter’s fault was not his courage but his reading of the situation. He had heard about the cup and the hour and the Good Shepherd laying down his life, and he arrived at the garden believing his job was to stop it. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable for zealous people. Ask what you are currently defending God from. If the honest answer involves preventing something he has already said he intends to do, a loss, a humbling, a door closing, then the sword is out, and the most likely outcome is somebody else’s ear.

How can I tell whether my zeal is Peter’s sword? Ask three questions. Is it in line with what Christ has actually said, or with what I assume he must want? Am I using the weapons he gave, truth spoken in love, prayer, patient witness, or the world’s weapons of force, manipulation and contempt? And who is getting hurt? Zeal that wounds the people Christ came to save, or that would have kept him from the cross, is zeal without knowledge (Romans 10:2). Real zeal for Christ looks like his own: it is willing to suffer, quick to heal, and never needs to win by cutting someone down.

In a sentence. This fulfilled Jesus’ word that he would lose none the Father gave him; then Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest’s servant Malchus.

On a Tuesday. Zeal without understanding does harm. Peter fought with the wrong weapons for the wrong cause. Our weapons are not fleshly (2 Corinthians 10:4). Think of the last time you defended the faith in a way that left someone bleeding: the cutting comment online, the argument won and the person lost. If you can, go back and help heal the ear.

For worship. Even in the moment of his arrest, the Lord kept every word he had spoken, guarding his disciples’ bodies as a sign that he would guard their souls for ever. And he was still healing. The last miracle before the cross was performed on a man who had come to arrest him, mending what his own follower had broken. Such is the Saviour we have: faithful to every promise, and gentle with his enemies even while they bind him.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.

Put your sword into its sheath. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (v. 36; Matthew 26:52). He has to rescue his disciples not only from the soldiers but from themselves.

Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had appointed for him. In the Old Testament the cup is often the cup of God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus will drink the cup of God’s anger against sin, so that his people never have to. The other Gospels record his prayer in the garden, “remove this cup” (Mark 14:36); John gives us his resolve: shall I not drink it? And notice whose cup it is: the cup the Father has given. Not Judas’s cup, not Caiaphas’s, not Pilate’s. Behind every human hand that night stands the Father’s purpose, and the Son receives it from him.

Where is Gethsemane? That word cup should prompt a question, because of what John has not told us. All three of the other Gospels place at this spot the most famous prayer ever prayed in a garden: Jesus falling on his face, sweating, asking three times that the cup might pass, and the disciples asleep a stone’s throw away. John gives us none of it. He brings Jesus across the Kidron, and the next thing that happens is that Judas arrives with lanterns. He is not concealing the anguish, and the proof is that he assumes it here. Jesus speaks of the cup the Father has given him as of something already settled between them; you cannot resolve a struggle you never had, and the sentence only makes sense if there was one. John has written the agony in his own place and his own way. He put it in chapter 12, in daylight, in public, before a crowd: now is my soul troubled, and shall I ask to be saved from this hour? No, for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). That is the same prayer, the same request raised and the same refusal to press it, only moved out of the dark and into the open where everyone could hear.

Both pictures are needed. That is the shape of the whole passion in this Gospel. The others show us a man overtaken by horror and holding on; John shows us a man walking into it with his eyes open, going out to meet the soldiers rather than waiting to be found, asking whom they seek, knocking them off their feet with a word, and then holding out his hands. Both are true and the church has always needed both. Take John without the others and you may forget what it cost him. Take the others without John and you may forget that nobody took his life from him.

Did Jesus resist the Father’s will in the garden? No. In Gethsemane his human soul shrank from the cup with all the horror of a holy man facing the wrath of God against sin, and he said so honestly. But every time he said it he added, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). To feel the full weight of something terrible and still embrace God’s will is not resistance; it is the deepest obedience there is. And it means that when you pray in agony, asking God to take something away while longing to do his will, you are not sinning. You are praying the way your Lord prayed.

So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him. “Captain” (chiliarchos): commander of a thousand, a senior Roman officer. They bind the one who had just floored them. He lets them. There was a man in Israel’s memory who had been bound by his father and laid on wood on a mountain, and who was old enough to have resisted and did not (Genesis 22:9). Jewish tradition called it the Akedah, the Binding, and it was much on people’s minds at Passover. Isaac was released and a ram was found. This time the ropes stay on.

In a sentence. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword, for he would drink the cup the Father had given him, and the soldiers, their commander and the temple officers arrested and bound him.

On a Tuesday. When suffering comes, ask not first who caused it but who gave it, and whether you can receive it from your Father’s hand. That is not passivity: Jesus objected to injustice within the hour. It is trust. And when you pray about something you dread, pray as he prayed, honestly and with surrender together, and do not think your fear disqualifies the prayer.

For worship. Christ drank the cup of wrath to the last drop. There is none left for those who are his. The cup we had filled by our sins was handed to the Son, and he did not push it away; he asked, shall I not drink it? The hands that had healed Malchus a moment before were held out for the ropes. Isaac went free and a ram was caught in the thicket. Here no substitute was found for the Son, because he was the substitute, and the ropes stayed on so that ours could come off.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.

First they led him to Annas. A word about who Annas was, because the arrangement is odd and the oddity matters. He had been high priest himself from AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him. But five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, so for roughly half a century the high priesthood of Israel was a family business run out of one house. He was the real power behind the throne. The Romans had deposed him, but many Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life. Luke can write of the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3:2), naming two men for an office that had one holder, because everybody understood who was actually in charge. Only John records this preliminary hearing.

For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. The family controlled the temple and its lucrative trade, the very trade Jesus had disrupted (2:13–16). So Jesus is taken first not to a court but to the house of the man whose family had the most to lose. It is not a legal step. Annas holds no office. It is a private call before anything official begins.

It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people. John reminds us of 11:49–52. The verdict was decided before the trial. And John had told us then that Caiaphas spoke a prophecy he did not know he was uttering: that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God scattered abroad. Now the prophet is the presiding judge, accomplishing his own prophecy without understanding it.

A night of irregularities. Jewish law as later written down forbade capital trials at night, forbade them on the eve of a festival, required a day to elapse before a death sentence, and required the court to sit in its own chamber. Every one of those appears to be broken in the next few hours. How much of that later law was in force in the AD 30s is genuinely disputed, and the point should not be pressed further than the evidence allows. But the men conducting this are the guardians of the law, and they are working in the middle of the night in a private house.

Why did God let such corrupt men hold the high priesthood? Because he was bringing the old priesthood to its end and replacing it with a better one. The very men who should have recognised the Lamb of God handed him over, and in doing so fulfilled the purpose of the priesthood without knowing it: a sacrifice was offered for the people. God often lets human corruption run its course in order to show that salvation comes from him and not from human institutions. The true High Priest stood bound before the false ones, and within days the temple curtain would be torn in two (Matthew 27:51).

In a sentence. They took Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year, who had advised that one man should die for the people.

On a Tuesday. Jesus faced a rigged trial with a predetermined verdict. When you face injustice, he knows. If you are caught in a process that has already decided against you, at work, in a family dispute, in a court, tell him plainly. Do what is right within it, speak the truth, and leave the final verdict with the Judge who cannot be bribed.

For worship. The religious powers of Jerusalem had settled the outcome weeks before, and they thought they were managing a nuisance. They were in fact carrying out the eternal counsel of God. Caiaphas said one man should die for the people, and he was right in a way he could never have imagined: one man did die for the people, and for children of God scattered through every nation and century, and we are among them. God turns even the schemes of the wicked into the means of his mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.

Simon Peter followed Jesus. Brave, after the others had fled (Mark 14:50). The rest had taken the option of distance. Peter had not, and whatever is about to happen, he is the only one of the Twelve to fail in a place none of the others went.

And so did another disciple. The other disciple raises a real question, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a confident one. He is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John himself (20:2), which fits the way this Gospel refers to its author in the third person and never by name. The difficulty is the next clause: he was known to the high priest, and a Galilean fisherman’s acquaintance with the household of Annas is not obvious. How he was known is uncertain: perhaps through business (supplying fish), or family connections (some traditions say John was of priestly descent). Some think the disciple is someone else entirely, unnamed. The Gospel does not say, and neither should a commentary.

He entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. A large house with a central courtyard. Annas and Caiaphas may have shared the residence.

But Peter stood outside at the door. Until the other disciple brings him in, and into temptation. What is not in doubt is what he does with his access. He goes back out to the door and speaks to the servant girl who kept it, and gets Peter in.

A door opened in kindness. That is one of the small ironies of the passion. The man with the connections uses them to bring his friend inside, and inside is precisely where Peter will fail. Nobody intended it. The kindness was real. If Peter had been left standing in the street, he might have gone home, and the worst night of his life would not have happened. That is not a reason to be careful about kindness. It is a reason to be honest about how failure actually arrives: not usually through malice, and often through a door somebody opened for us out of love. And notice that the door is kept by a servant girl. She is about to ask Peter a question, and the weight of the most famous denial in history will come down on an exchange with a young woman doing a menial job at a gate.

Should I avoid places where I might be tempted? Often, yes, and with no shame in it. Scripture tells us to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22) and to make no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). But Peter’s problem was not that he went into the courtyard; following his Lord into danger was right. His problem was that he went in sure of his own strength, having brushed aside the warning (13:37–38). Go where Christ calls you, even into hard places. But go praying, aware of your weakness, and leaning on him, not on your record of loyalty.

In a sentence. Peter and another disciple followed Jesus, and the other, known to the high priest, went into the courtyard and then spoke to the girl at the door and brought Peter in.

On a Tuesday. Before you walk into the place where your faith will be tested this week, the meeting, the family dinner, the night out, pray one sentence: Lord, I am weaker than I think; keep me. And if you have opened a door for someone that led them into trouble, do not torment yourself. Pray for them, and be the friend who stands with them when they fall.

For worship. Following Jesus into danger is good; following him in your own strength is dangerous. Ask for his strength. And worship the Lord who, while Peter was being let in through a door, was being led bound into the same house to stand trial for Peter’s sins and ours. He knew exactly what was about to happen at that fire. He had already prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and that prayer was holding him even as he walked in.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.” Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.

You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you? Look at the form of the question, because it makes what follows worse rather than better. The Greek form expects the answer no. She is not accusing him. She is a girl at a door, making conversation, and the way she frames it hands him the answer she assumes, probably without much interest either way. An easy question to answer wrongly. “Also”: like the other disciple, whom she knows to be one of them and who has come to no harm.

I am not. No threat has been made. No soldier is looking at him. And Peter, who a few hours ago swung a sword at an armed man’s head in the dark, says ouk eimi, I am not. The contrast is deliberate. Inside, Jesus says, “I am” (vv. 5, 6, 8). Outside, Peter says, “I am not.” The Lord identifies himself and a cohort goes over backwards; the disciple un-identifies himself to a girl minding a gate. The man who drew a sword against a cohort is undone by a servant girl’s question.

A charcoal fire, because it was cold. Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John’s eye for it is the eye of a man who was there. “Charcoal fire” (anthrakia) appears only here and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus cooks breakfast and restores Peter beside another charcoal fire. John is the only writer who mentions either, and he did not explain the connection. Smell is the sense most closely tied to memory, and anyone who has cooked outdoors knows what charcoal smells like. The smell may have taken Peter back to this night, and the second fire was lit to heal what the first had witnessed.

Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself. Standing with the enemies of Jesus: among the officers who arrested his master, at their fire, getting warm.

How denial usually happens. Here is the test, and it does not require anybody to have faced a tribunal. Denial in the New Testament is rarely dramatic. It is much more often what Peter does here: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward and nothing much seems to be at stake. The conversation at work where it would be easier not to say. The assumption left standing. It costs nothing at the time, which is exactly why it is so easy, and Peter’s began the same way.

Is keeping quiet about my faith the same as denying Christ? Not always. There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and not every conversation calls for a testimony. Wisdom, tact and timing are not cowardice. But silence becomes denial when someone asks you directly, or assumes something false about you, and you let it stand to protect yourself. The test is the motive. Am I silent because this is not the moment, or because I am ashamed of him? If it is shame, Jesus’ words apply: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (Mark 8:38). Ask him for courage before the question comes.

In a sentence. The girl at the door asked Peter if he was one of Jesus’ disciples, and he said he was not, and stood with the servants and officers warming himself at a charcoal fire.

On a Tuesday. Denials often begin with small questions in ordinary places. Be ready to say “I am” when asked about Christ. Think now of the easiest place for you to deny him: the colleague’s casual assumption, the friend’s joke, the form that asks your religion. Decide in advance, quietly, what you will say. Courage is far easier to find when the answer has been prepared before the fire is lit.

For worship. While Peter warmed his hands and said I am not, his Lord stood inside saying I am, and was about to be struck for it. The faithfulness that saves us is not ours but his. And the same Lord who heard the first denial already had another fire in mind, on a beach, where he would cook breakfast for the man who failed him. He does not forget our worst nights. He redeems them.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.

The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Annas, called high priest by courtesy. He fishes for evidence: how many followers, what doctrine? Perhaps looking for a charge of sedition or false teaching. He is trying to establish the size of the movement and the content of the doctrine, which is what a security official asks.

Which high priest is this? John calls both Annas and Caiaphas high priest. Annas had held the office and still bore the title, and many read v. 19 as his questioning, with Jesus then sent to Caiaphas (v. 24). Others read vv. 19–23 as Caiaphas. The first is the more likely.

Why John leaves out the trial before the council. A reader comparing the Gospels will notice what John does not give us here. Matthew and Mark record a full session of the Sanhedrin with witnesses, the charge about destroying the temple, the high priest’s direct question under oath, and the verdict of blasphemy. John has none of it. He gives us this brief and irregular interview with Annas and then, in a single sentence at verse 24, sends Jesus on to Caiaphas without describing what happened there. The likeliest reason is the one that explains most of John’s omissions: the other accounts were long in circulation and he supplies what they lacked. Nobody else records the Annas hearing at all, and the other disciple, very probably John himself, was inside the courtyard that night.

He would not name them. Jesus answers only the second question, and refuses the first entirely. Not one word about the disciples. He has just got them out of the garden; he is not going to name them in a courtyard. Meanwhile, a few yards away, one of those disciples is refusing to name him.

I have spoken openly to the world. Jesus has no secret movement or hidden doctrine. The word for openly (parrhēsia) is the one John uses of speaking with boldness, in public, without concealment, and it is a claim that can be checked, because everything he taught was taught in the two most crowded buildings available.

I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret. Not that he never taught privately (chapters 13–17), but that his teaching was public, with nothing to hide (Isaiah 45:19). And I have said nothing in secret does not deny that Jesus taught the Twelve privately. His private teaching explained the same message he preached openly (Mark 4:34); there was no secret doctrine for insiders.

The contrast not stated. His answer lands where it was aimed. He is standing in a private house, in the middle of the night, before a man who holds no office, being asked about a movement, and he replies that his practice has been to say everything in daylight in front of everyone. The contrast is not stated. It does not need to be.

Is there any hidden teaching for advanced Christians? No. Christianity has no secret inner doctrine reserved for an elite. Every generation has had teachers claiming special knowledge beyond the Bible, from the Gnostics of the second century to modern movements promising a deeper revelation, and every one is answered by this verse. What Jesus taught he taught openly, and what the apostles received they wrote down for the whole church (1 John 1:3). The deepest things of God are in the same Scriptures that a child can read. Growth in Christ is not access to hidden knowledge; it is going further into what has been openly given.

In a sentence. When the high priest questioned him about his disciples and teaching, Jesus answered that he had always spoken openly in synagogues and the temple and said nothing in secret.

On a Tuesday. Live so that you have nothing to hide: no private version of your faith that contradicts the public one, no conversations you would be ashamed to have reported. And when you are asked about other believers by someone who means them harm, gossip, an employer’s probing, a hostile questioner, follow your Lord and protect them.

For worship. Christ’s gospel is public truth, not a secret society. Proclaim it openly. The Word made flesh never whispered his way into anyone’s confidence; he spoke in the temple courts in broad daylight, and the light he brought is for the whole world. And even bound and interrogated, he would not hand over his friends. The Shepherd who has nothing to hide hides his sheep.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said. When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”

Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me. Under Jewish law, a case should be established by witnesses, not by forcing the accused to testify against himself (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus calls for a proper trial. The hearing is already procedurally compromised, and he says so.

One of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand. The slap should be allowed its full weight, because familiarity has made it almost decorative. “Struck” (rhapisma): a slap, perhaps with a rod, but here almost certainly an open-handed blow across the face. The first blow. Illegal and humiliating. It is not mainly a way of causing pain. It is the standard gesture for putting an inferior back in his place.

Is that how you answer the high priest? Showing off to his master. The officer explains himself in exactly those terms. So the first violence done to Jesus is not judicial and not even angry. It is an act of etiquette enforcement by a junior official who thought the prisoner’s tone was wrong. This is the man through whom all things were made, standing bound in a courtyard, being corrected on his manners by a member of the temple staff.

I gave my back. Isaiah had described it, and the wording is worth having beside the scene: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). Note the verbs. I gave. I hid not. The Servant in that passage is not overwhelmed; he presents himself.

Why did God allow his Son to be humiliated like this? Because our sin is not only guilt but shame, and he came to bear both. We dishonoured God; the Son received dishonour. We exalted ourselves; he was struck and put in his place. Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and the shame began here, with a slap from a servant. If you carry shame, for what you have done or for what was done to you, look at this courtyard. Your Lord knows what it is to be treated as worthless, and he bore it so that you could be clothed with honour as a child of God.

In a sentence. Jesus told the high priest to ask those who heard him, and an officer slapped him, asking if that was how he answered the high priest.

On a Tuesday. When you are put down, talked over, corrected unfairly by someone who enjoys a little power, remember who else was. You do not need to win the exchange. And notice whether you ever do the officer’s work: the cutting word to a junior, the public correction meant to impress someone above you. Repent of it.

For worship. The hand that made the officer’s hand was struck by it. He bore it for us. The Lord of glory gave his cheek to a servant’s blow without lifting his own hand, and he did not hide his face. The face that was slapped in Annas’s courtyard is the face we will see in glory, and the shame he carried there is the reason we will be able to look on it without shame.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? Calm and dignified. The reply is a small masterclass in what to do with an injustice, and it is worth taking apart because most of us have only two settings. He does not absorb it silently, and he does not retaliate. He states the principle: there are two possibilities, and the blow is wrong under both. If what he said was wrong, produce the evidence; that is what a court is for. If it was right, the blow has no justification at all. Either way the officer has skipped the only step that mattered. And notice that he does not appeal to who he is. He could have. The argument he uses is one that would protect any prisoner in any courtyard.

Turning the other cheek. Jesus does not literally turn the other cheek here (Matthew 5:39), but neither does he retaliate. He appeals to justice. Turning the other cheek does not mean silence before injustice; it means refusing revenge. Whatever the saying means, it evidently permits a man to say plainly that what has just been done to him was unjust.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Peter, who was near enough that night, wrote about it afterwards, and his summary is the best there is: “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The last clause is the mechanism. It is possible to say plainly that a thing is unjust and still not fight it, provided one genuinely believes there is a court that will sit later.

Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. To the official high priest and the council, for the formal trial, which the other Gospels describe (Mark 14:53–65). John passes over it. Still bound. He has been questioned by a man who holds no office, struck by a member of that man’s staff, and is now passed on with the ropes still on him to the next stage of a process whose outcome had been decided weeks earlier (11:53). Nothing has been established. Nobody has produced a charge. He is simply being moved.

When should I speak up against wrong done to me, and when should I stay silent? Speak when truth or justice needs it, calmly, without insult or threat, as Jesus did here and as Paul did when he appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Use the proper channels: a complaint, a court, the elders of the church; and if you are being abused, tell someone and get safe, because Scripture never asks you to stay under harm. Stay silent when speaking would only be revenge, self-display, or a fight for your pride. In both cases, the heart beneath is the same: you entrust yourself to God, who judges justly, and you refuse to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19).

In a sentence. Jesus asked the officer to testify to any wrong he had said, or explain why he struck him if it was right, and Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas.

On a Tuesday. You can speak up for justice without hitting back. Jesus did. The next time you are wronged, try his two-part answer: state plainly what was unjust, and then let it go into God’s hands. Write down the wrong if you must, pray over it, and refuse the second reply, the one that wants to wound.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth stood before a false court and asked only for justice, and when he did not get it he committed himself to his Father and went on, bound, to the next humiliation. He did not threaten. He did not revile. He trusted. And because the righteous Father heard him, every injustice ever done to his people will one day be put right in a court that cannot be rigged, presided over by the one who was struck in Annas’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.” One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”

Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. John cuts between Jesus and Peter: Jesus standing firm inside, Peter falling outside. He has interleaved the two scenes deliberately. Verses 15 to 18: Peter denies. Verses 19 to 24: Jesus is questioned and struck. Verses 25 to 27: Peter denies twice more. The two men are within a few yards of each other, and both are being asked who they are. One is asked, you are not one of his disciples, are you?, and says no. The other is asked about his disciples and will not name a single one of them.

He denied it and said, I am not. The second denial. Watch the pressure increase, because the sequence is exact. The first questioner was a servant girl at a gate, asking idly. The second is a group at the fire, several men at once (they said to him), with the same expected-no form of question.

A relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off. Another eyewitness detail. The danger is real: this man saw him with the sword. He is not asking whether Peter is a disciple. He is saying he saw him.

Did I not see you in the garden with him? The Greek expects the answer yes. That is a different order of danger. This man was there. He has a family grievance and an eyewitness identification, and Peter is standing in the household of the injured party warming his hands.

Before we feel superior to Peter. The escalation is real, and the honest thing to say is that by the third question Peter had something to be afraid of. The first denial cost him nothing and was therefore inexcusable. The third might have cost him his life. Nothing in the account suggests that a braver man would have done differently, and the others, apart from the unnamed disciple who got him in, are not in the courtyard at all. He failed in a place none of them went.

Courage in the wrong form. Note also what the questioner’s memory contains. The ear. Peter’s one act of courage that night has become the evidence against him, and the thing he did to prove his loyalty is what makes him identifiable when he wants to deny it. Bravery in the wrong form does not bank anything for later.

In a sentence. As Peter warmed himself, others asked if he was one of Jesus’ disciples, and he denied it; then a relative of Malchus asked whether he had not seen him in the garden with Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Notice how one compromise makes the next easier. Peter’s first lie made the second necessary, and the second made the third almost automatic.
