If you have told a small untruth to avoid embarrassment this week, go back and correct it before it grows. It is far easier to undo one denial than three.

For worship. Peter warmed himself at the world’s fire while his Lord was struck. How often we do the same. Thank God for his forgiveness. And look at the two figures John has set side by side: the disciple who would not own his Lord, and the Lord who would not betray his disciple. Our salvation has never depended on the faithfulness of the one by the fire. It depends on the faithfulness of the one inside, who kept his silence about Peter and went on to die for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.

Peter again denied it. The third denial. The other Gospels say he swore and called down curses (Mark 14:71). John says nothing else. No weeping, no look, no comment. The most catastrophic failure in the New Testament is reported in a dozen words, and then the narrative simply moves to Pilate.

And at once a rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (13:38). Luke is the one who supplies what happened next, and it is almost unbearable: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Perhaps he was being moved from Annas to Caiaphas at that moment. He turned his head. Then Luke’s next clause: Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). The crow did not condemn him. It reminded him of something Jesus had said in advance, which meant that the worst moment of his life had been foreseen and spoken about by the man he had just disowned, and had not stopped him being at that supper, or having his feet washed, or being prayed for by name.

The mercy hidden in the prediction. That is why Jesus made it. A failure nobody warned you about is evidence that everything has come apart. A failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is inside the story rather than the end of it. Here is the test, for anyone carrying a particular memory. Ask whether Christ knew about it before it happened. He did; that is what it means that he knows all things, and this chapter is the demonstration. Then ask what he did with that knowledge in Peter’s case. He announced it, washed the man’s feet anyway, prayed for him by name, arranged his escape from the garden, and three days later sent word specifically to him by an angel: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7).

The four accounts. The Gospels differ in who asked Peter each question, a servant girl, another girl, the bystanders, a relative of Malchus, and in where he stood. They agree on three denials and the rooster. In a crowded courtyard several people may have spoken at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. Mark adds that the rooster crowed twice (Mark 14:72).

The fire still to come. John, who leaves the weeping out here, has not forgotten. He is saving it. John says nothing of Peter’s tears here, but he will tell of his restoration (21:15–19). There will be another charcoal fire, on a beach, and three questions to match the three denials, and a man given his work back. Three denials will be met by three questions of love.

Judas and Peter. Both failed Jesus that night. Judas betrayed him and despaired; Peter denied him and repented. The difference was not in the size of their sin, but in what they did with it, and above all in Jesus’ prayer for Peter (Luke 22:32). Peter was one of those given to the Son; Judas was not.

Can a Christian who has denied Christ be forgiven? Yes. Peter is the proof, and he became the preacher of Pentecost. Jesus’ warning that he will deny before the Father whoever denies him (Matthew 10:33) speaks of a settled, final rejection of Christ, the life that disowns him and never returns. It does not speak of a believer who falls in weakness and comes back weeping. The warnings of Hebrews 6 describe those who fall away for good, not those who are grieved by their fall; if you are troubled that you have denied him, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Confess it, as plainly as Peter wept over it, and believe that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7–9).

In a sentence. Peter denied Jesus a third time, and immediately a rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. If you have denied Christ, do not despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back. He restores. And if someone you know has fallen badly, do not write them off. The Lord who sent a message to Peter by name on Easter morning may be asking you to carry one to them.

For worship. The rooster crowed, and the Lord turned and looked. It was not a look of rejection. It was the look of the one who had foreseen this moment, prayed against it, and was going to the cross to pay for it. Peter’s three denials were nailed there with the rest of our sins. And the Lord who heard them answered them, three days later, not with three accusations but with a message by name and, after that, three questions of love by a fire. There is no failure of ours that his faithfulness has not already outrun.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At daybreak Jesus is taken to the Roman governor’s headquarters. His accusers stay outside to avoid defilement before eating the Passover, so Pilate comes out to them. They give no charge but insist he is a criminal; told to judge him by their own law, they say they are not allowed to execute anyone, fulfilling Jesus’ word about the kind of death he would die. Inside, Pilate asks Jesus if he is the King of the Jews. Jesus asks whether that is Pilate’s own question. Pilate retorts that he is no Jew; Jesus’ own people handed him over. Jesus answers that his kingdom does not come from this world, or his followers would fight. Pilate presses: so he is a king? Jesus says he was born to testify to the truth, and those who belong to the truth listen to him. Pilate asks what truth is, then goes out and declares him not guilty, offering to release him by the Passover custom. The crowd shouts for Barabbas, a bandit, instead.
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question Pilate must answer, and his ironic placard — THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS — will become the most accurate theological statement of the passion narrative. Jesus' kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword (as Peter demonstrated), does not require political coercion, does not depend on earthly armies. It advances by truth — by the witness of the one who is the truth, received by those who are of the truth. Pilate's question — What is truth? — is asked by the man standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free, the innocent is condemned. Barabbas is released while the Son of the Father is crucified. He is a robber and insurrectionist — exactly the kind of person Jesus' opponents had accused Jesus of being. The crowd chooses the wrong son. In choosing Barabbas, they choose the kind of liberation they wanted — political, violent — and reject the liberation they needed — spiritual, sacrificial.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”

To the governor’s headquarters. The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium: either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city, or the Antonia Fortress beside the temple. Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived in Caesarea, but came to Jerusalem at feasts to keep order. John’s account of what happens there is built like a drama in seven scenes, with Pilate going out to the accusers and in to the prisoner and out again. Hold that picture; it is the picture of the man.

It was early morning. Roman officials began work at dawn. The night’s proceedings have produced a prisoner and no case, and the leaders want the matter finished before the festival crowds wake.

They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, unfit to eat the Passover. A Jew who went into a Gentile dwelling was held to contract a defilement that would bar him from the festival meals of that day. So they stand in the street and make Pilate come out. The irony is crushing: they scrupulously avoid ritual defilement while plotting the murder of an innocent man (Matthew 23:24). Men who will not step over a threshold because of a ceremonial rule, arranging a judicial killing on the other side of it.

A conscience pointed at the wrong object. It is worth being careful here, because it is the easiest thing in the world to read as a lesson about somebody else. The mechanism is not hypocrisy in the crude sense of knowing better and pretending. These men were, as far as we can tell, sincere about the purity rule. That is what makes it frightening. It is entirely possible to keep a real conscience about small things in perfect working order while the large thing goes past unnoticed. The scruple is functioning. It is simply pointed at the wrong object.

But could eat the Passover. This raises a famous question. The other Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16). Here, the Passover seems still to come. The question is treated more fully at 13:1.

Where Christians differ: the date of the Passover. Some say John has moved the date for theological reasons, so that Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered; others that different groups followed different calendars. Verdict: “eat the Passover” can refer to the whole seven-day feast of Unleavened Bread, which was also called Passover (Luke 22:1), including the festal offering eaten on the next day (2 Chronicles 30:22). The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and the leaders here wished to stay clean for the feast’s continuing meals. The Gospels do not contradict one another.

What accusation do you bring against this man? Pilate starts a formal Roman trial. And notice that Pilate goes out to them, which is the first move of the trial and sets its direction. A Roman governor was not obliged to conduct business in the street to accommodate the religious sensibilities of a subject people. He does it anyway, and by the end of the morning he will have conceded everything. When authority loses the will to be just, it becomes the instrument of injustice, however correct its procedures appear.

How do I know if I am straining gnats and swallowing camels? Look at where your conscience is loudest. If you are troubled about small matters of practice, the right wording, the right music, the right habits, while untroubled by bitterness, greed, a harsh tongue or an unreconciled brother, the scale is wrong. Jesus did not say the small things do not matter; he said these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others (Matthew 23:23). Ask God to recalibrate you by his word, especially by the weightier matters of justice, mercy and faithfulness, and ask a trusted friend where they think your blind spot lies.

In a sentence. At dawn they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters but would not go in, to avoid defilement before eating the Passover, so Pilate came out and asked what charge they brought against him.

On a Tuesday. Before your next communion service, examine not only your small observances but the large things: whom you have not forgiven, what you have done to someone this week that you would rather not name. Come to the Lord’s table clean in heart, not merely tidy in practice.

For worship. They kept themselves clean for the Passover while delivering the true Passover Lamb to death. Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Outside the governor’s door, men guarded their purity for a meal of lamb; inside, the Lamb of God waited to be slain for their impurity and ours. Every Passover since the exodus had pointed to this morning. God brought the shadow and the substance into the same street, and the substance was led to the slaughter so that we could eat the feast for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”

If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you. Their first answer is not an answer, and Pilate notices. They do not name a charge. They expect Pilate to take their word for it. Which is to say: trust us. They are asking a Roman court to ratify a verdict already reached without hearing the grounds for it.

Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law. Pilate does not want to be involved in a religious quarrel. His reply is procedurally correct and also an attempt to get rid of the case. Rome generally left internal religious matters to local courts.

It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death. Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea. The Jewish leaders could not legally execute (though stonings sometimes happened in mob violence, as with Stephen, Acts 7). They want Jesus dead, and only Rome can do it. Now they show their real goal. Historians have debated this, since Stephen is stoned in Acts 7 and the woman in chapter 8 was nearly stoned in the temple. The distinction is between mob action, which happened and which Rome punished when it noticed, and a formal judicial execution, which in a Roman province was reserved to the governor. What they are saying is not that killing him is impossible but that killing him legally requires Pilate.

Why does John keep saying the Jews handed Jesus over? He uses the phrase for the Jerusalem leaders and those who followed them, not for the whole people; Jesus, his disciples and the first believers were all Jews. Pilate himself says Your own nation and the chief priests (v. 35). The guilt for the cross belongs to those who planned it, to Pilate who allowed it, and, in the deepest sense, to all of us whose sins put him there. Peter says the Jerusalem crowd and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and the gospel was preached to them first. The charge of collective Jewish guilt, used to justify persecution, has no ground in John or anywhere in Scripture.

In a sentence. They told Pilate they would not have brought him if he were not doing evil, and when Pilate told them to judge him by their own law, they said they were not allowed to put anyone to death.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief often hides its real aims. Ask God to show you the true motives of your heart. When you find yourself saying, trust me, I would not raise this if it were not serious, about a colleague or a fellow church member, stop and ask whether you have actually got a case, or only a conclusion you want someone else to act on.

For worship. The leaders thought they were working the system, and they were. But it was God’s system they were working. Every legal technicality, every jurisdictional wrangle, every refusal and every demand that morning was being folded into a purpose older than the temple: that the Son would die, not in a riot of stones, but lifted up, in the manner he had foretold. The wrath of man was made to praise him (Psalm 76:10), and the guilt that put him on the cross, ours included, was the guilt he went there to carry.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”

This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. John’s note turns the whole exchange. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” meant crucifixion, the Roman penalty (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–33). If the council had been able to act alone, he would have been stoned. By handing him to Rome, the leaders ensure he will be crucified, fulfilling his word. The jurisdictional technicality that looks like an accident of Roman administration is the means by which the manner of his death was secured.

Hanged on a tree. And there is more in it than the shape of the execution. Being hanged on a tree meant being under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Paul builds on that very verse: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”. He became a curse for us. He had to die that way, under that sentence, and the men insisting on the correct paperwork were arranging it.

What does it mean that Christ became a curse? It means he stood where the law’s judgment falls. The law pronounced a curse on everyone who does not keep it (Galatians 3:10), and that is all of us. On the cross the Father treated his Son as the bearer of that curse, not because Jesus had sinned, but because our sin was laid on him (2 Corinthians 5:21). The tree was the outward sign of the inward reality: the Holy One under God’s judgment in our place. So the curse is not merely lessened for the believer. It has been exhausted on Christ, and the blessing of Abraham comes to us instead (Galatians 3:14).

Are you the King of the Jews? The charge is now political. Luke says they accused him of forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be Christ a king (Luke 23:2). In Greek, Pilate’s “you” is emphatic, placed first: su, you? This beaten, bound man? A king? It is contemptuous, and understandably so. In front of him is a man in his thirties, unarmed, tied up, handed over by his own nation’s leadership, with no supporters visible anywhere in the building. Pilate has spent years managing real insurgencies in this province, and he has seen what a claimant to a throne looks like. This does not.

The only charge that could interest Rome. That is why the question sits at the centre of the trial. It is the only charge that could interest a Roman court, treason, a rival king, and everything the priests want depends on making it stick. They have not brought a charge of blasphemy to Pilate, because he would have thrown it out. They were right that he was a king, and wrong about what kind, and Pilate is about to be right for the wrong reasons and write it on a board (19:19).

In the room they would not enter. Pilate has gone back inside to ask this. The accusers would not enter; so the heart of the trial, the one conversation in which Jesus explains himself, happens in a room they refused to walk into. They arranged the whole thing and were not present for the only part of it that mattered. And Pilate goes out (v. 29), comes in (v. 33), goes out again (v. 38), and will keep moving for the rest of the morning. He never settles anywhere, not with the accusers, not with the prisoner, not with his own verdict, and by noon he will have signed a death warrant for someone he three times declared innocent.

In a sentence. This fulfilled Jesus’ words about the kind of death he would die, and Pilate went back inside and asked him if he was the King of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. When events in your life seem to turn on technicalities, a missed form, a rule applied against you, a decision made by someone who did not care, remember that the death that saved the world turned on one. God is not limited to dramatic interventions. He governs the paperwork too.

For worship. Even the manner of his death was foretold. Nothing happened by accident; it was all for us. The Son had said he would be lifted up, and the scheming of priests and the procedures of Rome combined to lift him up exactly as he said. The curse of the law that hung over us was hung on him. And the man they mocked as King of the Jews was, all along, the King of kings, choosing his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?” Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”

Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? Something remarkable happens here, and it is easy to miss because it is phrased as a question. The prisoner starts interrogating the judge. Jesus asks what Pilate means. If Pilate means a political rebel king, the answer is no. If he means the Messiah, the answer is yes. That is not evasion. It is the question that separates two entirely different conversations. If a Roman governor genuinely wants to know whether this man is a king, there is an answer worth giving. If he is merely processing somebody else’s accusation, the word king means rebel. So Jesus asks him which he is doing. In effect it is an offer: the offer he made to Nicodemus and the woman at the well and the man born blind, extended to the Roman prefect of Judea in the early morning.

Am I a Jew? Contempt. Why would a Roman care about Jewish religious ideas? And it is the most self-revealing sentence Pilate speaks. He is declining to be personally involved. Whatever this is about, it is not his world and he does not intend to enter it. The effect is to shut the door on the only conversation in the room that could have done him any good.

Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done? Pilate wants a simple answer. And immediately after refusing to be interested, he does still want to know. That is the tragedy of Pilate throughout this narrative: he is not a monster and he is not stupid. He asks good questions and repeatedly declines to stay for the answers. His words also concede something. He has already worked out that this is an internal matter being routed through him, which is the first thing an experienced administrator would notice and the reason he keeps trying to hand it back. He knows he is being used. He says so out loud. And he goes through with it anyway, which is the difference between seeing a thing clearly and being willing to pay for acting on it.

Can I keep Jesus at arm’s length, like Pilate? You can try, and many do: interested in him as a historical figure, a moral teacher, a subject for discussion, but unwilling to let the question become personal. Jesus will not leave it there. He asked Pilate, in effect, are you asking this for yourself? and he asks every reader the same. Neutrality about Christ is not available, because he claims to be the King to whom every person will answer (Acts 17:31). Pilate tried to be a spectator at his own trial of Jesus, and ended as the man whose name is spoken in every recitation of the Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether Pilate said this himself or had been told it, and Pilate retorted that he was not a Jew; Jesus’ own people had handed him over, so what had he done?

On a Tuesday. Pilate thought Jesus’ claims had nothing to do with him. He was wrong. They have everything to do with us all. When you read the Gospels this week, ask the question Jesus put to Pilate: am I reading this of my own accord, wanting to know him, or only processing what others say about him?

For worship. Bound and accused, the Lord of all still turned the questioning around and offered a hardened Roman official a way into the truth. He did not need to. He was the one on trial, and he spent his breath trying to reach his judge. Such is his mercy, extended even across a courtroom to the man about to sentence him. He is still making that offer, to people who keep him at arm’s length, and he is the only one in the room who can save them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.” Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”

My kingdom is not of this world. One preposition in this answer carries more weight than anything else in the trial. The Greek is ek, out of, from. It is a statement about origin, not about location. Not that his kingdom has nothing to do with this world, but that it does not come from it, or work the way the world’s kingdoms do. Its source is heaven. Its power is truth, not swords. He is not saying his kingdom is somewhere else, purely spiritual, not down here. He says it does not come from here. Its territory is very much this world, which is why he is standing in a Roman courtroom.

Why the preposition matters. Getting it wrong has done real damage. Read as a statement about location, the sentence becomes a charter for a Christianity that concedes the actual world to other powers and retreats into private religion, which is precisely the arrangement every tyranny has been happy to grant the church. Read as a statement about origin, it says something far more disturbing to Pilate: there is a kingdom operating in his province whose authority did not come from Rome, does not depend on Rome, and will outlast Rome.

If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting. The proof: he stopped Peter fighting. Jesus gives the evidence in the form of a fact Pilate can check. There had been exactly one sword drawn in the garden and its owner had been told to put it away. The absence of a fight is the proof of the kingdom’s origin. Every time the church has reached for the sword to advance the faith, and it has, repeatedly, and worse than Peter did, it has contradicted the sentence its Lord spoke at his own trial.

But my kingdom is not from the world. Its origin is God.

So you are a king? Pilate seizes on the word.

You say that I am a king. A cautious yes. He is a king, though not in Pilate’s sense.

For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world. Born, and came: a man born, and one who came from elsewhere. Incarnation in a phrase. It is the only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth. Everything else has been I came, I was sent, I came down. To a Roman, who would have no framework for descending from heaven, he says it the ordinary way as well: I was born for this.

To bear witness to the truth. His kingdom is the reign of truth. He conquers by testimony. And the purpose named is not to reign, or to conquer, or even to die. To bear witness to the truth. He describes himself to the Roman governor as a witness, which is the humblest possible job description, and it is the one that gets him killed.

Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice. His subjects are those who hear him, as the sheep hear the shepherd (10:27). An invitation even to Pilate. To be of the truth is to belong to God’s side of reality, made able by him to hear the one who is the truth.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and the state. Some have sought to establish Christ’s kingdom by political power or force; others have concluded that faith has nothing to say to public life. Verdict: Christ’s kingdom advances by the word and Spirit, not by the sword. The church must not use the state’s weapons to spread the gospel. Yet Christ is king over all, and his truth addresses rulers too, as here.

Does this mean Christians may never fight? Some Christians, pacifists, read it so. But Jesus is speaking of his kingdom: it will never be advanced by force. That does not abolish the state’s God-given sword (Romans 13:4), nor forbid a Christian to serve as a soldier or police officer (Luke 3:14), nor to defend life. The church must never use force to spread the gospel; a Christian citizen may share in the just defence of others.

What does it mean to be of the truth? It means to belong to the truth rather than merely to hold opinions about it: to have been born of God, so that his voice is recognised as the voice of home. Jesus is not saying that some people are naturally better at truth than others. He is saying that those whom God has drawn will hear the Shepherd when he speaks (6:44–45; 10:26–27). In practice it shows in a willingness to be corrected by Christ, to come to the light even when it exposes you (3:21), and to keep listening to his word when it is unwelcome. If his voice is the one you want to hear above all others, you are of the truth.

In a sentence. Jesus said his kingdom is not of this world, or his servants would fight, and when Pilate asked if he was a king, he said he was born and came into the world to testify to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s kingdom comes through truth, so serve it with truth. In your workplace, your vote, your conversations about public life, speak honestly, act justly, and refuse the weapons of slander, manipulation and contempt even when your cause is right. And give one unhurried time today simply to listening to his voice in Scripture, as a subject listens to his king.

For worship. Christ is King, and his kingdom comes through truth. Listen to his voice. Bound and on trial, he told the representative of the greatest empire on earth that he too was a king, that he had been born for it and had come from beyond the world for it, and that his throne needed no soldiers. Rome has fallen. His kingdom has spread to every nation by nothing but the word of the cross and the power of the Spirit, and it will stand when every throne on earth is dust.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”

What is truth? The question deserves better than the contempt it usually gets, because there are two ways to say it and they are not the same. It can be a sneer: the tired cynicism of a career official who has watched every faction in a difficult province dress up its interests as principle, and who has concluded that truth is a word people use when they want something. That is the usual reading and it fits the man. It can also be genuine, and something in the scene allows it. He has just been told by a bound prisoner that there is such a thing as truth and that men can be of it. Pilate may be, for one moment, actually asking. Cynical, weary, or dismissive, Pilate does not wait for an answer. The irony: the Truth is standing in front of him (14:6).

He did not stay. What settles it is not the tone but the timing. John records that he asked the question and then went back outside. Whatever he meant by it, he did not wait. Francis Bacon wrote: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” The distance between Pilate and the answer was about four feet, and he had the authority to keep the man there as long as he liked. He asked the largest question a person can ask, in the presence of the only one who could have answered it, and left the room. Many still ask the question without wanting the answer.

How do I answer a friend who says there is no such thing as truth? Gently, and with a question of your own. Is that statement true? If it is, there is at least one truth; if it is not, there is no reason to believe it. Then move from argument to a person. Christianity does not claim merely to have found some true ideas; it claims that the Truth became a man, lived, died and rose, and that his resurrection is a public fact that can be examined (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Invite your friend to read one of the Gospels with you. Pilate’s problem was not lack of evidence; it was that he would not stay for it. Ask your friend to stay.

I find no guilt in him. The first of three times Pilate declares Jesus innocent (19:4, 6). The judge declares him innocent, and still sentences him. The innocent dies for the guilty. Three times the Roman court, in the person of its highest local representative, returns a verdict of not guilty, and three times it proceeds anyway.

But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. Note what he does immediately after acquitting him. He does not release him, which is what an acquittal requires. He offers a deal, which means that from this moment Jesus is no longer being tried. He is being negotiated over. An honest note: no source outside the Gospels attests this amnesty, though it is consistent with Roman practice of clemency at festivals, provincial governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd, and Pilate would hardly be the first official to invent a precedent when he needed one.

Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews? Pilate tries to wriggle out, and mocks the leaders with the title.

In a sentence. Pilate asked what truth is, then went out and told the Jews he found no guilt in Jesus, and offered to release the King of the Jews to them under their Passover custom.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask “What is truth?” and walk away. Stay for the answer: it is Jesus. When a hard question about your faith troubles you, do not leave the room. Take it to him, open the Scriptures, ask someone wiser, and stay with it until you have heard what he says. Truth is not found by those who ask and walk off, but by those who ask and wait.

For worship. The Truth stood four feet from the man who asked what truth was, and was not offended by the question. He was declared innocent three times by the court that crucified him, so that we who are guilty might be declared righteous by the court of heaven. Pilate found no fault in him, and neither has anyone, before or since. He is the true and faithful witness, and he is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.

Not this man, but Barabbas! Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7). So the man the crowd asks for is a real one: an armed nationalist with blood on his hands, of exactly the kind Rome crucified in batches, and of exactly the kind Jesus had been accused of being.

Son of the father. His name means “son of the father” (bar abba). Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17), which, if it stood, would mean Pilate asked the crowd to choose between Jesus son of the father and Jesus who is called Christ. The evidence is divided, and it should not be leaned on. The surname alone is enough. The guilty son of a father goes free; the innocent Son of the Father dies.

Now Barabbas was a robber. “Robber” (lēstēs): bandit, insurrectionist, the word used of the thieves and robbers in 10:1, 8, who climb into the sheepfold by another way. It is the violent kind of intruder, as opposed to the sneak-thief, and it is what the historian Josephus calls the insurgents of the period. They chose the robber over the Good Shepherd. In choosing Barabbas the crowd chose the kind of liberation, violent and political, that Rome could crush, and refused the liberation no power can overcome.

The exchange acted out. What happens next is the doctrine of substitution acted out in a courtyard, once, in front of witnesses, before anybody had a word for it. Two men. One guilty of insurrection and murder, one three times declared innocent by the judge. The crowd chooses, and the guilty man walks out of a Roman prison free while the innocent one is taken away to the cross that had been prepared. Barabbas is the first person whose life was saved by Jesus’ death in a literal sense. That morning he was a condemned man, and somebody else was nailed up in his place, and he went home. He is a picture of every sinner: guilty, condemned, and set free because Jesus took his place.

What became of him. Nothing is recorded of what became of Barabbas. He walks out of the story and out of history: no conversion, no repentance recorded, nothing asked of him and nothing given. He did not choose it, did not deserve it, and as far as we know never thanked anybody. Which is the exchange, and there has never been a clearer picture of it. Not a bargain, not a reward, not a transaction anybody entered into. A guilty man’s sentence served by an innocent one, arranged by people who were trying to do something else entirely, on the morning of the Passover.

Was Barabbas saved? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not guess. His release was physical; he was spared a Roman cross, which is not the same as being forgiven by God. To be saved from the judgment of God a person must trust in the one who took his place (3:16, 36). Barabbas is a picture of substitution, not proof that everyone it pictures receives it. That is why the picture ends with a question for us rather than for him: you have heard that Christ died in the place of sinners; have you received him as dying in yours?

Is it just for an innocent man to be punished in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if the substitute were unwilling, or a third party dragged in against his will, or if the judge simply waved the guilt away. None of those is true at the cross. The Son came willingly (10:18); the Judge whose law was broken is the same God who provides the substitute (Romans 3:25–26); and the Son is united to his people as their head, so that what he does, he does as one of us and for us. Barabbas’s release was an injustice by Pilate. Our release is the justice of God satisfied by the love of God, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

In a sentence. They shouted for Barabbas instead of Jesus, though Barabbas was a robber.

On a Tuesday. You are Barabbas. When you are tempted today to think you deserve God’s favour, or that you have earned your standing with him, remember the prison door opening for a man who had done nothing to earn it. And when someone wrongs you, remember how much you were released from, and let that make you quick to forgive.

For worship. You are Barabbas. Jesus took your place, and you walked free. The crowd chose a murderer over the Son of God, and God turned their choice into a picture of his own: the guilty set free, and the innocent Son of the Father bearing the sentence. He did it for rebels with blood on their hands, for people who did not ask and could not repay. The prison door stands open because the cross was occupied, and the one who hung there was the King of the Jews, the Son of the Father, our substitute.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.<sup>2</sup>Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons.<sup>4</sup>Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, “Whom do you seek?”<sup>5</sup>They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.<sup>7</sup>So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.<sup>19</sup>The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.<sup>20</sup>Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world— to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden across the Kidron, when soldiers and temple police come with Judas, Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; at his “I am he” they fall to the ground. He protects his disciples, rebukes Peter’s sword, and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is taken first to Annas, the former high priest and power behind the office, and questioned about his teaching, while outside in the courtyard Peter, warming himself at a charcoal fire, denies three times that he is a disciple, and the rooster crows.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders will not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled before Passover, while they hand over the true Passover Lamb to be killed. Pilate moves in and out between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside. To his question, “Are you the King of the Jews?”, Jesus answers that his kingdom is not of this world; he came to bear witness to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice. Pilate replies, “What is truth?”, declares Jesus innocent, and offers to release him for Passover; the crowd demands Barabbas instead. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as king with a crown of thorns and a purple cloak, striking him. Pilate brings him out to the crowd to show he finds no fault, and presents him: “Behold the man!” The chief priests demand crucifixion. When they add that he claimed to be God’s Son, Pilate becomes more afraid and questions Jesus, who first stays silent, then tells him that his authority comes from above, and the one who delivered Jesus bears greater guilt. Pilate seeks to free him, but the leaders threaten that this would make him no friend of Caesar. At noon on the day of Preparation, seated on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Pilate offers them their king; they cry for his death and declare Caesar their only king, and Pilate gives him up. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, beneath Pilate’s trilingual notice, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews”, which Pilate refuses to alter.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate's two presentations of Jesus to the crowd — each one a deeper truth than Pilate knows. Ecce Homo is the great statement of the incarnation: here is humanity in its representative, here is the man who is also the king. Pilate intends mockery and irony; the Spirit intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Gen. 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear the curse), the purple robe (borrowed royalty that will soon be stripped), and the reed scepter — all are parodies of kingship that are simultaneously truths about the king who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: They crucified him, and with him two others — one on either side (v. 18): the king flanked by his 'court,' the condemned alongside the condemned, the innocent among the guilty. The inscription in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek — the languages of religion, law, and culture — makes the proclamation universal: in every language, beside a road just outside the city, in the full light of Passover day, the truth is declared. The chief priests want it changed to 'he said he was king'; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.

Meaning first. John 19 tells of Jesus’ sentence, crucifixion, death and burial. John presents the cross as the King’s enthronement: crowned, robed, proclaimed king in three languages, lifted up. And it is the Passover sacrifice: he dies as the lambs are prepared, no bone broken, sprinkled with hyssop. At the centre stands his cry: It is finished. The work of salvation is complete. Everything in this Gospel has been moving toward this chapter: the Lamb of God John the Baptist pointed to (1:29), the serpent lifted up (3:14), the Shepherd laying down his life (10:11), the grain of wheat falling into the ground (12:24). Here it happens, and John tells it with a restraint that makes every detail weigh.

Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. It tore the flesh to ribbons, and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion. And the placement of this flogging is worth understanding, because it looks at first like a procedural muddle. Roman practice knew several grades of beating, and the severest was the standard prelude to crucifixion, done immediately before it. This one comes in the middle of the trial, before any sentence. Pilate may have hoped that this would satisfy the crowd, so he could release Jesus, and Luke supplies the reasoning in his own words: I will therefore punish and release him (Luke 23:16, 22).

A compromise worse than a miscarriage. So the flogging is an attempted compromise. Pilate has found no guilt, and he is trying to give the crowd something short of a death: a beaten man, visibly punished, whom they might let go. It is the classic manoeuvre of an official who knows what justice requires and is looking for a cheaper alternative. It did not work, and the attempt is in some ways worse than a straightforward miscarriage. Pilate has inflicted a savage punishment on a man he has publicly declared innocent, not as a sentence but as a bargaining position. Isaiah foretold it: with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5).

And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head. A mock crown, perhaps from a thorny plant, painful and humiliating. And the Greek word is not the one for a royal crown. A diadēma is what a king wears. What they twist together is a stephanos: the victor’s wreath, given to the winner of the games or to a general on his return. They meant it as part of the joke. It is the wrong joke. In three days the man wearing it will have won, and the word they chose is the one the New Testament uses for the crown he will give away: the crown of life, of righteousness, of glory that does not fade (James 1:12; 2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4).

The thorns of the curse. Thorns were part of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:18): the first visible consequence of the fall, the thing every farmer since has fought. A handful of it is pressed onto his head by men who are laughing. The King bears the curse on his head.

And arrayed him in a purple robe. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from costly dye. Perhaps an old soldier’s cloak. They dress him as a king to mock him. The soldiers are doing theology without knowing it: robing the King, crowning him, dressing him for his throne. They are adorning what they intend to destroy.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much? Would his death alone not have been enough? Scripture does not treat his sufferings as a mere preliminary to the real work. His whole humiliation, the flogging, the mockery and the pain as well as the death, was part of his obedience and his bearing of our sin. Isaiah links the wounds themselves to our healing (Isaiah 53:5), and Peter says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The suffering also shows us what sin is: not a small fault but a thing that, when it fell on the holy Son, looked like this. And it means that there is no pain you can suffer that he has not entered. He is a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In a sentence. Pilate had Jesus flogged, and the soldiers made a crown of thorns, put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple robe.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to offer God a compromise, a partial obedience, a cheaper alternative to what you know he asks, remember Pilate’s whip. Half-measures with the truth are rarely merciful. And when you suffer in your body, tell the Lord who was flogged. You do not have to explain pain to him.

For worship. The King of glory wore thorns for us. By his wounds we are healed. The curse that sprang from the ground when Adam fell was twisted into a crown and pressed onto the head of the second Adam, and he wore it. The soldiers meant a joke and made a victor’s wreath. They laughed at a king and robed the King of kings. And every crown that will ever be given to his people, the crown of life, the crown of glory, was won by the head that wore the thorns.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, “See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him.”

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” These are Roman auxiliaries; they know exactly what they are imitating. The soldiers mock him with the truth. What the mockery does, without anybody intending it, is stage a coronation. There is a robe, a crown, an acclamation, and a court paying homage. Every element of an accession is present and every one is inverted. John, who tells us the mockery in detail, is the evangelist most interested in the kingship. He wants the reader to see the crowning.

And struck him with their hands. Repeatedly, in the Greek. And it is worth remembering that this is happening between the flogging and the crucifixion, to a man who has been awake all night. The King receives blows rather than inflicting them.

That you may know that I find no guilt in him. The second declaration of innocence (18:38). Pilate’s plan: show them a broken man, no threat to anyone. Set the two things side by side and the horror is administrative rather than dramatic. The verdict is innocent. The prisoner has just been flogged and is being beaten by soldiers. Both facts are reported by the same man in the same breath, and he sees no contradiction, because the punishment is not a sentence; it is an offer. And notice how he puts it: I am bringing him out to you that you may know. He wants credit for the verdict. He is asking the crowd to notice his fairness, in the very sentence in which he produces a man he has had beaten half to death for no offence.

Why does God let people mock Christ, then and now? Because he is patient, and because he is not threatened. The mockery of the soldiers was not a defeat for God; it was the means by which the King was led to his throne. The mockery of today, the jokes, the contempt, the casual blasphemy, is no more a threat to his reign than theirs was. God is giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and some of the mockers will be his. The centurion at the cross was one of those soldiers (Mark 15:39). When you hear Christ mocked, grieve, speak up where you can with grace, and pray for the mocker. He may yet kneel.

In a sentence. The soldiers mocked him as King of the Jews and struck him, and Pilate brought him out to show the people that he found no guilt in him.

On a Tuesday. They mocked him as king; one day every knee will bow to him as King (Philippians 2:10). Bow now, gladly. And watch for the Pilate in yourself: the wish to be seen as fair while doing the unjust thing. If you have harmed someone and are now asking others to admire your reasonableness, stop, and put it right.

For worship. The soldiers hailed him in mockery and struck him with their fists, and he let them. Every word of their parody was true. He is the King, and his coronation was carried out by men who despised him, with a robe and a crown and a cry of homage, on the morning of his death. Heaven will one day ring with the same acclamation, sung in earnest by people from every nation, and some of them will be people who once mocked.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!” When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”

So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Bloodied, crowned, robed.

Behold the man! Three words, and no scene in the Gospels has been painted more often. In Latin, Ecce homo, the title of countless paintings. What Pilate means by it is fairly clear and entirely cynical. Look at him. Look at the state of him. This is your dangerous insurgent: a beaten man in a borrowed robe who can barely stand. He is inviting the crowd to be embarrassed by their own charge. Is he a threat?

Pity that did not come. Notice that the strategy assumes something decent about them. Pilate is betting that if they see the man they will stop wanting him dead. He has miscalculated, and the miscalculation is instructive: the sight of suffering does not reliably produce pity. It can produce the opposite, and here it produces a howl.

The true man. But John hears more. Here is the man: the true human being, the second Adam, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), suffering for all. There is a line in Zechariah that might be heard behind the words: behold, the man whose name is the Branch (Zechariah 6:12), a man who will be crowned, who will build the temple, and who will be a priest on his throne. Whether anyone in that courtyard caught it cannot be known; John has recorded the phrase that makes it audible. What is being pointed at is not a specimen of suffering but the human race’s representative. The old Adam was made in a garden and lost everything; this is the new one, and the curse that fell on the first is sitting on his head in the form of thorns. God’s verdict on humanity and his answer to it stand in one figure.

Crucify him, crucify him! The chief priests and officers lead the shout. Pity does not move them. The response is the only honest thing in the scene, and we should resist the instinct to distance ourselves from it too quickly. This is what happened when God became visible and stood in front of a crowd at close range without power: not indifference, not confusion, but a demand that he be removed. Anyone who has wondered why God does not simply show himself has an answer in this verse, and it is not a comfortable one.

Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him. The third declaration of innocence. A taunt: Pilate knows they cannot legally crucify.

Would I have shouted with the crowd? In one sense, yes. Not because you would have been in Jerusalem that morning, but because the same heart that shouted is in every one of us by nature: the heart that wants God out of the way when he comes too close (Romans 8:7). That is why the cross is not only something done by them; it was done for our sins, and in that sense by us. But the gospel does not leave you in the crowd. The man they rejected prayed for those who crucified him, and three thousand people from that same city were baptised seven weeks later (Acts 2:23, 36–41). The shout of crucify him is answered by the cry of it is finished.

In a sentence. Jesus came out wearing the thorns and the robe, and Pilate said, “Behold the man!”, but the chief priests and officers shouted for him to be crucified, and Pilate said they could crucify him themselves, for he found no guilt in him.

On a Tuesday. Take five minutes today and simply look at him: read this passage slowly and imagine the scene. Do not hurry to the lesson. Then ask what it would mean for you to receive him, rather than to want him removed, in the area of your life where he is most inconvenient.

For worship. Behold the man: crowned with thorns, for you. Look at him long. Here is everything humanity was meant to be, beaten and robed in mockery, and here is everything humanity has become, howling for his death. The true Man stood in our place, wearing our curse, and he did not come down. Behold him, and worship: the Son of Man who will come on the clouds came first like this.

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.” When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.

We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die. The law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). Before Pilate they say we have a law: their law, which a Roman court had no business enforcing. They had spent the morning translating a religious conviction into a political one because that was the only version Rome would hear. Now, frustrated, they revert to the real one, and hand Pilate a problem he has no competence to judge.

Because he has made himself the Son of God. The real charge comes out. Not sedition, but his claim to be the Son of God (5:18; 10:33). For an hour it has been the charge of kingship. Now, cornered by Pilate’s refusal, they say what the council had actually condemned him for. They are right that he had claimed it. Nothing in this Gospel lets a reader say they misunderstood him. Chapters 5, 8 and 10 are a record of them understanding him exactly and reaching for stones. They have understood his claim exactly. The only question is whether it is true.

When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. “Even more”: he was already uneasy, and John has not said so until now. Something about this prisoner has been unsettling him since the first interview. Matthew says his wife had warned him of a dream: have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matthew 27:19). Romans believed in sons of gods, divine men who walked among mortals. Augustus was officially called son of the deified Julius; the category existed and the emperors used it. And every Roman knew stories of gods walking about in disguise and of what happened to men who mistreated them without recognising them. What if this man really was one?

Fear that does the wrong thing. So the governor is now frightened, superstitious, out of his depth, and holding a verdict he cannot enforce. It is exactly the condition in which men do the thing they know to be wrong, because the wrong thing is the one that makes the fear stop soonest.

Did Jesus really claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies understood it better than many modern readers. He claimed God as his own Father in a way that made himself equal with God (5:18). He said, before Abraham was, I am (8:58). He said, I and the Father are one, and they took up stones because, as they said, you, being a man, make yourself God (10:30–33). He accepted Thomas’s confession, my Lord and my God (20:28). He did not die for claiming to be a good teacher; he died for claiming to be the Son of God. C. S. Lewis’s point still stands: a man who said these things would be either deluded, deceiving, or Lord. The resurrection settled which.

In a sentence. The Jews answered that by their law he should die for claiming to be the Son of God, and Pilate became even more afraid.

On a Tuesday. The question that frightened Pilate is the question for us all: is he the Son of God? If he is, then everything he says has the authority of God, including what he says about your money, your marriage, your fears and your sins. Ask which of his words you have been treating as optional, and bring that area under his claim today.

For worship. They condemned him for claiming to be the Son of God, and the claim was true. The eternal Son, who had been with the Father before the world existed, stood in a governor’s court accused of being exactly who he was. He did not withdraw the claim to save his life; he laid down his life and took it up again, and so was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). Fear him rightly, as Pilate did not, and love him, as Pilate never could.

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”

Where are you from? Not his hometown; Pilate knows that (Luke 23:6–7). He means: who are you, really? Where do you come from? The great question of John’s Gospel (7:27–28; 8:14; 9:29). It has been asked before by people who thought they knew the answer: the crowd at the feast who said they knew where he came from and therefore he could not be the Christ (7:27), the Pharisees who said they did not know where he came from (9:29). Now a Roman asks it, frightened, in a private room, and it is the right question at last.

But Jesus gave him no answer. After a night of speaking, to Annas about his teaching, to Pilate about kingdoms and truth and witness, the one question that goes to the centre is met with silence. Not sullenness, and not the silence of a man with nothing to say. Like the lamb led to slaughter that opens not its mouth: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). And something more specific: Pilate had already heard the truth (18:37) and brushed it aside. He had asked what truth is and walked out before the answer. A man who leaves before the answer to one question does not get an answer to the next. Jesus will not cast pearls before swine.

What if God is silent when I ask him something? There are people who have asked God something real, not idly, not to score a point, and received nothing. Not a refusal. Silence. The temptation is to conclude either that nobody is there, or that the asking was somehow disqualified. This verse establishes that the silence of God is not always what it appears. Jesus’ silence was not indifference; the man in front of Pilate was at that moment on his way to dying for sinners. The nearest thing to an answer Pilate was ever going to get was standing there in a purple robe with his hands tied. That does not explain any particular silence, and it is not offered as an explanation. It establishes something narrower and worth having: a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing. Keep praying, keep reading his word, and remember that he has already given his clearest answer at the cross.

Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you? Pilate falls back on his power. He thinks he holds Jesus’ life in his hands. It is the response of small authority everywhere to being ignored. He has just been frightened. Now he reaches for rank. Power has seldom been so mistaken about itself.

In a sentence. Pilate went back in and asked Jesus where he came from, and when Jesus did not answer, reminded him he had authority to release or crucify him.

On a Tuesday. When you have been wronged and long to defend yourself, consider whether silence would honour Christ more. Not every accusation needs an answer, and not every questioner wants one. And when you are tempted to remind someone of your authority over them, as a parent, a manager, an elder, ask whether you are reaching for rank because you have lost the argument.

For worship. Christ was silent before his judge, so that we might have something to say before ours: he died for me. The Word through whom all things were made stood wordless before a frightened governor, and his silence was the silence of the Lamb, going to the slaughter for the sins of the world. He held his peace so that we could have peace. And the one who would not answer Pilate answers every sinner who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.” From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. The word for from above is one this Gospel has used before, and it is not the obvious one. It is anōthen, the very word that baffled Nicodemus in chapter 3, where being born anōthen could mean again or from above. Here there is no ambiguity, and the claim is enormous. All human authority is delegated by God (Romans 13:1). The authority by which a Roman prefect is about to have the Son of God executed is authority that was issued to him, from above. Pilate is not ultimately in control. God is, and has ordained this hour (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Jesus is the one truly in charge of this trial. Pilate thinks he is, and says so. Jesus tells him he holds real power, and that it is on loan.

Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin. Probably Caiaphas, or Judas, or the leaders as a group. It is singular, he who delivered me, most probably Caiaphas, who had the Scriptures, the office, and full knowledge of what he was doing, as against a Gentile administrator out of his depth. They knew the Scriptures and the evidence. Pilate is guilty, but less so. There are degrees of sin (Luke 12:47–48). Scripture consistently weighs guilt by the light received, which is uncomfortable for the well-taught and merciful toward the ignorant.

Comfort under bad authority. There is a great deal of comfort here for anyone under an authority that is behaving badly, and it needs stating carefully so as not to become a defence of tyranny. It does not say that what Pilate is about to do is right. The next clause says the opposite: somebody in this affair has the greater sin, which means sin is being committed and measured. What it says is that the power being abused is derivative, borrowed and bounded, and that the man wielding it will answer for how he used what he was lent.

From then on Pilate sought to release him. He tries harder.

If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Then the sentence that ends the trial, and it is worth knowing why it worked. “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials. Pilate’s record was poor; he had offended the Jews several times, and the emperor Tiberius was suspicious and quick to punish disloyalty. He had provoked riots by bringing military standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem, and had been forced to remove them. He had put up shields in Herod’s palace and been overruled by Tiberius after the Jewish leaders complained over his head. Within a few years he would be removed from office and sent to Rome to answer for a massacre in Samaria. A report to Rome could end his career, or his life. The men making the threat know his file. They are telling a governor with two black marks against him that there will be a third.

Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. The threat works. Everything before this, the acquittals, the fear, the attempts to release him, collapses the moment his career is named.

If God is in control, was Pilate really to blame? Yes. God’s sovereignty never excuses human sin. Pilate’s authority came from above, but his decision to condemn an innocent man to save his own position came from his own heart, and Jesus calls it sin. Peter holds both together in one sentence: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordained the end; the men who did it did what they wanted, and they are answerable. That is not a puzzle to be solved by dropping one half. It is the comfort of the believer: even the worst human choices cannot escape God’s purpose.

Must I obey authorities who act unjustly? In general, yes, in everything lawful, because their authority is from God (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and that includes respecting rulers we did not vote for and employers we do not admire. But obedience has a limit: when a ruler commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Christians may also use lawful means to resist injustice: appeal, protest, the ballot, the courts. And abuse in a home or a church is never to be submitted to; get help and get safe. Above all, remember that every ruler is lent his power and will answer for it.

In a sentence. Jesus told Pilate his authority came from above, and those who handed him over had the greater sin; Pilate then tried to release him, but the Jews shouted that if he did, he was no friend of Caesar, for anyone claiming to be king opposes Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Whatever authority you hold was given you from above. Use it as one who will give an account. As a parent, a boss, a teacher or an elder, ask this week what your decisions would look like if you remembered that the power is on loan. And name your Caesar: the one person or pressure whose displeasure you fear so much that you would do wrong to avoid it.

For worship. Bound, flogged and on trial for his life, Jesus calmly told the governor of Judea where his power came from. The Son was never at the mercy of Pilate. The Father had given Pilate his authority, the Son had given himself into his hands, and the whole of that terrible morning was moving according to a purpose formed before the world began. The rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), and in doing so they fulfilled the plan by which he would rule them all.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your king!”

He brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat. The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave formal sentence (bēma). The Greek could even mean that Pilate sat Jesus on the judgment seat, in mockery. Either way, the irony is that Jesus is the true Judge (5:22, 27). Pilate sits on the seat of judgment over the one before whose judgment seat Pilate himself will one day stand (2 Corinthians 5:10).

At a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. An eyewitness detail. Gabbatha may mean a raised place.

Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. “Day of Preparation” (paraskeuē) was the regular term for Friday, the day of preparing for the Sabbath (v. 31; Mark 15:42). “Of the Passover”: Friday of Passover week. Jesus dies on the afternoon of the day the lambs were traditionally connected with the feast. John wants us to see that Jesus is the Passover Lamb (1:29).

But was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke say it was (Mark 14:12–16), while John seems to put the Passover a day later (13:1; 18:28).
