Some think different groups followed different calendars that year, or that Jesus held the meal early. The more likely answer is that the day of Preparation of the Passover means the Friday of Passover week, the day of preparation for the Sabbath (compare 19:31; Mark 15:42), and that in 18:28 the Passover means the meals of the festival week. On that reading the Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus died on the Friday of Passover.

It was about the sixth hour. About noon by Jewish reckoning. That clock reading needs a note, because it is one of the most frequently cited discrepancies in the Gospels. Mark says he was crucified at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25). Reckoned from sunrise, that is noon against nine in the morning, and the trial cannot be running three hours after the crucifixion. Two answers are offered and both are reasonable. The first is that John is counting hours the Roman civil way, from midnight, so that his sixth hour is about six in the morning, early enough for everything that follows. The second is simpler and may be truer to how anyone told the time before clocks: the day was divided into rough quarters, and a writer named the marker nearest the event. Mark reaches for the third hour, John for the sixth, and both are gesturing at a stretch of a morning that ran somewhere between the two. Notice that John writes about the sixth hour; he is not claiming precision, and nobody in that courtyard had a watch. The difference is no contradiction for people who told time by the sun’s position.

The day, not the clock. One honest consequence follows. If John is using Roman hours, then a neat correspondence with the midday slaughter of the lambs is not available, and that point should be held lightly. What does not depend on the hour is the thing that matters: Jesus was condemned and killed on the day of Preparation, in the week when the Passover lambs of that feast were sacrificed. John says so twice, and the symbolism he is pressing rests on the day, not on the clock.

Behold your king! Pilate mocks the Jews. He speaks the truth. It is his second presentation, this time from the seat of judgment, and the King he presents is still thorn-crowned and purple-robed. That is exactly what the King of the new covenant looks like: enthroned in suffering, crowned with the curse.

In a sentence. Pilate brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Gabbatha; it was the day of Preparation of the Passover, about noon, and he said, “Behold your king!”

On a Tuesday. When you meet an apparent contradiction in the Bible, do not panic and do not paper over it. Look carefully, as this note does, at what the writers actually claim, and remember that the Gospels are four honest witnesses, not four copies. Their differences in detail are the marks of independent testimony, and their agreement on everything that matters is the stronger for it.

For worship. Behold your King: bleeding, mocked, condemned, and reigning. Pilate sat on the judgment seat, and the Judge of all the earth stood before him, condemned on the day the Passover was prepared, so that the true Lamb would be sacrificed in the very week Israel remembered its deliverance. Every Passover lamb for fourteen centuries had been a rehearsal for this Friday. And the one Pilate presented in contempt is the King we will see on the great white throne, no longer standing before a governor, but with every governor standing before him.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.” So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,

Away with him, away with him, crucify him! Total rejection.

Shall I crucify your King? Pilate twists the knife.

We have no king but Caesar. This is the sentence to stop at, and it is easy to walk past because it sounds like ordinary political talk. It is said by the chief priests. Not the crowd, not a hothead: the men whose office existed to represent Israel before God. A shocking statement from the chief priests of Israel. God was Israel’s king (Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7; Psalm 5:2), and they longed for the Messiah, the son of David, to rule. Now, to get rid of Jesus, they renounce both.

What Israel was. Consider what Israel was: a nation founded on the conviction that its true King was God. When the people first asked Samuel for a king, the LORD’s verdict was that they had rejected him from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). Gideon refused a crown on exactly that ground: the LORD will rule over you (Judges 8:23). The psalms are full of it; the LORD reigns is the shortest summary of the religion. And this is said at Passover, which celebrated deliverance from a pagan king, in Jerusalem, a few hundred yards from the temple, by the priesthood, about the emperor of the occupying army, in order to secure the execution of their own Messiah. At the Passover, they bow to Caesar. In rejecting Jesus they reject God. Forty years later Caesar’s soldiers burned the temple to the ground.

Does this mean God has rejected the Jewish people? No. This verse has been used badly, and the guard must be stated. It is a sentence spoken by a group of officials in a particular courtyard on a particular morning, and it is not a verdict on a people. The Gospel’s author, its subject, Jesus’ mother and every one of his apostles were Jews, and Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians hold different views on what Romans 11 promises for Israel’s future, but none of them gives any ground for contempt. What this verse is, is a warning about religious leadership, and it lands nearest those who most resemble the men who said it: people who know the Scriptures, hold religious office, and find the real King inconvenient.

There is always a Caesar. Here is the test, and it is for anybody. There is always a Caesar available: something that can be appealed to as the real authority when the true King is inconvenient. Career, safety, respectability, the approval of a group whose good opinion is load-bearing. The chief priests did not stop believing in God that morning. They simply, under pressure, named somebody else as the one whose displeasure they could not risk.

So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. “To them”: to their will. Roman soldiers carried it out (v. 23). The verb is weighted. Judas delivered him to the priests, the priests delivered him to Pilate, Pilate delivers him to be crucified. And behind them all stands another delivering: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Human justice fails; divine love triumphs through the same event.

In a sentence. They shouted for him to be taken away and crucified, and when Pilate asked if he should crucify their King, the chief priests answered that they had no king but Caesar, so he handed him over to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you serve as king? If not Christ, then some Caesar. Choose your King. Finish this sentence honestly: the thing I could not bear to lose, even for Christ, is.... Whatever fills the gap is the Caesar you are tempted to bow to. Bring it to him today, and say aloud that he is your King.

For worship. They said, we have no king but Caesar, and the Father handed over his Son. Men delivered him out of envy and fear; God delivered him out of love. And the King whom his own leaders renounced did not renounce them: within weeks the apostles were preaching to the people of Jerusalem that God had raised him and made him both Lord and Christ, and thousands of them bowed the knee. Caesar’s throne is gone. His reigns.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.

And he went out, bearing his own cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. The upright post usually stood there already. The other Gospels tell us Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it, probably after Jesus collapsed (Mark 15:21). A reader comparing the Gospels will hit this at once, and the resolution does not require anyone to be wrong. The crossbeam was heavy, and Jesus started out carrying his. He had been awake all night, beaten by the temple guard, flogged by Rome and struck repeatedly by soldiers, and men in that condition often could not finish the walk. Luke’s wording is that they laid the cross on Simon to carry it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), which fits a man who has collapsed part of the way. Each writer keeps what serves his account. The others record the collapse and the stranger pressed into service. John, whose whole passion narrative insists that nothing was taken from Jesus and everything was given, records that he went out carrying it himself.

Isaac and the wood. John stresses that Jesus went out carrying it himself, perhaps recalling Isaac carrying the wood up Mount Moriah for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22:6). The son carried the wood up the mountain, and the father said God would provide the lamb. Here the Father provides the Lamb, and the Lamb carries the wood.

Outside the camp. “Went out”: outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27; Hebrews 13:12). The letter to the Hebrews makes a doctrine of it: Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, so let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:12–13). The place of rejection is where the sin offering went, and where his people go to meet him.

To the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. “Calvary” comes from the Latin calvaria, skull. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre probably marks the site, just outside the city wall of that time, and beside a road, because public execution was meant to be seen.

There they crucified him. John says it in a few words, the shortest sentence about the most important event in history. No description. Not one of the four Gospels describes the physical process of crucifixion, and every reader in the first century knew exactly what the words covered and did not need telling. Crucifixion was the most cruel and shameful death Rome could inflict, reserved for slaves and rebels. Nails were driven through wrists and feet; the victim died slowly of exhaustion and suffocation, often over days. Cicero said the very word “cross” should be far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts. This is how the Son of God died. And notice the restraint of the evangelists, in an age that has produced a good deal of Christian art and film determined to supply what they deliberately withheld. They want us to see not the gore but the meaning.

And with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them. Numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). The other Gospels call them robbers or criminals. John’s phrasing puts him in the middle: Jesus between them. The arrangement of the three crosses is Isaiah’s sentence carried out by a Roman work detail with no idea what they were doing.

What does it mean for me to take up my cross? Not to carry his cross; that was his alone, and no one can share the work of atonement. But Jesus said that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow (Luke 9:23). To carry your cross is to accept, for his sake, the cost of belonging to him: the loss of approval, the death of your own way, the hardships that come from obedience. It is not every misfortune, a bad back or a difficult neighbour, though he helps with those too. It is the shame and loss that come because you are his. And it is always carried following him, which means it leads, as his did, through death to resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus went out carrying his own cross to the Place of a Skull, Golgotha, where they crucified him between two others.

On a Tuesday. Go outside the camp with him this week. Identify one place where following Christ will cost you a little reputation, the joke you will not laugh at, the corner you will not cut, the friend you will not abandon when others do, and pay the cost gladly. It is a small share in the reproach he bore, and he is there.

For worship. He went out carrying the cross for you, to the place of shame, and was counted among sinners. The Lamb carried his own wood up the hill, and there was no ram in the thicket to take his place, because he was the provision. They crucified the Lord of glory between two thieves, and he hung in the middle, where sinners are, so that sinners could be brought to where he is.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.

Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. The charge was usually written on a board (titulus) and carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then nailed to the cross. It was part of the deterrent: the crowd would know what the state was punishing. Which makes this one remarkable. Every other such notice in the empire named a crime. This one names a person and a title, and states no offence at all, because there was none, and Pilate had said so three times.

Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. The charge was meant to mock and warn: this is what happens to would-be kings. But it proclaims the truth. On the cross, Jesus is enthroned as King. The Latin initials INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum) appear on many crucifixes. Pilate meant ironic humiliation; he wrote the gospel.

It was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek. Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman rule, Greek the common language of the empire. The King is announced to the whole world: in the language of religion, of government, and of culture. Aramaic, which the people of that land actually spoke, the language of home and of the synagogue. Latin, the language of the army and the law, in which the empire issued its orders. Greek, which everybody used for trade and thought from Spain to India. So the first public proclamation of the kingship of Jesus was in three languages, official, posted over his head beside a main road on the busiest day of the Jewish year, and paid for by the Roman government.

Many read it. John adds that it was well placed: the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. Golgotha was close enough to the wall and the gate that a crowd going in and out for the feast would pass it. Many read it, John says, and he means many.

Is Jesus King now, or only when he returns? Now. He was enthroned at the cross and the resurrection, and he is seated at the Father’s right hand, reigning until all his enemies are put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25; Ephesians 1:20–22). All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). His reign is hidden now, exercised through his word and Spirit as he gathers his people from every nation, and it will be visible to all when he returns. That is why the church can be confident in every age and every place. The board over the cross was not a joke that came true later. It was true when it was nailed up.

In a sentence. Pilate put an inscription on the cross, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,” which many read, since it was near the city and written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the gospel to go out in a language other than your own: for Bible translators, for missionaries learning a hard tongue, for a church in a country whose language you do not speak. The cross was first proclaimed in three languages. It will finally be praised in all of them.

For worship. The cross proclaims him King in every language. Let your tongue add its own. The Roman government paid for the first gospel tract, and the King of the Jews was declared to the world in the words of religion, law and culture while he hung dying under the notice. That proclamation has never been taken down. It has been translated into thousands of languages since, and one day people from every tribe and tongue will read it aloud before his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ‘This man said, I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

Do not write The King of the Jews. Write rather, “This man said, I am King of the Jews.” The chief priests are humiliated. The sign says that the Jews’ king has been crucified. Their objection is precise and grammatical. Not the King of the Jews, a statement, but this man said, I am King of the Jews, which converts it into a reported claim by a dead pretender. They are asking for the sentence to be turned into a quotation. It is the oldest way there is of disposing of a truth without denying it outright.

What I have written, I have written. And Pilate, who has spent the morning conceding everything, refuses. The perfect tense, twice: it stands written and it will go on standing. It is the flattest, most immovable sentence anybody speaks in the chapter, and it comes from the man who has just handed over somebody he knew to be innocent. Pilate, who could not stand up to them for justice, now stands firm out of spite. Almost certainly not conscience. It reads like a man who has been pushed around all morning and finds one thing he can refuse: a small, safe, spiteful assertion of the authority he failed to use when it mattered. There is nothing noble in it.

God served by a governor’s irritation. That is exactly what makes it worth having. But God overrules: the truth stays on the cross. Like Caiaphas (11:51), Pilate testified to the truth without meaning to. God’s purposes at Calvary were served by a governor’s petty irritation, as they were served by soldiers gambling and by a priest’s political calculation. Nobody in the chapter is trying to accomplish anything for God. Every one of them accomplishes it. And the result is that the only official document produced by the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, the one legal text, in three languages, over his head, unretracted, says that he is the King. God’s word stands written.

The proverb. The sentence has had a long life. Quod scripsi, scripsi passed into proverb, and it is usually quoted admiringly, as the mark of a man who will not be moved. It was said by somebody who had been moved on every question that mattered, about a notice, after the nails were in.

How do people today turn the truth into a quotation? Every time Jesus’ claims are reported as merely what he said, or what his followers believed, so that nobody has to reckon with whether they are true. It is the way of much modern talk about religion: Christians believe that Jesus is Lord, rather than Jesus is Lord. That can be honest description, and in the right setting it is fair. But watch for it in your own heart: the habit of holding Christ’s words at arm’s length, as interesting claims, rather than receiving them as the truth about the world. Scripture does not say he said he was King. It says he is.

In a sentence. The chief priests asked Pilate to change the sign to say that Jesus only claimed to be King, but Pilate answered that what he had written, he had written.

On a Tuesday. God can use even stubborn and spiteful people to declare his truth. He is never defeated. When you are discouraged by the people who seem to be in charge, in your nation, your workplace or your church, remember that God wrote the gospel that day with a reluctant governor’s pen. He is not hindered by the character of the instruments he uses.

For worship. What God has written, he has written. The chief priests could arrange an execution, but they could not edit the notice over the cross, and no one since has been able to edit the truth it proclaimed. The Lord who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11) made a spiteful man’s stubbornness serve his glory, and the title stands for ever: Jesus of Nazareth, the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes in four and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the psalm. Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, who takes her into his home. Knowing his work is complete, Jesus says he is thirsty, to fulfil Scripture, and is given sour wine on a hyssop branch. Then he says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. Because the Sabbath of Passover week is near, the leaders ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers break the legs of the two others, but finding Jesus already dead, one pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water flow out. The eyewitness testifies truthfully so that readers may believe; these things fulfilled the Scriptures that none of his bones would be broken and that they would look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, gets Pilate’s permission to take the body, and Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. They wrap the body with the spices in linen, as Jews bury, and, because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is near, lay him in a new tomb in a garden by the place of crucifixion.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished is the single most important word of the gospel. It announces a completed action whose effects are permanent: the work of redemption is done, accomplished, complete — it does not require addition, continuation, or supplement. Every subsequent act of piety, every religious effort, every moral striving — none adds to what is finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved; accepted, not earned.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross (with Mary, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas) is the model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost is highest, faithful where the others fled. He sees the blood and water from the soldier's spear — the sign that Jesus is truly dead, truly human, truly sacrificed — and testifies that what he saw is true. His testimony is the foundation of the gospel that will go to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things.

They took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier. The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned were the executioners’ perk. The number tells you this is a routine detail recorded by somebody who was watching. Four men sit down at the foot of the cross and divide a change of clothes: the outer cloak, the belt, the sandals, the head covering. One item is left over. Jesus was crucified naked, the final humiliation.

But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. The inner garment. Some note that the high priest’s robe was woven in one piece (Exodus 28:32; Josephus says the same). The coincidence has struck readers since the early centuries: the garment of the priest, on the body of the priest, preserved whole while everything else is divided. Jesus dies as our High Priest. Others have seen the unity of the church. It should be offered as an echo rather than an argument. John does not explain; he points to the fulfilment of Scripture.

This was to fulfill the Scripture. Psalm 22:18. Psalm 22 begins “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and describes in astonishing detail a man surrounded by mockers, with pierced hands and feet, his bones on display, his garments divided. Written a thousand years earlier, before crucifixion was invented. And it contains a line that had no obvious application to anything: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. Two different actions, dividing and gambling. It reads like ordinary Hebrew poetry, saying one thing twice. At Golgotha it turns out to be two things. They divided the garments and they cast lots for the tunic, and the reason they did both is a technical accident of weaving.

Psalm 22 read whole. The psalm is worth reading whole at this point. It opens with the cry Jesus quotes from the cross. It has men mocking and wagging their heads; it has hands and feet pierced; it has bones out of joint and a tongue sticking to the jaw; and it ends, unaccountably, in worldwide praise, with all the families of the nations worshipping and a people yet unborn told that he has done it. It is either the most extraordinary coincidence in literature or it is what it appears to be.

So the soldiers did these things. Every detail, even the gambling of soldiers, was under God’s hand. The soldiers noticed none of it. They were solving a practical problem about a garment that would be ruined if cut. Four men gambling on a hillside, entirely at liberty, fulfilling to the letter a poem they had never read.

Was Psalm 22 really about Jesus, or about David? Both, in their proper order. David wrote out of his own suffering, and the psalm makes sense in his life. But it goes far beyond anything David endured: the piercing, the stripping, the casting of lots, and above all the ending, where the sufferer’s deliverance brings the ends of the earth to worship God. David was a prophet and knew that God had promised a greater Son (Acts 2:30–31). The Spirit who moved him to write was speaking of the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:11). So Jesus could take its first line on his lips as his own, and John could see its details fulfilled at the foot of the cross. The psalm was always his.

In a sentence. After crucifying Jesus, the soldiers divided his clothes into four shares and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the Scripture about dividing his garments and casting lots for his clothing.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 22 today from beginning to end, slowly, and at each verse ask what it shows you of the cross. Then pray its last verses for the world: that the families of the nations would turn to the Lord. The psalm of the cross ends in mission.

For worship. He was stripped of everything, so that we might be clothed in his righteousness. The soldiers gambled for his last possession at the foot of the cross where he was purchasing an inheritance for his people. The God who wrote the psalm a thousand years before governed the dice that afternoon, and nothing in the suffering of his Son was outside his hand. The naked King on the cross clothes sinners in garments of salvation and robes of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10).
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”

But standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Count the women, and notice who is missing. Probably four women: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene, from whom Jesus had cast seven demons (Luke 8:2). The Greek also permits three, if the sister and Mary of Clopas are the same person. The men had fled; the women stayed. Peter is somewhere in the city. The men who had sworn to die with him a few hours earlier are absent, except one, and the people who stayed are the ones with no power to do anything at all.

Being there. That is worth saying to anybody who has ever stood beside a suffering they could not fix. These women could not stop it. They had no standing, no legal voice, no ability to intervene, and if they had tried they would have been moved on by soldiers. What they could do was be there, in full view, close enough for him to see them. It was not nothing. It is, in fact, the only thing anybody did for him that day, and John records their names.

A sword through her soul. Simeon’s prophecy to Mary is fulfilled: a sword will pierce through your own soul also (Luke 2:35). She was told it when the baby was forty days old. She has had some thirty years to wonder what he meant, and she is finding out.

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby. John, too, came back.

Woman, behold, your son! “Woman” is not cold but respectful, as at Cana (2:4). And it is the second time in this Gospel he addresses her so. He said it to her once before, at a wedding, when she wanted him to do something about the wine and he told her his hour had not yet come. John has bracketed the ministry with the word: Cana, where the hour had not come; Golgotha, where it has. In his agony, Jesus provides for his mother. As the eldest son, it was his duty. His brothers did not yet believe (7:5). He entrusts her to the beloved disciple. Even on the cross, he keeps the fifth commandment.

Where Christians differ: Mary at the cross. Roman Catholic teaching sees here Mary made the spiritual mother of all believers, and sometimes speaks of her as co-redemptrix, sharing in Christ’s saving work. Verdict: the plain meaning is that a loving son provides a home for his widowed mother. Christ alone is the Redeemer, and his sacrifice needs no human partner (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 10:14). Mary is honoured as a believer and the mother of our Lord, but she is not a mediator. This also suggests that Mary had no other sons who believed at that time, but it does not prove she had no other sons at all (Mark 6:3).

Does this make Mary the spiritual mother of all believers, as Roman Catholic teaching holds? The text shows a son providing for his widowed mother, and the disciple taking her to his own home (v. 27). Nothing gives her a role in the church’s salvation or prayers. Mary is honoured as the mother of the Lord and a believer among believers (Acts 1:14), but Christ alone is our mediator.

What if my own family does not believe? Jesus knows what that is like; his brothers did not believe in him at the time (7:5), and he still loved and provided for his own. Keep loving them, honour your parents, and pray for them patiently. Do not make them feel they are a project. The brothers who doubted came to faith after the resurrection: James became a leader of the Jerusalem church, and both he and Jude wrote letters in the New Testament (Acts 1:14; 15:13). And in the meantime, the church becomes family to you, as the beloved disciple became a son to Mary.

In a sentence. His mother, her sister, Mary wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene stood by the cross, and when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple he loved, he told his mother that this was now her son.

On a Tuesday. Even in agony, Jesus cared for his mother. Look after your parents, especially in their need. Ring them; visit; take care of the practical things. And when someone you love is suffering and you can do nothing to fix it, do not stay away for fear of being useless. Be there. It was the one thing anyone did for him.

For worship. The Son of God, bearing the sins of the world, turned his eyes from the weight of the cross to the face of his mother and made sure she would have a home. The Redeemer needed no partner in his work, and he did not ask for one; he asked only that she be cared for. Such is the heart of our Saviour: never so taken up with saving the world that he forgets the one standing in front of him.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”

Behold, your mother! A new family formed at the cross: the family of believers, bound by Christ. He had brothers; under any ordinary reckoning the eldest son’s responsibility passes to the next son. He passes it instead to a disciple. That is not a slight on the family. It is a statement about what the new family is founded on. The tie that binds this household together is not blood.

And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. John cared for Mary from then on. Tradition says she later lived with him in Ephesus. It is the first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, and it consists of somebody taking a widow in (James 1:27).

After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished. “Finished” (tetelestai): the same word as v. 30. Everything the Father gave him to do was complete, except his final words and death. And notice the timing of all this. He is in the process of being executed. Breathing requires pushing up on the nails. And what he does with that breath is domestic: settling who will look after his mother.

I thirst. He said it to fulfil the Scripture. Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink; and Psalm 22:15: my tongue sticks to my jaws. A reader may stumble here, as though the thirst were staged for the sake of a quotation. It was not. The man had been flogged, had lost blood for hours, and had been hanging in the sun since morning; dehydration is one of the ways crucifixion kills. The thirst is as real as thirst gets. What John means is that he knew what he was doing when he said it aloud. He is not manufacturing a fulfilment; he is naming, in the last minutes, the one thing left on the list.

The fountain thirsts. Hold on to the plain fact underneath the theology. The creator of the waters, the giver of living water (4:14; 7:37), thirsts. The one who told a woman at a well that he could give her water so that she would never thirst again, and who stood up at the feast and cried out about rivers of living water, died thirsty. His humanity was real, and so was his suffering. He thirsted that we might never thirst.

Did Jesus suffer as God or as man? He suffered as the one person who is both. God in his divine nature cannot suffer or die; the eternal Son did not cease to uphold the universe on the cross. But the Son took a true human nature, body and soul, and in that nature he truly thirsted, bled and died. Because it was the Son of God who suffered in that nature, Scripture can say God purchased the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). So the thirst on the cross was not play-acting by a divine being in a costume. It was the real thirst of a real man, who was also God.

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciple that Mary was now his mother, and he took her to his home; then, knowing that all was finished, Jesus said “I thirst,” to fulfil Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Take someone in. The first act of the church at the foot of the cross was to give a widow a home. Is there an elderly believer, a single parent, a lonely student in your church who needs a family? Invite them to your table this week. And when you thirst, physically or spiritually, remember who thirsted for you and go to him for living water.

For worship. The fountain of living water cried “I thirst” so that you might drink and never thirst again. The Maker of rivers and seas hung with a tongue that stuck to his jaw, and he made of his last breaths a new family and a fulfilled Scripture. Every drink of grace we have ever taken was paid for by that thirst. Come, everyone who thirsts, and drink.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

A jar full of sour wine stood there. Cheap, vinegary wine (oxos), the soldiers’ drink. Not the drugged wine he refused earlier (Mark 15:23).

On a hyssop branch. Before the great word, one detail that is easy to miss and is not decoration. Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), and in purification (Psalm 51:7). A small, bushy plant with a weak stem; it is not an obvious thing to hold a soaked sponge up with, and some think a long stalk is meant. But John wrote hyssop, and the reason is almost certainly that he knew what hyssop was for. On the night of the first Passover, Israel was told to take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the basin, and touch the lintel and the doorposts, so that the destroyer would pass over the house. Hyssop is the applicator of the Passover blood. And at the moment the true Passover Lamb is dying, a stalk of it is lifted to his mouth. John has recorded it and said nothing, which is his habit. The point is theological: the Lamb’s blood is applied.

It is finished. One word in Greek: tetelestai. Perfect tense: finished, and remaining finished, a thing completed with results that stand. It was used on receipts in the papyri to mean “paid in full.” Not “I am finished,” but “It is finished”: the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4). Not I am finished, which is what a dying man says. The subject is the work, not the man. The sacrifice for sin is complete. The debt is paid. The prophecies are fulfilled. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing needs to be.

The guard this word sets. Notice the guard this word puts on everything afterwards. If the work is finished, nothing can be added to it: not by penance, not by devotion, not by a lifetime of good behaviour, not by anything a person does on their worst day or their best. The commonest form of Christian misery is the suspicion that something is still outstanding. This word was cried from a cross to settle it.

And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit. John’s word order is deliberate, and it is backwards. A dying man’s head falls when he dies. John has him bow it first, as one lying down to rest, and then give up his spirit; the verb is one of handing over, of giving something into someone’s keeping. Not that his life was taken from him: he gave it up (10:18). Two thousand years of art have him hanging with his head fallen. John says he laid it down. The same man had said, in the Shepherd discourse, no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and this is the sentence where he does it. Luke records his last words, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

Nothing was taken. Nothing was taken from him that afternoon that he did not give. The clothes were taken, and the freedom, and the reputation, and the blood. His life he handed over, at a moment of his choosing, having first said that the account was settled.

Where Christians differ: what happened at the cross? Some say Christ’s death was mainly an example of love, or a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore God’s punishment for our sin. Verdict: Christ’s death was a victory and an example, but at its heart it was penal substitution: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). That is why “It is finished” can mean “paid in full.” Nor does the Mass repeat or re-present the sacrifice; it was offered once for all, finished (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

Was Jesus really forsaken by the Father? Yes, in the sense Scripture means, and it was the deepest part of his suffering. On the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). The Father did not stop loving his Son; the Son was never more pleasing to him than in this obedience. But as the sin-bearer, Christ endured the Father’s judgment on sin and the withdrawal of the felt comfort of his presence, the experience of the condemned. The union of the Trinity was not broken. What he bore was the forsakenness that our sins deserved, so that we would never be forsaken (Hebrews 13:5). John records the end of it: when the wrath was exhausted, he cried, it is finished, and committed his spirit to his Father.

If it is finished, why do I still struggle with sin and suffering? Because what was finished is the payment, not yet the whole renewal. The work that saves you is complete: your guilt is paid, your standing with God secure, your future certain. Nothing you suffer is punishment for sins Christ has paid for; it is a Father’s training (Hebrews 12:5–11). But the application of that finished work goes on: the Spirit is making you holy, and the creation still groans until Christ returns (Romans 8:18–23). You fight sin not to finish what he left undone, but because he has finished it, and the victory he won guarantees yours.

In a sentence. They lifted a sponge of sour wine on hyssop to his mouth, and when Jesus had received it, he said “It is finished,” bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

On a Tuesday. Notice today the thing you keep trying to add to the cross: the extra effort to feel forgiven, the penance of self-punishment after a sin, the private sense that God is still waiting for you to make it up to him. Name it, and then say the word aloud: it is finished. Confess the sin, receive the forgiveness, and get up and serve him out of gratitude, not to pay a debt that has been cancelled.

For worship. It is finished. Add nothing to it. Rest in it. With hyssop at his lips, the true Passover Lamb cried that the work was done, and bowed his head, and gave his spirit into his Father’s hands. The debt that no sinner could ever pay was stamped paid in full in the blood of the Son of God. Every sacrifice before it was a promise of it; nothing after it can be added to it. Glory to the Lamb, who did not die defeated but laid down his life as a finished work, and lives to make sure that not one of those he paid for is ever charged again.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.

So that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath. The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight: his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23); the coming Sabbath made it urgent. The Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, but in Judea they respected Jewish custom. And notice who does the asking. The Jews asked Pilate: the same officials, going back to the same governor, a second time in one day. The first request was for a death. The second is to have it hurried up so as not to spoil the evening.

For that Sabbath was a high day. The Sabbath of Passover week, especially solemn. John is flagging that this was no ordinary week’s end, the weekly Sabbath falling within the festival, which is why the pressure to have the bodies down was unusually strong, and why the burial that follows is done at such speed.

That their legs might be broken. Breaking the legs (crurifragium) with a heavy mallet sped death: the victim could no longer push up to breathe and suffocated quickly. Brutal mercy. Crucifixion killed slowly, by exhaustion and asphyxiation. A man could keep breathing only by pushing himself up on the nail through his feet, and every breath cost him that. It could take two days. Breaking the legs removed the ability to push up at all, and death followed soon after. It is the same irony as the governor’s doorstep (18:28), and it should be noted without being laboured. Men who would not enter a Gentile house in case it barred them from a meal are, that afternoon, arranging for the legs of living men to be shattered so that the evening’s observance is not spoiled.

So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other. Both criminals still lived. The soldiers work along the row. The first man’s legs are broken. The other one’s. And then they come to the middle cross.

What about the thief who believed? Luke tells us that one of these two men turned to Jesus and asked to be remembered when he came into his kingdom, and Jesus answered, truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:42–43). So one of the men whose legs were broken that afternoon died within the hour and went straight into the presence of Christ. He had no baptism, no record of good works, no time to make amends. He was saved by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and his broken legs could not keep him from paradise. There is no purgatory in that promise, only today, and with me.

In a sentence. Since it was the day of Preparation and the next Sabbath was a high day, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed, and the soldiers broke the legs of the two crucified with Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Even the timing of Jesus’ death and burial was bound up with God’s law and calendar. Nothing was random. When your days feel driven by deadlines and other people’s schedules, remember that the most important afternoon in history was hurried along by a religious calendar and a Roman mallet, and God was not hurried at all.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath died on the eve of the Sabbath, so that his body would rest in the tomb on the day God rested from his works. The law that cursed the hanged man was fulfilled in him, and the same law required that he be taken down before nightfall. And beside him, a dying thief with broken legs entered paradise that day on the strength of one request. Such is the grace of the crucified King: it reaches the man on the next cross, in his last hour.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.

When they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Jesus died quickly, after about six hours. Pilate was surprised (Mark 15:44). He had given up his spirit. Take the historical question first, because it is the one on which everything else rests: was he actually dead? The suggestion that he merely fainted and revived in the cool of the tomb has been made repeatedly since the eighteenth century, and it founders on this verse. The men at the foot of the cross were a professional execution squad. Killing people was their trade, and a soldier who let a condemned man off a cross alive would have answered for it with his own life. They looked at him and did not bother breaking his legs, which is the judgement of experts.

But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear. To make sure. The Roman soldier was trained to confirm death, and what came out settled it.

And at once there came out blood and water. Physically, this has been explained as blood and watery fluid from around the heart or lungs, proof that he was truly dead. Medical explanations vary, the separation of clot and serum after death, or fluid gathered round the heart or in the chest after the flogging and the strain, and no single account commands agreement. What is not in dispute is that this is what a corpse produces and a living man does not. This answers those who later claimed Jesus only appeared to die, or merely fainted.

Why John insists on it. By the time this Gospel was written, teachers were already circulating who held that the Christ could not really have suffered: that the divine had departed before the death, or that the body was only an appearance. John’s letters go after exactly that error: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (1 John 4:2–3). The blood and water are his answer, and he saw them come out. He is not making a devotional point first. He is a witness giving evidence about a body.

The sign in the wound. But John also sees a sign. Blood and water: the blood of atonement and the water of cleansing and life (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8). Many church fathers saw here the gospel’s two great gifts, forgiveness and the Spirit, and pictures of the Supper and baptism. That older reading is not to be dismissed, since John does write on more than one level; but the primary meaning is the plainer and harder one, the evidence of death. Zechariah 13:1 promised a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness. From the wounded side of the Lamb, it flows.

Does it matter whether Jesus really died? Everything depends on it. If he did not die, he did not bear the penalty of sin, which is death (Romans 6:23), and there was no resurrection, only a recovery. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17), and there is no resurrection without a death. The real death also means he has gone through what we will go through. He has tasted death for everyone who is his (Hebrews 2:9), and he knows the way out. When you stand at a deathbed, you are standing where he has been.

In a sentence. When they came to Jesus and found him already dead, they did not break his legs, but a soldier pierced his side with a spear, and blood and water flowed out at once.

On a Tuesday. When someone tells you the resurrection was a mistake or a swoon, do not be rattled. Ask them to read this chapter with you and notice who is giving evidence, and how carefully. And when you come to the Lord’s table or witness a baptism, remember the side from which blood and water flowed: these signs point to a real death, for real sins, by a real Saviour.

For worship. From his pierced side flowed blood to cleanse and water to give life. Come to the fountain. The spear that was meant to confirm his death opened the fountain the prophet had promised, and it has never been closed. Rock of Ages, cleft for me: the side of the Lamb was opened so that sinners could hide there, washed in the blood and given the living water of his Spirit.

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”

He who saw it has borne witness. His testimony is true. This verse is the author breaking cover, and it is worth noticing how unusual that is. John has written eighteen chapters without once stopping to vouch for himself. Here he stops the story and gives testimony, in the manner of a man swearing a statement: he who saw it has borne witness, his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth. John himself, the beloved disciple, standing at the cross (v. 26), insists he saw it. This is eyewitness testimony, sworn as in court (21:24). The doubling is deliberate and it is legal language: this is what I saw, I am telling the truth, and I know that I am. That is not the diction of piety. It is the diction of a witness. The Christian faith rests on historical events, seen and reported.

That you also may believe. The purpose of the whole Gospel (20:31). He is not recording the spear-thrust because it is moving. He is recording it because the reader’s faith depends on the man having actually died, and he was there.

Not one of his bones will be broken. The first of two fulfilments, and it is the one the whole Gospel has been building toward since John the Baptist pointed at him in chapter 1. The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12): it was to be roasted whole, eaten within the house, and not a bone of it broken. Every Passover for fourteen centuries, in every Jewish household, the lamb was handled under that rule. Psalm 34:20 says the same of the righteous sufferer: he keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken. Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood saves from judgment. Paul says: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

How the rule was kept. The soldiers had a routine and a schedule. They came along the row breaking legs, and at the middle cross they stopped, for the entirely practical reason that the man was already dead and there was no point. That is how the rule was kept. Not by anyone’s intention. A Roman work detail, hurrying to finish before sunset on the day of Preparation, left one body intact because there was nothing to be gained by damaging it, and in doing so handled the Lamb of God exactly as the law required.

Can I trust testimony written down decades later? Yes, for good reasons. John was there; he says so with unusual force, and he was writing while others who were there could still contradict him. The Gospels were written within the lifetime of eyewitnesses, as Luke says he consulted those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning (Luke 1:1–4), and Paul could appeal to more than five hundred who had seen the risen Christ, most of them still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). Ancient people remembered and passed on testimony carefully, and these witnesses gained nothing by it except hardship and, for many, death. And the Spirit who inspired the writing bears witness in the heart of the reader that it is true (1 John 5:6).

In a sentence. The eyewitness has given true testimony so that readers may believe, for these things fulfilled the Scripture that none of his bones would be broken.

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on a witness, not on a feeling. On a day when belief feels thin, go back to the testimony: read a Gospel account of the cross and resurrection as evidence, given by men who saw it. Then pass the testimony on. Someone near you may believe because you told them what was seen.

For worship. Behold the Lamb of God (1:29), his bones unbroken, his blood shed for you. For fourteen hundred years the Passover lambs were handled as the law required, and not one of them could take away sin. Then on a Friday afternoon Roman soldiers walked past the middle cross with their mallet lowered, and the Lamb to whom every lamb had pointed was kept whole in his death. God had written it, and God kept it. The witness saw, and wrote, so that we too might believe and have life in his name.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.” After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.

They will look on him whom they have pierced. From Zechariah 12:10, where the Lord says that the house of David and the people of Jerusalem will look on me, on him whom they have pierced, and mourn for him as for an only child. Notice: in Zechariah, it is the Lord himself who is pierced. It is one of the strangest sentences in the prophets, and John quotes it over a body with a spear-wound in its side. God was pierced at Golgotha. Some looked in mockery; many will look in repentance and faith (Revelation 1:7).

From looking to mourning to a fountain. The Zechariah passage is not about condemnation. What follows the looking is mourning, a whole land weeping, family by family, and then, in the next verse, a fountain opened to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1). The looking leads to grief and the grief to a fountain. That is the way every sinner comes to Christ: he looks at the one he pierced, grieves, and is washed.

Will Israel one day look on him and mourn? Christians differ on this, and the views should be stated fairly. Some believe Zechariah and Romans 11:25–27 point to a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, in which they will look on the one they pierced and mourn. Others understand all Israel to mean the whole number of God’s elect from Jews and Gentiles together, gathered through the age, and see the mourning fulfilled whenever Jews and Gentiles come to faith, from Pentecost onward (Acts 2:37). Both agree that John sees the prophecy beginning at the cross, that its full completion comes when every eye sees him at his return (Revelation 1:7), and that there is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: looking in faith to the pierced Christ.

Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council who had not agreed to its decision (Luke 23:50–51), and a rich man (Matthew 27:57). Fulfilling Isaiah 53:9: with a rich man in his death. John says he was a disciple secretly, for fear of the Jews, the same phrase used of the parents of the blind man and of the authorities who believed and would not say so (9:22; 12:42).

Asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus. A bold act. Mark says he took courage (Mark 15:43). The secret disciple comes into the open at the moment when following Jesus seemed most hopeless. The cross, which scattered the twelve, brought out the secret believers. And his timing is the point. Not during the trial, when a voice might have helped. Not while there was anything to gain. He goes to Pilate, with a private request to a Roman governor for the body of an executed rebel, which is not a small thing to be seen doing, at the exact moment when the movement seemed finished, the leader dead, and there was no possible advantage in being associated with any of it.

Courage at the costliest moment. That cuts against the way we usually rank courage. Joseph’s years of silence were real and this Gospel does not excuse them. But the moment he chose to break cover was the moment it cost most and profited least, and no one else in Jerusalem did it.

I have kept my faith quiet for years. Is it too late? No. Joseph kept silent too long, and when he finally came out, Christ received his gift. The Lord does not shame the timid who come; he welcomed Nicodemus by night and accepted Joseph’s tomb by day. But do not wait for the moment that costs most. Tell one person this week that you belong to Christ: a friend, a colleague, a family member. Ask to be baptised if you have not been, and join a church. Secret discipleship may begin in fear; it is not meant to stay there, and the cross is what draws it into the open.

In a sentence. Another Scripture says they will look on the one they pierced; afterwards Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple out of fear, asked Pilate for Jesus’ body, and with permission took it away.

On a Tuesday. If you have been a secret disciple, the cross calls you into the open. Take courage, like Joseph. And look today at the one who was pierced: read the account of the crucifixion slowly, and let it lead you where Zechariah says it leads, through grief over your sin to the fountain that cleanses it.

For worship. They will look on him whom they have pierced. The Lord of hosts promised it, and the one who was pierced was the Lord himself in human flesh. Every eye will see him one day, and for those who look in faith now, the sight that brings tears brings cleansing. The cross that drove the boldest disciples into hiding drew the most timid out of it. Such is the power of the pierced Christ: he makes cowards brave and mourners clean.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.

Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night. The man who came in the dark (3:2) now comes in the light. His journey from night to day is complete. John will not let the man be seen apart from that first visit, and the whole arc is now visible. He came in the dark, cautiously, with a compliment and a question, and was told he must be born again and could not follow it. He turned up again in chapter 7, in a council meeting, making a careful procedural point, does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing?, and was slapped down for it (7:50–51). And now he is here in daylight, in public, with a great weight of spices and his hands on a dead body.

A slow conversion. That is a slow conversion, and it is worth saying so for the reader who has been waiting a long time for somebody. It took Nicodemus years, and the visible steps were: a private conversation, one cautious question in a hostile room, and then everything at once at the worst possible moment. Keep praying for the Nicodemus you know.

A mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds, about 75 English pounds or 34 kilograms. An enormous amount, fit for a king’s burial (2 Chronicles 16:14): a load a man would struggle to carry, and worth a great deal of money. Ordinary burials used a fraction of it. Josephus records that five hundred servants carried spices at Herod the Great’s funeral, which is the register this belongs to. Nicodemus has brought a king’s burial to a criminal’s execution. Myrrh was a fragrant resin; aloes, a fragrant wood powder. They did not embalm the body, but covered and surrounded it with spices to honour it and mask the smell of decay.

So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices. Strips of linen wound around the body, with spices between. Compare Lazarus (11:44).

As is the burial custom of the Jews. Not Egyptian embalming, but Jewish burial. And it cost them more than spices. Handling a corpse made a Jew ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11). Both these men, on the eve of the great feast, disqualified themselves from it in order to bury him. They would spend the Passover unclean. They had missed nothing. The Lamb was already dead.

Does it matter how Christians bury their dead? Scripture does not lay down a law about burial or cremation, and the resurrection does not depend on what happens to the body; God who made it from dust can raise it from ashes or the sea (Revelation 20:13). But burial has long been the Christian custom, following the burial of Christ and the patriarchs, because it treats the body with honour as something that belongs to the Lord and will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Whatever your family chooses, do it with reverence and hope, not as disposal. The body you lay to rest is a seed, not rubbish.

In a sentence. Nicodemus, who had once come by night, brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, and they wrapped Jesus’ body in linen with the spices, according to Jewish custom.

On a Tuesday. Two rich men gave a king’s burial to the crucified King. Give him your best, too. Not your leftovers of time and money, but something costly, given when it looks as though it will gain you nothing. And if you are waiting for a slow-moving friend or relative, do not give up. Nicodemus took years.

For worship. The man who came by night to ask about new birth came in daylight to bury the one who gives it. Seventy-five pounds of spices, a fortune poured out on a corpse: they thought they were honouring a dead king, and they were preparing the body that would rise in three days and need none of it. Christ is worthy of every extravagance love can give, and none of it is wasted, even when it seems too late.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds — a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.

Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. Another garden. John has told us there was a garden once already in this passion, in the first verse of chapter 18, and he is the only evangelist who uses the word in either place. Now he closes the bracket. A garden at the beginning, where he was taken. A garden at the end, where he is laid. Eden was lost in a garden; the King is buried in one; and in this garden he will rise, and Mary will think him the gardener (20:15), which is either John’s finest touch or nobody’s, and he does not explain it. The new creation begins in a garden.

And in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own tomb, cut in the rock (Matthew 27:60). “New”: no other body there, so there could be no confusion about whose body was missing on Sunday. Two details in the tomb matter and both are evidential. It was new, and no one had been laid in it, which closes off the suggestion that the wrong body was found missing. And it belonged to Joseph, which means a wealthy man gave away the grave he had cut for his own family.

With a rich man in his death. Isaiah, describing the Servant, had said something that made no sense as a prediction: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9). Both halves came true within hours, and by opposite means: the state put him between two criminals, and a private citizen put him in a rich man’s tomb.

So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there. Time was short before the Sabbath began at sunset. The tomb was near. The last clause is very flat. They chose it because it was near and the light was going. There is no ceremony in the sentence, no reflection, no farewell. Two men who had been afraid of being seen with him work quickly against a deadline, put a body in a borrowed grave, and go home. And that is where the chapter stops. John does not close it with a promise or a hint. He leaves the reader at a sealed tomb on a Friday evening, which is exactly where everybody who loved him was left.

Why the burial matters. “He was buried” is part of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:4). It proves he truly died. And his burial sanctifies the graves of his people: he has lain where we will lie, and has come out.

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in Joseph’s tomb; his human soul went to his Father. He had said to the thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not sleep unconscious, and he did not go to a place of further suffering; his suffering was finished on the cross. When the Apostles’ Creed says he descended into hell, Reformed Christians have understood it of the hellish agonies he endured on the cross (Heidelberg Catechism, question 44) and of his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism, question 50). The same is true for believers: at death the body rests in the grave, while the soul goes at once to be with Christ, awaiting the resurrection (Philippians 1:23; Westminster 32.1).

In a sentence. In a garden near the place of crucifixion there was a new tomb where no one had been laid, and because of the day of Preparation and since it was close, they laid Jesus there.

On a Tuesday. When you stand at a believer’s grave, remember the garden tomb. Christ has been there, and it could not hold him. And on the days that feel like Friday evening, when everything you hoped for seems sealed behind a stone, remember that John left his readers there too, and that Sunday was already coming.

For worship. The Lord of life lay in a borrowed grave in a garden, wrapped in linen and spices by two frightened men, and the stone was rolled across the door. The one who had said, I am the resurrection and the life, was silent among the dead. But he had gone into the grave as a conqueror goes into an enemy’s fortress, and he had gone there for us. Every Christian grave since has been a garden plot, because his was first. He has lain where we will lie, and the tomb could not keep him.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death

Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!”<sup>6</sup>When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”<sup>7</sup>The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.”<sup>8</sup>When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.<sup>9</sup>He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.<sup>10</sup>So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”<sup>11</sup>Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.”<sup>12</sup>From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”<sup>13</sup>So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha.<sup>14</sup>Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your King!”<sup>15</sup>They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”<sup>16</sup>So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,<sup>17</sup>and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.<sup>18</sup>There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.<sup>19</sup>Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”<sup>20</sup>Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.<sup>21</sup>So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ’The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ’This man said, I am King of the Jews.’”<sup>22</sup>Pilate answered, “What I have written I have written.”<sup>23</sup>When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,<sup>24</sup>so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things,<sup>25</sup>but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.<sup>26</sup>When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.<sup>28</sup>After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”<sup>29</sup>A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth.<sup>30</sup>When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.<sup>31</sup>Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.<sup>32</sup>So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.<sup>33</sup>But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.<sup>34</sup>But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.<sup>35</sup>He who saw it has borne witness— his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth— that you also may believe.<sup>36</sup>For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”<sup>37</sup>And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.”<sup>38</sup>After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.<sup>39</sup>Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.<sup>40</sup>So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.<sup>41</sup>Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.<sup>42</sup>So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
19.overview:
John tells the crucifixion as the hour of Jesus’ glory and the fulfilment of Scripture. Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe.
