Pilate presents him to the crowd, “Behold the man!”, three times declares him innocent, and tries to release him; but when the leaders accuse Jesus of claiming to be Son of God, and threaten Pilate that releasing a rival king is disloyalty to Caesar, the governor gives way. At noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being slaughtered, Pilate hands him over, and the chief priests declare, “We have no king but Caesar.” Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others under a sign in Aramaic, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”

From the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple. Knowing that all was now finished, he says, “I thirst,” and receiving sour wine, says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. To hasten death before the Sabbath, the soldiers break the legs of the others, but finding Jesus already dead they pierce his side, and blood and water flow out. John, the eyewitness, insists that his testimony is true, and that these things fulfilled Scripture: not a bone of the Passover lamb was broken, and they will look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, secret disciples until now, bury him with a king’s quantity of spices in a new tomb in a garden. The work God gave him to do is complete.

20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before dawn on Sunday Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, fearing the body has been stolen. Racing to the tomb, they find the grave-clothes lying in place and the head cloth folded apart; the beloved disciple sees and believes, though they do not yet understand the Scriptures. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, and then Jesus, whom she mistakes for the gardener until he speaks her name. He tells her not to cling to him but to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and theirs, his God and theirs. She brings the disciples the news: she has seen the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John are structured around recognition: the beloved disciple sees and believes from the evidence of the linen cloths; Mary recognizes Jesus when he calls her name (the Good Shepherd and the sheep who knows his voice, 10:3); Thomas recognizes Jesus when invited to touch the wounds. Each recognition is different, calibrated to each person's need and capacity. This is the risen Lord — the same person, now transformed, who meets each disciple where they are.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection, commissioned by the risen Lord to tell the disciples: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. The announcement is simultaneously personal (my Father) and covenantal (your Father) — the resurrection makes the disciples' relationship to the Father the same as Jesus' own. The first gospel proclamation after the resurrection is spoken by a woman who was weeping at a tomb and heard her name called by the one she thought was dead. This is how the gospel always comes: to those who have not ceased to love the crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”

Meaning first. John 20 tells of the resurrection: the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meeting Mary, the disciples, and Thomas. Each meeting moves from grief, fear or doubt to faith and joy. The chapter ends with the Gospel’s purpose: these things are written so that you may believe. The resurrection is not a myth or a feeling; it is a historical event, attested by witnesses, which changes everything. John left us at the end of chapter 19 beside a sealed tomb on a Friday evening, where everybody who loved Jesus was left. Now the first day of the week dawns.

Now on the first day of the week. The first day of the week is Sunday. In Greek it is literally day one of the week, the ordinary idiom, but with an echo worth hearing. John opened this Gospel with in the beginning, deliberately echoing Genesis. Now, after a Friday of finishing and a Sabbath of rest, comes the first day. From then on, Christians gathered on the first day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). The day of resurrection became the day of worship. It is the first day of the new creation.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? The day of resurrection became the church’s day of gathering (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and John calls it the Lord’s day (Revelation 1:10). Christians who love the Scriptures hold two main views. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession (Westminster 21.7–8) and the 1689 Baptist Confession, regard the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath, the fourth commandment’s weekly day of rest and worship moved to the day of resurrection. Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), and see Sunday gathering as a glad privilege rather than a sabbath law. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest, and the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday; no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). Both agree that Christians should gather with the church each Lord’s Day, and should rest in Christ’s finished work.

Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark. The other Gospels mention other women too (Mark 16:1); her “we” in v. 2 shows she was not alone. Darkness outside, and in her heart. While it was still dark sits beside Mark’s when the sun had risen (Mark 16:2), and anyone who has set out early knows both are true of the same walk. She left in the dark and arrived as it was getting light.

And saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. Not rolled away so that Jesus could get out, but so that the witnesses could get in. The stone is not the beginning of the resurrection but the announcement that it has already happened.

They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him. Her first thought: grave robbers, or the authorities. Resurrection does not cross her mind. Her interpretation is wrong, and it is the sensible one. A tomb that was sealed on Friday is open on Sunday, and the obvious inference is that somebody has moved the body. It takes nothing away from her that she reached for the ordinary explanation; every one of us would have. The witnesses did not expect it, which makes their testimony more believable: they were not people who saw what they wanted to see.

The we that was left standing. There is a detail in Mary’s sentence that quietly confirms the other Gospels. John names only Mary Magdalene. Matthew has her with the other Mary; Mark adds Salome; Luke speaks of the women who had come from Galilee. A sceptical reader might call that a discrepancy. And then Mary opens her mouth: we do not know. We. John has written the whole scene around one woman and left the plural pronoun standing in her speech, which is exactly what happens when somebody reports a conversation accurately without tidying it. He tells the story through Mary because she is the one who matters for what follows; he has not troubled to remove the evidence that she was not alone. That is the mark of a man writing down what he remembers being said.

She ran to Peter. And her report has one more thing worth registering. She runs to Peter, the man who denied him, whom the others might reasonably have written off, and to the beloved disciple, and she treats them as the people to be told. Nobody in the account has excluded Peter from anything.

In a sentence. Early on Sunday, while still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, found the stone removed, and ran to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that someone had taken the Lord’s body.

On a Tuesday. Every Sunday is a small Easter. Prepare for it on Saturday: get to bed, plan to arrive early, come expecting to meet the risen Lord with his people. And on the dark mornings of your own life, when the obvious explanation is the worst one, remember that the first witnesses also reached for the sensible conclusion, and were wrong in the best possible way.

For worship. Every Lord’s Day celebrates this morning. Gather with joy. On the first day of the week God said, let there be light, and on the first day of the week the Light of the world came out of the dark tomb. The stone was moved, not to let him out, but to let us in to see. Every gathering of his people on the first day is a declaration to the world that the grave is empty and the new creation has begun.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.

So Peter went out with the other disciple. Peter, despite his denials, is still with the disciples, and runs. Two grown men sprinting through Jerusalem at first light on the strength of a report neither of them believed, because Mary’s message was that the body had been stolen, and that is what they were running to investigate. Whatever they expected to find, it was not what they found.

The other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. A vivid, almost humorous eyewitness detail, probably because John was younger. An invented story would have no reason to include it. John mentions it twice, here and again at verse 8. Whether it is the pride of a younger man remembering that he could outrun Peter, or simply the accuracy of somebody reporting the order in which people arrived, cannot be settled and does not matter much.

The pair. These two men appear together again and again in these chapters: at the supper (13:23–24), in the courtyard (18:15–16), at the tomb, and on the shore in the next chapter. John and Peter are consistently placed side by side, the one who sees and the one who acts, and the opening chapters of Acts have them still together, going up to the temple at the hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). Love arrives first; courage goes in first. The church has always needed both.

Why would the Gospel record such small details? Because they are the kind of things eyewitnesses remember and inventors leave out. Who ran faster, who stooped and who went in, how the cloths lay: none of these serves a theological purpose, and some of them do the disciples no credit. A man constructing a legend would not have built it around the testimony of a woman and then had two men arrive, look, and go home. The story does nothing to make its witnesses impressive. These small, unpolished details are part of why historians who are not believers still take the Gospels seriously as testimony.

In a sentence. Peter and the other disciple ran together to the tomb, and the other disciple outran Peter and got there first.

On a Tuesday. Run to Christ, whatever your past failures. Peter did. He had more reason than anyone to stay away from news about Jesus, and he ran. If you have been avoiding church, prayer or a Christian friend because of something you are ashamed of, go today.

For worship. The man who had denied his Lord three times ran to his tomb on the first report that something had happened. Grace had not let go of him, though he did not yet know it. The risen Christ draws his people to himself before they understand what has happened: the young and the old, the quick and the slow, the one who loved and the one who failed, all running toward the place where death had been undone.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,

Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there. Tomb entrances were low; the beloved disciple has to stoop to look in, which fits the rock-cut tombs of the period, with an opening a man had to bend to enter. “Lying” (keimena): lying flat, in place. Not thrown, not scattered, not gathered up.

But he did not go in. Perhaps from awe, or reluctance to defile himself.

Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. Peter, characteristically, goes straight in. Peter, who had denied his Lord a few days earlier and had every reason to hang back, walked past his friend into a grave. Neither is criticised, and John records the hesitation as his own.

He saw the linen cloths lying there. “Saw” (theōrei): looked carefully, studied. John describes the seeing in stages. At verse 5 the beloved disciple stoops and catches sight of the cloths. At verse 6 Peter goes in and takes stock. At verse 8 the other disciple goes in, and saw and believed. A glance, then a study, then an understanding: what happened in that small space over perhaps a minute, told by a man who was there.

What they were looking at. The position of the cloths is the thing. Grave robbers do not undress a body; the wrappings and the spices were worth more than the corpse, and anybody stealing it would have carried the whole bundle out. What these men are staring at is a set of grave clothes still lying where a body had been. Two Greek words are used for the burial wrappings in these verses, and they are not the same thing. The othonia are the linen strips that bound the body; the soudarion of the next verse is the cloth that covered the face and was tied round the head. John distinguishes them because their positions were different, and their positions are the whole point of what he is describing.

In a sentence. The other disciple bent down and saw the linen cloths but did not go in; then Peter arrived, went in, and saw the cloths lying there.

On a Tuesday. Faith in Christ is not a refusal to look; it is a willingness to look carefully. If you have doubts, do what these men did: go in, and study the evidence. Read a careful book on the resurrection, or simply read the four accounts side by side and ask what best explains them.

For worship. Look carefully at the evidence. It points to a risen Lord. The linen that had wrapped the dead body of the Son of God lay undisturbed in an empty grave. Death had been unwrapped from him without a struggle. He who said I lay down my life that I may take it up again had taken it up, quietly, before dawn, and left the evidence where his friends would find it.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

And the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the costly linen and spices; they would have taken everything, or the body wrapped. And they would not have folded the face cloth. The orderly state of the grave clothes shows that the body was not stolen. Some take “folded” (entetuligmenon) to mean rolled up, keeping its shape where the head had been. Either way, it looked as if the body had simply passed out of the wrappings. Compare Lazarus, who came out still bound (11:44). Lazarus came back to a life that would end again, and needed to be untied. Jesus came out of death for ever, and left the wrappings behind.

A story to set aside. A guard is needed here, because a sermon illustration about this verse circulates widely and it is not true. The story goes that a Jewish servant, clearing a master’s table, would leave the napkin crumpled if the meal was over and fold it neatly if he intended to return, so the folded face cloth is Jesus saying I am coming back. It is a lovely idea with one defect: there is no evidence for any such custom in any ancient source, and the word here is not about table linen at all. A face cloth is exactly that, used at burials. The story appears to be a modern invention, and the verse is strong enough not to need it.

Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed. The first to believe in the resurrection, before he had seen the risen Lord. What he saw convinced him: not an angel, not Jesus himself, but the empty grave clothes. He believed Jesus had risen. John writes the sentence about himself, in the third person, with no elaboration. Notice what he had at that moment. No angel had spoken to him. He had not seen the risen Lord and would not for another twelve hours. Nobody had explained anything, and the next verse says outright that he still did not understand the Scripture about the resurrection. What he had was an empty tomb and the way the linen was lying. That was enough. Blessed are those who have not seen (v. 29).

What about the other explanations? Every alternative has been tried, and each fails at a known point. The disciples stole the body: then they died for what they knew was a lie, and the grave clothes would not have been left. The authorities moved it: then they would have produced it when the apostles began preaching in Jerusalem weeks later. The women went to the wrong tomb: then the authorities would only have needed to show the right one. Jesus only fainted: Roman soldiers knew death, and a half-dead man could not have convinced anyone he had conquered it. The disciples hallucinated: hallucinations do not happen to groups, and they do not empty tombs. The only explanation that fits the empty tomb, the appearances, and the transformation of frightened men into bold witnesses is the one they gave: he is risen.

In a sentence. They saw the face cloth folded up by itself apart from the linen, and the other disciple went in, saw, and believed.

On a Tuesday. The empty tomb is a fact of history that no rival explanation has ever accounted for. Let it strengthen your faith. And when you share your faith, start where John started: not with your feelings, but with what happened. Christianity stands or falls on an event, and you are allowed to point to the evidence.

For worship. The grave clothes lay in order, and the face cloth by itself, because the one who had been wrapped in them did not need to fight his way out. Death had no hold on him. The beloved disciple stood in the empty tomb and believed, and every believer since has stood in the same place by faith: looking at a grave that could not keep the Lord of life, and knowing that it will not keep us either.
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.

For as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. They believed because of what they saw, not yet because of Scripture. The admission is remarkable for its candour, and it is worth asking why a writer would include it. Not they had forgotten. They had never grasped it, and Jesus had told them plainly and repeatedly that he would be killed and rise on the third day. Later, they understood that the Old Testament foretold it (Psalm 16:10; Isaiah 53:10–12; Luke 24:25–27, 44–46; Acts 2:24–32; 1 Corinthians 15:4). “Must” (dei): it was necessary, part of God’s plan.

Which Scriptures? The apostles later point to Psalm 16: you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption, and Peter builds his Pentecost sermon on it (Acts 2:25–31). Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4). Hosea has a third day (Hosea 6:2), Jonah has three days, and Isaiah 53 has a servant who is cut off and then shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10). It was all there. It had been there for centuries, and none of them had put it together, and one of them is writing this sentence about himself decades later without any attempt to look better.

Then the disciples went back to their homes. Probably where they were staying in Jerusalem. It is the flattest verse in the resurrection narrative. One of them has just believed something, and there is no announcement and no gathering and no prayer meeting. Two men look at the most important physical evidence in history and walk back to where they are staying. That is so unlike how a legend would be written, and so exactly like people. And it means that the first person actually to meet the risen Christ is the one who stayed.

How should I read the Old Testament, then? With Christ at the centre, as Jesus himself taught. On the road to Emmaus he began with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). That does not mean every verse is a hidden riddle about Jesus. It means the whole story is moving toward him: the promises to Abraham, the sacrifices, the kings, the psalms of suffering and vindication, the prophets’ hope. As you read, ask: what does this show me of the God who would send his Son? What problem is crying out for Christ to solve? Where does this promise land in him? Read it that way and the Old Testament will open to you as it opened to them.

In a sentence. They did not yet understand from Scripture that he must rise from the dead, and the disciples went back home.

On a Tuesday. Choose one of the passages the apostles used, Psalm 16, Isaiah 53, or Hosea 6, and read it this week with the empty tomb in mind. Then thank God that he wrote the resurrection into his word long before it happened, so that your faith rests not on a surprise but on a promise kept.

For worship. The resurrection was not plan B. It was written. Read the Scriptures with the risen Christ in view. The God who promised that his Holy One would not see corruption kept his word to the letter on the third day. He had been writing toward this morning since the first promise in the garden of Eden, and his slow, forgetful disciples were given the joy of discovering, too late to have helped and just in time to believe, that every word had been true.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.

But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb. The disciples leave; Mary stays. Her love keeps her at the grave. The but is doing all the work. The men have gone home; she has not. She had walked there in the dark, run to fetch them, walked back, and now stands outside a tomb that everyone else has finished with. And there is nothing constructive in what she is doing. She has no plan. She is not waiting for anything, because as far as she knows the body has been stolen, and the last service left to her, anointing it properly, has been taken away too. She is simply unable to leave.

The one who could not go home. That is worth saying plainly to anyone whose grief has outlasted everybody else’s patience with it. This is the person the risen Christ appears to first. Not the one who reasoned correctly from the evidence, not the one who went in first, and not the eleven. The one who could not go home.

She stooped to look into the tomb. The same verb used of the beloved disciple in verse 5, and it is a second look at a space two men have already searched. Grief does that too: it checks again.

She saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet. This time there is something there. And they are sitting: not standing guard, not blazing, not announcing. The most extraordinary beings in the account are described as sitting quietly in an empty grave, and Mary does not seem to realise they are angels. She is not frightened by them and does not remark on them at all. She answers their question as though they were attendants, and then turns away. Her grief is large enough that two angels do not register.

The mercy seat. One at the head and one at the feet, with an empty space between them where a body had lain. Like the two cherubim at either end of the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22), where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. Two cherubim of gold, one at each end, overshadowing the lid of the ark, with the space between them the place where God said he would meet with his people. John does not say so, but the picture is hard to miss. The place where Jesus lay is the true mercy seat (Romans 3:25). The Most Holy Place had been behind a curtain, entered once a year, with blood. This one has a woman crying at the entrance and, as the other Gospels record, the curtain torn (Matthew 27:51).

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve so deeply? No. Mary wept at the tomb, Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35), and nobody in this scene tells her to stop. Paul does not forbid Christians to grieve; he says we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christian grief is real grief, sometimes long and heavy, held in the hands of a risen Lord. If your sorrow has outlasted other people’s patience, do not be ashamed of it. Bring it to him, stay near him, and keep coming back to the place where he has met you before. He came first to the one who could not stop weeping.

In a sentence. Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and stooping to look in, saw two angels in white sitting where Jesus’ body had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.

On a Tuesday. Mary stayed when others left. Love lingers. Linger near Christ. And look around your church for the one who is still grieving after everyone else has moved on: the widow a year later, the parents after a miscarriage, the friend whose loss nobody mentions now. Sit with them. Say the name of the one they lost.

For worship. The place where the Lord’s body had lain became the mercy seat, guarded by angels, with nothing on it but the evidence of an accepted sacrifice. And the God who meets sinners there met first a weeping woman who could not go home. He is still the God of the mercy seat: the place where wrath has been turned away is the place where mourners are met.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Woman, why are you weeping? A gentle question. There is no need to weep. The angels ask her the same question Jesus will ask a moment later, and it is not an accusation in either mouth. It is the question that gets somebody to say aloud what is wrong. Nobody in this scene tells her to stop crying. Two angels and the risen Son of God, and not one of them says she should not be upset. They ask her why.

They have taken away my Lord. “My Lord”: personal, devoted. She still thinks of a dead body. Her answer has one word in it that was not there before. At verse 2 she said they have taken the Lord. Here she says my Lord. The public title has become a personal one. She is not making a theological statement; she is a woman explaining, to someone who has asked, why she cannot stop crying.

She turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. He was behind her. He had been there, for how long John does not say, while she was bent over an empty grave describing his disappearance to two angels. The risen Jesus was not always recognised at first (Luke 24:16; John 21:4). His resurrection body was the same body, with its wounds (v. 20), but transformed. And her eyes were full of tears, and she was not expecting him. Grief had already settled the range of possibilities, and a man standing in a garden at dawn could be one of several things, none of which was the man she had watched die. She was a few feet from the answer to her weeping and could not see it, and there was nothing blameworthy in that at all.

Will we recognise one another in the resurrection? Yes. The risen Jesus was recognised in the end by those who knew him: Mary knew his voice, the disciples knew his wounds, the Emmaus pair knew him at the breaking of bread. He was the same person in a glorified body. Paul expects to see his converts in the presence of Christ as his crown and joy (1 Thessalonians 2:19), and the comfort he gives the bereaved is that we shall be with them and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will not be strangers in the new creation. We will know as we are known (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the faces we loved will be there, made new.

In a sentence. The angels asked why she was weeping, and she said someone had taken her Lord, and then she turned and saw Jesus standing there, but did not recognise him.

On a Tuesday. When you are overwhelmed, it can be hard to see what God is doing. Ask him today: Lord, where are you standing in this? Look back over a hard season you have come through, and see where he was present though you did not recognise him at the time. Write it down, so that you remember next time.

For worship. Sometimes Jesus is standing beside us in our grief, and we do not recognise him. Look again. The risen Lord did not appear first to the powerful or the clever, but stood behind a weeping woman in a garden and waited for her to turn round. He is not offended by our blindness in sorrow. He asks us why we weep, and then he shows us himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).

Whom are you seeking? The question of 1:38 and 18:4. Not what, but whom. His first words to her are a question he has asked at the moments that matter in this book. He asked the first two disciples who followed him in chapter 1 what they were seeking, and he asked the arresting party in the garden, twice (18:4, 7). Now, in another garden, at the end, he asks it of a weeping woman. The whole Gospel is bracketed by that question, and it has always been aimed past the person answering it.

Supposing him to be the gardener. An understandable mistake, and a profound one. He is the gardener of the new creation, the second Adam in the garden (19:41). The first Adam was put in a garden to work it and keep it, and lost it. The last Adam stands in a garden at dawn on the first day of the new creation, and a woman mistakes him for the man who tends it. She is more right than she knows.

Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. Love that does not calculate. How would she carry a body wrapped in seventy-five pounds of spices? It is one of the most touching sentences in Scripture, because of what it takes for granted. She is proposing to collect a grown man’s body, dead two days, and carry it off herself. She has no plan for where to put it and no means of moving it. Love has produced an offer that makes no practical sense, and she makes it to a stranger without embarrassment.

Mary. Then one word, her name. Not an explanation. Not it is I. Not a rebuke for failing to recognise him, and no reference to the resurrection at all. He says her name, and she is turned round in an instant. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice (10:3–4). He had said that in a temple colonnade in winter. This is that sentence happening.

She turned and said to him in Aramaic, Rabboni! “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful form of “rabbi.” John keeps the word rather than translating it away. She uses the name she always used, because the man in front of her is the same man, and there is not yet a vocabulary for what has happened. She does not yet grasp all that he now is.

The first word of a risen voice. Consider what it took to reach that moment. The one who says her name has been dead. He has come out of death, walked into a garden at first light, and stood behind a woman who was crying for him. And the first thing he does with a resurrected voice, before any announcement, before the eleven, before anything, is say the name of one grieving person.

Does the risen Jesus really know me personally? Yes. He knows his sheep by name (10:3, 14), and his knowledge of you is not general but particular: your history, your sins, your griefs, the things you have never told anyone. The Father gave you to him by name before the world began (17:6), and he laid down his life for you by name. He calls you now through his word, and the Spirit makes that call personal in your heart, so that you know the voice is for you (10:27). You may feel forgotten in a crowd of eight billion. You are not forgotten by him.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why she wept and whom she sought, and thinking he was the gardener, she asked where he had put the body; then Jesus said her name, “Mary,” and she turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!”

On a Tuesday. Read 10:1–5 and 10:27–29 aloud, and put your own name where it fits: he calls me by name; I know his voice; no one will snatch me out of his hand. Then listen in Scripture today for his voice, not just for information. And when you speak to someone in grief, use their name. It may be the kindest thing you say.

For worship. The risen Lord knows your name. He calls you by it. Death could not make him forget one of his sheep, and the first word from his risen lips was a name. The Gardener of the new creation stood in the garden where they buried him and called a sinner out of her sorrow with a single word. One day he will call all his people by name out of their graves (5:28–29), and every one of them will turn and know his voice.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” — and that he had said these things to her.

Do not cling to me. “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume. She has grabbed hold of him, as if never to let go. Not “do not touch me” (the old translation), but “stop holding on to me.” The old Latin rendering, Noli me tangere, has produced a great many paintings of a recoiling Christ and a rebuked woman, and it misleads. The Greek is a present imperative, and with this verb it means: stop doing what you are already doing. She is not being kept at a distance. She has hold of him (Matthew records the other women taking hold of his feet, Matthew 28:9), and the instruction is to let go. Which is a completely different sentence. Not do not come near me, but you cannot keep me here. He has not come back to the old life in Galilee. A new relationship is coming, by the Spirit, after he ascends.

For I have not yet ascended to the Father. He is on his way. There will be time with him; but there is a task now. And a week later Jesus invites Thomas, Put your finger here (v. 27), so this is no ban on touching. I have not yet ascended means that Mary should not hold on as if the old way of being with him had simply returned. He is going to the Father, and from there he will be with them in a new way, by the Spirit (16:7).

But go to my brothers. “My brothers”: for the first time, Jesus calls his disciples brothers. After the cross, they are members of his family, children of his Father (Hebrews 2:11–12). At supper, three nights earlier, he had raised them from servants to friends (15:15), and that was already extraordinary. Now, after every one of them has run away, and one has denied him three times to strangers, he calls them his brothers. The first thing he does with a resurrected body is raise the standing of the men who abandoned him.

I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. Notice: not our Father, but my Father and your Father. His sonship is unique and eternal; theirs is by adoption, through him. And yet he shares his Father with them. The cross has made it possible. He does not once, anywhere in the Gospels, include himself with the disciples in a single our Father; even when teaching them to pray it, he gives it to them to say. His sonship and theirs are joined in one sentence and are not the same thing: he is Son by nature, they by grace. The two halves of the phrase keep both.

Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, I have seen the Lord. The first witness to the risen Christ was a woman, at a time when women’s testimony was not readily accepted in Jewish courts. No one inventing a story would have chosen her. She is sometimes called the apostle to the apostles. And her message is the simplest and fullest resurrection proclamation there is: personal, direct, certain. I have seen the Lord.

Does Mary’s witness mean women should be pastors? Mary was the first to announce the resurrection, and her witness was honoured by Christ himself. Every Christian, man or woman, is called to say what she said: I have seen the Lord, and this is what he told me. Women prayed, prophesied and laboured in the gospel throughout the New Testament (Acts 1:14; Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3). But Mary was sent with a message to the apostles, not appointed one of them, and the New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). That is not a judgment on women’s gifts or worth; Christ entrusted the greatest news ever told to a woman first. It is the pattern of ordered service he gave his church.

What does it mean that God is my Father because he is Christ’s Father? It means your standing with God is not a lesser copy of a relationship, but a share in the real one. By nature the Son alone is the Father’s child. But by adoption, through faith in Christ, the Father receives you as his son or daughter, with the Spirit in your heart crying Abba (Galatians 4:4–7). You approach him not as a servant hoping for wages but as a child at home. He knows what you need before you ask (Matthew 6:8), disciplines you because he loves you (Hebrews 12:6), and has given you an inheritance with his Son (Romans 8:17). The risen Christ came out of the tomb and called the Father yours.

In a sentence. Jesus told Mary to stop clinging to him, since he had not yet ascended, but to tell his brothers that he was ascending to his Father and theirs, his God and theirs, and Mary went and told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord.”

On a Tuesday. God is your Father because he is Christ’s Father. Go and tell someone: I have seen the Lord. And when you pray today, begin with the word Jesus gave you, Father, and remember that the risen Son himself put it in your mouth.

For worship. The risen Christ called deserters his brothers and gave them his own Father. Before he ascended to glory, he sent word to the men who had abandoned him that they were family, and that his God was now their God. The Son by nature has made us sons by grace. And the news of it was carried first by a weeping woman turned witness, running through the streets of Jerusalem with the best words ever spoken: I have seen the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That Sunday evening, with the doors locked for fear of the authorities, Jesus comes and stands among the disciples, greets them with peace, and shows them his hands and side, and they rejoice. He sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit; whoever’s sins they forgive are forgiven, and whoever’s they retain are retained. Thomas, absent, refuses to believe unless he touches the wounds. Eight days later Jesus comes again through locked doors and invites Thomas to touch and believe. Thomas responds, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing. Jesus did many other signs, John says, but these are written so that readers may believe he is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
verseByVerse.theology: Peace be with you (vv. 19, 21, 26): three times in this section Jesus speaks this word. The resurrection peace is not the absence of the disciples' fear but the presence of the risen Lord. He shows them his hands and his side — the wounds are still present, the marks of the passion carried into the resurrection body. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates it, glorifies it, makes it permanently the ground of peace. The scars of Jesus in his resurrection body are the permanent declaration that the atonement is real and its benefits are everlasting.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29): the beatitude of all post-apostolic faith. Every Christian since the first generation believes on the basis of testimony rather than sight — on the word of those who were there, preserved in the Scripture the Spirit inspired, applied by the Spirit who illuminates. Thomas's faith required the visible wounds; blessed are those who trust the testimony about the wounds. This is where the fourth gospel places us: in the company of the blessed who believe without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.” When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.

On the evening of that day, the first day of the week. Easter Sunday evening. Everything in these verses is worth slowing down for, because it is the reunion and John reports it in two verses.

The doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews. Frightened men behind locked doors, expecting arrest. That is where the church is on the evening of Easter Sunday: a room with the door bolted, containing men who have heard from Mary that she has seen the Lord and have made no visible use of the information. Luke says plainly that the women’s words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them (Luke 24:11). The contrast with the boldness of the coming months is the measure of what the risen Christ and his Spirit will do with them.

Jesus came and stood among them. Locked doors do not stop him. His resurrection body is real, physical, but not limited as ours are (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). John does not explain it and neither should anyone else. There is no suggestion of a door opening.

Peace be with you. “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom, the thing anyone said on entering a house. But from the risen Lord, to the men who deserted him, it is far more. Not a rebuke, but peace: the peace he promised (14:27; 16:33), now won by the cross (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17). He does not begin with a rebuke, or an explanation, or I told you so, all three of which were available and deserved. He greets them.

He showed them his hands and his side. Proof: the same Jesus, the one who was crucified. And it is worth asking why he had them to show. Nothing required a resurrection body to be marked. This is a body that can enter a locked room. And yet the wounds are there, and he displays them deliberately, and in eight days he will invite a man to put his hand into one. The marks were kept on purpose. The one piece of the old world carried out of the grave into the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. His wounds remain in his glorified body, the eternal marks of his love (Revelation 5:6).

Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. Sorrow turned to joy, as he promised (16:20–22). It is a plain word: they were glad. He had promised it three nights earlier: you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy; I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you. Three days. The sorrow arrived exactly as described and so did the joy, and the man who predicted both was standing in the room.

What will our resurrection bodies be like? Like his. Paul says Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21), and John says we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). His risen body was truly physical: he could be touched, he ate fish (Luke 24:42–43), he bore the marks of his history. Yet it was no longer subject to weakness, decay or death, and it was not hindered as ours are now. It is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The same you, made whole and glorious, with nothing lost that was truly yours and nothing left that sin had spoiled.

In a sentence. That Sunday evening, with the doors locked for fear, Jesus came and stood among the disciples and said, “Peace be with you,” showed them his hands and side, and they were glad to see the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Behind which locked door are you hiding this week: fear of a diagnosis, of a person, of the future, of being found out? Read these verses there. The risen Christ comes through locked doors with peace, and he shows his wounds as the proof that you are safe with him. Then unlock one door: tell a trusted friend what you are afraid of, and pray together.

For worship. The risen Christ comes to his frightened people with peace, and shows his wounds. Rejoice. He did not come to the men who had fled with accusation but with shalom, and the hands he showed them were the hands that had been pierced for their sin. In heaven he still bears those marks. The Lamb standing as though slain is the King on the throne (Revelation 5:6), and his wounds are the everlasting guarantee that his people’s peace has been paid for.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom — now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.” And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

Peace be with you. Again: peace for them, and now peace for their mission.

As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you. John’s Great Commission. The Son’s mission becomes the church’s mission (17:18). Sent as he was sent: to make the Father known, to serve, to suffer, and to bring people to God. And the comparison is the largest ever made about the church’s work. Not in the same general spirit. As. The pattern for how Christians are sent into the world is how the Son was sent into it, which meant coming all the way in, at their level, at his own cost, and remaining available to people who did not want him. And he says it while showing them the marks.

And when he had said this, he breathed on them. The verb (emphysaō) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and it is one of the most deliberate word-choices in the Gospel. Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the same Greek verb in the Greek Old Testament: the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. And it recalls Ezekiel’s vision of the Spirit breathing life into dry bones: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live (Ezekiel 37:9). Creation, and re-creation from a field of corpses. John has reached for the verb that carries both, in a locked room, on the first day of the week. A new creation begins.

Receive the Holy Spirit. The word for spirit is the word for breath in both Hebrew and Greek, which is why the picture works and why English cannot reproduce it. He breathes, and says: receive the Breath. How does this relate to Pentecost (Acts 2)?

Where Christians differ: this gift and Pentecost. Some see this as John’s version of Pentecost; others as a separate, partial gift. Verdict: this is a real gift, but also an acted promise, preparing the disciples for the full outpouring at Pentecost fifty days later, when Jesus had ascended (7:39; 16:7; Acts 1:4–5, 8). The Spirit was given to them here, and poured out in power there. Both show that the Spirit comes from the risen Christ.

Not a mere symbol. What no reading should do is make this only a gesture. John has just described a creation act. Something was given. And the commission in the previous verse shows what for: they are being sent, and no one is sent on that errand without the Spirit.

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit after conversion? No. The apostles stood at a unique turning point in history, between the resurrection and Pentecost, and their experience of the Spirit came in stages because redemption itself was unfolding in stages. Since Pentecost, every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), and in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). What you need is not a second blessing but a daily filling, to keep in step with the Spirit you already have (Galatians 5:25; Ephesians 5:18), through the word, prayer and obedience. Ask for more of his fruit and his strength. You do not need to ask for him to come, as though he were absent.

In a sentence. Jesus gave them peace again and said that as the Father sent him, he was sending them, and then breathed on them and told them to receive the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You are sent as Christ was sent. Think of the one place this week where you are most like a missionary: the office, the school gate, the club, the family table. Ask the Spirit for courage there, and do one concrete thing for one person in his name.

For worship. You are sent as Christ was sent, with his peace and his Spirit. Go. The breath that gave Adam life and raised the dry bones of Israel was breathed by the risen Christ on a roomful of frightened men, and the new creation began. The God who made us from dust has remade us by his Spirit, and every Christian alive is a person the risen Lord has breathed on.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld. Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.

If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld. The Greek perfect tense says: they have already been forgiven, they have already been withheld. The disciples do not create forgiveness; they announce what God has already done. By preaching the gospel, they declare forgiveness to all who believe, and declare that those who refuse remain in their sins (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; Acts 2:38; 13:38–39).

Where Christians differ: who forgives sins? Roman Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, giving priests power to absolve sins in confession. Verdict: only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). The words are given to the disciples as a group, and their exercise in Acts is the preaching of the gospel: forgiveness is proclaimed to all who repent and believe. Every Christian who declares the gospel speaks with this authority. Church discipline also applies it (1 Corinthians 5:4–5; 2 Corinthians 2:7–10). There is no special priestly power to absolve.

The reading that deserves an answer. The reading set aside there should be named carefully, since it is held by a great many Christians. Rome takes this verse as the institution of penance: the apostles, and the bishops and priests who succeed them, are given the power to absolve sins, exercised in the confessional, where the priest says I absolve you. The Council of Trent cited this text for it directly. It is not a frivolous reading, since the words plainly commit something about sins to these men, so it deserves an answer rather than a dismissal.

The grammar. Three things answer it. The first is in the grammar, and it is decisive. The words rendered they are forgiven stand in the Greek perfect tense: they have been forgiven, and stand forgiven. The forgiveness is not created by the disciple’s word; it is already in force, and the disciple announces it. It is the same construction Jesus used about binding and loosing (Matthew 16:19; 18:18), where the sense is what shall have been bound in heaven. Heaven does not ratify the church’s verdict. The church announces heaven’s.

The rest of the New Testament. The second is the absence of any such practice in the rest of the New Testament. Not once does an apostle hear a private confession and pronounce a man absolved. When Simon the magician needs forgiveness, Peter, who if anyone had this power, had it, does not absolve him but sends him to God: “Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you” (Acts 8:22). And John, who wrote this verse down, tells us in his own letter where a sinner is to take his sins: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Confession there is to God, and the promise rests on his faithfulness, not on a mediator’s word.

What the verse does mean. The third is what the verse does mean, which is not nothing. Christ has entrusted his church with the announcement that decides where people stand: the keys, as Matthew calls them. When the gospel is preached, forgiveness is really offered and really withheld. To the man who repents and believes, the church may say with full authority, your sins are forgiven; to the one who will not, it must say with equal authority that they are not. The Reformers kept the substance of this and were right to. They kept the declaration of pardon in public worship, and Luther valued private confession to a pastor for a conscience too troubled to believe a general promise. What they refused was the idea that the forgiveness waits on the minister. He is a herald carrying a message, not a judge holding a power, and the best thing he can do for a frightened soul is tell him what God has already said.

Should I ever confess my sins to another Christian? Yes, sometimes, though not to receive absolution. James says, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (James 5:16). Confessing a secret sin to a mature believer or a pastor can break its power, bring accountability, and let you hear the promises of the gospel spoken to you by name. Where you have sinned against someone, confess to them and make it right (Matthew 5:23–24). But the forgiveness itself comes from God alone, through Christ alone, the moment you confess to him. A brother can remind you that you are forgiven; only God can forgive you.

Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came. We are not told why. His absence will produce the encounter that brings the Gospel’s greatest confession.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they forgave anyone’s sins, they were forgiven, and if they withheld it, it was withheld; but Thomas, one of the Twelve, was not with them.

On a Tuesday. When you tell a friend that God forgives all who trust Christ, you speak with Christ’s authority. Say it with confidence. And if you know a believer crushed by guilt over a confessed sin, do the herald’s work: open the Bible with them and read them God’s promise of pardon, aloud, by name.

For worship. Only God forgives sins, and he has done it, once for all, through the death of his Son. Then he sent his people out with the most astonishing message ever entrusted to human lips: your sins are forgiven, for Christ’s sake, if you will turn and believe. The keys of the kingdom are not a power held over sinners but a door held open for them. Every gospel sermon, every word of witness, is the risen Lord announcing from heaven what he accomplished on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.” Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”

We have seen the Lord. The same testimony as Mary’s (v. 18).

Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails. Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet. The word for hand could include the wrist. Thomas has been badly served by the church, and it is worth putting the record straight, because doubting Thomas has become a byword and the text does not support the caricature. Look at what he actually demands: to see the nail marks and put his hand into the side. Now look at verse 20. When Jesus appeared to the other ten, he showed them his hands and his side, and only then were they glad. They had not believed Mary’s word either (Luke 24:11). Thomas is asking for exactly what the other ten were given. He is not demanding more evidence than his friends had; he is refusing to accept less.

And place my hand into his side, I will never believe. “Never” (ou mē): the strong negative. Thomas wants physical proof. He is not a cynic, but a realist who will not accept something so great on hearsay. His doubt, recorded honestly, adds to the evidence: the disciples were not credulous. And this is the man who, when the others were arguing against going back to Judea, said, let us also go, that we may die with him (11:16). Whatever his faults, cowardice and half-heartedness were not among them.

The week he spent. Consider the eight days that followed. Ten men he had lived with for three years, all telling him the same impossible thing, all glad, and he alone outside it, unable to make himself believe them and unwilling to pretend. He stayed, which is the thing to notice. He did not leave the group. He turned up on the following Sunday and was in the room.

Eight days later. The next Sunday, counting inclusively. The disciples gathered again on the first day of the week.

Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, Peace be with you. The same greeting, for Thomas.

What should I do when I struggle to believe? Do what Thomas did: stay where the others are, and keep turning up. Thomas did not reason his way out; he was in the room when Jesus came back. Do not withdraw from the church because you are struggling. Tell a trusted believer honestly what you are finding hard. Keep reading the testimony, especially the Gospels, and pray even if it feels like talking to the ceiling: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Distinguish doubt from unbelief. Doubt is a faith that is struggling; unbelief is a refusal. Jesus was patient with the first, and he came back for Thomas.

In a sentence. The others told Thomas they had seen the Lord, but he said he would never believe unless he saw and touched the nail marks and his side; a week later, with Thomas present and the doors locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”

On a Tuesday. If someone in your church is going through a season of doubt, do not treat them as a problem or a threat. Keep inviting them. Keep the door of fellowship open. Thomas was given a week among friends who did not throw him out, and that week ended with the greatest confession in the Gospel.

For worship. Christ came back for the one who doubted. He is patient with honest doubters. The risen Lord, who could have left Thomas to catch up from the others’ reports, came again on the next Lord’s Day for one man, and spoke the same peace to him. The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine for the one, and he comes through locked doors to find him.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.” Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”

Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Notice first that Jesus quotes him. Those are Thomas’s own words from eight days earlier, given back to him almost exactly. Jesus knows exactly what Thomas said, though he was not visibly there. He had heard. He offers Thomas exactly what he asked for. And there is no rebuke in the offer. He does not say, you should not have needed this. He gives him precisely what he asked, which is what he had already given the other ten without being asked.

Do not disbelieve, but believe. Literally “do not become unbelieving, but believing.” It is addressed to the whole direction of Thomas’s heart, not only to the moment.

Thomas answered him, My Lord and my God! The climax of John’s Gospel. We are not told that Thomas touched him; seeing was enough. John moves straight from the invitation to the confession, and most readers have concluded that the offer itself was enough. Thomas makes the highest confession in the Gospels: Jesus is Lord and God. The Gospel began, “the Word was God” (1:1); it ends with a disciple calling Jesus “my God.” And Jesus accepts it. A devout Jew, whose creed was “the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), calls Jesus “my Lord and my God.” Nothing in his upbringing permitted that sentence. He is standing in front of a man he watched die, and calls him God, and Jesus does not correct him, which is the point, because he had corrected people about far less. “My”: personal faith. Not the Lord, but my Lord. It is not a doctrinal formula; it is a man handing himself over.

The architecture of the book. This is the finest piece of construction in the Gospel. It opened: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. It now arrives, twenty chapters later, at my Lord and my God, and the first ending of the book is three verses away. John has framed the whole account between two statements of the deity of Christ. The first is his own, made about a Word nobody had yet seen. The last is spoken by the most reluctant man in the group, to a face, in a locked room, with the wounds visible.

Our lord and god. If this Gospel was written in the nineties, as many think, there is a further edge to it. The emperor Domitian is reported to have liked being styled our lord and god. Christians in Asia Minor were being pressed on exactly that point, and John hands them a sentence in which those words are addressed to somebody else.

Where Christians differ: what Thomas meant. Some, such as Jehovah’s Witnesses, suggest Thomas was exclaiming in surprise, like an oath, or addressing the Father. Verdict: the Greek says Thomas answered “him,” Jesus; and a Jew would never use God’s name as an exclamation (the third commandment). It is a confession, addressed to Jesus, and Jesus commends it in the next verse. Jesus is God.

Why did Jesus not correct Thomas, when he refused worship elsewhere? Because the confession was true. When people tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, or when John fell at an angel’s feet, they were rebuked at once: worship God (Acts 14:14–15; Revelation 19:10). Jesus receives worship throughout the Gospels without protest (Matthew 14:33; 28:9, 17), and here he receives the highest title there is. If he were not God, accepting it would be the very blasphemy he was crucified for. He accepts it, and blesses those who will say it after Thomas.

In a sentence. Jesus told Thomas to put his finger in the nail marks and his hand in his side, and not to doubt but believe, and Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God!”

On a Tuesday. Make Thomas’s confession your own: my Lord and my God. Say it aloud today, and then ask what it means for this week. If he is your Lord, what instruction of his are you resisting? If he is your God, what are you trusting instead of him? Two possessive words, and the whole of life is handed over in them.

For worship. The risen Christ stood before the doubter with his wounds open, and the doubter fell into the greatest confession in Scripture. My Lord and my God. The Word who was God in the beginning, who became flesh and was crucified, is confessed as God by a man who had touched death and now saw it defeated. He is my Lord: he has bought me. He is my God: I worship him. There is nothing higher to say, and nothing truer.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;

Have you believed because you have seen me? Not a rebuke, but a statement. Thomas is not cursed; he is standing there having just made the highest confession in the Gospel.

Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. The last beatitude of the Gospels, and it is for us. Every believer since the apostles has believed without seeing (1 Peter 1:8). We are not second-class believers; Jesus calls us blessed. Our faith rests on the testimony of those who saw (v. 31; 1 John 1:1–3). The beatitude is aimed forward, out of the room, at everybody who would ever read the book. There were at that moment a few hundred people alive who would ever see the risen Christ. Everybody else, for the next two thousand years, was going to have to rely on testimony, and Jesus, in one of his last appearances, pronounces them blessed for it.

Not blind faith. This answers a suspicion most Christians have had at some point: that faith would be easier and better if only one could have been there. This verse says the opposite. Not that seeing would be worse, but that not seeing is no disadvantage and carries a blessing of its own. And notice how the beatitude is worded. Not blessed are those who believe without evidence. John has just spent twenty chapters supplying evidence, and will say in the next verse that he selected it on purpose. The blessing is on those who have not seen, which is a different thing. They have the testimony of people who did.

Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book. John has been selective (21:25). It is the mark of an honest writer. Seven signs, out of many; a handful of days, out of three years. He is not claiming to have written everything and he does not want the reader to think he has. That is worth having when somebody objects that the Gospels leave things out, or differ in what they include. Of course they do. The author says so in the second-to-last verse of his book, and then explains what his selection was for.

Why does Jesus not appear to people today to settle their doubts? Because he has already given what is needed, and more sight would not change hearts that will not believe. Abraham told the rich man that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). The risen Christ appeared to chosen witnesses (Acts 10:40–41), whose testimony is written so that all may believe. Now he speaks through that word, and the Spirit opens blind eyes to see his glory in it (2 Corinthians 4:6). When he does appear again, it will not be to invite faith but to judge and to save (Hebrews 9:28). Today is the day of believing without seeing.

In a sentence. Jesus told Thomas that he believed because he had seen, but blessed are those who believe without seeing; and Jesus did many other signs not written in this book.

On a Tuesday. If you believe without having seen, Jesus calls you blessed. Do not envy Thomas, or the eleven. Thank God today for the witnesses who saw and wrote, and for the Spirit who has let you see by faith what they saw with their eyes.

For worship. If you believe without having seen, Jesus calls you blessed. On the evening he showed his wounds to Thomas, the risen Lord looked past the room to every believer of every century, and pronounced a blessing on us. Though you have not seen him, you love him, and you rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory (1 Peter 1:8). The day is coming when faith will become sight, and the blessed who did not see will see him face to face.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

But these are written so that you may believe. The purpose statement of the whole Gospel. The signs are selected and written for faith. This is the last sentence of the Gospel as John first ended it. Chapter 21 reads as an epilogue, and its own closing verse says something different. And it does what almost no ancient book does: it tells the reader what it is for. Not so that the record would be preserved, though it is. Not so that the church would have a history, though it does. He selected seven signs out of many and arranged twenty chapters around them with one outcome in view, and he states it in a single sentence and then stops.

Come to believe, or go on believing? The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.” An honest note on the Greek: one reading suggests that you may come to believe, which makes the book evangelistic, addressed to outsiders; the other, that you may go on believing, which makes it a book for the church. The manuscripts are divided and the argument has never been settled. The difference matters little: John writes both to bring people to faith and to strengthen those who believe. It is a happy dispute, because the book plainly does both. It has brought people to Christ who began it as sceptics, and it has held Christians steady for twenty centuries, and nothing in the sentence has to be given up.

That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The content of faith. Jesus, the man from Nazareth, is the Christ, the promised Messiah of Israel, and the Son of God, sharing the Father’s nature. Martha confessed it (11:27); Thomas confessed it in its fullest form (v. 28). Both titles have been fought over in this book. The Christ: the promised one of Israel, which is what the crowds argued about at the feast. The Son of God: which is what they picked up stones over, what the council condemned him for, and what Pilate was afraid of.

And that by believing you may have life in his name. The result of faith: life, eternal life, now and for ever (3:16; 17:3). “In his name”: through who he is and what he has done. And this is where the book started: in him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4). Everything in between, the water made wine, the bread on the hillside, the man who could see, the voice at the tomb of Lazarus, the towel and the basin, the cross, the empty grave, the name spoken in a garden, has been in service of that one word, and it is offered, at the end, to whoever is holding the book.

How do I know whether I have this life? Ask what you believe about Jesus and what you are trusting. Do you believe that he is the Christ, the Son of God, who died for sinners and rose again? Are you relying on him, and not on your record, for your acceptance with God? Then you have life, now, because he has said so: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life (3:36), and John wrote his letter so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). The evidence of that life will grow: love for God’s people, hatred of sin, a desire to obey him. But it rests on his promise, not on your feelings. If you are not sure, believe him now. That is what the book was written for.

In a sentence. These signs are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

On a Tuesday. Give a copy of John’s Gospel to someone this month, and offer to read it with them. That is what it was written for. And read it again yourself, slowly, one chapter a day, asking at each sign what it shows you of who Jesus is.

For worship. This is why the Gospel was written: for you to believe and live. Do you? The eternal Word, who was with God and was God, became flesh, died and rose, and then made sure that the testimony would be written down and handed on, so that people he would never meet in the flesh could believe and live. The life that was in him from the beginning is offered in his name to everyone who believes. Glory to the Son of God, the Christ, the Life.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.<sup>2</sup>So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>3</sup>So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb.<sup>4</sup>Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.<sup>5</sup>And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.<sup>6</sup>Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,<sup>7</sup>and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.<sup>8</sup>Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;<sup>9</sup>for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.<sup>10</sup>Then the disciples went back to their homes.<sup>11</sup>But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb.<sup>12</sup>And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.<sup>13</sup>They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>14</sup>Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?
