Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).<sup>17</sup>Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ’I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”<sup>18</sup>Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”—and that he had said these things to her.<sup>19</sup>On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”<sup>20</sup>When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”<sup>22</sup>And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.<sup>23</sup>If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.”<sup>24</sup>Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.<sup>25</sup>So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.”<sup>26</sup>Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.”<sup>28</sup>Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”<sup>29</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;<sup>31</sup>but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.overview:
On the first day of the week, while it is still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone rolled away and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that the body has been taken. The two run to the tomb; the beloved disciple arrives first, looks in, and sees the linen cloths lying there; Peter goes in and sees the head cloth folded by itself. The beloved disciple goes in, sees, and believes. Mary stays weeping outside, sees two angels, then turns and sees Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener, until he calls her by name. He sends her to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and their Father, to his God and their God. A woman becomes the first witness of the resurrection.

That evening Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows them his hands and side, and gives them peace. As the Father sent him, so he sends them; he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and gives them authority to declare sins forgiven or retained. Thomas is absent and refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus appears again and invites him to do so; Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospels, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus pronounces a blessing on all who will believe without seeing. John then states the purpose of his book: these signs are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By the Sea of Tiberias, Peter and six other disciples spend a fruitless night fishing. At dawn a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and the catch is too great to haul in. The beloved disciple realises it is the Lord; Peter plunges into the water to reach him. On the shore Jesus has a fire of coals with fish and bread; the net, holding 153 large fish, is unbroken, and Jesus serves them breakfast. Afterwards he asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and each time, as Peter affirms his love, commissions him to feed and care for his flock. He foretells that in old age Peter will be bound and led where he would not choose, the death by which he would glorify God, and calls him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus says that even if he wills him to remain until he returns, that is not Peter’s concern: Peter must follow. John corrects the rumour this started, identifies the beloved disciple as the author whose testimony is true, and closes by saying that the world could not hold the books needed to record all that Jesus did.
verseByVerse.theology: The threefold restoration of Peter — Do you love me? / Feed my sheep — is the most pastoral moment in the gospel. Three questions match three denials; three commissions match three failures. The charcoal fire (the same as 18:18) brings the smell of the denial back to Peter's senses; the same kind of fire is now the fire of restoration. Jesus does not ignore the failure or pretend it did not happen; he names it by re-enacting the scene in reverse. The gospel's answer to failure is not silence but renewed commission — the broken shepherd is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple as the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the gospel stakes its authority on eyewitness testimony. This is not mythology or legend but the account of one who was there — who saw the water turned to wine, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb, and watched Jesus break bread on the shore. The testimony is true because the witness is trustworthy; the witness is trustworthy because the one he testifies to is the resurrection and the life. The gospel ends not with a doctrine but with a person: if everything were written, the world itself could not contain the books. The Word is larger than any book.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.

Meaning first. John 21 is an epilogue. John 20 ended with the purpose of the book; now John adds a final scene in Galilee. It shows the risen Lord providing for his disciples, restoring Peter after his denials, commissioning him to shepherd the flock, foretelling his death, and correcting a rumour about John. It tells us that the risen Christ cares for failures, calls them to serve, and gives each his own path. Without this chapter, Peter’s denial would still be lying where chapter 18 left it, three times beside a charcoal fire, unhealed.

Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It is where he fed the five thousand and walked on the water, and the setting is thick with memory. Jesus had told them he would meet them in Galilee (Mark 16:7). “Revealed himself” (ephanerōsen): showed himself, made himself known. John uses the word twice in one verse, and it implies that the initiative is entirely on one side. These men did not find him and did not go looking; they went to work. He showed himself to them, in his own time, while they were doing something else, which has been the pattern of every meeting in this Gospel from the first chapter onward.

Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others. Seven disciples. Simon Peter is listed first: the denier who will be restored is the centre of this final scene. Thomas is here, and it is the last we see of him: back at work on a lake with the others. Whatever the caricature has made of him, John’s final picture is of a man who stayed. And Nathanael is given a home town for the only time in the Gospel. Nathanael came from Cana, where Jesus did his first sign (2:1–11). We were never told it in chapter 1, when he was sitting under a fig tree being sceptical about Nazareth. John has waited twenty chapters to mention that one of the men who watched the water become wine lived in the village. “The sons of Zebedee”: James and John, named only here in John’s Gospel, John characteristically hiding himself. And two are left unnamed, which is the sort of detail nobody invents; a writer constructing a scene supplies names.

The book closing its circles. The book began by the water with men being called, and it ends by the water with the same men. Seven of them, in a Gospel that has given us seven signs and seven I am sayings. John is tying the ends of his story together.

Does Jesus still reveal himself today? Yes, though not by appearing in a body on the shore. Those appearances were given to chosen witnesses for a limited time (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:5–8), and they ended with his ascension. Now he makes himself known through his word, preached and read, by his Spirit, who takes what is Christ’s and declares it to us (16:14). He is present when his people gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and he meets us at his table. And, as here, he often makes himself known in the ordinary places, at work and at home, when we are not looking for anything in particular. Do not wait for a vision. Open the book where he has already revealed himself.

In a sentence. Jesus showed himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, where Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee and two others were together.

On a Tuesday. The risen Christ comes to his people in their ordinary places. Look for him there. Before you start work today, ask him to make himself known to you in it, and at the end of the day look back and ask where he was.

For worship. The risen Christ comes to his people in their ordinary places. Look for him there. The Lord who had conquered death did not wait for his disciples in the temple or on a mountain, but on the shore of the lake where they earned their living. He revealed himself, as he always has, by his own choice and in his own time, to people who were not looking. He still does.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

I am going fishing. Some see Peter giving up and returning to his old trade. More likely he is simply doing something useful while they wait. Fishermen needed to eat. A guard is needed here, because the sentence is regularly preached as apostasy, Peter throwing in the towel and going back to his nets, and the text will not carry it. Consider where they are and why. The risen Jesus had sent word: tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me (Matthew 28:10; Mark 16:7). Galilee is where these men are. They have obeyed an instruction and are waiting for him in the place they were told to wait, with no date given. And men who are waiting have to eat. Peter owned a boat and knew a trade, and nothing in the story suggests that using it was a betrayal. Six of them go with him without hesitation, including the disciple whom Jesus loved.

The flatness of it. What is true, and sadder, is the flatness of it. A man who has seen the risen Lord twice, and denied him three times, says I am going fishing, which is what people do when they do not know what else to do with themselves. It is not rebellion. It is the ordinary, unglamorous business of filling the hours while waiting for something you cannot arrange.

They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Fishing on the lake was done at night, when the fish came near the surface and could not see the nets. A wasted night, as at their first calling (Luke 5:5). Professional fishermen, on their own lake, working the hours when the fish come up, and they take not one fish. It is the second time John has put them on that water in the dark with nothing going right (6:16–21), and both times the story ends with somebody standing where they did not expect him.

Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore. As at the tomb, at dawn. The detail is exact: at the moment the night’s failure is confirmed and there is nothing left to do but come in empty.

Yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. In the half-light, about a hundred yards away.

What should I do while I wait for God to show me the way? Do the next ordinary, faithful thing. The disciples had been told to go to Galilee and wait, and they waited by working. Waiting on God is not idleness, and it is not anxious searching for signs. Keep doing what is right in front of you: your job, your family duties, your place in the church, your prayers. Obey what he has already made clear, and trust him for what he has not. Guidance usually comes as it did here, to people already at their nets, not to people standing on the shore refusing to move until the heavens open.

In a sentence. Peter went fishing with the others, but they caught nothing all night, and at daybreak Jesus stood on the shore, though they did not recognise him.

On a Tuesday. Some nights of labour bring nothing. At daybreak, Christ is on the shore. If you are in a season of empty nets, a job search going nowhere, a ministry with no visible fruit, prayers that seem unanswered, keep at the work and keep looking toward the shore. The night is not the end of the story.

For worship. While seven tired men toiled in the dark and caught nothing, their risen Lord was already standing on the shore, watching for the dawn. He was not absent during the empty night; he was waiting for the moment to show himself. The Shepherd of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), and he is on the shore of every long night his people go through.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.” He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.

Children, do you have any fish? “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men, like “lads.” It is paidia here, not the tender little children of the upper room but the everyday word a man uses hailing a boat. And what he asks for is not fish in general but the bit of fish you eat with your bread. It is the question a buyer shouts from the beach at dawn: caught anything? The Greek form expects the answer no. So the risen Son of God opens the conversation of Peter’s restoration by asking for breakfast. Their answer is one word. No. John records it bare, which is how a man says it after a whole night of nothing.

Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some. A strange instruction to experienced fishermen. But they obey. The direction comes from the shore, from someone they do not yet recognise.

And now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish. A miracle, recalling their first calling, when Jesus said they would be fishers of men (Luke 5:4–10). Luke records that when Jesus first called these men, he got into Peter’s boat after a night in which they had caught nothing, told him to let down the nets, and filled them so full that the nets began to break and a second boat nearly sank. And Peter fell down and said, depart from me, for I am a sinful man. That is where Peter’s discipleship began: a wasted night, a stranger’s instruction, an impossible catch, and a man on his knees saying he was not fit.

The same lake, at the end. Here it is again, on the same lake, at the end. The empty night, the instruction from the shore, the catch, and this time Peter does not ask him to go away. He goes into the water to get to him. John does not mention Luke’s story. He does not have to. The men in the boat had lived it, and when the nets went heavy for the second time in their lives, at least one of them worked out immediately who was on the beach. Their mission will be fruitful only by his word. Without him, they catch nothing (15:5); with him, more than they can haul.

If I obey God, will he always give me success? Not always success as we would measure it, but always fruit as he measures it. Obedience is not a technique for guaranteed results; plenty of faithful servants in Scripture saw little visible fruit, like Jeremiah, who preached for forty years and was rejected. The promise is that whoever abides in Christ bears much fruit (15:5), and that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). The size and timing of the catch are his. What this scene teaches is the source: without him nothing, with him more than we can manage. So work hard, obey his word, and leave the results in his hands.

In a sentence. Jesus asked if they had caught anything, and when they said no, told them to cast the net on the right side, and they caught so many fish they could not haul it in.

On a Tuesday. Fruit in Christ’s work comes from his word, not our skill. Before you start the task you are most experienced at, the one you could do in your sleep, stop and pray over it. Experience is a gift, but it is not the reason the net fills.

For worship. Fruit in Christ’s work comes from his word, not our skill. Cast your net where he says. The Lord who called these men with a miraculous catch at the beginning recalled them with another at the end, and showed them that everything in between had been his doing. He is the Lord of the harvest, of fish and of people, and the nets fill at his word.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.

It is the Lord! John, quick to perceive, as at the tomb (20:8). He sees the sign and knows. It is the beloved disciple who works it out, as he was the first to believe at the empty tomb. And it is Peter who moves. One sees; the other jumps. The two men behave exactly as they have all the way through, and John clearly enjoys recording it.

He put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work. Fishermen worked in a loincloth or a short tunic. Peter dresses before meeting the Lord, out of respect. It is a small comic detail that has puzzled readers for centuries: he dressed to swim. Most people would do the opposite. The likeliest explanation is that a Jew did not greet a person of standing improperly clothed; a greeting was something close to a religious act. Peter is about to meet his Lord, and he is not going to arrive stripped for work, so he tucks up his garment and goes over the side in it.

And threw himself into the sea. Peter, quick to act, as always. He cannot wait. John sees first; Peter reaches him first. He was about a hundred yards out. He could have waited perhaps three minutes for the boat. That is the whole man. It is the same impulse that drew a sword in the garden and swore he would die first. Nothing about Peter’s temperament has been corrected by his failure, and Jesus is about to give him a job without asking him to become somebody else.

The others brought the boat in. And notice what the others do. They bring the boat in, dragging the net, doing the necessary work while one of them swims. John does not rank them. Both arrive.

About a hundred yards off. The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits, about 100 yards or 90 metres. There is one more detail of the sort that only a witness supplies. Somebody looked at the distance and remembered it. These small measurements run all through this Gospel: six stone jars holding twenty or thirty gallons, twenty-five or thirty stadia rowed on a dark lake, seventy-five pounds of spices, a hundred yards to a beach. They do nothing for the theology. They are what a man includes when he is describing something he watched.

Does Jesus want me to change my personality? He wants to sanctify it, not erase it. Peter was still impulsive after the resurrection, and John still quietly perceptive; Christ used both. Grace does not turn every Christian into the same kind of person. What it does is purge the sin that clings to our temperament: Peter’s rashness had to be humbled, and his boasting broken, but his eagerness was turned toward Christ. So do not envy another believer’s temperament or despise your own. Ask the Lord to cut away what is sinful in it and to use what is left for his glory. The church needs both those who see first and those who jump first, and those who quietly bring in the boat.

In a sentence. The disciple Jesus loved told Peter, “It is the Lord!”, and Peter put on his outer garment and jumped into the sea, while the others brought the boat in, dragging the net, about a hundred yards from shore.

On a Tuesday. Some see Christ first; others run to him first. Both are gifts. Learn from John’s insight and Peter’s eagerness. And thank God this week for a believer whose temperament is unlike yours, perhaps one who irritates you, and tell them something you value in them.

For worship. It is the Lord! The cry from the boat is the cry of every believer who has suddenly recognised Christ at work in the ordinary: in a filled net, an answered prayer, a word in season. And the Lord on the shore received both the man who swam and the men who rowed, the quick and the slow, the one who saw and the one who leapt. He does not need his people to be the same. He needs them to come.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”

They saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Everything about this fire matters. John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial (18:18). The word occurs exactly twice in the whole New Testament: here, and in a courtyard on the night Peter said I am not. Nobody else in the New Testament mentions one. John used it once when Peter was warming his hands among the men who had arrested his master, and he uses it again now, and he does not explain. It is deliberate. Smell reaches memory most directly, and anyone who has cooked outdoors knows what charcoal smells like. Peter comes up the beach soaked, and the wind is off the fire. He has been brought back to the scene of it. Peter denied his Lord beside one charcoal fire; he will be restored beside another.

Breakfast already cooking. And what is on the fire is the thing to notice: fish laid out on it, and bread. Before there was a catch. Before Peter had done anything at all, while seven men were still failing to fish, breakfast was already cooking. Jesus had already prepared breakfast, before they brought their catch. The risen Lord serves his disciples, as he did at the supper (13:4–5). And the fire is in place: already burning, already down to coals hot enough to cook on, which takes time. They had spent the night failing on the water, and he had spent part of it making a fire.

Bring some of the fish that you have just caught. He invites them to add what they have caught to what he has provided. He does not need them. He has fish. But he asks for theirs and puts them on the fire beside his own, which is one of the gentlest things in the Gospels: the risen Lord, who has provided everything, arranging for the men to contribute to a meal they could not have produced. That is very close to the whole doctrine of Christian work. In his work, he provides, and also uses what we bring. Nothing we bring is required. It is asked for anyway, and it goes on the fire with his.

What if the memory of my failure keeps coming back? Notice what Jesus did with Peter’s memory. He did not pretend the courtyard had not happened, and he did not leave Peter alone with it. He lit the same kind of fire and made breakfast beside it, so that the smell of failure would from then on be mixed with the smell of grace. When an old sin comes back to you, do not try to bury the memory or let it accuse you. Bring it to Christ and look at it in the light of the cross: it was real, it was forgiven, and he has given you work to do since. The Lord does not erase our history; he redeems it, until the worst memory becomes a place where we learned how much he loves us.

In a sentence. On land they saw a charcoal fire with fish and bread already cooking, and Jesus told them to bring some of the fish they had caught.

On a Tuesday. Bring what you have to Christ’s work this week, however small: an hour, a skill, a meal for someone, a few words of witness. He does not need it, and he asks for it anyway. And if there is a memory that still burns, take it to him in prayer today, beside the fire he has lit.

For worship. The risen Lord cooked breakfast for his tired, failing disciples. He still provides for his own. The Lord of glory, days out of the grave, knelt on a beach and lit a fire for the men who had abandoned him, and had the food ready before they knew he was there. Then he asked for their small catch, so that they could share in what he had already provided. Such is our Saviour: he goes before us, he provides for us, and he lets us bring what we have to his table.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.

Full of large fish, 153 of them. The number has attracted more ingenuity than any other detail in the Gospel, and the honest thing is to survey it briefly and then say what is probably true. Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest is that an eyewitness remembered the count. Augustine and Jerome offered symbolic readings. Jerome said there were 153 kinds of fish, standing for all nations, so that the catch would represent every kind of person gathered in. Augustine noticed that 153 is the sum of every number from 1 to 17, and built an elaborate structure on 10 (the commandments) plus 7 (the Spirit). Others have counted the numerical values of Hebrew letters. None of it commands agreement, and most of it could be done for almost any number.

Fishermen count the catch. The simplest explanation is much more likely and is not less interesting. Fishermen counted their catch to share it out. It was a remarkable haul, somebody sat on the beach and counted it, and decades later an old man still remembered the figure. That is worth more than any allegory. Legends do not carry inventory numbers. The precise number points to an eyewitness, and the great catch points to the worldwide mission.

And although there were so many, the net was not torn. In Luke 5:6, the nets began to break. Here they hold. The same lake, the same men, a similar catch, and nothing tears. Some see a picture of the church: gathering all kinds of people, and not torn apart.

Come and have breakfast. An invitation to fellowship. And it comes into a silence.

None of the disciples dared ask him, Who are you? They knew it was the Lord. Something about him was different, and yet they knew. Awe and certainty together. It is perhaps the most awkward sentence in the chapter. They knew, and nobody said anything. Seven men stand round a fire in a silence too large to break: not doubt, and not fear exactly, but the strangeness of being in the presence of someone you watched die and then abandoned. And into that silence: come and have breakfast.

What does the full net say about the church’s mission? That the gathering of people is Christ’s work, that it is great, and that his net holds. The disciples had been told they would be fishers of men, and their first attempt at fishing without him ended in an empty net. With him the net was full, and it did not break. The church today is gathered from every nation and kind, and it often looks as though the strain must tear it. It will not. Christ will bring in all whom the Father has given him (6:37), and not one will slip through. So pray for missionaries, support the work of the gospel, and cast your own net, knowing that the outcome is in his hands.

In a sentence. Peter hauled the net ashore full of 153 large fish, yet it did not tear, and Jesus invited them to breakfast, and none dared ask who he was, for they knew it was the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Come and have breakfast with Jesus. Start each day in fellowship with him. Before the phone, before the news, before the day’s demands, give the first minutes to him: a psalm, a Gospel passage, a prayer. He has already prepared the meal.

For worship. The net was full and it did not break, because the Lord of the harvest was on the shore. The risen Christ gathers his people from every nation and keeps them all, and he spreads a table for them in the morning of the new creation. Come and have breakfast: the invitation of the risen Lord to men who did not dare speak is the invitation of the gospel to every sinner, and one day it will be the invitation to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted — a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.

Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. Three verbs, and this Gospel has used them before. As he did at the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (6:11). On a hillside above this same water he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them to the crowd. The wording here is plain and familiar. The host serves his guests. Luke tells us the risen Jesus also ate (Luke 24:42–43): his body was real.

He serves them. That is the fact to sit with. The risen Lord of glory, days out of a grave, with the marks still in his hands, is crouched over a fire on a beach handing bread to seven fishermen who have been up all night. He had told them, at the supper, that he was among them as the one who serves (Luke 22:27), and he had knelt with a towel to prove it. Nothing about the resurrection has changed that. The one who washed their feet before he died is cooking their breakfast after.

This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead. The third appearance to the group of disciples in John (20:19, 26). There were others (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The first two were indoors, in a city, behind bolted doors, with fear in the room. This one is outdoors, at dawn, in their own country, over a meal, with the door of the world standing open.

The second meal of bread and fish. And the meal itself is bread and fish, which is what he had multiplied on the hillside above this lake for five thousand people, and the only meal this Gospel records him providing twice. The first time it was a sign, and the crowd wanted to make him king and then walked away when he explained what it meant. This time there is no crowd, no argument, and no discourse afterwards. Just seven men eating breakfast with him.

Is this a picture of the Lord’s Supper? Not directly; it is a real breakfast on a real beach, and John does not call it a sacrament. But it does echo the meals that point to his table: the feeding of the five thousand, where he spoke of himself as the bread of life, and the upper room, where he took bread and gave it to them. In all of them the same Lord feeds his people with his own hands. When you come to the Lord’s Supper, it is a memorial of his death and a means by which he nourishes your faith; you are not merely remembering an absent Christ. You are being fed by the risen one, spiritually present by his Spirit, who still takes bread and gives it to his disciples.

In a sentence. Jesus took the bread and fish and gave them to the disciples, the third time he had appeared to them after rising from the dead.

On a Tuesday. Serve someone a meal this week as he served his friends: a tired colleague, a new family at church, a neighbour living alone. The risen Lord of glory thought it worth his morning. And come to his table next time with the expectation of being fed, not only of remembering.

For worship. The risen Lord still feeds his people, by his word and at his table. He who fed five thousand with a boy’s lunch fed seven tired men with bread and fish from his own fire, and he has never stopped serving his people. The exalted King is still the servant who kneels with a towel and stands at a fire with bread in his hands. Worship him, and come and eat.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

Simon, son of John. Not Peter, the rock, but his old name, as at his first meeting with Jesus (1:42). Peter has not been a rock. And it lands hard, because Jesus gave this man a different name at their very first meeting: you shall be called Cephas, which means Peter. Now, on a beach, after a courtyard and a fire and three denials, he is addressed by the name he had before the promise was made. Three times. It is not cruelty. It is the necessary honesty of a restoration that refuses to pretend. A man who has failed badly cannot be repaired by being told the failure did not matter, and Jesus does not tell him that. He takes him back to Simon son of John, and starts again from there.

Do you love me more than these? “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me, since Peter had boasted that even if all fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29). Some take it as more than these things: the boats, nets and fish. The first is more likely. Jesus gently probes his pride. The comparison was Peter’s own. Jesus raises it once and then drops it, and never mentions it again.

The question nobody would predict. Not are you sorry. Not will you promise. Not do you understand what you did. Peter is never asked to explain himself, never asked to apologise, never once given the chance to make the vow he had made before and broken. Do you love me? That is the whole examination for restoration to apostolic ministry, put three times, and it is about love rather than performance. That is worth knowing for anyone who has failed and assumes that what is wanted is a better record.

Yes, Lord; you know that I love you. Peter no longer compares himself with others. He appeals to Jesus’ knowledge.

Agapaō and phileō. Jesus asks with agapaō the first two times; Peter answers with phileō each time; the third time Jesus uses phileō. Some see great significance: Jesus asks for the highest love, Peter can only offer friendship love, and Jesus comes down to Peter’s level. But John uses the two words interchangeably elsewhere (both are used of the Father’s love for the Son, 3:35; 5:20), and he varies other words in this passage too (lambs and sheep, feed and tend). The main point is the threefold question, not the variation.

Two things said even-handedly. The strongest argument that the change of verbs is a matter of style is that it does not stand alone. In these three exchanges John uses two different words for love, two for feeding and tending, two for lambs and sheep, and two for knowing. Four pairs of synonyms in three verses. A writer who varies his vocabulary that systematically is very likely doing it for the ear. That does not settle it, and the older reading remains available and moving: Jesus meeting a chastened Peter where he is, no longer pressing him to claim the higher love he had once boasted of. The point is that nothing in the passage’s meaning depends on the outcome: three questions answering three denials, and a full restoration to shepherd Christ’s flock.

Feed my lambs. Peter’s restoration is also his commission. The flock is “my” lambs: they belong to Christ, not to Peter. The shepherd must feed them, with the word of God.

Tend my sheep. “Tend” (poimaine): shepherd, care for, guide, protect. Feeding and leading.

Does Feed my sheep make Peter the head of the church and the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads it so. But the threefold question answers the threefold denial: it restores a fallen apostle to his work. It speaks of no office above the other apostles and of no successors. Peter himself later tells the elders, as a fellow elder, to shepherd the flock of God that is among you (1 Peter 5:1–2). The commission is for every faithful pastor.

What if I do not feel much love for Jesus? Then do what Peter did: take your love, such as it is, to the one who knows everything. Love for Christ is not measured by the intensity of your feelings on a given day, but by whether you want him, trust him, grieve when you fail him, and want to obey him. Weak love is still love. And love grows by looking at his love for you: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Read the passion narrative slowly, and this chapter, and see what he did for a man who had denied him. Then ask him to increase your love. It is a prayer he delights to answer.

In a sentence. After breakfast Jesus asked Simon son of John whether he loved him more than these, and twice Peter said Jesus knew he loved him, and Jesus told him to feed his lambs and tend his sheep.

On a Tuesday. Love for Christ shows itself in care for his people. Think of one lamb in your church, a new believer, a child, a struggling member, and do one thing to feed them this week: a word of Scripture, an invitation, a conversation over coffee. That is what love for Jesus looks like on an ordinary day.

For worship. Love for Christ shows itself in care for his people. Whom can you feed today? The risen Lord did not examine Peter’s record, which was a ruin. He asked about his heart, three times, and then trusted him with the people he had bought with his blood. Such is the grace of the Chief Shepherd: he restores failures by asking for love, and then gives them his sheep.
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me — Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”

He said to him the third time. Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. Each denial is answered by a confession of love. Jesus does not pretend the denials did not happen; he heals them. The restoration is as precise as the failure: a charcoal fire for a charcoal fire, three questions for three denials.

Peter was grieved. The third time stung. It reminded him of his threefold failure. The verb is strong: distressed, pained. And John tells us exactly what caused it: not the question, but the third one. He knew what the third meant. Nobody had to say it.

Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you. Peter throws himself on Jesus’ knowledge. He cannot prove his love by his record; only Jesus can see his heart (2:24–25). His answer changes. The first two times he says you know; the third time he says Lord, you know everything. That is the appeal of a man who has run out of evidence about himself. His record is a courtyard and a fire and a rooster. All he can do is appeal past his own performance to the one who can see what is underneath it. Not I have been faithful, which he could not say. Not I will do better, which he had said before and which had proved worthless. Just: you know everything, and you know that I love you. Jesus accepts it. That is the extraordinary thing. He does not require any more, and he immediately hands over the sheep.

Feed my sheep. Restored and recommissioned. Failure is not the end of service.

When you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted. Youthful independence. It is a description of Peter’s whole life so far, including the impulsiveness that had just put him over the side of a boat.

But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go. “Stretch out your hands” was an early Christian way of describing crucifixion, and the next verse says outright that it refers to his death. Tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, around AD 64–68, and asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord did. Peter had said he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37); now Jesus says he will. So the restoration comes with the truth attached. Peter is not told that everything will be well in the sense he might like. He is told, quietly, over breakfast, that he will die for his Lord, when he is old, and that he will not want to go. The Lord does not pretend the road is easy, and he does not withhold the commission because the man will suffer for it.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching sees this passage, with Matthew 16:18, as Christ giving Peter primacy over the whole church, passed on to the bishops of Rome. Verdict: this is the restoration of a fallen apostle, not the founding of an office. Peter calls himself a “fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1) and tells all elders to shepherd the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11). The New Testament says nothing of Peter’s successors. All pastors are under-shepherds of the one Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4).

Can a pastor who has fallen be restored to ministry? Every repentant sinner can be restored to Christ and to the fellowship of the church, fully and gladly. Restoration to the office of pastor is a different question. Peter was restored by the Lord himself, in person, to an apostleship that only Christ could give. Today the church must apply the qualifications Christ has set: an elder must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled and well thought of (1 Timothy 3:1–7). Some sins, especially abuse of the flock, betray a trust so deeply that the person should never again hold the office, however real his repentance; protecting the sheep comes first. Other failures may allow a careful return after time, accountability and proven change. Forgiveness is always offered. Office is a trust, not a right.

In a sentence. When Jesus asked a third time, Peter was hurt, and said Jesus knew everything and knew he loved him; Jesus told him to feed his sheep, and foretold that when he was old, others would bind him and lead him where he did not want to go.

On a Tuesday. Your past failure does not disqualify you from Christ’s service. He restores, and sends. If you have been sitting on the sidelines of the church because of something in your past that has been confessed and forgiven, ask your pastor this week how you can serve. And if the Lord is asking you to go somewhere you do not want to go, remember that he told Peter the truth about his road, and walked it with him.

For worship. The Lord who knows everything knew Peter’s three denials and Peter’s love, and he chose to speak to the love. He healed the wound with the same number of questions as the failure, gave back the work, and then told him the cost with tenderness. And Peter, who once could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Jesus, stretched out his hands for him in his old age. That is what the grace of the risen Christ does with a broken man.
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.” Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”

This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. Peter’s death would glorify God. A martyr’s death is not a defeat but a way of honouring God (Philippians 1:20). By the time John wrote, Peter had died. And notice the formula John uses. He has written that sentence once before, almost word for word, and it was about Jesus: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). The same construction, applied to the Master and then to the disciple. And the addition here is to glorify God. In this Gospel, glorifying God through a death has had one reference for twenty chapters. Peter is being told that his end will do what his Lord’s did, not atone, which is not given to anybody else, but glorify.

Follow me. Where it began (1:43; Mark 1:17), it ends. The whole Christian life in two words. Follow, all the way, even to a cross. They are the words he said to Philip as he set out for Galilee three years earlier, and the words Matthew records him saying to Peter himself beside this very lake, with a net in his hands: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matthew 4:19). Everything has happened in between. The confession and the rebuke, the walking on water and the sinking, the sword and the courtyard and the fire and the rooster and the weeping. And the instruction has not changed by a syllable.

The same terms. There was no new arrangement for a man who had failed: no reduced role, no probation, no adjusted terms. The same two words he was given at the beginning, given back to him at the end, as though nothing needed altering. And it is not a single decision but a way of going on.

Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. John, following too.

The one who also had leaned back against him during the supper. John reminds us who he is (13:23–25).

What does following Christ look like day by day? It means going where he leads, at his pace, by his word. In practice: beginning the day by listening to him in Scripture; taking his commands as your instructions for that day, at work, at home, in your thoughts; choosing his way when it costs you; confessing quickly when you stray and getting back behind him. It means being with his people, because he is leading a flock, not a set of individuals. And it means accepting the road he chooses, which for Peter included a cross and for John a long old age. Following is not admiring him from a distance. It is walking behind him, one step at a time, until the road ends where he is.

In a sentence. Jesus said this to show the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God, and told him to follow him; Peter turned and saw the disciple Jesus loved following them.

On a Tuesday. “Follow me.” Answer him again today. Write down one specific way you will follow him today that you did not yesterday: a conversation you will have, a habit you will drop, a kindness you will do. Then do it.

For worship. The first call was the last call. Follow me, he said to a fisherman by a lake, and three years and a cross and an empty tomb later he said it again on the same shore, without changing a word. He had not lowered the terms for a failure; he had paid for the failure and renewed the call. And the man who followed him to the end died glorifying God, because the one he followed had died first, and risen, and was waiting at the end of the road.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”

Lord, what about this man? Very human. Having just heard of his own death, Peter wants to know about John’s. The timing is what makes this so useful. He has just been restored, commissioned, and told how he will die. And within about one sentence he has turned round, spotted John walking behind them, and asked what is going to happen to him. It is not malice. It is the instinct that arrives the moment a person is given something hard: to find out what the other man is getting. Peter has just been handed a cross, and his first move is to check whether it is being handed out evenly.

If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Jesus will not satisfy Peter’s curiosity. Each disciple has his own path, appointed by the Lord. Comparison is a trap. It is one of the bluntest things Jesus ever says. There is no explanation offered. He does not tell Peter what John’s road will be, or justify the difference, or soften it. He declines the question entirely.

You follow me! “You” is emphatic. Mind your own call. Jesus’ will for John is not Peter’s business. He repeats the command with the pronoun brought forward for emphasis.

The comparison that corrodes. This is the most practically useful sentence in the chapter, and it applies far past martyrdom. Every Christian eventually notices that the terms are not identical: another believer’s marriage, health, children, work, or ease in prayer looks easier, and the comparison is corrosive in both directions. It breeds resentment when we come off worse and complacency when we come off better. Here is the test, and it is simple to run. Notice the last time a comparison with another Christian occupied more than a moment of your thinking. Then hear what Jesus said about that exact activity to the man he had just restored: what is that to you? The call is not comparative. It never was. By early tradition Peter’s road ended on a cross in Rome and John’s ended in extreme old age in Ephesus, and neither of them was owed the other’s.

Is it wrong to ask God why my life is harder than someone else’s? It is not wrong to bring your grief honestly to God; the psalmists did it constantly (Psalm 73). Asaph envied the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw their end. What is wrong is to keep the comparison as a grievance, as though God owed you another person’s road. Bring the question to him, and then let him answer as he answered Peter: your road is mine to choose; follow me on it. The comfort is that he chose it in love, that he walks it with you, and that every road his people walk ends in the same place, with him.

In a sentence. When Peter saw John and asked about him, Jesus answered that if he wanted John to remain until he came, that was not Peter’s concern: Peter must follow him.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing your path with others’. What is that to you? You follow him. When you catch yourself measuring your life against another Christian’s this week, stop, name it, and pray for that person’s blessing instead. Then go back to your own road.

For worship. The Lord of every life assigns each of his servants a road, and he does not consult us or explain himself. One apostle to a cross, another to old age; one believer to a long illness, another to a long and quiet usefulness. Every road is chosen by the same wise and loving hand, and every one ends at the same place: with him. You follow me. It is the sweetest command in the Gospel, because it means he is going ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?” This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.

So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die. The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Tradition says John lived in Ephesus until the reign of Trajan, around AD 98, the last of the apostles. It is a small window into the early church and oddly reassuring. The saying went round that the beloved disciple would not die. It is exactly the kind of thing that happens to a remark: a hypothetical gets repeated, the if falls off in the retelling, and within a generation people are treating it as a promise. Presumably as John grew very old the story hardened, and presumably it was causing difficulty by the time this was written.

Yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die. John corrects the rumour carefully, quoting Jesus’ exact words. A lesson in handling Scripture: pay attention to what is actually said, not what people think it says. The response is not indignation or embarrassment. Somebody simply quotes the sentence back exactly as it was said, with the if restored, and points out the difference. That is a community handling misinformation about its own founder by returning to the words. It is what the church has had to do ever since, and the first recorded instance of it is in the second-to-last paragraph of this Gospel.

This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things. The author identifies himself: the beloved disciple. The Gospel is eyewitness testimony.

And we know that his testimony is true. “We”: probably the elders of the church at Ephesus, or John’s circle, who knew him and endorsed his Gospel. They vouch for him.

Was chapter 21 added later? That shift to we know is worth stopping on, since it sounds like the community’s voice and a reader may fairly wonder what that implies. Some scholars argue that this whole chapter was added after John’s death by the church that preserved his teaching. The case is not silly: 20:30–31 reads like the end of a book, this chapter opens after that ending, and here at the close someone other than the author appears to be vouching for him. Two things weigh heavily the other way. The first is decisive and simply stated: no manuscript of this Gospel lacks chapter 21. Not one, anywhere, in any language. That is a completely different situation from the passage about the woman caught in adultery, or the long ending of Mark, where the copies genuinely divide and your Bible carries a footnote saying so. Whatever the history of how this book was put together, it was never in circulation without these verses. The second is that the we needs no editor to explain it. John writes this way elsewhere of the shared apostolic witness, we have seen his glory (1:14), and a document could carry the endorsement of the elders who published it without ceasing to be the author’s own, much as a preface signed by others does not make a book someone else’s.

Correct and unfinished. Consider what a Gospel that stopped at 20:31 would have left. Peter’s denial would still be lying there from chapter 18, three times by a charcoal fire, unhealed. This chapter puts him beside another charcoal fire and asks him three times whether he loves, and gives him back his work. A book that ended without it would have been correct and unfinished.

No ascension scene. And John never describes the ascension. Luke tells it twice because he is writing the sequel; John simply stops, on a beach in Galilee, with two words spoken to a man who had failed: follow me. He told us at 20:31 why he wrote, that you may believe and that believing you may have life, and once that is done he does not need a departure scene. He leaves you not watching the sky, but standing on the sand, with a command and an open road.

How do I guard against misreading Scripture as the rumour did? Do what John did: go back to the exact words. Read the whole sentence and its context, not a phrase lifted out of it. Notice the small words, the ifs and buts and therefores, because the rumour was born when an if fell off. Compare Scripture with Scripture, because the Bible is its own best interpreter. Be suspicious of any teaching that rests on a single verse read in isolation, especially one that promises something Jesus did not clearly say. And read with the church, past and present, whose careful reading has kept God’s people from many such rumours.

In a sentence. A rumour spread that this disciple would not die, but Jesus had not said that, only “if I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”; and this disciple is the one who testifies and wrote these things, and his testimony is true.

On a Tuesday. The next time you hear a claim about what the Bible says, a promise, a prediction, a rule, look it up before you repeat it. Read the verse and the verses around it. You will be doing what the church at Ephesus did with the rumour about John, and you will be protecting someone from a false hope or a false fear.

For worship. The Gospel you hold is true testimony from one who leaned on Jesus’ breast. Trust it. The beloved disciple outlived all the others, saw the church spread across the world, and set down his witness so that we who never saw the Lord could believe and live. The Spirit who brought Christ’s words to his remembrance (14:26) has kept those words for us, exact, if and all. God has not left his people to rumours. He has given them a true witness.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.

Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. John has told us only a selection (20:30). Twenty-one chapters can be read in an afternoon. A person could close the book thinking he now has Jesus of Nazareth, complete, between two covers. John’s last act is to say: this is a selection. There were three years. I have given you seven signs and a handful of conversations and one week in detail, and I chose them for a stated purpose (20:31), and what is not here would swamp the world.

Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written. A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of saying countless. The writer flags it himself with I suppose. He is not making a claim about library space. He is doing what a man does when he has finished writing about someone he loves, looks at what he has produced, and finds it absurdly inadequate. But there is truth in it. The person and work of Jesus are inexhaustible. If the Word through whom all things were made (1:3) became flesh, then the world itself is too small to hold the full account of him. The book is finished. The subject is not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we need other sources, traditions or revelations to know Jesus truly. What is written is enough to believe and have life (20:31). The Scriptures are sufficient, though not exhaustive.

The last picture. And so the Gospel ends: not with a doctrine, not with an ascension, not with a summary of what has been proved, but on a beach in Galilee, with a charcoal fire burning down, and a man who had failed being told to keep walking. He had made breakfast before they arrived. That is the thing to carry away from this book. Twenty-one chapters of signs and arguments and stones picked up and men walking away, and it ends with the Lord of glory crouched over a fire at dawn, cooking fish for seven tired men who had caught nothing and deserved nothing and had run away from him not long before. He had every right to be somewhere else. He was days out of a grave and about to go home to his Father, and what he did with that morning was light a fire on a beach and wait for a boat. Whatever else this Gospel has proved, it has shown the character of the one it is about, and this is the last picture it gives: not a throne, and not a cloud, but a meal cooking, and a question that is not are you sorry but do you love me, and then two words that had never changed and never will.

Will we keep learning about Jesus in heaven? Yes, for ever. Knowing him is eternal life (17:3), and an infinite person cannot be exhausted by finite creatures in any number of ages. Paul prays that we may comprehend the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:18–19), and the coming ages will show the immeasurable riches of his grace (Ephesians 2:7). We will know fully, in the sense of truly and without distortion (1 Corinthians 13:12), but never completely, because he is God. Heaven will not be the end of discovery. It will be its beginning, without sin to blur the view, and every new sight of him will be cause for fresh worship.

In a sentence. Jesus did many other things, so many that if each were written down, the world could not hold the books.

On a Tuesday. If you have read this Gospel through, do not put it away as finished. Begin it again, and ask for one new sight of Christ in every chapter. And tell one person this week something about Jesus you learned from it. The books the world could not contain are being written still, in the lives of those who follow him.

For worship. You will never come to the end of Jesus. Eternity will not exhaust him. Keep learning of him. The Word who was with God in the beginning, through whom the world was made, became flesh, died, rose, and cooked breakfast on a beach for his failed friends, and the world is too small for the story of him. We have been given enough to believe and live. We will spend eternity discovering the rest, and the last word of this Gospel is a promise disguised as a confession of inadequacy: there is always more of him.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
21.overview:
After the conclusion of chapter 20, John adds an epilogue set by the Sea of Galilee. Seven disciples go fishing with Peter and catch nothing all night. At dawn a figure on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and they cannot haul it in for the number of fish. The beloved disciple recognises him: “It is the Lord!” Peter throws himself into the water. On the beach Jesus has a charcoal fire burning with fish and bread, and invites them to breakfast; the net holds 153 large fish and is not torn.

Beside that charcoal fire, the same kind as the one where Peter denied him, Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, and three times commissions him: “Feed my lambs… Tend my sheep… Feed my sheep.” Peter, grieved at the third question, answers, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus foretells that Peter will one day be bound and led where he does not want to go, signifying the death by which he would glorify God, and says, “Follow me.” When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus replies that this is not his concern: “You follow me!” John corrects a rumour that the beloved disciple would not die, identifies him as the author of the Gospel, and closes by saying that if everything Jesus did were written, the world could not hold the books. The Gospel ends not with failure but with a forgiven disciple, a renewed calling and the command to follow.
